16024-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number forty-six, dated September 23, 1897, now under the Great Round World Publishing Company. News, science, and stories fill the paper in words young readers could follow. This number leads with India, where news runs encouraging. The paper kept children abreast of empire and war.

Britain's plan to send a strong force against rebellious tribes has had a good effect, the paper reports. The Afridis held a council of war and chose to return home and gather their harvests. Head men of the tribe, who made a strong stand, own the decision. Seen now, the issue shows how 1897 children learned of frontier war: brief, confident, and from London's side.
28532-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
January 1846 brought number 363 of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume 59, published by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London. Its lead piece mourns Sir William Follett, dead in his forty-seventh year while Attorney-General and head of the British Bar. The bar felt his loss at Michaelmas term, when his voice and figure were suddenly absent.

Other contents include The Last Hours of a Reign, A Campaign in Texas, The Greek and Romantic Drama, and My College Friends. The Student of Salamanca, Sicilian sketches, aesthetics of dress, a Christmas carol, and The Crisis complete the number. Together they show a monthly miscellany at full Victorian range.
29858-blackwoods-edinburgh-magazine-volu:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 365, volume 59, is dated March 1846. William Blackwood and Sons printed it in Edinburgh and London. The contents open with the twenty-fourth book of Homer's Iliad, attempted in English hexameters. The writer admits the risk, noting that even Southey seldom held the measure, though his happy lines show real progress.

The Student of Salamanca continues in part five, and Moses and Son offers a didactic tale. Vichyana, It's All for the Best in conclusion, and The Roman Campagna follow. Mr. Brooke of Borneo, The Smuggler's Leap in the Pyrenees, and Ministerial Measures close the number. The issue shows Blackwood's range: verse, fiction, travel, and politics in one monthly bundle.
29883-blackwoods-edinburgh-magazine-volu:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 366, volume 59, is dated April 1846. William Blackwood and Sons printed it in Edinburgh and London. The contents open with The Marquess Wellesley, a piece on noble recollection, great actions, and national character. The writer asks why Eastern kingdoms perished without reverence, while Greece and republican Rome still draw homage.

A letter to Eusebius and part six of The Student of Salamanca follow. How They Manage Matters in The Model Republic, Antonio Perez, and Recollections of a Lover of Society add variety. The Old Player, The Crusades, and The Burden of Sion by Delta close the literary side. Rhymed hexameters and The Surveyor's Tale end a full monthly number.
30388-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for May 1846, number 367, volume 59, comes from William Blackwood and Sons. Its Edinburgh address is 45 George Street, and its London address 37 Paternoster Row, printed by Ballantyne and Hughes and sold by all booksellers in the United Kingdom. The Student of Salamanca, part the last, leads, followed by Shakespeare and the drama, Birboniana on Italian antiquaries and antichità, and The Americans and the Aborigines, part one.

The state of Ireland, its condition, the life and property bill, the debate, and the famine follow. The Modern Pilgrim's Progress, the Iliad of Homer, book the first, in English hexameters, a prospectus, Truth and Beauty, and The Campaign of the Sutlej follow. The Student of Salamanca opens amid crowd and clamour in Pampeluna's principal coffee-house, on a July evening just after Don Baltasar escaped the town.
34026-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for June 1846, number 368, opens with an essay on the literature of the eighteenth century. Lord Brougham, the essay notes, had resumed his memoirs of eminent English writers, a task any lover of literature would welcome. The piece contrasts English statesmen after retirement with statesmen on the Continent.

The foreign statesman, it argues, fades from public sight once out of office, while the Englishman may still write and speak. The issue carries the magazine's usual mix of letters, politics, and review. It gives a snapshot of British literary talk in the summer of 1846.
548-project-trinity-1945-1946:
Carl Maag and Steve Rohrer compile this Defense Nuclear Agency review of the first atomic test, Project Trinity, in 1945 and 1946. The report covers the Alamogordo site, its organization, and its military and civilian hands. Preshot work, the detonation of 16 July 1945, and postshot surveys fill the core chapters.

Later sections treat radiation safety, site and offsite monitoring, and film-badge doses for participants. Figures show the shot tower, shelters, base camp, and Jumbo after the blast. The volume serves as a sober, factual record of a test that changed war, science, and the lives of all who stood near it.
612-the-constitution-of-japan-1946:
Japan's postwar constitution, promulgated in November 1946 and in force from May 1947, opens this short text. The Japanese people, through the National Diet, declare sovereign power resides with the people and renounce war forever. Government is called a sacred trust, its powers drawn from the people and used for their benefit.

Articles that follow set out rights, the Diet, the cabinet, courts, and local rule in plain, grave language. The text marks a sharp break from the 1889 imperial charter. It serves as a founding document of modern Japan, where peace, liberty, and popular rule replace empire and war.
all-s-well-that-ends-well-pg2246: Helena's daring drives this edition: she cures the King, claims Bertram, and wins him through the bed-trick and the impossible tasks. "All's well that ends well" is tested by a heroine who refuses to lose. The problem comedy at its most provocative.
an-exposition-of-dr-cobb-s-art-of-discov: An Exposition of Dr Cobb's Art of Discovering the Faculties of the Human Mind and Bodily Infirmities is a short American pamphlet of 1846, thirty-two pages long. Its subject is a method, credited to a Dr Cobb, for reading a person's mental faculties and bodily weaknesses, in the spirit of the character-reading sciences then popular. The piece is credited to Enos Cobb. It survives as a small specimen of the 1840s trade in practical mind reading.
arxiv-2412-00546:
Ask a language model a question about an unordered pile of items, like summing a column of a table, and it may silently skip some entries. Mohsen Dehghankar and Abolfazl Asudeh notice the answer should not depend on the pile's order, yet the model's accuracy does. Items sitting in certain positions get overlooked more than others.

Their fix is to shuffle smartly: rank the items first, then ask. Their algorithms estimate both how relevant each item is to the question and how much attention each position receives. A helper model supplies those estimates cheaply. On synthetic and real datasets, reranking lifted accuracy close to the best any ordering could reach, sometimes nearly doubling it. The trick makes no assumptions about the question itself.
arxiv-2412-00846:
Anand and a large team present a paper from twenty twenty-four on a geometry dataset for vision-language models. The set gathers over two thousand problems from school textbooks. Augmentation grows it past five thousand geometry questions. Both numeric and proof-style problems are included. Each carries a step-by-step solution in one consistent format. Rival sets offer only final-answer style questions. Tests show open models still struggle at geometry reasoning.

Fine-tuning on the set lifts model skill clearly. Captioning and retrieval tricks are also weighed for gains. An automated grader compares full solutions to ground truth. The authors offer the set as a benchmark for geometric reasoning.
arxiv-2412-01046:
Filling in a missing patch of a photo has many plausible answers, and the best current generators trade detail for structure because they compress features into a small set of codes. Kyungri Park and Woohwan Jung add a repair module in this 2024 paper that puts the lost detail back.

Their Feature Dequantization Module compensates for what the coding step discards, and a lean training scheme keeps its cost tiny. Plugged into a leading model, it clearly sharpened the detail of filled regions without slowing the system in any real way. The authors present it as a near-free upgrade for pluralistic inpainting tools.
arxiv-2412-01746:
Samuel McCarty and Liam Connor wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It forecasts how many strong gravitational lenses the next wide-field radio surveys will find, and what to do with them.

Optical surveys will swell the lens count soon, and radio arrays join the hunt. The Deep Synoptic Array and the Square Kilometre Array should each find tens of thousands of lensed systems, by cautious count. Many will be group and cluster lenses, not lone galaxies. The authors give tactics for the hard case where the lens ring is as small as the blur spot, with machine vision and cross-survey data. A few hundred flickering active nuclei among the finds could pin the Hubble constant to percent level.
arxiv-2412-02546:
Andrei Lixandru, Marcel van Gerven, and Sérgio Pequito present a 2024 paper on distributed optimization, the math behind training models across many machines. Such methods power federated learning, where data stay on local devices. They often stall on ill-shaped problems or trade speed against stability. The team introduces FrODO, a method that adds fractional-order memory terms, which weigh past steps with a long tail.

The authors prove the method converges at a steady rate on any strongly connected network. In tests it converged up to four times faster than rivals on ill-shaped problems. It also sped federated neural network training by two to three times while staying stable. The paper offers both theory and evidence for the design. The authors aim it at large, spread-out learning systems.
arxiv-2412-03546:
Laura Herold and Marc Kamionkowski present a 2024 cosmology paper asking whether the newest limits on neutrino mass rest on a shortcut. Data from the DESI survey, joined with maps of the early universe, give the tightest bound yet on the summed neutrino masses. Those analyses fake the true mass pattern with three equal-mass neutrinos.

Real neutrinos follow one of two orderings learned from Earth experiments. The authors reran the inference under both orderings, with two statistical styles. For the early-universe data alone, the shortcut holds up well, though answers lean on the assumed mass floor. With the survey data added, the checks grow sharper, and the paper reports how far the limits move.
arxiv-2412-05946:
Louis Arts tests whether a galaxy simulation can match a strange new class of far-off galaxies. A space telescope found little red dots, tiny and dust-red galaxies from the early cosmos. Their brightness hints at star masses and birth rates above what standard models allow. One idea says fierce star birth powers them, while another credits black holes at their centers.

Arts compares the FLARES simulation's output with the observed dots. The simulation makes far too many galaxies of the right mass, by orders of magnitude. It also overstates their star birth rates by a wide margin. The gap suggests the model damps star birth too weakly, missing feedback from black holes. Arts urges tests with a simulation where that feedback runs stronger.
arxiv-2412-06246:
Yi Han determines how small the smallest singular value of a large random rectangle can be when its entries have infinite variance. For well-behaved entries, classic results pin the scaled value to a clean limit. Heavy-tailed Lévy entries, whose extremes dominate, broke those arguments entirely.

For symmetric entries with power-law tails, Han traps the smallest singular value between two bounds differing only by logarithmic factors. The lower bound is new and answers, in weaker form, a problem posed by earlier authors. The same bound survives adding any fixed matrix, however large its norm. A diverging aspect ratio case is also treated. Earlier anti-concentration methods had only reached a much weaker lower bound.
arxiv-2412-07046:
Simon Bartlmae, Paul Jünger, and Elmar Langetepe settle a geometry problem in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The Euclidean Steiner tree problem seeks the cheapest network joining given points in the plane. Extra junction points may be added to shorten the tree. Their variants add a straight line of zero cost that must join the network.

In one variant the line is given as input. In the other, its best location must be found. Heuristics and a strong approximation existed, but NP-hardness was unproven. The authors prove both variants are NP-hard. They also prove both admit a polynomial-time approximation scheme. Known algorithms for the classic problem can be adapted to get it. Readers get a complete complexity picture for a natural Steiner variant.
arxiv-2412-07646:
Tom Kouwenhoven and co-authors test whether artificial languages shaped by large language models gain human-like structure, in this 2024 paper. Human languages became structured through generations of learning and use. The team ask whether the same shaping happens when AI agents, not people, pass a language along.

In a classic reference game, model agents learned and used invented languages to name things for each other. Starting from unstructured word sets, the languages picked up structural traits that eased communication. Passing them through generations made them easier to learn, echoing human experiments. Some runs, though, collapsed into degenerate vocabularies unlike any human tongue.
arxiv-2412-07946:
Ravi Jagadeesan and Alexander Teytelboym develop a theory of competitive equilibrium for goods that cannot be divided. Their twenty twenty-four paper builds the theory entirely on economic conditions on demand. The key move is to study complementarity and substitutability between bundles of goods, not just between individual goods.

From that starting point, the authors derive conditions for an equilibrium to exist that are sufficient and essentially necessary. The conditions unify settings dominated by complements with settings dominated by substitutes, which earlier theory treated separately. The analysis also carries implications for auction design, where indivisible items and bundle preferences are the norm. Economists get a cleaner account of when markets with lumpy goods can settle at prices that clear.
arxiv-2412-08646:
Jihao Liu and co-authors wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, on chatting with live video streams. A viewer may ask a question mid-stream, but most models answer from the single moment the question lands, missing what happens next.

StreamChat refreshes the model's view of the video at every step while it writes its reply. A cross-attention design keeps that constant refreshing cheap enough for live use. The team also built a dense instruction data set to train such streaming chat, and a coding scheme that stamps the relative time of words and frames. On standard image and video tests the model held its own with top systems. On live-stream tasks it beat them clearly. The authors aim at assistants that can follow events as they unfold.
arxiv-2412-10546:
Daniel Alabi and Eugene Wu present a vision for a data system built for computational science, in a paper from 2024. Computational science solves problems across the natural and social sciences by simulation and data analysis. The field has grown fast, but managing its huge data sets and simulation runs remains hard.

Their system, called EmpireDB, adapts ideas from database research to this setting. The paper maps the challenges scientists face and the chances for the database field to help. Early tests of its tuned parts show gains over current tools. The authors frame the system as a research agenda as much as a product. They invite database work aimed at the needs of simulation-driven science.
arxiv-2412-13846:
Gianmario Voria and co-authors ask why software practitioners adopt fairness toolkits in this 2024 paper. Toolkits that audit machine learning bias exist, but usage lags. The study surveys industry practitioners through a technology acceptance lens. A structural model tests which beliefs drive intention and real use.

Performance expectancy and habit emerged as the main drivers. Practitioners keep using tools that clearly help and that already fit their routine. Social pressure and ease mattered less in the model. Designers should prove concrete benefit fast and seed daily habits. Training and mandates alone will not spread fairness practice. Adoption research turns ethics tooling into a product problem with known levers.
arxiv-2412-14046:
ATLAS Collaboration presents a search from twenty twenty-four for rare Higgs boson decays at the Large Hadron Collider. The hunt seeks a Higgs that splits into two new spin zero particles. One of them then splits into a photon pair, and the other into a tau lepton pair. Hadronic decays of the taus are used, with a tagger built for close tau pairs.

The data span years of proton smashes at a set energy. The new particle's mass is sought across a mid range. No clear excess shows above the standard model haze. Caps are set on how often such a decay can occur, by mass. The caps run from a small share to a few percent at high trust.
arxiv-2412-15546:
Zhao-Rong Lai, Xiaotian Wu, Liangda Fang, Ziliang Chen, and Cheng Li extend a method for the Weber location problem in two thousand twenty-four. The problem picks the best site for a facility by weighing distance to a set of demand points. Its cost curve has kinks where the slope does not exist, which stalls standard methods.

A past fix handled only one norm and a narrow power range, with few kink points. The new work covers the rest of the range, where the kink set forms a full continuum and the shape is far more complex. Their algorithm, built on a classic update rule, is shown to descend and converge. Tests on six real data sets show a fast, steady rate in practice.
arxiv-2412-16246:
Ido Sivan-Sevilla and Parthav Poudel measure how web tracking merges the separate corners of a person's online life. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. People expect health, money, and news sites to stay apart, yet trackers follow them across all of them.

The team crawled seven hundred top sites across seven areas, from health and finance to education, for twenty-seven days. They mapped how cookie IDs and browser fingerprinting spread a person's identity within and between those areas. Earlier work counted trackers in bulk; this work tracks the collapse of context itself. The maps differ sharply by area. The authors use them to suggest how browsers could wall off storage and slow the collapse.
arxiv-2412-18146:
Jiancheng Wu and six co-authors model why some active galactic nuclei show twin-peaked emission lines that change over time. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. The broad-line region around a supermassive black hole encodes its geometry, but the code is hard to crack.

In their model, radiation pressure on dust at the disc's surface launches the line-emitting gas. Slow feeding gives double peaks; brisk feeding merges them into one. Matching the observed pattern, where wider peak splits pair with lazier feeding, demands metal-rich gas, at least five times the sun's share. When a nucleus's brightness swings, its line shape needs years to decades to follow. Long monitoring is the test.
arxiv-2412-18546:
Sandro Mereghetti, writing alone, reviews an odd pair of stars and the white dwarf that spins among them. His 2024 review covers a bright hot subdwarf star with a heavy companion. The white dwarf has more than the Sun's mass packed into a small body, and it turns once every few seconds.

The dwarf gives off pulsed X-rays powered by gas drawn from its partner's thin wind. That inflow is too weak to explain the tiny, steady speed-up in its spin. Mereghetti argues that the young dwarf is shrinking, which spins it faster. In time, added mass may push it past a known limit. It may then blow up as a supernova or collapse into a fast pulsar, and which fate awaits is still unclear.
arxiv-2412-18946:
Yassine Chemingui, Aryan Deshwal, and three colleagues help a safety-trained agent adapt when the safety budget changes after training, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Offline safe reinforcement learning learns from a fixed log of past behavior, maximizing reward while respecting cost constraints. Retraining for every new budget is impractical.

Their framework, CAPS, wraps around existing offline algorithms. In training, it learns several policies that share one representation but strike different reward-versus-cost trade-offs. At deployment, it switches between them state by state. In each state it picks the policy promising the best future reward among those that still satisfy the current cost limit. Tests on thirty-eight tasks from a standard safety benchmark show the switcher consistently beating rival methods. The trick is to prepare a portfolio of caution levels in advance. Deployment then becomes a matter of choosing, not relearning.
arxiv-2501-01046:
Youngjun Son, Chaewon Kim, and Jaejin Lee present SEDD, in a 2025 paper, a fast tool for removing duplicate texts from huge datasets. Clean data makes language models train better, but the standard hash-based hunt for near duplicates is slow. New graphics-chip tools still waste effort, shuffling data back and forth and leaving the chips underused.

SEDD replaces the shuffle with a streaming approach that flows data through the chips once. A partly reusable hash function cuts the core cost, and optimized chip code plus automatic parameter selection squeeze the rest. On thirty million texts, it beat a CPU-based tool by a huge factor and the best chip tool by close to eight times. Its duplicate calls stayed close to the standard method. A run over more than a trillion words took three hours on a mid-size chip cluster. The code is free online.
arxiv-2501-01546:
Tianqi Hu and co-authors published a paper, dated 2024 in the text where the catalog lists 2025, on a prototype detector that will trigger muon storage in a precision experiment. The muEDM experiment at Switzerland's Paul Scherrer Institute hunts for a tiny electric dipole moment in the muon, a clue to new physics. Its design needs a gatekeeper: spot a good muon fast, then fire a magnetic kicker to trap it in a storage magnet.

The prototype gate is a telescope of four scintillators, plastic panels that flash when particles pass, watched by silicon light sensors, with a fifth panel vetoing strays. It was tested with real muons at a PSI beamline, without the magnetic field. The team measured how it responds to different muon paths and how much light the plastic yields. Results matched detailed computer simulations closely. The agreement certifies the concept for the experiment's tight demands.
arxiv-2501-02246:
Bonte and four co-authors find the edge graphs for a set of chem graph scores in this twenty twenty-five paper. Chem graphs link atoms with a cap of three bonds at each atom. Each score sums bond-grade facts to grade the whole graph's shape.

Inside, the team works through thirty-three such scores in one full sweep. For each score they name the graphs that top it and those that floor it. Just five graph clans cover the edge cases for most of the scores in the set. That means the scores in the set split far less than their count would hint. The maps can speed hunts for drugs with set shape grades.
arxiv-2501-02746:
Zhengyu Wang and five co-authors show that the classic ESPRIT direction finding method turns inconsistent for large arrays, and fix it with random matrix theory. Array size and snapshot counts grow together in their regime. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

In that regime the sample covariance is a poor stand in for the true one, which poisons ESPRIT reads for both wide and close sources. Their improved G-ESPRIT restores consistency, proven in the same limit. A fresh bound on eigenvalue gaps between non symmetric matrices backs the proof and may serve elsewhere. Simulations match the theory.
arxiv-2501-02946:
Syed Yunus Ali, Rafna Rafeek, and Debasish Mondal wrote a 2025 physics paper on a geometric Brownian information engine. An information engine converts knowledge about a microscopic system's state into useful work. Here the system is overdamped Brownian particles, jittering randomly, confined in a two-lobed chamber.

An error-free feedback controller measures the particles' state and uses that information to extract work. The engine's performance depends on the cycle time, the measurement distance, and the feedback position. As the cycle time grows, the engine relaxes from a strongly non-equilibrium state to complete rest. The authors chart how extractable work, power, and efficiency evolve over the cycle, guiding the design of such nanoscale engines.
arxiv-2501-03846: Antonio Lei and Katharina Müller present a 2025 mathematics paper on graphs built from elliptic curves, enriched with extra structure. Isogeny graphs connect curves by special maps and matter for number theory and cryptography. The authors add level structures defined from the kernels of repeated applications of the Verschiebung map. They extend earlier results to this setting. As the map's power varies, the graphs stack into towers of coverings. Each connected component also shows a volcanic structure, with a crater and slopes like classical isogeny graphs.
arxiv-2501-05646:
Zixuan Liang, a solo author, presents new ways to encode category data with many distinct values for machine learning, in a paper from 2025. A common method turns each value into its own sparse feature. With many values, that swells the data, slows training, and invites overfitting.

Liang proposes three compact encodings based on means, low-rank structure, and a logistic model. Each builds a short, rich code for each category from the data itself. Theory and tests on varied data sets back the methods. They improved model scores and cut computing cost compared with standard baselines. The gains were largest where scalable handling of big data is needed. The paper frames the codes as summaries that keep the key signal.
arxiv-2501-05746: Shaun Cooper and Peter Schwerdtfeger study a family of lattices first considered by Conway and Sloane, two leading figures in the mathematics of sphere packing. Their paper came out in 2025. For each lattice they examine the Epstein zeta function, a sum over lattice points that measures how the points are distributed. They show that this function reaches a local minimum for the body-centred cubic lattice. Such minimum results identify which arrangement is most balanced, a question with echoes in packing and coding theory.
arxiv-2501-07646:
Manisha Garg and Igor Mineyev wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five about group rings. A group ring blends a group with a field of numbers. Two famous guesses by Kaplansky claim such rings have no odd zero divisors and no odd units, at least for groups without torsion.

One guess was disproved in two thousand twenty-one, so the hunt for more counterexamples is open. The authors build a step-by-step search tool that prunes the space of candidates by shape. They prove that a class of groups with curved, non-positive geometry cannot yield counterexamples. Computer checks also rule out all small cases up to a set size for both support sizes.
arxiv-2501-08946:
Robots that chat usually take turns by waiting for silence, which makes talk stilted, full of gaps and accidental interruptions. Gabriel Skantze and Bahar Irfan try two general turn-taking models, trained on human conversation, as the robot's sense of timing instead. One predicts the shape of the voice signal ahead; the other judges when a turn is complete.

Working together, the models tell the robot when to start preparing an answer, when to speak, and how to handle being cut off. No robot-specific training was needed. In a study with thirty-nine adults talking to a Furhat robot, people clearly preferred the new system. It also answered faster and interrupted less than the silence-based baseline. The authors present it as a first for human-robot conversation.
arxiv-2501-10046:
Brugnera described the LEGEND experiment in this article from twenty twenty-five. The experiment hunts a decay so rare it may not exist: neutrinoless double-beta decay. Seeing it would reshape our picture of neutrinos and the universe. LEGEND uses germanium detectors enriched in one isotope, run deep underground in Italy.

The first stage, LEGEND-200, is already taking data. Its background noise sits near the design goal. The team combined its first year of data with two earlier experiments. The joint result pushes the decay's half-life limit beyond a vast bound. A larger stage, LEGEND-1000, is planned to dig deeper. The article lays out both stages and the early findings.
arxiv-2501-11446:
Marius Tucsnak and Zhuo Xu prove that a point mass drifting in a simple fluid can be held steady forever. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The fluid follows a viscous Burgers equation, a one-dimensional stand-in for flow. A point mass moves inside it, pushed by the current. Feedback control can act on the mass. The authors ask whether calm is reachable from any start.

Two results answer yes, with exponential speed. First, the free velocity field settles globally on its own. Second, with feedback on, the mass also glides to a chosen target spot. A special test function keeps the mass away from the walls. A perturbed Lyapunov function then seals the decay. Control theory gains a clean benchmark for fluid-particle systems.
arxiv-2501-11646:
Hugo Hawkins, Chao Xu, Lie-Liang Yang, and Lajos Hanzo compare two radio schemes that both send data and sense their surroundings. Their 2025 paper joins a spreading method, long used in mobile networks, with a newer waveform built for delay and speed shifts. Few past studies had tested the joined scheme for sensing.

The team built three joined variants, spreading along delay, along speed shift, or along both. For each, they tested three standard spreading sequences. Two variants with a specific sequence beat the plain waveform on sensing error while holding data error rates about the same. The joined scheme also keeps decoding simpler than some rival multi-user methods. The results matter for future networks that aim to sense and communicate at once.
arxiv-2501-12446:
Mirko Consiglio and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on long-distance multipartite entanglement in a quantum spin chain. Three magnetic defects placed in the chain can host bound states, and the team asked when those states share genuine entanglement across all three sites at once, even over long distances.

Using both analytic and numerical methods, the team found that the defects' shared state carries this full entanglement across the whole parameter range studied. That holds even in regions where pairwise entanglement between two defects is zero. The team measured the effect with numerical lower bounds and an exact formula in simpler cases. The result suggests a route to build many-party entanglement by local control.
arxiv-2501-13046:
Josu Aurrekoetxea, Sam Brady, and a large team of colleagues release software for setting up relativity simulations in a 2025 study. Simulating black holes or uneven universes starts with initial data that must satisfy constraint equations from Einstein's theory. Solving those constraints is a hard numerical step before any evolution can begin.

Their code, GRTresna, uses a multigrid solver aimed at scenes with fundamental fields around black holes and lumpy cosmological spaces. It builds on a formalism the collaboration published earlier. The code is openly available for other groups to use. Reliable initial data tools widen who can run frontier simulations in numerical relativity.
arxiv-2501-13646:
Xuan Zhang and co-authors tune the links between qubits with a slow-swap method that needs no extra read wires, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Tunable links flex quantum chips, but most carry no own readout, which makes them hard to gauge. A slow swap with a neighbor qubit does the probing.

The team gauged and set links on their chips with the method. Warped control signals were fixed in a straight, exact way. The trick also retunes the talk between a fixed qubit and its reader across a wide span. Chip builders get leaner setup for bigger machines. Readers see control grow without hardware growth.
arxiv-2501-14146:
David Bowman, a solo author, wrote a math paper in 2025 on a barrier problem for a spread operator. The operator blends diffusion with drift and comes from pricing models for options that mix Asian and American traits. In a barrier problem, the solution must stay above a fixed wall.

Past work had set the best-known smoothness of solutions, matching what theory expects at the natural scale. Bowman improves the smoothness in the position variable beyond that mark. The gain comes from a classic trick paired with ideas from a major theory of rough equations. He then proves the first result on the smoothness of the free edge, where the solution leaves the wall. His proof leans on a new growth formula that the extra smoothness makes possible.
arxiv-2501-14346:
Boshko Koloski, Nada Lavrač, and Blaž Škrlj present a 2025 neural network design for tables that mix numbers with set labels. Such tables rule medicine, yet they often hold few rows with many columns, a hard shape for learning. Their design, HorNets, rests on a clipped polynomial-style switch. A routing part sends each input to the network part that fits its kind, with no told labels for the split.

The network can model part blends of traits or the whole space in one sweep. It reliably pulls out logic rules, even noisy twin-negation ones. On 14 real biomedical sets it topped rival scores. The team released the code and a fake-data maker under a free license. Small, messy tables gain a tool built for their shape.
arxiv-2501-14646:
Seven researchers wrote a computer graphics paper in two thousand twenty-five on making a talking avatar from sound alone. The avatar must move its lips, face, and upper body in step with speech, and do so live. Past methods cost too much computing, lacked facial detail, or let the face and body drift apart.

Their system, SyncAnimation, is built on a method that renders a person from learned scene data. One part matches body poses to the audio, and another matches facial expression to the emotion in the voice. A renderer then joins head and body into one smooth result. The authors report stable, real-time output.
arxiv-2501-14946:
Andrew Cooper, Annie Booth, and Robert Gramacy wrote a paper in 2025 that updates full posterior inference for surrogate models of computer simulation experiments with categorical outputs. Such surrogates mimic a simulation's binary output. Fully Bayesian, sampling-based inference for them is principled but slow, and it had been largely abandoned for large data in favor of faster shortcuts.

Those shortcuts give up a grip on doubt and model fit, both of which the team's work requires. Their driving case is a large simulation of how binary black hole pairs form. Their framework pairs elliptical slice sampling, a method for exploring the posterior distribution, with a Vecchia shortcut that prunes far data pairs for speed. In tests on the black hole simulation and on standard sorting tasks, the method beat the shortcut options. Input warping allows it to capture how the simulation acts across regions of its input space.
arxiv-2501-16546:
Feiyu Zhu, Jean Oh, and Reid Simmons show how plain-language know-how can help a robot learn a task from very few examples, in a 2025 paper. Copying an expert's moves, called behavior cloning, usually needs many demonstrations and fails on new situations. Experts can state general rules easily, but blending those rules with learned examples has been hard.

Their method asks a large language model to turn the expert's written rules into the skeleton of a control program, written as code. The few demonstrations then tune the numbers inside that skeleton. On lunar landing and car racing tasks, the system learned from as few as five demonstrations and stayed steady when noise was added to its actions. It beat a plain cloning model trained the same way.
arxiv-2501-18046:
Martin Jonáš, Jan Strejček, and Marek Trtík sharpen gray-box fuzzing, a software testing method, by searching near an already-run path, in a research paper from 2025. Their test programs record how numeric comparisons came out during a run. The goal is a new input that repeats the same path but flips the last comparison.

The authors define that search problem formally for recorded comparison data. They then give an algorithm that hunts the flipped input efficiently. Trials on a standard competition benchmark suite showed the method works in practice. Better local search helps fuzzers reach rare branches where bugs hide.
arxiv-2501-19346:
Mikhailov, a solo author, wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five about ultrametric spaces and clouds. In such spaces, distance obeys a stronger rule than usual, which suits tree-like data. Earlier work gave a natural way to build such a space from an ordinary space of distances.

The author shows that the building map keeps distances from growing for all spaces, not just bounded ones. He then studies the map's traits and finds a second map that acts as its inverse. That second map joins a space with a fixed, well-connected partner space. A closing result shows that far-apart classes of endless spaces cannot hold both space types at once.
arxiv-2502-00546:
In quantum physics, Lüders' rule tells how a system's state changes right after a measurement. Alisson Tezzin, Bárbara Amaral, and Jonte Hance argue that the rule, read in a natural way, says something about what would have happened if a different measurement had been made instead. They then ask whether a deeper layer of fixed hidden states, sitting beneath the quantum state, could fit with that reading.

Their answer is no. The counterfactual reading forces any hidden-state model to update its states through plain conditional probability. Once that link is in place, having such a model becomes the same as ruling out the very effects the rule describes. The two views cannot both hold.
arxiv-2502-00646:
Chang Dong and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on backdoor attacks against time series classifiers, the models that label heart traces, sensor streams, and the like. A backdoored model behaves normally until a secret trigger pattern appears, then answers as the attacker wishes. Older attacks poison the training data, which real attackers often cannot reach. TrojanTime works without that access. It first forges a stand-in data set from an unrelated public one by adversarial crafting, then keeps training the clean model on that set and its poisoned twin.

A second stage aligns the model's outputs and freezes some normalization layers, so clean accuracy survives the implant. Across four architectures and standard benchmark sets, the attack landed while clean performance held. The team also proposes a defense: an unlearning routine that strips the backdoor's effect while keeping the model accurate on honest data.
arxiv-2502-01646:
Miguel Cardona and co-authors push apart more of the cardinal numbers attached to the strong measure zero ideal, in this 2025 paper. Set theorists measure how sets of reals can be tiny in competing senses, and the strong measure zero ideal collects one such family. Separating its cardinals means building models where the numbers provably differ. The tool is forcing, the standard way to extend a set theory universe.

The authors introduce a new property of forcing notions. The property keeps control of the null ideal's additivity number through finite support iterations, a step where control is easily lost. With that lever they settle open questions left by Brendle and co-authors. The paper is a technical advance in the cardinal characteristics program.
arxiv-2502-01846:
Aashish Rai, Dilin Wang, and Mihir Jain lead a team flattening three-dimensional Gaussian scenes onto a spherical map, so image generators can create them directly. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Gaussian splatting renders scenes beautifully but resists generation. Its blobs are unordered and unstructured, unlike pixels on a grid.

Their UV map lays the blobs out as a multichannel image. Position, scale, color, transparency, and rotation become image channels. A small network compresses those channels into a three-channel shared space. Standard image diffusion machinery then works on the result unchanged. Raising the map's resolution simply fits more Gaussians. The team demonstrates unconditional and conditional generation plus inpainting. Tasks that were research projects become routine transfers. The representation unlocks a decade of image model progress for 3D.
arxiv-2502-02246:
David Touzeau and three co-authors develop a geometry test for cosmology in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Weak lensing surveys map how gravity bends light from distant galaxies. The bending patterns hold symmetries that depend only on the shape of the universe's expansion. Checking that these patterns cancel where they should is called a null test. The authors build a full method around tomographic cosmic shear nulling.

They show what the test can pin down, above all how distances grow with redshift. They also probe its weak spots, such as magnification bias and errors in galaxy distance bins. In a survey like the coming Euclid mission, the test performs well. Pure geometry checks, free of growth assumptions, add trust to cosmology results.
arxiv-2502-03246:
Simbarashe Aldrin Ngorima, Albert Helberg, and Marelie Davel improve how moving vehicles estimate their radio channel, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Cars that talk to each other use a Wi-Fi-like standard, but motion makes the radio path shift fast, and the guide signals used to measure it run thin. Weak estimates mean more bit errors.

The authors pair a temporal convolutional network with a method that reuses received data as extra guide signals, plus a smoothing step over time. They test the setup on a channel model for cars moving the same way beside a wall. Bit error rates fell by up to tenfold with smoothing, and by a large margin without it, beating the best classical estimator they compared against.
arxiv-2502-03446:
Alvise Sommariva and Marco Vianello present a cheap, steady way to compute integrals over many-sided solids. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Such integrals, called quadrature, sit inside many engineering codes, and the usual approach chops each solid into tetrahedra first.

Their method skips the chopping. It fits values inside a simple box that bounds the solid, and it works out the needed moments with a classic theorem from calculus. No matrix splitting or inversion is involved, so the usual numerical traps do not arise. The authors show the formula stays stable in theory, even when some of its weights come out negative. The gain is a simpler path to accurate integrals on complex shapes.
arxiv-2502-03546:
Oliver Biggar and Iman Shames present the preference graph as a basic tool for game theory, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The graph draws every strategy combination as a node. Arcs join combinations that differ in one player's choice, pointing toward the choice that player prefers.

The authors show this simple picture grows out of natural axioms. It sits beneath many core ideas, from dominated strategies and strict equilibria to named families such as potential and weakly acyclic games. It also shapes how learning rules behave, notably fictitious play and the replicator dynamic. Their aim is to hand game theorists a shared lens for new problems.
arxiv-2502-03646:
Byungkyun Kang, Myoung-Hwan Kim, and Chul Hong Park published this condensed matter paper in 2025 on UTe2, a uranium compound that becomes an unusual superconductor at low temperature. Its topological superconductivity is thought to need a three-dimensional Fermi surface, the boundary of the electron states that carry current. Yet some experiments suggested a flat, two-dimensional surface instead, raising doubts.

Combining two advanced calculation methods, the team finds both surfaces at once. Two Fermi surfaces sit at the same center point, each shaped by a different set of orbitals and by the Kondo effect, where electron spins entangle with local magnetic moments. At high temperature both look three-dimensional but faint. On cooling to 25 kelvin, one sharpens into a robust three-dimensional surface while the other flattens into a nearly two-dimensional sheet. The authors say both observations were right, and the three-dimensional surface needed for topology survives.
arxiv-2502-03946:
Yousef Koka and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on automating data cleaning for survival analysis. Preprocessing choices quietly make or break time-to-event models, yet automation tools mostly ignore them. CleanSurvival uses reinforcement learning, an extended Q-learning scheme, to pick the recipe of gap filling, outlier handling, and feature building that suits a chosen survival model.

Benchmarks on real datasets showed the learned cleaning beat simple baselines, most clearly where coverage was deepest. Simulations across missing-data patterns agreed. The authors argue that folding survival preprocessing into automated pipelines will make such studies faster, easier, and more robust as machine learning spreads.
arxiv-2502-04246:
Kangning Diao and Yi Mao build a fast stand-in for costly universe simulations in a 2025 paper. The target is the twenty-one centimeter signal from the era when the first stars lit up the cosmos. Surveys will map huge volumes, and matching fake data at full fidelity takes heavy computing. Their emulator uses a generative network to fake the images instead.

The trick is to train in two fidelities. The network first learns from a huge number of small, cheap simulations. It is then fine-tuned with only a few large, costly ones, a few-shot transfer step. The faked images matched key statistics to within a few percent on small scales. Errors grew only mildly on large scales. The authors estimate the full-scale training route would cost ten to one hundred times more computing.
arxiv-2502-05546:
Xing and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about the first lattice calculation of scattering between two charmed baryons. Lattice quantum chromodynamics simulates strong-force physics on a space-time grid. The pair studied is two Lambda-c baryons near their threshold energy. Finite-volume energy levels reveal scattering behavior through a standard method. The team used two simulation ensembles with a heavier-than-real pion. A related coupled channel was checked and found not to mix.

The interaction between the two baryons came out repulsive. Its strength is captured by a negative scattering length they determine. Statistical and systematic errors are reported separately for the value. Another possible channel lies above the studied energy range. The result is a first benchmark for charmed baryon interactions. Nuclear theorists can use it to model exotic matter.
arxiv-2502-05646: Mohamed Abbassi and Khadija Boulagouaz classify spiral-like curves on a three-dimensional bundle built over a curved surface, in a 2025 paper. The bundle collects every unit direction at every point of a pseudo-Riemannian surface of constant curvature. The curves are helices steered by the geodesic flow, space-like, time-like, or null. Their result is tidy: every such helix is in fact a circular helix, with curvature and torsion both constant.
arxiv-2502-05946: Vasily Buslov proposes an algorithm for building directed spanning forests of minimum weight in a graph. The method keeps the minimum forests for different numbers of trees as alike as possible, so the family stays related while the count of trees changes. Buslov checks the correctness of the algorithm and bounds its running time, which stays within cubic order for dense graphs. The output is the full set of related minimum forests, one for each allowed number of trees.
arxiv-2502-06146:
Annie Feng, Nishanth Kumar, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, and Leslie Pack Kaelbling tackle efficient exploration for robots learning relational world models in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Random exploration wastes effort on redundant data in large environments with long tasks. An earlier method, goal-literal babbling, improved matters by planning toward novel goals, but still chose goals and actions randomly. The authors identify two principles for doing better.

First, demonstrations should initialize operators so they cover the distinct effects planning needs. Second, exploration should target informative transitions by refining operator preconditions. The team tests these ideas in Baking-Large, a demanding new domain with huge state-action spaces. Oracle demonstrations and precondition-targeting guidance both improved sample efficiency and generalization in their experiments.
arxiv-2502-06446:
Claudia Pigini, Alessandro Pionati, and Francesco Valentini fix an estimation problem in twenty twenty-five. Binary choice models on panel data can hit complete separation. That happens when a variable perfectly predicts the outcome for some units. Separation biases average partial effects and blocks forecasts for units whose responses never vary.

The grouped fixed effects approach clusters units to shrink the number of effects estimated. Clustering with k-means discretizes the unobserved heterogeneity. Separation eases because transitions are counted within clusters, not within subjects. The authors propose a rule for choosing the number of groups. It balances approximating the latent trait against the incidental parameters problem. Simulations show unbiased estimates where the plain approach fails.
arxiv-2502-07046:
Daniel Rodriguez-Cardenas, Alejandro Velasco, and Denys Poshyvanyk introduce SnipGen in this two thousand twenty-five software engineering paper. Evaluating language models on code is tricky because test data may already sit inside the models' training sets. SnipGen is a repository mining framework that builds fresher, tailored evaluation data through prompt engineering. It works at the level of individual methods and aims to reduce this contamination problem.

In an exploratory study, the framework mined about two hundred twenty-seven thousand data points from roughly three hundred thirty-eight thousand recent GitHub commits. Its prompt templates can be chained into sequences resembling chain-of-thought reasoning, enabling nuanced assessment of code generation quality. The authors release the mining tool, the methodology, and the dataset. Their hope is that researchers and practitioners can evaluate code models more rigorously and interpret the results with greater confidence.
arxiv-2502-07446:
Arnob Mukherjee and co-authors design a two-dimensional topological superconductor in a 2025 paper. Topological superconductors can host Majorana modes, exotic states sought for quantum computing. Their recipe layers a magnetic crystal, CrInTe3, onto a standard superconductor. The magnet's atoms sit in a twisted, non-flat pattern that breaks time symmetry, while the superconductor keeps its pairing rules.

Computer models first mapped the magnet's exchange and twist forces, which favor a spiral ground state. On that spiral, the hybrid's surface states shifted from corner spots to edge channels as energy settings changed. Under a magnetic field, the magnet broke into skyrmions and spiral walls, and the system turned insulating with trapped states. The authors place the design in a symmetry class known to protect Majorana modes. They suggest microscope probes to test it.
arxiv-2502-08246:
Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré and co-authors speed up attention in transformer language models by looking up less memory. Attention normally compares every new word against all stored keys, which gets slow on long texts. Partitioning methods borrowed from vector search work poorly here, because keys and queries follow different distributions and the position encoding scrambles bucket assignment. Their method, Saap, partitions keys and queries separately, an asymmetric index that adapts the sparsity pattern to the data.

It runs on pre-trained models and needs only a small query classifier trained offline. On a long-context Llama model with sequences up to half a million tokens, Saap cut the memory fraction examined about twentyfold. That translated into roughly sixty percent time saved against a fast-attention baseline. The authors present asymmetric indexing as the fix that makes sparse attention practical, since attention's two sides were never symmetric.
arxiv-2502-08446:
Friedemann Landmesser and co-authors compare scanning methods for spectroscopy of ultracold atoms in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their approach blends femtosecond interferometry with acousto-optical phase control. It suits very dilute gases where fine spectral detail matters most.

They test two ways to scan the interferometer: stepwise and continuous rapid scanning. The rapid method performed better in direct comparison. With laser-cooled lithium atoms, they reached a spectral resolution of 250 megahertz. That is a ten-fold gain over earlier experiments. The result supports rapid scanning for high-resolution work on cold quantum systems.
arxiv-2502-09046:
Jin-Duk Park, Jaemin Yoo, and Won-Yong Shin propose a recommendation method in twenty twenty-five. Some shops rate items on many criteria at once, not just one score. Recommenders that use all those ratings can serve users better. But training-based methods for this task are slow and hard to scale.

Their method, CA-GF, needs no training at all. First it builds a graph of item likeness from a broader user graph that keeps the criteria apart. Then it applies graph filtering tuned to each criterion, choosing the best filter for each. Filters come from a family of polynomial low-pass types. The aim is top accuracy at very high speed. Readers get a lean path to multi-criteria suggestions.
arxiv-2502-10046:
Juyeong Hwang and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on how virtual characters move their heads. In games and virtual worlds, a character that looks around in a natural way feels far more alive. Older methods used fixed rules or heat maps of eye-catching spots, and they often missed why a person would look somewhere, such as danger or a search for clues.

The team's framework, called ViRAC, uses large vision and language models to reason about the scene. The character can weigh risk, seek information, and pick what matters most, much as a person would. Because it reasons rather than copying past motion, it can work in new settings it was never trained on. The goal is head motion that looks thoughtful, not just busy.
arxiv-2502-10146:
Prokhorov, Shohonov, Teryaev, Tsegelnik, and Zakharov model how matter speeds up when heavy ions crash, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Strong electric fields can form in head-on hits, and the Schwinger effect can then matter. The team asks what the same sort of push does when it acts through the motion of the fluid.

They use the PHSD frame to model gold-gold hits at mid-range speeds. The maps show where the push is strong at each point in time. The push can be very high, in both head-on and off-center hits, and it forms a core and outer ring. In the bound phase, heat stays below the Unruh heat. In the free phase, that link flips. The result backs the idea of such cool states early in a crash.
arxiv-2502-10746: Satoshi Ishizaka, writing alone, checks a proposed shortcut for locating the edge of quantum correlations in the simplest Bell test, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A tidy analytic test for the boundary had been suggested but not proven. Ishizaka attacks the question through the NPA hierarchy, a ladder of checks for quantum behavior. One hoped-for simplification fails, yet the boundary test at the plain level matches the next level up. That match moves the extremal condition to the simpler level, where it can be checked directly.
arxiv-2502-11646:
Yunzhe Hu, Difan Zou, and Dong Xu design transformer layers from a top-down energy view, in place of the usual hand-built parts. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, is called Hyper-SET.

Transformers win at many tasks, but their layers are built by feel, from the ground up. The team reads token play as a joint best-fit task on a sphere. Two marks guide it: tokens should line up in sense in the wide space, and spread in a fair way in the small one. Stated as bounds on an energy, that view yields matched focus and feed parts, with a scale rule. Run in a loop, it gives a new transformer with shared terms across layers.
arxiv-2502-12646:
Ciro De Simone, Vittorio De Falco, and Salvatore Capozziello wrote a paper from 2025 on whether a wormhole could sound like a black hole. A wormhole is a thin bridge between two parts of space, with no core of crushed matter and no edge of no return. When a black hole is struck, it rings with a set of fading tones. If a wormhole rings with the same tones, the two would be hard to tell apart by sound.

The team reshaped the wormhole's form near its throat with a few free dials. They worked out the main tone and first overtone for three kinds of shaking: plain waves, light waves, and gravity waves. They then searched for dial settings matching a standard black hole's tones. In one part of the dial space, the wormhole copied a subset of those tones, for single kinds of shaking and for mixes.
arxiv-2502-12846: Bonetti and co-authors work out WH birth at the LHC in the SMEFT frame. They reach next-to-next lead QCD grade for that birth path. The team weighs how ties from six-size parts sway the W-plus-Higgs yield. Those ties stem from the frame's own part set. Fresh QCD fix terms for the stock path sit next to the bent path in the same runs.
arxiv-2502-13046:
Mateo Londoño and Jesús Pérez-Ríos study how cold helium gas cools metal fluoride molecules in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Buffer gas cooling sheds molecular energy through collisions with a cold gas. How well it works rides on the molecule-atom collision details.

The team computed the forces between each fluoride and helium with quantum chemistry, then ran full quantum collision dynamics with the molecule treated as a stiff rotor. The cooling and spin-down rates were read through an approximation scheme that ties them to basic molecular traits. Their analysis exposes the physics that sets how fast such molecules settle in a cold bath.
arxiv-2502-15146:
Godoy and three co-authors fixed a distance problem for random fields in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Spatial models sometimes index randomness by whole sets, not points. Standard set distances, like the Hausdorff distance, break the math needed for valid covariance functions. The authors propose measuring distance between the smallest balls enclosing each set.

For well-behaved spaces, that ball-Hausdorff distance reduces to centers and radii. They prove it keeps the key definiteness property whenever the underlying space does. By a classical theorem, that unlocks standard covariance families for set-indexed fields. Families covered include the Matérn and powered exponential forms. Reducing sets to ball summaries also makes covariance cheap to compute.
arxiv-2502-15446:
Jiyun Li and four co-authors build a digital backend for radio telescopes in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Very long baseline interferometry links telescopes across the globe into one giant instrument. Each station needs a digital backend to process its signals. Existing products rely on costly, custom hardware with long build times. The team instead uses the ROACH2 platform, a flexible board made for astronomy signal work.

Their design adapts that board into a versatile backend. They then validate its performance against the needs of real observations. A cheaper, reconfigurable backend can serve more stations and switch modes as science demands. The paper targets observatory engineers who face tight budgets. It shows a proven open platform can carry a core telescope function.
arxiv-2502-17546:
Peter Denton and Charles Gourley use neutrinos to weigh the density profile of the Sun, in a research paper from 2025. Solar neutrinos proved that fusion in the Sun matches theory in broad terms. They also revealed that neutrinos have mass and change type as they travel, which lets them probe the solar interior.

The authors combine the latest solar neutrino data with reactor data on neutrino change. From that mix they set bounds on how dense each solar layer is. More reactor data from JUNO and more solar data from DUNE should sharpen the bounds. A rare neutrino type from helium fusion is a key missing measure.
arxiv-2502-17746:
Sebastián Donoso, Alejandro Maass, and Vicente Saavedra-Araya wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It proves a pointwise ergodic theorem along return times of systems that mix fast, a variant of Bourgain's return times result.

The authors bring in a new class of sparse sequences that are good for ergodic averages, meaning averages along them settle to the right limit for almost every point. The sequences arise as the times a fast-mixing system comes back to a small set. One concrete case comes from doubling a point on a circle and watching when it lands in a shrinking window. The proof adapts tools made for random sequences to ones that are not free of each other.
arxiv-2502-18246:
Hannah Lehr, Igor Lesanovsky, and Gabriele Perfetto wrote a 2025 physics paper on a gas of half-spin particles that annihilate each other as they spread through open space. Annihilation-and-spread behavior is a model for how populations thin out. On a lattice, weak loss of this kind was known to produce strange, slow decays of the population.

The team asks whether the same behavior appears in smooth continuous space, with no lattice. They use a time-dependent method suited to weak loss. For meetings of two or three particles that end in annihilation, the population decays by the same law as on the lattice. The same holds for pairs that merge into one. A hotter start speeds the decay but does not change its law. When the birth of new particles competes with the deaths, a sharp transition to an empty state appears, of a class.
arxiv-2502-18546:
Xuechun Li and Susu Xu grade earthquake damage to buildings from satellite radar in a 2025 paper. Radar images taken before and after a quake reveal ground movement, but sorting buildings into damage classes is muddied by noise and slow at regional scale. Fast, reliable maps guide emergency response.

Their framework blends the radar data with government ground-failure models and building fragility curves, using a causal Bayesian method with a fast quadratic approximation. Tested on five major quakes, from Haiti 2021 to Ridgecrest 2019, it scored high accuracy across damage classes. It improved on earlier methods by up to about a third while cutting computing cost by over forty percent.
arxiv-2502-18646:
Alessandro Ascani Orsini, Manan Bhatt, Pierce Perkins, Siyu Wang, Kiara Quinn, Kenzi Griffith, Fausto Kang, and Nitish Thakor wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents a way to rebuild rodent muscle in three dimensions from thin stained slices, then study where nerve and muscle meet.

The method uses classic image steps to stack the slices, find the junction sites, and even out counts across samples. It then lines the sites up with muscle signal records taken from the skin. In the soleus muscle, the sites found from tissue match the motor unit spots found from signals well. The tool joins structure and function in one view, which could aid muscle care and repair work.
arxiv-2502-19746: Takuma Byakuno proves a compact result in metric geometry in a solo 2025 paper. The setting is the Gromov-Hausdorff space, whose points are spaces, compared by a distance that says how alike two spaces are in shape. He takes two bounded parts of that space and pairs their points under the l-infinity rule, keeping the larger of the two distances. The paper proves this product can be placed back inside the Gromov-Hausdorff space with every distance kept exact.
arxiv-2503-00046:
Zhaoyi Hou, Adriana Kovashka, and Xiang Li wrote a 2025 paper on whether large AI models can judge creativity in advertisements. Evaluating creativity is hard even for people, because it is subjective and involves complex mental processes. Marketing research suggests breaking creativity into parts.

The authors split ad creativity into atypicality, how unusual an ad is, and originality, how fresh its idea is. They collected fine-grained human annotations on these dimensions for a set of advertisements. They then built a suite of tasks and tested how well state-of-the-art vision-language models align with human judgments. The results show both promise and clear challenges for automatic creativity assessment, a tool advertisers would value for screening ideas.
arxiv-2503-02046:
Jun Yin and Marian Verhelst wrote this engineering paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on finding where a sound comes from using tiny devices. Hearing aids and small robots need this skill in real time, but the best neural methods are too heavy for edge hardware.

The team starts from a robust network that reads SRP-PHAT features, a classic sound-location signal, and trims it for the extreme edge. Their paired methods cut the cost of building the features and shrink the network itself. Across settings, the network's compute cost fell by up to about three quarters, and its stored weights by far more. The most balanced version still matched top accuracy while running in under nine milliseconds per frame on a Raspberry Pi. That is more than seven times faster than the starting model. The work targets always-on listening on small, cheap chips.
arxiv-2503-02646:
François Bachoc, Tommaso Cesari, and Roberto Colomboni analyze a broker who must price trades without knowing what either side truly values. Two traders hold private valuations and accept or reject the broker's proposed price, guided by context. The broker aims to maximize the gain from trade against an oracle that knows the valuation distributions. Prices shift arbitrarily between rounds as the market value moves.

Similar contexts are assumed to carry similar prices, and valuations are zero-mean noise around that moving value. Two feedback regimes are studied: full revelation after each round, or only attempted transactions. Algorithms for both achieve tight regret bounds. A further result shows the distribution-knowing oracle already secures at least half the gain of an oracle that knows the realized valuations themselves. The half-approximation is also tight.
arxiv-2503-03846:
Massimo Villata, in a solo paper from 2025, asks whether a theory of gravity built on a deep symmetry can survive a recent antimatter experiment. The theory predicts that matter and antimatter repel each other, which could explain why the universe expands faster and faster.

The experiment dropped antihydrogen atoms and found that Earth pulls them down, just as it pulls normal matter. Villata offers two ways the theory can still hold. In one, the repulsion involves matter in an inverted space-time, not antimatter in ours. In the other, antimatter here cannot show the reversal that causes repulsion. A simpler approximation even suggests time reversal is not needed for the effect.
arxiv-2503-03946:
The CMS team reported in twenty twenty-five how much beam light hit their detector in lead-on-lead crashes in twenty fifteen and twenty eighteen. Knowing that total, called the beam load, lets staff turn crash counts into true rates. The crashes ran at a set high energy, and the later set was three times the size of the first.

Three small sub-tools tracked the beam, and beam scans set the true scale. The team lists the main sources of doubt in those counts. The final doubt was three parts in a hundred for the first year. It fell to under two parts in a hundred for the later year.
arxiv-2503-04046:
Zhipeng Zhou, Ziqiao Meng, Pengcheng Wu, Peilin Zhao, and Chunyan Miao present COST, a way to ease clashes when one model learns many tasks in two thousand twenty-five. Tasks trained together often pull the model in rival directions, and some tasks hog progress. Past fixes mostly reweight losses or gradients to calm the clash.

COST instead jumps the model to a twin point with the same loss but less clash, a move the authors call symmetry teleportation. A small add-on module makes that jump cheap and keeps the loss fixed by design. A replay of past paths lets the method keep gains from strong optimizers. The add-on lifts a wide range of past methods in tests.
arxiv-2503-05246:
Zheng and co-authors present a method for teaching AI agents new tasks in sequence without erasing old skills, in this 2025 paper. Agents must balance fast learning with stable memory. Their method, called SSDE, splits the network into frozen parts that carry old knowledge and free parts for new tasks.

A sparse coding scheme shares out the free capacity so each task gets enough room. The method also wakes up dormant neurons, units that have gone quiet, to restore flexibility as frozen parts pile up. The authors argue this mix keeps agents adaptable over long learning runs. Tests in the paper weigh the approach on continual learning tasks.
arxiv-2503-07746:
Sergio Martínez-González studies how supernova shocks disrupt dust grains by torque in two thousand twenty-five. Big stars shape interstellar dust through light and force. Gas hits can spin grains fast when shocks pass by. Past a critical spin, grains tear apart from the strain.

He tracks that process for old grains and for grains born in the supernova itself. Both sit inside wind blown bubbles around the star. Work runs on outputs of three dimensional fluid simulations. Before the blast, disruption takes millions of years in the thin bubble gas. Torque times run past sputtering times and near shattering times.
arxiv-2503-07946:
Zhongpai Gao and co-authors present a graphics method that renders moving scenes with shifting light effects in real time, in a paper from 2025. Past methods handled motion and view-based effects apart. Joining them while keeping speed was an open problem.

Their method, called 7DGS, describes each scene element with a seven-part spread. The parts cover place in space, time, and viewing direction. A slicing step turns those into the standard three-dimensional forms that current renderers use, based on the viewer's angle and the moment shown. That keeps the method compatible with existing tools and allows joint training. On hard test scenes, image quality beat past methods by a wide margin while running at hundreds of frames per second.
arxiv-2503-08446:
Andreas Katsanikakis and Nikolaos Bekiaris-Liberis design controls for systems that switch modes while their commands arrive late. Predictor feedback can cancel input delay, but switching breaks the usual recipe. Tomorrow's mode is unknowable today, and each mode may last any length of time. An exact predictor for the true system is therefore out of reach.

Their law averages the exact predictors built for each single mode alone. The average is not itself exact, so stability needs the modes' matrices and gains to differ only modestly. The authors argue that limit is unavoidable without restricting delay or dwell time. A Lyapunov functional proves uniform stability of the closed loop. The proof constructs a bound on the gap between the average and an exact predictor. Simulations, with comparisons to rival laws, show the design working.
arxiv-2503-08846:
Dmitry Melnikov, a solo author, gives a tutorial in 2025 on links between knot theory and quantum mechanics. The notes show how quantum states and operations can be encoded in the topology of spaces, following rules from topological quantum field theory. Values such as probabilities then come out as knot and link invariants, numbers that stay fixed when a knot is deformed.

The notes focus on how topology controls quantum features, offering a picture based way to think about the subject. Melnikov gives a topological classification of entanglement, the linking of quantum states. Entanglement entropy and basic quantum protocols are also covered. The aim is a fresh diagrammatic intuition for readers who know standard quantum theory.
arxiv-2503-09446:
Zhihua Tian and co-authors present a 2025 paper on erasing concepts from image generators. Text-to-image diffusion models can produce harmful or misleading content. Erasing a concept usually means editing the model, and edits often damage normal generation. The proposed framework, Interpret then Deactivate, works in two steps. A sparse autoencoder first reads each concept as a mix of features. Features tied to the target concept are then switched off for good.

The autoencoder doubles as a zero-shot classifier that spots prompts naming the concept. Removal can therefore be selective: only flagged prompts lose the concept. AI safety teams get precision erasure that spares unrelated skills. Feature-level surgery beats whole-model retraining in both cost and side effects. The interpret-first step matters because blind deletion is what degraded earlier erasure methods.
arxiv-2503-09746:
A large team of researchers solves inverse problems with diffusion models and reinforcement learning in a paper from 2025. An inverse problem works backward from blurred or partial data to the hidden original. Diffusion models can serve as prior knowledge about what originals look like. The team trains such a model to sample the full range of plausible originals, using a learning rule called Relative Trajectory Balance.

They test the method on hard vision and science problems, both straight and twisted. Extra exploration tricks help training find good solutions. Older training-free methods, they show, carry biases when working in compressed latent space. The approach aims at principled, optimal sampling rather than quick guesses.
arxiv-2503-10246:
Samuel Pawel, Małgorzata Roos, and Leonhard Held addressed a quiet inconsistency in drug regulation in 2025. Regulators require two significant trials to approve a drug, the two-trials rule. But when officials then estimate the drug's effect, they usually pool both trials in a fixed-effect meta-analysis. That pooled interval can exclude no-effect even when the two-trials rule itself was not satisfied, so testing and estimation can contradict each other.

The authors recast both procedures in one framework of combined p-value functions. In that view, the two-trials rule matches one classical combination method and meta-analysis matches another. From the unified frame they derive compatible p-values, effect estimates, and confidence intervals in closed form. Compatibility means a regulator never has to announce significance with one hand and take it back with the other. The paper also offers new proposals for combining evidence coherently.
arxiv-2503-10846:
Seyed Ali Akhavani, Bahruz Jabiyev, Ben Kallus, Cem Topcuoglu, Sergey Bratus, and Engin Kirda slip malicious requests past web application firewalls by exploiting parser disagreements. Their paper from twenty twenty-five, WAFFLED, runs advanced fuzzing over headers, body segments, and common content types. Five major firewalls are the test targets: AWS, Azure, Cloud Armor, Cloudflare, and ModSecurity.

The fuzzing found and confirmed 1207 bypasses across the five. A wild study adds sting: over ninety percent of websites take form-encoded and multipart bodies interchangeably, so the tricks apply broadly. All vendors acknowledged the flaws, some paying bounties. The team also ships HTTP-Normalizer, a proxy that checks requests against the RFC rules and blocks every bypass shown. Parser gaps are now a named attack lane.
arxiv-2503-12846:
Jia-Lin Pei, Guo-Liang Ma, and Adam Bzdak published this physics paper in 2025. It studies symmetric cumulants, statistical tools that reveal how flow patterns of particles from heavy-ion collisions vary together. When two nuclei smash at near light speed, the debris' spread carries fingerprints of the quark-gluon plasma formed inside.

The authors calculate two such measures, built from four and six particles. They trace three sources: the rule that total momentum is conserved, the collective flow of the plasma, and the interplay between them. Their four-particle results match data from the ATLAS experiment once a sub-event method is applied. That helps explain where the signal in small collision systems comes from. The six-particle numbers are fresh predictions for experiments to test. Cleaner theory, they argue, sharpens what collisions teach about the plasma's fluctuations.
arxiv-2503-13646:
Chiara Plizzari and co-authors build a tougher test of time sense for video models in this 2025 paper. First-person video is a stream of close-up hand and object action, where order matters. The team found current question sets leak: models score well from the words alone or one frozen frame. Their new set, EgoTempo, asks only questions that need the whole video watched in sequence.

Ten temporal skills are probed, and cheating by shortcut does not work by design. Leading multimodal models, strong elsewhere, fell well short on the new set. The gap shows how thin present time reasoning is in the egocentric domain. The authors release data and code, hoping the benchmark pushes models that truly track unfolding action.
arxiv-2503-14246:
Villani, Natale, and Mallmann-Trenn cut the communication bill for federated learning, where many devices train one shared model. Shipping model weights back and forth dominates the cost. Their trick encodes the full weights as a sparse random mixing of a much smaller trainable vector.

Only the small vector travels between server and clients. Shrinking it further keeps accuracy while the mixing matrix grows denser, a trade the team maps out in theory. The result beats earlier pruning-based schemes by orders of magnitude in compression. The authors also link their training-by-sampling view to random geometry. They frame the method as a path to learning on tight networks.
arxiv-2503-16346:
Xiangyu Ren, Yuexun Huang, Zhiding Liang, and Antonio Barbalace present a compiler for quantum graph states in a 2025 arXiv paper. Graph states are key resources for quantum algorithms and for linking machines in distributed quantum computing. The team works with a scheme that uses emitters plus photons and builds states in a fixed, step-by-step way.

Their framework splits a target graph state into parts, compiles each part, then joins and schedules the circuits. It also reshapes graph states to cut the cost of entanglement.
