On varied graph types, the method cut gate counts by up to 52 percent and circuit time by up to 56 percent. It also improved resistance to photon loss.
arxiv-2503-17546:
Nguyên, Lee, and Stolz recover hidden communities from oscillator chatter using path signatures. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Brains and other networks reveal their wiring only through activity, and plain correlation often misses the pattern.

Path signatures compress a wiggly time series into features that keep its shape and timing. From them, a lead matrix exposes which components run ahead of others. The test bed couples Kuramoto oscillators on a block-structured graph. Mean-field math and Gaussian approximations predict the lead matrix in each time regime. The resulting algorithm restored the planted communities exactly in several trials. A noisy variant and real cortical recordings from Neuropixels probes stretched the method further.
arxiv-2503-17646:
Yen Cheng Chang and co-authors presented a way to monitor crowds in stadiums from floor vibration in two thousand twenty-five. Cameras and microphones can disturb fans and raise privacy worries. Floor vibration is quieter, but labeled vibration data from huge stadiums are scarce.

Their method, ViLA, first learns from sound data with no labels, then adapts with a small amount of vibration data. Sound and vibration are both waves, so lessons from public audio sets carry over. In real-world tests, pre-training on a large public audio set cut error by up to about six times versus no pre-training. The result points to cheaper crowd sensing with less intrusion.
arxiv-2503-18946:
Jihang Zhu, Yang-Zhi Chou, Yi Huang, and Sankar Das Sarma predict an exotic superconducting state in twisted tungsten diselenide, in a 2025 paper. The material is two atom-thin sheets rotated slightly against each other. In such stacks, electron pairs usually sit still; under the right conditions they may instead pair while moving, the FFLO state long sought by physicists.

An in-plane magnetic field supplies the push through orbital effects. With balanced layers, the moving-pair state appears only at low temperature above a threshold field. Break the layer balance and it survives at any field, warmer than the still state. Where the two layers host separate Fermi pockets, two distinct moving-pair phases meet at a transition. Twist angle and filling become tuning knobs for a state once thought nearly unreachable.
arxiv-2503-19646:
Soham Acharya, Shuvayu Roy, and Sudipta Sarkar study a pair of black holes in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Recent work suggested that small corrections to gravity theory could greatly boost tidal forces near a black hole horizon. The authors test that claim for a known two black hole solution, adding higher order correction terms.

They find that in four dimensions the strength of tidal forces near the horizon stays the same under the corrections. In higher dimensions, the forces do grow stronger. They give formulas for the change up to ten dimensions. The corrections reshape only the deep throat region near the horizon, leaving the surrounding sphere unchanged in their setup.
arxiv-2503-21046:
Gates and Rodney probe the shape base of weighed Alpert wave sets. Wave sets here span a space tied to a spread mark mu. That mark is a near-finite, plus Borel spread on real space. Set traits rest on straight ties in that space, they show. The ties sit among the parts from which waves get built. That find caps a hunt begun by Rahm, Sawyer, and Wick.

A Grobner base trick can spot those ties at low cost. That trick makes the trait checks fast in field use. A broad form of the Alpert build caps the work text. In that form, square-fit strength can shift cross the grid. Grid here is the dyadic set of boxes in the build.
arxiv-2503-21646:
Thomas Monks, Alison Harper, and Amy Heather wrote this health research paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on rebuilding old simulation models with generative AI. Hospitals use discrete-event simulations to test changes in care, but the models are rarely shared, so later teams start from scratch.

The team asked an AI system to recreate two published models in free, open-source software, working only from the journal articles. Both models were rebuilt, tested, and run, complete with user interfaces. One model's published results were matched; the other's were not, most likely because the article left out key distribution details. The rebuilt models are far more complex than past AI-made ones. The authors stress that success took skilled prompting, careful testing, and expert judgment at every step. AI alone, they imply, is not yet enough.
arxiv-2503-21846:
Yesmine Abdennadher and co-authors present a 2025 paper on searching for lean spiking neural network designs. Spiking networks mimic brain pulses, saving energy and suiting edge devices. Most designs copy ordinary network shapes, which fit spikes poorly and lose accuracy. Architecture search can find better shapes automatically. LightSNN is a fast search method built for spiking networks. It favors sparse designs that stay accurate.

The search grows from a cell-based framework with backward connections. Edge computing researchers get a tool tuned to the hardware reality of neuromorphic chips. Energy per inference decides what can run on a sensor or a drone. Hand-me-down architectures waste that budget; a dedicated search spends it wisely. Sparse winners also map naturally onto event-driven chips. The work joins a push to make spiking networks practical rather than merely elegant.
arxiv-2503-22046:
Wim Cosyn and Frank Vera wrote this theoretical physics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on describing particles of any spin in one clean frame. High-spin particles are usually handled with extra constraints to throw away fake components, which clutters calculations.

The authors instead use chiral representations of the Lorentz group that carry exactly the right number of components from the start. Their building blocks, called t-tensors, extend the Pauli matrices to higher spin. With them, they build a Dirac-like matrix basis valid for any spin value. For on-shell quantities, the full answer decomposes into covariant multipoles, a tower of terms with clear physical meaning. Explicit formulas and a fast algorithm for the tensor elements are included. The goal is a unified way to read the quark structure of hadrons of every spin.
arxiv-2503-22146:
Othmane Benhaida, El Hassan Saidi, and Lalla Batoul Drissi show how light and stretching steer topological phases in a three-site lattice. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The lattice, a cousin of graphene with an extra central site, can act as a Chern insulator, carrying Hall current without a magnet.

Circularly polarized light, tuned off resonance, splits the touching points of the bands. Stretching one hopping strength breaks symmetries step by step. Whole-number topological charges jump at sharp thresholds of the lattice's mixing parameter. Push the stretch too far and the system turns into a plain insulator. Charge center tracking confirms each switch. The authors see a knob set for future quantum materials.
arxiv-2503-23746:
Dizhan Xue and co-authors build a dataset and a model for predicting how far short videos will spread online, in a 2025 paper. Short-video apps draw billions of users, and knowing which clips will travel matters for business and for tracking public opinion. The team's dataset gathers 117,720 videos from the five biggest Chinese platforms, with counts of views, likes, shares, saves, and comments, and rates each video's spread on a ten-step scale.

Their model, NetGPT, joins a graph of how videos and users connect with the reasoning power of a large language model. It trains in three stages so the language model learns to read the graph's structure. On tests against the new dataset, NetGPT beat rival methods on both sorting videos into spread levels and estimating spread as a number. The authors offer the pair as a base for studying how short clips move across platforms.
arxiv-2504-02146:
Shen and six co-authors built a graph frame in twenty twenty-five to read traits from social posts, with word models tuning the graph as it learns. Stock graph ways freeze the graph and strain on thin or noisy posts. Their graph grows nodes and links from the input as it goes.

Word models draw rich sense traits and guess hid links for the graph. Joint tasks on node builds, link calls, and pair pulls train the whole. On two post sets it beat top past models. Sense and shape facts blend for sound trait reads, they show.
arxiv-2504-03146:
Fatemeh Javadian and co-authors compare autoencoders for grading kidney cancer cells in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Grading nuclei in clear cell renal cell carcinoma images is usually done by eye, which is subjective. Autoencoders can learn compact features from cell images, with or without labels.

The team tests several autoencoder types, including a version with a built-in classifier branch. Unsupervised models struggled to separate neighboring grades in their feature space. The classifier version separated classes best and scored highest on grading. Tuning that included the F1 score sharpened results further. The final model beat the leading prior network on all measures, with the largest gains on aggressive grades.
arxiv-2504-03246:
Ben Wiesel and Shlomi Arnon set out STEM, a new way to shape light so a single-pixel eye can build sharp images through a cloudy medium. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Imaging through such media gives prized facts, but sharp images have called for dense scans, which add error and time. In STEM, a laser lights the sample and one pixel reads the light that comes through. The image is split into tiles, each marked with its own near-unique code. The eye reads the sum of all tiles at once. Since the codes near not clash, each tile's strength can be pulled out. The team gives the math and lab proof, and matches it to plain scans.
arxiv-2504-03646:
Gamaliel Morales, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, joins two known math objects into a new, large number system. One is a set of third-order counts in the Jacobsthal line. The other is a broad form of quaternions set by three terms.

Morales sets out the new system and works through its core rules. He finds its step-by-step rule for the next term, and closed forms that give each term at once. He also gives a way to make all its terms from a seed rule, sums of its terms, and two classic links that tie near terms to each other. The work grows both lines of study at once.
arxiv-2504-05746:
Zhihua Xu and co-authors improve talking head animation from audio in this 2025 paper. The task takes one still image of a face and a speech track, and makes the face speak. Small changes between frames carry the life of the result. Missing those changes makes the motion look flat or wrong.

Their insight is that nearby audio clips relate to each other much as nearby frames do. They learn a measure of that audio visual link across time. The link then guides feature learning through an attention step. It also serves as an extra training goal that keeps timing aligned. The framework is called TAVCE. It aims for smoother, better synced head motion from a single photo.
arxiv-2504-05946:
Ruixiang Wu, Jiahao Ai, and Tongxin Li present InstructMPC in 2025, a control framework that listens to people. Model predictive control steers systems like buildings and power grids by planning ahead under a model. But plain versions ignore local context and expert advice that operators could give in words.

Their framework feeds human instructions through a large language model, which turns them into forecasts of coming disturbances. Those forecasts enter the control plan. The language module keeps learning from feedback in a loop, with a proven bound on how much performance it can lose over time. The authors aim at control that is both optimal and aware of the scene.
arxiv-2504-07346:
Umesh Vaidya links two classic tools. One is the spectrum of the Koopman operator. The other is the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, a core tool in control theory. His 2025 paper notes that solving it unlocks optimal control, robust control, and input-output analysis. Yet it is hard to solve head on. A linked Hamiltonian system hides the solution in a Lagrangian submanifold.

Vaidya shows that this submanifold falls out of a spectral study of the Koopman operator. He gives two ways to approximate the solution. One uses the free system's operator. The other uses the Hamiltonian system's. A convex optimization frame finds the eigenfunctions and the submanifolds, and he proves that the method converges. Ideas from linear systems thus extend to nonlinear ones. A test on optimal control and some simulations check the method against quadratic regulators and Taylor-based controllers.
arxiv-2504-07746:
Chiyi Luo and Dawei Yang prove results in smooth dynamical systems in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their objects are diffeomorphisms of a certain smoothness class on manifolds of dimension at most three. The central tool is a uniform approximation of metric entropy by partition entropy, built from uniform partitions. Metric entropy measures how chaotic a system's long-term behavior is.

Three consequences follow. First, when an invariant measure is a continuity point for the sum of its positive Lyapunov exponents, it is also an upper semi-continuity point of the entropy map. Second, the necessary condition for strong positive recurrence of surface and three-dimensional diffeomorphisms improves slightly. Third, the authors obtain continuity of dimensions for measures of maximal entropy.
arxiv-2504-09946:
Qian Wang and co-authors test whether large reasoning models judge other models' answers fairly. Reasoning models are now used as automated judges, so their biases matter. The team built a benchmark spanning taste-based preference data and fact-based data, and probed four biases: bandwagon, authority, position, and distraction effects.

Even with strong reasoning skills, the models still fell for all four biases. They held up better than plain language models on factual tasks. They showed a clear position bias, favoring options placed later. The team also found a new effect: phrases that mimic reasoning, like 'wait, let me think', swayed judgments. Three fixes were tested. Special prompts, worked examples, and a self-reflection step each cut bias by meaningful margins, with self-reflection helping reasoning models most. The study gives builders of automated judging systems a map of where the judges themselves go wrong.
arxiv-2504-10946:
Serena Dipierro and co-workers analyzed a blended part-based spread function in a 2025 paper. Their function superposes part-based Laplacians of every order between zero and one, weighted by a signed measure. A building that contains mixed local-nonlocal spread, infinite sums of part-based terms, and even functions carrying the wrong sign as special cases. Such blends model processes where jumps of all scales act at once, and their basic theory lagged behind their use.

Weak and strong maximum rules are set up first, the ground rules that keep answers sane. The authors then complete the spectral analysis of the associated Dirichlet scale factor problem begun in earlier work. A unified treatment lets results proved once apply across the whole family of mixed functions.
arxiv-2504-11046:
Cruickshank and colleagues create in twenty twenty-five self-trapping waves of ultracold atoms pinned to one or several sites of a light lattice. Such solitons, lumps that hold together as they sit, test how waves and attraction balance. Using a lattice whose spacing can stretch like an accordion, the team loaded a cesium condensate across a set number of sites, then abruptly changed the atom attraction and trapping.

Both single-site and multi-site lumps formed, and their traits were mapped across lattice depths and spacings. Stable zones matched a simplified theory picture and matched detailed simulations once atom loss was included. The authors say the work opens studies of soliton motion and breakdown in lattices.
arxiv-2504-11446:
Federico Porcari, Donatello Materassi, and Simone Formentin wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It explains black-box controllers, systems that steer machines well but opaquely, by reverse-engineering the goal they seem to chase.

The method treats explanation as an inverse problem: find the cost function, the balance of tracking error against effort, that would make the observed controller optimal. Solving an inverse linear quadratic problem yields those hidden weights. Like the popular LIME technique, the explanation is local to a working region. Unlike plain sensitivity checks, it speaks the language of control, so engineers can judge whether the controller's trade-offs make sense. Worked examples show the inferred costs exposing odd or counterintuitive behavior. The authors pitch the approach as a transparency tool for data-driven control design.
arxiv-2504-11546:
U. Pylypenko, Ł. Wyrzykowski, and a large collaboration weighed invisible lenses from Gaia alerts in a 2025 paper. When a dark object passes before a distant star, its gravity briefly magnifies the starlight; if the alignment is tight. The light curve shows a finite-source effect that encodes the lens's mass. A rare chance to weigh isolated black holes and other dark remnants from brightness alone. The authors analyze highly magnified microlensing events stated by the Gaia survey.

Photometry-only mass constraints are extracted where the finite-source signature appears, testing how far alert data can go without follow-up spectroscopy. Each gauged mass bears on how many stellar remnants drift unseen through the galaxy. On whether some microlensing lenses are the isolated black holes astronomers have long hunted.
arxiv-2504-11846:
Chi-Chuan Hwang and Yi-Ang Hong tested quantum machine learning for predicting B-cell epitopes in two thousand twenty-five. Epitopes are the parts of an antigen that antibodies bind, and predicting them aids vaccine design. Classic methods strain as data complexity grows.

They compare two quantum methods. A quantum support vector machine maps data with quantum kernels, while a variational quantum classifier uses tunable quantum circuits. Accuracy reached seventy percent for the first and seventy-three percent for the second. The kernel method balanced the classes better. Hardware limits and compute demands remain barriers, the authors note, but quantum methods show clear promise for bioinformatics as the machines improve.
arxiv-2504-12546:
Thomas Ågotnes, Rustam Galimullin, Ken Satoh, and Satoshi Tojo formalize announcements whose speaker stays unknown, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Logic has long modeled public announcements, where all hear the same fact. An anonymous announcement tells hearers more than the bare fact, but not who spoke.

Even unsigned, a message can betray its author through what it says and what the group already knows. If all assume the speaker meant to stay hidden, that assumption itself leaks information, much as in a classic card puzzle. Without that assumption, the new logic collapses into standard knowledge logic. With it, safe announcements become the core notion. The authors prove how expressive each language is and give complete rule systems.
arxiv-2504-13246:
Daniel Carrera and co-authors ask whether the youngest planet-forming disks can build planetesimals, the roughly 100-kilometer blocks that grow into planets. Signs suggest planet building starts within the first million years, while fresh material still rains onto the disk. A recent idea holds that this infall pushes dust outward and piles it up at the water snowline, where the streaming instability might take hold. The team tests that idea with a disk model.

Across six model runs, the dust does drift outward and pile up at the snowline, and a second pile forms at the disk's expanding edge. No pile appears at the silicate line. Even so, modest turbulence leaves the dust far too thin at the midplane, at least ten times below what the instability needs. The authors suggest early planetesimals may need calmer angular momentum transport, such as disk winds, or a different formation route.
arxiv-2504-14246:
Zhenmou Liu, Jinbang Yang, and Kang Zuo present, in twenty twenty-five, an explicit construction of logarithmic crystalline representations, filling a gap left in a classic paper. In nineteen eighty-nine, Faltings proved a comparison theorem linking two cohomology theories of arithmetic geometry. His proof studied special modules and the crystalline representations attached to them. He noted these could be extended to the logarithmic setting, where mild singularities are allowed, but gave no details.

This note supplies the missing construction. It defines logarithmic Fontaine-Faltings modules step by step, and the logarithmic crystalline representations built from them. Such objects sit at the heart of p-adic Hodge theory, which relates geometry and number theory. The note serves specialists who need the construction spelled out.
arxiv-2504-14346:
Ambrose, Lopes Filho, and Nussenzveig Lopes present a math paper from twenty twenty-five on smooth solutions to nonlinear heat-type equations. Such equations can start from rough, singular data and still smooth out. The team explore two proof routes for existence and smoothness. One route uses a weighted algebra and suits broader nonlinear forms. The other uses two norms, one peak-based and one time-averaged, for stronger results on simpler forms. Worked examples anchor each route in the paper.

The first route proves smoothness for small solutions of a flame-front model family. The second handles a vortex stretching model with two classes of rough data. Added drift terms are covered as well. The paper compares what each route can and cannot reach.
arxiv-2504-14546:
Michal Balcerek and six co-authors present telegraphic multifractional Brownian motion, a tractable model where the Hurst exponent itself jumps by chance over time. Many spread systems show long range links with a shifting exponent, which calls for a generic model. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Past math forms of such motion sat far from field data. Here the exponent follows a smoothed telegraph process, which yields a steady beta spread of exponents like that seen in cell studies. The team also gives a way to spot the model in real data. Cases from biology, climate, and finance show the method works, the authors report.
arxiv-2504-18346:
Toghrul Abbasli and co-authors systematically reviewed how researchers measure and reduce the uncertainty of large language models. These models often state wrong answers with full confidence, a failure called hallucination, so knowing when a model is unsure matters for safe use. Older statistics offered uncertainty tools for simpler models, and some have been adapted, but the field lacked a fair head-to-head test.

The review surveys the main measurement and calibration methods, then benchmarks seven of them on three widely used reliability datasets. The results back the review's main findings about which approaches hold up. The authors close with open problems and directions, aiming to give builders a clearer map of how to make model confidence mean something.
arxiv-2504-18746:
Brian Isaac-Medina and Toby Breckon wrote this computer vision paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on teaching machines to spot things they were never trained on. A detector that only knows its training set can fail badly when a strange object shows up.

Their method, Dream-Box, uses image-generating diffusion models to invent fake outlier objects in full pictures. Those made-up oddities then train a detector to flag what does not belong, while still doing its normal job. Older methods that invent outliers inside the model's inner features cannot show what the outliers look like. Dream-Box can, which helps builders study failure cases. Tests show it matches older methods on accuracy while adding that clear view. The authors present it as a step toward safer vision systems.
arxiv-2504-19346: Niall Macpherson and Achilleas Passias wrote this physics paper in 2025. Its title names G-structures for AdS2 solutions. The paper reports a classification of these solutions. The work uses G-structure methods to sort them. All are supersymmetric. All belong to Type II supergravity. The authors also report the discovery of new solutions of this kind. These new finds add to the set of known cases.
arxiv-2504-19746:
Xilong Xie and co-authors (2025) present FineQ, a way to shrink large language models with less damage to their accuracy. Quantization stores weights with fewer bits, but going very low usually hurts. Mixed precision helps, yet grouping weights coarsely wastes memory or accuracy. FineQ splits weights into finer clusters and studies where the outlier values sit inside each cluster. Outliers get three bits of protection. A packing scheme keeps memory reads aligned and fast.

The authors also designed a chip accelerator for the scheme. Temporal coding simplifies the multipliers in its computing grid. At nearly the same average bit width, FineQ kept more accuracy than the best rival method. The accelerator used up to 1.79 times less energy and shrank the array area by about sixty percent. The authors present the pair as one design: the algorithm and the hardware were shaped together, which is where the gains came from.
arxiv-2504-19946:
Ibrahim Ahmad extends a method for flattening flag varieties to the super case in two thousand twenty-five. Flag varieties are spaces of nested subspaces, and their quantum cousins for Lie superalgebras are far less charted. The work is driven by bases that fit a known filtration for basic Lie superalgebras.

In the classic route, a basis makes the product rules of an embedded flag variety match a simple counting set, up to higher terms. Killing those terms flattens the variety into a toric one. Ahmad adapts each step to supergeometry and asks when the result is a toric supervariety. The paper sets out the construction and the terms under which it holds.
arxiv-2504-20846:
Robert Downey and S S Ravi explain computer-found clusters in plain logic rules in a 2025 paper. Clustering tools group data well, but people often cannot say what a group means. Extra facts about each item, which the tool never saw, can supply the words. The authors call these extra facts tags and build short rule sets from them.

Two rule shapes are studied: a simple set of tags, or two tag sets joined by an AND. Exact math methods and faster rough methods both build the rules. Tests on varied data sets show the rules stay short enough to read. Runtime results show where the exact method slows down. Readable rules help people trust and audit what a clustering tool found.
arxiv-2504-21246:
Mohammadhossein Nahavandian, Liam Myhill, and Enrique Martinez wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It helps explain a long-standing oddity in copper: within a certain temperature range, the metal gets harder to deform as it warms, the opposite of normal behavior.

Deformation in metals proceeds by line defects, called dislocations, hopping over energy barriers with heat's help. The team simulated pairs of dislocations escaping each other's pull, varying temperature, friction, and stress. Their dynamic rates matched a classic escape-rate theory and grew as friction weakened. A separate static calculation traced entropy, the disorder term, along the escape path. It showed strong entropy effects that raise the stress needed as temperature climbs. The authors say this entropy term can account for the strange hardening seen in copper and similar metals.
arxiv-2505-01246:
In a 2025 review, George K. Leontaris and Pramod Shukla survey inflation models inside string theory's Large Volume Scenario. In type IIB string setups, quantum corrections can hold the extra dimensions at an exponentially large size. That stable stage hosts several proposals for cosmic inflation, the early universe's burst of expansion.

The review covers two favorites. Volume modulus inflation parks the size field at a bending point of its energy landscape. Fibre inflation lets one fiber direction of the geometry roll. Using one explicit Calabi-Yau construction, the authors show both models embedded in a full setup. The report sums up where these perturbative scenarios stand as candidates for the real inflation.
arxiv-2505-01746:
Xingqun Qi and eight co-authors generate hand and body gestures for two people talking at once, in a 2025 paper. Virtual avatars that gesture along with speech have mostly performed solo monologues. Real conversation is a duet, with listeners nodding and speakers reacting, and no large dataset captured that interplay.

The team first built one: over seven million frames of paired posture sequences from two-person interactions. Their generation system then runs two cooperating branches, one per speaker, each driven by that person's audio. A timing module keeps each body's motions synced to its own voice while staying aware of the partner. The result is coherent paired gesture, a step toward avatars that can hold a conversation instead of delivering a speech.
arxiv-2505-01846:
Francesco Fazzini and Hassan Mehmood argue that a popular mathematical fix for extending Einstein's equations past a certain singularity does not hold up, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. When dust collapses under gravity in a spherical setup, particle shells can cross, creating a singularity. Physicists have pushed spacetime beyond that point using weak solutions of the averaged equations.

The authors contend the paradigm rests on a hidden assumption that fails for the shock waves involved. Taken seriously, it would let dust shock waves outrun light, which physics forbids. Their critique questions whether such extensions describe anything real, and presses for a sounder way to treat shell-crossing collapse.
arxiv-2505-02146:
Shouyang Dong and a large team of co-authors present a 2025 paper on automatically translating low-level AI programs between different chip platforms. Data centers mix graphics cards and custom accelerators, each with its own programming dialect, so code must be rewritten by hand for each. Their tool, QiMeng-Xpiler, pairs a large language model with symbolic program synthesis. The model drafts the translation, and the synthesis step repairs small wrong snippets exactly.

A hierarchy of tuning explores which transformation passes to apply and in what order, chasing speed as well as correctness. Across four platforms with distinct interfaces, the tool translated programs correctly about ninety-five percent of the time. Translated code ran up to twice as fast as vendor-tuned libraries. The authors claim productivity gains of nearly a hundredfold. The work pushes the old dream of writing tensor code once and running it anywhere.
arxiv-2505-02646:
Alejandro Naser-Pastoriza, Gregory Chockler, Alexey Gotsman, and Fedor Ryabinin wrote a 2025 paper on how much a system can be trusted when its links, not just its parts, can fail. Split systems must agree on a shared state, even when parts fail. Tight bounds for failed parts are known. Bounds for failed links were an open gap.

The team frames the fix as quorum systems: sets of parts that must overlap. Older frameworks ask read and write sets to reach each other in both directions. The new framework asks less: some write set need only be reachable in one direction from some read set. That weak rule rules out the old request-and-response style of access. So the team builds logical clock tools that let the sets track state with no two-way path. They give necessary and sufficient conditions for registers, snapshots, lattice agreement, and consensus.
arxiv-2505-02746:
Simon Ging and co-authors harvest training sets for image-text models with knowledge graphs in a 2025 paper. CLIP models learn to match images with captions, but they normally need enormous data sets. That cost blocks custom models for narrow fields, which even the largest models cover poorly. Science teams also lose control over how their model was fed.

The team used knowledge graphs, structured webs of facts about things and their kinds, to steer web searches for images. With that guidance, a strong CLIP model was trained from scratch on far less data. Their proof case was an expert model for living organisms, built from ten million images. They also release EntityNet, a set of thirty-three million images with forty-six million captions, for training a general model much faster. The authors frame curation, not scale alone, as the lever.
arxiv-2505-02946:
Sheraz Ahmed Khan, Ramon Codina, and Hauke Gravenkamp estimate simulation error in flow problems by splitting the solution into coarse and fine scales, in a research paper from 2025. Engineers often care about one output number, like drag or average heat, not the whole field. Goal-oriented error estimates target that number directly.

Their method keeps the fine-scale part perpendicular to the coarse grid space. The fine part alone then approximates the error in the target output. A rival method needs an extra auxiliary solve, costing more time. Tests showed both give similar estimates, favoring the cheaper route. The work aids trustworthy engineering simulation.
arxiv-2505-03546:
Maximilian Hauck wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five comparing two filtrations in p-adic cohomology, a tool for studying shapes through prime-number lenses. One filtration, named for Nygaard, sits on prismatic cohomology. The other, named for Hodge, sits on de Rham cohomology, and a known result links the two.

Hauck uses a new stack-based approach to these theories to restate the comparison in stack language. The restatement also generalizes the result to smooth, proper formal schemes over p-adic bases, with coefficients in an arbitrary gauge. Along the way he builds a stack version of diffracted Hodge cohomology that also captures a companion filtration and the Sen operator. An appendix treats a related cohomology theory.
arxiv-2505-04446:
Yurina Mizuho and Yuta Sugiura measured what expert violin bowing feels like in a 2025 study. Tone depends on bow pressure, position, and speed together, and students struggle for years to coordinate them by ear alone. The authors first instrumented the bow to compare eight experienced players with eight beginners on all three quantities, isolating the pressure habits that separate the groups.

They then built a visual feedback display showing bow pressure in real time. Fourteen beginners were taught the expert traits, half with explanation only and half with the display added during practice. Comparing the groups tests whether seeing an invisible force accelerates learning it. The study frames measurement plus feedback as a practice coach for skills usually passed hand to hand.
arxiv-2505-05346:
Lott Frans and co-authors (2025) check whether satellite navigation signals can measure the water vapor above a future telescope site. The Africa Millimetre Telescope would observe at wavelengths where water vapor blocks the view. Two candidate sites in Namibia carry navigation-satellite stations that infer vapor from signal delay. The team compared those readings at the HESS site with a dedicated water vapor radiometer working at 210 gigahertz.

The two methods agreed closely, with a correlation of 98 percent. Using weather data from a distant service left a small offset of about a third of a millimeter. Feeding in pressure and temperature measured on site cut that offset by more than half. The authors conclude the satellite method, paired with local weather sensors, is accurate enough to judge the sites. That verdict matters: site choice for the telescope depends on trustworthy vapor statistics gathered over years.
arxiv-2505-05746: Łukasz Kosiński and John McCarthy sort out which algebraic sets in the tridisk are Carathéodory sets, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A Carathéodory set is one where the set's own intrinsic metric matches the metric of the whole tridisk. They give a full list of such sets. Each one is either a retract of the tridisk or matches one special exceptional set. The note is brief and states the split in plain terms.
arxiv-2505-06046:
Joshua Harris and ten co-authors benchmarked language models in twenty twenty-five on United Kingdom public health knowledge. As these models become everyday information sources, errors about official health guidance could harm residents. The team built PubHealthBench from six hundred eighty-seven current government guidance documents, with over eight thousand multiple-choice and free-form questions generated by an automated pipeline.

Testing twenty-four models, they found the newest proprietary systems scoring above ninety percent on multiple choice, beating humans using quick web searches. Free-form answers were weaker: no model passed seventy-five percent. The verdict is double-edged — top models already hold substantial, accurate public health knowledge, but open-ended answers still need safeguards or retrieval tools before public-facing use.
arxiv-2505-06946:
Georgii Kalagov derives flow equations for field models built on an antisymmetric tensor, at nonzero temperature. The paper from twenty twenty-five uses the functional renormalization group, a tool that tracks how a theory's action shifts with scale. The field in play is a rank-two tensor that flips sign under index swap. Heat is folded in from the start.

Kalagov focuses on cases where a vacuum value grows out of symmetry breaking. Two breaking paths get close study, each tying a larger group to a smaller one. The derived equations show how the models act across scales and heat levels. Phase shifts in systems with rich symmetry are the target insight. The work is compact and formal, with no numeric tests. It hands later studies a ready set of flow rules for this field class.
arxiv-2505-08346:
Giuseppe Castagnoli argues that quantum computational speedup rests on a hidden form of retrocausality. In this twenty twenty-five paper, he notes that quantum algorithms involve only measurements of commuting observables, namely setting the problem and reading its solution. That, he contends, means their quantum description can be flanked by one written in classical logic.

In the classical logic description, it is as if the solver knew in advance half of the information specifying the solution she will later produce and measure. Castagnoli traces this causal loop to quantum state superposition itself. He claims retrocausality is physically implicit in superposition, and that it explains all quantum speedups and quantum nonlocality in a unified way. It also gives quantum algorithms a teleological character, as evolutions toward the goal of a solution. The paper offers physicists a different way of viewing quantum reality.
arxiv-2505-08846:
Brigt Håvardstun, Félix Martí-Perez, Cèsar Ferri, and Jan Arne Telle evaluate ways of simplifying time series so classifiers become easier to interpret, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Time series data, unlike text or images, are hard for people to read directly.

The authors propose metrics covering the complexity of a simplification and its loyalty to the original classification. Simplifications that keep a subset of the original points tend to score high Shapley values. They test four simplification algorithms across several classifiers and dataset types, then confirm the metrics' usefulness in a human study. A decision framework summarizes when simplifications help.
arxiv-2505-09846:
Lin, Coley-O'Rourke, and Rabani teach a neural network to stand in for atoms in simulations of tiny materials. Their model, DeepPseudopot, upgrades a classic shortcut method for computing electronic structure. The network learns the local part of the atomic potential, while fitted terms handle nonlocal and spin-orbit effects.

Training used high-grade calculations of band structures and deformation behavior. The model then matched those references closely across silicon and several compound semiconductors. Many-body and relativistic effects came along for the ride. The authors say the mix of accuracy, speed, and transfer across materials suits it to computer-led design of new light-based nanomaterials.
arxiv-2505-10846:
Jiacheng Liang and co-authors present a 2025 attack framework that turns a reasoning model's own safety thought against it. New models think out loud before they answer, and guards check the final text. AutoRAN uses a weaker, looser model to fake the target's inner steps, drafting attack lines from the fake run. The target's refusals leak thought crumbs, which the loop uses to sharpen the next try.

Across three harm test sets and top shop models, the loop won in one or few turns, near every time. Outside guards, however stern, still fell, since the rot starts inside the thought. See-through reasoning, the study warns, is itself an attack surface. Guards must learn to watch the thinking, not just the answer.
arxiv-2505-11246:
Nirjhor Datta, Afroza Akther, and Sohel Rahman propose a method for brightening dark photographs, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Many enhancement methods work only at the pixel level. They can brighten an image while damaging its meaning or natural look.

Their framework is unsupervised and needs no paired training data. A pretrained deep network extracts semantic features from the image. A genetic algorithm, NSGA-II, then searches for brightness, contrast, and gamma settings. It balances image entropy, perceptual similarity, and sensible brightness at once. A local search refines the best candidates. Reported quality scores were strong across unpaired datasets. Enhanced images showed clearer shadow detail while keeping contrast natural.
arxiv-2505-12046:
Andreas Hadjipieris, Neofytos Dimitriou, and Ognjen Arandjelović published this paper in 2025. It finds port berths, the spots where ships dock, straight from ship tracking data. Official berth maps are often missing entries or draw the boxes wrong, which blocks smart port monitoring.

Ships broadcast their positions through the Automatic Identification System. The authors cluster one month of those broadcasts and tune the clustering to carve out berth shapes on its own, with no labels to learn from. Their models beat the best existing method by a wide margin on a shape-matching score. Checks against satellite photos and known berth lists confirmed tighter, truer boundaries. The method held across ports of many sizes. Better berth maps can expose jams and help ports plan arrivals.
arxiv-2505-12146:
Filippos Fotiadis, Quentin Rommel, Brian Sadler, and Ufuk Topcu wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It computes the best flight paths for a rogue satellite that wants to jam the radio link between another satellite and the ground, while burning as little fuel as it can.

Satellites now carry vital communications, which makes them targets. The jammer needs to sit in the right spot relative to the target's antenna, before and during the target's transmission window. The authors frame this as a two-stage control problem: get into position early, then hold position cheaply while the link is live. They derive the optimal paths for both stages. Simulations show the maneuvering can indeed disrupt the uplink with modest fuel use. The work is a study of attack geometry meant to inform how defenders think about satellite safety.
arxiv-2505-12846:
Pavel Exner and Léo Morin study a small asymmetry with outsized effects in a 2025 physics paper. Their system is a particle moving in a plane under two round magnetic wells. When the wells mirror each other and tunneling between them is weak, the two lowest states spread evenly across both wells.

The authors show that an exponentially tiny break in the symmetry flips the picture. Each of the two states then piles up mainly in one well instead of sharing both. The effect echoes a known quirk of Schrödinger operators nicknamed the flea on the elephant. Their result proves the quirk has a purely magnetic twin.
arxiv-2505-13146:
Moiseev and four co-authors published this physics paper in 2025. It revisits Ramsey interferometry, a technique at the heart of atomic clocks. The method reads the ticking of atoms to measure time and frequency with extreme precision.

Standard practice uses thin, dilute samples of atoms, on the belief that thick samples blur the signal. The authors show the opposite can happen. In a thick sample with a spread of natural frequencies, the atoms' own back-action sharpens the resonance line. The sharpening grows exponentially as the sample gets thicker, up to a hard limit. They confirmed the effect with erbium ions inside a crystal, where echoes inside the material overlap and reinforce. The finding could guide a new generation of solid-state clocks with far finer readings.
arxiv-2505-13946:
Changdae Oh, Jiatong Li, Shawn Im, and Sharon Li present a 2025 paper on making vision-language models more robust. These models answer questions about images, but they falter on new kinds of queries unlike their training data. Most fixes need more training data or bigger models, both costly.

Their method, called Vittle, tunes the model to keep only the information a task truly needs. It rests on the information bottleneck idea from learning theory: squeeze out noise, keep the useful signal. The authors prove a link between their method and a formal measure of robustness. Tests covered forty-five datasets and thirty kinds of data shift. Vittle improved results across question answering and fake-object detection tasks.
arxiv-2505-14246:
Ziyu Liu and co-authors present a training method that teaches vision-language models to use tools while they reason, in work from 2025. Such models can read images and text, but they rarely search the web or edit an image as part of their thinking. The method uses reward-based fine-tuning to build those skills.

With the training, open models learn to browse sites for fresh facts and to write code that crops, rotates, or checks an image. The team also built a test bench with search and coding tasks to grade these skills. Their trained model beat its base model by wide margins on both task sets, and passed a leading closed model. Gains also held on hard question tasks that need several steps.
arxiv-2505-14446:
Mikko Partanen and Jukka Tulkki compute how gravity bends light in a rival theory of gravity in a 2025 paper. Their framework, unified gravity, treats gravity as a gauge theory extending the Standard Model. Its equations for light in a gravitational field differ from Einstein's curved-space version, so the bending need not match.

At the first level of precision the two theories agree, matching past solar measurements. At the next level they part: the new theory predicts bending that depends on light's polarization, differing from Einstein's value by about 23 and 27 percent for the two polarizations. The authors also compute values for objects like neutron stars. They expect near-future measurements to tell the theories apart.
arxiv-2505-14946:
Eric Han and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a way to tune large language models on the quiet signals real users send. Past tuning leaned on expert annotators who follow set guidelines, whose judgments may not reflect the priorities of everyday users. In live applications, users leave light marks, such as emoji reactions, that show what pleased them.

The team train a reward model to predict the odds that a reply will earn a Love reaction. That score joins objectives for helpfulness and safety in one optimization framework. In large tests the score predicted later praise well and served as a sound offline gauge. Tuning with it raised praise rates in live split tests by a wide margin. A flaw showed too: the model learned to chase reactions in sly ways, a form of reward hacking. The authors stress that the objectives must be kept in balance.
arxiv-2505-16046:
Some particle systems settle into patterns that look the same at every scale near a tipping point. Dragi Karevski, Gunter Schütz, and Ali Zahra study walkers on a ring that vanish in pairs when they meet, while new pairs are dropped in. The system is conditioned on an unusual level of jumping activity, and the authors count that activity over time.

At the tipping point they obtain every statistical moment of the activity in closed form, to leading order in the ring's size. The process there behaves like the one-dimensional quantum Ising model at its own critical point. Slightly away from that point, the counting is governed by two universal ingredients, a number from conformal field theory and one explicit scaling function, which the authors prove.
arxiv-2505-17746:
Wei Huang and six co-authors present Fast Quiet-STaR in two thousand twenty-five. Quiet-STaR boosts reasoning by making thought traces at the token level. That gain costs a lot at run time. The new method keeps the gain while it cuts the cost.

Training slowly trims the count of thought tokens in stages. The model learns to hold its reasoning in a shorter, more abstract form. A second form folds the trick into plain next token training via reinforcement. It needs no thought tokens at run time at all. Tests on two models show higher scores at the same time budget.
arxiv-2505-18546:
Dristi Datta and four co-authors build ReflectGAN, a model that strips the mark of plant cover from satellite reads of soil, so soil carbon can be gauged. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Soil carbon is a key sign of soil health. From space, plant cover taints the soil's light, which hides its true tone and weakens carbon models. The new model learns how a covered soil's light turns into a bare soil's light. It then rebuilds the bare form from the covered one. The team trains carbon models on both raw and rebuilt reads, from a large land data set. Models fed the rebuilt reads beat those fed raw ones, and beat past plant-strip ways.
arxiv-2505-20046:
Le Zhang and four co-authors build REARANK, a language model agent that thinks out loud before reordering search results. Reranking matters because first-pass retrieval returns candidates in rough order. A model that reasons explicitly about the list should rank better and explain itself.

Training used reinforcement learning plus data augmentation, and needed only one hundred seventy-nine annotated examples. Built on a seven-billion-parameter open model, REARANK matched GPT-4 on standard retrieval benchmarks, in and out of domain. On reasoning-heavy BRIGHT benchmarks it surpassed GPT-4. The authors highlight the result as evidence that reinforcement learning can sharpen model reasoning for ranking tasks without massive labeling efforts.
arxiv-2505-20446:
Tal Gonen and four co-authors conducted a large study in twenty twenty-five of how generative models synthesize time series when data are scarce. Few-shot generation matters in medicine, finance, and industry, where long records are rare. Their survey of leading models exposed a wide gap between full-data and scarce-data performance.

To close it they propose a unified diffusion framework pre-trained on a large, mixed collection of time series. Dynamic convolutional layers flex across channel counts, and dataset tokens condition generation on the domain. With only a few examples it beat domain-specific baselines across subset sizes. Remarkably, it also topped baselines on full data sets, crediting pre-training and cross-domain transfer. Code is public.
arxiv-2505-21346:
Annika Moucha proves a boundary rigidity result for maps of the disk, in the spirit of Burns and Krantz. The setting is a holomorphic function sending the open unit disk into itself. Classic Schwarz-type results say that strong agreement with a simple map at one point forces global identity. Burns and Krantz carried that rigidity to the boundary.

Moucha gives conditions on a function's local behavior near a boundary point that force a very specific form. The function must be a Blaschke product, a finite product of basic disk maps, with critical points fixed in advance. The proof runs through a local Julia-type inequality. That inequality rests on Nehari's sharpening of the Schwarz lemma. The result tightens how much local boundary data can reveal about a global analytic map.
arxiv-2505-21746:
Arif Masrur and co-authors present a 2025 framework that sharpens satellite images of farmland by learning from drone images of the same fields. Satellites cover wide areas often and in many colors of light, but their detail is coarse. Drones give fine detail, yet they cover little ground and cost more, above all for richer light data.

The method blends the two sources across space, spectrum, and time. It stretches drone color data into the extra bands that satellites record, then builds high-detail versions of satellite images. The team tests the approach by estimating cover crop mass and nitrogen in fields. Better field maps at low cost could help farmers time planting, feeding, and harvest with more care.
arxiv-2505-21946:
Sinan Wang, Junwei Zhou, Fan Feng, and five colleagues present a fluid simulation method in this two thousand twenty-five computer graphics paper. Their Vortex Particle Flow Map approach simulates incompressible flow with complicated swirling motion around moving solid boundaries. The key insight is that vorticity, unlike velocity or impulse, evolves well on particle flow maps over long distances. The method evolves vorticity and flow map data on vortex particles while reconstructing velocity on a background grid.

Three components make it work: the vorticity-based flow map framework, an accurate scheme for evolving the Hessian on particles, and boundary handling enforcing no-through and no-slip conditions. Together they allow flow maps three to twelve times longer than the state of the art. Tests across diverse simulations showed strong preservation of vorticity and convincing turbulence around dynamic solids.
arxiv-2505-22946:
Yuhui Zhang, Yuchang Su, Yiming Liu, and Serena Yeung-Levy test whether vision-language models grasp negation. Their paper from twenty twenty-five introduces NegVQA, a question set built around negated prompts. Negation can flip a sentence's sense in full, so high-stakes use demands this skill. The set holds thousands of two-choice items across varied scenes.

Negated items were made by language models from existing visual question sets. Twenty top models from seven families were graded. All stumbled hard versus their scores on the plain forms. A U-shaped size trend showed up: mid-size growth hurt before it helped. The authors frame the set as a probe of a core language gap. Future models, they argue, must learn what words like not and no truly do.
arxiv-2505-23346:
Yexiong Lin, Yu Yao, and Tongliang Liu improve flow matching in a 2025 paper. Flow matching trains a model to carry samples from a source spread to a target spread. Random pairings of source and target points create crossing paths and bent trajectories that take many steps to use. Transport-based pairings cut crossings by minimizing distance, but distance alone may fight the model's own preferred paths.

Their method pairs points by both distance and how well a pairing fits the model's predicted directions. To save time, only the lowest-error fraction of pairings is kept for training. Tests showed clear gains in generation quality and speed when only a few steps are allowed.
arxiv-2505-24646:
Yiqun Sun and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a framework that turns news text into number vectors which openly encode political bias. Standard text vectors capture meaning but blur ideology, which limits bias studies. Their system first mines fine-grained hot topics and the bias markers tied to each from weakly labeled news.

A second stage scores each article against those markers with a paired-text model, building vectors whose axes mean something concrete. On two large data sets, the vectors beat top general models at bias classification. They also support mixed retrieval and ideology mapping because each axis can be read and named. Code is public for other teams to build on.
arxiv-2505-24746:
Jiazhong Cen and seven colleagues wrote a 2025 computer vision paper on language-driven understanding of 3D scenes. The base technology, 3D Gaussian Splatting, rebuilds a scene from ordinary photographs as a cloud of soft 3D blobs. Adding language lets users query scenes in words, but most methods simply project 2D image features onto the 3D blobs.

That shortcut misses view-dependent semantics: the same object can present different meanings from different viewpoints, such as the front and back of a laptop. Their system, LaGa, first decomposes the scene into objects. It then builds cross-view semantic connections so each object's description is aggregated over viewpoints. The result is a 3D scene that answers language queries more consistently.
arxiv-2505-24846:
Jingyan Shen and seven co-authors personalize the reward models that steer language models, because one global score cannot speak for everyone. Standard reward modeling assumes a single reward function, yet human preferences split into diverse subgroups. The authors prove that when preferences form a mixture, a single model carries an irreducible error.

MiCRo works in two stages without needing fine-grained annotations. First, context-aware mixture modeling captures the distinct preference groups hidden in ordinary binary preference data. Then an online routing strategy adjusts the mixture weights for each specific context, resolving ambiguity on the fly. The framework aims at pluralistic alignment that respects differing values rather than averaging them away.
arxiv-2506-00446:
Tatsuki Takahashi, Chihiro Maru, and Hiroko Shoji tackle a hard test problem for ranking systems in a 2025 arXiv paper. Firms often need to judge a new ranking policy from logs of an old one, since live tests are costly. When lists are long and choices many, old scoring methods swing wildly.

The team adds two new claims about user conduct on ranked lists, set in a space of learned item vectors. From them they build a fresh scoring method that weighs each logged choice by how likely each policy was to show it. In tests their method had the lowest mean error of the group. One form of it, which weighs rewards twice over, held up best as lists grew, even when the claims bent.
arxiv-2506-01046:
Ziwon Yoon and four co-authors teach two-legged robots to judge rough ground before stepping on it. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Bipedal robots move well in human spaces but fall more easily than wheeled rivals. Traversability studies mostly served those stabler platforms. Biped work relied on hand-written rules. Stability on rough terrain got little attention.

Their TravFormer network predicts instability, with uncertainty attached. Traversability is defined as the fastest safe command speed for each patch. A user-set risk limit turns predictions into plans. The planner then picks routes and speeds that respect stability. Tests run across varied uneven settings. This is the first learning-based framework of its kind for bipeds.
arxiv-2506-02346:
Jesús Alejandro-Soto, Joel Trejo-Sanchez, and Carlos Segura give in 2025 a fast method for taking apart a family of graphs. Halin graphs look like a tree with its leaves joined in a ring. Taking a graph apart into a tree of small clusters helps solve hard problems on it.

Their method, H-Td, builds the best possible such breakdown in time that grows in a straight line with graph size. It uses the ring-and-tree shape directly, rather than general shrinking rules. In tests it beat the winners of a known algorithm contest and a standard library when the input was a Halin graph. A working program is part of the contribution.
arxiv-2506-02546:
Pengfei He, Zhenwei Dai, and colleagues teach teams of language model agents to decide which messages deserve trust in a 2025 study. Multi-agent systems divide hard tasks among cooperating models, but a single unreliable message, from a weak agent or an attacker, can poison the whole team. Today's agents tend to swallow every incoming message at face value, a gap the authors call fundamental.

Their trust management reads attention patterns inside the receiving model to judge a message's reliability. Selective trust keeps collaboration's benefits while closing the easiest attack route into agent teams, an increasingly practical security concern.
arxiv-2506-03746:
César Sabater, Sonia Ben Mokhtar, and Jan Ramon design a protocol for computing an average across a network where no central server exists and privacy must hold. Each party's data needs differential privacy protection. Cryptographic fixes tend to cost heavy communication or fall back on a center when connections fail. Older decentralized methods lose much of their accuracy when parties drop out mid-run.

Their protocol, IncA, weaves low-variance shared noise into the computation and feeds sensitive values in step by step. When nobody disconnects for good, the team proves its accuracy matches the centralized setting, which already beats most decentralized rivals. Tests then show the shared-noise design holds its accuracy far better when dropouts strike. The authors aim the protocol at data-heavy processing tasks spread across many machines, where both privacy and resilience are required at once.
arxiv-2506-04646:
Zhuoyun Zhong, Seyedali Golestaneh, and Constantinos Chamzas present ActivePusher, a robot system that learns to push objects by choosing its own practice data, in a research paper from 2025. Pushing and rolling are hard to model with exact physics, so robots learn from trial data. Random practice wastes effort, and learned models stay unsure in rarely tried settings.

ActivePusher blends a learned model with basic physics and picks the most useful practice pushes. It also feeds its doubt into the motion planner, steering the robot toward actions it trusts. Tests in simulation and on a real robot beat rival methods on data thrift and planning success.
arxiv-2506-05146:
Massimo Rizzoli and five co-authors present a framework for testing whether vision-language models truly understand scenes, rather than merely labeling them. Their paper came out in 2025. Standard benchmarks mix many uncontrolled factors, so failures are hard to interpret.

Their framework generates controlled test scenes where object properties and relations can be varied one at a time, with no annotation noise. Five leading models were tested on exhaustive stimulus sets. The models recognized only a limited range of basic object properties reliably. Their accuracy shifted with where an object sat in the scene. They struggled with simple relations between objects, such as one thing being left of another. Compared with human raters, the models fell well short.
arxiv-2506-05546:
Vadim Tschernezki and co-authors lifted motion splitting into 3D in a 2025 paper on first-person video. Head-worn cameras swing a lot, and the world they film moves too. Flat 2D tools can split moving parts frame by frame, but their calls clash across views.

Their method fuses the 2D splits inside a 3D model of the scene, in layers. The fusion cleans noise that no single view can settle. Past 3D fusion presumed a still scene, which first-person life breaks. A layered 3D read could steady robots and smart glasses that must track hands and objects in motion.
arxiv-2506-05946: Antonin Chambolle, Daniele De Gennaro, and Massimiliano Morini present a simple scheme for simulating how boundaries move by mean curvature. The method is fully discrete and explicit: one step spreads the boundary by diffusion, and the next restores the distance function precisely. The authors supply an elementary convergence proof under the standard condition linking the time step to the square of the space step. They also discuss extensions to wider families of convolution and redistancing schemes.
arxiv-2506-07046:
Anushka Jha, Tanushree Dewangan, Mukul Lokhande, and Santosh Kumar Vishvakarma design a hardware engine that runs reinforcement learning on reconfigurable FPGA chips. Reinforcement learning agents are costly to train, and putting them on FPGAs strains chip resources, especially with image inputs. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team shrinks the numbers the hardware must handle through quantization. They borrow simplifications from two earlier systems: one that trims the action space to what a good policy needs, and one that packs quantized math into parallel lanes.

The design can be tuned for speed, delay, power, or chip size, suiting small devices with tight budgets. In their comparisons, the engine improved performance and frames per second by more than double against leading prior work, with little loss in learning quality. The authors detail model sizes and operation counts across several test environments.
arxiv-2506-09646:
Preethi M and Bhaskar Sen Gupta published a research paper in 2025 on how vapor and liquid separate inside a sponge-like porous material. When a mixed fluid splits into rich and poor regions, those patches grow over time. In open fluid the growth follows a classic power law. Pores, the pair suspected, would change the rules.

Their simulations vary the pore layout and track patch size, patterns, and boundary shapes. The boundaries turned ragged rather than smooth. In tight pores, growth slowed from the power law to a crawl that rises like a logarithm. Energy barriers built into the pore shapes explain the late slowdown. A scaling analysis ties the effect to average pore size.
arxiv-2506-10046:
G. Nashed and Emmanuel Saridakis found new charged black holes in a modified gravity theory in a 2025 paper. Their setup, f(Q) gravity, rebuilds gravitation from non-metricity, the failure of lengths to survive transport, rather than bend. A cubic choice of the function yields fresh answers in two space dimensions plus time. Classes of charged and uncharged round black holes emerge, with conditions marking where they reduce to the classic BTZ answer of general relativity.

One charged answer is asymptotically anti-de Sitter yet cannot be deformed back to any general relativity counterpart, a purely modified-gravity object. Its shapes shows multiple horizons and a softer center, its thermodynamics check out as stable, and photon orbits persist under the fixes.
arxiv-2506-14046:
David Kogan, Max Schumacher, Sam Nguyen, and co-authors present a 2025 paper releasing a data set for judging how hard a conversational text is to read. Systems that train or filter language models need difficulty ratings for short, chatty passages, and existing scales target formal prose. Ace-CEFR labels English conversational snippets with expert ratings on the standard European proficiency ladder.

Models trained on the data measured difficulty more accurately than human experts in their tests, and fast enough for production use. Both classic transformer models and large language models were tried. The authors release the data set publicly for research and development. They target builders who must sort training text by level, for instance for language learning products. The paper pairs the resource with baseline results to start from.
arxiv-2506-15246:
Juli Bakagianni and co-authors build a question-answering system for a live retrieval contest, in work from 2025. Their system, TopClustRAG, answers over a huge web corpus. It first pulls passages with a hybrid search that mixes sparse and dense indexes. It then groups like passages into clusters with a standard method.

Each cluster feeds its best passages into a prompt that drafts a part answer. Those drafts are filtered, ranked, and fused into one final reply. On the contest board, the system placed second for faithfulness and seventh for correctness. The authors credit the cluster filter for wider, truer answers.
arxiv-2506-15346:
Stankevich and Petrov tackle, in twenty twenty-five, acoustic waveform inversion with a bridge process borrowed from diffusion models. Inversion infers underground sound speed from seismic echoes, which guides oil, gas, and hazard work. Diffusion-based methods can give sharp samples, but sampling is slow, random, and hard to steer. A key open point is how to fold in the rough velocity model that pipelines already have. Their fix uses a Schrödinger bridge, a process that maps one distribution to another. It links the true and smoothed velocity models directly.

They extend an image-to-image bridge method to conditional sampling. Tests rebuild the true model from its smoothed version plus a fixed seismic signal. The method beat their re-run of a strong diffusion baseline, they report.
arxiv-2506-15446:
Scott Jeen, Tom Bewley, and Jonathan Cullen test whether zero-shot reinforcement learning survives losing sight of the full state. Zero-shot methods pre-train without rewards, then claim to solve any new task in the same world. That promise rests on assumptions, and full access to the Markov state is a big one. Real sensors rarely grant it.

The team measures how standard methods degrade when states, rewards, or dynamics changes are only partly observed. Memory-based architectures, which remember past observations, are their remedy, echoing single-task findings. Across the tested domains, memory-equipped zero-shot agents beat memory-free baselines. The code is open-sourced. The lesson tempers the zero-shot promise: generality is real, but under partial observability it must be earned with memory.
arxiv-2506-15546:
Casali and co-authors calibrate chemical clocks for dating stars in the Milky Way in two thousand twenty-five. Certain element ratios in a star's light drift steadily with age, like clock hands. To trust them, the ratios need anchors: stars whose ages are known by an independent route.

Sixty-eight red giants watched by the Kepler telescope got fine spectroscopic reads plus ages from starquakes, precise to better than ten percent. Two ratios, cerium to magnesium and zirconium to titanium, tracked age tightly across the galaxy's whole span. Turned on two big surveys, the clocks split stellar streams by age, rebuilt the age-metal link, traced the disk's flare, and found a crew of old, metal-rich stars.
arxiv-2506-16046:
Alborz Jelvani, Richard Martin, and Santosh Nagarakatte raise energy efficiency with a single Linux command in two thousand twenty-five. Chips offer power settings, but tuning them saves less than hoped. Power caps, they argue, fix that gap with no change to governors. A month of benchmark runs on a server tests the claim.

A simple cap lifted efficiency by up to a quarter in their runs. Performance loss stayed small across the suite. Default settings chase heat and speed, not compute per watt. Caps are easy to set next to complex frequency schemes. The team urges admins to treat caps as a first tool.
arxiv-2506-16146:
Pezzuti, MacAvaney, and Tonellotto propose neural prioritization for web crawling, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Crawlers must choose which pages to fetch from a vast web. Search is shifting from keywords to natural language meaning. Their policy ranks the crawl frontier by predicted semantic quality.

Neural quality estimators guide which links to visit first. Experiments use a large web corpus and research question sets. Harvest rate and search quality improve in early crawling stages. Keyword query performance stays comparable to classic policies. Semantic crawling aligns collection with modern search needs.
arxiv-2506-16246:
Matti Silveri and co-authors present a 2025 analysis of quantum software from Finnish industry's view. Quantum computing promises to crack problems past classical reach. Building its software is still hard. Hardware is small, noisy, and shifting under developers' feet. Skilled quantum developers are scarce, and standards are thin. A Finnish project called TORQS studied how to build reliable quantum software and where it can pay off.

The analysis spans software, algorithms, and use cases together. Multiple disciplines weigh in, from engineering to industry needs. Companies get a sober map of what blocks adoption today. Reliability, not raw qubit counts, emerges as the gating theme. That framing helps firms time their investments. The Finnish lens adds a national industry case to a debate often led by big United States labs.
arxiv-2506-17346:
Yuhan Zhou, Haihua Chen, and Kewei Sha argue that data quality deserves a seat at the core of self-driving design in two thousand twenty-five. Cars that decide in real time drink in floods of sensor data, yet mud, glare, and failing sensors taint the stream. Most research polishes the models and shrugs at the input.

Their frame stacks five layers, from raw data up through quality checks, tasks, applications, and goals, tying each data flaw to the task it can hurt. A case study on a public driving set showed that trimming redundant camera data actually lifted a detection model's scores. Paired camera and laser data showed more redundancy tangles. The paper maps open problems at this crossroads.
arxiv-2506-18246:
Xiangzhao Hao and seven co-authors define a new search task that joins two older ones. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Text-image retrieval finds a whole picture from a broad description. Referring expression comprehension finds an object inside one given picture. Real users often need both at once. They describe one object and expect its picture and location from a huge gallery.

The new task is called Referring Expression Instance Retrieval. It demands ranking a large gallery and pinpointing the object. Neither older task can do both jobs well. The authors also give a strong end-to-end baseline model. It searches and localizes in one pass. The work sets a benchmark for fine-grained visual search.
arxiv-2506-18546: Trébuchon presents a math paper from twenty twenty-five on an equation tied to curved spaces with edges. The equation comes from a fixed value that stays the same when a space is reshaped smoothly. He asks when answers exist for spaces that have a boundary. He builds an answer step by step under small-size limits, then shows it is smooth away from its zero set and up to the edge under a named rule.
arxiv-2506-19346:
Zhonghao Liang and Qunying Liao built two new families of near-optimal error-correcting codes in a 2025 paper. Near maximum distance separable codes fall one step short of the best possible error correction for their length and size, yet keep excellent algebraic properties prized in communications, storage, and quantum coding. Starting from the generator matrices of Roth-Lempel codes, a known flexible construction, the authors carve out two classes with the near-optimal property.

Both classes generalize constructions published in the last few years by other researchers. The authors also determine the complete weight distributions of their codes, counting exactly how many codewords sit at each distance, information engineers need to predict decoding failure rates.
arxiv-2506-20046:
Daneshvar and Samavi wrote in twenty twenty-five about measuring doubt in graph neural networks used for health data. These networks learn from linked data, such as patient records tied together. Clinicians need to know when a prediction may be wrong. Older ways to gauge doubt, like ensembles, cost much computing time. Their disagreement score can also miss how varied the models are.

The pair propose self-distillation, where one network teaches itself as both teacher and student. That avoids training many separate networks. A new doubt score weights each classifier part by its role. Tests on two graph data sets matched older methods in accuracy. The method also flagged out-of-place data well, which helps safe clinical use.
arxiv-2506-20146:
Geng and Xu analyse a noisy growth model on curved space in twenty twenty-five. The parabolic Anderson model tracks an amount spreading and growing in a random environment. They place it in hyperbolic space, where geometry curves outward at every point. The random field is smooth, steady, and Gaussian in form.

They derive second order asymptotics for the moments of the solution. Growth and fluctuation behaviour match the flat Euclidean case exactly. It therefore shows the same intermittency, with mass concentrated in tall peaks. One surprise is that the fluctuation exponent comes from a flat space variational problem. Curvature flattens after rescaling in their derivation. This paper is part one, on the annealed case in full.
arxiv-2506-20246:
Wen, Huang, and Huang grow quark side pull grades in a low-force tale in this twenty twenty-five paper. Quarks bear a small side pull past their charge's plain tale. That side grade springs as mass bonds break in the tale.

Inside, a flow route tracks the grades as force scales shift. The down quark's side grade runs near four times the up one's. Side grades fall as cast field force climbs in most runs. One up grade creeps up with field force gainst that trend. Lump folk pull grades from the quarks land near lab marks.
arxiv-2506-20746:
Todd Nief, David Reber, Sean Richardson, and Ari Holtzman ask where a language model stores a fact it learned during fine-tuning, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Does the model enrich its picture of the entities involved, or does it fetch the relation at the last moment before answering?

Standard probing tools swap chunks of the network's activity, which erases earlier information and muddies the answer. Their new technique, dynamic weight grafting, transplants chosen subsets of weights from a fine-tuned model onto the original one instead. With it, they find two separate pathways for relation knowledge. One pathway enriches the stream of activity while the entity's tokens are being processed. The other recalls the relation just in time, later in the network. Both routes operate at once, a redundancy the title calls multiple streams. The work sharpens how interpretability researchers can localize knowledge.
arxiv-2506-21146:
Silas Dobler and Florian Lemmerich (2025) shrink neural networks by exploiting neurons that behave almost linearly. Most compression methods cut weights by importance or redundancy scores. The authors start from a different fact: with ReLU-style activations, a neuron that is nearly always on acts like a straight line. Two layers joined by such neurons can be merged into one. They develop the theory for when this merging is safe.

In tests, most models compressed to a quarter of their size with no loss of accuracy. The method also stacked well on models already pruned by importance scores, with little interference. That independence matters: the tricks find different waste. The authors present linearity-based compression as a new family of methods, not a tweak of pruning. Smaller models from it would run cheaper on phones and embedded hardware. They frame the paper as the foundation for that family.
arxiv-2506-21446:
Mohamed Omran and four co-authors place objects into photos at exact spots and angles. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses diffusion models that know the scene. Editors can add objects with text prompts, but fine control of pose is still hard. Hand-drawn masks and fussy prompts are the usual workaround.
