Their method feeds the model a visual map plus rough object masks. That signal clears up where the object goes and how it turns. The background stays untouched by design. Tests in car scenes score edits on looks, pose, and place accuracy. Hard cases that need shape changes are included. Fine place control can also join with style control.
arxiv-2506-22846:
Altinok improved speech recognition in this paper from twenty twenty-five with help from language models. CTC-based recognizers are fast because they decode in one pass. Their weakness is shaky handling of language patterns. Attention-based rivals model language better but decode slowly, which blocks real-time use.

The new loss, LAIL, borrows linguistic knowledge during training only. Small connector layers feed middle encoder outputs into a large language model's space. A language modeling loss there teaches the encoder better habits. At run time the recognizer stays a plain, fast CTC system. Tests on three speech corpora cut word errors to state-of-the-art levels for CTC systems, with minimal extra cost.
arxiv-2507-02546:
Ruicheng Wang and eight co-authors build MoGe-2, a model that reads the true-scale shape of a scene from a sole image. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A past model gave the scene's shape up to an unknown scale. The team finds ways to add true scale, with no loss to the shape's fine form. They also find that noise and flaws in real data blur the fine grain of the result. Their fix cleans and fills real data from many sources, with sharp fake tags as a guide. The model is trained on a large mixed set. It gives both true size and sharp detail.
arxiv-2507-03846:
Nicola Bernold, Moritz Vandenhirtz, Alice Bizeul, and Julia Vogt present an image generator in two thousand twenty-five whose reasoning can be inspected. Diffusion models build pictures by clearing noise step by step under the guidance of a text prompt. They often drop or garble parts of the prompt, and those slips are hard to catch automatically.

The team rebuilt the generator from modules with a built-in explanation trait. Each word of the prompt yields a map showing which pixels it influenced. That makes prompt-to-image mismatches visible at a glance. The authors show the model still produces high-quality images while giving useful insight into alignment. The work points toward generators whose failures can be diagnosed rather than guessed at.
arxiv-2507-04146:
Gunnar Schwertfeger and co-authors model a frustrated magnet with a twisted honeycomb-like lattice in a 2025 paper. The material HoAgGe arranges its atoms on a twisted Kagome net of corner-sharing triangles. It behaves as a two-dimensional spin ice with an unusually rich phase diagram.

In a magnetic field the compound's magnetization climbs in steps at simple fractions of saturation. Earlier simulations with fitted parameters explained only part of that behavior. The team combined a reduced-configuration search with density functional calculations to ground the model in first principles. Their approach aims to explain the full plateau pattern and the strong in-plane anisotropy behind it.
arxiv-2507-04246:
Daniel Akamatsu and five co-authors study how to measure temperature in quantum systems. Their 2025 paper treats a set of two-level atoms probed by a single beam of light. Heat blurs quantum behavior, so knowing the temperature is a first step in judging noise. The team asks how precise such a measurement can ever be.

Their exact analysis, with no shortcuts, caps precision at the standard quantum limit for the light used. They then build a thermometer inside a quantum simulator based on a split-beam device. The setup can start the atoms at ordinary or even effective negative temperatures. That range makes it a handy testbed for checking how well real quantum devices sense heat.
arxiv-2507-04346:
Li and van Kampen smoothed an adaptive flight controller in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Learning-based controllers can adapt in flight, but a twitchy one may command jerky moves. Jerks stress the actuators and can shake the aircraft. The target task is tracking a set angle of attack under changing dynamics.

Their scheme caps how fast control actions may change, with a penalty weight that adjusts itself online. A low-pass filter in the layered network trims high-frequency commands while keeping learning valid. Simulations on a longitudinal aircraft model showed smoother control and better tracking than the base method. Oscillations fell, and the trained policy stood up better to model errors. The authors stress the method's low computing cost.
arxiv-2507-04846:
Anna Zigelman, Zitao Yu, Rom Levy, and Yizhar Or study a robot drive in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The Twistcar is a wheeled platform that moves by wiggling. In most models its steering angle is set as a periodic input. In this kind, a rotor on the body swings in a cycle while the steering joint swings free, passively. Wheels that roll with no skid set nonholonomic constraints that link the joint's motion to momentum balance.

The acts that come out are rich: computer runs showed periodic solutions, some symmetric, some not, plus stability shifts and bifurcations. With perturbation expansions, harmonic balance, and scaling claims, the team near-called when the symmetric solution loses stability through a pitchfork bifurcation, as a function of drive frequency and build terms. Their far-limit calls fit the numbers. The work shows how passive joints make multi-stable locomotion.
arxiv-2507-05146:
Aadi Srivastava and five co-authors present VERITAS, a system that flags AI-made images and explains its call. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with the flood of synthetic images from GAN and diffusion models. Most detectors just give a label, which leaves users unsure why an image was judged fake.

VERITAS works on small images and does two jobs: it decides if the image is real or generated, and it points to the artifacts that drove the call, with a plain-language account. The design gives clear reasons even in zero-shot tests, where no examples of the new generator were seen. Code and prompts are shared on GitHub.
arxiv-2507-05346:
William Fleshman and Benjamin Van Durme present LAG, a 2025 method for tapping libraries of small expert adapters, called LoRA modules, that fine-tune a language model for narrow jobs. As such experts multiply, picking and blending the right ones per task becomes the problem. LAG needs no extra training and no access to the experts' data. It filters and fetches adapters during generation, choosing them token by token and layer by layer.

On knowledge-heavy tasks, LAG beat rival data-free methods. Where extra data does exist, it also paired well with retrieval-augmented generation, the standard trick of fetching documents at answer time. The authors present LAG as a practical way to reuse a growing shelf of expert modules instead of training one giant model per job.
arxiv-2507-06846:
Franco Dassi, Andres Rubiano, and Ivan Velasquez develop error estimators for a numerical method applied to the vibration of thin plates. Their paper came out in 2025. Engineers simulate plate vibration for structures from bridges to aircraft panels, and they need to know how large the simulation error is.

Their method belongs to the virtual element family, which handles meshes made of many-sided cells in two and three dimensions. The estimators are computed after the simulation, from the leftover imbalance in the equations, and they flag where the mesh needs refinement. The authors prove the estimators are both reliable and efficient, with an argument that does not depend on dimension. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions confirm the method performs as theory predicts.
arxiv-2507-07346:
Boris Bolliet and a large collaboration publish working notes and examples for a cosmology code that computes sky observables at unusual speed. The software extends a standard Boltzmann solver with the halo model and survey statistics. It produces galaxy shear and clustering, microwave background lensing, thermal and kinetic Sunyaev-Zeldovich signals, the cosmic infrared background, cross-correlations, and three-point functions. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the notes walk through calculations in varying detail and rigor. Implementations exist in three languages, including a differentiable version for gradient-based pipelines.

Speed is the headline: emulators plus efficient integration return most outputs in under half a second. Core spectra take about a millisecond. That pace enables fast parameter inference for current and upcoming surveys. The authors stress the notes are a living showcase, not a finished manual.
arxiv-2507-08246:
Hashimoto, Liu, Dong, Liu, and Muto wrote in twenty twenty-five about dust grain size around a very young star. Grain size controls how planets can start forming in disks of gas and dust. Even infant stars show rings and gaps that hint at early planet building. The team observed the young star WL 17 with a large radio array. They covered seven frequency bands, from centimeter to millimeter waves.

The dust ring was detected at nearly every band, though its fine structure stayed unresolved. By matching the observed energy pattern to models, they estimated the largest grains. Some inner structures held grains up to about four millimeters across. The authors also weigh the ring's stability against collapse. They estimate what core mass pebble growth could build there.
arxiv-2507-08646:
Melvyn Nathanson, writing alone, settles a pattern spotted in computer experiments about adding sets of numbers to themselves, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Take a set of four whole numbers and add it to itself many times; the size of the result can vary. Experiments hinted that the most common sizes are not random: they cluster at values given by differences of tetrahedral numbers, which count balls stacked in a pyramid.

Nathanson proves that these popular sizes always occur. For each such size, he builds an explicit set that reaches it, using a construction based on digit patterns. The paper turns a pattern first seen in raw computation into a proved result with concrete examples.
arxiv-2507-08846:
Serdar Metin looks again at Dominant Resource Fairness, the widely used scheme to share many resource types fairly in clouds and data centers. Fair shares were long studied for one resource type. Dominant Resource Fairness spread max-min fairness to mixed demands across several resources. It has prized traits such as sharing incentive, envy-freeness, Pareto efficiency, and strategy-proofness.

Metin studies the structure of the first method with care. He proposes a new form, Precomputed Dominant Resource Fairness, named for its main work rule. The new method comes close to the first method's shares in fewer steps. Faster shares matter where schedulers must split compute power, memory, and other resources among many users all the time. The paper refines a core cloud method in theory.
arxiv-2507-08946:
Yves Brihaye and Betti Hartmann study frozen states of charged boson stars in a 2025 arXiv paper. These star-like objects are smooth solutions of a charged scalar field tied to gravity. They mimic a known solution with a de Sitter core, a black hole outside, and a thin shell between.

The shell replaces the event horizon in their construction. The authors show plain electrodynamics suffices to find these states, but the scalar field must interact with itself. Adding a modified gravity term removes that need. The states carry two light rings, one stable inside the shell and one unstable outside.
arxiv-2507-10446:
Sudarshan Babu explores how neural networks can carry useful prior knowledge into brand-new tasks when data is scarce. The work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Giant pretrained models transfer beautifully, but fields like computational chemistry and medical imaging cannot feed such giants.

Neural memory designs learn from shifting data streams with only a few samples. Hypernetworks, which generate other networks' weights, then prove to learn more reusable priors under a standard meta-learning scheme. The approach speeds text-to-3D scene generation from a handful of examples. It also segments novel 3D scenes by borrowing priors from scenes seen earlier. Finally, a molecular generation method is repurposed as pretraining, improving molecule property prediction. Small-data learning is the thread throughout.
arxiv-2507-11446:
Jona Dirks and Alexandre Vigny proved hardness results in twenty twenty-five for reconfiguring dominating sets on sparse graphs. A dominating set touches every vertex; reconfiguration asks whether one such set can be morphed into another by sliding tokens along edges, staying dominating at every step. The jumping variant of the problem is tractable on sparse graph classes, raising hopes for sliding too.

Those hopes fail. Even with parameters that make related problems fixed-parameter tractable — solution size, pathwidth, and the length of the reconfiguration — sliding domination is W-two-hard. On graphs of modest treewidth it stays hard without the length parameter. For directed graphs on acyclic digraphs the problem is NP-hard at small treewidth and hard in depth-three cases as well.
arxiv-2507-11646:
Langer, Löscher, Steinbach, and Yang develop a state-based method for boundary control of the Laplace equation, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The control lives on the boundary in its natural fractional Sobolev space. Cost is measured in that same norm, doubling as regularization. Finite element error estimates guide method design.

An optimal balance links mesh size to the regularization parameter. That relation proves crucial for building efficient solvers. Box constraints on control and state are also treated. Numerical examples confirm the theory, including a constrained case. The work sharpens theory and practice for boundary control problems.
arxiv-2507-12046:
Sarah White and eight co-authors give a first look at quasars found in the MIGHTEE radio survey of two sky fields. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The sample holds one hundred four bright quasars with firm spectra and full near-infrared data. Their sky spots span a wide range of redshifts, from near to far.

Deep radio reads found that just five percent of the group count as radio-loud. The team then asked how much of each quasar's radio glow comes from its black hole versus new stars. The split hinged a lot on which star-rate gauge was used. Once redshift was weighed in, more sources looked like star bursts, and that share rose with redshift.
arxiv-2507-13046:
Llibert Aresté Saló and colleagues report the first full merger simulations of unequal black hole pairs in an alternative gravity theory. Scalar-Gauss-Bonnet gravity adds a scalar field to Einstein's picture. Simulating its full nonlinear dynamics only recently became possible. Unequal pairs, with mass ratios of two or three to one, kept breaking before merger.

The team follows both ratios through merger and inspects what the waveforms claim. The key worry is dephasing, the drift from Einstein's prediction, which fakes can imitate. Weak couplings matched the expected post-Newtonian dephasing. Stronger couplings instead picked up false deviations from wobbles in the starting data. The authors pinpoint which setup choices corrupt the signal. Their lesson: better initial data methods are the bottleneck for trustworthy beyond-Einstein waveforms.
arxiv-2507-13246:
Matthew Walker and Keith T. Butler wrote a research paper in 2025 about the hidden climate cost of searching for new solar cell materials. Computer screening is now a common way to hunt for such materials. Most searches use a heavy physics method to estimate how well a material might turn sunlight into power. Machine learning models can stand in for that method and use far less energy.

The authors rerun a standard search and swap in learning models step by step. They track the carbon cost of each mix of the two methods. Some mixed plans match the old accuracy while cutting emissions a lot. They also find that guessing a single score, such as top efficiency, works better than guessing a full spectrum first. The study gives labs a clear way to weigh speed, accuracy, and climate cost.
arxiv-2507-13446:
Lina D'Aoust, Ben Coull-Neveu, Eve Lee, and Nicolas Cowan test if the air of hot Jupiters can tell us how these huge, close-in worlds were born. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

How hot Jupiters reached their tight orbits is still not settled. Shifting them in from far out fits some facts, but clashes with what we see in kin worlds. The team turns to air traits that later dirt, added after birth, would leave. They test three such paths in models. Just one, growth by small stones in a metal-rich disc, leaves a sign we could see. A planned space scope will give the even set of air data to test it.
arxiv-2507-13546:
Dmitrii Mikhailov and co-authors present a faster attention method for video generation in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Transformer models make strong videos, but full attention grows quadratically, a heavy cost for high-resolution, long clips. Their method, NABLA, works at the block level and adapts to where attention is actually needed.

Neighborhood blocks are kept or skipped by a sparsity-driven threshold that adjusts as it goes. The method needs no custom low-level code and plugs into a standard PyTorch operator. Tests showed training and generation up to two point seven times faster than the baseline. Quality scores and human ratings barely moved, the authors report.
arxiv-2507-14646:
Junke Zhang and Yiqian Wang study flickering sync in coupled chaotic maps in a 2025 math paper. Coupled map lattices model systems spread across space, from fluids to power grids. Most theory assumes weak coupling between sites. The authors tackle the strong-coupling case for two linked sites running the same piecewise linear expanding map.

Their geometric counting method yields an exact condition for when the system holds a single steady statistical pattern. The same condition decides whether orbits drift in and out of sync forever, a behavior called intermittent synchronization. Strong coupling is where real systems live, so exact tests there carry weight beyond this two-site case.
arxiv-2507-15046:
Fayçal Djebari and three co-authors forecast oil price swings with a network model fed by carefully built weights, in a paper published in 2025. Volatility forecasts in large markets are hard to compute. Their base framework spreads swings across a network of linked prices. Most such networks set links by crude distance rules. Theirs sets links from joint volatility fits, a richer source of information.

In rolling tests on OPEC crude oil prices, the new weights won on statistical grounds. The framework matched the accuracy of a heavy standard model. It did so at a tiny fraction of the computing cost, smaller by tens of thousands of times. Its spread terms stay plain to read, which helps sense checks. The authors present it for risk work in linked markets, where speed and clarity both count.
arxiv-2507-16446:
Martin Guillot and nine co-authors build a measuring tool for a subtle property of light in patterned chips, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Many systems carry a two-part internal state that can be pictured as a point on a sphere. Light polarization is the classic case, but the same math fits which sublattice of a pattern a wave sits on.

Their tool reads that sublattice state in arrays of coupled light cavities arranged like graphene. By shining light with controlled phase shifts on each sublattice and recording the glow, they rebuild each wave mode's size and phase across the whole pattern. Precision beat the modes' own line width. The method unlocks the full energy map of the system and extends to richer patterns.
arxiv-2507-16746:
Ang Li and co-authors release a dataset that teaches AI models to think with pictures interleaved, in a 2025 paper. People sketch diagrams mid-argument when solving hard problems. Models that reason only in text miss that tool, and training them to draw their reasoning has been blocked by missing data.

Their collection holds over one hundred eighty-two thousand worked examples where text and images alternate in coherent chains. Tasks span geometry and physics problems, visual search and jigsaw puzzles, three-dimensional inference and robot planning, plus chess and logic games. Fine-tuning two open models on the data lifted test accuracy by about twelve points, with gains up to thirteen points on standard benchmarks. The resource aims to make visual chain-of-thought a trainable skill rather than a party trick.
arxiv-2507-18546:
Urchade Zaratiana and co-authors present GLiNER2, an information extraction system that runs on plain CPUs. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with pulling facts from text: named entities, text classes, and nested structured records. Past tools needed one model per task, or a costly large language model.

GLiNER2 unifies all three tasks in one compact model, built on a pretrained transformer encoder. A schema-based interface lets users declare what to extract in a simple form, and tasks can be composed. Tests show it rivals bigger options on extraction and classification while being far easier to deploy. It is released as an open-source package.
arxiv-2507-20646:
Castillo and Gordillo-Núñez show that a claimed new test for classical orthogonal polynomials was already covered by older general theorems. Their note appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Two recent papers proposed judging a polynomial family from its first recurrence coefficients. The note checks those claims against the record.

The authors show both papers' results follow from two theorems published years earlier. They also supply a symbolic algorithm that automates the check. The program runs in a standard algebra system and works on quadratic lattices. As a test case, they treat a family said to live on a double lattice. It turns out to be a classical family on a plain linear lattice after all. Its properties then drop out of the older theorem. The note restores priority and simplifies the theory.
arxiv-2507-20846:
Lorenzo Sala and Stefano Vitale derived exact Bayesian formulas for low-rate spectral estimation in a 2025 paper. Below one hertz, tests like the LISA gravity-based wave observatory and its Pathfinder precursor cannot average many free-standing spectra. Gaussian approximations for noise estimates break down precisely where precision matters most. Their method works straight with periodograms and Wishart stats for multivariate Gaussian time series. It yields closed-form posterior distributions at each rate for single power spectra, pairwise and multiple coherence, and the full cross-spectral matrix.

For noise projection, they model one channel as filtered versions of others plus background. Posteriors for the filter responses and background spectrum are also closed form. Applied to LISA Pathfinder data, the method decorrelated heat level-induced disturbances effectively. Exact stats replace hopeful approximations in precision gravity-based tests.
arxiv-2507-21446:
Dibyendu Samanta and Sudeep Kumar Ghosh show that a chain of magnetic atoms on a special magnet can act as a one-way valve for supercurrent, with no outside field. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such valves most often need a field to break a time rule, which blocks scale and ease of build. The chain here sits on a magnet whose spin pattern has a rare form. The team solves the pair state in a self-set way. They find a state where pairs carry a set drift, which hosts prized end modes that can be tuned. The drift is set by a current fed in from outside, a knob labs can turn. The same state bears a strong valve effect.
arxiv-2507-21546:
Tianxiang Zhan and a large team show long-range free-space quantum key distribution with continuous variables. The method lets far-off users share secret keys with strong safety. It also fits with old-style light-based networks. In the past, tests with this method worked only indoors or over short outdoor runs.

The team beat extra noise from the air, even in daylight. They did so with no extra wavelength change and no extra filtering. Their steps include state control that does not rest on channel swings. They also use sharp signal capture and fine pointing and tracking. They sent safe keys over a 7-kilometer inland link and a 9.6-kilometer sea link. Both spans beat the depth of the air layer.
arxiv-2507-21846:
Chenyuan Zhang and four co-authors teach observers to actively hunt for another agent's goal in a 2025 paper. Guessing hidden goals from behavior is central to teamwork and safety in shared spaces. Most older methods watch passively and wait for clues to accumulate.

Their probabilistic framework lets the observer plan information-gathering moves. A joint belief update tracks what each new observation implies. A tree search planner picks moves that shrink uncertainty fastest, without hand-built domain knowledge. Tests in a grid world show the active method beating passive guessing clearly. It also matches a strong greedy baseline that was tuned to the domain. The result points toward assistants that ask and probe rather than merely watch.
arxiv-2507-22446:
Yunrui Yu and colleagues propose a new activation function for neural networks in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Activation functions shape how each unit in a network responds. They affect both accuracy on new data and resistance to attacks. Crafted inputs can fool networks in ways that matter for safety. The authors aim to build a function that improves both traits at once.

Their design, RCR-AF, blends traits of two known functions. It keeps smooth gradients and some negative signal, like GELU, and steady growth, like ReLU. Built-in clipping, set by two dials, controls sparsity and model size. Theory based on Rademacher complexity shows how these dials govern generalization. The paper offers network builders a new knob for robust design.
arxiv-2507-22646:
Nathan Hayford wrote this work in two thousand twenty-five. It looks at a special solution of the (3,4) string equation. That equation comes up in the multicritical quartic two-matrix model. Hayford asks how the solution acts in one set range of parameter values.

In that range, he shows that its tau-function has an asymptotic expansion. The expansion is topological, and it shows the solution does exist, at least in that form. The solution he finds is the one with a set choice of Stokes data. Along set curves in the same space, the tau-function becomes the tau-function for a tritronquée solution of Painlevé I. That solution comes up in the critical quartic one-matrix model. The shift points to a renormalization group flow between these critical points. It also backs a conjecture made in nineteen ninety.
arxiv-2507-22846:
Yi-Ting Lee, Bibek Pokharel, Jeffrey Cohn, André Schleife, and Arnab Banerjee run spin transport tests on a quantum device. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Spin transport matters for spin-based electronics and for spin qubits. Past quantum runs used a spin-spin measure, but a spin-current measure gives more direct facts and costs many more gates.

They use a superconducting transmon device and a direct measure plan that leans on mid-circuit checks. That route dodges the cost of the classic test trick. On a chain model with many sites, they cover three regimes of spread. They recover the known power-law in the middle regime and the loss of steady flow in the slow one.
arxiv-2507-22946:
Yixuan Mi, Yiduo Yu, and Yiyi Zhao present a course advising system, in a 2025 preprint, that gives undergraduates advice shaped by their own records. Standard advising tools list courses but ignore the student's history. SmartCourse, built for computer science majors, reads the transcript and the degree plan together. A locally run language model turns that context into personal suggestions. The system also handles accounts, enrollment, grades, and four-year plans, through both a command line and a web screen.

The team scored the advice on twenty-five sample questions. They invented measures for plan fit, personal fit, and recall. With full context, the suggestions were far more relevant than with context stripped out. Retakes and missing requirements were spotted when the record was visible. The authors conclude that transcript-aware advising is not a luxury but the core of useful guidance. Privacy stays local since the model runs on site.
arxiv-2508-00046:
Ruo Yu Tao and co-authors build a test suite for learning agents that see only part of their world, in work from two thousand twenty-five. Agents may miss a foe's intent, a blocked view, or a hidden place. Most past tests hid the world in only one or two simple ways.

The suite spans many kinds of hidden state, from mapping and sight control to games. Each task is built so memory truly matters, not luck or raw speed. The open code base runs fast on graphics chips and ships with tuned settings. That gives researchers a fair way to compare memory methods.
arxiv-2508-01046:
Sander Kammeraat and seven co-authors settle a debate about how healing skin grows finger-like protrusions. Epithelial sheets seal wounds by migrating collectively, and fingers often lead the advance. Specialized leader cells, chemical signals, and cell division were all candidate explanations.

Combining live imaging, agent-based simulation, and continuum theory, the team shows correlated active motion of ordinary cells is enough by itself. Motion that lines up between neighbors naturally buckles the edge into fingers. Leader cells, signaling, and proliferation tune the pattern but never trigger it. The authors frame wound closure fingers as a generic outcome of dense active matter physics, not a bespoke biological program.
arxiv-2508-01446:
Gabriel Arenas-Henriquez, Luca Ciambelli, Felipe Diaz, Weizhen Jia, and David Rivera-Betancour study gravitational radiation through the fluid-gravity correspondence. They probe anti-de Sitter spacetimes with radiative traits. They use null gauges that allow a flat limit. The radiative content of the bulk is caught by values at the edge. Those values are grouped into a radiative vector, read as fluid values in the dual theory.

For algebraically special solutions, they link bulk radiation to dissipative fixes in the boundary stress tensor. That link ties radiation straight to entropy production in the boundary fluid. For the flat limit, they build a Carrollian form of it. They also bring in celestial observables such as energy detectors. Bulk radiation sources the Carrollian viscous stress tensor and heat current, which encode the Bondi news. Clear cases in the paper include Robinson-Trautman spacetimes and black holes that speed up.
arxiv-2508-01746:
Shiyang Duan and colleagues built HypoAgents in 2025, a team of cooperating software agents that proposes and improves scientific hypotheses. With knowledge growing exponentially, a good hypothesis must be novel, feasible, and valuable at once, and language model generators typically score none of those systematically or learn from feedback. The authors imitate the working loop of a human scientist instead.

The framework runs three stages in a closed loop: generating hypotheses, validating them against evidence, and refining them. Diversity sampling produces a broad first set, scored by a composite of novelty, relevance, and feasibility to set prior beliefs. A retrieval step then gathers literature evidence, and Bayes' rule updates each hypothesis's standing. The most uncertain hypotheses, flagged by an entropy measure, receive focused refinement, and the loop repeats, coupling Bayesian bookkeeping with information-driven search.
arxiv-2508-02446:
Yichao Zhang and co-authors present TeraNoC, a chip wiring scheme that lets a thousand processor cores share one fast memory without choking, in a 2025 paper. Two classic layouts fail at this scale: grids keep wires short but force long trips across the chip, while crossbars answer fast but grow in cost with every added port.

TeraNoC mixes the two, running several 32-bit channels of grid wiring studded with crossbars. A remapping router spreads traffic evenly across the channels. The team built a cluster of 1,024 small cores sharing a memory split into 4,096 banks, in a modern 12-nanometer process. On heavy AI-style kernels the cores stayed busy at high rates, and the wiring took a small slice of total power. The design is open source.
arxiv-2508-03446:
Erico Souza Teixeira, Lucas Barros Fernandes, and Yara Rodrigues Inácio tried quantum neural networks at predicting how tightly proteins bind in a 2025 paper. Binding affinity governs molecular interactions and sits at the heart of drug development and vaccine design, where machine learning already helps estimate it classically. Whether quantum models offer any edge was the open question. The authors built thirty variants of multilayer perceptron style quantum networks: three architectures, each fitted with ten different quantum circuits configuring its quantum layers.

Those quantum models were benchmarked against classical counterparts on the binding prediction task. The study is a feasibility exploration, mapping how architecture and circuit choices move performance rather than claiming quantum advantage. Systematic comparisons like this are how a young field learns which of its ideas deserve the scarce quantum hardware time available.
arxiv-2508-03746:
Xinhui Duan and Lu Lu solve a spectral extremal problem about powers of cycles. Their twenty twenty-five mathematics paper works with graphs that avoid a fixed pattern. A cycle power joins vertices that sit close along the cycle. Two measures matter here: the most edges possible, and the largest spectral radius.

The authors pin down the single best graph for large vertex counts. That graph wins on both measures at once. Earlier work often handled edge counts and spectra separately. Getting one unique winner for both sharpens the picture. Graph theorists can use the result as a benchmark for related forbidden pattern problems.
arxiv-2508-05546:
Rasman Swargo, Engin Arslan, and Md Arifuzzaman present a modular system for fast data transfer in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Big science applications must move huge data sets between distant sites. Classic transfer tools often waste resources or stall because their settings are fixed.

Their system, AutoMDT, uses a learning agent to tune read, network, and write parallelism at the same time. A light simulator lets the agent train offline in under an hour, avoiding slow live training. The modular design separates input-output from network work, so the agent can adapt to changing conditions. On testbeds it cut transfer times by up to sixty-eight percent versus leading tools.
arxiv-2508-07846:
A large T2K team presents a new time calibration method for multi-channel particle detectors, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Kit like that in the T2K neutrino experiment reads out through many channels. Each channel has its own electronics. Small gaps in timing from one channel to the next cap how sharp the time readings can be.

The new method works step by step and rests on Markov chain ideas. It fixes tiny gaps in sync across channels, and it does so with little waste. The team shows it at work on two T2K detectors, SuperFGD and the time-of-flight system. Good timing counts for a lot here. Such experiments rebuild events from the exact times at which hits arrive. A method that squeezes out offsets helps the whole detector do its best work. Staff from many sites took part in the work.
arxiv-2508-08246:
Zhiyang He, Quynh Nguyen, and Christopher Pattison introduce composable fault-tolerance, a framework for proving that quantum computers can work reliably despite noisy parts, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Threshold proofs are long, formulaic, and hard to assemble from pieces published separately.

The framework separates the probabilistic analysis of noise from the combinatorial analysis of circuit correctness. Gadgets analyzed once can then be composed rigorously into full threshold proofs. The authors supply a library of standard gadgets, including memory and logic for quantum low-density parity check codes and distillation. Sample applications give a surface code threshold proof and re-derive Gottesman's constant-overhead scheme.
arxiv-2508-08646:
Naama Kashani, Mira Cohen, and Uri Shaham build a feature picker that chooses patient data step by step under a budget, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Health records are rich but patchy, and each extra test costs money and time. Their frame picks the next most useful feature for each patient, not one list for all.

Costs and price swings per feature enter the choice, fitting real screening work. The method handles sparse, mixed-type records and scales to large clinics. It aims to raise diagnostic confidence while sparing resources. The authors pitch it as decision support for doctors facing long test menus.
arxiv-2508-08946: Hasami and Mansoury present a study from twenty twenty-five on fairer explanations for product suggestions. Their fix adds a step before a what-if explanation is built: a large language model filters out history items that do not fit the user's character. Tests on two public datasets show the filtered method yields what-if cases that match each user's taste in popularity better than the base method alone.
arxiv-2508-09946:
Amin Nassiri-Rad, Haidar Sheikhahmadi, and Hassan Firouzjahi extended a tool for studying the early universe in 2025. During inflation, the universe expanded at a furious pace, and random quantum noise stretched into the seeds of galaxies. A stochastic method tracks that noise with random equations to compute cosmic correlations beyond simple approximations, but it needs the noise strength as a starting input, known exactly only for non-interacting fields.

Real fields interact, and the noise inherits those interactions. The authors rewrite the governing random and diffusion equations with quantum corrections included. In a three-stage inflation example used to form primordial black holes, they compute the correction from a one-loop change in the power spectrum. Noise strength shifts by a factor tied to that fractional change.
arxiv-2508-10446:
Halima El Badaoui and colleagues tackle a paperwork problem in safety analysis: good methods find more hazards than teams can act on. Systems Theoretic Process Analysis of a complex vehicle can generate hundreds of unsafe control actions. Prioritizing them objectively, and explaining the ranking, is where projects stall.

Their framework scores each action by severity, by the influence of the controller issuing it, and by expert rankings of criticality. A Monte Carlo simulation then washes out some subjectivity from those combined inputs. Results are communicated through a prioritization matrix whose scaling adapts dynamically. The case study applies everything to electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft operations, a fast-moving development program.
arxiv-2508-11346:
Puja Das and co-authors study a light particle predicted by a five-dimensional version of the Standard Model, in a physics paper from 2025. In that model, all known particles sit on a wall inside an extra dimension. Because the wall breaks the symmetry of sliding along that dimension, a Nambu-Goldstone boson appears.

The particle couples to ordinary fermions and to their heavier copies from the extra dimension. The team bounds it from three sides: cooling of exploding stars, the chemistry of the early universe, and collider searches. Collider data gave the strongest limits, setting a firm floor on the heavy copies' masses. The authors also sketch how future lepton colliders could produce those copies and tell them apart from similar predicted particles.
arxiv-2508-12746:
Muhammad Ammad, Paul Schwarzbach, Michael Schultz, and Oliver Michler locate tags inside an aircraft cabin with a residual neural network fed by likelihood maps. Their paper from twenty twenty-five serves indoor positioning, where satellite navigation cannot reach. Simulated cabin measurements supply ranges and angles between a tag and fixed anchors. Residuals against a grid turn those readings into maps where each cell scores its chance of holding the tag.

The network trains on the maps paired with true positions. Hyperparameter tuning squeezes the setup before final training. The payoff is centimeter-level localization inside the cabin mock-up. Airlines and cabin system makers care because crew, equipment, and passenger services all ride on knowing where things are indoors.
arxiv-2508-15446:
Harbir Antil and Anna Lentz gave an algorithm for nonconvex optimization with a sparsity penalty in two thousand twenty-five. The penalty uses an Lp norm with p between zero and one, which pushes many variables to zero. That term is both nonconvex and nonsmooth, which makes the problem hard.

Their method smooths the penalty, then builds a convex upper bound for the smoothed form. Descent steps follow a special point found by a line search along a proximal path, inside a trust-region scheme. They prove convergence properties for the smoothed method. Numerical examples show how it performs, and they discuss fast solvers for the subproblems that arise at each step.
arxiv-2508-16446:
Xuan Cao and Kyoungjae Lee give fast Bayesian tools for wide multi outcome regression in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such models guess many outcomes at once from many inputs, and must also learn how the errors link. Bayesian routes give honest doubt bands but often crawl, or cut corners that break the math.

The team gives two routes. The exact one pairs a spike and slab prior on the weights with a graph based prior on the error links, at a cost near the best known shortcut. The fast one ignores the links while fitting weights, then reads the error graph off the leftovers. They prove both routes pick the right terms in the long run. Tests on fake and real data show the pair works in practice.
arxiv-2508-17246:
Takuma Sumi and Georgi S Medvedev published a research paper in 2025 on a math method for reading signals from very large networks, applied to brain-like circuits. Classic tools treat a network as fixed, but real networks vary and grow. Their method uses a smooth limit object, called a graphon, that stands in for a whole family of networks at once.

They tackled a hard reverse task: guess the input a network got from the output it gave. In spiking network models and in real calcium recordings from tissue, their projections gave compact codes for the input. Those codes sorted inputs better than two standard methods. They also stayed steady when network size or noise changed.
arxiv-2508-18046:
Ekaterina Kononov and Mary Knapp design a space array to image the whole radio sky below ten megahertz. Their 2025 paper targets a band Earth's air blocks completely. Science there spans the cosmic dark ages and planet auroras. Only a space array can listen, but classic designs need thousands of antennas.

Vector sensors pack three dipoles and three loops into one unit. Each unit senses direction and polarization on its own. Fewer, smarter units could shrink the array and loosen distance demands. The team shows the sensors suit interferometry for all-sky maps. Interference resilience adds a further edge. The concept opens a quiet band that ground radio has never seen.
arxiv-2508-18546:
Akbar and Kais move a method for telling mirror image molecules apart onto gate based quantum computers in twenty twenty-five. Mirror twins of a molecule can act very differently in the body, so sorting them matters. Classic sorting schemes use smooth, analog control pulses. Digital quantum machines take only step by step gate commands, which clashes with that style.

The pair sliced the smooth pulses into small steps a gate machine can run. They simulated the plan on a small chiral molecule. They then ran it for real on IBM quantum hardware. The runs worked, they report. The result lays ground work for handling molecular handedness on common quantum machines.
arxiv-2508-21746:
Jiachen An, Bing Sun, and Zhoujian Cao ask, in twenty twenty-five, whether gravitational wave data can bound how fast the gravitational constant changes. Theory says a varying constant first corrects wave amplitude, then, at next order, phase. Phase matters more, since detectors match signals by phase. The team used data from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detectors to constrain the variation. Their findings are sobering: distances or signal strengths must grow by large factors before phase corrections can pin the variation down.

For events with light counterparts, which fix the source distance, phase corrections can almost always be neglected for this purpose, they find. The paper sets expectations for future detector eras.
arxiv-2509-00846:
Woon Yee Ng, with three co-authors, proposes Causal SHAP for explaining model predictions. SHAP is a widely used method that scores each feature. It tells how much each feature counts for a prediction. But it cannot separate cause from mere correlation. It can thus give wrong credit when features move together.

Causal SHAP weaves causal links into the scores it gives. It keeps many good traits of the original SHAP. The method combines the Peter-Clark algorithm, which finds causal graphs. It also uses the IDA algorithm to measure causal strength. Tests use both synthetic and real-world data. Scores fall for features that are merely linked to the target. The gain is clearest in high-stakes fields such as healthcare.
arxiv-2509-01346:
Ozan Hur studies a robust finance question: what is the worst-case chance that an asset Y beats a benchmark X, when Y's distribution is only known to lie near the benchmark's? Nearness is measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence, a standard gauge of how far one probability law sits from another. The problem takes a max-min form over ways of coupling the two outcomes.

Hur shows that problem has a tractable dual, reached through optimal transport, and its solution tilts the benchmark law exponentially. The answer forms a one-parameter family, with the parameter acting as a budget for the allowed information shift. As it grows, probability mass moves steadily from lower to higher outcomes. Because the method needs only the baseline distribution, Hur offers it as a tool for wide scenario generation and robust performance testing.
arxiv-2509-01446:
Ireland's population will shift over the coming decades, and planners need local detail, not just national totals. Sean Caulfield Curley, Karl Mason, and Patrick Mannion present a dynamic microsimulation model for Ireland running from 2022 to 2057. The model follows individuals through four main events: births, deaths, internal migration, and international migration.

Each simulated person carries seven traits, including age, sex, marital status, citizenship, education, and economic status. Those traits change over time by chance, using transition rates drawn from Irish data. People are placed at the fine Electoral Division level, allowing close local analysis. Curley and the team offer the model as a tool for academic study and for testing how demographic change and policy choices might play out across Ireland's regions.
arxiv-2509-01546:
Testing solid-state sensors for particle physics needs a way to excite charge at a precise point inside the material. Enoch Ejopu, with nine co-authors, commissions a femtosecond laser system whose wavelength can be tuned across a very wide range, from ultraviolet to deep infrared. Two-photon absorption in the sensor gives three-dimensional resolution for creating electron-hole pairs at a chosen spot.

The system pairs a commercial laser with an optical amplifier unit that tunes the output. Beam measurements set the focused spot's size and its Rayleigh length, the span over which the beam stays tight. First tests on silicon and diamond samples show the expected quadratic rise of signal with pulse energy, and models explain extra signal from reflections. The silicon results match a one-dimensional model well, marking the facility ready for detector work.
arxiv-2509-01646: Mohammad Adarbeh and Mohammad Saleh introduce a new notion in module theory. It is uniform S-projectivity relative to a module, or u-S-projectivity for short. A module P has this trait when maps out of it respect a class of surjections tied to a set S. The dual notion, relative u-S-injectivity, is defined alongside it. The pair discusses traits of both notions. They give characterizations of u-S-semisimple modules through them. Quasi forms of both notions are also introduced and studied.
arxiv-2509-01846:
Takashi Onaka, Itsuki Sakon, Takashi Shimonishi, and Mitsuhiko Honda hunt for missing oxygen hidden in large ice grains between the stars. At least a quarter of oxygen in thin space clouds sits in no known form. Ice marks in near infrared light hint that a fifth of the missing share lies in big water ice grains. But those marks weaken and tangle for the largest grains, so they cannot settle the count.

Far infrared ice marks at two longer wavelengths can pin down crystal ice up to larger sizes. Reading them over a bright background needs a sensitive tool like the PRIMA spectrograph. Broad marks need only modest sharpness but very accurate calibration. Solving the oxygen gap matters for cloud chemistry and star birth studies.
arxiv-2509-01946:
Aarsh Shah, Cleyton Magalhaes, Kiev Gama, and Ronnie de Souza Santos present Tether, a desktop aid for software engineers with ADHD. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder can hinder focus, task starts, and self regulation at work. Few tools target those hurdles inside coding workflows, despite growing awareness of neurodiversity in the field. Tether uses a large language model to give adaptive, context aware support.

The app tracks system activity locally to prompt engagement at the right moments. Its chatbot draws on ADHD specific resources through retrieval, so replies stay relevant. Games style rewards add motivation for steady work. Early self use showed sharper context accuracy after prompt and retrieval tuning. User trials with the target group remain future work.
arxiv-2509-02046:
Kaiyue Wen, David Hall, Tengyu Ma, and Percy Liang benchmark pretraining optimizers fairly and find smaller speedups than often claimed. Optimizers steer model training by updating weights from gradients. AdamW has long dominated language model pretraining despite rivals claiming large speed gains. The team blames unequal tuning and narrow evaluation setups for the confusion.

Ten optimizers are tested across four model scales and varied data to model ratios with rigorous tuning. Rankings can flip mid training, so only end of training scores count. Real speedups shrink with scale, falling to a modest edge at the largest size tested. The fastest methods all use matrix preconditioners rather than per entry scaling. Careful methodology, the authors argue, is the real bottleneck.
arxiv-2509-02546:
Nathan R. Sandford and sixteen co-authors, with the S5 Collaboration, present a 2025 astronomy paper on Boötes I, an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way. New survey spectra are merged with about fifteen years of archived data.

The combined sample is the largest of its kind for such a galaxy, with well over a hundred confirmed members reaching far from the centre. It includes new members, binary candidates, pulsating stars, and many iron abundance measures. Correcting for perspective rotation for the first time in this setting reveals a velocity gradient aligned with the galaxy's orbit, hinting at tidal stretching. Metal content falls with radius. A Jeans model of the motions mildly favours a cusped dark matter profile, and chemical modelling suggests rapid, wasteful star formation with strong outflows.
arxiv-2509-02646:
Shivam Kumar Mishra, Jackson Levi Said, and B. Mishra present a 2025 cosmology paper working out how small disturbances evolve in a modified gravity theory. The theory is teleparallel gravity extended with the Gauss-Bonnet invariant, a curvature quantity with deep geometric roots.

Background expansion alone cannot judge such models; perturbations test their stability and health. The authors take a gauge invariant approach, so results do not depend on coordinate choices, then illustrate popular gauge options. They derive the equations of motion for every perturbative mode. New contributions from the Gauss-Bonnet coupling are interpreted physically, mode by mode. The work supplies a needed check for whether these cosmologies can match structure formation data without hidden instabilities.
arxiv-2509-02746:
Saarang Panchavati, Corey Arnold, and William Speier present a 2025 biomedical AI paper exploring foundation models for EEG, the brain wave recordings used to diagnose epilepsy and other disorders. EEG data is noisy, high-dimensional, and strongly nonlinear, which limits older automated methods.

Their model uses a Mamba architecture, a selective state space design built for long sequences. Training first teaches the model to reconstruct masked EEG in a self-supervised way, then tunes it for seizure detection on a large set of seizure and non-seizure recordings. Ranking accuracy on test data held out from training was solid but not spectacular. The authors frame the work as a step toward large, clinically usable EEG foundation models, rather than a finished diagnostic tool, with scale and generality as the main goals.
arxiv-2509-02846:
Siddharth Mansingh and twelve co-authors wrote a 2025 scientific computing paper. It brings test-time thinking to foundation models for partial differential equations. Those equations sit behind most physics simulation. Such models falter on long rollouts and unfamiliar cases. They also demand huge training sets.

Inspired by language model reasoning tricks, the authors spend extra computation at inference time instead. Reward models grade candidate predictions for spatio-temporal consistency. They guide a stochastic base model toward better trajectories. Tests use compressible Euler simulations from the PDEGym benchmark. Test-time computing improved predictions over standard autoregressive rollout. It did so with smaller models and fewer training samples. The authors frame it as a first step toward fuller reasoning algorithms for physics workflows.
arxiv-2509-03046:
Divyansh Agrawal, Venkateswaran P. Krishnan, and Vladimir A. Sharafutdinov worked in 2025 on describing which outputs a ray transform can produce. The transform adds up a tensor field, a grid of directional quantities, along every straight line. Knowing its range, the set of reachable outputs, is key to undoing it in imaging problems.

Earlier work settled the question in three or more dimensions on weighted smoothness spaces. The two-dimensional case behaves very differently, and the authors handle it in higher order versions of those spaces. Their main tool is a formula named after Reshetnyak that equates the sizes of a field and its transform. They treat fields with no net source, called solenoidal. The result sharpens inverse problem theory for planar tensor data.
arxiv-2509-03446:
Niteesh Midlagajni and Constantin A. Rothkopf taught a graph neural network in 2025 to simulate liquids being manipulated by moving rigid bodies. Faithful fluid simulation matters for design, graphics, and robotics, yet learned models usually cover only static free-fall scenes or simple primitive objects. Real tasks involve containers and tools that move and collide with the liquid.

In their framework, particles become graph nodes and collisions with objects are handled through surface representations accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy, a tree that speeds up contact checks. Training covered single-object manipulation tasks only. The model still generalized to new objects and new manipulation tasks, and it also worked as a plain free-fall simulator. Its learned dynamics could then drive control through gradient-based optimization.
arxiv-2509-03646:
How reinforcement learning builds reasoning in large language models, layer by layer, is the question in a 2025 research paper by Haozhe Wang and five co-authors. Reinforcement learning clearly improves complex reasoning, but the mechanism behind the gains stayed unclear. Odd phenomena reported by others, like sudden aha moments and shifting entropy, are treated here as clues to one underlying pattern.

Their analysis finds an emergent hierarchy resembling human cognition, where high-level strategy sits above low-level procedure. Early training is bottlenecked by procedural correctness, so models first sharpen basic execution skills. Later the bottleneck moves upward, and gains come from exploring and mastering strategic planning. Standard algorithms like GRPO push on all tokens equally, diluting the learning signal. Their method, HICRA, concentrates credit on high-impact planning tokens instead. Many experiments show it beats strong baselines by a wide margin.
arxiv-2509-03746:
A 2025 research paper by Anushya Subbiah and five co-authors focuses on giving each product its own single token inside a large language model recommender. Recommendation systems built on language models gain broad world knowledge, but real catalogues hold millions of items. The field's standard view held that item identifiers must be split into several tokens, which slows real-time serving badly.

The authors challenge that practice and treat item IDs as full members of the model instead. Simple changes to training and inference allow one-token representations per item and single-step decoding of a recommendation. On Amazon shopping datasets, recommendation quality improves over existing techniques on recall and ranking measures. Inference also runs many times faster, between five and fourteen times in their tests. The work opens a different route for integrating huge identifier sets into language models, with code released for others to build on.
arxiv-2509-04446:
Kiymet Akdemir and four co-authors present a framework for drawing and then polishing multi-frame stories with image generators in a 2025 research paper. Text-to-image diffusion models paint detailed scenes from words, and story visualization strings those scenes into narratives. Creators need to revise frames afterward, though, without breaking consistency of characters, style, or plot across panels. Existing tools rarely allow both fine and coarse edits while holding a story together.

Their zero-shot framework, Plot'n Polish, needs no task-specific training. It generates consistent story frames and supports disentangled editing, meaning one aspect can change while others stay fixed. Writers and illustrators gain a drafting partner that accepts revision instead of forcing a fresh start.
arxiv-2509-04646:
Health simulations can inform policy, yet their complexity often shuts out the people they should help. Philippe J. Giabbanelli and one co-author address that gap in a 2025 mixed-methods paper on personalised explanations. Stakeholders include clinicians, policymakers, patients, caregivers, and health advocates, each with different needs.

The authors present a step-by-step framework to identify what each group needs from an explanation. The framework then guides large language models in producing tailored summaries of simulation outputs and model design. Their aim is to replace one-size-fits-all summaries with explanations matched to audience and purpose.
arxiv-2509-04746:
The Efimov effect, where three particles show a repeating pattern across scales, appears as a limit cycle in renormalisation group language. Langxuan Chen, lead author with five co-authors, ask whether its mathematical form stays universal across regulators in a 2025 paper. Regulators are tools that tame short-range behaviour in calculations.

Working through two classic three-body equations, they derive a universal functional form for general separable regulators. The form follows from a real Möbius transformation with three parameters. Numerical checks confirm the shape across regulators, although the parameter values depend on the regulator. The result broadens understanding of three-body renormalisation.
arxiv-2509-05046:
The internal quark structure of the spin-1 deuteron includes tensor-polarised distributions that experiments are only beginning to reach. S. Kumano and one co-author calculate one such twist-3 distribution in a 2025 paper. They use relations modelled on classic spin-half results, together with known twist-2 distributions of the same type.

The resulting curve has a shape similar to its twist-2 counterpart and a comparable size. Because the energy scale at a current facility is not far above the hadronic scale, higher-twist effects could be sizable there. The authors argue upcoming experiments at several facilities could measure these curves directly.
arxiv-2509-05146:
Translating text inside a photograph is harder than translating clean documents, because real images have messy backgrounds and varied fonts. Yanzhi Tian, lead author with six co-authors, tackle that practical setting in a 2025 paper on in-image multilingual machine translation. Existing research relies on synthetic data that cannot reflect real conditions.

The team annotate a dataset of real captured one-line text images with complex backgrounds, diverse fonts and positions, and many translation directions. Their end-to-end model processes visual text and background separately, aiming for better translation quality and visual effect. Experiments show gains over other models in their tests, and code and data are public.
arxiv-2509-05446:
Shrinking deep image networks in one pass, without a slow search, is proposed by Iftekhar Haider Chowdhury and three co-authors in a 2025 paper on filter pruning. Large convolutional networks perform well but cost too much memory and computing for many devices.

Their method scores each filter by fusing three importance measures: gradient sensitivity, a first-order Taylor estimate, and how activation patterns shift. Filters whose scores disagree across measures are scaled up in importance ranking as unstable or less critical candidates. In tests cutting half to seventy percent of filters, the method removed most floating point operations while keeping nearly all baseline accuracy at the deepest cut. It needs only one forward and backward pass.
arxiv-2509-05646:
Stable states that follow a slowly changing field can survive energy loss in three-level quantum systems, Emil A. Gazazyan, Gayane G. Grigoryan, and Vanush Paturyan show in a 2025 quantum optics paper. Adiabatic states support gentle transfer methods used in atomic control.

The authors derive the needed stability conditions, both necessary and sufficient, and check them in numbers across setups held at exact two-photon resonance. In every scheme the state's lifetime is set by the dephasing time between levels not linked by an allowed transition. They also show efficient transfer through a middle state at room temperature despite slow relaxation. They match one special state's lifetime to the dark state's under large detuning.
arxiv-2509-05746:
Sharpening a photo should depend on how far away each part of the scene is, Tianhao Guo and three co-authors argue in a 2025 image processing paper. Standard super-resolution assumes one blur model everywhere, while real optics add distance effects like haze, focus falloff, and perspective distortion.

Their variational framework treats reconstruction as a spatially varying inverse problem with distance-dependent blur, giving theory for reconstruction limits by depth. A neural network implements the resulting energy flow with depth-aware convolution kernels and learned smoothness that adapts to local geometry. Spectral rules from atmospheric scattering theory guard far regions against noise blow-up. Across five benchmarks the method led on outdoor driving scenes at two scales.
arxiv-2509-06546:
Movement between regions in a network is rebuilt from basic physics by Hadrien Oliveri and two co-authors in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. Their cases range from infections between countries to toxic proteins between brain areas. Standard network models move quantities between nodes using a graph Laplacian, a rule based on connections alone. That shortcut ignores what happens inside each link.

Taking flow, reaction, and spreading along each link as the true mechanism, the authors derive the network-level transport rule from first principles. The resulting effective graph Laplacian is fully fixed by the small-scale physics inside the edges. They show the operator captures transport correctly and study how it scales when edges grow longer. The work gives network modelers a transport rule with a clear physical basis instead of a fitted guess.
arxiv-2509-06646:
Gravity emerging from a matrix model of string theory is the subject of a 2025 theoretical physics paper by Pei-Ming Ho and two co-authors. Matrix models define string theory without assuming spacetime; spacetime is supposed to arise from the matrices themselves. Fluctuations around that background should then represent both matter and gravity.

The authors focus on the IIB matrix model and ask how coordinate-change symmetry, called diffeomorphism invariance, appears, and how unitarity, the rule that probabilities behave sensibly, is guaranteed. They treat matrices as bilocal fields, objects living on pairs of points, and describe the Lorentz-invariant vacuum and its low-energy excitations in those terms. Conditions for unitarity are rewritten for bilocal fields. In the low-energy limit, they argue, the fields reduce to a finite set of massless local fields plus infinitely many massive ones, all consistent with unitarity.
arxiv-2509-06746:
A honeycomb magnet candidate for exotic quantum states is probed with X-rays by M. M. Ferreira-Carvalho and ten co-authors in a 2025 paper on condensed matter. The compound, a barium cobalt arsenate, is a possible host for Kitaev physics. Its cobalt atoms sit inside oxygen cages whose exact shape shapes the magnetism.

Absorption and magnetic circular dichroism readings at the cobalt edges used a fluorescence method fit for insulating samples. A strong linear dichroic signal showed a marked trigonal twist of the cages. Fitting the spectra with a full-multiplet cluster model showed the key hole density focused in one orbital, and sum rules gave the spin and orbital moments. The twist energy came out larger than the cobalt spin-orbit coupling, showing how local form drives this material's electronic and magnetic conduct.
arxiv-2509-06846:
A fresh map of how stars move in the Milky Way's central bulge is built by Carlos Quezada and nine co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. Bulge motion is complex, mixing several stellar components, and dust plus crowding leave the region near the galactic plane poorly measured. Better maps are needed to test dynamical models.

Radial velocities from the GIBS and APOGEE surveys were combined with published and new MUSE observations, including nine new fields close to the plane. The total came to fifty-seven fields and about twenty-three thousand measured velocities. A custom Python tool extracted spectra from the instrument's data cubes. Statistical sampling corrected for foreground contamination and produced new analytical fits. The updated maps confirm the bulge's cylindrical rotation and reveal a boxier shape in the velocity dispersion pattern, with its central peak preserved.
arxiv-2509-07346:
Itzhak Bars, writing alone in 2025, argues that the Higgs field does far more than give particles their masses. The Higgs boson is famous as a ripple on a universe-wide field whose background value fills all space. Bars claims that near singularities, the points where gravity becomes extreme inside black holes and at the universe's start, the field changes character completely.

In his account, the field there becomes strongly varying and builds new spacetime domains governed by antigravity beyond the singularities. Gravity and antigravity regions join through traversable singularities, making the whole spacetime geodesically complete, with no paths that simply end. Electroweak symmetry is restored at the singularities, he argues. He also claims the picture resolves the black hole information paradox in a manifestly unitary way. Detailed calculations sit in a companion paper, and these remain his claimed results.
arxiv-2509-07446:
Nikhil Yewale and 2 co-authors draw an analogy in 2025 between a standing wave on a pool of liquid and a mechanical oscillator. A standing wave sloshes in place rather than traveling, and its free oscillations are the motions it makes when left alone. The authors show the equations for the liquid surface and for the mechanical model share the same kinds of solutions.

Both systems admit quiet solutions and time-periodic ones with finite amplitude, and the periodic ones can turn linearly unstable depending on amplitude. A new Mathieu-like equation, derived by a simpler route, governs stability of the standing wave against a super-harmonic disturbance. Analytic predictions are checked against numerical solutions of the full nonlinear equations for both systems. Agreement is good in most cases, and the mismatches are analyzed to mark where the analogy breaks down.
arxiv-2509-07546:
Sungjun Eom and 1 co-author extend differential dynamic programming in 2025 to control problems whose target is an ellipsoid, a stretched ball region, rather than a single point. Many real tasks, such as parking a vehicle, accept any final state inside a safe region. Differential dynamic programming, or DDP, is an efficient optimal control method, but it needs smooth cost functions, and the ellipsoid version creates costs with kinks.

Their ETS-DDP reformulates the problem with an orthogonal projection operator and smooths the cost locally around the previous iteration's path. A statistical inference method designs the ellipsoid itself from target points shown in expert demonstrations. In an autonomous parking simulation, the method finds an admissible trajectory efficiently and runs much faster than a comparison point-target approach. Region targets could make optimal control fit real tasks more naturally.
arxiv-2509-07746:
Samvit Kumar and 3 co-authors test Lighthill's mechanism for concentrating vorticity near walls in turbulent flow in a 2025 paper. Vorticity measures local spinning in a fluid, and the logarithmic layer is the region of wall turbulence where average velocity grows with the log of distance from the wall. Lighthill proposed long ago how motion toward and away from the wall gathers spanwise vorticity there.

Using a channel flow database at high Reynolds number, the team computes flows conditioned on motion toward or away from the wall. The results support Lighthill's proposal across the whole logarithmic layer, extended by counterflows that explain an anti-correlation between two vorticity transport routes. Vorticity transport also looks like a cascade through a hierarchy of eddy scales. Townsend's attached hairpin eddies account for half the cascade; necklace-like shawl vortices wrapping turbulent sweeps supply the other half.
arxiv-2509-08746:
Ryan McGaughey and 2 co-authors challenge a core belief about defenses in federated learning in a 2025 paper. In federated learning, many clients train a shared model without pooling raw data. Robust aggregation tries to spot and exclude harmful client updates.

Their Chameleon Poisoning keeps harmful updates inside the main distribution, so they look normal. Feedback from aggregation tells the attacker whether its update was accepted. The attacker then balances a harmful part with a camouflage part. Across two datasets, attack success rises sharply against nine defenses. The result shows detection based on outliers alone is not enough.
arxiv-2509-08946:
Stellar evolution codes produce grids of thousands of star models, and mining those grids by hand is slow. D. Tarczay-Nehéz presents MESAlab in a 2025 research paper written alone. MESAlab is a Python pipeline for post-processing output from MESA, the standard open-source stellar evolution code. It is modular, so users can adapt the stages to their own grids.

The pipeline spots selected evolutionary features automatically. One example is the blue loop phase in the life of classical Cepheid stars. It can also prepare inputs for, and launch, two companion tools that compute how stars pulsate. Visualization tools draw evolutionary tracks on standard diagrams, including the Gaia color-magnitude diagram. For researchers running huge model grids, MESAlab turns weeks of file handling into a repeatable workflow. Pulsation analysis comes attached to the phases that matter.
arxiv-2509-09146:
Internet providers gain speed and control by peering directly with each other, but choosing partners is a slow, manual courtship. Md Ibrahim Ibne Alam and 4 co-authors automate that choice with machine learning in a 2025 research paper. Providers otherwise pay transit services to carry their traffic. Peering through exchange points is preferred, yet arranging it eats time and expertise.

The team assembled public data on providers from databases like PeeringDB and CAIDA. They compared tree-based, neural network, and transformer models at predicting which pairs should peer. Tree-based models won on both accuracy and efficiency. The best one predicted peering partners with very high accuracy and stayed robust across time, region, and missing data. The authors envision providers automating partner selection entirely, making the internet's connective tissue grow faster and with less friction.
arxiv-2509-09446:
Hazem Hassan's 2025 paper develops a p-adic tool aimed at conjectured objects called Stark-Heegner cycles. Heegner cycles are higher-weight relatives of Heegner points, and their intersection numbers show up inside modular forms. A proposal by Rotger and Seveso predicts matching cycles over real-quadratic fields, whose existence would follow from deep conjectures of Bloch and Beilinson.

Hassan lifts the rigid meromorphic cocycle theory of Darmon and Vonk into higher weight, building a pairing on the p-adic upper half-plane for divisors coming from real-quadratic fields. Values computed for principal cycles appear to land in abelian extensions of real-quadratic fields. That algebraic behaviour counts as indirect support for the predicted cycles actually existing.
arxiv-2509-09946:
Vu-Minh Le and 5 co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a way to lift ordinary two-dimensional multi-camera tracking into three dimensions. Tracking people across many cameras is key for large-scale surveillance, and depth data plus camera calibration can place each target in real space. Rebuilding a whole tracking system for 3D, though, is often not practical for teams with working 2D setups.

Their method keeps the 2D tracker, then uses depth to rebuild each target as a point cloud and recover its 3D box by clustering and heading correction. An improved matching step uses local identity consistency to assign global identities across frames. On the 2025 AI City Challenge 3D tracking data set, the system placed third on the leaderboard.
arxiv-2509-10146:
Mathijs van Noort and 2 co-authors show that a temporal logic can shed its best-known operators in a 2025 logic paper. It loses nothing by the cut. Reasoning over time often leans on negation. That habit suits closed data sets. It breaks down when data arrive late or never. Sensor networks and the Semantic Web face just that risk. Negation-free fragments keep reasoning monotone and scalable. They might be too weak, though, to say all that is needed.

The authors work inside negation-free metric temporal logic. They drop the always operators first. Once, since, and until carry the load instead. Then once is dropped as well. A fragment built only from until and since remains. Broad claims about all past or future time survive the cut. Such claims were long thought to need the muscle of negation.
arxiv-2509-10246:
Amir Bahador Javadi, Amin Kargarian, and Mort Naraghi-Pour use machine learning to lighten a heavy power-grid planning problem in this 2025 paper. Grid operators must commit power plants a day ahead while renewable output stays uncertain, a two-stage stochastic problem whose transmission constraints grow enormous.

Their idea replaces the flood of line-flow limits with a much smaller set learned by a support vector machine. The swap rests on the geometry of the feasible region under a standard DC power flow approximation, and training data comes from fast optimal power flow runs. On the IEEE 57-bus and 118-bus test systems, the learned constraints stayed highly accurate, planning ran about forty-six and thirty-one percent faster, and generation costs barely moved.
arxiv-2509-10446:
Rui Lu and 8 co-authors present DeepDive, a system that teaches language models to search deeply, in this 2025 paper. Browsing tools can turn a model into a research agent, but open models still reason poorly over long searches and lack hard training questions. The team attacked both problems together.

First, they generate tough, hard-to-find questions automatically from open knowledge graphs. Second, they train the model with multi-turn reinforcement learning, with a penalty that discourages asking the same query twice. Their 32-billion-parameter model set a new best among open systems on the BrowseComp benchmark, ahead of several named rivals. All data, models, and code were released in public.
arxiv-2509-10746:
Medical chatbots often sound emotionally flat, and Adarsh Srinivasan with five co-authors fix that openly with RECAP in this 2025 health AI paper. Their framework works at inference time, no retraining, and is grounded in cognitive appraisal theory, the psychology of how people evaluate events. A patient's message is decomposed into auditable stages: reflect, extract, calibrate, align, produce.

Across benchmarks and models from eight to one hundred twenty billion parameters, RECAP improved agreement with human judgments, with the biggest gains on the smallest models. Its intermediate steps expose a blind spot: models systematically underweight relational factors like social support. In blinded tests, oncology fellows preferred RECAP's responses over baselines in roughly three quarters to seven eighths of comparisons, suggesting careful prompting can raise emotional intelligence while keeping reasoning visible for clinicians.
arxiv-2509-11246:
Krystian Gajdzica, Bernhard Heim, and Markus Neuhauser classify a sign pattern in this 2025 number theory paper. Partitions count ways to break a whole number into pieces. The authors study counts from restricted infinite products. Some factors are left out by an exception set.

One quantity compares neighboring partition counts. Its sign shows local log-concavity or log-convexity. The simplest case gives regular partitions. There, no part is a multiple of a fixed number. The authors find that large-parameter signs follow a pattern. The pattern depends on the small numbers two through five. It depends on which of them are exceptions. It also depends on the remainder of n. A value set by the exception set fixes that remainder.
arxiv-2509-11346:
