Connor Ligeikis, Heath Hofmann, and Jeff Scruggs built a self-powered vibration controller in this 2025 control engineering paper. The system harvests energy from the shaking it suppresses. The prototype works at a larger scale than earlier demos. It handles forces around a kilonewton. Power flows exceed a watt.

The hardware couples a linear ballscrew to a synchronous machine. That machine uses permanent magnets. A custom inverter steers power flow. A converter moves energy in and out of a storage capacitor. Real circuits waste some energy. The control law must meet a feasibility condition stricter than passivity. The authors give a workable design method respecting it. Hardware-in-the-loop tests used a stochastically shaken tuned absorber. The design behaved as intended.
arxiv-2509-11646:
Cristiano Spotti surveys a borderland between two fields in this 2025 discussion paper. Differential geometry is one side. Algebraic geometry is the other. His topic is Kähler-Einstein metrics. These are special curved geometries on complex spaces. What happens to them under limits and rescalings is the thread.

The discussion centers on moduli spaces. Those catalog all varieties of a kind. Singularities get equal weight. Those are points where spaces fail to be smooth. Spotti walks through basic examples and reviews recent results. Tentative conjectural pictures link the two sides. Rescaled metric limits mirror algebraic ways to complete moduli spaces. The paper maps an active frontier for readers who want the lay of the land.
arxiv-2509-11746:
Jian Cao and 9 co-authors simulate a newly seen exotic particle in a 2025 hadron physics paper. A detector team recently reported an axial-vector particle, X(2300), in a specific decay process. What the particle is made of is still unknown.

Using a parton and hadron cascade model, the authors simulate its making in electron-positron collisions. They propose candidate inner structures for the first time, among them four-quark states and a bound system of a strangeonium with a light hadron. Each candidate forms by coalescence steps in the simulated final states. They compute the particle's angular momentum in its rest frame and classify each candidate. Estimated rates differ by an order of magnitude between candidates, and their momentum spreads differ a lot, giving tests for experiments.
arxiv-2509-11946:
Vibrating beams stiffened with carbon nanotubes get a fast new analysis method from Maryam Jalili and one co-author in 2025. Their subject is the nonlinear free vibration of composite beams whose nanotube content can be spread evenly or graded through the thickness.

The authors build boundary-adapted Chebyshev functions that satisfy clamped and simply supported end conditions exactly, then apply a Ritz procedure with geometric nonlinearity included. Material properties come from a modified mixing rule, and the reduced model converges fast. With a dozen basis functions, the lowest frequency already sits within a tenth of a percent of published benchmarks. It also costs far less computing time than fine finite-element models. Raising the nanotube share lifts the frequency, they find, though the method still assumes a slender beam.
arxiv-2509-12846:
Junlin Song, Antoine Richard and Miguel Olivares-Mendez give in 2025 a fast way to align a motion sensor and a camera in space and time. Drones, phones, and robots need that match set in advance, or their sense of place drifts.

Most past methods use smooth curves over time, which are exact but slow. The new method uses step-by-step states instead and fixes the weak point of such states for time shifts. The gain is large at scale: saving one minute per device across a million devices saves thousands of work days. Code is shared openly so labs and firms can use and check it.
arxiv-2509-13046:
Eyal German, Daniel Samira and two co-authors attack fake table data in 2025 to test if rows leak their source. Diffusion makers can craft true-like tables for health and finance share. They may also store real rows and leak them.

Their MIA-EPT attack is black-box: it sees only fake output. It masks row fields, rebuilds them, and reads miss size as a member clue. Tests span three makers with fair leak scores. In a 2025 contest run it placed second in its track. The lesson is stark: fake data is not safe by default.
arxiv-2509-13246:
Samuel Escribano, Alfredo Levy Yeyati and Elsa Prada derive in 2025 a compact band model for III-V crystals under strain. Strain tunes electronic traits, but full band models cost too much for device-scale runs. Simple strain-aware forms for these quantum-grade materials lagged behind.

Starting from an eight-band model with corrections, they fold down to one band. Closed forms give mass, potential, spin coupling, and g-factor under strain. Small to mid strain matches full results. Wire and layered cases test the form. Spintronic and quantum designs gain a fast, trusted tool.
arxiv-2509-13546:
Nam Nguyen and five co-authors lay out a full cost analysis in a 2025 quantum computing paper for simulating the extended Jaynes-Cummings model. That model describes light interacting with matter across several modes and underlies technologies such as photon addition, but classical simulation becomes impossible for large systems.

The team develops explicit quantum algorithms and circuits for the model's time evolution, using first and second order product formulas in two different pictures of the dynamics. They prove closed-form error bounds, handle both pure and mixed states, and check their cost models numerically. Finally they compile the circuits for a surface-code fault-tolerant architecture, giving concrete estimates of physical qubits and run times for future machines.
arxiv-2509-13646:
Kexue Fu and six co-authors present Vistoria in a 2025 human-computer interaction paper, a writing system where text and images act as equal partners in fictional storytelling. Most writing tools are text-only, even though people naturally think and remember in pictures, which limits how authors plan and develop ideas.

A co-design study with ten writers, run in Wizard-of-Oz style, showed how sketches, images, and annotations drive ideation and organization. Vistoria supports operations borrowed from image editing, such as lasso selection, collage, filters, and perspective shifts, applied to narrative material. In a controlled study with twelve participants, co-editing improved expressiveness and immersion and strengthened feelings of authorship, though it also raised mental effort.
arxiv-2509-13846:
Puru Vaish and four co-authors challenge a quiet assumption in representation learning in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Self-supervised methods usually assume that loosely related views of the same scan are enough to teach a model useful structure. The team argue that meaningful structure in the hidden representation does not appear on its own; it has to be induced.

Their method, Consistent View Alignment, aligns representations from different views so complementary information lines up without creating false matches. Applied to foundation models for three-dimensional medical image segmentation, it improved downstream performance over standard self-supervised baselines. Entries using the method took first and second place in the MICCAI 2025 SSL3D challenge with two different backbone networks.
arxiv-2509-14346:
Muqaddar Abbas and three co-authors model a light effect in 2025 inside a tiny optical cavity holding a bilayer of graphene. The photonic spin Hall effect splits light by polarisation. Left and right circular parts shift sideways in opposite directions.

In their setup, pump and probe fields drive one mirror of the cavity. Radiation pressure sets the second mirror vibrating. The two polarisation parts of a probe beam then separate across the incidence plane. The split can be tuned with cavity fields, mechanical coupling and phonon links to electronic states. Phonons are quantised vibrations in the material. Results hold also for standard optomechanical systems without those extra links, widening where the tuned effect could be used.
arxiv-2509-14546:
Zhilun Zhou and six co-authors benchmark the rationality of large language models in 2025, across both thinking and acting. Models now simulate people and assist decisions widely, raising a plain question: do they reason and choose as rational agents should? Rationality has theoretical and practical sides.

Their benchmark is presented as the first omnibus test of model rationality across many domains. It probes consistency of beliefs, preference logic and decision quality under varied framings. Multiple leading models are compared on the same suite. Human like fluency can mask systematic irrationality, such as framing effects or inconsistent trade offs. A shared rationality scorecard helps buyers and researchers see where a model can be trusted as a simulated or advising agent.
arxiv-2509-15046:
Shu Yang, Konstantinos Zinelis, Sourojeet Chakraborty, and C. Ricardo Constante-Amores simulate a liquid thread breaking inside a yield-stress material in a 2025 fluid dynamics paper. A Newtonian thread drains and pinches off while surrounded by a viscoplastic medium, a material that flows only where stress passes a threshold. Such setups appear in embedded printing, where ink threads rest inside support gels.

Simulations and theory agree that breakup happens below a nearly universal threshold set by the balance of capillary force and yield stress. The viscosity contrast matters little at low Ohnesorge numbers, which compare viscous and capillary effects. Maps over the parameter plane reveal distinct regime boundaries, and a scaling law predicts the minimum thread radius accurately. Stress localization inside the viscoplastic surroundings emerges as the key mechanism.
arxiv-2509-15446:
Yahui Qu and Benedek Valkó study how points spread in a random pattern called the Sine beta process. This pattern is the large scale limit of a family of random tables used in physics and math. A key question is how likely two points are to sit at a given gap. That likelihood is the pair correlation function, the object of this paper.

The pair write that function through a random differential equation and through an endless system of such equations. They show the function varies smoothly with the key parameter and bound how fast it fades. For even values of the parameter, a finite set of equations pins it down, and they expand it as a series. Their formulas recover the known cases.
arxiv-2509-15546:
Ran Hong leads a team that boosts a video cutting tool guided by words. The task is to cut out, in each frame, the objects a text query names. A recent system joins a language model with a strong cutter. The team improve it with no extra training, using two added parts.

One part checks that the named subject and action truly appear in the video, which cuts false hits. The other part picks key frames with care, catching early views and long range context. On a known test set, the boosted system scores well and takes second place in a 2025 contest track. The work shows checks and frame choice can lift a strong base system.
arxiv-2509-15646:
Sharan Banagiri, Eric Thrane, and Paul Lasky sort merging black hole pairs into groups. The fourth catalog of gravitational wave events gives a detailed view of these pairs. How the black holes formed is unclear, and each birth path may leave its own marks. The team take a data led approach, letting mass ranges define the groups.

They find support for at least three groups, split by the heavier hole's mass with sharp borders. The lightest group mixes mass ratios evenly and spins slowly. The middle group strongly favors near equal masses. The heaviest group shows support for fast spins. Each group's traits hint at a distinct birth path. More data will test the split.
arxiv-2509-15946:
Sound in a room bounces off walls and spreads in ways that shape what listeners hear. Sungho Lee and five co-authors present DART, a fast computer method that tracks how sound energy moves between small patches of a room's surfaces. Their work builds on an older method that treats walls as having flexible material traits.

Because DART can be tuned step by step, users can adjust wall materials and see how the sound field changes. Tests show it predicts sound for new speaker and listener spots well, even when few measurements are given. It beats older signal methods and neural nets on those sparse tests, stays easy to read, and comes with open code.
arxiv-2509-16346:
Airborne laser scans map a forest canopy well but miss the tangled growth beneath it, which ground scans catch at high cost. Juan Castorena and three co-authors train a generative model to infer that hidden undergrowth from the canopy view alone. The model learns from paired air and ground scans of the same woods, so its guesses stay true to the real layout.

At tree, plot, and landscape scales, the fake ground scans match real ones in shape and in measures like tree height and crown size. A new quality score helps judge outputs where no ground truth exists. Richer forest maps aid fire and ecology work.
arxiv-2509-16446:
Recommendation models that generate item codes can stumble when two like items receive the very same code. Ruohan Zhang and three co-authors insist the codes stay purely semantic, with no random tag tacked on to split ties. They loosen the usual nearest-center rule and give two methods that assign each item a unique code while keeping its meaning.

Tests span series recommendation, product search, and document retrieval. Both methods lifted overall results and did even better for cold-start items with little history. The lesson is that code uniqueness itself, not extra tokens, drives much of the gain.
arxiv-2509-16646:
Xiyong Yan studies loops in signed graphs in a 2025 solo math paper. Each edge in the graph carries a label from a small set. A loop that visits every vertex once is called Hamiltonian. Its total label, summed around the loop, is its double sign. Yan asks when loops can achieve all four possible signs.

He proves that three distinct signs among small triangles are enough. The proof leans on triangle bases in a binary cycle space. It also uses the structure of tiny subgraphs and builds loops by hand. The result ties a local clue, signs on triangles, to a global trait of the whole graph.
arxiv-2509-16846:
Aryan Dhar, Siddhant Gautam, and Saiprasad Ravishankar speed MRI scans in a 2025 medical paper. MRI can skip some data and still rebuild a good image, if the skipped pattern is chosen well. A pattern tuned to each scan beats a fixed one. Their network predicts such a pattern from low-frequency data at scan time.

Tests used a public knee dataset with many coils. Image quality matched top prior methods at high speed-up rates. The cost of predicting a mask does not grow with the training set size. Faster scans mean less time in the machine for patients and more scans per day for hospitals.
arxiv-2509-17546:
Nathan Grieve, writing alone, works on stability theory for projective varieties in a 2025 arXiv paper. His tools are CM-line bundles, built from the Chow-Mumford line bundle theory of Arezzo and co-authors, with key insights from Paul and Tian. The paper gives an explicit intersection-theoretic account of Donaldson-Futaki invariants, the numbers that test K-stability.

The invariants here arise by deforming to the normal cone along subschemes, for line bundles that are big and nef rather than ample. That step generalizes the slope stability theory of Ross and Thomas to the broader bundle class. A load-bearing fact is that the CM-line bundles vary continuously with the ample cone. The paper is dense, technical work aimed at specialists in K-stability, where explicit formulas for these invariants guide both proofs and examples.
arxiv-2509-17646:
Denis Burgarella and seven co-authors lay out survey plans for a future far-infrared space observatory. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes PRIMA, a cryogenically cooled mission expected to serve astronomers by the early 2030s. Its PRIMAger instrument will image from the mid to the far infrared, with hyperspectral, photometric, and polarimetric modes.

The paper defines the General Observer programmes, above all a wide survey covering a quarter of the sky. That survey would gather data on millions of galaxies out to large redshifts. Medium-resolution spectra can trace dust and gas emission line by line, while the broad bands and polarization add shape and magnetic clues. The authors present the survey as the shared backbone that guest observers will build on, with smaller targeted programmes filling the rest of the mission's open time.
arxiv-2509-17746:
Yuval Kern and nine co-authors photograph single flashes of an intense quantum light source, one shot at a time. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies bright squeezed vacuum, a state with no mean field but wild swings in photon number. It is strong enough to drive extreme nonlinear processes, yet the shape of a single pulse had never been fully pinned down.

The team built a femtosecond source in a single spatial mode and read each shot with spectral interferometry against a known reference pulse. The group delay stayed consistent from shot to shot. The mean pulse length came out far shorter than the pump pulse, with a modest spread across shots. The interferograms also show a nodal pattern that betrays the source's random phase flip of half a cycle. The authors argue this light is a viable femtosecond source for probing ultrafast electron dynamics.
arxiv-2509-17846:
Timmi G Jorgensen and Ross P Church model young star clusters in the galaxy M51. Their 2025 paper asks how hits with giant gas clouds shape the fate of those clusters. They run thousands of cluster sims, each twice: with cloud hits and without.

Most seen mass and age trends in M51 came out of the runs. Old, light clusters near the galaxy core were the most prone to break up. Cloud hits cut the chance to survive for old light clusters by a fair share. In a few cases, cloud hits oddly shielded a cluster and helped it keep more stars.
arxiv-2509-18046:
Yinuo Wang and 4 co-authors train a humanoid robot to walk with a Mamba encoder at its core. Their 2025 frame, HuMam, learns control end to end, from body state to joint targets. Past such policies can train in a shaky way, fuse inputs poorly, or burn too much power.

One Mamba layer blends body state, footstep goals, and a phase clock. A reward with six parts weighs contact, swing, foot place, posture, and body steadiness. On a known humanoid in a sim, HuMam learned faster and ran with more stability than a strong base policy. It also cut power use and peak joint force.
arxiv-2509-18146:
Madi Yerlanov, Qi Wang, and Nancy Rodriguez model crime, targets, and guardians as a three-way moving system. Their 2025 paper builds a flow-and-spread model of a city, with police as an active third part. Past crime models held two parts; adding guardians changes the maths and the tale.

With classic split tools, they set exact terms for when a flat state breaks. Past a policing threshold, hotspots can lock in or pulse in cycles. Guard moves act as the tipping force in that split. Sims show still patterns, pulses, and even chaos. The frame gives new tools for multi-agent social systems.
arxiv-2509-18346:
Fast methods for finding the lowest point of a smooth function often use momentum, a push from past steps. M Parimi and four co-authors revisit why the famous Nesterov method speeds up at all. Their 2025 paper argues that most past accounts work backward from the method to a matching equation. That reverse route, they say, hides the deeper reason for the speed-up.

Instead, the team starts from control theory tools and builds the dynamics first. Their frame explains each term in the Nesterov method and the order of its steps. It covers both strongly curved and plain curved cases. The same frame also yields the triple momentum method's speed-up. It even explains why the older heavy-ball method can fail to reach the best point. The goal is a clear origin story for acceleration.
arxiv-2509-18746:
Difference equations with fractional orders model systems whose present depends on a long past. Janardhan Chevala and Sachin Bhalekar study a linear equation with two fractional difference operators in this 2025 paper. The two orders sit between zero and one. They give a sequence form of the solution that is easier to work with.

A Z-transform approach then traces where the stable region ends, working in the complex plane. When one coefficient turns slightly negative, that boundary folds into multiple points. The folding creates several separate stability regions. The authors chart all possible bifurcations, the qualitative changes, in terms of the parameters. Many worked examples support the claims. The results help predict when such fractional systems stay stable. That matters for control and signal models built on fractional differences.
arxiv-2509-18946:
Kamaljeet Singh and two co-authors study matter made of quarks and gluons at extreme heat and density. Such matter forms for a brief time when heavy atomic nuclei crash into each other. Heat tends to spread through it, but the authors ask a subtler question: can a heat gradient push particles to drift, and can a particle gradient drive heat to flow?

These two linked effects are named the Soret and Dufour effects, and the team studies them in this setting for the first time from first principles. They use a transport equation for fast-moving particles, with terms for both heat and chemical imbalance. They derive formulas for both effect strengths in the free quark phase and in the later phase made of ordinary particles.
arxiv-2509-19146: O. A. Veliev, writing alone, gives a brief explanation of the spectral expansion method for a class of differential operators on the whole real line. The operators are not self-adjoint, which means their behavior is less tidy than in the classic textbook case, and their coefficients repeat periodically along the line while taking complex values. The note's stated aim is narrow: to explain the expansion problem for these operators clearly and briefly, rather than to report a broad new research program.
arxiv-2509-19446:
Magnetars are neutron stars with magnetic fields beyond a hundred trillion gauss, and Rachael E. Stewart and fifteen co-authors use one to test a quantum prediction about empty space. In such fields the vacuum should act like a crystal, bending light differently by polarization, an effect called vacuum birefringence. It has been predicted for decades but never confirmed. The team coordinated X-ray and radio observations of a radio-loud magnetar with three observatories.

In the soft X-ray band the light is strongly polarized, reaching about sixty-five percent at low energies, then dropping sharply. At some rotation phases the polarization nears eighty percent. Radio and X-ray polarization angles both track the star's rotating field geometry. Standard surface models cannot explain the pattern. Propagation through the birefringent vacuum can. The authors call it a significant advance toward confirming the effect.
arxiv-2509-19646:
Sixth-generation mobile networks are still on the drawing board, and Salma Tika and three co-authors survey where the work stands. They start from the strict demands expected of 6G: very high reliability, wide coverage, and support for huge device counts. Enabling tools include terahertz radio, smart reflecting surfaces, massive antenna arrays, and AI-run network control.

The survey maps likely uses, from automated industry to merged physical and digital spaces. It also lists the hard gaps: hardware limits, energy cost, security, and standards that do not yet exist. As 5G still rolls out, such stock-taking guides research money toward the true bottlenecks. The authors write for both industry and academic readers. The paper serves as a status report on a technology a decade from daily use.
arxiv-2509-19846:
Boreal forests hold a huge share of the world's land carbon, much of it locked in permafrost soils that thaw as the climate warms. Kevin Bradley Dsouza and seven co-authors build BoreaRL, a reinforcement learning playground for managing those forests. Its simulator couples energy, carbon, and water flows on physical grounds. Agents learn harvest and care policies under two modes: one tuned to a single site, one trained to stay robust across random conditions.

Trials expose an asymmetry: gaining carbon is far easier to learn than preventing thaw. Policies that guard permafrost struggle where carbon policies thrive. That gap warns managers that the two goals need unlike strategies. A shared testbed lets algorithms compete on the trade-off openly. Climate adaptation needs such tools before thaw locks in losses.
arxiv-2509-19946:
Slurred, hard-to-parse speech from conditions such as cerebral palsy or Parkinson's is called dysarthria, and detecting it automatically could speed referrals. Lovisa Wihlborg and ten co-authors grade seventeen ready-made speech embedding systems on that task. Six datasets of varied origin supply the tests. Small, skewed recordings make naive scores untrustworthy, so repeated cross-validation runs are compared against a crafted null model.

Only scores that beat the null distribution count as real detection. Within one dataset, results swung widely by dataset, whatever the system. Training on one dataset and testing on another exposed still sharper drops. The study is a reality check for a field short on data. Clinics need detectors that travel across recording setups, not just leaderboards.
arxiv-2509-20046:
Fiber optic cables can listen: scattered light reveals sounds along their length. Knut H. Grythe and Jan Erik Håkegård localize an underwater acoustic source with a fiber read from both ends. Their transceiver setup works in forward mode rather than backscatter. A bistatic radar analogy guides the design: two vantage points, one source.

Delay differences between the signals arriving at the two ends fix the source position. Standard distributed acoustic sensing localizes along the fiber; this scheme adds position finding for communication sources. Underwater acoustic links serve vehicles, sensors, and divers where radio fails. Knowing where a caller sits, not just what it said, aids coordination and rescue. The proposal integrates that positioning into the decoding setup.
arxiv-2509-20346:
Sensors built at exceptional points promise extreme sensitivity. Todd Darcie and J. Stewart Aitchison test that promise against noise in a 2025 arXiv paper. At such a point, a sensor's split in tone grows as a root of the push it feels, which hints at endless response. In ideal linear gear, shot noise grows just as fast, so the gain cancels out. Nonlinear gear was predicted to show new blow-ups.

The team studies two linked resonators with gain that can saturate. When the noise math is done with full care, the predicted blow-ups vanish. Patches of instability ring the exceptional point, where phase noise leaks into the size of the wave. Those patches cap both the response and the noise a real sensor can reach. Full stochastic runs of the system back the math, right down to zero detuning.
arxiv-2509-20446:
The faintest galaxy yet confirmed at extreme distance is measured by Marusa Bradac and twenty-two co-authors in a 2025 arXiv letter. A massive cluster, the Bullet Cluster, magnifies the galaxy about fourteenfold, acting as a cosmic lens. Spectroscopy with the James Webb Space Telescope confirmed its redshift near eleven. Its light dates from the universe's first few hundred million years.

Webb imaging and spectra reveal three star-forming clumps, two of them smaller than ten parsecs across. The clumps hold about half of the galaxy's total stellar mass. Most of its stars formed in a burst roughly one hundred fifty million years before the epoch observed. A damping wing in the spectrum signals neutral gas along the line of sight, typical so deep in the reionization era. Despite the magnification, the galaxy's true luminosity is the lowest yet confirmed at such distances.
arxiv-2509-20746:
Designing an optimization algorithm usually means guessing a method and then proving it works. Ibrahim Ozaslan and four co-authors automate that process in a 2025 paper accepted for the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control. They target strongly convex problems with linear equality constraints.

Their approach grows out of robust control theory, which merges design and analysis into one step. The synthesis yields a single-loop, gradient-based algorithm. Its convergence rate does not depend on the condition number of the constraint matrix, an improvement over earlier algorithms. Because the framework exposes performance limits first, the resulting method is built to sit near those limits. The paper shows how control theory can systematize algorithm design.
arxiv-2509-20946:
Laser power meters must measure energy accurately, but scratches and heat damage on their sensor coatings skew readings. Dongqi Zheng, Wenjin Fu, and Guangzong Chen present a real-time inspection system in a 2025 paper. The system runs on the device and learns without labeled defect examples.

Their framework trains only on images of good sensors, learning what a normal coating looks like. Anything that departs from that pattern is flagged as an anomaly, whether or not that defect type was seen before. Preprocessing uses edge detection and clustering to isolate the coating area. The authors target medical and industrial lasers, where bad measurements carry real costs. Unsupervised learning sidesteps the need for large labeled defect libraries.
arxiv-2509-21446:
Forecasting seismic waves before they arrive could help future gravitational wave detectors cancel ground noise. Waleed Esmail and 3 co-authors built a transformer model for that task in a 2025 paper. The setting is the planned Einstein Telescope, a next generation observatory. The model, SeismoGPT, learns from three component seismic waveforms directly.

Trained in an autoregressive way, the model predicts step by step from past motion. It can run on a single station or on an array of stations. Learned time and space patterns give realistic ground motion forecasts. Accuracy is strong in the immediate window and fades further ahead, as expected. The authors frame the work as groundwork for Newtonian noise mitigation and real time control.
arxiv-2509-21646:
Making X-ray photoelectron spectra of strongly linked molecules needs multireference methods that stay fast. Shuhang Li and 2 co-authors formulate such a method in a 2025 paper. Their approach joins core valence splitting with an equation of motion driven similarity renormalization group. Core ionization values come out accurately with favourable scaling in basis set size. A modification of the ground state formalism ensures rigorous core intensivity.

Three variants are developed and compared. Two derive from low order perturbative approximations, at second and third order. One uses a non perturbative scheme truncated to one and two body operators. Benchmarks compute vertical core ionization values for a representative molecular test set. The variants are weighed on hit rate and robustness for strongly linked systems.
arxiv-2509-21746:
Wrong labels are common in real data sets, and most sample-picking methods act as if they were not there. They also force the user to fix in advance how much data to cut. Brian B. Moser and six co-authors built HyperCore to handle both problems. Their 2025 paper offers a coreset method that adapts on its own.

HyperCore fits a simple ball-shaped model, called a hypersphere, for each class in the data. Points of a class should sit near the ball's center, while stray or mislabeled points sit far away. A standard statistic then sets the cut level with no hand tuning. In tests, the method beat its rivals most clearly when labels were noisy or data was scarce, keeping small samples that still teach a model well.
arxiv-2509-21846:
Lu Wei, writing alone, works out exact formulas for a basic quantity in quantum information in this 2025 paper. The quantity is relative entropy, a measure of how different two quantum states are. Wei studies it for random states, drawn from two standard families of random state models. The goal is the average value of the measure when both states are picked at random.

Wei derives exact, explicit formulas for that average, for states of any size. The formulas cover two states from the same family and pairs drawn from two different families. A key step is a splitting pattern the author spots in the averages after doing a hard integral over rotations. For one family, the new exact formula completes earlier work that had only an approximate version for equal-size states, found by a replica method.
arxiv-2509-22246:
Xiaoyang Liu and seven co-authors build a better ruler for judging automatic translation of math statements into formal language. Autoformalization is growing, but scoring its output is hard: string comparisons ignore meaning, while proof-based checks give no graded score when a proof fails. Their 2025 framework, ASSESS, accepted at ICLR 2026, scores a formal statement on both meaning and structure.

On those trees, a new metric measures edit distance while allowing semantic transformations, so equivalent rewrites are not punished as errors. To validate it, the team built a benchmark of over a thousand expert-annotated statement pairs from two known collections. Each pair is labeled both for whether one statement can prove the other and for how alike they are structurally. On that benchmark, the new metric beat existing methods on accuracy and on agreement with the human labels.
arxiv-2509-22546:
Jinfeng Zhou and 6 co-authors teach language models to reason about social life, not just logic puzzles. Logic training gives step-by-step deduction toward checkable answers. Social scenes instead demand reading ambiguous cues with no single right outcome. Their paradigm, Cognitive Reasoning, breaks that reading into linked units like observation and attribution, which combine as needed.

Their framework, CogFlow, first builds data by simulating human-like thought with tree-structured planning. Fine-tuning installs the basic skill. Reinforcement learning then refines it, with rewards for both the thought flow and the final reply. Tests showed clear gains in social decision-making for models, and even for humans who used the approach.
arxiv-2509-22846:
Philippe-André Luneau and Jean Deteix accelerate fixed point iterations with a reduced model built on the fly. Fixed point schemes solve nonlinear equations, optimization problems, and dynamical systems across the sciences. Reduced-order modeling shrinks such problems, but classic versions need offline training and a precomputed basis tied to one geometry. Their on-the-fly version builds a low-dimensional, self-correcting approximation during the iteration itself.

When the iteration map is contractive, inexact fixed point theory keeps the error within a user-set tolerance. Error estimates propagate through block Gauss-Seidel steps for systems of partial differential equations. A multiphysics lid-driven cavity flow in two and three dimensions illustrates the method. The authors also probe when speedups appear and where the method's limits lie.
arxiv-2509-22946:
Matthias Beck, Benjamin Braun, and Alvaro Cornejo study generating functions for q-chromatic polynomials. These polynomials count proper graph colorings, weighted by a chosen linear form. A recent paper showed the count is a polynomial in a q-analog sum. Beck and his co-authors ask what these counts can tell apart.

For one set of weights, the polynomial can tell apart all labeled graphs on a fixed vertex set. Using permutation statistics and polyhedral geometry, they find a formula for the full generating function. For the all-ones weights, they rewrite the polynomial in a q-binomial basis. Some numerator coefficients turn out to be palindromic in q.
arxiv-2509-23346: A short comment paper on Kahler Ricci flow clears up one definition. Xiuxiong Chen and Bing Wang clarify what polarized canonical radius means in a recent study of Laplace comparison on Kahler Ricci flow and convergence. The note is brief and definitional, aimed at readers of that earlier work. The note adds no new theorems or data. It pins down the term so that later work on the flow can use it in one shared sense.
arxiv-2509-23546:
Flood analysts lean on a 1949 formula that links two ways of stating how rare an extreme event is. Francesco Dell'Aira and 2 co-authors extend Langbein's formula to cases its assumptions miss. The formula ties the return period from annual maxima to the average recurrence interval from peak-over-threshold counts. It assumes exceedance counts follow a steady Poisson process, which real rivers can break.

Three breaks are covered: conditions that drift over time, mixed populations of events, and counts that spread more or less than Poisson predicts. For the first two, the classic form survives once terms are redefined. Spread in counts needs a wider form, with the classic result as a limiting case.
arxiv-2509-23746:
Vision-language models point at objects far worse than people do, partly because they must answer in one shot. Wenjie Yang and Zengfeng Huang propose Poivre, a self-refining loop named for its steps: point, visualize, then refine. The model marks its guessed point on the image, looks again, and adjusts if needed, like a person checking a fingertip. Reinforcement learning trains that habit, guided by a process reward with tidy theoretical properties.

Their trained model, Poivre-7B, set a new best score on Point-Bench. It beat closed models such as Gemini-2.5-Pro and large open ones such as Molmo-72B by over three percent. Code, data, and the model are released.
arxiv-2509-24046:
Picking a business partner means weighing many firms on mixed facts: numbers, types, and free text. Lingyao Li and 7 co-authors built PartnerMAS, a team of language-model agents that splits this job into layers. A planner sets the plan, expert agents judge set parts, and a boss agent merges their views.

To test the system, the team built a data set from venture capital deals, where true partner groups are known. Across well over a hundred cases, PartnerMAS matched true groups more often than a lone agent or a debate-style team. Gains reached about a tenth or more. The split of roles, not a bigger model, drove the edge.
arxiv-2509-24346:
Highest weight modules of exceptional Lie algebras carry two key invariants that are hard to compute by hand. Zhanqiang Bai and 3 co-authors develop an explicit algorithm that finds both for any infinitesimal character. The first invariant, the Gelfand-Kirillov dimension, measures the module's growth. The second, its annihilator variety, is the closure of a nilpotent orbit of twice that dimension.

The method reduces the dimension to a known function on a Weyl group, then splits the root system into factors. Classical factors use classic insertion algorithms, while exceptional ones use index reduction and dedicated software. Springer theory and Sommers duality then recover the orbit. An online implementation takes the weight as input.
arxiv-2509-24546:
Before any video plays, it passes through ingest, transcoding, packaging, and delivery, and those steps now sprawl across distributed systems. Matthias Neugebauer reports on nagare media engine, an open-source research prototype for network-based media processing. It implements an MPEG standard that describes such workflows in a uniform way.

The engine runs on Kubernetes, making it native to both cloud and edge settings. It aims to meet current demands for describing and running complex multimedia workflows. The report details how the prototype is built and what the standard requires. Such systems matter as media pipelines outgrow the single-machine tools they began with.
arxiv-2509-25446: Dale Worley, a solo author, opens a notebook of unsolved problems in a 2025 paper. The subject is the combinatorics of tableaux, the grid-like arrangements used across algebra and combinatorics. The notebook is modeled on a famous group-theory problem collection that gathered open questions for decades. Worley presents the problems as an invitation: other researchers are welcome to contribute their own unsolved questions to the collection. The paper is a community resource rather than a results paper, meant to focus attention on what the field still cannot answer.
arxiv-2509-25846:
Dazhuo Wang and co-authors published this wireless engineering paper in 2025. It deals with OTFS, a waveform proposed for future 6G networks that stays reliable when users move fast. The paper asks how the same signal can serve two jobs at once: carrying data and sensing the surroundings like a radar, a pairing known as integrated sensing and communication.

The authors present a fast radar algorithm that builds a range-and-speed map of targets from the returning signal. It works for both a single device sensing its own echoes and a two-device setup, at far lower computing cost than current methods. They then add a pilot-aided way to estimate the channel, using one shared symbol for both sensing and estimation. Cutting the usual guard symbols also lowers the signal's peak power. Simulations show the scheme beating the methods it was compared against.
arxiv-2509-25946:
Lee Jung-Mok and co-authors present a pipeline for automated model discovery in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Model discovery means searching a large space of candidate models to fit a data set well. Good models must capture fine detail yet generalize beyond the training data, without growing too complex.

Their pipeline uses two vision-language modules in an agent-like loop. One plans analyses over several steps and proposes candidate models. The other judges the candidates on numbers and on visual fit, weighing local detail against overall trend. Tests showed the pipeline finds models that balance both aims. Further checks confirmed that using images and multiple steps each play a key role.
arxiv-2509-26146:
Nagur Shareef Shaik and co-authors published a 2025 paper on grading diabetic eye disease with an AI that respects the disease's order. Eye damage from diabetes comes in stages, from none to severe. The stages are ordered, and the severe ones are rare in datasets yet most urgent to catch. Standard models treat the grades as unordered labels and learn lopsided lessons from the common mild cases.

Their framework encodes the order directly. A generative model shapes its internal space with a skewed prior that preserves the rare stages' structure. A custom loss keeps grades separated in the right sequence. A second loss punishes under-grading more than over-grading, matching clinical priorities: missing severe disease is worse than a false alarm. On public benchmarks the method topped standard scores for agreement, accuracy, and balanced detection. The authors argue medical AI should borrow the clinic's values, not just its labels.
arxiv-2510-00046:
Zou exposes a security hole in the commercial prompt-trading market, where creators sell carefully curated text-to-image prompts that carry trademark styles. By showing those prompt templates can be stolen from just a few public sample images. His RLStealer frames template stealing as a sequential decision problem and trains a reinforcement learning agent. Using several similarity-based feedback signals as rewards, to search the full prompt space efficiently in this study.

Solved with the PPO algorithm, the attack reaches reported state-of-the-art stealing performance while cutting total attack cost to under 13 percent of what existing baselines need. And it also generalizes across image styles to unseen templates and subjects. An ablation against random search confirms the gains come from guided policy learning, and Zou urges the community to build defenses and protective standards for prompt marketplaces in the future.
arxiv-2510-00446:
Yuling Shi and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on LongCodeZip, a tool that shrinks the code fed to language models. Repository-scale tasks force models to read enormous code contexts, which costs money and time. General text compressors ignore how code is structured, so they cut the wrong pieces. LongCodeZip compresses in two stages built around that structure.

First it ranks whole functions by how relevant they look to the instruction, using conditional perplexity. Only the top functions survive to the second stage. There, each function splits into blocks, and a budgeted subset is chosen to maximize relevance. Across completion, summarization, and question answering tasks, the tool beat baseline compressors. It reached compression ratios up to about five and a half times with no loss in task performance. The framework needs no training and works across different code models.
arxiv-2510-00946:
Andleeb, Kantorski, and Carver study what ChatGPT does to first-year programmers in this 2025 paper for the ACM SIGCITE conference. Introductory students now routinely ask chatbots for code, debugging, and explanations, which could build skill or quietly replace it. The authors ran a counterbalanced quasi-experiment in a CS1 course: students alternated between ChatGPT and no-ChatGPT conditions across two C programming assignments, one on functions and one on structures. Rubrics graded the code, and post-surveys probed concepts and perceptions.

With ChatGPT, students produced significantly higher code quality scores and finished faster than without it. Conceptual gains were uneven: lower for the functions topic, higher for structures. Students liked the tool for debugging and practice, while worrying about its accuracy and their long-term skill growth. The authors recommend structured integration and complementary teaching strategies so the efficiency gains do not crowd out independent problem solving.
arxiv-2510-01146:
Anugraha and five co-authors release mR3 in this 2025 arXiv paper, a multilingual reward model that judges language model outputs by rubric. Reward models grade candidate answers during training and evaluation, but strong judges exist almost only for English. Building one for many languages is hard, since human judgements are costly and evaluation habits differ across datasets. The team trained their model on material spanning seventy-two languages, the broadest coverage reported for reward modelling.

Their study compares data sources and curriculum choices systematically, including reasoning traces written in the target language. The resulting model beat existing reward models on multilingual benchmarks, including systems up to nine times larger such as GPT-OSS-120B. Ablations showed English still works best as the reasoning language, while targeted multilingual training made target-language inputs far more robust. Models, data, and code are open source.
arxiv-2510-01446:
Milyushkov tests whether machine learning prices options better than the classic formulas that finance has trusted for decades. Black-Scholes and Heston assume tidy markets, while real prices bend with frictions and shifting volatility. Neural networks, random forests, and a boosting method enter the contest.

Synthetic data with controlled distortions came first, then real market options. The learning models captured nonlinear price patterns the formulas missed. In several settings they beat both traditional benchmarks outright. Feedforward networks and the boosting method looked strongest in the three-stage comparison. Closed-form elegance loses to learned flexibility on messy markets. Hedging and arbitrage both depend on prices being right. Linear and nonlinear distortions stress the models in stages. Constant volatility is the assumption reality violates daily. Data-driven pricing reflects market dynamics the equations idealize away. The title's question gets a qualified yes.
arxiv-2510-01546:
Wang and co-authors give language-vision models the ability to generate images without giving up what they already understand. Unified models often trade away either meaning or fine detail, and hybrid designs break the clean next-token pattern. Their model, Bridge, grows generation onto a pre-trained understanding model through a mixture-of-transformers design.

A two-layer visual code carries compact meaning tokens alongside fine pixel tokens. Understanding scores stayed intact while generation quality climbed toward specialist tools. One prediction stream now handles reading images and producing them. The approach offers a practical upgrade path for the many strong understanding models already deployed. Pure autoregressive design keeps training and serving simple compared with bolted-on diffusion parts. Semantic tokens keep generated scenes faithful to the prompt's meaning. Pixel tokens then restore texture and small detail. Both token kinds share one vocabulary with the text stream.
arxiv-2510-01846:
Provenzano and Ferraresso study how electromagnetic vibration frequencies behave on very thin domains in this 2025 mathematics paper. Their domains are thin tubes built around surfaces inside three-dimensional space. As the tube thickness shrinks toward zero, they track Maxwell's eigenvalues for the full field problem. The question is whether those values settle into a simpler limit.

They prove the Maxwell eigenvalues converge to the Laplacian eigenvalues of the underlying surface. The proof recasts the problem through the Hodge Laplacian acting on differential forms with relative boundary conditions. That limit has sharp side effects for spectral geometry. It yields new domains where the Faber-Krahn inequality fails for Maxwell's eigenvalues. It also produces domains with any chosen number of arbitrarily small eigenvalues. The authors further construct Maxwell eigenfunctions explicitly on product domains, extending older Euclidean constructions.
arxiv-2510-01946:
Master and Moeller recast colored Petri nets as functors in this 2025 category theory paper. Petri nets model systems of processes and resources as places, transitions, and tokens. Colored nets attach extra data to those pieces, which tames repetitive structure in complex systems. Their classical definition, though, hides how the color data acts like a semantic interpretation.

The authors show each colored Petri net is exactly a monoidal double functor from a syntactic category into spans of commutative monoids. That framing yields canonical definitions for standard constructions on colored nets. Morphisms between colored nets become natural transformations between the functors. The unfolding construction, which expands colors away, is characterized through free symmetric monoidal categories. A displayed-category result equates lax double functors with ordinary functors into a reworked domain. The payoff is a compositional foundation for colored nets inside applied category theory. Open nets with boundaries are the conjectured next step.
arxiv-2510-02146:
Požar and five co-authors simulate water-amine mixtures to explain a puzzling X-ray signal in this 2025 chemistry paper. Water-rich amine mixtures show a prominent scattering pre-peak, while pure amines barely show one and water-rich alcohols show none. Atom-level simulations were needed to see what the molecules actually arrange into.

The pair correlation functions revealed micro-segregation rather than uniform mixing. Amine head groups coat the surfaces of water domains, and longer tails stabilize that coating better. The amine regions form disordered bilayers, like an inverse micelle melt or a precursor micro-emulsion. This stable micro-segregation creates the long-range oscillations behind the pre-peak, plus destructive anti-peaks. Only when water dominates and amines grow scarce does the coating fail and demixing threaten. The microscopic picture resolves the scattering paradox completely.
arxiv-2510-02246:
Hosseinabadi and co-authors build a minimal model for atoms held inside optical cavities. Their 2025 physics paper joins two kinds of interaction in one system. Cavity light links atoms across long distances. Excited Rydberg atoms, by contrast, block their near neighbors from firing. That blockade creates strong short-range rules. The team calls the combined setup the squared PXP model. They study it in one dimension under a strong blockade.

At rest, the model shows plain magnetic phases and an ordered Neel phase. Away from rest, special states called quantum scars appear. Scar states keep memory of their start far longer than normal states. Long-range links reshape those scars in new ways. The model gives experiment teams a clean test bed. It also helps theorists compare short-range and long-range forces inside one system.
arxiv-2510-02946:
Lieskovský and co-authors build the simplest possible swinging robot. Brachiation is how gibbons swing hand over hand between branches. Most robots copy it with many linked arms. This one is a single rigid rod. A gripper at each end grabs a horizontal bar. A crank-slide unit shifts the rod's center of mass. That shifting pumps the swing, much like a child on a playground swing.

Two control strategies drive the mass shifting. A bang-bang plan gives the best swing growth in theory. It demands more force than the small motor can give. A second, continuous plan respects the torque limit and the mechanism's shape. It rests on a method that flattens the nonlinear dynamics. Both plans were checked in simulation first. The continuous plan then ran on cheap STM32 hardware. Real tests confirmed both the swing and full rotation stages.
arxiv-2510-03146:
Alvarado-Gómez and co-authors chart the magnetic cycle of a young Sun-like star. The star, iota Horologii, is active and spins fast. HARPSpol watched it for nearly three years of campaigns. Zeeman-Doppler imaging rebuilt its surface field eighteen times. Those maps span about one hundred thirty-nine rotations. The team tracked poloidal and toroidal parts separately.

Toroidal strength pulsed in step with chromospheric activity. For the first time, stellar butterfly diagrams were reconstructed. They trace how magnetic features migrate across the surface. A polarity reversal takes roughly one hundred rotations there. Field-weighted latitudes gave the first drift speeds beyond the Sun. Some features drift poleward while others slide equatorward. Unlike the Sun, axisymmetry rose near activity maxima here. The toroidal-to-poloidal energy ratio followed activity most cleanly. Young dynamos may thus run on a different balance than ours.
arxiv-2510-03246:
Song, Bai, and Zhao make global structured pruning of giant language models fit on ordinary hardware. Pruning trims models, but global methods need memory for everything at once. Local pruning fits one layer yet ignores how layers interact. Structured patterns suit real GPU kernels, unlike scattered zeros. Those patterns suffer most under purely local decisions, though. Their STRUPRUNE framework splits the global problem across modules. An ADMM optimizer coordinates the pieces toward one solution.

A closed-form rule allocates sparsity layer by layer. An energy-based scheme softens that rule into a softmax form. Heterogeneous layer importance shapes the allocation automatically. Memory demand falls from linear to square-root scaling in model size. Billion-parameter pruning becomes practical on limited cards. Experiments on OPT models confirmed the savings. Perplexity stayed close to full global structured pruning. Hardware-friendly masks add real speed at inference time.
arxiv-2510-03346:
Shi, Chiesa, Maguire, and Kostic present a 2025 arXiv paper on how language models in a team can talk to each other more cheaply. Teams of models now tackle hard jobs together, but chat in plain words is slow and lossy. Sharing raw hidden states has its own flaws, including bias and bulk. The authors propose KVComm, which shares selected key and value pairs, the memory traces models keep while reading text.

A scoring rule picks the most informative layers to send, guided by attention strength. In tests across many tasks and model pairs, KVComm matched the score of a no communication upper bound. It did so while sending as few as thirty percent of the layers' pairs in some setups. Communication cost fell by up to three times in the reported runs. Leaner model teamwork could cut the price of agent systems that must reason together at scale.
arxiv-2510-03846:
Howell and Aravkin wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on estimating hidden states of a moving system from noisy measurements. This task, called smoothing, matters for tracking and navigation. Two families of methods compete: unscented Kalman smoothers, which push sample points through the system, and optimization-based smoothers. The authors compare the two families across standard settings.

They show that the classic extended Kalman smoother can be read as an optimization method, which makes fair comparison possible. In their tests, the optimized smoother matched the unscented one when noise was low. It pulled clearly ahead for strongly nonlinear systems and higher noise levels. Extra computing could also improve the optimized result, with no clear way to do the same for the unscented method. The study gives clear guidance on which smoother to pick.
arxiv-2510-04046:
Nishimura, Sakumura, and Ikeda present this 2025 arXiv paper on classifying data where one class vastly outnumbers the other. Imbalance plagues tasks like medical diagnosis and fraud detection, where the rare class is the one that matters. Classifiers trained on such data favor the majority and miss the minority, and standard remedies fail when imbalance is extreme. The authors adapt kernel density estimation so the decision boundary responds to local crowding.

Their method, KOTARO, tunes the width of each Gaussian kernel by the density around its sample. In dense majority regions the kernels shrink, stopping the majority territory from bleeding outward over minority ground. In sparse regions the boundary stays generous, recognizing minority areas that rival methods erase. Experiments on synthetic and real imbalanced datasets showed KOTARO beating conventional approaches. Its advantage was largest under severe imbalance, exactly where help is most needed.
arxiv-2510-04146:
Kim and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper comparing the raw performance of diffusion and autoregressive language models. Autoregressive models generate one token at a time, which keeps arithmetic intensity low and hardware underused. Diffusion language models generate text in parallel, better hardware efficiency. Whether that promise survives long contexts and batched serving was unclear.

Combining theory with profiling, the authors find diffusion models do achieve higher arithmetic intensity across the sequence. Plain diffusion decoding, however, scales poorly as context grows. Block-wise decoding fixes that weakness, keeping the intensity while matching autoregressive scaling to long contexts. Batching flips the verdict: autoregressive models gain more across sequences and win on throughput. Open-source diffusion models could beat autoregressive latency mainly by needing fewer steps. The study gives systems builders a grounded map of when each paradigm pays off.
arxiv-2510-04646:
Johanna Sommer and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on speeding up molecule generation with flow matching models. Such models draw high quality three dimensional molecule shapes, but each shape costs hundreds of network passes. Sampling a million drug candidates at that price is out of reach. The team caches hidden features inside the network and predicts them ahead across solver steps. No retraining of the base model is needed.

The cache works directly on the symmetry aware backbone that these models use. It also stacks with other speedups instead of competing with them. On a standard drug like molecule data set, caching halved the generation time at equal sample quality. Pushed harder, it reached a threefold speedup with only slight quality loss. Combined with other lossless tricks, the total speedup rose to about sevenfold. The method is training free, so any lab can bolt it onto a released model.
arxiv-2510-04746:
Eze, Handler, Kahraman Aliçavuş, Pawar, and Miszuda wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on measuring massive stars that orbit each other. Massive stars show a stubborn puzzle: masses from spectra disagree with masses from evolution models. The likely cause is that models understate the size of the churning core. Eclipsing pairs offer a rare check, since their geometry reveals true sizes and masses. The team adds starquake data, which probes the deep interior directly.

They observed their sample from space with the TESS telescope between 2021 and 2024. Ground spectrographs in South Africa, Chile, Europe, and Slovakia added radial velocity data. Fits yielded the orbital shapes and the absolute sizes, masses, and temperatures of the stars. Seismic analysis then exposed how their cores move and mix. The paper presents itself as groundwork for later theoretical modeling. Precise numbers for these stars will test whether bigger cores fix the mass mismatch.
arxiv-2510-04846:
Aprile and the XENON Collaboration wrote this 2025 physics paper measuring a rare nuclear decay spectrum with a dark matter detector. The XENONnT experiment hunts dark matter underground with a tank of liquid xenon. The same tank records other rare events, including decays of bismuth 214. This decay drops the nucleus to the ground state of polonium 214. Its energy spectrum shape tests nuclear theory and matters for background modeling.

The collaboration measured that spectrum and compared it with calculations. Precise spectral shapes feed the background budgets of rare event searches. A misunderstood decay tail can mimic or mask the signals these experiments seek. Bismuth 214 seeps from radioactivity in detector materials, so its behavior must be known well. The measurement also checks the nuclear models used across the field. Ground state transitions are the cleanest case for such tests. The paper adds a reference spectrum that other low background experiments can reuse.
arxiv-2510-05346:
Hui-Huang Chen solves exactly how a quantum chain evolves after a sudden quench in this 2025 arXiv paper. The starting state is a thermal pure quantum state, already encoding thermal averages. An integrable system like the spin-half XX chain should then simply sit still. Instead, its entanglement evolves in a surprisingly structured way.

Chen derives the behavior three ways: conformal field theory, exact numerics, and a quasiparticle picture. Local observables settle at their thermal values after dephasing. The entanglement entropy, however, rises through a characteristic double plateau. That non-monotonic shape traces to coherent dephasing of anomalous pairing correlations in the initial state. The result defines a third dynamical paradigm, between chaotic stillness and standard non-thermal relaxation.
arxiv-2510-05446:
Zhou and colleagues study how a learning agent can reuse lessons across many tasks. In meta-reinforcement learning, an agent faces a stream of related problems in sequence. Knowledge from early tasks should speed up learning on later ones. Their 2025 paper builds that transfer into Thompson sampling, a classic exploration strategy.

The method assumes that good action values across tasks follow one shared prior pattern. Two algorithms learn that prior from experience, with the second also learning its spread. A new prior-alignment proof links the learned prior to an all-knowing oracle version. The proof yields the first regret guarantees of this kind for finite-horizon tasks. Recipes cover warm starts and prior widening tricks. Simulations on a recommendation setting show the methods beating rivals that ignore prior knowledge. The gains appear once enough tasks have taught the prior, matching the theory.
arxiv-2510-05846:
Lasbordes and Gad specialize small language models for French. Large models remain English-centric, leaving French performance far behind. Small models suffer the gap most, yet adapt cheaply when targeted. Their 2025 Luth family post-trains compact models on curated French data.

Five models span from three hundred fifty million to under two billion parameters. A French instruction dataset of five hundred seventy thousand pairs drives the training. Luth beats every open-source counterpart of comparable size on French benchmarks. English capability survives the specialization intact. Strategic model merging then improves both languages further. The largest average gain reaches about eleven points across six benchmarks. The family sets a new state of the art for French small models. French has over two hundred eighty million speakers worldwide. The recipe transfers plausibly to other under-served languages.
arxiv-2510-05946:
Heilmann and colleagues teach sum-product networks without any party revealing its data. Sum-product networks support fast, exact probabilistic inference. Hospitals and similar parties cannot simply pool sensitive records for training. Their 2025 protocol privately learns both network structure and parameters.

Secret sharing protects privacy against honest-but-curious participants. Privacy holds even if up to half the parties collude. A forest of randomly generated networks is trained and weighted privately. Private inference on new data points follows after training. Log-likelihood matches non-private learning on homogeneous and heterogeneous partitions alike. Scales tested reach one hundred thirty-five features and twelve parties. Homomorphic encryption alternatives can take thirty hours on smaller data. End-to-end runs finish in under an hour at realistic scales. Runtime and memory scale favorably against neural network protocols. Privacy regulation like GDPR motivates the whole design.
arxiv-2510-06346:
Nelson, Rajakumar, and Gullans sharpen the known limits of noisy geometrically local quantum circuits in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Noisy circuits eventually converge to uniform and become trivially simulable. With geometric locality, structured classical algorithms succeed at shallower depths than that trivial limit suggests.

They consider arbitrary local lattice circuits from product states, with depolarizing noise of any constant strength. Once depth passes a threshold scaling like noise inverse times log size, outputs are approximately samplable in quasipolynomial time. The proof rests on new information-theoretic bounds. Local regions decorrelate and turn maximally mixed before the whole system becomes uniform. Structural results suggest a sharper transition at depth set only by the noise rate. After coarse-graining, Pauli weight on long paths truncates with exponentially small error. The percolation-like picture motivates their constant-depth simulability conjecture.
arxiv-2510-06746:
Zhiliang Zhu and four co-authors build a model that removes rain from photographs. Their 2025 paper improves image deraining, which also helps later vision tasks work in bad weather. Recent Mamba-based models handle sequences efficiently. They struggle, though, to keep fine detail and to use frequency information about rain streaks.

Their model, DeRainMamba, adds two new parts to the state space design. A frequency-aware module uses the Fourier transform to separate rain streaks from true fine detail. That balance lets the model erase rain without smearing textures. A multi-directional convolution part then rebuilds local structures from gradient cues in several directions. Tests on four public benchmarks beat leading methods on both quality scores used. The model also needed fewer parameters and less computation than rivals. The authors note that extreme rain still challenges the method. Better generalization to complex storms is their stated next step.
arxiv-2510-07346:
Nemati builds a real-time ship-spotting system for cameras at sea, trained partly on synthetic images. The 2025 paper uses RT-DETR, a fast transformer-based detector. Maritime targets are often tiny and pale against glittering water. Labeled real photos are scarce, so fake ones must help without corrupting judgment. All scoring uses real images only. Multi-scale feature blending sharpens small, low-contrast vessels. A query selection step favors the most reliable candidate detections from the start.

A domain-aware weighting scheme balances synthetic against real training samples. Augmentation also evens out the class mix in the data. On the test collection, the system reached a strong mean accuracy score and beat its baseline. A component analysis shows what each added module contributes. Harbor surveillance and autonomous shipping need detectors that stay fast in ugly conditions.
arxiv-2510-08146:
Sharma and Chopra wrote this 2025 paper using a model's own uncertainty to stop its reasoning early and save compute. The authors compute Shannon entropy from token probabilities as a confidence signal. When entropy stays low, the model likely already has its answer, and generation can stop. Across models and datasets, the framework saved between a quarter and a half of the compute while holding accuracy steady.

The catch is that the signal only exists in some models. Entropy-based confidence calibration appeared as an emergent property of advanced post-training in modern reasoning models. It was absent in standard instruction-tuned and pretrained models tested, including a large Llama model. Where the property exists, the stopping threshold calibrates from a few examples in one shot. Advanced models often know when they are right long before they finish talking. Exploiting that self-knowledge cuts cost and latency.
arxiv-2510-08646:
Eric Hanchen Jiang and co-authors steer language models away from false refusals at inference time in a 2025 arXiv paper. Safety alignment teaches models to reject harmful prompts, but over-caution makes them refuse benign ones too. Their Energy-Driven Steering framework fixes behavior without fine-tuning the model itself. A lightweight external energy-based model scores internal states as desirable or undesirable.

Undesirable states, false refusals and jailbreak successes, get high energy; helpful replies and safe rejections get low energy. During generation, the energy function's gradient nudges hidden states toward low-energy regions in real time. Model weights never change, decoupling behavior control from core knowledge. On the ORB-H benchmark, compliance rose from 57.3 percent to 82.6 percent, while baseline safety performance was maintained across their experiments.
arxiv-2510-08946:
Chen and co-authors force AI-generated molecular structures to obey basic physics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Foundation models now draft the shapes of interacting biomolecules with impressive skill, yet their all-atom structures often place atoms impossibly close, violating simple steric rules. A shape that cannot exist is useless for drug design, no matter how plausible it looks. The team enforces physical validity as a hard constraint during both training and use.

Their module projects each draft structure onto the nearest physically valid arrangement. A Gauss-Seidel scheme, which fixes clashes one neighborhood at a time, makes that projection fast and stable at scale. Because the step is differentiable, models fine-tune through it end to end. With the module in place, just two cleaning steps produced complexes as accurate as leading diffusion systems that need two hundred. The wall-clock speedup was about tenfold, with validity guaranteed.
arxiv-2510-09046:
Yu and colleagues take a census of pulsars, the spinning remains of dead stars, at a low radio frequency, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They mined archival data from the Murchison Widefield Array in Australia, gathered as the sky drifted overhead. Forty-eight such drift scans covered some thirty thousand square degrees, reaching faint sensitivities in the deepest patches. A search pipeline built on standard pulsar software ran on a Chinese SKA computing center.

The search found all eighty known pulsars in its sights, about sixty percent more than the previous census at this frequency. Thirty of them had never been detected at this frequency before, and the paper presents their pulse shapes and brightnesses. The team also measured how the pulses spread and scatter on their way to Earth. Those properties constrain where signals fade at low frequencies and how pulse width grows with spin period.
arxiv-2510-09146:
Mikkola, Acerbi, and Klami reconstruct what an expert believes from nothing but their pairwise preferences, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Asking an expert for a full probability distribution is hopeless, but asking which of two options they prefer is easy. The team's goal is to turn many such comparisons into the underlying belief distribution. The bridge is the winner density, the distribution of whichever option tends to win each comparison.

Winners follow a tempered, meaning flattened or sharpened, version of the true belief. The authors prove the two distributions' score vectors, the arrows pointing uphill in probability, point the same way, linked by a tempering field they can write down and estimate. A diffusion model then learns the winner density from comparisons, and undoing the tempering recovers the expert's belief. In simulations, a few hundred to a few thousand comparisons sufficed to learn complex beliefs over several variables.
arxiv-2510-09246:
Daugulis and co-authors fill in missing entries in a dataset by asking which completed version stays closest to the data's main patterns, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Missing values plague real datasets, and guessing them well, called imputation, shapes everything computed afterward. Their method mixes classical mathematics with a machine learning flavor. The known data is summarized by a flat subspace, spanned by its first principal components, the directions of greatest variation.

A candidate completion is shifted and compared against that subspace, and distance decides the winner. The completion whose geometry hugs the principal subspace most closely supplies the imputed values. The authors work out the solutions explicitly for the Euclidean metric, the ordinary straight-line distance. The appeal is transparency: unlike a black-box predictor, the geometry can be inspected and the choice justified. The paper presents the method as a principled alternative for data scientists facing incomplete tables.
arxiv-2510-09546:
Julia Gehrlein, Joachim Kopp, Margot MacMahon, and George Parker propose a new use for a neutrino detector technique in a 2025 arXiv paper. Upcoming long-baseline experiments, which fire neutrino beams across hundreds of kilometres, will be limited by uncertainty in the beam's flux and in how neutrinos strike nuclei. The PRISM technique answers by measuring the spectrum at several angles to the beam and combining the measurements into a data-driven prediction for the far detector.

The authors ask how far the off-axis measurements alone can pin down the beam model. Their method, called LENS, extracts the fluxes and spectra of the different meson species in the beam separately. They show this sharpened flux model further constrains the far detector prediction. The improvement feeds directly into better oscillation measurements, the experiment's main goal, since the beam is characterised by measurement rather than by simulation alone.
arxiv-2510-09946:
Chen derives a regularity estimate for spacetimes in this 2025 arXiv paper in differential geometry. Regularity asks how smooth the metric of a spacetime must be, given bounds on its curvature. The paper works with any four-dimensional spacetime.

Chen's estimate rests on two a priori bounds, limits assumed before solving. One bounds the Ricci curvature, which measures how spacetime volume bends. The other bounds the Lie derivative of the Lorentzian metric along an arbitrary timelike vector field, which tracks how the metric changes along a flow of time. From those bounds alone, the paper extracts control on the metric's regularity. Such estimates underpin proofs that rough initial data still evolve into well-behaved spacetimes.
arxiv-2510-10246:
Shi, Zhongwen Li, and Xiaoqi Li review password security in this 2025 arXiv paper on system security. System passwords guard login to operating systems and applications, and a valid password opens the door to system resources. Frequent cracking attacks have made password defense a severe concern for information systems.

The authors survey attack and defense mechanisms for system passwords. Attacks range from guessing and brute force to theft of stored password data. Defenses include hashing choices, rate limits, and policy design. Organizing both sides in one review helps administrators see which defenses answer which attacks. The paper treats password security as an ongoing contest, not a solved problem with one best setting.
arxiv-2510-10446:
Makrehchi analyzes reverse supervision in this 2025 arXiv paper on machine learning theory. Standard supervision labels a training set and fits a model. Reverse supervision flips the search: it hunts over labelings of a large unlabeled set, scoring each by error on a small labeled set.

Makrehchi ties this strategy to the economics of annotation, where labels cost money and unlabeled data is cheap. The search space over labelings grows as two to the power of the set size, and the complexity stays exponential even under huge constant-factor speedups from quantum or parallel hardware. That hardness result sets honest limits: reverse supervision cannot be made cheap by hardware alone, so its use must be rationed wisely.
arxiv-2510-10746:
Kshitij Duraphe and eight co-authors mine twelve years of X-ray observations of the black hole Cygnus X-1, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They analyze 26 observations from NASA's NuSTAR telescope, taken between 2012 and 2024. Their timing analysis characterizes how the accretion flow, the gas spiraling into the black hole, varies across spectral states. They find that hard X-rays, from 8 to 79 keV, split into two well separated flux peaks, making them the best diagnostic of which state the system is in.

Characteristic frequencies shift from 0.050 hertz in the hard state to 0.074 hertz in the intermediate state, which the team links to the disk's inner edge moving inward. Time lags between energy bands shrink toward zero in soft states, quantifying the collapse of the hot corona. Most strikingly, one observation caught a failed state transition with anticorrelated band behavior. The authors say this challenges standard transition models.
arxiv-2510-10846:
Kaixuan Ren, Preslav Nakov, and Usman Naseem benchmark how vision language models handle requests that mix harmless text with risky images, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Safety training can backfire into over-refusal, where models decline benign requests from excess caution. The visual side of this problem lacked a systematic benchmark. Their DUAL-Bench tests over-refusal and safe completion, the ideal behavior of fulfilling the benign part of a request while flagging the harmful element.

They evaluated 18 models across 12 hazard categories, using meaning preserving visual perturbations. In dual use scenarios, models showed extremely fragile safety boundaries.
