They fell into a binary trap: either refusing defensively or generating dangerous content. Even the best model, GPT-5-Nano, managed only 12.9 percent safe completion, with the GPT-5 and Qwen families averaging 7.9 and 3.9 percent respectively in the reported results. The authors hope the benchmark pushes alignment strategies that balance safety with usefulness in multimodal systems.
arxiv-2510-10946:
Onil Boussim identifies treatment effects when outcomes are unordered categories, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The setup is an instrumental variables model: a binary treatment, a binary instrument, and an outcome like a chosen category with no natural ranking. Yet most tools in this area were built for ranked or numeric outcomes, not for plain labels. Boussim introduces an assumption called association similarity. For each instrument value, it requires the odds ratio link between potential treatment and outcome to be the same whether the outcome is evaluated under treatment or under no treatment.

Under this assumption plus a testable condition called categorywise dominance, the data pin down the full distributions of potential outcomes exactly, and estimation uses sample frequencies. Boussim also studies weaker limits on departures from the assumption, which lead to sharp partial answers instead. He tests the method on the effect of insurance on health.
arxiv-2510-11046:
The Tutte polynomial is a classic counting tool in graph theory that also encodes information about matroids, abstract structures that generalize the idea of linear independence. Xiaxia Guan, Xian'an Jin, and Weiling Yang study its extension to polymatroids in this 2025 arXiv paper. Earlier work defined the polymatroid Tutte polynomial through a bases expansion and through a rank generating function, and a recursive formula appeared in 2025.

For ordinary matroids, three definitions of it are known to agree, including a deletion-contraction recursion that builds it by removing or shrinking one element at a time. Guan and co-authors show that the existing recursive formula for polymatroids can stand on its own as a definition. That result completes the parallel with the classical theory. It now rests on the same three independent foundations as the original.
arxiv-2510-11146:
Methylidyne, a simple molecule known as CH, is widely used to trace molecular gas, but it is rarely observed in cold, dense clumps. Gan Luo and co-authors observed CH toward 27 Planck Galactic Cold Clumps in this 2025 arXiv astronomy paper. They used the Arecibo 305-meter telescope and combined the CH data with carbon monoxide emission, atomic hydrogen absorption, and dust-based gas column estimates.

The team found CH velocity dispersions that are almost everywhere subsonic, unlike the mostly supersonic carbon monoxide, suggesting CH traces dense, low-turbulence gas. Their upper limits on the cosmic-ray ionization rate favor an attenuation model whose low-energy cosmic-ray spectrum matches Voyager spacecraft measurements. The abundance of CH falls as column density rises and grows with the ionization rate. Fitting the abundance constrains the atomic oxygen and ionized carbon content, linking CH formation closely to ionized carbon regulated by cosmic rays.
arxiv-2510-11246:
Multi-agent systems built from language models let several AI agents collaborate through shared tools, creating attack surfaces that single-agent security work does not cover. Pengyu Zhu and co-authors present the first distributed backdoor attack designed for such systems in this 2025 arXiv security paper. The work is a red-team study: it builds the attack to expose the weakness.

The attack splits a backdoor into small primitives hidden inside the system's tools. Each primitive stays dormant on its own, and the full backdoor assembles only when agents collaborate in a specific sequence, enabling targeted actions such as data exfiltration. The authors also built a benchmark of multi-role collaborative tasks and a sandboxed evaluation framework. In their experiments the attack succeeded more than 95 percent of the time without degrading performance on benign tasks, arguing that defenses must move beyond single-agent protection.
arxiv-2510-11946:
Fabrizio Canfora and four colleagues argue that a crystalline phase of nuclear matter is nearly unavoidable. The chiral soliton lattice is a stack of evenly spaced domain walls made of hadrons. Theory predicts it becomes the ground state of quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons, at high baryon density in a strong magnetic field. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks how robust that prediction is when the underlying model is made more realistic.

From the gauged Skyrme model, they include the electromagnetic field's back-reaction. The lattice survives unchanged. More surprisingly, it survives the sub-leading corrections of the large-color expansion, fiercely nonlinear as they are. The Callan-Witten term lets baryon number appear even where the usual topological charge density vanishes. The magnetic field may even be generated by the hadronic layers. The formulation also opens a way to couple the lattice to quark matter.
arxiv-2510-12246:
Wang and colleagues present PromptFlow, a framework that trains prompts for language models much like neural networks are trained, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Good prompts can adapt a general model to a specialized task without retraining, but writing them by hand is slow and expert dependent. Automated methods exist, yet most use fixed update rules and rewrite the whole prompt at each step.

PromptFlow is modular, combining meta prompts, operators, optimization, and an evaluator in the style of TensorFlow. It explores prompt refinement paths through gradient based meta learning and needs little task specific training data. A reinforcement learning component recycles experience gathered during the prompt engineering process, so past attempts inform later ones. The framework also edits prompt sections at a finer grain instead of replacing everything. Across a range of datasets, the authors report that PromptFlow effectively finds strong prompts and can host the latest optimization methods.
arxiv-2510-12446:
Lu and Xi connect periods of certain automorphic forms to sums of special values of L-functions, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Automorphic periods are integrals of automorphic forms over subgroups, and often encode deep arithmetic information. The setting is a Hamiltonian variety whose dual side has a specific form built from a general linear group and a Levi subgroup.

For some cuspidal Eisenstein series, the authors prove that the associated period equals a fixed sum of special values of L-functions. These L-values come from evaluating the zeta like functions of number theory at specific points. The sum is organized by the fixed points of its associated extended L-parameter acting on the dual variety. The result confirms a conjecture of Ben-Zvi, Sakellaridis, and Venkatesh in this case. That conjecture, part of a broad program linking periods to L-values through duality, gains concrete new evidence.
arxiv-2510-13046:
Jiang and colleagues classify heart abnormalities from electrocardiograms in this 2025 arXiv paper. A twelve-lead ECG records the heart's electrical activity from many angles. Detecting multiple simultaneous abnormalities in these long signals matters greatly for clinical decisions. Residual networks and transformers have been applied, but both struggle when sequences grow long.

Their hybrid model pairs a convolutional front end, which spots local waveform patterns, with Mamba. Mamba is a selective state space model built for efficient sequence modeling. They use a bidirectional variant adapted from Vision Mamba. The pairing strengthens how the model captures dependencies across the heartbeat. On the PhysioNet Computing in Cardiology Challenge datasets from 2020 and 2021, the model scored far higher than the best published algorithms on standard ranking metrics. The authors highlight uses in early diagnosis, telemedicine, and resource-limited care.
arxiv-2510-13246:
Sisodia and Jalan explain how reservoir computing predicts crises in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reservoir computing trains only a simple readout on top of a fixed recurrent network. Yet it forecasts chaotic time series and even discontinuous transitions called crises. In a crisis, a system's attractor suddenly changes size or vanishes. Why the black box works so well was unclear.

The authors dissect good predictions of boundary crises and attractor-merging crises, showing how the reservoir's internal dynamics come to mimic the true system's dynamics. That mirroring lets the reservoir reproduce the correct scaling exponent near a boundary crisis, the number that governs how behavior changes as the crisis approaches. They show the mechanism at work in two distinct test systems, the logistic map and the Gauss map, giving a dynamical explanation that should guide more robust forecasting methods.
arxiv-2510-13646:
Quintela and co-authors compute how strain reshapes light absorption in monolayer CrSBr, a two-dimensional magnet. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a material prized for its high magnetic ordering temperature and stable, lopsided lattice. Its optical response is dominated by excitons, bound electron-hole pairs. Magnetism and optics intertwine here in ways still largely uncharted.

The study is theoretical, working out the material's optical response under several distinct strain layouts. Stretching a sheet that is only one atom thick is easy, so strain is a practical tuning knob. The authors track how each strain pattern shifts the excitonic absorption peaks. They also follow changes in the overall shape of the conductivity response along each direction. Because the lattice is anisotropic, the two in-plane directions respond differently. The work maps a playground for devices that couple light with magnetism.
arxiv-2510-13946:
Rei Nishiura and Tsuyoshi Inoue investigate how cosmic rays, high-energy particles from space, gain energy at shocks driven by ultrafast outflows from active galactic nuclei, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These outflows are winds of gas moving near light speed from the centers of galaxies. A process called the Bell instability can amplify magnetic fields at such shocks, which should help accelerate particles.

The authors use a one-dimensional model that follows cosmic rays, magnetic fields, and the shock together over time. They find a sharp transition set by the background field strength. With weak background fields, the instability amplifies turbulence efficiently and the maximum particle energy settles into a self-regulated state. With stronger fields, the escaping cosmic-ray current is too weak to drive the instability, turbulence decays, and acceleration likely suffers. They discuss whether these shocks could reach the extreme energies needed for PeV to EeV particles.
arxiv-2510-14146:
Arman Maesumi and co-authors introduce PoissonNet, a neural architecture for learning on 3D surfaces such as character meshes, in this 2025 arXiv paper, published in ACM Transactions on Graphics. Mesh learning architectures usually trade off against each other: they may miss high-frequency detail, see a small neighborhood, depend on how the mesh is triangulated, or cost too much to run.

PoissonNet borrows the local-global strategy from mesh processing. Each block applies learned local transformations in the gradient domain of the mesh, then solves a Poisson equation, a partial differential equation, to spread those updates across the surface. This preserves the frequency spectrum, gives a global receptive field, ignores triangulation details, and needs far less computation than other methods. Experiments reach state-of-the-art results on semantic segmentation and on parameterizing detailed animated surfaces. As a headline application, learning deformations of shapes outperforms previous surface-learning methods.
arxiv-2510-14346:
Dingding Li and Chao Zhang prove results for solutions of perturbed fractional 1-Laplace equations, a class of nonlocal equations with singular traits, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The theory asks how smooth solutions must be, which controls whether the answers can be trusted. The fractional 1-Laplacian is a rough one, tied to total variation and image processing.

Assuming weak solutions are locally bounded, the authors show the subquadratic case behaves like the superquadratic case, understood before. Guided by a threshold value of the fractional parameter, they split the analysis into two cases. They establish Sobolev regularity, membership in function spaces with integrable weak derivatives. The result strengthens once it crosses the threshold. Their analysis combines a nonlocal finite-difference quotient method with a Moser-type iteration scheme. It gives a step-by-step approach to such singular problems.
arxiv-2510-14746:
Rémond and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a quantum algorithm for simulating how cracks open in materials, a task that normally eats large amounts of classical computing. Their variational algorithm stores the displacements of a mesh's nodes as quantum amplitudes in a parametrized circuit. The circuit is tuned to minimize the elastic energy of the structure, computed by the finite element method, and the energy needs only a polylogarithmic number of measurements to evaluate.

Once the solution has converged, useful quantities such as the stress intensity factor, which predicts crack growth, can be extracted efficiently. Scaling up is the hard part, because optimization landscapes flatten into barren plateaus. The authors counter with a warm start: solve a coarse mesh first, then remesh finer and reuse the solution. They validated the approach on Quandela's photonic quantum processor, Ascella, and in simulations across growing system sizes.
arxiv-2510-14946:
Aalishah, Navardi, and Mohsenin build, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a navigation system for robots whose computers are too weak for deep learning. Edge devices have little memory and compute, yet navigation needs object detection in real time. The authors pair a reinforcement learning navigation policy with a detector built on Mamba, an efficient architecture. They train it on a dataset of shapes photographed in varied indoor settings.

The detector finds objects and passes their bounding boxes to the policy, which steers toward goals. The student model shrank by sixty-seven percent relative to its teacher. On two edge platforms, an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 5, it used up to seventy-three percent less energy per inference while matching the teacher's performance. In the MiniWorld and IsaacLab simulators, it kept high detection accuracy with thirty-one percent fewer parameters than the baseline.
arxiv-2510-15046:
Yang presents, in a 2025 arXiv paper, an analytic framework for how cosmic structure grows when dark matter comes in several species at once. Mixtures blend parts with varied masses, speeds, and abundances, from cold particles to warm species to sparse objects like primordial black holes or solitons. Two wrinkles matter: each species has speed dispersion, warmth, and discrete populations fluctuate randomly, Poisson noise seeding its own patterns.

It solves a truncated BBGKY hierarchy, the chain linking a distribution to its correlations, by way of Volterra integral equations. An algorithm delivers the total power spectrum plus the spectra within and between species. Worked examples with two-component mixtures show that isocurvature patterns, born from the Poisson noise, and ordinary adiabatic fluctuations evolve quite differently depending on the warm or sparse fraction's properties. Free-streaming and Jeans scales control the outcome, and the results match estimates and N-body simulations.
arxiv-2510-15146:
Qili Hu and seven colleagues report the first femtosecond laser built entirely on a chip, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Femtosecond lasers fire pulses lasting quadrillionths of a second and underpin work from chemistry to precision sensing, but they have stayed bulky bench instruments. Shrinking one onto a chip, within tight size and power limits, had resisted decades of effort.

The breakthrough is a new mode-locking mechanism, the process that keeps a laser's pulses regular, assisted by photorefraction, a light-induced change inside the chip material. Running from a simple low-voltage supply, the device switches on reliably and emits pulses shorter than ninety femtoseconds. Its settings can be retuned electronically, and its optical comb, the evenly spaced set of colors it emits, showed an exceptionally narrow linewidth of 53 hertz. The authors see the result clearing a key barrier for chip-scale sensing, communications, and computing hardware.
arxiv-2510-15246:
Hsuan-Lin Liao and Van Tien Nguyen construct a new kind of failing solution for a model of micro-electromechanical systems, tiny devices where a membrane can snap down and touch an electrode. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies quenching, where the solution reaches zero in finite time and the model breaks down. All earlier quenching examples were radially symmetric, looking the same in every direction from the center.

The pair build a solution on a disc that quenches only at the origin, yet its final shape is genuinely non-radial, depending on direction in a mixed pattern of the two coordinates. To their knowledge it is the first such example. The proof starts from a carefully built approximate solution in self-similar variables. Spectral analysis and an energy method then show a true solution stays close to that approximation all the way to the quench.
arxiv-2510-15346:
Heecheol Yun, Kwangmin Ki, Junghyun Lee, and Eunho Yang ask when combining several language models mid-sentence helps and when it hurts. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies ensembling, where models pool their next-token probabilities to pick each word. Pooling at every token works for short answers, but the team shows it often degrades long-form writing.

Two factors decide where pooling is safe. One is tokenization mismatch, since models chop words into different pieces. The other is consensus, meaning the models roughly agree on what comes next. Their framework, SAFE, ensembles only at points that pass both checks. A sharpening step merges probabilities spread across sub-word pieces of the same word into one representative token. On benchmarks including MATH500 and a broad reasoning suite, SAFE beat existing ensemble methods in accuracy and speed. Remarkably, it gained while ensembling fewer than one percent of tokens.
arxiv-2510-15546:
Marwa Ennaceur and Amel Jadlaoui study Hodge Laplacians, operators that generalize the familiar Laplacian to networks and higher-dimensional meshes, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is weighted simplicial complexes, where edges and triangles carry weights. The key questions are how large these operators can be and when they are essentially self-adjoint, a property that makes their physics and spectra well behaved.

For regular unweighted graphs they prove a clean universal bound on the operator's norm. Weighted versions follow with a sharp comparison constant. The bounds need no assumptions about curvature or geometric completeness, which widens their reach. The approach extends to higher degrees using up and down degree data, and a unitary equivalence links the skew and symmetric versions on colorable complexes. For periodic lattices they compute exact constants, confirming the general bounds grow at the right rate.
arxiv-2510-15746:
Yang Gao and colleagues propose a new way to judge chatbots in a 2025 paper. The models would judge each other. Fixed tests with reference answers fit modern chatbots poorly. Their behaviour is open-ended and subjective. So the authors built a mutual evaluation framework. Models review each other's outputs. They do this through self-play and peer assessment.

Voting methods from game theory then combine the reviews. The output is a ranking of the models. The team compared these rankings with human voting. This tested how well the method matches human judgement. The framework is offered as a scalable option. It suits qualities with no single correct answer. Static benchmarks handle such qualities badly.
arxiv-2510-15846:
Pramod Rao and a large team present a relighting system in a 2025 paper. It works from a single portrait image. It renders the face under new lighting in three dimensions. The problem is underconstrained from one image. A head's geometry, skin material, and lighting must all be rebuilt. Classical pipelines lean on many simplifying assumptions. Those assumptions limit realism.

Their method is called 3DPR. It brings in generative priors. These are patterns learned from large portrait collections. They fill the gaps one image leaves open. The system does not fully split the photo into geometry, material, and light. It leans on the learned priors instead. The result is novel relit views of the head. They stay plausible from new angles.
arxiv-2510-16046:
Xiao Sun, writing alone, frames long-term emotion in small stable groups as a complex system with memory and weak chaos. Short facial clips, the usual data for emotion tools, hide multi-stable attractors, long-range memory, and sparse uneven coupling that unfold over months. CARDIO-Affect models each person's emotion as a multi-stable stochastic system and group emotion as a sparse network with emergent shared states.

Four pillars carry the framework: statistical mechanics with a neural Hamiltonian model, information geometry on a high-dimensional manifold, topological analysis of trajectory signatures, and variability analytics borrowed from heart-rate work. Validation uses a thirty-month in-the-wild facial corpus and reports three testable paradoxes about contagion, persistence, and crisis response. Synthetic tests match a strong baseline on linear data and fail openly on nonlinear data, a limit Sun documents rather than hides.
arxiv-2510-16146:
Thanh-Huy Nguyen and eight co-authors propose DuetMatch, a semi-supervised system for outlining structures in brain MRI scans when only some scans carry expert labels. Teacher-student training is popular for this task, but optimizing the whole network at once can destabilize learning, especially with noisy labels.

DuetMatch splits the network into two branches that take turns: while one branch trains its encoder the other freezes, and vice versa for the decoder. Added pieces include decoupled dropout for steadier predictions, paired CutMix exchanges of pseudo-labels between branches, and a matching step that cleans labels using stable teacher predictions. On the ISLES 2022 and BraTS benchmarks, the system consistently beats earlier methods, showing resilience across labeling conditions.
arxiv-2510-16246:
M Pignatari and ten co-authors trace a radioactive clue left inside ancient dust grains. The grains formed in exploded stars before the Sun was born, and some carry a neon mix that points to decayed sodium-22. That sodium forms when hydrogen seeps into a dying star's helium shell and survives until the blast.

The team's supernova models make sodium-22 mostly in that shell, in amounts spanning a wide range. The decay could feed the fading blast's glow from five hundred days on, for years, before titanium-44 takes over. It would also shine a distinct gamma-ray line that telescopes might catch from a near blast. The same decay may add to a galaxy-wide glow from antimatter electrons meeting their twins. The work links grain chemistry in the lab to what sky watchers might see after the next near supernova.
arxiv-2510-16746:
Aiichi Iwazaki, in a single-author proposal, describes a way to hunt for axions, a leading dark matter candidate, using a cylinder placed in a strong magnetic field. An axion passing through the field should drive a tiny oscillating electric current in the sample. With a very conductive sample, that current stays at the surface.

Iwazaki instead chooses a material with low conductivity, so the current flows through the bulk of the cylinder and grows with its cross-section. For axions in a low mass range, a large sample gives a signal that can rise above thermal noise even at a few degrees above absolute zero. The paper works out the expected current under a standard axion model.
arxiv-2510-16946:
Erfan Darzi, Aldo Pareja, and Shreeanant Bharadwaj hunt sudden slowdowns in shared graphics processors in a 2025 paper. Cloud and supercomputing centers rent GPU power to many users. Brief latency spikes hurt performance and are hard to trace. Existing monitors lack the detail needed for root-cause work.

Their system watches from the host machine using lightweight kernel probes. It links host signals with events inside the graphics processor. In tests it found causes with high diagnostic accuracy. Spikes were flagged within five seconds of appearing. Full root-cause analysis finished in only a few seconds more. The overhead stayed near one percent of processor time. Causes found included network contention, bus pressure, and processor interference.
arxiv-2510-17346:
Splitting a heart sound recording into its beats normally takes deep learning models trained on large labelled sets. Peihong Zhang and six co-authors offer a route that needs far less labelled data. Their system, TopSeg, first turns the sound pattern into shape based features that capture its form at several scales, then a light network reads those features to mark beat boundaries.

Trained only on one public heart sound collection, TopSeg was checked on a second, separate collection. The shape features beat sound picture and envelope inputs, with the widest gaps when training data was scarce. Zhang and her co-authors report that every scale helped, which supports use where expert labels are hard to obtain.
arxiv-2510-17746:
Casey Y. Lam and five co-authors hunt for heavy black holes with old, metal-poor companion stars. Theory says the heaviest stellar black holes form from stars low in metals. A recent find, Gaia BH3, pairs such a hole with a metal-poor giant. The team searched for more systems like it.

They picked about nine hundred candidates from Gaia spacecraft data. The candidates showed odd motion, shifting speeds, and low metal content. The team then took sharp spectra for over six hundred sources. After removing false leads, about fifteen strong candidates remained. Later Gaia data should let astronomers pin down their orbits.
arxiv-2510-17946:
Sanjan C Muchandimath, Joaquim R R A Martins, and Alex A Gorodetsky speed up a costly step in aircraft safety work: estimating uncertain model settings from data. Airflow models are fast but imperfect, and honest error bars matter when planes are certified by analysis. Full Bayesian sampling with pricey simulations runs far too slowly for routine use.

Their method couples transport maps with sampling at several fidelity levels, mixing cheap and costly runs. The mix targets the same answers at a fraction of the cost. For engineers who must state how much a prediction can be trusted, the paper offers a workable path.
arxiv-2510-18046:
Mahsa Valizadeh and three co-authors use language models to enrich the thin records behind shopping recommendations. A recommender that sees only clicks and buys often lacks the context of why a user wants an item. LaMAR asks a language model, with a few examples, to infer hidden aspects of intent and of how items relate.

Those inferred notes, such as use cases and themes, are added back into the behavior sequence. Standard sequence models then performed better across benchmark tasks. Checks suggest the added signals are faithful and readable. Retail and media readers get a way to add meaning to sparse logs.
arxiv-2510-18146:
Konrad Aguilar, Samantha Brooker, and Jack Spielberg build a geometry for a family of algebras tied to irrational numbers. Effros-Shen algebras grow from towers of matrix blocks whose sizes follow the continued fraction of the chosen number. A newer view rebuilds them from a category of paths, with infinite-dimensional stages instead of finite ones.

On that path picture the authors define a spectral triple, borrowing a construction from earlier work. Spectral triples are the core tool of noncommutative geometry, pairing an algebra with a space-like operator. The paper gives this classic algebra family a fresh geometric handle.
arxiv-2510-18346:
Jiayu Zhang, with Shuo Ye and four co-authors, presents AV-Master in a 2025 paper on audio-visual question answering. The task asks models to answer questions using both sound and video together. Long scenes carry much redundant content, and fixed sampling misses the moments a question actually needs.

AV-Master samples adaptively over time, focusing step by step on the most relevant segments. It also weighs each modality, meaning sound versus vision, according to what the question needs. A dual-path contrastive loss, which pulls matching views together and pushes others apart, ties both dimensions together. Tests on four large benchmarks show clear gains on complex questions.
arxiv-2510-18446:
Anna Oliveras and her eight co-authors introduce LAND, a model that creates artificial three-dimensional chest CT scans for training and teaching. Real scans are costly to share, so synthetic scans guided by anatomy maps could help. LAND is a diffusion model, meaning it builds images by removing noise step by step, and it takes three-dimensional masks that outline the lungs and any nodules as its guide.

The model produces full chest volumes at one millimeter detail on a single mid-range graphics card, far cheaper than earlier approaches. Experiments carried a warning: guiding the model with nodule masks alone produced anatomically wrong scans, while adding the whole lung shape fixed the problem. With both guides, LAND can make varied scans with or without nodules of different traits, giving trainers and students fresh material without exposing patient data.
arxiv-2510-18546:
Zebin Yang and his eight co-authors move a robot task onto the device itself. The task is object-goal navigation. An agent must find a named item in a new space. Cloud agents read online maps well. Small local models fail far more on the same maps. Long map text also slows local planning. Their system, EfficientNav, attacks both flaws at once.

A memory step prunes repeated detail from the map. It keeps the parts with real scene meaning. A small model can then grasp the scene. A cache scheme saves past computation for reuse. It groups stored attention data to cut repeated work. Tests used a standard indoor benchmark. EfficientNav beat cloud-based rivals on success rate. It also answered several times faster. Capable home robots, the authors argue, need no remote servers.
arxiv-2510-18946:
Meredith Neyer and six co-authors use the THESAN simulations to test whether Lyman-alpha emitters can reveal the size of ionized bubbles during reionization. Early galaxies lit up hydrogen gas around them, and the bright line they emit is easier to see when the bubble nearby is large.

The team builds realistic emitter catalogs with dust and gas outflow effects, matched to observed counts. Before the midpoint of reionization, galaxies in larger bubbles along the line of sight shine brighter in that line. The link fades as bubbles merge, but early on the emitter share works as a size tracer.
arxiv-2510-19146:
Yoshiyuki Kabashima and Kazushi Mimura build a theory of associative memory. Their networks use neurons with non-monotonic response curves. The classic Hopfield model stores patterns through Hebb's rule. It recalls them by sliding down an energy surface. Older work showed odd neurons can recall far better. No clear theory explained why.

The usual tools fail here, since there is no energy function. The authors use dynamical mean-field theory instead. It tracks recall step by step. Their treatment works for the non-monotonic model. It opens a path to memory networks built to use the effect.
arxiv-2510-19946:
Dylan Hebrail, Óscar Jiménez-Arranz, and Santi Roca-Fàbrega quantify how tidal encounters stir stars radially in galaxies like the Large Magellanic Cloud. Radial migration is usually studied in isolated disks, where bars and spirals do the stirring. The LMC, currently interacting with the Small Magellanic Cloud, is a natural test case. The team used six high-resolution simulations from the KRATOS suite, comparing isolated and interacting versions.

Interacting galaxies show wave-like migration fluxes. These move up to about forty percent of the disk's stellar mass per billion years. They pulse at each close passage of the satellite, almost regardless of disk stability. The waves also dent the inner disk's metallicity by a few percent. The authors propose this tidal migration wave as a new dynamical response with chemical consequences.
arxiv-2510-20746:
Nesta Benno Joseph, Arka Bandyopadhyay, Ajit C Balram, and Awadhesh Narayan propose layered oxide structures as a tunable stage for a nonlinear Hall effect driven by band geometry. In materials that keep time reversal symmetry, a sideways voltage can still grow in a nonlinear way when the band shape has a dipole pattern.

Their stacks alternate thin metal like oxide layers with an insulating ferroelectric layer whose distortion breaks mirror symmetry and allows the dipole to appear. First principles calculations show two allowed dipole parts of equal size and opposite sign. Changing the number of metal layers or swapping the metal atom tunes the effect, pointing to oxide stacks as a flexible test bed for geometric transport.
arxiv-2510-20846:
Dennis Tang leads ten co-authors on ProtoEEG-kNN, an interpretable system for spotting epileptiform discharges in brain wave recordings, a key marker of epilepsy. Even trained neurologists find these spikes hard to catch, yet most machine tools cannot explain their calls, so doctors cannot check or correct them well.

The model reasons by direct comparison, judging a new recording against similar past recordings from its training set. It shows its logic through both spike shape and scalp location, matching how experts weigh evidence. Accuracy reaches the level of leading methods while expert users prefer its explanations over rival approaches, giving clinics a tool whose reasoning can be audited case by case.
arxiv-2510-20946:
Lidiya Ahmed leads four co-authors on calibrating Faraday cup plasma detectors by learning from a well calibrated sister spacecraft in a similar orbit. Ground truth is prepared from the reference craft by aligning time series with dynamic time warping, a pattern matching method.

A neural network then learns to reproduce that ground truth from the target craft raw measurements, even when those measurements are poorly calibrated or taken at low level. Because training targets come from the reference, calibration errors in the target stream do not poison the result. The scheme offers a path to rescue plasma data from aging instruments whose settings have drifted.
arxiv-2510-21746:
Harris Song and Long Le reframe robot control as three-dimensional reasoning instead of learned reflexes. Most vision-language-action models read flat images. They are trained end to end on action demonstrations. That ties them to their training tasks and viewpoints. It also hides their decisions inside opaque policies.

Avi, their architecture, works on 3D point clouds. A multimodal language model predicts the next point cloud of the scene. The robot's action is then computed from that prediction with classical geometric transformations. There is no training on action tokens at all. Because the reasoning lives in 3D, the behavior should survive occlusions and moved cameras. New viewpoints that break flat-image policies should also be handled. Early results support 3D vision-language reasoning as a scalable, sturdier foundation for general robots.
arxiv-2510-21846:
Yongchao Huang, Pengfei Zhang, and Shahzad Mumtaz study membership inference, the attack that asks whether one specific record was used to train a model. A yes answer can expose private data, yet most attack methods need costly shadow models or heavy access to the target, which limits how practical they are.

Their method, GP-MIA, works after the fact from ordinary clues a single trained model leaves behind, such as its accuracy, its uncertainty, and dataset statistics. A Gaussian process classifier then separates likely members from non-members and reports how confident each call is. Trials on synthetic data, fraud records, image benchmarks, and text showed strong accuracy and good transfer, making the approach a lighter and more readable auditing tool.
arxiv-2510-21946:
Kieu Dang, Phung Lai, NhatHai Phan, Yelong Shen, Ruoming Jin, and Abdallah Khreishah attack a defense of commercial language model services. The defense is watermarking. Providers hide faint patterns in their models' answers. Copied services can then be traced. A thief who trains a rival on those answers should carry the mark too.

Their attack is named δ-STEAL, and it breaks that chain. The thief first collects the provider's answers. Then the thief fine-tunes a local model on blurred word embeddings. The blur is tuned to meet local differential privacy. That formal standard limits what any single example can reveal. The laundering strips out detectable watermarks. Yet the stolen model stays useful. Providers take the warning: marks that survive plain reuse may fail against privacy-style noise.
arxiv-2510-22046:
Daniel G. P. Petrini and Braz Izaias da Silva Junior revisit a design exercise in splitting a job between hardware and software. The job is a converter that turns pulse-code signals into pulse-width signals, the core of a Class-D audio amplifier. The question is which parts deserve dedicated circuits and which can run as code.

Working through the SpecC system-level method, first published in two thousand five and reissued with refreshed formatting in twenty twenty-five, the pair modeled the converter, estimated costs, and simulated options quickly. Their chosen partition met real-time demands while avoiding both the price of an all-hardware build and the expensive processor a pure software version would need. The case study argues that system-level co-design pays off early, when architectural insight is cheapest to gain.
arxiv-2510-22146:
Can Cui and Nung Kwan Yip generalize their work on direction-dependent surface motion to containers of any dimension. The flow moves a hypersurface by anisotropic mean curvature, meaning the local speed cares about orientation. At the boundary two different rules are in play across the paper's problems: meet the wall at a prescribed contact angle, or obey a Neumann condition on the slope.

The technical heart is a prior gradient estimate, a bound on steepness proved before knowing the solution, which demands care because the anisotropic operator can degenerate, losing grip in some directions. With the estimate secured over a bounded, strictly convex, smooth domain, both boundary problems yield the same clean conclusion. Solutions converge to a profile that is invariant under translation in time, a shape that travels without deforming.
arxiv-2510-22246:
Keonhee Lee, Seunghee Lee, and C. A. Morales rebuild the idea of topological stability so it depends on a measure, a way of weighing which starting points matter. Classic stability asks whether a system perturbed slightly behaves like the original everywhere. Their version asks the same question relative to a chosen measure, so rare behavior can count for less, or for everything.

The anchor result is clean: a map is stable for the point measure concentrated at one spot exactly when that spot is itself a stable point. On closed manifolds of dimension at least two, stability for finitely supported measures brings a matching shadowing property. The notion survives relabeling by conjugacy and restriction to full-measure invariant sets. For expansive maps, the collection of good measures is convex, and for measures with densities the authors relate their notion back to the established set-valued theory.
arxiv-2510-22346:
Atsuhisa Ota asks whether hot radiation can dress gravity the way a plasma dresses electric fields. In a thermal plasma, soft gauge fields reorganize into collective modes. They gain a gap and Landau damping. For gravity, the thermal scale lands on the Hubble rate. Any such effect lives at the horizon, where the background cannot be treated as still.

Radiation is modeled as a conformal scalar field on an expanding flat universe. Ota computes the linear response to metric ripples on that moving background. The answer is checked against the diffeomorphism Ward identities. The spectrum yields a gapped collective mode set by the expansion rate. Its apparent damping turns out to be the expansion itself, not Landau damping. Tensor modes obey a memory-laden equation. It reproduces Weinberg's classic damping result.
arxiv-2510-23246:
Jonas Thoen Faber and six co-authors study fine structure inside solar flare ribbons, the bright chromospheric footprints where flare energy lands. That fine structure probes how magnetic reconnection accelerates particles during a flare. They combine data from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly with sharp images from the Swedish one-meter Solar Telescope.

Aligned data sets for three flares let them examine ribbon morphology in detail and gather statistics on small features. Patterns at the smallest scales trace the reconnection process itself. Better ribbon statistics help modelers connect telescope images to the physics that powers solar eruptions.
arxiv-2510-23346:
Xinyu Wang, Jonas M Kubler, Kailash Budhathoki, Yida Wang, and Matthaus Kleindessner remove communication overhead when serving many LoRA adapters on a tensor-parallel language model. Serving one base model with several adapters at once cannot merge adapters into the weights, or batching across requests breaks. The S-LoRA sharding strategy aligns adapters with tensor parallelism but still incurs communication cost.

Their block-diagonal LoRA design eliminates that overhead while keeping adapter computation separate from the base model. Cheaper multi-adapter serving lets providers offer many personalized models on shared hardware without a speed penalty.
arxiv-2510-23546:
Rui-Hao Li, Semeon Valgushev, and Khadijeh Najafi work on preparing Gibbs states, the quantum states that describe systems in thermal balance. A key step, computing the von Neumann entropy, is costly and hard to store for large systems. The team uses matrix product states, a compact classical format, to judge and tune the preparation circuits without storing the full quantum state.

They test two circuit layouts on small spin chains, including the transverse-field Ising and XXZ models. One layout, based on a thermofield-double design, did better at high temperature, while a hardware-friendly layout did better when cooling. They also find a ceiling on the entropy the second layout can hold, set by its layering. On larger test grids, an interleaved layout usually cut free-energy errors, though it costs far more classical computing as ancilla qubits grow.
arxiv-2510-23646:
R. Scott Johnson introduces Hamming Graph Metrics, a way to compare graphs by their connection patterns at every distance at once. Classic centrality scores rank how important single nodes are, but they miss whether a network's multi-scale wiring is unusual or redundant. That structural fingerprint matters for judging resilience and function, yet tools for it have been thin.

The framework encodes a graph as a stack of tables recording which node pairs sit exactly k steps apart, for every k. The distance between two graphs is then a Hamming-style count of mismatches across that stack. Johnson proves the measure ignores relabeling, behaves as a true metric, and stays stable when edges change, with explicit bounds. Around it he builds per-scale spectral summaries, node and graph-level dissimilarity scores, and extremal results. The package gives network scientists a principled ruler for structural difference.
arxiv-2510-23746:
Laura Mismetti and three co-authors build a system that reads a molecule's structure straight from its tandem mass spectrum. Mass spectrometry is a workhorse for identifying unknown small molecules in metabolomics, natural products, and environmental work. Yet the shattering process is probabilistic, chemical space is vast, and today's tools mostly match against databases of known spectra or chain several costly steps.

Their transformer framework takes the spectrum plus the molecular formula and generates candidate structures end to end, with no hand-built annotations between. Pretraining on simulated spectra supplies transfer learning, and a test-time tuning step adapts the model to fresh experimental data on the spot. On two benchmarks it beat conventional fine-tuning clearly, and even wrong answers stayed chemically close to the truth, scoring high on structural similarity. The authors pitch the tool as guidance for experts facing spectra nobody has seen before.
arxiv-2510-24046:
Tu Anh Hoang Nguyen and five co-authors propose a new way to make fake table data that still respects cause and effect. Real tables are often blocked by privacy rules, so teams make copies instead. Older methods match basic patterns in the data but can break the links between causes and results.

Their method, CA-GAN, first learns a cause graph from the real data and then builds the fake data step by step along that graph. A reward signal also pushes the fake data to keep the same cause links. Tests show strong use for later tasks while keeping privacy and data quality high.
arxiv-2510-24346:
Benjamin D. C. Lowe and seven co-authors present a detailed chemical analysis of sixteen candidate metal poor stars using the X-Shooter spectrograph. The stars were first flagged by an earlier survey, and the team confirms their low metal content with spectral synthesis software. Six stars prove extremely metal poor, with iron below one thousandth of the solar level.

Two of those stars, including the most metal poor in the sample, are kinematically tied to the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger event, raising its known extremely metal poor members to eight. The team measures abundances for sixteen elements, generally matching high resolution studies. This is the first paper in a series on unusual chemistry in halo stars.
arxiv-2510-24446:
Viktoriia Zinkovich leads a team of nine authors on AI vision safety. Reasoning segmentation asks a model to outline things named in words. A user might ask for the object that fits a short text clue. Past safety work mostly warped the image to fool the model. The team instead warps the words while keeping the same meaning.

Their method, SPARTA, rewrites a query so the mask gets worse. The rewrite must stay smooth, grammatical, and true to the first sense. A text autoencoder gives a small space where rewrites are searched. Learning from rewards guides that search without seeing model internals. SPARTA beat prior methods by up to two times on two data sets. Even top models proved weak against careful word swaps.
arxiv-2510-25546: Tommaso Grigoletto, Lorenza Viola, and Francesco Ticozzi shrink models of quantum systems. Their 2025 paper deals with Markov type systems under outside control. The rules of motion change with time in such systems. Their method builds on Krylov spaces and algebra tools made for fixed rules. The small model tracks the key read-outs of the full one in an exact way. It also keeps the Lindblad form that such rules must have.
arxiv-2510-25646:
Elias Fink, Carlo Contaldi, and Giorgio Mentasti cross-correlate gravitational wave observables. Astrometric and timing residuals from distant sources are mixed. Pulsars and galaxies supply those distant observables. Nearby solar system bodies give equivalent observables. A unified spin-weighted formalism derives angular correlations.

They compute expected signal-to-noise and sensitivity for readings. Focus falls on pulsar timing array redshift signals. Pulsar-only surveys currently constrain backgrounds more strongly. The method offers a complementary higher-frequency probe. Future wide-field surveys could reach sub-milliarcsecond precision. That could make the method viable for finding. Varied reading domains share fewer systematic errors. The technique bridges pulsar and LISA frequency bands.
arxiv-2510-25846:
Luis A. Anchordoqui, Dieter Lust, and Severin Lust set out a short note on what they call species quantum mechanics. In gravity theories, the species number counts how many light particle types exist, and a tower mass scale marks where a tower of heavy states begins. Both ideas appear in the swampland distance idea, which limits how far field values can move in a valid theory.

Anchordoqui and his co-authors treat the species number and tower scale as quantum operators with partner variables. They discuss the commutation rules, a possible wave function, and duality swaps between the partners. They argue a known pattern in these theories follows from those basic rules, and they link the setup to Calabi Yau geometry.
arxiv-2510-25946:
Brandon Massett and Walter Shmayda test whether a saturated drying bed can prefer heavy water over light water. Dryer beds with molecular sieves, materials full of tiny pores, are used in fusion plants to trap tritiated water vapor, where tritium is a heavy form of hydrogen. A passive control system could exploit a bed that favors heavier forms of water.

Massett and Shmayda send a humid heavy water stream through a bed first saturated with light water. Clear displacement appears, as heavy water takes over and light water leaves. After capture, the rise in heavy water pressure depends on its humidity, with higher humidity giving faster, steeper transfer that fits a sigmoid curve well.
arxiv-2510-26246:
Alcides Gomes Andrade Junior and Akira Matsubayashi show a limit on using quantum walks to solve the maximum matching problem. A matching pairs up vertices of a graph, and the maximum matching problem asks for the largest possible set of pairs with no vertex reused. Quantum algorithms are judged by query complexity, the number of input lookups, and the best known quantum algorithm beats the trivial bound but may not be optimal.

Quantum walks turn a classical random walk search into a quantum search and have given tight results elsewhere. Andrade Junior and Matsubayashi prove that, when the underlying classical walk does not depend on the input graph. In that case this technique cannot improve the known query bound. Any such design also carries a time cost beyond polynomial limits in their analysis.
arxiv-2510-26346:
Robin Schmöcker, Alexander Dockhorn, and Bodo Rosenhahn study how game-playing search programs can work faster. Their field is Monte Carlo tree search, a method that tests many possible moves and keeps score for each. Grouping states that act alike lets a program share those scores, but in noisy games or games with many moves, such groups are hard to find.

The three authors prove why the groups stay rare, then loosen the grouping rule a little. Their method, called IPA-UCT, gives up a small amount of exactness and finds far more groups. In tests across many domains and time budgets it beat the older OGA-UCT method. The paper also shows how both methods fit inside one wider frame.
arxiv-2510-26846:
Tomasz Matulewicz reports a measurement from the NA61/SHINE experiment at CERN that models of hadron production cannot explain. Isospin symmetry, rooted in the similar masses of up and down quarks, predicts equal numbers of charged and neutral kaons from collisions of isospin-symmetric nuclei. The experiment measured kaon production in argon-scandium collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of eleven point nine giga-electronvolts per nucleon pair.

Matulewicz reports that charged kaon production at mid-rapidity is about eighteen percent higher than neutral kaon production. The stated uncertainty is about six percent. Models of hadron production, including the known effects that break isospin symmetry, fail to account for the gap. The result stands as an open puzzle for hadron physics.
arxiv-2510-26946:
Rebeca Beltran, Chandan Hati, Martin Hirsch, and Ana Martin-Galan study two proposed new particles at the Large Hadron Collider. Heavy neutral leptons are heavy cousins of neutrinos, and axion-like particles are light particles that may link to them. If the second type couples strongly to gluons, the particles that hold quarks together, the collider should make many of them.

The team simulates how future detectors, including the main ATLAS detector and planned far detectors, could spot long-lived heavy neutral leptons made through this route. For very heavy axion-like particles, production acts through a high-order interaction with gluons. The results map where the high-luminosity collider could reach new ground.
arxiv-2510-27246:
Mohammad Tavakoli leads five co-authors in BEAM, a benchmark for long-term memory in language models, plus LIGHT, a memory system that improves it. Existing memory tests often lack narrative coherence, cover narrow domains, and probe only simple recall. The team first builds a framework that auto-generates long, coherent, diverse conversations up to ten million tokens with probing questions across many memory abilities.

BEAM itself holds a hundred conversations and two thousand validated questions. Even models with million-token windows, with or without retrieval help, struggle as dialogues lengthen. LIGHT adds three human-inspired stores: episodic long-term memory, short-term working memory, and a scratchpad for salient facts. It improves every backbone tested, and ablations confirm each component contributes, clarifying what long conversations demand.
arxiv-2510-27446:
Daniel Plummer, Pontus Svensson, and four other co-authors model hot, dense plasma with moving wave packets in this 2025 paper. Dense plasma, gas stripped of electrons at high pressure, sits inside stars and fusion tests. Part of it stays ionized, part binds back into atoms. Tracking both parts at once is hard.

Their method, wavepacket molecular dynamics, follows atoms as fuzzy packets rather than points. A chemical model counts bound states, the allowed orbits of still-attached electrons. Charge shares come from minimizing free energy, the usable energy of the system. Hydrogen serves as the test case. They compare steady traits like structure against path integral Monte Carlo data, a trusted heavy method. The comparison shows where their lighter model's shortcuts hold and where they strain.
arxiv-2511-00146:
Michael Landry and Mingda Li introduce chimeric states of matter, phases where traits of broken and unbroken symmetry coexist in a way enabled by mixed anomalies of higher-form symmetries. Ordinary sorting says solids break translation symmetry and superconductors break gauge symmetry, but anomaly-based generalization widens the options. Their headline example concerns the Meissner effect, the pushing out of magnetic fields taken as the key sign of superconductivity.

Using an effective field theory building, they show that effect can occur in media that are lossy or even insulating under electric probing. Condensed matter readers get a phase concept that scrambles textbook expectations, splitting magnetic pushing out from superconductivity itself.
arxiv-2511-00346:
Kayua Oleques Paim and four co-authors report an attack method against large language models that exploits gaps in their latent space, the internal map where meanings are encoded. Sparse training data leaves discontinuities in that map, and the authors craft inputs that steer models through them. The aim is twofold: universal jailbreaks that bypass safety rules, and extraction of data the model should not reveal.

Unlike many earlier attacks tuned to one system, theirs transferred across seven leading language models and one image generator. Even layered defenses failed to hold consistently in their tests. The authors frame the flaw as architectural, not a surface bug, which would make it a systemic risk that model makers need to address at the design level.
arxiv-2511-00446:
Xin Yao and five co-authors attack CLIP, the model that learns to match images with text from web-scale data. Because CLIP trains on uncurated internet pairs, poisoned data can plant hidden backdoors. Most studied attacks poison images, leaving the text channel oddly unexamined. Their framework, ToxicTextCLIP, crafts adversarial texts that corrupt the model during pre-training itself.

Two hurdles shape the design: poisoned texts must fit the target class's background, and such background-matched texts are scarce. A selector picks texts whose backgrounds align with the target, and an augmenter generates more coherent, varied samples in that style. In classification and retrieval tests the attack reached very high poisoning and backdoor success rates, and it slipped past three published defenses. The study exposes text as a serious entry point for supply-chain attacks on foundation models.
arxiv-2511-00546:
Loukas Kokkinos and Joo-Von Kim survey the behavior of spin-torque vortex oscillators, nanoscale devices where magnetic vortices spin and emit microwave signals. Most studies fix one layer as a polarizer that drives the other. Here both layers are free vortices, and each acts as the moving polarizer for the other, doubling the interplay and the possible dynamics.

Extensive micromagnetic simulations, run with the open-source Mumax3 code and the authors' own coupled equations, map how the relative vortex arrangement and layer asymmetry shape current-driven motion. Regimes include self-modulated gyration, where the orbit rhythmically swells and shrinks, and a distinct C-state pattern. Chaotic transitions between steady gyration and the C-state also appear. The overview helps designers predict which regime a dual-layer device will land in.
arxiv-2511-00746:
Andrew Moore links two computing worlds that rarely meet: Ising machines and neural networks. Ising model computation powers quantum annealers, adiabatic quantum computers, and thermodynamic classical devices, and tradition equates the computed answer with the machine's ground state, its lowest energy configuration. Moore generalizes the picture from ground states to spin averages, letting computation happen at high temperatures instead of only in the cold ground state.

On that basis he builds a systematic correspondence between Ising devices and neural networks, plus a simple method to run trained feed-forward networks on Ising-type hardware. A mathematical proof shows these implementations always succeed. For builders of unconventional hardware, the result means a trained network need not wait for specialized chips: it can be compiled onto the physics of spins.
arxiv-2511-00846:
Zhihao Peng and a large team introduce OmniBrainBench, a benchmark for testing how well multimodal language models read brain images. Existing question answering benchmarks cover few imaging types or only coarse descriptions of disease, so they miss much of the clinical workflow.

The benchmark spans fifteen imaging modalities from thirty verified medical sources, with more than nine thousand validated question pairs and over thirty thousand images. Its fifteen tasks follow clinical stages and were checked by a professional radiologist. Testing twenty four leading models, the team finds the best proprietary model scores far below physicians. All models struggle with complex reasoning before surgery, exposing a gap between seeing an image and clinical judgment.
arxiv-2511-00946:
Fenglong Song, Roland Schwan, Yuwen Chen, and Colin Jones speed up a core computation inside the PIQP optimization solver. Multistage problems, such as model predictive control and racing trajectory planning, repeatedly produce Karush-Kuhn-Tucker systems, the linear equations an interior point method must solve at every step.

Their contribution is a parallel Cholesky factorization and triangular solve designed for the block structured matrices these problems generate, with a banded part plus an arrow shaped border. It is implemented as a new backend for PIQP and released as open source. On chain of masses benchmarks and on a minimum curvature racing line problem, the solver shows substantial speed gains over other state of the art solvers.
arxiv-2511-01046:
Vedant Acharya and colleagues show VayuChat, a conversational tool for air quality analysis in India, where air pollution contributes to about one point six million early deaths each year. The data needed for decisions sit scattered across agencies, and existing tools demand expertise and offer only static dashboards.

VayuChat lets users ask plain language questions about air quality, weather, and policy programs. Answers come back as both executable Python code and interactive charts. The system unifies monitoring data from the Central Pollution Control Board, state level demographic data, and funding records from the National Clean Air Programme, all driven by a large language model. The platform is publicly deployed for policymakers, researchers, and citizens.
arxiv-2511-01446: Eva Horvat studies the symmetries inside a link diagram's cube of smoothings, a knot theory structure where each crossing can be resolved in two ways, generating a cube of related surfaces. A labeled barycentric subdivision adds extra combinatorial structure to that cube. She studies the symmetries preserving this structure, and from them constructs a combinatorial link invariant based on the symmetries of triangulated smoothings.
arxiv-2511-01646:
Bastian Castorene, Francisco Peña, Martin Groves, and Patricio Vargas count, exactly, the states of a classic magnet model at its critical point. The one-dimensional antiferromagnetic Ising chain, spins on a line preferring to oppose their neighbors, has a ground-state level crossing when the magnetic field reaches twice the coupling strength.

At that crossing, the number of ground states follows the Fibonacci sequence for open chains and the Lucas sequence for closed rings. The authors extend the counting to the full excitation spectrum: states are built from topological defects counted through Diophantine equations and repeated Fibonacci convolutions. Open chains step through energies in units of twice the coupling, rings in units of four times, and near full polarization some top energy levels are strictly forbidden. Closed forms and residual entropies follow.
arxiv-2511-01846:
Thang Luong and a large team of collaborators introduce IMO-Bench. It is a benchmark suite pitched at the level of the International Mathematical Olympiad. It measures real mathematical reasoning in foundation models, rather than easy short answers. Every problem was vetted by a panel of top specialists.

IMO-AnswerBench holds 400 diverse Olympiad problems with verifiable short answers. IMO-ProofBench goes further, grading full proof writing at basic and advanced levels with detailed grading guidelines for automatic scoring. The benchmarks were central to the team's gold-level Gemini Deep Think result at IMO 2025. The model scored 80 percent on AnswerBench and about 66 percent on the advanced ProofBench. It beat the best non-Gemini models by wide margins. A companion GradingBench, with a thousand human-graded proofs, supports progress in automatic evaluation.
arxiv-2511-02046:
Soham Joshi, Shwet Kamal Mishra, and Viswanath Gopalakrishnan tackle a data bottleneck for systems that answer questions about text visible in images, such as signs and labels. Building such datasets normally needs skilled human annotators, which is slow and costly. Their alternative is an automated pipeline that manufactures question and answer pairs from scene text in a given image.

The pipeline chains optical character recognition, region detection, caption generation, and question generation, then validates what it produces. The authors report a dataset of about seventy-two thousand question and answer pairs drawn from about forty-four thousand images. They present the method as the first pipeline able to synthesize and check a text-based visual question answering dataset at this scale.
arxiv-2511-02546:
M. H. Naghizadeh Ardabili, Omid Yahyayi Monem, Morteza Nattagh Najafi, and Hosein Mohammadzadeh invent a dial that slides between bosons and fermions, the two great families of quantum particles. Bosons follow Bose-Einstein statistics and fermions Fermi-Dirac statistics. Haldane's exclusion statistics long ago pointed to something in between. Their alpha scheme, built around a changed filling weight, slides between the two. For negative values of its dial setting, it pushes past bosons into a hyperbosonic regime.

Thermodynamic geometry supplies the test: the sign and singularities of its curvature reveal whether the interactions act attractive or repulsive. A crossover temperature marks where the curvature flips sign. Its ratio to the condensation temperature depends only on the dial's setting. In that regime it blows up at certain fugacities, signalling condensation unlike usual Bose condensation.
arxiv-2511-02946:
Srikumar Sastry and six colleagues introduce ProM3E, a model that embeds ecology data of many kinds into one shared space. Field ecology mixes photos, sounds, and text, and a useful model should generate any missing kind from the ones at hand. Their 2025 model learns by masked reconstruction in the embedding space, hiding one modality and inferring it from the rest.

Because the model is probabilistic, it can judge which modality mixes are feasible for a task, in effect learning what is worth fusing. It also supports flipping a query inside the embedding space. Their retrieval method blends cross-modal and same-modal similarity and topped all retrieval tests they ran. Linear probes on the hidden features further showed strong representation learning for ecology tasks.
arxiv-2511-03146:
Kaiyuan Zhang and twenty-one colleagues built MME-CC, a benchmark that probes the visual thinking of multimodal models. Existing tests lean on text reasoning or skip whole kinds of visual cognition. Their 2025 benchmark organizes eleven tasks into three groups: spatial reasoning, geometric reasoning, and knowledge-based reasoning, all grounded in images, with fine-grained scoring per group.

Sixteen leading models took the test. Closed models led overall, with the best near 43 points against about 30 for a strong open rival. Spatial and geometric reasoning stayed weak almost everywhere, at or below thirty percent. The team catalogued common errors: flipped orientations, losing track of objects across views, and ignoring counterfactual instructions. Thinking traces tended to run in three stages: extract, reason, then verify.
arxiv-2511-03446:
Anwesh Ray and Tanushree Shah study the zeros of Alexander polynomials for torus knots and links through an arithmetic lens. The knot-prime analogy has long guided such work. Their family wraps a torus with two winding numbers, and the polynomial is taken against the total linking cover.

As both windings grow, the zeros spread evenly around the unit circle. The authors give an explicit rate at which primitive roots of unity appear among them. A moment sequence for the zero pattern gets a closed-form generating function, capturing finer statistics. Iwasawa invariants for the linked branched covers are also determined, plus growth control from a logarithmic measure. Knot theory and number theory meet cleanly in the shared formulas.
arxiv-2511-03946:
Marcelo P Fiore, Ohad Kammar, Georg Moser, and Sam Staton develop modular abstract syntax trees for programming languages that include second-class sorts. Some calculi, such as call-by-value lambda calculus and call-by-push-value, forbid certain sorts from appearing in variable contexts, which breaks the standard treatment of syntax with binding and substitution.

Banning second-class sorts from variable contexts changes the algebraic picture from monoids in monoidal categories to actions in actegories, the authors argue. Much of the classic development is rebuilt through bicategorical arguments. As an application, substitution lemmas for varieties of call-by-value calculus are proved, giving language designers a firmer formal base.
arxiv-2511-04046:
Guoming Zhang, writing alone, tackles the Kato problem for degenerate elliptic operators of arbitrary even order in weighted spaces. Coefficients are measurable and complex-valued. They satisfy a Garding inequality against a Muckenhoupt weight, extending earlier work by Cruz-Uribe, Martell, and Rios to this broader setting.

As an application, the unweighted Dirichlet, regularity, and Neumann boundary value problems for such operators are solved when the exponent lies close enough to two. Kato-type results link a hard square-root estimate to well-posed boundary problems. Extending them to higher order, degenerate, weighted operators widens the class of equations with a firm boundary theory.
arxiv-2511-04146:
Xiumin Huang, Dong Lai, and Bin Liu calculate the largest eccentricity an inner binary can reach in a restricted hierarchical three-body system. An outer companion perturbs the pair there, and general relativity pushes back. Octupole-order effects can drive extreme eccentricities and orbital flips, while short-range forces can cap that growth.

In highly hierarchical systems, double averaging works well, and flipping orbits share one limiting eccentricity computable from the quadrupole Hamiltonian alone. Adding the Brown Hamiltonian correction for moderate hierarchy does not change that limit. Single-averaging analysis completes the picture. Knowing the cap matters for systems from satellite-planet-star triples to binaries near supermassive black holes.
arxiv-2511-04546:
Goureesankar Sathyanathan and two colleagues improve how sky maps separate signal from foregrounds. Component separation must pull the faint cosmic microwave background out of brighter galactic emission. If the noise model is wrong, the recovered maps and spectral laws pick up bias.

Their extension models linked low-frequency noise as a power law in harmonic space. A modified ridge method sits inside an ensemble-average process for the fit. They derive an analytic correction for the bias that noise creates in foreground leftovers. Tests serve as proof of concept for cleaner microwave background maps from future surveys.
arxiv-2511-04646:
Narjes Nourzad leads four authors with DR. WELL, a framework for embodied multi-agent teamwork. Robot teams must plan together with partial views and limited communication. Planning raw trajectories fails easily, since small timing slips cascade into conflicts.

Symbolic planning raises the level of abstraction and gives agents a shared action vocabulary. DR. WELL runs a two-phase negotiation: agents propose roles with reasons, then commit jointly. Consensus and environment limits shape the final allocation. Each agent then plans and acts on its own symbolic share, which keeps coordination stable while work proceeds.
arxiv-2511-04846:
Jonathan Shaki and two colleagues ask how a principal can persuade agents into a stable matching. Two-sided matching pairs agents by preference, and stability depends on those preferences. In uncertain settings, preferences also reflect what agents believe about the world.

The principal sees the true state and can shape beliefs through Bayesian persuasion. The goal is a stable matching that scores best on the principal's own utility. General cases are intractable on both the matching and persuasion sides. Two special cases get the focus: few agent types, and a second structured setting the authors develop.
arxiv-2511-04946:
Lei Chen and co-authors look at fully homomorphic encryption from the side of storage input and output. This form of encryption lets a machine compute on locked data, which guards user privacy, but its real-world speed has a less studied weak point.

The team tests how storage traffic slows such systems in practice. They report that slow storage can cut the speed of special chips by a very large factor, and can slow graphics chips by a large factor too. Their lessons show where builders must fix data flow, not just math.
arxiv-2511-05146:
Luigi De Masi and co-authors give two variational forms for robust optimal transport, where a network must still partly work when parts of it are damaged. The task weighs build cost against the gain of keeping some flow after harm.

One form models the network as a measure and repair plans as currents, and lets flow switch path after damage, though damage is set as whole closed sets. The other form tracks paths directly. Both frames give math tools to design transport that degrades with grace, a need for roads, grids, and supply lines.
arxiv-2511-05346:
Olaf Adan, Dimitra Dritsa, and Steven Houben introduce semantic interactivity, a way for people at one table to act on a shared display through meaning, not just touch. Most team systems back solo tasks done side by side, not true joint acts.

Their mechanism uses language processing to let a group shape shared content together. It was built into CollEagle, a tabletop system for joint externalization, where a team makes its thoughts visible. The work argues that shared sense-making needs tools built for the group act itself, not a stack of single-user tools.
arxiv-2511-05446:
Zehua Cao and co-authors compute a two-loop correction to superallowed beta decays, the decays that give the sharpest value of the quark mixing term Vud. That reading rests on exact radiative corrections, counted as a series in the charge of the nucleus and the fine structure constant.

They give the first model-free result for the long-distance part at this order, with nuclei treated as heavy point particles. A renormalization group study adds new terms at the next order for double-log parts. Tighter corrections mean a tighter test of whether quark mixing sums as the standard model demands.
arxiv-2511-05746:
Nicola Bariletto, Nhat Ho, and Alessandro Rinaldo make a classic stats method work where its usual summaries break down. Bayesian methods state doubt as a spread of likely values after seeing data. But when the unknown is a grouping of data, or lives in an endless space, a mean or a standard range may not exist at all.

Their method, Conformalized Bayesian Inference, treats the task as a forecast over the space of guesses. From samples alone it gives a best guess, a range with a coverage promise that needs no added premises, and a map of the spread's peaks. A grouping step picks out the main peaks. Tests on fake and real data show the method works at scale.
arxiv-2511-05946:
Ba-Thinh Nguyen and co-authors read pulse signals from face video alone, a technique called remote photoplethysmography. Tiny color changes in the skin betray heart and breathing rates, enabling contactless checks for telemedicine, driver monitoring, and more. The pulse is strongly periodic, yet past methods model that rhythm only weakly.

Their framework, Reperio-rPPG, mixes a relational graph network with a graph transformer to capture the repeating structure of the signal. A tailored mixing augmentation widens the training variety, since data sets in this field are narrow. On three benchmarks the method reached state-of-the-art results. It stayed robust under head motion like talking and walking, and under lighting from dim LED to bright natural light.
arxiv-2511-06146:
Akshar Tumu, Varad Shinde, and Parisa Kordjamshidi use referring expressions, phrases that single out one object in a scene, to probe spatial understanding in vision-language models. Spatial reasoning is core to human cognition, and current models show strain there. Most tests lean on captioning or question answering, which probe the skill only shallowly.

Their platform stresses three hard cases: ambiguous detection, long expressions stacking several spatial relations, and expressions using negation. Both specialized architectures and large models were tested. All struggled, but their strengths split by the kind of spatial meaning involved, such as topological versus directional relations. The authors map which spatial semantics break which models, and point to the research gaps that follow.
arxiv-2511-06446:
Bohan Yu, Wei Huang, and Kang Liu plug live knowledge bases straight into a language model's memory. Retrieval pipelines usually fetch facts with an outside search tool before the model reads them, a chain that can break or lag. SR-KI instead encodes a knowledge base as key-value pairs and loads them into the model's own cache.

Training runs in two stages: first find the model layer best suited to retrieval, then supervise attention at that layer toward the right entries. Retrieval then happens inside the model during a single pass, and updates stay dynamic. The system held forty thousand entries in a seven-billion-parameter model on one graphics card with strong recall.
arxiv-2511-06546:
Nagaraj Vernekar and colleagues introduce LRPayne, a tool that reads stellar chemistry from blurry, low-resolution starlight. Big galactic surveys gather spectra too coarse for classic analysis, yet each spectrum hides a star's temperature, gravity, and elemental mix. A model-driven neural network trained on seventy thousand synthetic spectra does the decoding.

The network predicts what a spectrum should look like for any set of stellar labels, covering two dozen elements. Fitting an observed spectrum then reduces to finding the synthetic match with the smallest error. Tests on benchmark stars and metal-poor stars agreed well with published values for most elements, though a few, like oxygen, stayed stubborn in certain star types.
arxiv-2511-06846:
Federico Vasile, Ri-Zhao Qiu, Lorenzo Natale, and Xiaolong Wang estimate the physical features of objects from video, a task called system identification. Recent methods optimize geometry, appearance, and physics together using differentiable simulation, but they assume flat surfaces for collisions. Real objects collide with curved, complex shapes, where those methods fail.

Their system, AS-DiffMPM, extends the differentiable Material Point Method with a collision mechanism that handles arbitrarily shaped rigid bodies while keeping the whole pipeline differentiable. A falling or rolling object can thus be fitted against the true geometry of what it hits. The system plugs into various novel view synthesis methods, widening the range of scenes where substance features, shape, and appearance can be recovered from plain video observations.
arxiv-2511-07046:
Fabian Kresse and Christoph H Lampert shrink continuous-control reinforcement learning policies until they run on integer-only hardware. Embedded deployments face tight latency and power budgets that small FPGAs can meet, but only if floating-point pipelines are avoided. The authors study quantization-aware training for such policies and build a learning-to-hardware pipeline that automatically selects low-bit policies and synthesizes them onto an Artix-7 FPGA.

Across five MuJoCo control tasks, the selected networks stayed competitive with full-precision policies while using as few as three, or even two, bits per weight and activation. That holds provided input precision was chosen carefully. On the chip they answered in microseconds and consumed microjoules per action, beating a quantized reference design.
