Message passing, run in sync and out of sync, spreads that agreement across the whole plan with no new training. Tests beat earlier baselines and reached start-goal pairs never seen in training. Long plans stay coherent because every seam is checked.
arxiv-2603-03546:
Radu-Andrei Cioacă and five colleagues fuse satellite and inertial navigation in real time, loosely. Autonomous systems need precise positioning, and satellite signals falter exactly where streets get interesting. Factor graph optimization, which blends satellite fixes with motion-sensor data on one graph, is accurate but usually too heavy for live use. Their 2026 paper builds a loosely coupled version and tests whether it can run in real time.

Loose coupling merges finished position solutions rather than raw signals, which keeps the graph light. On a Hong Kong urban dataset known for canyon-like streets, the method ran in real time and stayed available more often than batch processing versions. The gain costs some positioning accuracy. The authors map the three-way trade-off between accuracy, availability, and computing effort in detail, giving designers honest numbers for live systems.
arxiv-2603-03646:
Mohamed Elmoghany and twenty-nine colleagues, from Adobe Research and partner institutions, generate story videos that can run for an hour without losing the plot. Long-form synthesis usually breaks three ways: backgrounds morph between shots, characters pop in and out, and quality collapses as length grows. Their 2026 framework, InfinityStory, attacks all three, with character-aware transitions as its signature.

A background-consistent pipeline holds scenery, character identity, and spatial relations steady across scenes. A transition module then choreographs smooth shot changes for several subjects entering or leaving the frame at once, beyond the single-subject limits of earlier work. A synthetic dataset of ten thousand multi-subject transition sequences trains the skill. On the standard VBench suite, InfinityStory records the highest background and subject consistency scores and the best overall average rank.
arxiv-2603-04246: Wu, Lindgren, and Hanson study areal disaggregation from a small area estimation perspective. Yet many surveys release outcomes only at coarser levels, limiting relevance for choice-making. They propose a fully Bayesian, one-stage spatial models method for areal disaggregation generating fine-scale indicator figures straight from coarsely aggregated survey data.
arxiv-2603-04446: Nordlund and Jiao present Threadle, a memory efficient network engine in C#. Population networks hold millions of nodes and billions of edges, and old libraries handle two mode data poorly. Threadle queries two mode layers as one mode layers without building the heavy projection. A 20 million node network equal to 8 trillion projected edges fits in about 20 GB, above 2000 to 1 compression. Multilayer support, an attribute manager, and a large command CLI complete the tool, plus an R frontend.
arxiv-2603-04546: Okoroafor and colleagues push hybrid online learning toward best results plus speed. Data arrive on their own from an unknown source while labels come from a rival. Earlier work split into best but unusable methods and fast oracle methods that were weak on stats. Here the rival picks labels only from a fixed rich function class. A new method runs fast with an ERM oracle, gaining regret tied to Rademacher complexity of a class built from learner and rival classes.
arxiv-2603-04646: Abdollahi and colleagues generate Verilog code with two-stage HDLFORGE. The framework balances generation speed against accuracy. A coder plus a mid-size LLM runs in Stage A. It escalates to a bigger coder plus a huge LLM only when diagnostics say so. A counterexample-guided agent turns checking traces into micro-tests for reuse, cutting detection time. The escalation controller wraps existing Verilog pipelines without changing their internals. HDLFORGE-Qwen reaches over 91 percent Pass at 1 on VerilogEval Human and V2, and over 97 percent Pass at 5 on RTLLM.
arxiv-2603-05246: Toni Ikonen and Stefan Wenger extend the ultralimit of bounded Lipschitz-map sequences in pointed metric spaces to p-bounded Sobolev-map sequences, preserving its desirable properties. They use this to prove Dehn-function stability under ultraconvergence of pointed length spaces, resolving a problem posed by several researchers. As an application, they give a simpler proof of a recent Stadler-Wenger result characterizing spaces of curvature bounded above through an isoperimetric inequality for curves.
arxiv-2603-05346: Alba de las Heras and team reveal pulse-length effects on solid harmonics, where intraband speedup and recombination interplay. Longer pulses stretch them by promoting conduction band excitations. It appears in silicon, is narrow in magnesium oxide, and peaks in RhSi. RhSi picking rules for attosecond locally chiral light follow. Its chiral structure makes a local electric field with uneven torsion. Circular dichroism emerges when helicity aligns or opposes handedness. Findings spur chiral Weyl semimetal tests tracking band crossings and locally chiral light, toward compact sources and topological electronics.
arxiv-2603-05546: Chao and team build a digital twin-driven V2X chain forecasting multi-agent motion at intersections from shared vehicle and infrastructure sensing. Their model pairs a Bi-LSTM generator with mean squared error and twin losses. The twin loss captures infrastructure limits, collision dodging, mode range, and rule-based priors. The MSE term keeps point-wise results right, while the twin loss counts rule breaks, forecast collisions, and mode collapse against it. Tests on real urban V2X data show serious breaks fall a lot with similar accuracy.
arxiv-2603-06046: Tripathi and team explore secure talk in an under-sea relay network. The optical hop uses a Gamma-Gamma channel with pointing errors, at times blocked. A spy watching the sound hop creates a secrecy concern. The authors frame power sharing as an endless-view Markov choice plan. A model-based reward learning sharing maxes long-term secrecy until the network stops. Lower-cost options include Greedy and Naive plans. Models show the reward learning sharing tuning to battery moves and link uptime, hitting the highest secure sending.
arxiv-2603-06346: Kirsz and his team explain complex methane crystal forms as packings of near round supermolecular clusters, despite nearly cubic symmetry and sluggish reshuffle. Density functional molecular dynamics finds Phase A built on a 13 molecule regular icosahedron, plus 8 molecules closing the 21 molecule unit cell. Phase B packs 17 molecule Z16 polyhedra in a body centred cubic layout, with 12 more molecules per cell in four sided gaps. Their separation likes hinge sharply on their orientation, giving slow rotation and low entropy. Packing trades against entropy.
arxiv-2603-06546: Li and team present PEACOCK, a Monte Carlo radiative transfer tool tracing ultraviolet emission and absorption lines from mixed galactic winds. Applied to spectra of 50 nearby star-forming galaxies, it reproduces 220 profiles spanning dark, bright, and P-Cygni-like shapes within one halo model. Monte Carlo runs with deep-learning boost and nested sampling enables settled inference at a small share of grid cost. Radial speeding flows often fail to match dark shapes, while big velocity dispersion produces uneven troughs, pointing to turbulence as an outflow component.
arxiv-2603-06746: Karmore presents ButterflyViT, a compression method for sparse Mixture-of-Experts vision Transformers on edge devices. Storing each expert separately scales memory linearly, beyond edge budgets, and standard compression only trims constants. Here experts become learned rotations of one shared quantized ternary prototype, so diversity comes from viewing shared capacity at different angles. A spatial smoothness regularizer calms routing between adjacent patches. Tests show a huge memory cut at many experts with negligible accuracy loss.
arxiv-2603-06946: Kaya and colleagues present joint MDPs for learning in coupled-motion settings. Many amounts in learning span actions, including gap spreads and winning odds. Yet standard MDPs give only single-action laws, leaving the joint law of what-if results across actions at a state open. They study settings with a multi-action sampling link that samples what-if results for several actions under shared random noise. Joint MDPs add a sample step model that couples what-if results across actions, while keeping standard play as single-action views.
arxiv-2603-07146: Kosiuk and colleagues study fine-grained table retrieval for complex natural-language questions over databases. Their DCTR mechanism splits queries into typed parts and tracks global links across tables, tackling the hard cases of open-domain question answering over relational data. They judge the two mechanisms by retrieval complexity along query and data axes. On industry-aligned benchmarks, DCTR proves robust for tangled queries and tightly linked databases, where coarse retrieval often misses the right tables.
arxiv-2603-07346: Khallaf and Sharoff ask how much noisy training data a BERT-style classifier can take in sentence difficulty detection. They test cleanup tricks on crowdsourced labels, including label smoothing, co-teaching, noise transition matrices and mixture models. Explicit noise filtering lifts scores a lot on the smaller dataset, while the larger dataset barely moves from a strong pre-trained baseline. Dropping roughly a fifth of noisy sentences still yields a cleaner corpus, now released as a multilingual resource.
arxiv-2603-07446: Li and colleagues present GeoVisA11y, a question-answering system that opens geovisualizations to screen-reader users. Maps normally lock out blind users, so the system handles analytical, geospatial, visual and contextual queries through natural language. Studies with screen-reader users and sighted participants show it bridges access gaps while revealing distinct interaction patterns between groups. The work contributes the open system, empirical findings on query behavior and a geospatial query dataset.
arxiv-2603-07546: Gross demonstrates a tool for verifying and explaining reinforcement-learning maintenance policies for bridge networks. Learned rules offer no formal safety proof and stay opaque to staff, so COOL-MC checks a trained policy on a three-bridge network with a shared budget cycle. Probabilistic model checking finds a small safety-violation chance slightly above the ideal minimum, flagging mild shortfall. An explanation pass also exposes a systematic bias toward one bridge over the others.
arxiv-2603-07646: Murshid, Sarkar and Mandal bring certified deletion to registered attribute-based encryption without trusted centers. This erasure makes encrypted data vanish for good even if keys later leak, but existing schemes rely on trusted centers with escrow risks. The authors design in-private and in-public open schemes, plus forever versions where privacy turns total once proof appears. Public checks use witness locks, one-shot signatures and signed quantum states.
arxiv-2603-07746: Hattab and Palti study type II0 loci in type IIB string theory on Calabi-Yau spaces. Near these infinite distance loci, the leading gauge matrix and prepotential look like a threshold correction from a BPS state with an effectively complex charge. Splitting low-energy supergravity between graviphoton and matter sides, they find a strongly-coupled sector with light electric and magnetic states. They propose the leading matrix comes from removing it. A Heterotic picture has a Kaluza-Klein monopole lighter than the basic string, hinting at infrared emergent loci.
arxiv-2603-07846: Arthamonov and colleagues study fixed points of the genus two surface group character variety under finite symmetry groups. Working in a generator frame for the genus two double affine Hecke algebra and its classical limit. They find fixed sets tied to distinct subgroups that match in surprising ways, with shifts in genus and irregularity. The new subvarieties offer geometric candidates for symmetry-reduced moduli spaces tied to four-dimensional supersymmetric field theories.
arxiv-2603-07946: Wang and colleagues generate synthetic mobility trajectories that stay lifelike during large events, where language models handle routine movement but miss event-driven shifts. Two gaps: no event-annotated datasets exist, and frameworks cannot reconcile habits with event constraints. ELLMob closes both gaps, first by building an event-annotated dataset covering Typhoon Hagibis, COVID-19, and Tokyo 2021 Olympics. Its self-aligned framework extracts reasons between habits and event constraints, drawing on Fuzzy-Trace Theory, and aligns them into habit-grounded, event-responsive trajectories that beat state-of-the-art baselines.
arxiv-2603-08246: Hojny and colleagues study single-source multicasting over a communication network facing restricted adversaries. When the adversary can only touch a prescribed subset of edges, classical cut-set bounds lose tightness. Reaching capacity then typically needs a joint design of the outer code and the inner network code. That contrasts sharply with unrestricted adversaries, where capacity follows from linear network coding plus rank-metric outer codes. Building on network decoding, the authors pin down the exact one-shot capacity of one fundamental family of 2-level networks.
arxiv-2603-08346: Kezerashvili reviews bound trions in two-dimensional layers. Trions are Coulomb-bound three-particle states made of two like-charge carriers and one reverse-charged carrier, and they are central units in flat semiconductors. Reduced dielectric screening and quantum trapping strongly enhance their binding strength, making them robust and easy to observe. The review surveys theory and lab gains in trion physics, stressing strict few-body methods and the role of screening setting and outside charge and magnet fields. Methods for describing trions in flat spaces are analyzed.
arxiv-2603-08446: Conde and colleagues prove a general sparse domination principle that respects the cancellative structure of the functions studied. It covers general measure spaces, one- and two-parameter martingale settings, and the Euclidean case. In the one-parameter martingale setting they obtain a sparse characterization of the H1 norm, with proofs leaning on sharp level-set estimates for generalized medians. The results yield new quantitatively sharp weighted results for martingales and Calderón-Zygmund operators acting on Hp spaces.
arxiv-2603-08646: Juha Kontinen and Ivano Ciardelli compare how much two inquisitive logics can say. For plain sentences, team logic matches first-order logic, but for open formulas it says strictly more. Adding a range-making quantifier lets the logic express finiteness, breaking compactness and pushing complexity beyond arithmetic, and the same reach extends to standard inquisitive first-order logic.
arxiv-2603-09246: Quanchen Zou and colleagues describe a jailbreak for large vision-language models that chains benign pieces into harmful logic, in analogy to return-oriented programming. Safety tuning mostly screens explicit bad patterns at the input, leaving compositional reasoning exposed. Their automated framework builds visual gadgets kept apart in meaning and space, so the harmful logic forms only late in reasoning. Tests on SafeBench and MM-SafetyBench show this route slips past perception-level alignment.
arxiv-2603-09446: Tran Bao Sam and colleagues reframe multi-view medical diagnosis as relationship modeling and propose GIIM, a graph-based method. Automated diagnosis often misses how abnormalities relate within a view and how lesions change across views, and missing data weakens it further. GIIM models links among abnormalities inside each view and their dynamics across views in a single graph. Built-in handling of incomplete inputs adds robustness, and broad tests on medical image tasks show the approach generalizes.
arxiv-2603-09646: Ilkka Helenius and colleagues compute dimuon production in neutrino-nucleus collisions at next-to-next-to-leading order in perturbative QCD. Dimuon final states from charm production constrain the strange-quark distribution, and have long favored a smaller strange PDF at small x than LHC data suggest. Their self-contained calculation rests on semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering, fixing flaws of the older fully inclusive route. NNLO corrections shrink scale uncertainties at large x and turn negative at small x, easing the dimuon-LHC tension.
arxiv-2603-09846: Vincent Cohen-Addad and coauthors sharpen the known running time for near optimal clustering in low dimensional Euclidean space. The task is to pick centres that minimise summed distances, or squared distances, to each input point. Their method cuts the heavy factor in a prior near linear algorithm. A near matching lower bound, under a standard hardness assumption, shows little room remains for k-means.
arxiv-2603-09946: Igata and Takamori set out the strong bend limit for heavy bits moving on timelike geodesics in still, round, flat at far distance spaces. As spin nears its top value, a bit winds many times around an unstable round path and its bend angle grows with no bound, in a log way. With the geodesic deviation law, they show the growth rate is set by that path's radial instability, per unit of angle round the centre. In general relativity, matter enters through one local mix of density and pressures.
arxiv-2603-10046: Reza Rahimi Azghan and coauthors tackle continual learning for human activity recognition from wearable sensors. On device models must adapt to new people with distinct movement styles without forgetting earlier users or sending private data to the cloud. Their method gates channels of a frozen pre trained representation, scaling existing features rather than generating new ones. Theory shows this bounded diagonal change limits drift while still allowing subject specific tuning.
arxiv-2603-10346: Leo Maynard-Zhang, Zhihan Xiong, Kevin Jamieson, and Maryam Fazel study best-arm identification in non-stationary linear bandits under a fixed time budget. The best arm has the largest total reward, while unknown parameters can shift in an adversarial way. Standard G-optimal sampling gives a minimax rate, yet they call that view too pessimistic, since it hides gains from richer arm-set geometry. They prove an arm-set-dependent lower bound and propose an adjacent-optimal design whose error matches it, pinning down the true complexity here.
arxiv-2603-10646: Thong Hoang and co-authors propose an agentic framework for managing the whole ESG reporting lifecycle with large language models. ESG reports are hard to align with standards because data are unstructured, terms vary, and requirements are complex. Their framework weaves AI agents into five stages, from identification to improvement, so agents extract information, verify performance, and update reports. The authors set out technical requirements for four core tasks and compare single-model, single-agent, and multi-agent designs.
arxiv-2603-11046: Emmanuel Gnabeyeu tackles Merton's portfolio problem inside a fake stationary Volterra-Heston market with many factors, where the usual approach breaks down. The paths are neither Markovian nor semimartingales, so the usual tools do not apply here. He uses a stochastic factor to solve a Riccati backward stochastic differential equation, guided by the martingale optimality principle. Optimal strategies come out in semi-closed form tied to Riccati-Volterra equations. Tests on a two-dimensional rough Heston model show how stationary rough volatility moves them.
arxiv-2603-11146: Kaz Gary and coauthors argue that weighing planets around Habitable Worlds Observatory targets is key. Mass lets us read their atmospheres and judge habitability. Masses to ten percent are needed to name the gases in an Earth-like atmosphere. Space-based astrometry is a must for face-on systems and for planets around fast-rotating or active stars. They propose an astrometric survey with its high-resolution instrument. In its photon-noise budget, reference-star counts and brightness drive the uncertainty near the Galactic poles.
arxiv-2603-11246: Christos Chatzisavvas and coauthors fix a waste in object-centric learning. Several latent slots can compete for the same region of an image. They compete instead of dividing it into distinct objects. Slot counts are normally fixed in advance, and slots only get refined. They add a lightweight merging step that combines overlapping slots during training. Overlap is scored between slot-attention maps. Merged pairs update barycentrically to keep gradients flowing. The threshold comes from overlap statistics. This improves factorization and mask quality in the DINOSAUR pipeline.
arxiv-2603-11346: Yuto Shibata and coauthors teach humanoid agents to assist a human partner through force-exchanging contact. Caregiving robots must give this help, but motion tracking alone cannot. They cast imitation of assistive human-human motion as multi-agent reinforcement learning. Supporter and recipient train together inside a physics simulator. Priors from single-human tracking controllers ease exploration. Dynamic reference retargeting adapts its motion to the partner's live pose. A contact-promoting reward pushes for meaningful support. It is the first to track assistive interactions on established benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-11446: Liang, Ma, and Zhu aim to make legal judgment prediction rest on legal logic, not word patterns alone. Older models lean on fact-outcome links, so they can learn false links and break under change. The team's fix mixes language model priors with statistical causal discovery. A coarse-to-fine step first pulls clean legal factors from noisy case text. The model then helps prune unclear causal directions into candidate graphs. Those graphs steer attention in the final model, which beats best prior systems on three data sets.
arxiv-2603-11546: Zhou and co-authors present MTAC, a multi-task anti-causal learning framework for inferring causes from effects. Many tasks share mechanisms, yet each keeps local parts. MTAC learns a structural equation model that splits outcome generation into one shared mechanism plus local deviations. Inference then uses maximum a posteriori estimation to rebuild causes. The test case rebuilds urban events from resident reports on parking, abandoned properties, and unsanitary conditions. On data from Manhattan and Newark, MTAC cuts MAE by up to 33.04 percent over strong baselines.
arxiv-2603-12046: Cappellazzo, Petridis, and Pantic ask how speech models split their trust between sound and sight. Their Dr. SHAP-AV framework uses Shapley values to score what each modality adds. Six audio-visual models faced two benchmarks at varied noise levels in three linked analyses. Models lean more on vision as noise grows, yet audio keeps a strong share even under heavy damage. Balance shifts while text is generated, alignment holds, and noise level drives the weighting most.
arxiv-2603-12246: Liu and co-authors examine reasoning LLMs as judges in post-training where answers cannot be checked directly. Static benchmarks favor reasoning judges, but their effect inside real policy training stayed untested. A gold-standard judge labels preferences in a controlled setup used to train smaller judges. Non-reasoning judges invite reward hacking with ease in these runs. Reasoning judges yield strong scores, yet their policies win by crafting outputs that fool other judges. The study flags both promise and clear room to improve judge-based training.
arxiv-2603-12546: Abid Afridi and co-authors tackle uneven load in satellite networks beyond Earth. Some satellites sit idle while others clog at their ground links. The team frames the whole set as an anycast flow problem. A linear program then picks a ground station for each satellite. When needed, it shifts traffic to nearby satellites across optical links. In tests, the worst downlink rate rose by more than 25% with rain. It also rose by over 10% when no rain fell.
arxiv-2603-12746: Yuzhi Huang and co-authors ask whether multimodal language models can think in dynamics, tracking how scenes change over time. Static image skill is strong, yet motion and interaction may be read inconsistently. Their Dyn-Bench gathers dynamic scenes from real and synthetic video for robust tests. It probes spatial reasoning and object grounding at region level. Models could not hold top scores on both skills at once. Structured tools like mask-guided fusion helped far more than plain prompting.
arxiv-2603-13046: Sneha Srikanth and Andres Arrieta use transition waves in multistable materials to trap energy and harvest it at once. Multistable structures show hysteresis, which suits shock absorption without a set frequency. Their system locks transition waves so impact energy stays at chosen spots. The wave dynamics link to solitary waves of a phi-four equation, which yields design estimates. Tests beat linear materials on damping, and energy splitting adds a second loss path. The same setup also harvested more energy than linear rivals.
arxiv-2603-13546: Eshed Gal, Samy Wu Fung, and Eldad Haber present Probabilistic Gaussian Homotopy, a new take on nonconvex optimization. Classic Gaussian homotopy smooths the objective and averages gradients in a uniform way. Their method instead deforms the Boltzmann distribution, so perturbed gradients are weighted toward low-energy regions. They show it matches a log-sum-exp soft-min homotopy that returns to the true objective as the scale goes to zero. A dynamical system tracks how minimizers move along the annealed path. Their PGHO algorithm did well on benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-13846: Wegmann and co-authors test how well people spot and judge synthetic videos, known as deepfakes. Two experiments vary visual and audio distortions and measure effects on credibility ratings and learning. A third study looks at artifacts left by deepfake generation itself. Across the studies, distortions and artifacts tend to lower how credible a video feels. The authors say the results show a need for better theory on how people process synthetic media.
arxiv-2603-14046: Menon and Adhikari extend the theory of null, force-free electromagnetic fields, used for magnetospheres around compact objects. Such fields rest on two-dimensional field sheets that foliate spacetime. The open task is to say which null geodesic families can carry a force-free solution. The authors prove that a local rotation of the cross-plane basis can always meet the equipartition condition. They also show that a shear-free geodesic family is enough to build a null field sheet foliation.
arxiv-2603-14446: Bahri and co-authors study self-assembled naphthalocyanine lattices as tunable quantum superlattices. The team grows a square monolayer of metal-free H2Nc molecules. They combine density functional theory with photoemission and tunneling microscopy. A free film shows both flat, molecule-bound states and wider dispersive bands. Each band type fits a tight-binding model with direction-dependent hopping. Changing the metal base tunes hopping and Coulomb forces. Silver and gold bases give two working examples, the authors show.
arxiv-2603-14646: Nguyen, Phan and Gonzalez treat dynamic theory of mind as a temporal memory problem. Most tests ask for a belief judgment at one moment. Real social tracking needs beliefs kept and updated over time. Their DToM-Track frame probes multiturn conversations for three skills. Models must recall old beliefs, infer current ones and spot belief change. Current beliefs come easily to the models tested. Past beliefs fade once updates land, across model families and scales. The pattern mirrors recency bias known from cognitive science, they note.
arxiv-2603-15146: Bartoli and Stanica build new infinite families of APN permutations in three variables over binary fields. They extend two families of Li and Kaleyski by letting a scalar parameter range over the whole field. For each family, a permutation arises exactly when a linked one-variable polynomial has no root in the field. The same root test also decides the APN property. Counting arguments show many parameter values work. The authors prove strong inequivalence results, so the families are genuinely new and differ from each other.
arxiv-2603-15646: Lan and co-authors rework how rubric rewards guide reinforcement learning. Rubric methods score answers on several traits at once. Fixed weighting then crushes those scores into one number. That step is touchy and hides links between traits. Their ARL-RR method trains on one rubric class at a time. A light search picks the next class from task results. On HealthBench, the method beat scalarized rivals at four model sizes. It also trained faster in their tests.
arxiv-2603-16146: Strouwen and Micluţa-Câmpeanu make experiment design for dynamic systems run in real time. Classic adaptive design re-solves costly inference between each step. Their blend pairs Deep Adaptive Design with differentiable models. A neural policy, trained offline, picks each next experiment. Transformer policies respect the time shape of dynamic systems. Contrastive training extends to cover nuisance parameters cleanly. Four test systems rise in complexity across the study. A fed-batch bioreactor and a DC motor bookend the set. Live deployment closes the demo chain.
arxiv-2603-16546: Wang, Huang, and Dragut read document-level sentiment with a team of agents. Aspect-based analysis usually works sentence by sentence in narrow domains. Whole documents with informal style are much harder. Their DanceHA framework splits the long task into small sub-tasks. Specialized agents then solve the pieces together. A human-AI step, HA, helps build fine-grained labels. Their Inf-ABSIA dataset covers many domains. Agent knowledge also transfers into smaller student models.
arxiv-2603-16646: Zhao and co-authors co-design AI auditing tools with teachers in Hawai'i. Classroom AI can misrepresent cultures and carry bias. The risk grows in Indigenous and low-resource language settings. Hawai'i schools must weave Hawaiian language and culture into lessons. Four workshops drew 22 public school educators. Teachers wanted tools rooted in Hawaiian values and practices. One idea traces the genealogy of knowledge in source material. Auditing, the team argues, is community work.
arxiv-2603-17146: Baigutanova and co-authors build a multilingual system that flags Wikipedia claims in need of references. Wikipedia's verifiability rule asks that claims be backed by reliable sources, but editors must check this by hand amid a flood of daily edits. Their machine learning system assists editors by spotting claims that require citations. It was tested in 10 language editions and beat existing benchmarks for reference need assessment. The team weighs accuracy against computing cost under real infrastructure limits. The system is deployed in production, with data and code released.
arxiv-2603-17246: Restrepo and co-authors study the modality gap in medical vision language embeddings. In such models, image and text embeddings cluster in narrow cones, leaving a gap between the two modalities. Their tool is a light post hoc mechanism that freezes the pretrained encoders and steers the gap's size with one parameter. They test general and medical models on medical and natural datasets. Cutting an excessive gap improved downstream results, with medical data most sensitive. Fully closing the gap was not always best.
arxiv-2603-17446: Awad argues that prediction markets give a test for backward time travel. If rational travelers could return, binary contract prices would jump to zero or one at once. Large sets of resolved contracts show no such pattern, he reports. Traders would have no reason to hide bets on events that prices cannot sway. Many-worlds views escape the test, he grants, but single-timeline travel looks ruled out.
arxiv-2603-17946: Zhou and co-authors convert grouped-query attention into multi-head latent attention with CARE. Latent forms promise richer attention at the same cache size. Plain SVD swaps track weights only and let activations drift, they note. CARE factors weights against real activation covariance instead. Rank then flows to the layers that need it most under one fixed budget. Perplexity fell sharply on Qwen and Llama tests, and a short heal tune restored full accuracy.
arxiv-2603-18146: Cipressi, Langhoff, and Opferkuch study heavy new vector states at future muon and wakefield colliders. Wakefield machines make beamstrahlung, which spreads beam light from the peak energy down to lower ones. That spread is most often seen as a flaw. They show it can help: the spread scans many hit energies at once and lifts the reach for such states. Their test case is a heavy Z prime with kinetic mixing.
arxiv-2603-18346: Liu studies the large friction limit of the almost pressureless Euler-Poisson system with repulsive force. The leading limit equations form a hyperbolic-elliptic Keller-Segel system of consumption type. Under set conditions on the starting data, unique global solutions exist for both systems. Global stability holds in the large friction limit, and no singularity forms there. The time behavior of the one-dimensional Keller-Segel flow with vacuum is also covered.
arxiv-2603-18646: Mitchell and Wild study orientable sequences, where each n-tuple occurs at most once in either direction. Such sequences were first used for position location tasks in the early 1990s. They focus on a known way to build negative orientable sequences. In those, each n-tuple occurs at most once in the sequence or its negated reverse. They show how to add more n-tuples to that method. The new sequences reach asymptotically optimal period, and they also yield orientable sequences with optimal period.
arxiv-2603-19146: Lys and co-authors improve how discrete diffusion models pick their next draft when they write text. Standard beam search does not fit these models, since each step holds full draft texts, not word prefixes. Their method, D5P4, picks a batch of drafts with a point process that scores both quality and spread. No outside checker is needed. On open writing, questions, and math tasks, it widens the range of good drafts. Quality stays at or above the base methods.
arxiv-2603-19246: Coles and co-authors ask how solo and team researchers differ when they respond to world crises. They track over 1.5 million papers on 25 crises from more than 3 million authors. Solo authors publish their responses faster than teams. Yet team work draws more notice in journals, news, and policy. Gains from team size fade as teams grow, and the edge varies by crisis. Other traits, like state strength and lead expertise, also shape impact. The old proverb on speed and reach holds up.
arxiv-2603-19346: Boudouma and co-authors use Juno data to pin down how Jupiter's narrowband radio waves arise. Two wave families are tracked, one at 20 to 141 kilohertz and one lower. Both seem to start in plasma near the Io torus at low latitudes. The team sorts each burst by whether its mode is trapped or escaping. Three-dimensional models then bound the source spots, beam shapes, and wave modes. High-latitude bursts fit the O-mode, while low ones fit X-mode. Both families seem born near the base plasma frequency.
arxiv-2603-19646: Hong proves a sharp Minkowski-type inequality in Cartan-Hadamard 3-spaces. The proof uses harmonic mean curvature flow. Keeping the volume term in the monotonicity step sharpens the result. The work improves known estimates for total mean curvature in hyperbolic 3-space. It sharpens an earlier result of Ghomi and Spruck. A corollary follows as a comparison theorem. It links the total mean curvature of convex surfaces in these spaces to the volume they enclose.
arxiv-2603-19946: Abou Samra and Madore embed the Turing degrees, with their order reversed, into a broader degree structure. The Arthur-Nimue-Merlin degrees generalize Turing degrees through a three-player game. That game adds both angelic and demonic nondeterminism to oracle queries. The structure also describes subtoposes of the effective topos. The authors call their embedded copy the co-Turing degrees. They then study how these co-Turing degrees relate to the plain Turing degrees inside the larger order. The work links computability theory with topos theory.
arxiv-2603-20346: Muneeb and Ascher present G2DR, a framework that turns genetic signals into drug target leads. Human genetics can point to new therapies, but usable ranking tools remain scarce. Their method traces inherited variants through predicted gene expression and pathway tests. Network context, druggability, and drug-target evidence then shape the final ranks. In a migraine case study with 733 UK Biobank participants, results held up. Gene-level ROC-AUC reached 0.775 on held-out data. The authors stress the tool generates hypotheses, not clinical advice.
arxiv-2603-20746: Varun and co-authors study attacks on graph neural networks that train with local differential privacy. Graphs often hold sensitive data, so privacy tools matter here. Yet how privacy noise affects attack risk was not well known. The paper tests how well known attack methods work on protected models. It also notes the hurdles in crafting attack inputs under privacy rules. The authors then sketch defense paths for future work. Their theme is the push and pull between privacy and security.
arxiv-2603-20846: Wu and Zheng set out a framework for outage odds in fluid antenna systems with a continuous aperture. They treat the antenna as one smooth surface in place of fixed ports. A Gaussian kernel stands in for the true link between points in space. Three paths give the outage math: mode expansions, two sided bounds, and extreme value theory. The bounds dodge the rosy bias of block models. The final formula needs just the aperture size and the threshold. Checks show less than ten percent error for small apertures.
arxiv-2603-21346: Wang and co-authors study differential resistance in the hydrodynamic regime of an electron liquid in GaAs/AlGaAs quantum wells. At zero magnetic field, a Lorentzian profile appears in nonlinear transport driven by a U-turn current loop. With added dc bias, a minimum in the resistance deepens as the bias grows. Their analysis ties this transport valley to Joule heating of the electron temperature. The results match the dc-current induced electronic Gurzhi effect in several measurement setups.
arxiv-2603-21446: Ahmed and Admal tackle the design of strain soliton networks in bilayer two-dimensional materials. These networks shape the structure and electronic behavior of the bilayer, but the space of possible deformations is huge. They build a geometric framework that maps each deformation to a network described by line and Burgers vector pairs. Topology from the stacking fault energy landscape limits which networks can occur. The map runs both ways, so a target network can be turned back into the deformation that creates it.
arxiv-2603-21546: Zhang probes what world models in reinforcement learning store inside. Such models learn to mimic an environment, which makes training cheap on samples. Probes, causal tests, and attention maps are applied to two models: a token transformer and a diffusion model. Both trained on Atari Breakout and Pong. Game facts like object positions and scores could be read out with simple linear probes. Shifting hidden states along probe directions changed predictions as hoped. So the stored codes are used, not just present.
arxiv-2603-21646: Wang and co-authors derive fluid limits from the Boltzmann equations for a two-species gas mixture. The species have different particle masses, which breaks the symmetry of the linearized collision operator. That loss of symmetry is the main technical hurdle. Using a Hilbert expansion at small Knudsen number, they construct the hydrodynamic limit for the mixture. They pin down precise properties of the collision operators, including extra terms from the mass difference. Under scaling assumptions on the initial data, they also rigorously justify the acoustic limit.
arxiv-2603-21746: Alghisi and co-authors study why asking vision-language models to point first improves their counting. In the Point-then-Count setup, the model lists coordinates for each target object, then gives the total. Across fine-tuned and training-free variants, it earned the highest accuracy on zero-shot counting. The predicted points landed on the right objects in over 94 percent of cases. The gain comes from spatial facts encoded in the coordinates. Pointing also helped on new kinds of images, though grounding strength varied by region.
arxiv-2603-22046: Endrodi and co-authors use lattice simulations to study QCD with three quark flavors of equal mass. At a set imaginary isospin chemical potential, this theory has an exact center symmetry. The team tracks the Polyakov loop across system sizes with a multi-histogram method. They report a first-order deconfinement phase transition between the two regimes. Runs at other quark masses sketch how QCD behaves in this corner of its phase diagram. The results shed light on how chiral symmetry breaking relates to deconfinement.
arxiv-2603-22346: Caraker and co-authors name a bias that creeps into gradient boosting explanations. In boosting, early trees grab importance that later trees would share. Correlated features make the effect worse and attributions unstable. Scaling one model up makes the problem worst of all. Their fix, DASH, averages SHAP values across independent models. Plain seed-averaging works too, since both break the chain of sequential fitting. DASH also ships two diagnostics that flag the bias with no ground truth. On breast cancer data, stability jumps sharply under DASH.
arxiv-2603-22446: Meng and co-authors study how reward-based fine-tuning changes a language model token by token. They find the shifts are sparse: only a small share of token choices differ much from the base model. Swapping tests show how much those few choices matter. Adding a small share of tuned tokens to base output recovers most of the gains. Adding base tokens to tuned output collapses the gains instead. The work frames fine-tuning as targeted refinement, not broad change.
arxiv-2603-22846: Liu and co-authors present CoMaTrack, a framework for embodied visual tracking with language goals. One agent must follow a target named in words. Single-agent imitation needs costly expert data and adapts poorly. CoMaTrack trains agents in a competitive multi-agent game instead. A tracker faces adaptive opponents across varied scenes and instructions. The team also built a Habitat-based benchmark for such duels. Their tracker beats prior methods on standard tests and the new benchmark. A small three-billion-parameter model beats larger imitation-based rivals.
arxiv-2603-23146: Pudasaini and co-authors ask why AI text detectors fail outside their benchmarks. Many detectors score high on test sets yet prove shaky in real use. Their framework blends linguistic features, machine learning, and explainable AI. Trained on 30 language features, it matches top leaderboard scores on two corpora. Cross-domain and cross-generator tests then show sharp drops. Explanations reveal the key features differ by dataset. Detectors lean on dataset style cues, not stable signs of machine writing. The team releases an open tool with per-text explanations.
arxiv-2603-23346: Mai and Liang present RelayS2S, a design that makes dialogue systems answer faster. Pure speech-to-speech models reply at once but write weaker text. Cascaded recognition plus model chains write better text, yet lag grows with model size. RelayS2S runs both paths at once when a turn starts. The fast path streams a short draft prefix to speech output. The slow path writes a stronger continuation from that prefix. A learned verifier approves the handoff or falls back. First-chunk lag drops sharply.
arxiv-2603-23446: Filzinger and six co-authors report a multi-ion optical clock with record-low uncertainty. Single-ion clocks are superb but slow to average down noise. Running up to ten strontium ions at once cuts measuring time by a factor of 4.8. Ion-by-ion readout keeps position shifts tiny, below one part in 10 to the 20. The clock's fractional uncertainty reaches 5.3 times 10 to the minus 19. A check against an ytterbium clock gives a clean frequency ratio. The result shows many ions can run at top accuracy.
arxiv-2603-23746: Xu and co-authors propose a new model for events spread over space and time. Classic Poisson and Hawkes models rest on narrow assumptions. Neural models are more flexible but hide event links in a black box. Their model, called KSTPP, uses Gaussian processes for background rates and for influence between events. Kronecker structure and a special quadrature scheme keep training fast on large event sets. Tests show the method can reveal clear event relationships while staying flexible.
arxiv-2603-24246: Matela and Krüger describe a system for matching software mentions across scientific documents. The system entered the SOMD 2026 shared task on cross-document coreference. It mixes dense embeddings from a Sentence-BERT model with a knowledge base lookup built from training cluster centers. FAISS speeds retrieval, and HDBSCAN clusters mentions that match nothing with confidence. Name normalization and abbreviation handling improve matching. A blocking strategy adapts the pipeline to the largest subtask. It scores CoNLL F1 of 98, 98, and 96 percent on the three subtasks.
arxiv-2603-24446: Xi and co-authors explain how a three-dimensional spin supersolid can arise in a metallic antiferromagnet on a stacked triangular lattice. Recent work on the rare-earth alloy EuCo2Al9 found such a phase with a giant magnetocaloric effect. The team combines electronic structure analysis, an effective spin model, and Monte Carlo simulations. RKKY and dipolar interactions together produce the model, which matches the measured thermodynamics well. The ground state breaks both lattice translation and spin rotation symmetry. They also map the field-temperature phase diagram.
arxiv-2603-24546: Abreu and co-authors analyse multidimensional convolutional codes. These codes extend one-dimensional ones, with codewords indexed over a grid. An upper bound on free distance, the generalised Singleton bound, defines the best codes, called MDS codes. The main result gives new constructions of MDS multidimensional codes based on special matrices. New families of rate 1/n codes come from generator matrices with set row degree conditions, expanding known constructions a lot.
arxiv-2603-24846: Dineva and co-authors benchmark vision language models for clinical reasoning on brain disorders. Their NeuroVLM-Bench uses curated MRI and CT datasets with multiple sclerosis, stroke, tumours, other cases, and normal controls. Models must output diagnosis, subtype, modality, sequence, and plane at once. Scores cover abstention, calibration, output validity, and efficiency. Across twenty frontier models, traits such as modality and plane are nearly solved. Reasoning, above all subtype calls, stays hard; tumours are easiest, while multiple sclerosis remains difficult.
arxiv-2603-24946: Fakorede and co-authors introduce MobileDev-Bench, a benchmark for issue resolution in mobile app development. Existing software benchmarks use library-style repositories, leaving mobile work untested. Their set holds 407 real issue-resolution tasks from 19 production apps across Android, React Native, and Flutter. Each task pairs a verified developer issue with executable test patches for automatic validation. Fixes are complex, touching 12.9 files and 334.6 lines on average, and 41 percent span several artifact types. Four frontier models resolve only about three to six percent of tasks end to end.
arxiv-2603-25046: Tran and co-authors forecast heavy rain in Vietnam with a mixture-of-experts model guided by pattern matching. Raw weather models drift in the tropics, where terrain and storms are complex. Standard fixes score each time point alone, which punishes small timing slips twice. MP-MoE adds a matrix profile loss that scores whole rain shapes, not single points. This helps the model pick the right expert and keeps storm shapes intact. On two river basin datasets, it beats raw forecasts and rivals on heavy rain scores.
arxiv-2603-25446: Zhang and co-authors run a near-live alarm for solar radio bursts at the Owens Valley array. Bursts flag storms in the Sun's corona and feed space weather forecasts. Their system clips data from a live buffer and streams a radio spectrogram. A YOLO-style deep net, trained on physics-made fake bursts, spots type III events in that stream. Reports go out about ten seconds after a burst hits. The setup pairs raw sensitivity with the low delay that forecasters need.
arxiv-2603-25546: Tocher and co-authors simulate how fuzzy dark matter reshapes the birth of the first stars. In this picture, dark matter acts as waves, and its ripples steer gas inside young halos. Their AREPO runs track halos across a span of axion masses with early chemistry in play. Gas collapse stalls twice: the flat soliton core holds gas back, and wave jitter adds push and spin. Star sites scatter into many small clusters instead of one core peak. Cosmic Dawn may start later than mass cutoffs alone suggest.
arxiv-2603-25946: Koran and co-authors build a collision-aware add-on for self-driving systems. Crashes and near misses cause most failures in closed-loop driving tests. Their detector, VLAAD, learns from video and language data to flag collision risk early. To train it, they built CARLA-Collide, a large dataset of varied crash events. Plugged into a pretrained TransFuser++ agent, the module raised the driving score by 14.12 percent. They also release Real-Collide, a dashcam dataset for open-loop tests. The module kept working on real-world footage, they report.
arxiv-2603-26046: Hwang and Kwak build a pipeline that pulls nurse observations out of spoken dictations. Nurses spend heavy time on notes, and language models could ease that load. Their method uses retrieval-augmented generation to ground each extraction. Relevant reference material is fetched before the model writes its answer. This keeps the extracted observations accurate to the dictation. On the MEDIQA-SYNUR test set, the system reaches an F1 score of 0.796. The authors present it as a step toward lighter clinical paperwork.
arxiv-2603-26146: Tran and co-authors study how fluctuations shape transport in two-dimensional superconducting films. The films sit under electric drive and an out-of-plane magnetic field. Their theory uses the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau equation with thermal noise, with fluctuating Cooper pairs interacting at the Gaussian level. The authors derive closed forms for the pair density, resistance, and nonlinear response. A key result is an S-shaped current-voltage curve with a negative-slope segment. Tests match recent data across many thin-film materials.
arxiv-2603-26246: Kumar and co-authors study how past turns in a chat can help a language model transcribe speech. After multi-turn training, context mainly helps the model catch names and other context-bound facts. Raw past audio is costly, since its embedding grows with each turn. Their method, Abstract Compression, swaps each past turn of audio for a fixed set of learned tokens, while keeping past transcripts. Tests in and out of domain recover part of the gain at lower cost.
arxiv-2603-26446: Linder and co-authors extend a topography-aware contact model to fully dynamic simulation of jointed structures. Friction in connections drives much of a structure's damping, and real surface shape matters most in partial slip. Their multi-scale method couples finite element and boundary element models of the true contact surface. They show it works with time stepping and Harmonic Balance runs, checked against quasi-static results on the S4 Beam test case. The runs reveal that load history can shift the settled equilibrium.
arxiv-2603-27146: Wang and co-authors train language models to propose research that the future actually pursues. Judging proposal quality is hard because novelty resists automatic scoring. Their trick reframes generation as scientific forecasting with a time cutoff. Models see a question and papers before the cutoff, then draft a structured proposal. A Future Alignment Score checks the draft against papers published later. Training used 21,835 paper occurrences with synthesized reasoning traces. Future-aligned tuning raised the score by up to 10.6 percent. Two generated proposals were even implemented with gains.
arxiv-2603-27546: Bonnerjee and co-authors locate odd patches hidden in spatial data. Their SPLADE method finds several axis-aligned patches at once. It works even when nearby values are strongly linked. A fast sampling step first handles the single-patch case. A two-stage search then tackles many patches jointly. Proofs back both the patch count and each edge. Tests on synthetic data show gains in speed and accuracy. A video surveillance task shows real-world value.
arxiv-2603-27646: Qiu and co-authors test whether AI agents can redo physics papers end to end. PRBench holds thirty expert-built tasks from eleven subfields. Each task gives an agent a paper and instructions. The agent must code the method from scratch. Output numbers must match the published results. Tasks come from over twenty Peking University groups. Ground truth and scoring rubrics were verified by hand. Coding agents are then graded across key skills.
arxiv-2603-28846: Babbush and co-authors assess how quantum computers could break elliptic curve cryptocurrencies and how to respond. They give resource estimates for the 256 bit discrete log problem. Shor's algorithm could run it with under 1,200 logical qubits and under 90 million Toffoli gates, by one option. On superconducting hardware, the circuits could run in minutes with under half a million physical qubits. Fast clock systems could enable on-spend attacks on mempool transactions. They survey risks for smart contracts, staking, and abandoned assets, and urge a move to post-quantum methods.
arxiv-2603-28946: Ramírez Ovalle studies how a logic can be read from a class of neural architectures. The start point is a category of zone labelled blocks, with records of which copying, discarding, and zone shifts the design allows. From that category, a subexponential signature is extracted. A sequent calculus is then defined, with rules indexed by the zones. Three results follow: the category is symmetric monoidal, the proof system admits cut elimination, and derivations are sound for the diagrams. Subexponential structure is thus read from data, not assumed.
arxiv-2603-29246: Jeong and co-authors analyze the chemistry of an actinide-boost star in the halo. The star, J1222, is very metal-poor but rich in r-process elements. High-resolution Gemini spectra gave abundances for 47 elements, including thorium. Its pattern matches yields expected from neutron star mergers. Some match also comes from black hole and neutron star mergers. Motion data place the star in the I'itoi substructure. Neighboring stars show widely varied r-process enrichment. That spread points to many events and uneven mixing.
arxiv-2603-29846: Avsian and Heck build SNEAK, a benchmark for secret-aware talk by language models. Multi-agent settings often demand messages that inform allies but hide facts from rivals. Each test gives a model a category, a word list, and a secret word. The model must hint at the secret without giving it away. An ally agent and a rival agent score utility and leakage. Humans beat all tested models by up to four times.
arxiv-2603-29946: Sena and Galuppo Azevedo present ShapPFN, a tabular model that explains itself in real time. Tabular foundation models predict well, but tools like SHAP explain too slowly for interactive work. ShapPFN bakes Shapley value regression into its design. One forward pass then yields both a prediction and its explanation. On standard benchmarks, accuracy stays competitive. Explanation quality is high, with R squared at 0.96. It runs over a thousand times faster than KernelSHAP.
arxiv-2604-00046: Pagels and team propose a large language model to spot and measure Enterprise Architecture Debt in documentation. It arises from poor decisions and mismatched parts harming an IT estate. Early signs, EA Smells, are found by hand or from set files. Using design science, the team builds and tests a tool for auto finding. The tool ingests process notes and plans, applies fine-tuned models, and outputs smells. A case study with fake firm documents, against a custom GPT-based model, shows language models detect known smells in text.
arxiv-2604-00146: Chaudhuri and Mukherjee give unitary representations of mixed braid groups on cohomology groups of Abelian branched covers over the complex projective line. Complex reflections generate the image of each representation. The authors also link the construction to the multivariate Burau representation, giving a full account of this monodromy picture. The paper works out the maps in full detail.
arxiv-2604-00346: Lee builds a forecasting method for gaps between orders in fast electronic markets, where waiting times cluster and stretch into long tails. His self-exciting residual point process keeps the observed shape of those gaps while preserving bursts and decay, and he checks that the process settles into a stable long-run pattern. Tests on very fast trading records beat several rival approaches at predicting the next gap.
arxiv-2604-00546: De Micheli and colleagues present a lightweight system for encrypted face recognition with GPU support. Face recognition runs client-server. The client turns a face into a compact embedding, and the server searches a store. Facial data is sensitive, so privacy concerns run deep. Fully homomorphic encryption allows encrypted search, but protocols cost heavily in compute and memory, burdened by rotation-key sets and bandwidth-bound operations. Building on HyDia, the team adds algorithmic improvements for edge clients, with BSGS-Diagonal, a fast, memory-efficient similarity algorithm.
arxiv-2604-00646: Salone and colleagues work out non-leptonic hyperon decays in relativistic chiral perturbation theory to next-to-leading order, the first such treatment. Recent lab gains prompted the work. Loop corrections are computed from ground octet and decuplet fields. Low-energy constants for weak transitions are gauged by resonance saturation, following a non-relativistic tree-level calculation. The spin-1/2-minus and spin-1/2-plus octets are used. The rest are fitted to decay amplitudes, giving a joint account of s- and p-wave amplitudes, though not tightly pinned. Resonances matter most.
arxiv-2604-00746: Deepanshu Kush proves an unconditional barrier to proving superpolynomial lower bounds for multilinear algebraic branching programs with the min-partition rank method. He exhibits a full-rank multilinear polynomial that a polynomial-size branching program can compute, so the method cannot deliver the separation. His proof settles an open problem about the size of 1-balanced-chain set systems, showing the key quantity grows only polynomially.
arxiv-2604-00946: Zain and colleagues study near-Earth asteroids in Main Belt-crossing orbits, selecting objects brighter than magnitude 18 and integrating their orbits for 10 million years. Objects split by initial semi-major axis into three groups, with median lifetimes falling as axis grows, from about 13 million years to about 0.9 million years. Collisional erosion barely changes the global size distribution over a million years, though the asteroids spend much of their lives inside the Main Belt under frequent small impacts.
arxiv-2604-01246: Musielak, Fry, and Kanan consider complex scalar fields under a novel Klein-Gordon equation from gauge and group theories, at Schwarzschild black hole singularities. They show the field stays well-behaved near these singularities and reaches zero at both of them. The field also forms a scalar hair outside the event horizon, while the interior field is tachyonic and settles into its lowest-energy state at the central singularity. This behavior differs sharply from the minimally coupled Klein-Gordon equation, with implications for black hole interiors.
arxiv-2604-01546: Reinhardt and colleagues propose Tensor-ComBat, a spatial matching for brain scan data that gauges and removes tech shifts between voxel images from sites or scanners. Tensor-ComBat uses a Bayes tensor model to gauge spread scanner effects via a low-rank PARAFAC split, then removes them via a ComBat step. Unlike plain ComBat, which treats voxels as same, Tensor-ComBat uses voxel layouts when gauging settings, aiding matching. Applied to over 2100 T1w-MRI scans in ADNI-1, it shows greater effect removal, body prediction, and better reruns versus ComBat.
arxiv-2604-01646: Jung and colleagues propose a method for thinly labeled monocular 3D finding with two key modules. Monocular 3D finding does well on densely labeled sets but falters when labels cover only some objects, a common setting given the high cost of 3D labels. Road-Aware Patch Augmentation uses sparse labels by placing cut patches onto road regions while keeping 3D shape fit. Prototype-Based Filtering makes good pseudo-labels by sifting guesses through model match and depth doubt, picking labels matching learned models with reliable depth guesses.
arxiv-2604-01746: Macheda and Sohier study interactions between electrons and phonons, and among electrons themselves, over long ranges in doped 2D materials, including interlayer couplings in van der Waals stacks. They assess transport effects with dynamic coupled Boltzmann equations for electrons and for active excitations. The theory claims validity and is applied to simple parabolic models and to a boron-nitride-encapsulated graphene system in a second paper. Dynamic screening proves fundamental to describing transport right, in particular polar phonon scattering, whether from the semiconductor or nearby layers.
arxiv-2604-01846: He tracks p-adic Hodge parameters for semistable Galois representations with regular weights. Merging crystalline case methods with counts of extension groups for Steinberg representations, he reads the full parameter data off Steinberg pieces and the crystalline data between them. The results also restate in geometric and Lie algebraic terms on flag varieties. He builds an explicit locally analytic representation and shows that when its monodromy rank is small, it pins down the target.
arxiv-2604-02246: Mahato and Blaschke study the thermodynamics of a graphene inspired Gross Neveu model in two plus one dimensions. Focusing on entropy from Gaussian fluctuations beyond mean field, they find fluctuations contribute nearly as much as the mean field itself. Feedback from fluctuations to the mean field must be included, cutting mainly Landau damping contributions. A generalized Beth Uhlenbeck treatment suppresses low energy terms while keeping bound state effects, giving a sharper crossover in the degrees of freedom.
arxiv-2604-02346: Liu and colleagues benchmark language models for drug discovery with DrugPlayGround. The frame tests text accounts of drug traits, drug protein interactions, and body responses to drug perturbations. It also pairs predictions with expert guided reasons to probe chemical and life science reasoning. The goal is an objective account of where language models help or falter against older drug discovery platforms across all stages of the pipeline.
arxiv-2604-02546: Mao and four colleagues propose UniScene3D, a transformer system that learns one shared 3D scene code from multi-view RGB-Pointmap inputs. It borrows priors from a pretrained 2D base model and enforces shape and meaning consistency across views through two alignment tricks. Fine-tuning on viewpoint grounding, retrieval, classification and 3D question answering reaches top results in low-shot and task-specific settings.
arxiv-2604-02646: Abe and three colleagues refine bounds on contractible edges that preserve 4-connectedness in graphs, focusing on plane triangulations. They show that a 4-connected plane triangulation with at least seven vertices holds at least as many such edges as the count of vertices of degree five or more, plus two. They also determine the extremal graphs that meet the bound.
arxiv-2604-02746: Chen, Shao and Shi study zero-free regions of the hard-core model partition function on finite graphs and their implications for free energy analyticity. Classical results reach the tree uniqueness threshold set by maximum degree, but the connective constant measures structural complexity more precisely for lattices. Defining the connective constant for finite graphs via self-avoiding walks, they prove zero-freeness below the threshold set by that constant.
arxiv-2604-02846: Shi and four colleagues propose adaptive local frequency filtering for Fourier-encoded implicit neural representations. Such models learn continuous signals from discrete samples. Fixed Fourier mappings use one frequency set everywhere, fitting signals with varying local spectra poorly and converging slowly on fine details. A parameter that varies in space tunes encoded Fourier components, sliding smoothly among low-pass, band-pass, and high-pass response across locations. The method improves reconstruction quality and speed over fixed-frequency baselines. Tests cover 2D image fitting, 3D shape work, and sparse data rebuilding.
arxiv-2604-02946: Nagano and five colleagues train models on synthetic data with help from provenance records made during synthesis. Each input region is marked as target or non-target, and gradients over non-target regions are suppressed. That push steers the model toward features of the target object itself, instead of quirks and artifacts left by synthesis. Tests across weakly supervised object localization, spatio-temporal action localization, and image classification show the method works across tasks and modalities.
arxiv-2604-03346: Wang and colleagues use quantum circuits to solve the partial differential equations behind portfolio choice. Their circuit builds a polynomial from tensor rank breakdown, cutting resource needs from exponential to polynomial when rank is modest. Built into quantum and quantum-inspired physics-informed networks, the models beat standard networks on the Merton problem while using far fewer weights.
arxiv-2604-03546: Ohno and Togawa revisit three ways to shrink large coefficients in quantum annealing Hamiltonians under minor-embedding rules. A wide coefficient range hurts results there. They test how far the methods shrink the range of the minor-embedded Hamiltonian. They also test sample scores on the D-Wave Advantage annealer. The interaction-extension method lifts sample scores well by shrinking the range. Bounded-coefficient integer encoding and the augmented Lagrangian method show only small effects.
arxiv-2604-04046: Jiale Huang and team named the dismagicker, a non-Clifford unitary gate that cuts non-stabilizerness, or magic, in quantum many-body states. Tools that cut entanglement are standard in tensor networks, but no matching tool existed for magic cutting. They steer states toward stabilizer states a classical machine can mimic, built by tuning within matrix product states. Joined with Clifford untying steps, the method raised scores for old-style simulation and quantum state setup.
arxiv-2604-04146: Lai and Nguyen extend a tiling count for cross-shaped regions built from overlapping Aztec rectangles. Ciucu had shown that the number of domino tilings of such a cruciform region follows a simple product formula. The authors generalize that result to a generating-function formula, which packages the counts across region sizes. The work grows out of Di Francesco's Aztec triangle conjecture and its connection to the twenty-vertex model.
arxiv-2604-04646: Cha and five colleagues propose the Flow Divergence Sampler, a training-free framework for flow matching. Flow models learn a target distribution from a marginal velocity field averaging sample velocities from a prior to target data. When sample velocities conflict at one state, the mean velocity can misguide samples toward low-density regions. This misguidance is quantified by the divergence of the velocity field. The sampler steers states toward clearer regions. As a plug-and-play framework for solvers, it improves fidelity across tasks including text-to-image synthesis.
arxiv-2604-04846: Mony and Dhir study the Bc meson spectrum with a Bayesian approach, testing three confining potentials: the Cornell form, a logarithmically modified version, and a screened Cornell form. They sample each potential's parameters by Markov chain Monte Carlo, keeping correlations among fitted values. The resulting distributions yield masses, spin splittings, mixing angles, and wave-function measures through the 6D multiplet, checked against Regge trajectories. Low-lying states stay stable across potentials, while higher states diverge as they probe larger distances, with growing uncertainty.
arxiv-2604-04946: Hu, Glatt, and Liu tackle phase drift in graph-based models for fluid dynamics, where forecasts stay plausible yet lose time alignment with observations. That drift limits digital twins and control, while retraining a frozen surrogate is costly and impractical. They ask whether drift can be corrected by steering latent space. Their phase-steering framework for pretrained CFD models pairs sparse autoencoders, which yield disentangled codes, with an intervention mechanism. Steering latent space aims to restore temporal alignment without new training.
arxiv-2604-05046: Kunnumkai and four co-authors ask whether gravitational-wave merger rates can explain the observed short gamma-ray burst rate. Binary neutron star detections are scarce in the latest LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA run, raising doubt that merger rates suffice. Using fourth-run merger constraints and published local burst rates, they test reconciliation. For burst rates near one to seven per cubic gigaparsec per year, if over 55 percent of binary neutron star mergers launch a jet, the current merger rate suffices.
arxiv-2604-05346: Gretarsson and ten colleagues study ruthenium tribromide, a layered magnet prized for Kitaev magnetism, where competing spin links frustrate ordinary order. With X-ray scattering tuned to ruthenium, they watch its zigzag spin pattern melt at the Neel point. Zigzag correlations survive well above that point, however, and shift strength along the stacking direction. Extended bromine orbitals strengthen links between layers, the team argues, locking in correlations across layers that the chloride cousin lacks.
arxiv-2604-05446: Lee and Kim improve mean estimation when labels are scarce but unlabeled traits abound. Their MEC method reweights labeled cases to match the target group, using split-sample fits and Bregman projections to stay steady when predictors err. It meets the efficiency bound under weaker rules, with coverage near its stated level and tighter gaps than prediction-powered rivals.
arxiv-2604-05546: Zhang and nine colleagues review fast inference for large vision-language models, where image tokens swamp cost across encoding, prefilling, and decoding. They sort tricks by life-cycle stage and by three axes: information density, long-context attention, and memory limits. The review ends with four frontiers, from hybrid compression to split-stage serving, backed by pilot tests.
arxiv-2604-05846: Sun and four colleagues turn graph learning into agentic navigation plus language-model inference with AgentGL. Graph-native tools enable multi-scale exploration, search-limited thinking balances accuracy and efficiency, and graph-shaped curriculum reinforcement learning steadies long-horizon policy learning. Gains reach up to about 18 percent on node classification and about 28 percent on link prediction.
arxiv-2604-05946: Spaeth and Roberts show that small ensemble size bends conditional reliability checks in weather forecasting. Finite samples shrink the slopes of spread-error links and reliability diagrams even for perfect forecasts, so flat slopes need not mean bad forecasts. They work out exact shrink formulas and give estimators from ensemble data alone, then show the bend bites hard in ECMWF sub-seasonal temperature forecasts.
arxiv-2604-06346: Alansary, Mohamed, and Hamdi propose severity-aware weighted loss for Arabic models. Fine-tuning treats all cases evenly, ignoring severity, though severe errors carry higher risk. Their method scales loss by soft severity probabilities, prioritizing critical interactions. Labels and scores come from an AraBERT-based classifier at loss level only. Experiments use the MAQA dataset of complaints and responses, across ten Arabic large language models. Standard fine-tuning yields modest improvements, while severity-aware optimization improves AraGPT2-Base from 59 to 66 percent and gains up to 12.1 percent over baselines.
arxiv-2604-06746: Chen, Liu, and Shao protect long-context inference from memory blowup with StructKV. As context windows pass one million tokens, key-value caches grow linearly and choke memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors rank tokens by local saliency at one layer, discarding tokens that act as global hubs yet look dormant there. StructKV aggregates attention across network depth to find those hubs, detects the best compression layer adaptively, and separates compute budget from storage budget. Tests on LongBench and RULER show it preserves long-range links and retrieval strength.
arxiv-2604-07046: Dabbaghi, García Lastra, and de Silva recast density models so they use the full bend of electron density rather than only its slope hints. Standard models lean on kinetic energy density or a density laplacian, which can blur apart one electron cases that look alike. The authors present a simple no fit model, theta PBE, and lay out a path to run it in full self agreement inside a common wave method. Tests show sound chemisorption energies, though bulk lattice spacings stay hard to pin.
arxiv-2604-07246: Elokda and three colleagues design a karma economy for sharing scarce charging power among electric vehicles. Each driver holds non-tradable karma tokens and bids them in each time slot, with winners paying their bids into a pool that is then redistributed. The scheme handles changing charge levels, private trip deadlines, and varying urgency. A stable equilibrium is shown to exist, and it balances deadline pressure against urgency better than standard scheduling rules.
arxiv-2604-07346: Borchia, Knolle, and Nunnenkamp show that links between particles can spread one-way motion from a bath to parts it never touches. Their test case is a line of spin-1/2 fermions with Hatsugai-Kohmoto links joining all pairs and a built bath. In that setup, the motion stays exactly solvable. Links reshape how excitations move and drive drift even in spin parts with no direct bath link. The same effect holds for short-range links in a driven Fermi-Hubbard chain, giving a solvable test bed for such motion.
arxiv-2604-07446: Bala and three colleagues build a Super-Grassmannian integral form for n-point functions in N equals 1 superconformal theory in three dimensions. Conformal, supersymmetry, and special superconformal invariance show up plainly through operator-valued delta-function constraints. Simple algebraic links among component correlators let any component follow from just one of them. The form also builds AdS4 boundary correlators with contact diagrams from pure exchange terms, shown by the Yang-Mills gluon four-point function.
arxiv-2604-08046: Zhao and nine colleagues tackle the integration bottleneck in RAG, where retrieved files often fail to change model answers, even when matching. Current research stresses lookup quality but overlooks a key failure: models ignore matching files that conflict with internal parametric memory. Resolving that conflict quietly in a single generation pass proves weak. Their GuarantRAG framework openly splits reasoning from evidence integration. An Inner-Answer from built-in knowledge alone captures the model's reasoning flow, while a Refer-Answer built with a contrastive training goal ensures faithful evidence use.
arxiv-2604-08146: Tian gives a simpler proof of a descent conjecture of Wittenberg for certain torsors. The conjecture says a smooth base inherits weak approximation with Brauer-Manin obstruction when every twist of a rationally connected torsor over it satisfies it. Tian proves the claim for certain torsors under connected linear groups, using Cao's descent formula. The argument offers an alternative route to Wittenberg's result in these cases.
arxiv-2604-08246: Carstensen and Tran present a local discontinuous Galerkin finite element method for convex minimization. Error control in convex minimization hinges on tight control of the discrete-exact minimal energy gap. Conforming discretizations for p-Laplace minimization give energy-difference bounds at optimal rates. Even for smooth solutions, known rates for higher-order non-conforming discretizations stay suboptimal. Thus popular a posteriori error control via the two-energy principle, generalizing hyper-circle identities, looks unbalanced. The authors offer a refined analysis as a new starting point.
arxiv-2604-08846: Luo and seven colleagues introduce DACO, dictionary aligned concept control for safeguarding multimodal language models. Prompt engineering, response classification, and fine tuning often fail against evolving malicious patterns, need query reruns, or cost heavily, while activation steering of a frozen model offers flexible control. DACO curates 15,000 multimodal concepts from over 400,000 caption image stimuli into concept directions, forming DACO-400K, and uses sparse coding plus a sparse autoencoder initialized from the dictionary to steer activations. Tests across models and safety benchmarks show much better safety with general capabilities intact.
arxiv-2604-08946: Fan, Huang, and Lei settle a long-open question for the compressible Navier-Stokes-Poisson equations: do global smooth solutions exist for general large initial data? The answer is yes under ball-shaped symmetry on solid balls, with density-linked thickness meeting a BD-type entropy rule. By using the coupling between effective speed and speed, the authors prove bounds for key values, yielding density bounds. The result is the first for any large initial data in a truly multi-way domain with rich traits.
arxiv-2604-09146: Rivière, Malo, Varlin Grassi, and Prié study breaks in presence, moments when a distraction snaps a virtual reality user out of feeling present. From close interviews with 14 users of a height exposure program, they model 57 episodes in fine detail. Four patterns emerge: episodes users reflect on, episodes they discard, episodes tied to self-protection, and episodes with mixed signals. The authors read these against a model of presence and offer an awareness-based definition plus three design ideas.
arxiv-2604-09246: Ghosh, Sinha, and Stober improve voice masking for atypical speech in the DDSP-QbE pipeline.
