Tests show much better search speed and success in complex real-world scenes.
arxiv-2605-09546:
Zhong and three colleagues propose PolarNet, a neural net design for modeling Lyapunov functions with a single critical point guaranteed by design. Lyapunov functions certify stability of dynamical systems, but learning them jointly with controllers is fragile. Past neural methods can fail in training because nothing in the design guarantees the learned function acts like a valid Lyapunov function. The authors trace those failures to missing design guarantees.

PolarNet structurally guarantees a single critical point, with theory results on properness and universality for Lyapunov modeling. Used as a drop in swap for past learned control methods, it dodges the training troubles caused by the missing guarantees. Number tests confirm PolarNet keeps a single critical point and avoids training failures, giving users a safer building block for provably stable learned control.
arxiv-2605-09746:
Ahmad and two colleagues asked which satellite channels a landslide detector truly needs, rather than feeding it everything available. Most models pile up correlated spectral and terrain inputs, which muddy interpretation, inflate compute, and can even hurt accuracy through the Hughes Phenomenon. Their explainable framework for the Landslide4Sense benchmark combined Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery with ALOS PALSAR terrain data plus 16 engineered indices.

Instead of dropping one band at a time, they used Sequential Forward Floating Selection, building and pruning a feature pool with a lightweight U-Net++ proxy. A compact 8-channel subset matched or beat the segmentation F1 score of setups using up to 30 channels. The selection trail also reveals which physical cues, spectral or topographic, the models genuinely lean on.
arxiv-2605-09846:
Liu and three colleagues built ChladniSonify, a real-time system that turns Chladni patterns, the sand figures formed on vibrating plates, into sound for new media art. Visual-acoustic mapping in art tools is usually subjective, and existing tools demand heavy physical simulation, cannot run in real time offline, or offer uncontrollable mapping rules. The team grounded mapping in Kirchhoff-Love thin-plate vibration theory.

They built a paired dataset of patterns and vibration frequencies. It was calibrated with ANSYS finite-element simulation. Pattern modes were classified with a lightweight convolutional network enhanced by attention, focusing on slender nodal lines. The core module hit 99.33 percent accuracy on synthetic tests, at 7.03 milliseconds per image. It mapped patterns to sine-wave audio at matching frequencies, with no deviation from theory on correct samples.
arxiv-2605-09946:
Max Horwitz and three colleagues rethink how language models learn from human tastes. Nash Learning from Human Feedback recasts that tuning as a zero-sum game over policies, but it optimizes mean pairwise payoffs. Strong mean scores can then hide routine failure across prompts, raters, or safety-critical groups. Their 2026 paper introduces risk-aware games to expose those tails.

Players instead optimize convex risk measures of their loss, exploiting structure in feedback doubt. A shift-invariance trait of many risk measures preserves monotonicity, so sample-efficient self-play still converges fast. The authors prove stability and sample bounds that scale with risk, and add a layered game plus a two-timescale algorithm with bias correction. Risk-tuned policies proved robust across data strata and matched or beat risk-neutral scores, gaining robustness without a performance tax.
arxiv-2605-10746:
Tong Liu and Gao Xianlong frame key states as a dual-space Lyapunov trait, giving duality-proof marks of key states. The authors prove a Fourier ban rule: tight packing in one view cannot sit with tight packing in its Fourier-twin view.

This turns the Liu-Xia rule, that both real-space and momentum-space Lyapunov exponents fade to zero, from a seen rule into a hard length-scale claim. A key state is marked by the joint lack of tight packing in real and momentum space. In quasiperiodic models that can be solved by hand, it yields closed-form key lines and an exact finite key zone with one more key branch. It also yields a tangled key face in a non-Hermitian non-self-dual spectrum. It thus makes the rule an exact solvability guide for finding key sets.
arxiv-2605-10846:
Andrew Lingenfelter and Aashish A. Clerk solve exactly the steady states of a class of driven, dissipative fermionic systems, the kind of open quantum matter now built from cold trapped atoms. Such systems balance coherent motion against loss, and exact non-equilibrium solutions are rare.

Generalizing the coherent quantum absorber trick to fermions, the pair uncovers a hidden time-reversal symmetry in these models. The steady state jumps in density at a first-order phase transition, a jump that survives finite dissipation, while mean-field theory finds the bistable region but misses the transition line. The hidden symmetry also forces an Onsager symmetry on two-time correlations. Theorists get exact ground truth for a lively experimental frontier.
arxiv-2605-10946:
Xue-Ying Han and seventeen colleagues of the Lattice Parton Collaboration compute heavy-meson shape functions from lattice quantum chromodynamics, tightening predictions for B-meson decays. These functions rank among the largest theory errors clouding B anomalies and CP-violation results.

Building on the HQLaMET framework with lattice work on expansion moments, the team runs many simulations toward the continuum limit and true pion mass, with full error budgets and cross-checks. Total error on key inverse moments falls threefold against the prior analysis. Flavor physicists get sharper form factors for B decays into K-star states at large recoil.
arxiv-2605-11046:
P. Castorina, A. Iorio, J. Kriš, and M. Shams Nejati ask which dilaton gravity models can mimic two-dimensional analogue black holes built in labs, such as superconducting quantum circuits. Analogue systems let researchers probe regimes of inaccessible systems through accessible stand-ins, following Feynman's analogue-simulation idea.

The team identifies the assumptions such models must satisfy and finds which ones let the Hawking temperature's state-dependence switch on and off, a feature absent in four-dimensional black holes. When temperature runs state-independent, its motion rules split from the entropy rules. Number work shows the given analogues match no known dilaton model, limiting their theory payoff. Reversing the logic, established dilaton models yield conditions lab setups must meet, shifting the challenge to experiment.
arxiv-2605-11146:
G. Diniz and four others map the BCS-BEC crossover in trapped one-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard chains. Trapping breaks translational symmetry and reshapes correlation patterns. Confined ultracold atoms in optical lattices mimic strongly correlated lattice models, but in trapped setups the crossover allows odd phases with no uniform analogue.

The team pairs density-matrix renormalization-group runs and entanglement checks with simple models of tightly bound fermion pairs. They map how trap-plus-interaction effects yield insulating zones that still host persistent superfluid correlations. Conditioned correlation functions with power-law decay give a clear test for telling crossover regimes apart. Cold-atom researchers get entanglement-based signs for a crossover that trapping makes subtle.
arxiv-2605-11246:
Yonghan Yang and seven colleagues present SPADE, support-proximity augmented diffusion estimation for offline black-box optimization. Offline black-box search seeks novel designs with high quality scores from a static dataset alone, challenged by out-of-sample guessing.

Existing routes split into inverse methods, struggling with the ill-posed mapping from scores to designs, and forward methods, often lacking the expressivity to measure uncertainty. SPADE rethinks forward surrogate modeling through conditional generative modeling. It models forward likelihood with a diffusion model plus two extras. A Calibrated Diffusion Estimation module keeps global match in moments and paired rankings. A Support-Proximity Regularization tool holds the data manifold constraint via kNN density scores. Theory shows this rule equals raising a Bayesian guess from a valid design prior. In tests, SPADE reaches state-of-the-art Design-Bench performance. Builders get a forward method that respects the data manifold.
arxiv-2605-11546: Daniels, D'Ambrosia, DeWeese and Sahai give an analytic estimate for the entropy of floating-point numbers, with bounds on its error. Differential entropy links tightly to the discrete entropy of a uniformly rounded random variable. Their approximation uncovers a different quantity that provides that link for floating-point quantization. They also prove floating-point entropy stays nearly unchanged under scaling. Closed-form expressions for common distributions are provided and checked against exact results.
arxiv-2605-11646: López studies circles-layered steady sheets of the Dirichlet energy in flat space. He proves non-spinning sheets exist with zero uneven mean bend, layered by circles in flat planes. These sheets extend the known Riemann cases of minimal surface theory into the uneven Dirichlet-energy context. He sorts all zero-bend sheets layered by circles: either axially even about the z-axis or one of the new cases. He also studies the case of non-zero constant uneven mean bend.
arxiv-2605-11746: Wenkai Li and four colleagues test whether chain-of-thought traces faithfully report how a language model reaches its answer. Across nine models and seven reasoning benchmarks, the model's hidden commitment and its stated answer lined up on only 61.9 percent of steps on average, with most mismatches being confident-looking continuations written after the answer had already settled. Their 2026 study concludes that such traces stay useful but cannot be trusted as a record of when the answer formed.
arxiv-2605-11846: Moritz Gögl, Hanwen Xing, and Christopher Yau bring martingale consistency to self-taught learning under changing information. When views are coarse or partial, a coarse guess should match the mean guess expected after update, yet standard goals do not enforce this. Their system constrains only the mean refined guess, letting guesses update as information arrives without steady drift. Tests on time-series, tabular, and image benchmarks showed better toughness and tuning under partial views.
arxiv-2605-12046: Ge Yan, Shanchuan Li, and Yuxuan Du rethink neural decoders in quantum error fixing under stated accuracy-latency limits. They unify representative neural units into five design patterns for surface-code work up to distance 9, or 161 real qubits. They build an end-to-end squeeze chain for FPGA testing. Tests show near-term results depend more on data scale than design size. Built-in bias matters most for high scores, and INT4 rounding is a must for µs FPGA latency.
arxiv-2605-12246: In a 2026 paper, Renato Vieira dos Santos presents kappa to test whether charge couples to gravity. The number sets the motion difference equal to kappa times the charge-mass gap. Pooling precise equivalence tests gives a bound: kappa stays below 2.1 times ten to the minus four kilograms per coulomb at 95 percent trust. That bound is about eleven orders weaker than bounds on makeup breaks, leaving the charge axis open. A future find at reachable levels would point beyond gravity theory, perhaps to light scalar fields.
arxiv-2605-12646: Benz, Straitouri and Gomez-Rodriguez study learning to decide with AI help when human and AI confidence align. When AI helps high-stakes decisions by predicting an outcome, it should share prediction confidence. Yet people often struggle to judge when to trust a prediction from confidence alone. Recent work links use of AI-aided decisions to match between AI confidence and people's confidence in their own guesses. The paper asks how far that match shapes learning optimal choices through repeat rounds, in the case of binary guesses and binary choices.
arxiv-2605-12946: Akita, Hamaguchi, Kitagawa and Yokoyama study minimal Majoron dark matter, built on the Type-I seesaw model plus a singlet scalar. Staying agnostic about the Majoron mass, they compute its abundance from freeze-in and misalignment production and map the viable parameter space. Without fine-tuning the initial misalignment angle, the mass sits below about 10 MeV. Successful leptogenesis with two right-handed neutrinos instead favours misalignment production with mass below about 100 eV.
arxiv-2605-13246: Hattori, Kobayashi and Sakayori build DrvHorn, a tool that hunts reference counting faults in Linux kernel drivers. Such faults miscount live references to resources and can cause leaks or security holes. By modelling the driver interface and slicing programs aggressively, the tool found 545 faults across platform drivers, with 424 previously unknown. The authors submitted fixes, and 45 of their patches were merged into the kernel.
arxiv-2605-13346: Angioli and colleagues adapt contextual bandits, online choice problems under partial feedback, for tiny devices. Standard linear methods scale badly in memory and compute, while hyperdimensional HD-CB grows action values until low precision hardware overflows. Their probabilistic HD-CB updates only a random subset of components each step, with a decaying chance and bounded values. At just 3 bits per component it beats binarized HD-CB and nears full precision HD-CB on standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-13446: Andrzej Puc and Joanna Janczura propose a framework for forecasting intraday power price paths and turning those forecasts into trades. Continuous intraday markets matter for short-term trading and balancing, yet prices move fast. Building on a fixed support vector model, they stretch point forecasts into path forecasts through scenarios built from forecast errors. A new support vector sorting step picks typical scenarios. Tests on German intraday trade data show gains over benchmarks in both accuracy and profit, and dynamic reweighting adds further profit with limited downside risk.
arxiv-2605-13846: Ziheng Zhang and three colleagues introduce WARDEN, an early tongue model system writing and turning Wardaman, a rare Aussie native tongue, into English from only 6 hours of audio. WARDEN uses split writing and turning models: it first turns Wardaman audio into sound writing, then the writing into English turning. For writing, the Wardaman token is seeded from Sundanese, a tongue sharing similar sounds with Wardaman, to speed fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-13946: Pfeifle and fifteen co-authors report 157 twin active black-hole candidates split apart in mid-infrared light, drawn from the Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer. Imaging from the Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey marks them as galaxy merger candidates. Spectra now cover about two thirds of the set. Seventy-six are confirmed to sit in galaxy mergers, a phase thought key to giant black-hole growth.
arxiv-2605-14146: Arvanitis, Aslanidis, Sommer and Rugamer offer bde, a Python package for Bayesian deep ensembles that is friendly to use, with tabular data as its main focus. It builds on a fast JAX implementation of Microcanonical Langevin Ensembles, a sampling method known as MILE. The package supplies scikit-learn compatible estimators for fast training, Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling, and uncertainty scores. Both regression and classification tasks are covered, so users can gauge how much to trust its predictions.
arxiv-2605-14246: Liu and six co-authors propose a light risk-gated reinforcement learning approximation for risk-aware control with partial views. Safety-critical control uses risk-aware Markov decision processes with partial views. The method builds a finite-history proxy state and learns a forecaster of near-term safety breaches per candidate action. That predicted risk serves as a penalty in value learning and as a gate between optimistic and conservative value estimates. In adult and teen glucose cohorts, the method improves glycemic tradeoffs and cuts runtime against a belief baseline.
arxiv-2605-14546: Wang, Liu, Wang, Chen, Ren, Li, Hao, Kong, Zhang and Ni probe what fine-tuned neural PDE experts actually learn in weight space. Starting from a shared anchor, they separate endpoint experts' updates into two parts. One part is shared across the family, and the other points along the physical parameter. Their Calibration-Conditioned Merge then reads a target coordinate from metadata or a short rollout and deploys one merged checkpoint, with claimed error cuts over fifty percent in extrapolative regimes.
arxiv-2605-14846: Chen and Cannon propose a data-driven model predictive control method using a transformer encoder for multi-step forecasts. The nonconvex attention is handled by deriving difference-of-convex forms, embedded in a successive convex loop. Feasibility and convergence of the loop are guaranteed, with each step meeting problem constraints. Under mild assumptions, the loop reaches a locally optimal solution of the control problem, shown on a benchmark control problem.
arxiv-2605-15146: Sabya Sachi Chatterjee and Antonio Palazzo propose that sterile neutrinos feeling a new matter potential could explain several oscillation anomalies. At low energy the 3+1 model acts like a three-flavor beyond-standard scheme. It eases tension between the NOvA and T2K tests when it is negative and two sterile mixing angles are nonzero. The same effect explains a Super-Kamiokande electron-like excess. At high energy a new resonance near 10 TeV matches an IceCube hint.
arxiv-2605-15246: Stavros Bouras and seven others examine whether generative models for trajectory data really protect privacy. Made paths from GANs, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models are often assumed private simply because they are made. The team maps usable observed privacy-evaluation methods and finds a major gap in how such models are judged. Running member guessing attacks against typical models, they show generative nature alone does not remove privacy risk.
arxiv-2605-15546: Bingwen Qiu and seven colleagues address 3D object detection in point clouds, where distant objects are sparse yet need wide context. Their 3DTMDet network pairs state-space models, which capture long-range interactions cheaply, with transformer modules that preserve fine local geometry, in a hybrid block balancing both demands. A voxel block inspired by LiDAR physics diffuses features along viewing direction to rebuild occluded and distant shapes. Tests on KITTI and ONCE beat leading detectors.
arxiv-2605-15746: Yuki Nakamura derives the linear Kyle equilibrium for a Bayesian market maker watching Gaussian noise-blurred order flow. Price impact and informed-trader strategy rescale by factors of the parameter, inversely, so their product stays fixed. A split then names a closed-form transfer from the LP pool to traders, the privacy subsidy. It is the break-even fee any privacy exchange must charge. It is the closed-form analog of Loss-Versus-Rebalancing. Shielded market makers with noise injection are the main use; other designs need separate frames.
arxiv-2605-15846: Xinbo Xu and fifteen colleagues introduce RoadmapBench, a benchmark for long-horizon agentic software development across version upgrades. It holds 115 coding tasks drawn from real open-source upgrades across 17 repositories and five programming languages. Each task asks the agent to build a target version's features from a source snapshot, with a median change of 3,700 lines across 51 files. Testing thirteen frontier models, the authors find even the strongest, Claude-Opus-4.7, solves only 39.1 percent of tasks, against 5.2 percent for the weakest. Long-horizon development remains largely unsolved.
arxiv-2605-15946: Benjamin Rainer and Barbara Kaltenbacher study an inverse problem for ultrasound imaging. They seek to recover sound speed, diffusivity, and nonlinear effects from edge readings. The model is a cyclic Westervelt equation for strong sound waves in varied media. They show smoothness of the forward map and prove a single answer in the linearized case through a baseline approach. They then build a frozen Newton-type rebuild scheme. Test runs show that the approach can work.
arxiv-2605-16246: Fuller and four others present FRESH, a method that tunes patient-level models to pooled evidence such as trial notes and record data. The method retunes a model trained on patient-level data so its outputs match set stats for a target group. The retuning is a minimal tweak of the first joint spread in an information-shape sense. Uses include framing single-arm trials against current standard of care, mocking trial designs, and weighing on-market drugs.
arxiv-2605-16446: Liang and Li spot a conflict in tabular fair semi-supervised learning: under confidence-gated pseudo-labels, fairness rules trigger Masking Collapse and Trivial Saturation. They propose Online Primal-Dual Allocation, an online system setting fairness and stability costs using breach, risk, and pseudo-label health signals. On Adult, ACSIncome, and COMPAS, OPDA eases degenerate regimes seen under static weighting and single-signal rivals. On Adult and COMPAS it yields working points matching the static frontier; on ACSIncome it preserves utility.
arxiv-2605-16546: Kilpatrick and five colleagues probe mass-loss histories of Type IIn and II-L supernovae with late radio observations. The Very Large Array data come from roughly 1,000 to 7,000 days after explosion. Radio emission appears from four of the 16 targets, while the rest yield only upper limits. The detected sources span about two orders of magnitude in brightness, reflecting varied circumstellar gas. Steep spectra point to optically thin synchrotron emission with internal free-free absorption. The intermediate object PTF11iqb supports a continuum between the subtypes rather than a sharp divide.
arxiv-2605-16646: Campos Junior and Murta compare two paradigms for resolving software merge conflicts: large language models and search-based software engineering. Testing MergeGen against a hill-climbing search method on thousands of real conflicts in Java, C#, JavaScript, and TypeScript, they find clear trade-offs. Language models handle imbalanced content well but falter on non-English text and large inputs. Search generalizes better and wins on balanced conflicts, motivating hybrid tools.
arxiv-2605-16746: Wang and colleagues study a failure mode they call memory laundering in agents that reuse persistent state. Toxic or adversarial context can be compressed into memory summaries that pass standard toxicity detectors, while still steering later outputs toward hostile framing. Paired counterfactual rollouts show toxic-origin summaries staying below toxicity thresholds yet raising downstream toxicity. The team measures this with the sub-threshold propagation gap. Sanitizing toxic state before summarization cuts the gap sharply, while cleaning only the finished summary leaves laundered influence intact.
arxiv-2605-16846: Zabolotnii presents a frequentist option to least-squares fractional polynomials for skewed dose-response and survival. Fractional polynomials model nonlinear curves, but least-squares fitting falters with skewed or heavy-tailed errors, as with survival times and biomarkers. His replacement keeps the model but estimates coefficients with a moment score tuned to skewness and kurtosis, giving an efficiency gain. Across skewed errors, slope variance falls 10 to 20% for skew and up to 60% for heavy-tailed log-normal cases, with near-nominal coverage. On a breast-cancer cohort, tumor intervals narrow 26%.
arxiv-2605-16946: Che's team shows voltage-controlled, reprogrammable magnonic logic in a bismuth ferrite and lanthanum strontium manganite film stack. Ferroelectric domain design in the bismuth ferrite layer tunes the magnon dispersion of the manganite layer, shifting frequencies by up to about 150 megahertz and forming tunable waveguides. Brillouin light scattering images them in detail, showing non-volatile, reversible control set by voltage rather than current. Inverse-design runs show the platform can also split signals, opening a path to magnonic logic and neuromorphic computing.
arxiv-2605-17146: Yasar Yanik and colleagues pair weighted flow matching with a physics-informed Kalman filter to keep digital twins in step with real systems. The generative part reweights training samples toward parameter regions that best explain the evolving state. The filter then tracks state and parameters under noise and weak excitation. In a spacecraft twin it recovered the moment of inertia steadily and beat two standard Kalman filters, the authors report.
arxiv-2605-17346: Onuki examines thermal fluctuations of polarization, charge density and electric field in dilute electrolytes held between metal electrodes at fixed applied potential. When the film is thinner than the Debye screening length, polarization and field correlations gain global parts inversely proportional to volume, uniform across the plane. For much thicker films, global correlations of polarization and charge fade in the bulk, while the field's global part persists across the whole cell.
arxiv-2605-17546: Yang, Tacchella and Xue study redshift-conditioned galaxy image synthesis, comparing diffusion samplers with one-step pixel-MeanFlow on GalaxiesML-64 data. Standard DDPM sampling gives the best distributional fidelity at high cost, while second-order samplers improve efficiency over DDIM. One-step pixel-MeanFlow matches many morphology statistics at far lower cost but trails many-step DDPM on fine structure. The work opens a path to efficient conditional simulators for large cosmological surveys.
arxiv-2605-17846: Attia Nafees ul Haq and four colleagues build UrduSpeech, a 156-hour Urdu speech corpus for a language with 230 million speakers. A language-model-driven pipeline curates audio across twelve categories, from news and drama to rare forms like Bait-Bazi, handling right-to-left script and code-switching. Each clip carries twelve dimensions of paralinguistic metadata, and the set holds a 60-40 gender balance across 71,792 utterances. A nine-hour benchmark set, hand-corrected, anchors evaluation. Human ratings give the main corpus a mean opinion score of 4.6.
arxiv-2605-18346: Peiliang Cai and ten colleagues propose Focused Forcing, a training-free way to shrink the key-value cache in autoregressive video diffusion, where each new chunk of frames conditions on past frames. Instead of sharing one history choice across a chunk, it picks the most relevant and distinctive past frames per frame and gives larger budgets to more important attention heads. Reported in 2026, the result runs up to 1.48 times faster while improving visual quality and text alignment.
arxiv-2605-18446: Adrià Marín-Salvador shows in a 2026 paper that the representation category of a conformal net is canonically a balanced W-star tensor category. The balance comes from the action of the rotation generator on the circle, and the paper gives a more accessible proof for the case with no group acting. A companion paper generalizes the result to nets with a group action.
arxiv-2605-18646: Francis Kulumba and four co-authors identify, in a 2026 paper, the circuit behind a language-switching backdoor in an 8B-parameter autoregressive language model. A three-word Latin trigger redirects English output to French. Early attention heads compose trigger tokens at the last position. The signal then travels mid-layers in a subspace orthogonal to the natural language-identity direction. The final-layer MLP converts it into French logits. Corrupting the single-position bottleneck at any layer kills the trigger but also harms capabilities.
arxiv-2605-18746: Yining Hong and seven co-authors introduce ESI-Bench, a 2026 benchmark for spatial intelligence. Agents act to gain views and reason about how they change with action, uncovering occluded structure and dynamics. Spanning 10 categories and 29 subcategories on OmniGibson, it asks agents to sequence perception and manipulation. Active exploration beats passive sensing, with agents finding strategies. Yet most failures come from action blindness: poor actions yield poor views and errors. Models also commit early with high confidence regardless of evidence, a gap better perception and interaction cannot close.
arxiv-2605-18846: Yusuke Hayashi diagnoses a quiet failure in variational autoencoders, where the decoder may read latent codes not as the encoder wrote them. Standard checks confirm only that a code is used, never that both halves agree on its meaning. His codebook channel measures that agreement, backed by a bound on disagreement drawn from the variational gap. Audits on small datasets, a two-dimensional model, MNIST and a quantized model show the bound holding, exposing mismatches that simple counts cannot reveal.
arxiv-2605-18946: Vinay Kumar and Axel Brandenburg simulate how the magnetic Prandtl number shapes plasmoid-mediated reconnection between merging magnetic islands. Before the plasmoid instability sets in, the reconnection rate follows Sweet-Parker scaling and falls as the Prandtl number rises. Once the current sheet turns plasmoid-unstable, that dependence weakens sharply, and in the plasmoid regime rates stay independent of the Prandtl number. The fastest rates come from nonlinear phases of plasmoid interaction and merger, and the authors explain why boundary-driven Taylor-problem simulations show a stronger dependence.
arxiv-2605-19246: Whanhee Cho and colleagues address bundle retrieval, where a group of items must jointly meet several constraints. Users often struggle to state such multi-part intent, and a strict query can return nothing at all. Their Ex2Bundle system learns package queries from example bundles a user supplies, then gently relaxes limits when the inferred limits cannot be met. Tests on real data plus a user study show it returns bundles that match intent even when the target data shifts.
arxiv-2605-19746: Patterson presents a Hartree-Fock-based GW and Bethe-Salpeter method for solids, using Gaussian orbitals and density fitting instead of the usual plane-wave density-functional starting point. Screening comes from the random-phase approximation without a plasmon-pole shortcut, and high-energy states enter at second order to converge the self-energy. Tests on carbon, silicon, magnesium oxide and two forms of titanium dioxide correct Hartree-Fock's oversized band gaps and valence widths. Diamond and silicon band widths land close to experiment, showing the approach works.
arxiv-2605-19846: Faure, Chen, Yeh, Su and Hsu present FineBench, a benchmark for fine grained human action in long videos. It packs nearly two hundred thousand choice questions across sixty four fifteen minute videos, probing close motion, contact and object handling. Closed models do fairly well, but open source models lag, above all on space sense in multi person scenes and subtle motion gaps. Their FineAgent framework, pairing a Localizer with a Descriptor, lifts open models, giving a plain path to sharper video reading.
arxiv-2605-20246: Xiongbin Wu and nine co-workers present GROW, a framework for open-world vision-language agents. Vision-language agents show promise on open-world tasks, but supervised fine-tuning with demos dominates, while group relative policy optimization needs full trajectories, giving long noisy context. GROW splits trajectories into state-action samples and compares advantages across samples. An analysis shows grouped samples keep the relative optimization signal under simplifying assumptions, despite different local states. Tests on over 800 Minecraft tasks show top performance.
arxiv-2605-20346: Adam Wills, Theodore J. Yoder and Isaac Chuang build a post-selection strategy that works across decoders for high-rate quantum codes. After a baseline run, the decoder runs per logical observable, flipping it; flipped results at near odds drop. Relay-BP tests use 72-qubit and 144-qubit bivariate bicycle codes. Versus priors, it cuts logical error rates by more than 4 times at the same circuit and physical error rate, same post-selection rate. It uses FPGA-friendly belief propagation, not prior repeated high-latency rounds.
arxiv-2605-20446: Lucassen and two co-workers screen blended refrigerants in activated carbons for heat storage and refrigerant recovery. Adsorption storage packs high energy density and pairs well with renewable heat. Their workflow mixes Monte Carlo simulation, thermodynamic models and breakthrough runs to predict storage and separation from pure-component data alone. Blends beat pure fluids on storage density through cooperative adsorption and tighter packing, while carbons split key blend components.
arxiv-2605-20646: Ruichen Yao and eight colleagues present DisImpact, a two-stage framework for sizing up disaster impacts from social media. Disasters cause physical harm plus cascading social effects that surveys capture slowly. Their method first sorts posts into ten impact categories spanning physical and social domains. It then builds an index that weighs each category by its share of posts and by weekly public engagement, giving one scale across categories.
arxiv-2605-21146: Samuele Pasini, Jinhan Kim, and Paolo Tonella present MIST, a detector for Trojans implanted when neural networks are fine-tuned on untrusted data. Instead of reconstructing triggers, MIST tracks how a model's pre-activation spectra evolve during fine-tuning and flags updates that stray from benign patterns. Across four datasets and eight attacks, spectral distances separated Trojaned updates from clean ones after a single update, without knowledge of poisoned data or triggers.
arxiv-2605-21246: Valeria Formisano and colleagues ask who is most at risk from phishing. They test one thousand eighty-six people with a lifelike phishing task from the Spamley set. Five traits emerge from factor analysis: seniority, expertise, creativity, stability, and risk. People who decide fast are more at risk, and fast choices match self-reported impulsivity. Sorting by seniority and creativity yields two groups: aware users and high-risk users.
arxiv-2605-21346: Onur Danaci and co-authors present evidence of quantum machine learning advantage with tens of noisy qubits. Noiseless results show coherent processing of quantum data beats fixed-measurement schemes followed by classical processing. Whether that gap persists at finite scale under unavoidable device noise was uncertain. Simulating existing hardware on a problem with known long-run advantage, they find a clear gap at just thirty to forty noisy qubits. At that scale, data acquisition, not classical computation, becomes the bottleneck.
arxiv-2605-21546: Satyadev Nandakumar, Akhil S, and Chandra Shekhar Tiwari study resource-bounded Kučera-Gács theorems. The Kučera-Gács theorem states that every infinite sequence X is Turing reducible to a Martin-Löf random sequence R. They study resource-bounded analogues at polynomial-time and finite-state bounds. They prove a quasi-polynomial-time theorem: every X is quasi-polynomial-time reducible to a polynomial-time random R, with oracle use n plus little-o of n bits for n bits of X.
arxiv-2605-21646: Jacek Karolczak and Jerzy Stefanowski present alike parts, a feature-guided approach to local and global prototype accounts. Prototype examples help read black box models with cases, but often lack feature-level detail. Locally, alike parts use feature weight scores to highlight the key feature subsets between a sorted instance and its nearest prototype. For global choice, they add a feature weight term to the choice goal, raising mix in feature credits. Tests on six sets show the boosted choice keeps or raises stand-in model faith.
arxiv-2605-21846: SeyedSina Seyedi HasanAbadi and coauthors study causal discovery in linear Gaussian structural VAR models under equal noise variance. Causal effects may span time and intervals, a point for neuroscience, where sampling is coarse. Unlike the DAG equal-variance case, time-series data do not find a unique causal graph, since several parameterizations can give the same law. The authors define observational equivalence and describe its class by orthogonal transformations plus a global positive scale. They propose ENVAR, a sparsity-based search of that class for a sparse representative.
arxiv-2605-22046: Alberto Merici, Kay Rulling, and Shuji Saito refine structure-sheaf cohomology for smooth, proper schemes over a complete non-archimedean field. They build an A1-invariant cohomology theory for smooth schemes, not necessarily proper, taking values in lattices over the ring of integers. The same holds in positive characteristic in dimensions at most 3. As an application, the automorphism group of a variety of dimension at most 3 in positive characteristic acts quasi-unipotently on the structure sheaf cohomology in this setting.
arxiv-2605-22446: Sun and colleagues present Pre-VLA, a runtime verification system for vision-language-action models and world models. Poor actions can cause physical failures or misleading rollouts with wasted rendering. Pre-VLA checks action validity before execution or imagination, using a multimodal backbone and a light dual-branch head. It predicts safety confidence and critic-derived advantage scores for candidate action chunks. Training blends focal classification, advantage regression and soft calibration to handle class imbalance. On the LIBERO benchmark, success rises from 30.79 percent to 37.62 percent, with fewer steps.
arxiv-2605-22746: Hayta and others simplify evidential deep learning, which estimates uncertainty in one pass through Dirichlet distributions over class probabilities. They replace complex expected objectives with a plug in loss at the Dirichlet mean. The approximation error shrinks as evidence grows for broad loss types including squared error and cross entropy. As a special case, this justifies the standard softmax classifier under a given evidence mapping. On Google Speech Commands, the simpler losses match older learning on correct calls and selective prediction while using standard training.
arxiv-2605-23146: Aryal and fourteen coauthors implement infra-Bayesian learning agents for worst case robustness under model misspecification. Classical reinforcement learning assumes an environment apart from agent policy. That fails when other actors anticipate the agent, as with predictors, humans, and institutions. Bayesian methods then yield surely wrong beliefs and endless regret. Infra-Bayesianism splits chance uncertainty from Knightian uncertainty, where no prior can be fairly chosen, and judges actions by worst case outcomes. Their agent shows lower worst case regret than agents and picks the optimal strategy in Newcomb's problem.
arxiv-2605-23346: Kim and colleagues speed up reward-guided sampling from discrete diffusion models, which generate structured categorical data such as text or DNA. Twisted sequential Monte Carlo can target reward-tilted distributions exactly in the limit, but estimating its twist function costs dearly at inference. Their contrastive distribution matching learns that twist from positive and negative samples, adding under 5 percent overhead to a forward pass. Tests span toxic text, DNA design, protein design, and language-model alignment, beating baselines at equal run time.
arxiv-2605-23446: Hordan, Dym, and Seppelt prove that the Weisfeiler-Leman test cannot tell apart all non-isomorphic graphs with a simple spectrum, no matter how high its order k runs. Since that test caps the power of widely used graph neural networks, the gap hits every such network family. Their PRiSM method, short for Partition, Refine, Solve, Match, gives the first provably complete canonicalization of simple-spectrum eigendecompositions. Paired with DeepSets or a Transformer, it achieves universal approximation on these graphs, and tests match or beat prior spectral methods.
arxiv-2605-23546: Wang and colleagues propose a scalable recipe for multi-flux Aharonov-Bohm caging, the complete trapping of wavefunctions in lattices through destructive phase interference. The trapping phases come from gauge fields such as magnetic fields, linking the effect to novel topological states of matter. Computer runs confirm the predicted caging directly. The recipe scales to many fluxes at once. The authors also probe how the effect breaks under onsite detuning, decoherence, and non-Hermitian transitions, offering another route for quantum simulation of exotic matter states.
arxiv-2605-23746: Nguyen and colleagues investigate lithium evolution in the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus galaxy, using GALAH, Gaia-ESO, SAGA. Lithium is hard to explain over time. They present a model for the galaxy, agreeing with data, including the low-metallicity plateau in both star types. At higher metallicities they see lithium-enriched stars from nova explosions. The results reinforce the Spite plateau's universality and suggest the red-giant-branch plateau is too. A hint of low nova lithium yield comes from GALAH sample, but few high-metallicity stars block nova study.
arxiv-2605-23846: László Kérchy studies cross sections of the commutant of upper triangular operator matrices. He builds similarity models from nearly unchanged half spaces. Squeezing commutant operators through a standard map yields a linear manifold. In that manifold, every element drops to rank at most two. A cyclic trait makes the manifold transitive. Earlier work mapped its three dimensional cross sections and their standard bases in three by three matrices. This paper adds matching rules between side by side cross sections, tightening the picture.
arxiv-2605-23946: Vakhnovskyi argues that AI-driven indoor farming should be judged as backup infrastructure for produce, not as a cure-all for food security. His framework, CEA-RIF 2.0, scores seven fronts: supply, climate isolation, energy links, water reuse, cyber-physical reliability, economics, and governance. Drawing on reports, literature, and 2025-2026 financing and policy signals, he finds AI earns its keep only when it improves climate stability, energy flexibility, yield steadiness, fault detection, and safe recovery. The paper closes with a research agenda for testbeds, open data, shared metrics, and pilots.
arxiv-2605-24046: Moreira and three co-authors place a Schwarzschild black hole inside a Hernquist dark-matter halo, building its metric from the halo profile. They verify null geodesic solutions and trace how the halo bends photon paths, then derive mass, horizon condition, Hawking temperature, entropy, Gibbs free energy, and heat capacity. The halo shifts the thermal structure and stability of the configuration, and scalar perturbations show nontrivial corrections to optical, thermodynamic, and perturbative behaviour. Overall, dark-matter parameters move the black hole away from the standard vacuum solution.
arxiv-2605-24146: Vyugin and Dutta study the K-Fibonacci sequence modulo a prime p, estimating the sizes of its sum set and product set. They also lay out a method for estimating the doubling constant of certain m-dimensional recurrent sets in the finite field. That gives a tool for measuring how fast such sets grow under addition.
arxiv-2605-24646: Abel Azze and others study robust ergodic control with steady swings plus rare shocks. Drift and jump intensity both carry uncertainty, common in inventory, cash, and capacity planning. They frame regulation as ergodic singular control with two-way actions, where ambiguity enters through entropy-penalized shifts. The long-run average goal yields a max-min problem. Its HJB equation becomes a nonlinear integro-differential free-boundary problem. The worst model takes a bang-bang form, the policy uses reflecting walls, and exponential jumps reduce it to an ODE system.
arxiv-2605-24746: Hough and others report three decades of VLBI work on quasar 3C207's nucleus. X-band observations from 1981 to 2010 span 29 years. The nucleus is the strongest and most variable in its sample. Core outbursts recur about every seven years, two from a stationary core feeding a swinging eastern component. That component drifts about 40 degrees over the long term with a short reversal. A curved jet extends eastward at apparent speeds near ten times light speed, fitting a precessing, recollimating model.
arxiv-2605-24946: Alexey Kravets leads VISTA, a bridge carrying language interpretability into vision without dedicated vision autoencoders. Labeling visual concepts is hard and fuzzy, so past language gains stalled visually. VISTA steers a visual projector in a LLaVA model to map visual tokens into the language model's labeled textual autoencoder space. Regularized by that autoencoder's reconstruction loss, and the matching rate between top textual concepts and image elements roughly triples. The same lens shows DINOv2 localizing space better than rival encoders, and object removal and replacement tests prove alignment.
arxiv-2605-25146: Philipp Mayer and Ho Yun embed quantum measurements into a geometric framework built from kernel methods, a tool for comparing data through similarity scores. Their quantum covariance embedding turns each measurement into an object in a combined space, giving a distance that orders measurements by difference. Applied to quantum state tomography, rebuilding an unknown quantum state, the setup recasts estimation as kernel regression. It frees estimation from basis-tied sparsity limits. The pair also proves optimal error rates and introduces an estimator tuned to real hardware layouts.
arxiv-2605-25346: Keyi Shen and Glen Chou build a reachability framework that gives bounds for neural dynamics and controllers, staying differentiable and fast. Existing tools over-approximate reachable states, cannot differentiate, and move too slowly for learning and planning. Their JAX framework merges Taylor-model flowpipes with bound propagation, keeping affine links for GPU batches and differentiation. On top of it they add certified training and a sampling-based controller with gradient refinement. Tests on manipulation and quadrotor tasks, including hardware runs up to 72 dimensions, show online planning with bounds intact.
arxiv-2605-25646: Wang and colleagues present G-DRAGON for outdoor robot navigation over long distances. Visual-language navigation handles only short ranges, while map-based methods hallucinate and cannot finish the last mile. G-DRAGON turns spoken commands into coordinates from versioned local OpenStreetMap entities, plans global routes, and projects waypoints through SLAM. It then switches to frontier exploration with open-set semantic voxel mapping for the final approach. In simulation it beats leading baselines, and a ground vehicle completes person-search missions on unseen urban streets.
arxiv-2605-26046: Darshan and Divekar probe what breaks when a language-model judge is tuned for several criteria at once. Textual gradient methods write critiques in words, not numbers, so classic multi-task fixes do not apply. The authors extend TextGrad to the multi-objective case and vary how much the loss, gradient and optimiser models share across criteria. When one gradient model must judge all criteria jointly, its task focus falls 59 percent, from 9.0 to 3.7 out of 10. Simply merging singly tuned prompts also degrades performance, the authors find.
arxiv-2605-26146: Calboreanu names Augment Engineering, a new discipline for orchestrating several purpose-built AI tools across domains. Organisations now deploy separate tools per domain and hire specialists for each, recreating old staffing patterns. The author argues the meta-skills behind effective tool use, prompt engineering and context engineering, transfer across domains. A practitioner fluent in both can serve many tools in many fields. The paper presents a six-phase orchestration methodology. Four portability metrics come with it, illustrated by a five-month case study of one practitioner.
arxiv-2605-26546: Runxi Huang and three colleagues speed on-device inference for mobile GUI agents with MobileExplorer. Cloud models raise privacy and latency worries, yet on-device agents remain underexplored. Their framework exploits slow vision-language reasoning with lightweight parallel interface exploration, storing traces as structured memory. A two-level rollback restores the initial state when naive backtracking fails. Traces compress into concise hints injected into the next prompt. On AndroidWorld and harder custom tasks, reasoning steps and latency fall 23 percent, with success rates holding or rising 5 percent.
arxiv-2605-26646: Yiqun Chen and sixteen others present UnityMAS-O, a training frame for language-model teams that split jobs across roles. Most teams stay hand-run by prompts and rules, while existing trainers optimize one policy at a time. UnityMAS-O treats the whole workflow as the unit, with roles, graph paths, rewards, and model maps as first-class parts. A star-topology runtime runs workflows and PPO-style updates. On question answering, search, and code tasks, team training lifts hand-set workflows, most for small models.
arxiv-2605-27146: Florindo presents Chaos-SSL, a method for medical image sorting using chaotic maps as a complex twist for contrast learning. Standard methods rely on simple shape and color twists. They may miss fine texture details needed for subtle illness, so stage one pre-trains with Logistic, Tent, and Sine maps for harder, richer views. A second stage fuses cues with general ones from a larger ImageNet model through focus. The Tent-map variant with focus fusion reaches top scores on skin and retina sets, beating rivals.
arxiv-2605-27246: Benzmüller and co-authors argue for logical pluralism in formal reasoning. Their case draws on two decades of embedding non-classical logics inside classical higher-order logic. That line of work grew into the LogiKEy method, which hosts many object logics inside one unifying meta-logical frame, grounded here in computational metaphysics. The paper urges proof assistants to support such pluralism in principle, and warns against logical imperialism, the rigid use of one foundation logic for large theory building, which blocks reuse across fields.
arxiv-2605-27346: Abhinaba Roy, Junyi Liang, and Dorien Herremans build MERIT, a music similarity framework that separates melody, rhythm, and timbre. Training pairs conditional audio generation with source-separated stems so each factor varies on its own. Each head then tracks its own dimension strongly while staying near chance on the others, on synthetic and real audio alike.
arxiv-2605-27546: Abeer Badawi and colleagues build keyphrase summaries of youth crisis chats beyond fixed label lists. Growing a 19-label issue list into a 39-label tree with 96 percent expert agreement, they generate short chat-specific keyphrases with a constrained language model. Expert review finds most keyphrases accurate and clarifying, and topic lookup accuracy jumps from 25 percent to 70 percent over hand analysis.
arxiv-2605-27646: Kabir Swain and colleagues propose Hurwitz Quaternion Multiplicative Quantization, a calibration-free method for compressing key-value caches. Each 4-element chunk becomes a quaternion whose unit direction is quantized to a product of two codebook entries. A Hurwitz group element times a secondary entry yields many codewords from few stored parameters. The method matches full precision within a few hundredths of a perplexity point at about 5 bits, and shrinks a large-context cache from 43 GB to about 9 GB.
arxiv-2605-27746: Vicente Vergara develops square-function bounds for Fourier multipliers whose local oscillation scale sits between dyadic and power-subdyadic scales at high frequency. For symbols meeting a localized Sobolev test, he proves a pointwise square-function bound and a weighted L2 multiplier inequality. Adding a smooth low-frequency part yields unweighted Lp bounds. At p equals 2 the multiplier is bounded for all beta, with a sufficient beta test for other p and Lorentz endpoints at critical equality.
arxiv-2605-27946: Yibo Jacky Zhang, Zeyu Tang, and Sanmi Koyejo ask whether backpropagation is truly the most sample-efficient way to train neural networks. In a unified feedback framework, they show synthetic gradients can estimate gradients with lower error under certain conditions, sometimes by an arbitrarily large margin. Bandit and reinforcement experiments support the theory.
arxiv-2605-28046: Li and colleagues turn agent memory from a passive lookup tool into part of reasoning itself. MemCog links user knowledge into a navigable store, lets agents wander it step by step as they reason, and prompts them to explore memory on their own from conversation cues. It led on standard question tests and far outpaced rivals on a new proactive-memory benchmark.
arxiv-2605-28246: Mohamed Aarif A and Soumya Chakrabarti model a heavy scalar field falling in on itself in a flat-angled, round spacetime. Exact answers show the fall easing off with no shell-pinching breaks in finite time, joined to Schwarzschild or Vaidya outsides. Self-similar falls need heat-flow drag, and the fluid part breaks usual energy rules.
arxiv-2605-28546: Werner Kasselman offers a deliberately tiny executable proof for multi-language contract traceability. Six 'Hello, world!' programs in Rust, Go, C, Java, TypeScript, and AWK link to one observable-output contract, one implementation graph, a traceability file, a readiness gate, and an evidence matrix. The contract demands the exact greeting bytes, no stderr output, and exit code zero. The harness reported five passes and one skip for Java, whose compiler was missing, with no failures, showing contracts, graphs, and gates checked against runnable witnesses.
arxiv-2605-28946: Matthew Blakeney, Luke Corcoran, and Marius de Leeuw review Yang-Baxter integrability for spin chains with constrained Hilbert spaces, such as a Rydberg blockade. They focus on anyonic chains, where fusion rules set the constraints, and present a result on which chains host Temperley-Lieb algebras. Results extend to several fusion categories up to rank seven, and a modified boost-operator method yields new integrable chains. Examples include spin three-halves models, Tambara-Yamagami chains, product categories, and Haagerup-Izumi chains, with numerics for one rank-five model.
arxiv-2605-29446: Chengliang Xu and colleagues introduce CrystalXRD-Bench for vision-language models on XRD peak indexing. Miller-index identification requires reading a narrow peak location from a rendered curve and multi-step crystallographic reasoning. The benchmark contains two hundred fifty samples from ten public databases. The task is to recover the Miller indices contributing to the highest-intensity peak in an XRD pattern. The best score remains below six tenths, with exact-match below four tenths, so the task is far from solved.
arxiv-2605-29946: Zitao Lin and colleagues report Rossiter-McLaughlin measures for AU Mic's two Neptune-size worlds. The pair transited on back-to-back nights in late August 2024, watched by Magellan's spectrograph plus ground and space photometry. Planet b's orbit stays aligned with the star's spin, while planet c leans aligned too, though a polar path stays possible. Wider stability and transit checks also back the aligned picture. A stray stellar signal and weak timing forecasts block a read on c's tilt, showing how stellar activity clouds young, restless systems.
arxiv-2605-30046: Lixing Zhang, Yuchen Liang and Liyan Xie propose MaskDiff-AD for spotting anomalies in categorical, mixed-type and discrete sequence data. The model trains only on normal data, learning to refill masked values from visible context. For a test sample, the score reflects how hard masked spots are to rebuild. This gives a content-sensitive discrete-state score without reverse-time sampling. A non-parametric variant and error guarantees under a threshold accompany the method. Tests give it the best average rank against twelve tabular baselines.
arxiv-2605-30246: Zucheng Gao, Zvonimir Vlah and Anthony Challinor compute the tree-level unequal-time bispectrum in real and redshift space. Results express the bispectrum as a sum of products of two power spectra, enabling a flat-sky approximation that improves efficiency. It preserves line-of-sight information while discarding extraneous full-sky contributions. Validation against full-sky integration shows agreement across scales and redshifts, and at redshift one, sub-percent agreement for multipoles over five. At small scales, results align with the Limber approximation, and Python code is on GitHub.
arxiv-2605-30346: You-Zhe Xie and five co-authors present YoCausal, a benchmark asking how far video models are from a world model. By flipping videos as reversed samples, YoCausal sets up a test plan. Level 1 brings the Reverse Surprise Index, measuring time perception via noise removal. Level 2 brings the Causality Cognition Index, which uses a VLM to split sets into causal and other subsets, freeing causal thought from time bias. Tests on 13 models reveal seeing time flow does not imply grasping causality, and a gap persists versus causal cognition.
arxiv-2605-30546: Chang and Guan study how radio networks combine values held at scattered nodes into one global aggregate, such as a sum. Nodes run on batteries and radio activity dominates energy use, so the goal is to minimize awake time, the rounds any node must stay on. Their randomized distributed algorithm builds and runs an aggregation schedule in near-linear rounds with energy close to the best possible tree degree. A matching lower bound shows no schedule can do better: some node must stay awake at least that many rounds.
arxiv-2605-30646: Alkaeed and colleagues test whether medical language models stay stable when the same patient case is rephrased. Small phrasing changes can flip answers, a danger in safety-critical care, yet vector likeness often misses negation, timing, or severity gaps. Their meaning check uses meaning-based logic to filter truly meaning-preserving rewrites, refined by model judging and checked by a medical expert. Across sixteen general and medical models, domain focus proves mixed: some focused models rank most robust, while strong general baselines stay strong.
arxiv-2605-31246: Ziqing Yang and colleagues plant a backdoor in visual prompt learning by compromising the backbone model itself. Rather than attacking the prompt step, BadBone uses bi-level optimisation so only downstream tasks that use prompt learning inherit the flaw. Attacked models score highly on targeted and untargeted attacks while keeping utility on pretraining and downstream tasks. Six leading model-level defences prove largely ineffective against them, leaving effective defence as open future work.
arxiv-2605-31546: Katona and Mao present weak Ramsey-Turán numbers and strong ones for t-chains in host poset families. They focus on the Boolean lattice family. For any poset, the weak number never exceeds the strong number, with equality when the poset is a chain. For t equal to 1, both numbers equal the product of k minus 1 and l minus 1 for chains. For fixed k, l, and t, the strong number grows like n to the power t.
arxiv-2606-00446:
Benson and co-authors tune each gate of a silicon quantum dot rig with gate-held light. Such dot bits need far-split volts on each gate to sit right. That spread makes set-up slow and fiddly for each chip. Their trick moves trapped charge at the chip's face skin in a firm, set way.

Near heat-band light is shone while gate volts are held in place. The light shifts charge in a pat the team can steer and redo. Gate volts then fall in a much more matched range. A triple dot is tuned to small, matched volts as a show case. Wave-and-charge sims back the tale of how it works. Charge noise stays the same through the shift.
arxiv-2606-00846:
Nguyen, Liu, and Senanayake match people to language models in this 2026 paper. Users face a fast-growing pool of models with opaque traits. Many users also lack the words to say what they value in a reply. Picking the right model by hand is slow and hit-or-miss.

Their system, CUPID, learns tastes by duels. It shows pairs of models, takes the user's pick, and updates its view of their hidden preferences. A fresh upper-confidence rule balances probing new models against using what it has learned. Cost and time budgets set by the user bound the search. Tests with real models and human studies back the design. The authors report that CUPID finds well-matched models at lower cost than naive search. The work treats model choice as a learning problem in its own right. It aims to give each user a 'dream' model without a long quiz.
arxiv-2606-01246:
Luo and co-authors anchor text-to-SQL in live execution feedback. One-pass SQL on complex schemas is often wrong. Many systems draft many queries and vote on them. Votes alone miss key flaws. Drafts from one model tend to repeat each other. One fix for all error types fits none well. SIRIUS-SQL attacks all three flaws at once.

A tuned 32B model drafts diverse, runnable SQL. A general model fills gaps the specialist leaves. Each run result is classed by type, then fixed in a targeted way. A hybrid selector weighs result match and SQL form. It scores 75.88% on BIRD dev. It scores 91.20% on the SPIDER test set.
arxiv-2606-01446:
Bicer and Laneman shrink radio data so many receivers can hunt emitters jointly. Each receiver hears a short burst of complex IQ samples. It turns the burst into a time-frequency picture. Then it codes that picture into a small latent vector. A central unit fuses the vectors from all receivers. It estimates the set of active emitters in the band.

For each emitter it gives a location and frequency offset. It also gives bandwidth and waveform family. A training loss that ignores order handles the shuffled emitter list. Tests use synthetic scenes where spectra overlap. Small vectors still support counting and waveform calls well. Larger vectors are needed for sharp locations, they find.
arxiv-2606-01746:
Wang studies a weak point in neural nets in this 2026 work. Small, crafted changes to inputs can fool such nets. Wang traces part of that risk to the final layer. That layer sorts inputs with sharp, quick shifts. A plain distance-based sorter is far more robust. Yet it tends to sort less well.

Wang builds a new sorter to gain both traits. It mixes stable prototypes with fresh ones from each batch. The mix keeps sharp sorting but adds distance-based strength. Wang also adds a strict test for attacks. The test uses stand-in models to probe the new sorter fairly.
arxiv-2606-02146:
León and co-authors explain why black hole ringdown tails are hard to see in merger waveforms. Price's law predicts a late time power law tail for black hole perturbations, and that tail is a generic feature of the theory. Yet numerical relativity waveforms of binary black hole mergers show the tail only weakly or not at all. The team trace that suppression to the spectral structure of oscillatory sources that drive the perturbation.

For a generic perturbation with a carrier frequency and a characteristic width, the branch cut coefficient that governs the tail is suppressed by their product. For a Gaussian pulse, the suppression takes an exponential form in that same parameter. Time domain Regge-Wheeler evolutions confirm the effect exactly, the authors report. They also derive the leading and next to leading tail coefficients in analytic form.
arxiv-2606-02446:
Abbasi and co-authors model how charge fluctuations evolve in the hot matter made in heavy-ion collisions. Such fluctuations are key signs of the QCD critical point. They shift while the quark-gluon fireball lives and dies. The standard baseline is Fickian diffusion. In that model, the current follows the density slope at once. Real currents need time to respond.

The authors extend the baseline to Maxwell-Cattaneo diffusion. Current now relaxes over a finite time, so it keeps a memory. They derive closed equations for multi-point Wigner functions. Freezeout results become acceptance-dependent cumulants along paths in the phase diagram. Fickian flow already lags behind equilibrium. Added memory suppresses, shifts, and reshapes the cumulant pattern. Higher-order cumulants show the effect most. The work sharpens how critical-point signs should be read.
arxiv-2606-02846:
Botnan and Dong study Cheeger inequalities for persistent Laplacians. These operators track how a simplicial complex grows into a larger one. The work extends a classic link between a graph's smallest cuts and its Laplacian spectrum into the persistent setting.

The authors define a persistent up p-Laplacian for p at least one. At p equal to two it gives the usual persistent up Laplacian. At p equal to one it yields a nonzero persistent Cheeger constant. They prove an inequality that ties that constant to the smallest nonzero eigenvalue. They then treat two structured cases in depth. One assumes a locally complete skeleton. The other covers orientable pseudomanifolds, where a Kron reduction turns the operator into a weighted graph Laplacian. In that case they obtain two-sided inequalities and describe the constant through the dual graph.
arxiv-2606-03046:
Putra, Duong, Pham, and Kim present ZK-Flex, a framework that speeds up zero-knowledge proof generation. Such proofs let a prover convince a verifier that a computation is correct without revealing private data. Generation is compute-heavy, dominated by polynomial and elliptic-curve operations. Accelerators struggle with large-precision modular multiplication and with workloads that shift between stages.

ZK-Flex is a software-hardware co-design. Software optimizers trim polynomial and elliptic-curve work with hardware-aware choices. The hardware centers on TCore, a Toom-Cook-based multi-precision core. A flexible network-on-chip and a linked-list memory scheme raise parallelism under tight memory limits. Across representative benchmarks, ZK-Flex ran 5 to 11 times faster than the state of the art. Area efficiency rose by up to 3.8 times. The authors offer it as a foundation for reconfigurable proof acceleration.
arxiv-2606-03246:
Henriksson, Asadi, Majd, and Kalliovaara make synthetic sea images to train ship perception systems. Self-driving ships need data from bad weather and low light. Such paired images cannot be gathered at sea, since the same scene cannot be shot in two weathers. Unpaired image translation fills the gap, but past models lose small objects in the process.

Their framework uses CycleGAN-turbo, a one-step unpaired translator. Zero-convolution skip links bypass the autoencoder bottleneck that blurs detail. Small objects such as far ships and sea marks thus survive the transfer. A set of 7,000 sea images trains three transfers: day to fog, day to sunset, and day to night. The fog and sunset models kept scene structure well. The night model showed a flaw: fake coastal lights, traced to skewed training data. The pipeline gives a structure-aware way to grow training sets for sea autonomy.
arxiv-2606-03446:
Fernández and Villegas extend multiple orthogonal polynomials to the unit ball. A standard build pairs a Jacobi-type radial part with a spherical harmonic angular part. The authors bring Jacobi-Piñeiro multiple orthogonality into that frame. Both Type I and Type II polynomials are defined on the multidimensional ball.

To show the definitions earn their keep, key results are carried over from the one-variable theory. Several basic theorems of univariate multiple orthogonality gain multivariate forms. The build then widens past the ball itself. Multiple orthogonality is set up for radial weights on more general domains. Readers get a firm base for work on approximation in several variables. The radial extension opens the door to new domains in future studies. The paper links a classic construction to a broader modern setting.
arxiv-2606-03546:
Benoit, Hacquard, Fillion, and Bertin measure how sulphur dioxide sticks to water ice. Sulphur species drive chemistry in the interstellar medium and on icy moons. Yet the total sulphur budget stays poorly known. Sulphur dioxide is seen as a main sulphur store in icy settings. Its grip on water ice thus matters for astrochemical models.

Temperature-programmed desorption tests were run under ultra-high vacuum. Sulphur dioxide was laid on gold, compact amorphous water ice, and crystalline water ice. A Polanyi-Wigner model then extracts adsorption energy distributions for each surface. The ice results show a two-part structure. One layer is loosely bound, the other held much more strongly. The two ice types differ only slightly in behavior. Mean binding energy on water ice is about 439 meV. Modelers get firm numbers for solid-gas exchange of a key sulphur carrier.
arxiv-2606-03646:
Meng and co-authors build the first benchmark for semi-supervised multi-modal crowd counting. Crowd counting from paired data types lacks a shared test ground in the semi-supervised setting. The team first defines that setting formally. A standard protocol fixes how labeled and unlabeled data split at varied ratios. Solid reference points come next.

Baselines are tailored from two families. Fully supervised multi-modal methods form one group. Semi-supervised single-modal methods form the other. Each is evaluated under the new benchmark rules. The comparison gives the field its first common yardstick. Code and the data partition are set for public release. Future methods can now be judged on equal terms. The benchmark should steer semi-supervised crowd counting toward fair, repeatable progress.
arxiv-2606-03846:
Cao and co-authors estimate language model uncertainty by clustered self-assessment. Models often answer with plausible but wrong text. Missing uncertainty scores leave users unable to judge trust. Entropy over sampled replies is the usual proxy, yet it is hard to read. It also wastes the model's own judgment skill.

Sampled replies are grouped into clusters that differ in meaning. The clusters become options in a structured multiple-choice question. The model's probability on each option serves as the confidence estimate. Tests across models and datasets beat baseline methods throughout. Two extra samples already give competitive performance. The method is both effective and cheap to run. Teams deploying language models get a clearer reliability dial. Self-assessment turns out to beat indirect entropy signals.
arxiv-2606-04046:
Xiao and co-authors target a perceptual bottleneck in embodied vision-language decisions. Such models serve robot handling and navigation tasks. Vision-language models plan well over long horizons. Action models react fast in control. Both fail when they cannot tell key objects from distractors. Visual hallucinations follow from that mix-up.

Their SceneDiver method builds focus plans in a coarse-to-fine way. It first builds a whole scene graph for context. Then it splits the task into simpler sub-problems in cycles. Each cycle runs recognition, understanding, and analysis again. A light adapter passes the focus skill into action models. Tests show far fewer hallucinations for both model types. Speed for fast tasks was kept, they report.
arxiv-2606-04246:
Prashanth Vijayaraghavan and colleagues present StepPRM-RTL in 2026, a framework that teaches language models to write hardware description code, the register-transfer level code behind digital chips. The task demands long chains of reasoning under strict correctness rules in Verilog and VHDL.

Their system builds training trajectories from reference solutions, where each step pairs a rationale with an incremental code change. A process reward model grades the intermediate steps, giving dense feedback instead of a single pass-or-fail at the end, and a tree search explores alternative reasoning paths to enrich the data. Fine-tuning uses retrieval to ground the model further. On benchmark Verilog and VHDL sets, the framework beat prior methods by over ten percent in functional correctness and reasoning quality.
arxiv-2606-04546:
Dutta, Barui, Mitra, and Balakrishnan model how two wear measures on the same equipment degrade together over time, in a 2026 arXiv reliability paper. Each degradation path is modeled with an inverse Gaussian process, a standard choice for gradual damage. Dependence between the two paths is introduced through a shared unobserved frailty factor. Earlier work forced that frailty into a specific distribution, such as normal or gamma, a choice that is hard to justify because the frailty is never observed.

Their IG-GG framework lets the frailty follow the generalized gamma family, which contains the exponential, gamma, Weibull, and lognormal distributions as special cases, so the data can pick the shape. The authors develop estimation procedures and verify them in simulations. Applied to fatigue-crack data, the model fit better than several frailty-based and copula-based rivals, and they discuss estimating whole-system reliability under the framework.
arxiv-2606-04946:
Dütting and colleagues keep a near-optimal selection fresh while the underlying set keeps changing, in a 2026 arXiv theoretical computer science paper. Submodular maximization picks items with diminishing returns, and dynamic settings add a consistency requirement: maintain a near-optimal solution at all times while adjusting it only slightly per step. Prior work handled insertion-only streams and cardinality constraints. This paper addresses the fully dynamic setting, with a general framework for designing consistent algorithms.

Instantiating it, they obtain the first constant-factor approximations with sublinear consistency in this setting. For cardinality constraints, their algorithm achieves roughly a one-half approximation while changing the solution by an amount depending only on the parameter. For rank-k matroid constraints, they achieve roughly a one-quarter approximation with consistency growing only logarithmically in k.
arxiv-2606-05146:
K.-R. Hinds and a large collaboration report early multiwavelength observations of AT 2026fgk in this 2026 arXiv paper, the afterglow of the sub-luminous gamma-ray burst GRB 260310A. Sub-luminous bursts tied to broad-lined Type Ic supernovae are poorly understood, partly because their afterglows are faint. This one's optical afterglow was identified without a gamma-ray trigger, through optical survey data streams.

Follow-up over the first 50 days showed a rapidly rising, red transient and confirmed a broad-lined supernova with ejecta of about three solar masses. At redshift 0.153 it is the nearest afterglow ever identified blindly by an optical survey, and one of the brightest seen. Basic afterglow modeling points to either a low initial Lorentz factor around 40 or an off-axis viewing angle under three degrees. Its rate matches that of on-axis long bursts, sharply constraining how common slow, weakly beamed bursts can be.
arxiv-2606-05646:
Xuehang Guo and colleagues give coding agents a memory that improves with use in a 2026 arXiv paper. Software agents solve each new task from scratch, repeating old mistakes. Bolt-on memories exist, but nobody had a fair yardstick for memory quality. The team defines memory utility by measured downstream impact instead. That yardstick doubles as a training signal that needs no hand labels.

Their framework, MemOp, runs memory as a closed loop: store, distill, reuse, and grade. Tests cover both single-task help and carry-over across tasks. Agents with MemOp gained up to about five points in success rate. They also resolved issues about five points more efficiently. Computing cost fell by at least about ten percent. The gains held across settings, which suggests the loop, not a single trick, does the work. Memory, the authors argue, should be optimized like any other part of an agent.
arxiv-2606-06146:
Jakkapat Seeyangnok, Udomsilp Pinsook, and Graeme Ackland study magnetism in an atom-thin material in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their subject is bilayer Janus 1T-MnSSe, two stacked layers whose faces are made of different atoms, so the sheet is asymmetric like the two-faced god Janus. How the layers register, called stacking, can change whether their magnetic moments align or oppose.

Using first-principles calculations, the team finds that the nonmagnetic state is unstable for every stacking they tried. One arrangement, labelled AA2, is the ground state and orders antiferromagnetically between layers, while other stackings favor parallel alignment. Monte Carlo simulations put Néel temperatures above three hundred kelvin for the antiferromagnetic stackings and Curie temperatures up to two hundred fifty kelvin for ferromagnetic ones. Several stackings act as half-metals, conducting one electron spin only, with nearly full spin polarization that doping and strain can tune.
arxiv-2606-06346:
Roberto Vila, Eduardo Nakano, and Chang Dorea unify several classical probability formulas in this 2026 arXiv paper. Conditional expectations, conditional distributions, and hazard rates are usually derived separately for smooth, discrete, and mixed random variables. The authors show that one mechanism sits underneath them all. Their tool is the distributional derivative, expressed through Dirac delta representations that localize a variable at a point.

Within that single framework, general identities cover every variable type at once. Joining the approach with copula methods, which describe how variables depend on each other, they turn to transport and spread measures. Using the Fréchet Hoeffding bounds, the extreme cases of dependence, they derive sharp bounds for absolute difference moments when the marginal laws are fixed. The machinery yields compact quantile formulas for the Wasserstein distance, a standard cost of morphing one law into another, plus new forms for the Gini mean difference.
arxiv-2606-06546:
Tao Liu and co-authors automate the grading rubric for AI teachers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Judging a tutoring model means judging how it teaches, not just what it knows. Hand written rubrics cannot cover the long tail of classroom situations. Their Elmes Plus framework builds rubrics itself. A multi agent engine stages teacher, student, and judge interactions. A self evolving module, SceneGen, refines the scoring criteria and the test scenarios.

With it they built Edu 330: three hundred thirty scenarios across eleven subjects, three grade bands, and ten task types, scored on over a thousand indicators. The results show teaching skill has many dimensions. Top models differed mainly in creativity and values integration. Some knowledge strong models failed at Socratic scaffolding, guiding by questions. An education specialized model, InnoSpark, earned the best human evaluated average. Model judges matched human rankings with lower variance, though they favored themselves.
arxiv-2606-06646:
Jakub Bąba and Jarosław A Chudziak teach machines to diagram an argument properly in this 2026 arXiv paper. Argument mining extracts claims and premises from text. Richer frameworks like Carneades also demand premise types, proof standards, and argument schemes, structure that shallow tools miss.
