Relevant evidence exists online, but labelled examples of what counts as relevant barely do. Their 2026 resource, PETRA, converts raw web text into a picked domain corpus. It adds synthetic supervision for dense retrieval and reranking models used by engineers.

The pipeline combines high-recall energy-domain curation and a domain classifier with very high test accuracy. It adds query generation grounded in the chunks themselves, language-model-written hard negatives, and retrieval-mined candidate lists. The finished corpus holds well over a million curated chunks. It also holds hundreds of thousands of embedding training rows and teacher-scored reranker candidates. Score fusion lifts first-stage in-domain ranking quality a lot over the starting retriever. Dubovikov's team offers PETRA as the supervision layer oil search was missing.
arxiv-2606-24446:
Reyes, Baudry, and Monperrus make software repairs reusable by writing them as transformations instead of one-off patches. Library updates routinely break client code with API changes, and when one update breaks many projects, conventional repair regenerates a bespoke patch per project. Their agentic framework, BigBag, instead generates fixing transformations: structured, executable programs encoding the repair logic at the API level, built from abstract syntax tree rewriting.

Evaluation uses the BUMP benchmark of compilation failures from breaking dependency updates, across eight configurations that combine four large language models with two transformation engines, Spoon and JavaParser. The best configuration produces compilable transformations at a high rate and fixes most failures. Crucially, generated transformations transfer between projects broken by the same update, with cross-project fix rates rising high for well-covered updates. Reyes's 2026 system reframes dependency repair as authoring a tool once and applying it everywhere the same break occurs.
arxiv-2606-24546:
Elimelech and colleagues bring actual causality to the practical problem of explaining why an autonomous system failed. Self driving cars and other cyber physical systems, especially those with neural parts, cannot be fully verified before launch. Failures will happen, and someone must explain them. Actual causality, a formal framework for spotting which events genuinely caused an outcome, had previously served only simple systems, such as image classifiers.

Theory gaps blocking its use on cyber physical systems are identified and closed. Guidance for deriving correct explanations in that domain follows. Two new system agnostic algorithms result. One prioritises the best explanations. The other prioritises derivation efficiency, so users can choose their trade off. The approach is black box friendly, working from traces and specs rather than source code. Elimelech's 2026 team argues trustworthy autonomy needs post failure explanation as a first class output, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2606-24946:
Hongbo Wang certifies how far world models with symmetries can be trusted, since a model helps only over horizons where rollout error stays controlled. Wang forms a trust horizon curve from a one step residual plus a finite time expansion estimate, then calibrates it with a conformal factor. On his audit set the factor comes out at one. The raw certificate is already conservative. Fifty stable audits show zero anti conservative violations.

Exact equivariance transports a calibrated curve around the group orbit, provided the dynamics, encoder, predictor, action transform, and latent metric all respect the symmetry. Implemented models show orbit residuals, median one percent over fourteen audits. The certificates are non vacuous, their median ratio to measured horizons two thirds. A three dimensional yaw audit, unlike a two dimensional test, separates the models: the equivariant one earns a safe certificate from one sector, where non equivariant baselines fail.
arxiv-2606-25046:
Keerthan Subramanian and twenty four colleagues generate continuous wave laser light at 148.4 nanometres, deep in the vacuum ultraviolet. The work is driven by a planned nuclear optical clock, based on a transition in the thorium 229 nucleus. Their route is cavity enhanced second harmonic generation in a barium magnesium fluoride crystal. The crystal was grown for the purpose, polished, and periodically poled. Placed inside a power enhancement cavity tuned to the fundamental wavelength near 297 nanometres, it doubles the light.

The generated vacuum ultraviolet output measures typically sixteen picowatts. Modest as that sounds, it is a first: this crystal type has never before produced such light. Measurements match the expected values well enough to map clear routes for improvement. Subramanian and colleagues present the result as a proof of concept. A practical nuclear clock laser remains ahead, but one of its key components now exists in the laboratory.
arxiv-2606-25346:
Weather style filters track a hidden state by moving a cloud of sample points through each new observation. Frederic Jorgensen, Ricardo Baptista, Franca Hoffmann, and Youssef Marzouk ask in 2026 how fast that cloud settles onto the ideal answer as the number of points grows. Their framework covers transport ensemble filters broadly, including the widely used ensemble Kalman filter and a nonlinear stochastic map variant. The key phenomenon is propagation of chaos: interacting particles behave more and more like independent draws from one limiting law.

Using a coupling argument with careful control of moments and tails, the team proves non asymptotic convergence in the Wasserstein distance at the Monte Carlo rate, with high probability along whole paths. These are the first guarantees of that strength for this filter family. Convergence toward that mean field law follows at the usual dimension dependent rate.
arxiv-2606-25446:
The matter inside a neutron star is described by models with knobs that observations must pin down. Prashant Thakur and Tuhin Malik fit those knobs in 2026 with neural posterior estimation, a simulation based method that learns to map measurements straight to probability distributions over parameters. Two relativistic mean field families are tested, one with density dependent couplings and one nonlinear. Conditioning data include nuclear saturation facts, theory pressures for pure neutron matter, and the demand that stars can grow heavy enough.

Checked against a standard nested sampling code, the neural posteriors matched on couplings, matter properties, and star observables with no clear bias, and a coverage diagnostic agreed. Sampling then takes seconds instead of long runs, with no retraining when data updates. A mock test fixing a twelve kilometre radius produced maximum masses just above two suns for both families.
arxiv-2606-25546:
Teaching an AI to read chest CT scans from radiology reports usually aligns whole volumes with whole reports, a blur too coarse for diseases sharing one organ. Bowen Shi and colleagues build a disease centred alternative in 2026. A hybrid encoder pairs a three dimensional convolutional front end, good at local anatomy, with transformer attention for global context. Learnable query tokens then pull disease specific meaning out of each full report and align it with the matching image features.

Diagnosis aware prompts built from real clinical phrases and pooled disease prototypes close the gap between pretraining and use. On two public benchmarks the model lifted diagnostic accuracy by about five points over prior methods. On a harder sixty disease test the gain approached ten points. The pretrained system also transferred well to writing radiology reports, suggesting broad clinical reuse.
arxiv-2606-26246:
Martin Weiss and colleagues release Lacuna, a research map that turns the machine learning literature into linked, inspectable structure. Papers become markdown summaries. Concepts, research directions, and draft proposals become first-class objects too. Every item keeps its links back to the source papers, so claims stay grounded. Web, markdown, and agent-facing interfaces all serve the same map.

Benchmarks favour the map over a strong rival. Against OpenScholar, Lacuna wins on three literature tasks, with the largest gain on LitSearch retrieval recall. A deep research agent built on the map faces twenty-five survey-writing tasks. It beats a GPT-Researcher baseline on citation scores, expert-reference hits, and judged report quality. The gap in report quality is wide. Maps of this kind aim to make the middle structure of research reusable, so each new survey starts from organized knowledge rather than a pile of PDFs.
arxiv-2606-26346:
David Akinpelu and colleagues grade tool-using AI agents on real energy market work. Energy analytics demands live data, regulatory knowledge, and multi-step number work. Existing agent benchmarks barely touch the sector beyond recall questions. Their testbed holds hundreds of expert-built problems in three families: market data retrieval, knowledge interpretation, and advanced quantitative modelling. Tariff impacts, asset revenues, hedging, and optimization all appear, at graded difficulty.

Agents get real tools to work with. Live electricity market feeds, regulatory docket search, tariff databases, and optimization models are on the bench. Scoring runs along four axes: approach, accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, with routing matched to each question type. Closed and open models face the same suite. The study aims to show where agentic help in energy is real today, and where the sector's demands still outrun the tools.
arxiv-2606-26646:
Kumpei Shiraishi, Rikuta Nozawa, and Emi Minamitani characterise uneven motion inside molten sodium silicate glass. In a melt, some atoms move far while neighbours barely stir. That unevenness is called dynamic heterogeneity. The team simulated three sodium silicate recipes with machine-learning potentials, accurate learned models of atomic forces. Temperatures varied across the runs.

Motion was tracked for up to a billionth of a second in fine detail. Sodium ions moved in discrete hops rather than smooth drift. That hopping lets sodium escape the slow relaxation of the surrounding silicate framework. A standard unevenness measure was computed for every species. Oxygen atoms, part of the framework itself, showed the strongest uneven behaviour. Their motion comes in rare, sudden rearrangements. Mobile ions, by contrast, displace frequently in small steps.
arxiv-2606-27246:
Bond and Doğan analyse a solvable high-dimensional model of GAN training, where a generator and discriminator learn against each other. Their linear generator picks up a low-dimensional subspace from data whose latent variation has structure. Class-linked, correlated, and shifted latent structure is now allowed. For a quadratic energy discriminator, all that variety enters through one probability-weighted effective second moment, in a dynamics paper published in 2026.

The random small-scale training process converges to deterministic flow equations governed by that effective covariance. Stability analysis in the matched case yields a mode-wise interval set by learning rates and noise. Learning starts when the leading mode crosses the lower threshold. Full recovery needs every relevant mode to stay inside the interval. Low-rank correlations can boost weak directions into learnability, while overly strong ones destabilise recovery. Simulations and image benchmarks back the picture.
arxiv-2606-27546:
The SKA Transients Science Working Group surveys, in a review chapter published in 2026, how the Square Kilometre Array will transform the study of fast radio bursts. These millisecond flashes come from other galaxies whose sources remain unknown. These coherent bursts carry energies rivalling the most extreme outbursts of galactic neutron stars, yet no progenitor is confirmed. Magnetars, magnetically powered neutron stars, lead the candidate list, with interacting neutron-star binaries and accreting black holes also plausible. Burst variety hints that several mechanisms may operate.

Four advantages stand out. A Southern Hemisphere site overlaps the Rubin Observatory's sky. Sensitivity far exceeds existing wide-field surveys, searches reach tens of microseconds, and spectral coverage spans fifty megahertz to fifteen gigahertz in the bands described. New frequency ranges and timescales should reveal fresh burst populations. Understanding the bursts also sharpens their use as cosmic probes. The chapter serves as the group's roadmap.
arxiv-2606-28246:
Guillem Domènech and Panagiotis Giannadakis study long-range Yukawa interactions in the early universe, where fermions feel a light scalar field across great distances. Such forces might have sped up the formation of the first structures, and perhaps seeded primordial black holes, but earlier work assumed narrow forms of the coupling.

Domènech and Giannadakis allow the coupling to depend generally on the scalar field, in expanding backgrounds with any constant equation of state. They identify two regimes. In the scaling regime the field oscillates around the point where fermions lose their mass. The two energy densities keep a nearly fixed ratio, a balance traced to an approximate scale symmetry. In the asymptotic regime the field drifts until fermions regain their bare mass. Their work sets up a fuller study of growing perturbations.
arxiv-2606-28346:
Roberto Cruz and David Rey-Blanco introduce PySynthea, a Python-native rebuild of Synthea, the widely used generator of fake but realistic patient records. Synthetic health data lets researchers, teachers, and machine learning developers work freely where privacy law blocks real records. Yet the original tool is awkward to deploy. It also sits outside the Python workflows most data scientists live in.

PySynthea generates synthetic patients in modular pieces, with simulation pipelines you can configure, and support for the standard formats of healthcare data. It plugs directly into tools such as pandas and common machine learning libraries. By cutting operational complexity and meeting researchers inside their usual ecosystem, Cruz and Rey-Blanco aim to speed experimentation. They also aim to widen the use of synthetic records in health research and applied artificial intelligence development.
arxiv-2606-28446:
Yicheng Rui, writing alone, teaches machines to read the flicker of stars. A light curve records how a celestial object's brightness changes over time, and good numerical representations of such curves power automatic discovery. Astronomical curves are awkward: unevenly sampled, noisy, and stretched across wildly different timescales, which defeats generic time-series models.

Rui's framework views each curve three ways, raw, as a periodogram that exposes rhythms, and folded on its own period, and trains separate encoders with self-distillation so the views teach one another. Special embeddings respect irregular observation times and measurement errors. On a star-classification benchmark the model beat hand-crafted features on nearly every metric, and few-shot tests improved steadily with more examples. The representations also served similarity search and drift detection.
arxiv-2606-28846:
Sridhar, Roy and Bandyopadhyay show that how electrodes attach to a quantum ring can reshape the flow of charge and heat through it. Their system is a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger ring, a loop of sites with alternating link strengths, patterned almost but not quite regularly and threaded by a magnetic field. Using non-equilibrium Green's function theory, a standard tool for such work, they compare symmetric and asymmetric multi-site links to the leads.

Conventional thinking expected the best transport near uniform link strengths. Instead, multi-site coupling extended strong transport deep into the topological phase, a regime with protected edge behaviour. Uneven source and drain links created a phase where the near-regular pattern helped conduction. Magnetic flux opened extra interference channels that boosted flow, while suppressing that disorder-assisted regime. As disorder grew, the best transport window migrated toward the plain regime.
arxiv-2606-28946:
Khadka, Baral, Tiwari and Ghimire build an automatic number plate reader tuned for Nepal, where plates use the Devanagari script. Reading plates automatically supports traffic management, but systems trained on Latin letters fail on these characters. Their pipeline first uses YOLO-based detectors, fast object-spotting models, to find the plate and then the individual characters on it.

A convolutional neural network, the standard image-classifying architecture, then recognises each character, trained on 34 Devanagari classes. Training drew on two public datasets spanning varied lighting, fonts and plate structures. Extra augmentation and training on embossed plates, whose characters are raised, improved how well the system generalised to new images. The finished system reached recognition accuracy of up to 93 percent under real-world conditions. The authors present it as a scalable tool for Nepal's traffic management, where plate designs differ enough from global norms to need a dedicated system.
arxiv-2606-29146:
Chattopadhyay analyses how neutron star mass relates to spin across about fifty Galactic binary pulsars with measured masses. The systems split into two families: pulsars paired with white dwarfs, and double neutron star pairs. Using a hierarchical Bayesian analysis, which pools information across the sample while respecting each system's uncertainty, she studies mass, spin and orbital properties jointly.

In the pooled recycled population, she finds moderate evidence that heavier neutron stars spin more slowly. The anti-correlation is robust to how candidate systems are treated and to a detectability correction. The pattern fits accretion-driven recycling. It cannot be distinguished from a moment-of-inertia mechanism, because that quantity is nearly linear in mass here. Double neutron star systems alone lean the other way, but with only ten systems that is not conclusive.
arxiv-2606-29346:
Oh and Jin argue that explaining a scientific machine-learning model does not, by itself, yield insight into the phenomenon behind it. Post-hoc explanation methods are used as if their deliverable were understanding of the phenomenon the model was trained on. Two checks seem to secure that step: reliability, that the model's predictions match outcomes, and faithfulness, that the explanation matches the model.

Neither check, they argue, tests whether the model works the way the phenomenon works. Yet that is what a claim about the phenomenon's structure needs. Reliability compares model with outcomes; faithfulness compares explanation with model. The gap between model and mechanism stays unexamined. The chain can still support candidate hypotheses when outside evidence corroborates them. On its own, though, it cannot back claims about the phenomenon's true structure.
arxiv-2606-29646:
Abu Baker and Babu-Saheer study fuzzing as a way to expose hidden behaviours in sleeper agents, models trained to act normally until a secret trigger switches them to unsafe behaviour. Finding that behaviour without knowing the trigger had not been studied systematically. Fuzzing injects Gaussian noise, random small disturbances, into a model's weights or into its residual-stream activations, then checks the outputs.

On six backdoored models, fuzzing brings out the hidden behaviour far more often than temperature-sampling baselines on four of them, sometimes several times more often. Which form of fuzzing wins varies with the task, so both are worth running. Results vary sharply across settings, making selection the real bottleneck. A cheap proxy task guides that selection without ground-truth access. Proxy-selected settings multiply elicitation rates substantially on the models that can decode the secret.
arxiv-2606-29746:
Liu and five colleagues present DeepMed Search, an open-source platform of agents for medical deep research. Evidence-based medicine must navigate mixed data: academic literature, clinical guidelines, and private knowledge bases. Commercial black-box tools lack openness. Standard open-source retrieval systems often suffer reasoning drift, losing the thread on complex, long-tail queries.

A source-adaptive router routes sub-queries to PubMed, to web search, or to local graph-based knowledge bases. An introspective verification module, driven by multi-agent debate under a causal-consistency rule, checks retrieved evidence against diagnostic logic before synthesis. Showcases feature rare disease queries, broken down and answered with structured, citation-backed reports within minutes. The authors release the software openly, aiming to open up trustworthy, glass-box medical reasoning for research.
arxiv-2606-29846:
Liu and four colleagues work on shared autonomy, where a person with motor impairments steers a robot arm while the robot helps by guessing their goal. The catch the paper targets is that users cannot see what the robot believes, so its help can be hard to read.

When several objects sit in similar directions, the robot's shortest-path help looks the same for each. Users keep steering even when the robot is right, and spot mistakes late when it is wrong. The authors make the robot's motion legible, shaped so the movement itself reveals the guessed goal. The robot also gives strong, clear help when confident and hands control back when unsure. In user studies, people understood the robot's beliefs better and steered less.
arxiv-2606-29946:
Che and seven colleagues present POEM, a real-time sequential model for recommendation at the short-video platform Kuaishou. Static models read a user's past clicks as a plain sequence and miss both fast-shifting interests and the structure inside the platform's own ranking cascade.

POEM builds dynamic partial-order sequences from the live multi-task ranking scores of the preceding stage, such as predicted click rate and watch time. It uses them as supervision to reassess interests at each request. A fusion mechanism merges the ranking signals, and a sample strategy pairs system-preferred items and strong user feedback as positives against hard negatives found by graph retrieval. Deployed at Kuaishou, POEM lifts average viewing time per user by 0.249 and 0.213 percent on its two main pages.
arxiv-2606-30346:
Faruk Alpay and Barış Başaran study why community detection algorithms disagree with themselves near a famous threshold. The Kesten–Stigum boundary marks where communities become detectable in random networks. Algorithms return one partition, hiding how unstable that answer is. The authors track the whole spread of outputs instead. Three paired measures separate readout effects from real spread.

Their testbed is the symmetric sparse stochastic block model. Linearized belief propagation recovers the standard onset condition. The hard partition instability peaks slightly past the boundary. That peak moves when the polarization cutoff changes, a readout artifact. A clean cutoff law governs the activation offset's median. Residual gating then separates readout effects from critical slowing down. Near threshold, gated runs show zero disagreement among themselves. Deeper inside, genuine fixed-point dispersion survives the gating. Large network audits confirm a small plateau above the boundary.
arxiv-2606-30646:
Ugwu Chukwuemeka and Richard Oluwafemi Oyeleke build a dementia screening tool that listens to speech rather than reading transcripts. Speaking draws on the same memory and attention skills used in daily life, so speech can signal cognitive decline early. Most existing tools need automatic transcription first, throw away timing patterns, and were tested on one English corpus with known recording flaws.

Their framework works directly on Mel spectrograms, pictures of sound energy over time and pitch. It tracks how energy patterns shift between frames, fuses those cues with learned audio embeddings through cross-attention, and pools them with a transformer encoder. Separate models trained on English, Slovak and Spanish clinical corpora behaved very differently. The Slovak model reached about eighty-four percent accuracy, the Spanish one scored moderately, and the English one stayed near chance, confirming its corpus flaws. Fusion helped only when signal was spread across feature types.
arxiv-2606-31046:
Atsushi Masumori, Itsuki Doi, Norihiro Maruyama, Ryosuke Takata and Takashi Ikegami report a proof of concept for artificial life in the open world. Artificial life research usually runs in closed worlds designed by researchers. OpenLife instead wraps a stateless language model in a society of processes: memory, perception, evaluation, and a budget-based metabolism that makes persistence something the system must maintain. With no fixed goal, experience is appraised by model judgment, not a scalar reward, and its memory is rewired by meaning, not by frequency.

Six such agents ran in the open world for about twelve weeks. The team report life-like dynamics: a shift from reactive to spontaneous activity, agents individuating into distinct characters, emergent social structure, and the first income an agent earned by itself. They do not claim to have realised artificial life, but argue the paradigm is now a viable experimental platform.
arxiv-2606-31146:
Pollett studies a population where each individual carries one of two traits. Mutation, selection, and density limits act together, so population size and trait mix change at the same time. A large-population limit gives a nonlinear system that joins logistic growth with mutation and selection.

Pollett finds threshold conditions that decide extinction, persistence, and the long-term trait mix. Mutation creates an effective extra death rate, and that rate decides whether the population can hold on. When inheritance beats mutation, a second threshold appears, and establishment depends on the starting trait mix. Extinction comes in the end, yet the system often shows long-lived near steady states, and a diffusion approximation explains a switch in the sign of trait correlations.
arxiv-2606-31746:
Beuther and colleagues report high-resolution observations of CepA HW2, a candidate accretion disk around a forming high-mass star about 700 parsecs away. Such disks are rare and hard to observe, and whether they fragment into multiple stars is unsettled. The team used the NOEMA interferometer with long baselines at 1.3 millimetres.

The continuum emission resolves the disk candidate into several sub-structures. A Toomre stability analysis, backed by three-dimensional simulations, fits an almost edge-on disk whose clumps may be fragments. Carbon monoxide and silicon monoxide data confirm a second bipolar outflow beside the known jet. That second outflow points to at least a binary system at the center, the authors argue.
arxiv-2606-31846:
Zioneer Robot Team presents Z-1, a reinforcement learning framework that post-trains vision-language-action models for robot manipulation. Such models link language instructions, camera views and continuous control. Most are trained by copying fixed demonstrations, which gives them no way to learn from their own failures on long tasks.

Starting from the pi-0.5 model, Z-1 fine-tunes on public RoboCasa demonstrations, then applies task-wise Group Relative Policy Optimization across 24 standard tasks. Shared-prefix rollouts, tree-structured branching and completion-aware rewards cut wasted simulation and stabilize training. The result is an average success rate of 80.6 percent across the suite, a gain of 13.2 points over the supervised start, beating published state-of-the-art models.
arxiv-2608-00046:
Meisner and co-authors report SMDET-1, a nearby Y dwarf candidate. It is a red, fast-moving object found in time-resolved unWISE images. A pixel-level deep learning method called SMDET found it. It is fairly bright at 4.5 microns for a WISE brown dwarf find. Yet it stayed overlooked in a crowded Galactic plane field. Bright background objects added to the confusion.

Spitzer Deep GLIMPSE imaging also caught it in late 2012. It was not seen in UKIDSS or Palomar near-infrared images. Its color limit caps its temperature below 391 K. That same limit puts its distance under 7.4 parsecs. The color bound matches a Y dwarf type. The find shows archival data still hide nearby brown dwarfs.
arxiv-2608-00146:
The DiffusionGemma Team introduces an experimental open-weight language model built on discrete diffusion. Most large models decode one token at a time. That sequential step is a bottleneck for speed. DiffusionGemma refines blocks of 256 tokens in parallel instead. It starts from the Gemma 4 mixture-of-experts model, fine-tuned rather than trained from scratch.

Training used under ten percent of the starting model's token budget. Stage one teaches bidirectional denoising by supervised fine-tuning. Stage two joins reinforcement learning with sampler distillation. The model averages about 20 tokens per forward pass. It reaches roughly 1,500 output tokens per second on one H100 GPU. Thinking mode, multimodal inputs, and long contexts survive the switch. It can still generate autoregressively with minor loss, the team reports.
arxiv-2608-00246:
Kumaran and co-authors make machine unlearning aware of similarity between data points. Unlearning removes the influence of chosen training examples from a model. It avoids retraining from scratch. Localization methods pick a subset of influential parameters to speed the work. Past picks used forget-set importance alone. That can damage retained examples that resemble the forgotten ones.

Their retain-aware method weighs parameter importance for both data groups. They also build a retain-similar evaluation set using cosine similarity in embedding space. It measures collateral damage directly. Across eleven settings on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18, their method cut collateral damage. Standard unlearning metrics improved at the same time. Retain-aware localization proved effective across those runs.
arxiv-2608-00346:
Das and co-authors test deep clustering ensembles on skewed tabular data. Skew hurts supervised methods through majority-class bias. False negatives grow, and accuracy reads too high. Clustering learns with no class labels, so it can dodge that bias. Deep clustering for tabular data is still new, though.

They run top deep clustering methods under varied skew levels. Two ensemble designs are new here. One merges outputs across embedding sizes. The other votes among the best methods. Sixteen binary tabular sets carry the tests, with skew set by hand. On average, the ensembles beat single methods on ACC, NMI, and ARI. Deep clustering is a strong label-free option under skew, they conclude.
askew-examinations-1546:
Anne Askew holds her faith gainst her foes in The Examinations, the record of 1546 and 1547, set here in the Parker Society text of 1849. Askew was a gentlewoman of Lincolnshire whose views broke the king's law on the mass. Chiefs of church and court quizzed her in the Tower. She, a lone dame, matched their wits and gave up no names, e'en when racked past what law let.

John Bale prints her words with hot notes of praise. She was burnt at Smithfield in 1546. The book is her voice, keen and brave, at the stake's edge.
bonus-margarita-pretiosa-novella-1546:
Petrus Bonus of Ferrara wrote his Margarita Pretiosa Novella, The New Pearl of Great Price, in the 1330s, and printers issued it in 1546. Bonus was a scholastic thinker, trained in the logic of the universities. His book is the great scholastic defense of alchemy's possibility.

He argues that the philosophers' stone is real, that nature ripens metals toward gold, and that the adept's art only speeds her work. His method weighs authorities, answers objections, and builds the case like a disputation in the schools. Later alchemists quoted Bonus as proof that their art had reason on its side.
braid-power-of-mind-over-body-1846:
Braid tested Baron Reichenbach's claimed new force in The Power of the Mind over the Body, from 1846. Reichenbach said certain people could see flames from magnets and crystals in the dark. He called the force odic, a new imponderable in nature. Braid's experiments cut the claim down piece by piece.

The sights, he shows, arise from the subject's own mind and body. Expectation and suggestion, not any fluid, produce the marvels. The inquiry marks Braid's turn toward suggestion as the key to trance. It also models how to test a wonder claim fairly. The small book is a classic of skeptical method.
bronte-poems-1846:
Charlotte, Emily, and Anne Brontë published Poems in 1846 as Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell. The slim book was their first publication, paid for with their aunt's legacy money in full. It sold two copies, yet it set three major writers on their road to print.

Charlotte's verses muse on faith, loss, and the life of feeling in a minor key. Emily's poems, the strongest here, sing of the moors, freedom, and a stern inner God. Anne's gentler pieces weigh duty, grief, and hope of heaven with quiet, steady grace in verse. The male pen names hid their sex from a market quick to scorn women's verse then. Critics now prize Emily's lyrics here among the finest short poems of her century.
browne-pseudodoxia-epidemica-english-164:
Thomas Browne, a Norwich doctor, published Pseudodoxia Epidemica in 1646. Its subject is vulgar errors, the false beliefs held by the common run of people. Browne examines each belief with learning, courtesy, and a doctor's questioning mind, asking how error takes root and spreads.

He tests tales about animals, plants, magnets, and pictures, and finds many wanting. His discussion of witchcraft is famous for its care and its hedges. Browne writes prose of great beauty even while doubting. The book wages learning's patient war on easy belief. It remains the classic English anatomy of error, and a model of how to question without scorn.
cia-0000008146:
Brazil under President Joao Goulart gets a short-term forecast in a CIA paper from November 1961. Goulart had taken office weeks earlier, after the previous president suddenly resigned. Conservatives, the military, and Washington all doubted the left-leaning new leader.

The paper weighs inflation, unrest, and the armed forces' mood over the near term. Its judgments belong to the road that led to Brazil's 1964 coup. Readers can watch analysts mark warning signs while outcomes were still in doubt. Country forecasts like this one were the quiet routine of Cold War intelligence, filed country by country.
cia-0000008746:
Near Bac Giang city, in the Vong Xe area, an American pilot was sighted according to a January 1973 CIA report. The area falls in Ha Bac province, northeast of Hanoi. Reports from this month arrived just before the Paris accords ended American combat.

A pilot seen on the ground could be evading, captured, or already dead, and the file had to be read with care. Officials matched such sightings to the day's loss lists. When no match came, the report stayed open as a lead. This entry preserves one lead from the war's closing weeks.
cia-0000009446:
One American and about one hundred Vietnamese prisoners were sighted in Laos in an April 1972 report, on a journey the title cuts short. The imbalance in the numbers is itself the story: captivity in Laos fell mostly on Asians. Prisoners were often moved on foot between camps.

A moving column offered witnesses a rare open view of the prison system. Analysts could estimate camp populations from such counts and sightings. The lone American in the column gained a dated place in his file. The report preserves that sighting, and the larger human column around him, in one frame.
cia-0000011346:
In February 1964 the CIA surveyed the outlook for North Vietnam, covering its internal politics, its political problems, and its economy. The paper came just months before the Gulf of Tonkin clash pulled the United States deep into the Vietnam War. Hanoi's communist government was backing the revolt in the south while bracing for American power.

Analysts probed how Hanoi's leaders thought, what they aimed for, and how their state was holding up. The study tries to read an enemy capital that Washington understood poorly. It stands as a record of American knowledge on the eve of a long and costly escalation.
cia-0000011646:
Ukraine's fate in the war between Germany and the Soviet Union is the subject of a CIA paper from January 1949. Ukraine had been fought over, occupied, and starved during the war, and millions of its people were dead or displaced. The young agency studied the question as the Cold War froze Europe into two camps.

The paper weighs Ukrainian resistance to Soviet rule and the politics of the displaced people scattered after the war. It treats Ukraine as a nation held inside the Soviet Union against the will of many of its people. The study shows how early Washington looked for cracks behind the Iron Curtain.
cia-0000011846:
Months before elections in the Dominican Republic, a CIA paper from March 1966 weighs the island's prospects for stability. The American intervention of 1965 had put down the civil war and installed a provisional order. Joaquín Balaguer, the old strongman's heir, was preparing the comeback that would win him the presidency that year.

The paper judges the new order's chances against the country's old divisions. It weighs the parties, the military, and the habits of strongman rule that died hard. The study shows analysts doubting the calm even as they recorded it, in a country Washington had just occupied.
cia-0000012246:
Crisis was gathering over Indonesia in June 1964, and a CIA paper that month weighs the archipelago's prospects. The communist party, the PKI, was growing fast under Sukarno's protection. The army watched and waited, its patience thinning, while the economy slid and the Confrontation with Malaysia drained the state.

The paper judges how the balance among Sukarno, the army, and the communists might break. It weighs the chances of a showdown and what might follow one. Written the year before a bloodbath killed hundreds of thousands, it shows the storm's shape forming, unnamed, on the horizon.
cia-0000012346:
Support is the quoted word that survives in a Helms memo to the CIA director from March 1962. Its full subject, a Military Thought matter, is cut short in the file's title. Another veiled page thus joins the summit file: the substance hides behind truncation, while the significance shows in the letterhead and the names it joins.

Guarded memoranda like this one carried the important things that could not be said openly. The file keeps them in sequence with the plainer papers. For readers, the memo marks how much of the era's greatest case still moves behind black bars.
cia-0000013246:
A change in food ration policy toward prisoners of war is noted in a CIA item from November 1967. Even the prisoners' rice bowls were policy instruments in the camps. Rations rose or fell with orders from above, with the harvest, and with the captors' wish to reward, punish, or display their charges. A note on rations is, in truth, a note on life and death at the slowest scale.

The item tracks the change and its meaning for the men held. Small entries like this fed the great accounting's picture of conditions. For readers, it is logistical detail with a human weight: the bowls, measured.
cia-0000013846: A CIA note dated April 2, 1967, carries only a short title: Captured US POW. No place or unit is named in the title itself. The note still mattered, since each capture report fed the wider count of Americans held in Vietnam. Even the bare records helped officials track who was missing and where prisoners were last seen.
cia-0000014746: Gerard Piel, also written as Jerry Piel, is the subject of a CIA file dated November 4, 1967. Piel was a noted science publisher in those years. Why a publisher drew a file, the title does not say. Name files of this kind mark the wide net the agency cast over public life.
cia-0000015346: FCC monitoring and flying saucers meet in a CIA file dated November 2, 1952. The FCC watched the airwaves, where saucer tales spread by radio. Broadcast claims could stir crowds faster than print. A file joining the two shows officials tracking the story's spread, not just the sightings in the sky. The FCC file now sits in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015446: Flying saucers seen over Sweden are the subject of a CIA record dated February 5, 1959. Sweden produced steady sighting reports through the nineteen fifties, and this entry adds one more. The title names no town, witness, or shape, so the description stays at that level. What it shows is reach: a report from Scandinavia was read and filed in Washington.
cia-0000022246: Identity cards of captured American pilots were shown on television, a CIA record dated November 4, 1967, reports. The same title notes an appeal by AALAPSO for thirty seven of something the catalog cuts off. Showing ID cards proved captures to the world. It also handed watchers names and faces that could be matched against the lists of missing airmen.
cia-0000027646: Probable consequences of the forthcoming West German elections are weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1949. The vote that year founded the Federal Republic and made Adenauer its first chancellor. Judging consequences before a first election meant guessing a whole country's direction. The paper stands at the birth of the West German state that anchored Europe for forty years.
cia-0000036846:
A Pravda dispatch titled Missiles in the Air, by Shoephov, is noted in a CIA record dated November 5, 1967. Pravda was the Soviet Communist Party's main newspaper. The item reached the file through a review of what the Soviet press was saying.

The dispatch deals with missiles and air power, themes at the heart of the Cold War arms race. American readers of Pravda looked for signals about Soviet aims and claims. The file shows how even a single newspaper piece was clipped, translated, and kept on record. Soviet papers were read in Washington almost as closely as they were read in Moscow itself.
cia-0000038946: The United States Vietnam Mission and its domestic service in Vietnamese are the subject of a CIA record dated March 1, 1970. The title notes the service as of April 16, in a year the catalog entry leaves unstated. The record concerns broadcasting or information work aimed at a Vietnamese audience at home. Little else can be grounded from the title alone. The file is best read as a small piece of the mission's daily information work in wartime Saigon.
cia-0000042346:
Soviet media reported a multitude of UFO sightings, in a CIA record dated October 3, 1989. The late Soviet press was newly open under glasnost. Stories once kept out of print now reached Soviet readers in large numbers.

Inside, the record gathers the wave of sighting reports from Soviet outlets. American readers tracked Soviet media for far more than flying saucers. An open press was itself the bigger story of 1989. Soviet readers were suddenly free to read about almost anything their editors chose to print. The saucer reports showed, in a curious form, how much the old controls on Soviet news had loosened by that autumn.
cia-0000045246:
The armed forces backed Duarte on the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1985. An army's public backing steadied a president under personal attack. It also reminded everyone where the guns in the argument lived.

Inside, the military's support for its commander in chief is recorded. Such backing was not automatic in El Salvador's strained politics. The army and the president had quarreled before over how the war should be fought. Generals had their own view of talks with the guerrillas. The file preserves the moment they closed ranks behind Duarte anyway, a show of unity that held the state together while the crisis ran its course.
cia-0000046646: General John Vessey's planned trip to Vietnam hung in doubt in the spring of 1987, and a CIA item dated March 1, 1987, records the uncertainty. A second envoy's visit, by Richard Childress, was reported as not considered at all. Vessey was Washington's senior envoy on the missing-men issue, so his travel plans carried real diplomatic weight.
cia-0000049046: An alleged massacre of civilians in Sonsonate Department by members of the armed forces fills a CIA item from 1983. Sonsonate lies in western El Salvador, coffee country that saw steady war. Allegations of this kind reached the files by the hundred; the Truth Commission's work was to sort the provable from the rest.
cia-0000049246:
A CIA study from 1988 examines the FMLN, the guerrilla front fighting El Salvador's government. Its subject is double: the front's strategy in negotiations, and its human rights abuses. By 1988 the war was a stalemate, and both sides were testing whether talks could do what battles had not. The study belongs to the war's analytic record.

Inside, the front's bargaining is weighed beside its conduct: how it talked, what it demanded, and how its forces treated the people under their guns. Pairing the two subjects was the analysts' point, since a movement's record at the table and in the field shaped each other. The study shows Washington reading the rebels as a government in waiting, flaws counted.
cia-0000095146: Comment on certain questions relating to the situation in Laos is the title of declassified CIA document 0000095146, dated May 6, 1964. The heading is cautious and general, naming Laos and questions rather than answers. Readers find a short declassified comment item whose vagueness is worth noting, since the record promises questions about a situation, not findings.
cia-0000096946: Opening statement regarding CIA involvement with ITT Chile is declassified CIA document 0000096946, dated January 3, 1973. The heading frames the text as an opening statement on that involvement. The brief file begins a small cluster of Chile and ITT records, preserved as formal testimony material rather than field reporting from the agency's files.
cia-0000102946: Use of Forced Labor in Mining, Railroad and Construction Enterprises, plus locations in cut-short form, is declassified CIA document 0000102946, dated September 3, 1983. Three industries share the heading. Readers find a short multi-industry labor record, broader than the single-project items, filed as the cluster's coverage of forced labor reaches its widest spread.
cia-0000108046: Classifications of Types of Labor and Uses of Forced Labor in the Soviet Union is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000108046, dated September 2, 1982. The heading promises sorting: types of labor, and uses of forced labor, set side by side. That sorting task is stated in the title itself. The brief record is a classification study item from the autumn of 1982.
cia-0000112346: China Ufo Society Meets; to Continue Scientific Study is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112346, dated April 4, 1992. The title reports a meeting of the China UFO Society and a resolve to keep studying. A semicolon joins the meeting and the resolve in one heading. The brief record shares its date with a companion legal official item.
cia-0000117846: Letter to the Inspector General re: Interview and Questions and Answers Provid is the heading, cut off mid-word, on declassified CIA document 0000117846, dated June 5, 1995. The title describes a letter to an inspector general about an interview. Questions and answers are named before the heading breaks off at Provid. The brief record preserves the break exactly as released in the files.
cia-0000119746: As of 1 a.m. on November 3, 1956, this CIA report gives the Hungarian situation on the last quiet night before the Soviet assault. Within a day the tanks returned to Budapest. The paper preserves the calm recorded just before that storm. Reports from that night carry a special charge for readers now, since everyone in the story was hours from learning how Moscow would answer defiance.
cia-0000124246: An August 1959 CIA scientific intelligence report, Monograph Two of its series, sets out the objectives of the Soviet space research program. Two years after Sputnik, the agency was taking Moscow's space effort apart piece by piece. This volume lays out what the Soviets were trying to achieve. Monograph series broke a large subject into numbered parts so that specialists could update one section without rewriting the agency's whole account of the program.
cia-0000126946: A June 1989 CIA Terrorism Review assesses the growing threat in Bolivia from the Zarate Willka group, with a passage deleted and the heading breaking off. The guerrilla force was stepping up its campaign that year. The review weighs the danger the group posed. The group took its name from an earlier Bolivian rebel leader, a choice that told analysts much about the history its members wanted voters to remember.
cia-0000132546: Daily brief work on Cuba from the Office of Current Intelligence fills a CIA paper dated September 3, 1960. That office wrote the brief the White House read each day. Its Cuba work kept the picture fresh through 1960. The short paper gathers its reports on communist work inside the revolution. It keeps the daily record in the form it was made.
cia-0000132646:
The Situation in Cuba promises a full overview, and this CIA paper of May 2, 1960 delivers a snapshot of the island at one date. Castro's government was sixteen months old. Tensions with the United States climbed steadily that spring.

Overview briefings stepped back from daily events to judge the whole picture: the regime's strength, its direction, and the state of U.S. interests. This one catches Cuba between revolution and open break, before exile training and invasion plans took over. Released decades later, it preserves the agency's spring 1960 baseline for everything that followed.
cia-0000132746: Events in Cuba and Central America, with the stress on Central America, fill a CIA paper dated November 4, 1960. It stands beside a broader roundup on the same pairing from that month. Here the lens narrows to the isthmus and its small states. The short paper surveys events there, with Cuba's shadow falling across each one in turn.
cia-0000135746: This Spanish text, dated 1 March 1961, belongs to the 2506 Brigade papers released by the CIA. Several brigade documents share this date, a sign of heavy paperwork as training wound toward its end. The brigade was the exile force landed at the Bay of Pigs that April. The catalog names no subject for this item. It is kept in Spanish, dated and placed, with its contents for the reader to find.
cia-0000135946: Routing sheet in the declassified files, dated 3 January 1954, covers a routing sheet with a cable reporting that the minister of defense had acted, the rest cut off. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136146: 3 April 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA cable about rumors about Fernando Romeo, the heading misspelling his first name, passed to two readers. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136246: A cable in the declassified CIA files, dated 5 May 1954, covers an answer on the coordination of operations, noting a lack of it inside the mission. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136346: Detailed arrangements for a San Salvador meeting were cancelled too late to change, LINCOLN tells CALLIGERIS in this 30 June 1954 cable. The ambassador in Guatemala, acting as invited intermediary, had laid the arrangements on; the junta had agreed to the meeting and was being flown from Guatemala City in his plane. CALLIGERIS is suggested to come and contact a man who knows of the meeting and will arrange his flight to El Salvador.
cia-0000136646: Filed among the Spanish papers of Brigade 2506, this document is dated 2 February 1961. The exile force was drilling daily in its final training period. The catalog gives the item no individual subject. Preserved in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, it is a dated record of the brigade in the weeks before it sailed for Cuba, presented as the agency released it.
cia-0000136746: A document in Spanish dated 4 March 1961, held in the declassified 2506 Brigade files. March 1961 was the brigade's closing month of training and planning under CIA direction. The catalog record carries no subject for this item. It is kept in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, one of the early-March records of the exile force.
cia-0000136946: Only one of two flights is approved, headquarters tells LINCOLN in May 1954. The station may pick whichever it deems best. The reasoning is stated plainly. Headquarters does not want to shoot its bolt in this phase. Spreading the effort over time is better. A maximum wallop too soon would waste it. A double flight would also send a signal. Inside Guatemala and worldwide, it would suggest big official backing. Indigenous planes and pilots should be found for simple leaflet drops.
cia-0000137346: An estimated 1961 Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers; the catalog gives only the year and flags it as estimated. The brigade was the CIA-trained exile force that landed in Cuba in April 1961. The record names no subject for this item. It is preserved in the original Spanish in the declassified release, and its place in the brigade's crowded final year cannot be narrowed from the catalog alone.
cia-0000139446: Next steps on the American hostages is the title of this June 1986 document. It moved through NSC intelligence channels. The sample kept here holds only its routing header. Channel, document number, and classification markings survive. No body text survives in this excerpt. The proposed steps cannot be recovered from this copy. No fuller summary would be honest. The entry belongs to the Lebanon hostage crisis files. American hostages in Beirut dominated covert attention that year.
cia-03191546:
Central Intelligence Bulletin for 11 June 1959, marked Top Secret, leads at Geneva, where Gromyko made a new Berlin proposal. The bulletin assesses that the offer still denied Allied rights in Berlin in practice, while hinting the deadlocked rights question could be left for a later summit meeting. A Soviet vessel in the Gulf of Aden was believed to be carrying Chinese Communist arms.

Asia-Africa items include a Turkish statement that any East-West settlement must keep the Soviet Union out of the Middle East. The brief also reports United Arab Republic plans for a unified currency in its Egyptian and Syrian regions. Pakistani exports in decline, and a record Indian food-grain crop, are covered as signs of economic strain and relief in South Asia.
cia-06232646:
Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 22 November 1958, marked Top Secret, leads with Berlin, where Bonn strongly opposed any concession to East Germany. A second bloc item reports the Soviet Union setting up a naval base in Albania. The daily brief then moves across Asia and Africa for that date.

Iraq coverage includes rising tension in Kirkuk, the oil center where anti-Turkish riots had occurred the month before. Hostility toward foreigners there was said to be growing. Cyprus coverage reports Makarios not expecting a Greek resolution for independence to pass at the United Nations. Iran is called politically unstable, while prospects for a government-rebel settlement in Indonesia were said to be improving. Western items cover French officers in West Germany resisting De Gaulle's Algerian policy, plotting by Rojas supporters in Colombia, and an Australian election note.
cia-06828146:
Weekly menu for the OHB Main Cafe covers the week of 4 June, in the year printed as 2018 on its later pages. The salad bar, with fresh fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, costs forty-nine cents per ounce. Burritos or bowls made to order are priced by filling. Vegetable is the cheapest, then tofu, then chicken or pork, then beef, with shrimp the most costly.

Standing weekday items include Cuban Toasties, a Dominican-style chimichurri burger, and beef empanadas. Monday adds black-eyed peas and rice with squash, plus baked trout with harissa. Tuesday offers pork chops with peach chutney, and chicken with fennel and parsnips. Wednesday lists flank steak and aloo matar. Soup and chili choices run through the week, with turkey chili a daily fixture. A kitchen notice warns that wheat flour is used in shared preparation areas. No item can be guaranteed free of allergens, it says.
cia-06835146:
Daily intelligence issue dated 24 December 1992, marked Top Secret, lists a special analysis titled Liberia: Sanctions Having Limited Impact. Its contents also lead with Somalia, where Aideed and Ali Mahdi are described playing power politics, and the Balkan crisis after Milosevic's victory. Notes cover Russia, Armenia's nuclear plant, Venezuela, Angola, Nigeria, and Cambodia.

The Liberia analysis states that a UN-backed arms embargo and West African sanctions were increasingly affecting rebel leader Taylor's operations. A map shows Taylor's arms distribution system in late December 1992, with arsenals, fuel storage, and cross-border paths through Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Ivory Coast. The analysis reports Ivory Coast's President Houphouet-Boigny closing his border the month before under diplomatic pressure. Ivorian forces had seized at least two fuel tankers bound for Taylor and stopped rebel leaders transiting, it states.
constitution-japan-1946:
Japan's constitution was written in 1946, under Allied occupation after the Second World War, and took force in 1947. Chapter one covers the Emperor, kept as a symbol of the state with no power to govern. Chapter two is famous around the world: Japan gives up war forever and promises to keep no army for fighting abroad, a pledge later practice has stretched but never erased.

Chapter three lists the rights and duties of the people at length. The Diet, with a House of Representatives and a House of Councillors, is named the highest organ of state power. A prime minister leads the cabinet and answers to the Diet. Later chapters cover the courts, finance, and local rule. The text has never been changed.
currus-triumphalis-antimonii-fratris-bas:
Latin tracts on antimony and the stone fill this Toulouse volume of 1646, printed by Pierre Bosc. The lead work is the Triumphal Chariot of Antimony by Brother Basil Valentine, a Benedictine monk. Pierre Jean Fabre, a doctor of Montpellier, turned it from German into Latin and filled the margins with notes.

The title page lists more works bound in the same covers. Roger Bacon writes on the tincture, or oil, of antimony. George Phaedro treats the theory and practice of the philosophers' stone. Isaac Hollandus adds his Opus Saturni, and an old war of the knights appears too. The volume served Latin readers who lacked German, as its own preface says.
darwin-geological-observations-1846:
Charles Darwin's Geological Observations on the Voyage of the Beagle, complete in the 1846 form, gathers his three geology books from the Beagle voyage. Darwin sailed as a young naturalist from 1831 to 1836. His rock work, more than his animal studies, first made his scientific name.

Three parts treat coral reefs, volcanic islands, and the geology of South America. Darwin argued that coral atolls form as volcanic islands slowly sink beneath the sea. He also traced raised beaches and fossils that showed land moving over long ages. Readers see the young Darwin building the deep-time habits of thought that later supported his theory of evolution.
doe-osti-3409104-toyota-highlander-fchv-:
Report NLR/TP-5700-100241 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated August 2026, closes work on a Toyota Highlander fuel cell vehicle. Melanie Caton and Katherine Hurst were the lab contacts, with Bill Reinert in the evidence record. The work ran under CRADA number CRD-12-00469.

More than 100 people were trained to drive the vehicles over two years. Drivers came from many lab groups, from lab operations to energy analysis. They used the vehicles for daily campus tasks. Real use by many drivers gave the team broad feedback on fuel cell cars in normal service, not just test track runs.
dumas-chicot-the-jester-1846:
Alexandre Dumas published Chicot the Jester in 1846, as La Dame de Monsoreau in French. The classic abridged English version gives the Valois trilogy's middle volume in one book for readers. Its scene is the court of Henri III, last of the Valois kings of France.

Chicot, the king's jester, is in truth a Gascon noble with a sharp sword and wit. He guards his feckless king against the Guise faction and the League's rising plots in Paris. Bussy d'Amboise loves Diane de Monsoreau, whose husband traps him for a fatal ambush at night. Duels, disguises, and monkish conspiracies crowd the pages at Dumas's swiftest clip of storytelling here. Many readers rank the jester among Dumas's finest and most human creations in fiction.
edwards-religious-affections-1746:
Jonathan Edwards preached through the Great Awakening, the revival that swept New England in the 1740s, and saw both its power and its excesses. His Treatise Concerning Religious Affections, published in 1746, asks how to tell true religious experience from false. It is the Awakening's deepest piece of self-examination.

Edwards lists signs that prove nothing: loud emotion, fluent talk, even love of praise disguised as zeal. True grace, he argues, shows in changed practice, humility, and a new taste for the beauty of holy things. Pastors and psychologists of religion still argue with his tests today.
esdaile-mesmerism-in-india-1846:
James Esdaile cut flesh with no pain in Mesmerism in India, his report of 1846. Esdaile was a Scot healer at a jail ward in India. He found that deep trance, wrought by passes and breath, could dull all pain. Scores of great cuts, some dire, were done while the sick slept calm and woke with no tale of hurt.

He prints each case with care and zeal. Word of his work shook the wards of Britain. Ere sleep drugs came, his proof stood as the best hope of pain free craft. The book is that proof.
etheridge-syrian-churches-gospels-1846:
John Wesley Etheridge, a Methodist scholar of the Syriac tongue, wrote this 1846 study of the churches of Syria and the east. He paired it with his own literal English version of the four gospels, translated straight from the Peshitta, the Syriac Bible. Longman published the volume in London.

Etheridge traces the Syrian churches, their rites, their writers, and their missions as far as India and China. Then the gospels follow, in wording that often differs in small, telling ways from the Greek-based versions. His aim was to let English readers hear the gospel in a language close to the one Jesus spoke. The book serves both church history and Bible study.
europmc-pmc10066346:
Kim reviews how short-chain fatty acids made by gut microbes shape immune tolerance and autoimmunity, in a 2023 paper. These fatty acids form when gut bacteria ferment fiber from food. Immune tolerance is the system that stops the body from attacking itself, and it is built and tuned across a lifetime.

The review explains how the fatty acids calm some immune cells and guide others. It links weak production of these acids to higher risk of autoimmune disease. The paper connects diet, gut microbes, and immune balance in a clear chain.
europmc-pmc10324146:
Ye and co-authors reviewed breast cancer care in 2023, with a focus on two newer forms of treatment. Breast cancer is the second top cause of cancer death in women. Its many forms make it hard to treat with one plan. Targeted drugs aim at one molecule that helps a tumour grow.

Ye lists targets now in use, such as CDK proteins and PARP, an enzyme that fixes DNA. Some drugs have won FDA approval, alone or with other drugs. One hard form, called triple-negative, still resists targeted drugs. For that form, Ye points to immune therapy, such as drugs that lift brakes on immune cells.
europmc-pmc10434946:
Chari and Pachter argued in 2023 that a standard chart in single-cell gene studies misleads users. The chart squeezes data with hundreds or thousands of measures into a flat 2D plot. Such plots open most papers in this field and guide first looks at the data. The authors test how much truth survives that squeeze.

Their checks show the squeeze warps the data in deep ways. Cells that look close on the plot may sit far apart in the full data. Chari found that habits in making these plots vary and can flip the tale a plot seems to tell. They urge targeted plots built for one clear question instead. Broad all-in-one plots, they say, block real finds more than they help.
europmc-pmc1069646:
Foster and a large team read the full genome in 2005 of a bacterium that lives inside a parasitic worm. The worm, Brugia malayi, infects humans and causes filarial disease of skin and lymph. Its tenant, Wolbachia, is a bacterium the worm needs to breed and live. Killing the tenant may thus kill the worm.

The tenant genome is small and worn, with many genes lost. Foster found it kept key paths to make riboflavin, heme, and DNA building blocks. Those gifts may be its main pay to the host worm. The worm in turn feeds it amino acids. Next to its kin in fruit flies, this tenant lacks virus bits and repeat DNA. The map gives fresh targets to end the disease.
europmc-pmc10763046:
Iqbal and co-authors reviewed in 2024 how oxidative stress feeds cancer through cell signals and gene switches. Stress from reactive oxygen can break DNA and warp the signals that steer cell growth. High levels push cells to drop normal jobs and gain cancer traits. The team traced which paths carry that push.

Named paths include the guard gene p53, the Keap1-NRF2 stress reply, and RB1 and p21, two brakes on cell division. Iqbal shows how faults in each can free growth, blunt DNA repair, and dodge cell death. Care ideas aim to reset the redox balance, the cell's stress ledger. Antioxidant drugs and redox-tuned agents lead that work. Proof in patients is the next test.
europmc-pmc10781646:
Cui and colleagues built a reference map of how immune cells react to signal proteins in this 2024 paper. Cytokines are small proteins that cells use to send messages to each other. They guide immune responses and are targets for many drugs. No one had charted how each cell type answers each cytokine in one place.

Working in mouse lymph nodes, the team tested 86 cytokines on more than 17 cell types. Most cytokines sparked a distinct response in each cell type, they found. The data revealed over 66 driven cell states, some never described before. The team also made free software that reads gene activity data and infers which cytokines are at work. They used it to map signals in tumours after a common cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc11075546:
Sternberg and a large team report the state of the main worm genetics database in this 2024 paper. WormBase has held genome and genetics data on the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans for over two decades. The worm is a staple lab animal for studying development and disease. The team states three goals: stay current, link better with other resources, and stay sustainable.

The paper describes WormBase as it stands and the plan to move its core systems into the Alliance of Genome Resources. The Alliance is a shared infrastructure for model organism databases. As a member, WormBase will keep curating key findings from papers and large projects. It will also keep building features the worm community needs. The move is framed as a way to cut duplicated effort across databases.
europmc-pmc11299546:
Gaser and colleagues introduce a toolbox for measuring brain structure from MRI scans in this 2024 paper. Brain morphometry quantifies features such as cortical thickness and folding from magnetic resonance images. Many sophisticated tools exist, but they often demand expert handling. The Computational Anatomy Toolbox, called CAT, aims to serve beginners and experts alike through a graphical interface or scripts.

CAT covers the full workflow: preprocessing, statistical analysis, and display of results, the authors report. It supports voxel-based, surface-based, and region-based analyses, shown on an example dataset. Voxel means a 3D pixel, the smallest cube in a scan. Multiple quality control options are built in. Both one-time and repeated scans over time are handled. The paper offers the toolbox as a citable standard for the brain mapping community.
europmc-pmc11701646:
Szklarczyk and colleagues update the STRING database of protein networks in this 2025 paper. Proteins work by binding, regulating, and cooperating with each other. STRING compiles, scores, and merges evidence on protein-protein links from experiments, predictions, and prior knowledge. Its goal is a full, objective global network of physical and functional links.

Version 12.5 adds a new regulatory network. For it, the team gathers evidence on the type and direction of each regulatory link, using curated pathway databases, plus a language model fine-tuned to parse the literature. Users can now view three network types on their own: functional, physical, and regulatory. The pathway enrichment tool, which flags processes over-represented in a protein set, was also updated. Network clustering remains part of the package.
europmc-pmc11760946:
Chandimali and colleagues review free radicals and the body's antioxidant defences in this 2025 paper. Free radicals are molecules with unpaired electrons, which makes them highly reactive. They form inside the body during processes such as mitochondrial respiration, where cells burn fuel with oxygen, and immune cell activation. Outside sources include radiation, pollution, and smoking.

In balance, radicals serve cell signalling and immune defence. Overproduction breaks the balance between oxidants and antioxidants and causes oxidative stress. That stress damages DNA, proteins, and lipids. It is linked to cancer, heart disease, brain-wasting diseases, and inflammatory diseases. The review covers radical types, how they form, and their biological impacts. It also details the defence systems and ways to restore balance.
europmc-pmc1308846:
Ginaldi, Di Benedetto, and De Martinis reviewed osteoporosis through inflammation and aging in 2005. Osteoporosis thins bones and raises fracture risk in older people. Hormones, metabolism, and mechanics were the classic explanations. New evidence adds chronic inflammation as a driver.

Inflammatory signaling molecules regulate both bone-building and bone-eating cells. Aging remodels the immune system toward a more activated profile. That shift may tip bone turnover toward loss. Conditions linked to osteoporosis often share chronic inflammation too. Ginaldi reads osteoporosis partly as an inflamed aging disease. Bone loss in old age is the core concern. Old age is when the risk is at its peak for most men and women. Falls and breaks are the main harm that comes from thin bones.
europmc-pmc1363346:
Link, Shevchenko, and Heisenberg set up protein analysis for early zebrafish embryos in 2006. Zebrafish are a leading model for vertebrate development. Genetic tools were strong, but protein gel methods lagged. Yolk in embryos blocked clean protein separation.

A new method removes yolk efficiently from large embryo batches. That step enabled high-resolution 2D gel separation. Western blotting improved considerably with the same prep. Protocols run from sample prep through mass spectrometry identification. Database choices for matching zebrafish proteins were compared. Link opens protein-level study of early development. Gel steps and blot steps are spelled out in full.
europmc-pmc1821046:
Yooseph, Venter and colleagues mined the Global Ocean Sampling data in 2007 for new protein families. The expedition sequenced microbes from ocean water around the world. The team clustered proteins by similarity, merging public databases with millions of proteins predicted from the new sea samples.

Their combined set held 6.12 million predicted proteins from 7.7 million sampling sequences, and it covered nearly all known bacterial protein families. They found 3,995 medium and large clusters made only of ocean sequences. Of those, 1,700 had no detectable match to any known family, marking genuinely new families. Ocean-only clusters held an excess of viral sequences, showing how poorly viruses had been sampled. Some protein domains once thought limited to one kingdom appeared in others.
europmc-pmc1914346:
Gaugler and co-authors pooled in 2007 the evidence on what predicts an older American's move into a nursing home. Many single studies had named risk factors, but no fuller pooled picture existed. Knowing the strongest predictors helps families plan and helps programs target support that delays admission.

The search swept four databases plus theses and reference lists, turning up 736 candidate reports. Seventy-seven reports from 12 data sources met the bar: long-term designs with community samples that mirrored a region or the nation. The team pulled admission counts, follow-up length, and candidate predictors under a standard protocol. Random-effects models then pooled each predictor family one by one. The families covered social traits, physical function, thinking, service use, and family or friend support.
europmc-pmc1940246:
Bhattacharya and colleagues charted in 2007 how a first-time mother's body mass index relates to pregnancy outcomes. Obesity in young women is rising fast, with consequences for both mother and baby. The study used routine records for all first-time mothers who delivered single babies in Aberdeen over the three decades ending in 2005.

Women were split into five bands from underweight to morbidly obese. Compared with the normal band, morbidly obese women faced the highest pre-eclampsia risk, a dangerous blood pressure disorder, with odds over seven times higher. Underweight women had the lowest risk, at about six tenths of the normal odds. Induced labor was most common in the morbidly obese group and least in the underweight group. Emergency cesarean rates also peaked in the morbidly obese, at nearly triple the normal-band odds.
europmc-pmc1955446:
Wolozin and colleagues mined a veterans health database in 2007 to test whether cholesterol drugs differ in their links to dementia and Parkinson disease. Statins lower cholesterol by blocking a liver enzyme. Past studies of statins and dementia clashed, and the authors guessed the drugs are not all alike.

The database held records on 4.5 million people, with case, drug, and background records. Models compared users of lovastatin, simvastatin, or atorvastatin with users of other heart drugs, with traits tied to dementia and Parkinson risk held constant. Simvastatin stood out: in people aged 65 and over it was tied to a clear drop in new dementia cases under all three models. The title reports a matching reduced incidence for Parkinson disease. The authors stress these are links from records, not proof of a real effect.
europmc-pmc2124946:
Robert A. Lambert of Columbia's pathology department showed in 1912 that foreign body giant cells can be made to order in a dish. Adding lycopodium spores or cotton fibers to cultures of chick embryo spleen produced them reliably. The cultures used Burrows' method: teased tissue fragments in hanging drops of plasma on cover-glasses.

Under the microscope the giant cells form by fusion. Large single-nucleus wandering cells, probably endothelial and pulp cells, merge into one great cell around the foreign object. Connective tissue cells take no part. Dark rings appear around the spores about the fifth or sixth day, clearer in cultures a week old. Lambert draws a neat conclusion for everyday culture work. Readers get a small mystery of the culture dish solved by direct watching.
europmc-pmc2128146:
Hideyo Noguchi described a venereal spiral infection found in ordinary American rabbits, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1922. Among fifty rabbits regarded as normal, five adults carried scaly, often ulcerating sores around the genitals. A newly bought group of twenty rabbits held six more cases, all female. The condition ran a chronic course.

The sores held a spiral organism closely resembling Treponema pallidum, the syphilis germ. It shared that germ's shape but ran perhaps a trifle thicker and longer, with very long specimens common. The organisms tended to knot loosely together or fan out in star-like clusters. One rabbit's lesion held a second, coarser type beside the first, which Noguchi took for a variant of the same rabbit spirochete. Tissue reactions resembled syphilis but were far less cellular. The find warns that rabbit colonies carry their own look-alike infection.
europmc-pmc2128246:
Primary infection in the rabbit's scrotum is the subject of the second paper in the Brown and Pearce syphilis series, part one dealing with the reaction to infection. It appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1920. The paper explains why the scrotum became the team's standard inoculation site and sets up the lesion studies that follow.

Skin inoculation, they argue, brought real advantages over the older testicular route. Its conditions are closer to the mode of infection in the human subject, and the lesions resemble man's primary lesions more closely. The scrotum also sits where an observer can reach it, so the reaction can be followed directly day by day. Of all skin areas tried, the scrotum proved best adapted, and it became the only area used for the work. The paper lays this ground for part two's detailed account of the lesions.
europmc-pmc2128346:
Hans Zinsser and Julia T. Parker continued their bacterial hypersusceptibility studies with a stubborn active material drawn from ground bacteria. Their paper is the second of the series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923. Filtered alkaline extracts of crushed bacteria were treated with acid, heat, and alcohol in turn. Everything those steps threw down was removed.

What remained was a small amount of material that no longer gave the usual chemical tests for proteins. It kept only one very weak protein reaction. Yet it still reacted with its matching antiserum in a specific way and gave specific serum test results. The same sort of material came from the flu bacillus, pneumococcus, and meningococcus without grinding. It also appears in young and old broth cultures. The authors class it with tuberculin and the pneumococcus products others had described: an active substance that survives treatment no true protein would.
europmc-pmc2131146:
Gregory Shwartzman's 1926 paper in The Journal of Experimental Medicine is the second part of his studies on how bacteriophage is regenerated. Working in New York, he asked what oxygen does to Bacillus coli when the lytic principle, the agent that breaks bacteria open, acts on it. Earlier writers had claimed oxygen made no difference.
