Shwartzman found that oxygen changes how the bacterial cells behave toward the lytic principle. At set acid levels, cultures grown with or without air could be made resistant even when no lytic principle was present, and that resistance held. Resistant cultures still rebuilt the lytic principle when it was added, yet they did not break open themselves.
europmc-pmc2131246:
Fred Stewart, at The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, wrote part two of his 1927 series on local treatment of pneumococcal meningitis. Part one had used rabbits; this part produces the disease in dogs and treats it there. Injected into the cisternal space, virulent Type I pneumococci gave the dogs a severe, pus-forming meningitis much like the human disease.

Stewart washed the meninges in a set way and applied mixtures of optochin and serum through a four-puncture method. Cures followed when the drug reached every region of the membranes often enough. Where contact failed, germs survived and infection returned. He stresses repeated clear spinal fluids, on smear and on culture, before a cure can be trusted, and notes that recovered dogs resisted a second attack in part.
europmc-pmc2131346:
Fred Stewart wrote part three of his local therapy series in 1928, turning from cure to the side damage of pneumococcal meningitis in dogs. In parts one and two he had produced Type I pneumococcal meningitis in rabbits and dogs and treated it by washing the membranes. Here he records what else the disease does inside the cord and membranes.

Involvement of the central cord was common after the second day and could grow into wide, pus-forming myelitis. Abscesses were rare, arising along blood vessels or at infected skin spots. In long, untreated cases the pus-like exudate did not clear as it does after pneumonia crisis. Instead it organized, and late lesions showed a strong growth of scavenger cells around the vessels.
europmc-pmc2140946:
Young roof rats on an inclined plane steer upward at an angle set by gravity, and W. J. Crozier and G. Pincus test whether that rule matches their earlier work on another rat species. Their 1927 study, from Harvard's Laboratory of General Physiology, compares Rattus rattus with Rattus norvegicus under the same creeping-plane setup.

Orientation in the roof rat follows the same equations found for the Norway rat, yet the constants differ clearly between the two forms. The roof rat also proves more sensitive to gravity's pull. Readers get a careful early attempt to turn animal movement into exact formulas, plus a discussion of what the species difference may mean for how excitation controls orientation.
europmc-pmc2180246:
Two separate outbreaks of mouse typhoid swept the Rockefeller Institute's cancer-breeding mouse colony within a few years, and Harold L. Amoss and Peter P. Haselbauer compare the germs behind each. Their 1922 study uses immune reactions to test whether the two strains, taken from colonies of 2,500 to 4,000 mice, are really the same.

The two strains prove antigenically different, meaning their surface markers trigger different immune responses. The first strain sits near, but not with, two enteritidis strains. The second sits near human paratyphoid B strains instead. A linked paper by Webster ties the second strain to Bacillus pestis caviae and a mutton-associated group. Careful strain identity, the study shows, matters even within one animal house.
europmc-pmc2206446:
Mehta and co-authors, for the Acute Kidney Injury Network, reported an initiative in 2007 to standardise acute kidney injury care. The disorder ranges from tiny rises in blood creatinine to complete kidney failure, yet it had no accepted definition. Experts from critical care and kidney societies met in Amsterdam in September 2005. Three workgroups drafted recommendations, refined them with the full group, and gained endorsement from participating societies.

The group proposes the term acute kidney injury to cover the whole spectrum of acute renal failure. Diagnosis rests on sudden changes in urine output or in serum creatinine. Severity is then graded by a staging system using the size of those changes. The network itself offers a standing forum for collaboration across disciplines. Its standards now need validation in future studies.
europmc-pmc2211546:
Thomas and co-workers identified in 2008 a family of proteins that sit in plasmodesmata, the channels linking plant cells. Those channels carry signals and materials between cells and shape growth and defence, yet how proteins are targeted to them was unknown. The new family, called PDLP1, resembles cell-surface receptor proteins. The team studied the first member, PDLP1a, tracing its route through the cell and testing altered versions.

PDLP1a reaches plasmodesmata through the secretory pathway, in a route blocked by the drug Brefeldin A. Changing its expression altered how much traffic passed between cells. Its single membrane-spanning segment holds all the targeting information. That segment alone could drag unrelated proteins to plasmodesmata. The finding gives plant biologists a delivery tag for probing these channels.
europmc-pmc2233646:
Bui, Sidney, Li, Fusseder and Sette built a software tool in 2007 for measuring how conserved immune epitopes are. Epitopes are the protein fragments that trigger antibody or T-cell responses. Vaccine designers prefer conserved epitopes, shared across many strains, for broad protection. Diagnostic designers may want strain-specific ones instead. Either way, the degree of conservation must be measured concretely before choosing.

Their tool analyses epitope variability across any given set of protein sequences. It was implemented as part of the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) and its linked Analysis Resources, a public resource for immunology. Users can check how widely an epitope is preserved before committing to it. The authors expect the user-friendly tool to aid design of epitope-based vaccines and diagnostics alike.
europmc-pmc2289846:
Fedorova and a very large team compared genomes in 2008 of the pathogenic fungus Aspergillus fumigatus and two close relatives. This fungus is a major allergen and a dangerous invader in immunocompromised patients. The team sequenced a new clinical isolate plus Neosartorya fischeri and Aspergillus clavatus, rarely pathogenic species. Comparing all three against the first sequenced isolate revealed which genes are core, variable or unique to each genome.

Core genes were 99.8 percent identical between the two Aspergillus fumigatus isolates. Variable genes dropped as low as 40 percent identity. Species-specific genes made up 8.5 to 12.6 percent of each genome. They clustered in thirteen chromosomal islands rich in pseudogenes and jumping elements. At least twenty percent of the pathogen's unique genes appear functional. Their origin likely involves duplication and differential loss, not horizontal transfer.
europmc-pmc2374446:
Zeng and co-authors summarised twenty years of rheumatic disease surveys in China in 2008. Rheumatic diseases cover joint, bone, and connective tissue disorders that cause pain and disability. The team pooled 38 population surveys with 241,169 adults from 25 provinces and cities, covering 1980 to 2006.

Joint and muscle complaints ranged from 11.6% to 46.4% of adults depending on place and method. Symptomatic osteoarthritis, worn-joint disease, hit the spine and knees most. Beijing's older women had more knee osteoarthritis than US women, while hip and hand rates stayed far below Western rates. Rheumatoid arthritis ran lower than in rich countries. Gout rose over time, and Taiwan's aboriginal people showed the highest rate, at 11.7% in the records.
europmc-pmc2375446:
da Fonseca and co-authors traced how mammal mitochondria adapted over evolution in 2008. Mitochondria are the cell's power stations, making up to 95% of its energy through a process called oxidative phosphorylation. Their small genome holds 12 protein-coding genes that the team compared across 41 placental mammal species.

Change clustered at working hotspots. One energy protein, cytochrome b, varied at key regions in animals with special needs. These included low-energy diets in sloths and pangolins, diving in whales, flight in bats, and thin air in alpacas. The ATP8 piece, which helps assemble the energy turbine, showed the strongest adaptive signal of all. Another part, ATP6, varied in its loop regions, which affect how the turbine spins. The authors mapped these shifts onto protein shapes to guide future lab tests.
europmc-pmc2440546:
Wu and colleagues reported a first human trial of malaria vaccines meant to block transmission in this paper. Most malaria vaccines protect the vaccinated person. These two, Pfs25 and Pvs25, target proteins the malaria parasite shows while in the mosquito, so antibodies would stop it passing to the next person.

The dose-rising trial at Johns Hopkins planned 72 healthy volunteers but was halted early for unexpected reactions, enrolling 36. Groups got 5 or 20 micrograms of either vaccine in an oil-based booster called Montanide ISA 51, or the booster alone. Local reactions were frequent. Two volunteers developed erythema nodosum, a painful skin inflammation, judged probably linked to the vaccine mix. Still, those finishing the lowest Pfs25 dose made real antibody responses. Their antibody levels matched the strength of transmission blocking measured in lab tests. The authors said the concept works, but this formula is too reactogenic to develop further.
europmc-pmc2631046:
Ware and colleagues conducted an ethnographic study in 2009 to explain a puzzle: HIV patients in sub-Saharan Africa take their antiretroviral therapy more faithfully than patients in wealthy countries. Adherence above 90 percent of doses was routine, defying early fears that extreme poverty would make treatment fail. The team interviewed 252 patients, their treatment partners, and health workers at clinics in Nigeria, Tanzania, and Uganda, with 136 observation sessions.

Patients overcame money obstacles deliberately: borrowing or begging transport funds, making impossible choices to fund treatment first, and doing without other needs. Help flowed from treatment partners, family, friends, and providers, who expected adherence in return. Patients stuck to their regimens partly to preserve goodwill, keeping help available for future needs. The authors frame adherence as fulfilling social responsibilities that protect social capital.
europmc-pmc2673046:
Ribeyre and colleagues found in 2009 that a yeast enzyme guards the genome against a knot-like DNA structure. Certain DNA stretches rich in the letter G can fold into four-stranded knots called G-quadruplexes. The team planted a human repeat prone to such folding into baker's yeast and watched what happened with and without the unwinding enzyme Pif1.

Without Pif1, the planted repeat kept changing length, a sign of genomic instability, while other repeats stayed calm. Knocking out a different unwinding enzyme did nothing. In test tubes, the repeat did fold into the knots, and Pif1 unwound them faster than ordinary DNA. When the team edited the repeat so it could no longer fold, the instability vanished even without the enzyme. Pif1, they conclude, patrols the genome for these knots and undoes them before they cause damage.
europmc-pmc2736946:
Stewart and co-authors described in 2009 a new case register. It was built from electronic records at South London and Maudsley. That trust is Europe's largest secondary mental health provider. Older registers used manual data entry, which limited depth. Full electronic records plus search software that strips identity offer a richer, safer research resource.

Their CRIS tool lets researchers search anonymized numerical and free-text clinical data under strict security rules. By October 2008 the register held over one hundred twenty-two thousand cases, reasonably matching the local population by sex and ethnicity. Mood disorders were the commonest primary diagnosis, followed by schizophrenia-related disorders, substance misuse, neuroses, and organic disorders. About thirty-five thousand patients were under active case management.
europmc-pmc2763246:
Bouayed, Rammal, and Soulimani reviewed in 2009 the relationship between oxidative stress and anxiety, in both normal and pathological forms. The brain uses much oxygen and holds rich fat stores. Its antioxidant defenses are modest. That mix leaves it prone to redox imbalance and damage. Oxidative stress had already been tied to depression and anxiety disorders, raising the question of whether it helps cause anxiety itself.

They weigh findings linking oxidative status to normal anxiety levels in people and animals. They also examine claims that cellular oxidative stress could generate emotional stress, and they set out the methods used to test a causal link. The evidence, they conclude, supports an association, while the direction of cause and effect remains disputed and needs direct tests.
europmc-pmc2795146:
Rutherford and co-authors used brain scans to check whether cooling newborns after oxygen loss at birth truly protects brain tissue. Babies in the TOBY trial had hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, brain harm from low oxygen and blood flow, and were cared for with or without moderate cooling. The 2010 substudy read scans from one hundred thirty-one of the infants.

Cooled babies showed fewer injuries in deep brain areas that steer movement, and fewer damaged tracts in the white matter, the brain's wiring. They were also more likely to have normal scans and less likely to show patterns that predict later movement problems. Scans predicted death or disability equally well in both groups.
europmc-pmc2827546:
Zijnge and colleagues mapped the layout of bacterial films on natural teeth in 2010, using glowing probes that light up set species in place. Dental plaque causes gum disease and cavities, yet its mature structure below the gumline had barely been studied since the nineteen seventies. The team examined seven pulled teeth from four people.

Below the gum, five groups dominated, including Actinomyces and the gum disease germ Tannerella forsythia. One little-known group sat right against the gum tissue, close to immune cells. Lactobacillus formed the core of clumps below the gum, while above it, Streptococcus and the yeast Candida albicans built corncob-shaped clusters. Gum pathogens arrived late and colonized films already built.
europmc-pmc2833246:
Heddleston, Li, Lathia, Bao, Hjelmeland, and Rich reviewed in 2010 how low oxygen inside tumors protects cancer stem cells, the rare tumor cells that can regrow a whole cancer. Solid tumors are riddled with oxygen-poor zones because their blood vessels grow in chaos. Oxygen-sensing proteins called HIFs switch on survival programs in those zones.

Brain tumor stem cells cluster in two homes, near blood vessels and beside dead tissue, the review reports. Low oxygen grows their numbers and pushes ordinary tumor cells toward a stem-like state. These cells depend on HIFs for survival, self-renewal, and tumor growth. That dependence raises a hard problem: killing stem cells may fail while oxygen-poor zones keep minting replacements, so therapy may need to strike the zones themselves.
europmc-pmc2841246:
Sobolewski, Cerella, Dicato, Ghibelli, and Diederich reviewed in 2010 the role of COX-2, an enzyme switched on in inflammation and cancer, in tumor cell growth and death. COX enzymes drive the making of prostaglandins, hormone-like signals. The always-on family member COX-1 handles housekeeping, while COX-2 rises sharply in many solid tumors, colorectal, breast, and prostate among them, and lately in blood cancers too.

Evidence ties COX-2 to faster tumor cell division and slower programmed death. Pairing COX-2 blockers with standard treatments may sharpen those treatments, the authors argue. They survey the combination studies run so far and judge COX-2 control a promising field for improving future cancer care.
europmc-pmc2859946:
Low oxygen inside tumors triggers a survival program, and Favaro and colleagues traced in 2010 how one tiny RNA drives much of it. The RNA, called miR-210, rises when oxygen falls and marks tumors with a poor outlook. It works by silencing a helper protein named ISCU, which builds iron-sulfur clusters that many cell enzymes need to function.

In cancer cell lines and real tumors, Favaro found that silencing ISCU was the main cause of harmful free radicals building up under low oxygen. Blocking ISCU also weakened energy-making parts of the cell, pushed cells toward sugar burning, and helped them survive. Tumors with low ISCU levels belonged to patients who fared worse, tying the pathway to real disease course.
europmc-pmc2893946:
Gold and colleagues gave in 2010 the first clear job description for MAIT cells, an unusual T cell subset that patrols mucosal tissues like the gut and lung lining. Unlike ordinary T cells, which each target one specific germ, MAIT cells respond broadly across bacterial infections. The team tested what switches them on using infected human cells.

MAIT cells detected airway lining cells infected with the tuberculosis bacterium and with other bacteria as well. They read the infection through MR1, a display molecule that is nearly identical across all mammals, the most conserved of its family. That unusual conservation now makes sense: the molecule flags bacterial chemistry rather than variable germ proteins, letting one cell type watch for many invaders at body surfaces.
europmc-pmc2941746:
Parri and Chiarugi reviewed two families of molecular switches, Rac and Rho, that govern how cancer cells move, in a 2010 article. Both families reorganise the cell's actin skeleton, the inner scaffolding that sets shape and motion.

Tumour cells invade in three broad styles: moving as a linked cohort, crawling singly with a stretched shape, or squeezing along in a rounded amoeba-like mode. Rac drives the stretched crawling style, while high Rho activity powers the rounded style through strong contraction. Cells can switch styles as conditions change, a flexibility that helps them spread.
europmc-pmc3081346:
Liu and coauthors traced in 2011 how one small RNA pushes tumors to grow their own blood vessels. The RNA, called miR-21 in short, is abundant in many cancers and tied to growth and spread, but its role in vessel growth was unclear. Forcing prostate cancer cells to make extra copies raised two vessel promoting factors and sparked new vessel growth in a standard membrane test.

The chain ran through a brake protein the RNA normally suppresses. With the brake down, two signaling routes switched on, which in turn raised a low oxygen master switch and the vessel growth factor it controls. Blocking the RNA, restoring the brake, or drugging either route each cut the effect. Removing the oxygen switch alone erased it completely. The pathway gives drug makers several linked points to attack tumor blood supply.
europmc-pmc3134446:
Michael Clark and a large group of colleagues defended a bold claim about the human genome in a 2011 paper in PLoS Biology. Only a tiny share of DNA codes for proteins, yet many studies reported that most of the genome still gets copied into RNA. A rival paper had blamed that signal on lab artefacts and background noise.

The authors rechecked the rival data and found its arrays unusual and its sequencing too shallow to catch faint copies. Several independent methods, from copy catalogues to genome-wide chips, agree that copying is widespread across cell types. They conclude the copying is real, while granting that the purpose of many of these RNA copies remains unknown and needs study.
europmc-pmc3169446:
Benjamin Solomon reviewed a rare pattern of birth defects in a 2011 paper in the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases. The pattern, known by an acronym of its parts, is diagnosed when at least three of six defect types appear together. The six are spine, blocked anus, heart, a windpipe-food pipe link, kidneys, and limbs. It occurs in roughly one in tens of thousands of newborns.

Diagnosis is clinical and requires ruling out a long list of look-alike syndromes, several of them genetic. The cause remains unknown in most patients, likely because many different causes converge on the same pattern. Surgery soon after birth fixes the most urgent defects, followed by lifelong management of lasting effects. Thinking ability is typically unaffected, and with good surgical repair the outlook can be fairly positive, Solomon reports.
europmc-pmc3234246:
Torsten Schaller and colleagues mapped how HIV's capsid uses helper proteins to enter the nucleus, in this 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. HIV infects non-dividing cells, so its core must cross the nuclear pore. The team showed the capsid binds directly to a cyclophilin domain on Nup358, a protein of the nuclear pore itself.

Grafting that domain onto a viral restriction factor created a new HIV blocker, confirming the interaction matters in living cells. Blocking the other capsid partner, cyclophilin A, changed which import machinery the virus depended on, suggesting it steers the choice of route. Capsid mutations shifted where the virus inserted its DNA in the genome, toward or away from gene-rich regions, and weakened replication in test cells and macrophages. The work links capsid helpers to import route, insertion targeting, and fitness.
europmc-pmc3276346:
Ernestina Schipani, Christa Maes, Geert Carmeliet, and Gregg Semenza reviewed how blood vessel growth and bone growth are coupled, in this perspective in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. Bone is richly supplied with vessels, yet what angiogenesis does in shaping and maintaining the skeleton was poorly defined. Work in altered mice had recently thrown the coupling into relief.

The mouse experiments highlight a pathway in which the oxygen sensor HIF drives production of VEGF, a vessel-growth signal, linking low-oxygen sensing to both vessel ingrowth and bone formation. The authors review the current understanding of the mechanisms that keep the two processes in step during development and throughout adult remodeling. They argue that clarifying this coupling will deepen knowledge of bone biology and may yield therapies that speed bone regeneration and repair. The signals that summon vessels also instruct bone-forming cells.
europmc-pmc3291446:
Chomel and colleagues reviewed germs of the Bartonella group carried by pets in a 2006 article. These bacteria live in blood, spread through insects such as fleas, and can pass from animals to people. Cats are the main source of the species behind cat scratch disease, a common infection after a scratch or bite.

The review counts eleven species or subspecies thought to harm people, six of them found in pet cats and dogs. Dogs can carry several kinds for long periods and sometimes develop heart valve infection. Infection rates in cats range from almost none in cold Norway to very high in the warm Philippines. The authors update the germs, symptoms, and spread patterns known at the time.
europmc-pmc3313946:
Collins and Koechlin explored how the brain's frontal lobes juggle competing strategies while making decisions, in a 2012 article. Everyday choices unfold in changing settings where no single approach always works. A person must track several possible strategies, judge which is paying off, switch when one fails, and sometimes invent a fresh one altogether.

Drawing on computer models and behavior experiments, the authors argue the frontal system can keep watch over about three or four strategies at once. One part of the system adjusts the strategy in use by its recent rewards, while monitoring functions estimate how trustworthy each option is. The open puzzle is how the brain decides to create new strategies instead of recycling old ones, a problem the authors connect to statistical models that grow their own categories.
europmc-pmc3328746:
Pester and colleagues built a master family tree of microbes that turn ammonia into nitrite in soil, reporting in 2012. These archaea, single celled organisms distinct from bacteria, drive a key step of the nitrogen cycle that fertilizers depend on. Researchers use one of their genes, called amoA, as an identity marker, and the team assembled every public sequence of that gene into one agreed tree.

The tree sorts the organisms into five major clusters, one of them newly recognized, holding eighty three species level groups. Deep sequencing of soils from Austria, Costa Rica, Greenland, and Namibia found each soil home to anywhere from a handful to dozens of species. One cluster dominated almost everywhere, and the mix in each place tracked geography, hinting that travel limits and history shape these communities as much as soil conditions do.
europmc-pmc3352246:
Hunter and Hölscher asked whether two diabetes drugs modelled on the gut hormone GLP-1 can reach the brain and act there. Liraglutide and lixisenatide strengthen insulin signalling, and because type 2 diabetes raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease, a brain effect could matter beyond blood sugar control.

Injecting the drugs into mice, the researchers tracked them across the blood–brain barrier and measured receptor activation through cyclic AMP levels. Both compounds entered the brain; lixisenatide did so at every dose tested and proved the stronger activator. Both also increased the formation of new neurons. The authors suggest these agents merit study as treatments for neurodegenerative disease.
europmc-pmc3374546:
Neter and Brainin surveyed Israeli adults in 2012 to test whether the digital divide follows people into online health searching. eHealth literacy means the skill to find, judge, and use health information from electronic sources. Their telephone survey reached a representative sample of more than four thousand adults.

Adults with high eHealth literacy tended to be younger and better educated than those with low scores. The skilled group searched more, used more strategies, and checked information more carefully. They also gained more, from understanding to managing their own care and talking with doctors. The authors warn that online health tools may widen social gaps unless weaker groups get training and simpler designs.
europmc-pmc3419346:
Boeing led a panel that critically reviewed in 2012 whether eating more vegetables and fruit prevents chronic disease. These foods supply nutrients, fiber, and plant chemicals, but the strength of the protective evidence was unsettled. The panel weighed study quality, size, and design across a long list of conditions, from heart disease to dementia.

For high blood pressure, coronary heart disease, and stroke, the evidence that higher intake lowers risk was judged convincing. A general cancer benefit looked probable, and possible benefits covered weight control, some eye diseases, dementia, and bone loss. For a few conditions the data were too thin to call. National campaigns urging more vegetables and fruit, the panel concludes, stand on justified scientific ground.
europmc-pmc3563746:
Sumitra Datta, Rene Christena, and Yamuna Rani Rajaram gave an overview of enzyme immobilization in 3 Biotech in 2013. Immobilization fixes enzymes onto a solid support so they can be used again and again, instead of being washed away after one reaction. Industry wants enzymes that last longer on the shelf and keep working through large, low-cost production runs.

Supports covered range from natural materials to synthetic ones, and methods from simple adsorption to trapping inside gels or beads. Fixed enzymes stay available to their target molecules far longer than free enzymes, which cuts later purification steps. Weak points remain, including cost and loss of activity in some setups. The review closes by urging smarter trapping methods and better-designed supports, so plants can reuse these biological catalysts with less waste.
europmc-pmc3580446:
Julia Oh and colleagues charted how the microbes on human skin change with age in Genome Medicine in 2012. Healthy adult skin communities were already mapped, giving a reference for disease studies. Children were a blank spot, even though skin changes greatly on the way to adulthood and several skin diseases begin in childhood. The team sampled twenty-eight healthy volunteers aged two to forty at the National Institutes of Health.

Swabs came from the nose, the inner elbow and back of knee where eczema strikes, and the forearm as a control. Gene sequencing showed nose communities in young children differed strikingly from adults: whole bacterial families common in small children gave way to others after puberty. Skin sites shifted too, though less sharply. Adult maps, the authors warn, cannot simply be borrowed for children's skin disease.
europmc-pmc3588146:
Ludmil Alexandrov and colleagues set out a method for reading the fingerprints of cancer-causing processes in Cell Reports in 2013. Every cancer genome carries thousands of mutations gathered over a lifetime, left by DNA damage and faulty repair. A small share drive the cancer; the rest are passengers. Global projects were cataloguing these mutations by the thousand, yet no framework existed for sorting the catalogue back into the separate processes that wrote it.

Treating the task as blind source separation, borrowed from signal processing, their framework teases apart the mixed mutation patterns into distinct signatures, one per underlying process. Each signature reflects the kinds of DNA change a process favors and the sequence letters around them. With the maths in place, catalogues from many cancers can be mined the same way. The authors present the approach as the doorway to learning how each cancer was made, process by process.
europmc-pmc3671546:
A guardian protein fails in Parkinson disease when rust-like damage builds, Ariga and five colleagues review in a 2013 article in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. The protein, DJ-1, is the product of a gene whose faults cause a family form of the disease. Its jobs span gene switching, stress defence, guiding other proteins and guarding the cell's power plants. One sulfur point on it sets its working state.

Too much oxidation at that point switches the protein off, and just such damage is found in the brains of patients with the common, non-family form of the disease. The protein rises under many kinds of stress, acting as a stress sensor for the cell. The review gathers what DJ-1 does against oxidative stress, then asks how losing that guard may drive both disease forms.
europmc-pmc3682446:
Bacteria dismantle one of nature's toughest polymers outdoors, Beier and Bertilsson review in a 2013 Frontiers in Microbiology article. The polymer is chitin, the shell and wall material of fungi, insects and shellfish, and one of the most abundant natural polymers on earth. Its breakdown feeds both carbon and nitrogen cycles. Reviews of the process were some twenty years old when new gene-based methods, which read germs without growing them, redrew the picture.

The review walks through the molecular steps of breakdown and the main enzyme families at work. It then links which germs are present in a place to measured breakdown speed and uptake of the pieces. Because the polymer must be cut outside the cell first, neighbours cross-feed on the fragments. Climate, particles and nutrient state are named as chief drivers of the pace of decay.
europmc-pmc3691846:
Sully and colleagues revisited how well randomized trials recruit, reviewing multicentre trials funded by two British agencies, the Health Technology Assessment programme and the Medical Research Council. Of 440 trials screened, 73 met the criteria, covering recruitment between 2002 and 2008.

Just over half reached their original target sample size, though more than three quarters reached eighty percent of it, and there was no sign of improvement across the period. Nearly half received an extension, and extensions did not make success more likely. Trials designed with eighty percent power recruited worse than those set at ninety. The authors recommend planning for ninety percent power where possible. They also urge trial teams to build recruitment strategies into the design from the start, rather than reaching for an extension once enrolment is already falling behind.
europmc-pmc3710246:
Matthew Brentnall and four co-authors reported a cell biology study in BMC Cell Biology in 2013 on three proteins called caspases. Caspases help carry out apoptosis, the planned death of a cell from inside. The group asked what caspase-9, caspase-3, and caspase-7 each do on their own during this kind of cell death.

Blocking caspase-9 still let a key signal leave the cell's energy centers, but it stopped changes in their shape and stopped the rise of harmful oxygen by-products. Caspase-9 was shown to cut a protein called Bid, and that cut was needed for the oxygen by-products to form. Cells lacking caspase-3 were harder to kill but made more of those by-products, while cells lacking caspase-7 stayed attached to their surface instead of letting go.
europmc-pmc3717046:
Rakesh Sharma and three colleagues review, in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology in 2013, how everyday habits shape fertility in both women and men. About 10 to 15 percent of couples face infertility. Unlike fixed causes, lifestyle factors can be changed: when to start a family, nutrition, weight, exercise, stress, and exposures at work and in the environment.

The review works through the evidence factor by factor. Cigarette smoking, illicit drugs, and heavy alcohol and caffeine use harm fertility, while preventive care can help. Age sets hard limits: semen quality declines from about age 35, and the paper traces the same clock on the female side. The aim is a practical map couples can act on before treatment.
europmc-pmc3737546:
Ryan McClure and seven co-authors presented a software system called Rockhopper in Nucleic Acids Research in 2013. RNA sequencing can reveal all the genes a bacterium is using, but the tools for making sense of bacterial data had lagged behind the flood of new data sets. Rockhopper was built for the shape of bacterial genomes and transcripts.

The system aligns reads to a genome, builds transcript maps, measures gene activity, tests for changes between conditions, finds operons, and displays results. The team tested it on 2.1 billion reads from 75 experiments across five bacterial species. Its transcript maps matched careful hand-checked data closely, and it found new small RNAs, operons, and start sites. The authors offer it as an open tool for bacterial transcript studies.
europmc-pmc3753746:
Geeta Ramesh, Andrew MacLean, and Mario Philipp wrote a review in Mediators of Inflammation in 2013 on cytokines and chemokines in nerve inflammation. These small proteins coordinate immune responses. When they fall out of balance, they help drive inflammation in the nervous system, nerve degeneration, and neuropathic pain.

Activated microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, release such factors, which can injure nerve and support cells but also help clear germs and dead cells. When inflammation runs too long, a feedback loop can keep it going and deepen the damage. The review traces these processes in bacterial meningitis and brain abscesses, Lyme disease of the nervous system, HIV encephalitis, and neuropathic pain. The outcome, the authors stress, hinges on the balance between repair and inflammatory factors.
europmc-pmc3760646:
Kenneth Witwer and a large group of co-authors wrote a standardization report in the Journal of Extracellular Vesicles in 2013. Extracellular vesicles and the RNA they carry have drawn intense interest as disease markers and treatment targets, above all in cancer. Yet knowledge of vesicle types, origins, and cargo remains incomplete, and lab methods vary widely.

The report grew out of a workshop of the field's international society in New York City in October 2012. Round-table talks produced an evidence-based framework for collecting samples, isolating vesicles, and analyzing them and their RNA. The authors stress standard handling, proper controls, and shared techniques so results can be compared, while noting that many points still lack consensus and that methods must keep evolving.
europmc-pmc3765446:
Jietang Mai, Anthony Virtue, Jerry Shen, Hong Wang, and Xiao-Feng Yang proposed a new paradigm in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology in 2013: endothelial cells as conditional innate immune cells. Endothelial cells line all blood and lymph vessels, forming the barrier between blood and tissue. They are among the first cells to meet germs and danger signals in the bloodstream.

When activated, these cells make inflammatory signals that recruit immune cells, acting as both fighters and mobilizers. They also steer immune cells by switching their activity up or down, and in set conditions they can present antigens to T cells like dedicated immune cells. The authors argue that this flexible, changeable behavior earns endothelial cells a place inside the innate immune system, at least under the conditions where they perform these roles.
europmc-pmc3771246:
Maricela Maldonado and Jin Nam wrote a review in BioMed Research International in 2013 on cartilage matrix changes in osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis is a joint disease with no therapy that fully stops it. Cartilage is its main target, and the cartilage cells, chondrocytes, actively remodel their surrounding matrix as the disease advances.

Under lasting inflammation, the new matrix the cells lay down differs in makeup and structure from healthy matrix. That altered matrix changes the forces the cells feel, which drives further breakdown, a self-feeding loop. The changed matrix also blocks repair: stem cells that might rebuild cartilage fail to convert into cartilage cells in that environment. The review focuses on how this inflammation-driven remodeling stops the joint from healing itself, and why grasping it matters for treatment.
europmc-pmc3807846:
Kamran, Patil, and Gude reviewed in BioMed Research International in 2013 the role of STAT3, a signaling protein, in the spread of cancer. In resting cells STAT3 waits in the cytoplasm until a phosphate mark at one key site switches it on, sending it into the nucleus to turn on genes.

In healthy tissue this switch is brief and tightly held, but in many cancers it stays on, driving cell growth, invasion, movement, and the growth of new blood vessels that feed metastasis. The review first explains how STAT3 is controlled, then how it aids spread, and finally surveys small-molecule drugs designed to block its signal. Such blockers are still experimental, the authors note, rather than proven treatments.
europmc-pmc3824146:
Heimo Mairbäurl wrote a solo review on red blood cells in sport in Frontiers in Physiology in 2013. Red cells carry oxygen from lungs to working muscle and carry waste gas back. Training changes both their count and the blood around them, and Mairbäurl sorts fact from myth.

Endurance athletes often show a low share of red cells in blood, a state dubbed sports anemia. It is not true anemia, since their total red cell mass is in fact higher than in inactive people. Extra plasma volume explains the low share. Hard effort also bursts old red cells as they squeeze through tight vessels in muscle, feet, and palms. The review weighs how the body balances cell gain and loss.
europmc-pmc3873446:
Celsa A. Spina leads a large team in comparing HIV lab models in PLoS Pathogens in 2013. HIV can hide in resting immune cells, silent and out of drug reach, which blocks a cure. Labs study that hidden state in cell models, yet each model behaves in its own way.

Drugs that wake the virus in one model often fail in another, and in real patient cells. The team ran the same wake-up tests across many models and on resting cells from patients with no virus in blood. Response patterns differed a lot by model. That gap can mislead drug hunts that lean on one system. The study maps each model's traits so future screens can pick models that match patient cells best.
europmc-pmc3874546:
Bradley C. Lowekamp, David T. Chen, Luis Ibáñez, and Daniel Blezek describe image software design in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics in 2013. The Insight Toolkit is a vast C++ library for medical image work, powerful but hard to use. Its template-heavy style shuts out many scientists who code in simpler languages.

SimpleITK wraps that library in a clean, plain face for languages such as Python. It hides the inner pipeline, drops the template burden, and adds handy extras like ready install packs and math symbols on images. A hand-built list of each filter feeds code generation behind the scenes. The open-source package aims to bring pro-grade image tools to teaching and fast lab prototyping, not just to expert C++ coders.
europmc-pmc3898746:
Siim Pauklin and Ludovic Vallier report a stem cell timing study in Cell in 2013. Stem cells must both renew themselves and mature into body cell types, and the cell division cycle is tied to both. A glowing reporter system that marks cycle phases let the team watch fate choices live in human pluripotent stem cells.

Cells' power to mature varied with their cycle phase. A family of cycle drivers steered that link by gating a key maturation signal path. Blocking the cycle at a set phase pushed cells toward chosen fates. A small drug that tweaks the cycle could thus steer production of cell types wanted for medicine. The work shows fate choice is not set apart from the cycle clock but wound into it.
europmc-pmc3974746:
Billie Bonevski and colleagues review how health research can reach disadvantaged groups. Their paper appeared in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2014. The groups in focus face social, cultural, or money disadvantage. They are the hardest to enroll in studies. They are also the hardest to keep in them. Yet their health needs are often the greatest. Evidence ends up thinnest where it matters most.

The team searched five databases for work to May 2013. Studies of many kinds qualified for the review. Barriers and strategies were sorted by research phase. The phases run from sampling to recruitment and consent. Data collection and retention follow. Mistrust, cost, literacy, and logistics recur as blocks. The review catalogs which tactics have been tried against each block. It is written as a practical map for study designers.
europmc-pmc3989046:
Amy Reeve, Eve Simcox, and Doug Turnbull ask why old age is the largest risk factor for Parkinson's disease, in Ageing Research Reviews in 2014. The disease affects more than one in a hundred people over sixty. A small share of cases start early and link to gene faults. Most cases, though, rise steeply with age alone.

Attention centres on the substantia nigra, a brain area that loses the nerve cells that make dopamine. Those cells also show more age-linked change than cells elsewhere. Ageing brings stress on cell power plants, called mitochondria, and on systems that clear worn proteins. Weakened in this way, the cells cope poorly with added disease stress. The review ties these threads into one account of why age drives the loss.
europmc-pmc3994246:
Damjan Krstajic, Ljubomir J. Buturovic, David E. Leahy, and Simon Thomas warn of traps in cross-validation, in the Journal of Cheminformatics in 2014. Cross-validation is a standard way to pick and test models that sort or predict values. It splits data into folds, trains on some, and tests on the rest. The authors work in drug research, where weak models waste real effort.

A single split can give a lucky or unlucky score by chance alone. That spread, they show, must be counted when a model is chosen and when its error is judged. Their fix repeats the process many times, and nests one loop inside another when judging error, so tuning does not leak into the test. Tests on seven drug data sets back the claim. Cheap cloud computing, they note, now makes these heavier routines practical for routine work.
europmc-pmc3995046:
Javier Lopez-Calderon and Steven J. Luck present ERPLAB, a free toolbox for brain wave research, in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2014. The toolbox handles event-related potentials, small shifts in the brain's electrical signal that follow a sight, sound, or action. It runs inside MATLAB and works closely with EEGLAB, a widely used package for brain wave data.

ERPLAB adds tools for cleaning signals, spotting artefacts, sorting events, and re-setting reference points. It averages signal segments into clean waveforms, builds difference waves by simple maths, and plots waveforms and scalp maps. It also measures the size and timing of peaks in the signal. Users can work through a clear point-and-click screen or through scripts, and a history tool turns clicks into script lines. Guides, a step-by-step lesson, and videos support new users, so the package suits both simple and complex studies.
europmc-pmc4155246:
María José Nueda, Sonia Tarazona, and Ana Conesa updated their maSigPro software package for gene expression studies that track change over time. Their update note appeared in Bioinformatics in 2014. RNA sequencing had replaced microarrays, and time-course designs were growing, but the package was built for the older data type.

The new version adds generalised linear models, the right statistical family for count data, while keeping the package's familiar features. Tests on simulated time courses and one real data set showed good performance. The package is written in R and distributed freely through the Bioconductor site under an open licence. The update lets labs that relied on maSigPro for array time series carry the same workflow into sequencing data without relearning their analysis.
europmc-pmc4220146:
Rebeca Blazquez, Javier G. Casado, and five co-authors tested stem cell exosomes on immune cells in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Mesenchymal stem cells from fat tissue calm inflammation, and they shed exosomes, tiny sacs that may carry that calming effect without the cells themselves.

The team collected exosomes from human fat stem cells and added them to T cells stimulated in the dish. Treated T cells divided less, released less interferon gamma, and showed weaker activation and differentiation markers in both helper and killer subsets. In short, the sacs alone reproduced part of the parent cells' immune-damping action. The authors propose exosomes as a cell-free product for treating inflammation-driven diseases, safer to store and dose than living cells.
europmc-pmc4283646:
Thi Loan Anh Nguyen, Sara Vieira-Silva, Adrian Liston, and Jeroen Raes ask how far mouse gut studies can speak to human health. Their article appeared in Disease Models and Mechanisms in 2015. Mice are the main test animals in gut microbe research because their microbes can be changed in controlled ways, which helps prove cause and effect.

The authors compare the core gut microbes of mice and humans through a pooled analysis of existing data. The two share broad groups but differ in detail, and housing, diet, and strain all shift the mouse side. The article lists the traps to watch when carrying a mouse result over to people, and where the model still earns its place.
europmc-pmc4307746:
Tesfaye B Mersha and Tilahun Abebe examine how the race and ethnicity labels used in genome research can mislead studies of health gaps. Their review appeared in Human Genomics in 2015. Race describes outward traits, ethnicity describes shared culture and language, and genetic ancestry is computed from DNA markers; the three often fail to match for the same person.

Someone who reports one identity may carry ancestry from several populations, and grouping by self report can hide or invent genetic patterns. The review shows where the mismatch distorts findings on disease risk and drug response between groups. It urges researchers to state plainly which measure they used and why, especially when the aim is to explain disparities.
europmc-pmc4310146:
Abigail M Methley, Stephen Campbell, Carolyn Chew-Graham, Rosalind McNally, and Sudeh Cheraghi-Sohi compared three frameworks for searching the literature in qualitative health reviews. Their study appeared in BMC Health Services Research in 2014. The standard PICO frame fits treatment trials well but searches for interview and experience studies often miss papers or flood the results.

Using a review of health care experiences in multiple sclerosis, the team ran the same terms through PICO, a modified PICOS, and the newer SPIDER frame across three databases. SPIDER returned fewer, more relevant hits, while PICO cast a wider but noisier net. The comparison gives reviewers tested grounds for choosing a search frame for qualitative work.
europmc-pmc4356746:
Gail Davies led a very large CHARGE consortium team in a 2015 Molecular Psychiatry study of the genetics of general thinking ability. Thinking ability runs in families across life, but which common gene variants shape it was unclear. The team combined genome-wide studies from 31 groups with 53,949 middle-aged and older adults, each scored on several thinking tests combined into one general measure.

Thirteen variant sites reached strong support, falling in three regions of the genome, near genes already linked to brain and mental traits. A gene-level test also flagged a gene on chromosome 21. Common variants together accounted for roughly 29 percent of the spread in scores in two large groups. The pattern fits many small genetic effects adding up, rather than a few large ones.
europmc-pmc4385146:
Katie Williams and the European Eye Epidemiology Consortium pooled eye studies to size up focusing errors across Europe. The consortium combined data gathered between 1990 and 2013 from fifteen population studies, totaling 61,946 adults. Results were pooled by five-year age bands and by sex. People whose eyes had been altered by surgery or disease were left out of the counts.

Age-standardized rates were 30.6 percent for myopia and 2.7 percent for high myopia. Long sight, called hyperopia, affected 25.2 percent, and astigmatism affected 23.9 percent. Short sight was far more common in the young: 47.2 percent of those aged 25 to 29 were myopic. Just over half of European adults had some refractive error. Such numbers guide planning for eye services and glasses provision across the continent.
europmc-pmc4495346:
Leigh McGarvie, Hamish MacDougall, G Michael Halmagyi, Ann Burgess, Konrad Weber, and Ian Curthoys measured normal balance reflex values across the lifespan in Frontiers in Neurology in 2015. The video head impulse test checks each of the six semicircular canals, the inner-ear organs that sense head rotation, by measuring how well the eyes counter-rotate during a sudden small head turn. That ratio, called VOR gain, is the main sign of a healthy canal.

Clinicians lacked reference values by age and head speed, without which a patient's result cannot be judged. The team tested healthy volunteers in every decade from the teens to the eighties, for all canals and a range of head velocities, using a prototype video system. Their tables give age-specific norms for each canal, so an abnormal result can be told apart from normal aging.
europmc-pmc4566946:
Rita Haapakoski and four co-authors run a running tally of inflammation in depression, in Brain, Behavior, and Immunity in 2015. Major depression is a leading cause of disability, and one theory blames a constantly aroused innate immune system. Blood studies had found higher inflammatory signals in depressed people, but the strength of proof varied by marker.

A cumulative meta-analysis adds each new study in date order, showing when the evidence settled. The method confirmed a robust link between depression and two markers: interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein. For tumor necrosis factor and interleukin-1β, the signal stayed uncertain. The authors call for deeper work on how interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein act, and whether calming them can treat depression.
europmc-pmc4594046:
Aysha Akhtar wrote a solo 2015 essay arguing that animal experimentation is flawed and harms people as well as animals. The paper appeared in the Cambridge Quarterly of Healthcare Ethics. Akhtar questions the common claim that animal models predict human responses well enough to justify their use. She builds her case from published scientific critiques of animal studies.

The essay argues that animal tests are often unreliable across many research areas. Misleading safety results can expose people to risk, she writes, and promising treatments can be dropped after failing in animals. Money spent on animal work could instead fund human-based test methods. Her conclusion is that the costs and harms outweigh the gains, so research funding should shift toward methods based on human biology.
europmc-pmc4603346:
Qian Wang, Ying Liu, and Jiawei Zhou published a 2015 review of inflammation in the brain in Parkinson's disease. The disease kills dopamine neurons in a midbrain region and leaves clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein. Long-lasting brain inflammation is now seen as part of the process. The review appeared in Translational Neurodegeneration.

Brain immune cells, astrocytes and microglia, stay switched on in patients and release factors that speed neuron loss. Immune cells from outside the brain also enter the affected regions. The authors sum up recent findings on these immune roles and weigh treatment ideas that target inflammation. If inflammation drives part of the damage, calming it could slow a disease that now has no cure.
europmc-pmc4732746:
Karsten Bartels, Lena M. Mayes, Colleen Dingmann, and four colleagues surveyed opioid use after surgery in PLoS ONE in 2016. Pain pills after operations aid recovery, but leftover tablets in home cabinets invite accidental use by others. The team surveyed patients sent home after cesarean section or chest surgery. They asked how much of each prescription was actually taken, and how the rest was stored. Thirty women and thirty-one chest patients answered.

Most took half or less of what was prescribed. Over half in each group took almost none at all, while a minority finished nearly everything. Patients who used more opioids in hospital also used more at home. The pattern implies routine over-prescribing, with the surplus sitting at home. The authors argue for tailoring prescription size to expected need and for clearer disposal guidance.
europmc-pmc4758946:
Ming Xu leads a wide author team in eLife in 2015 on how worn-out cells drag down fat tissue in old age. Senescent cells, which have stopped dividing, build up in fat as animals age. The team had earlier shown that clearing them saves fat in fast-aging mice. Here they find the signal the old cells use.

Senescent fat stem cells release activin A, a protein that blocks young stem cells from maturing into fat cells. Aged mice given a cell-clearing switch shed activin A, kept their fat, and switched fat-building genes back on within weeks. A drug that mutes the senescent cells did the same work. Old mice on that drug for eight weeks kept more fat, wasted less fuel, and handled sugar better.
europmc-pmc4806646:
E. R. de Kloet and M. L. Molendijk rethink a classic animal test in Neural Plasticity in 2016. In the forced swim test, rodents placed in water they cannot escape gradually stop struggling and float. Drug screens treat that stillness as surrender: a compound that delays it looks like an antidepressant. Yet over two thousand papers now read the same stillness as a sign of depression in the animal itself.

The authors argue the reading is wrong. Stillness is a smart, energy-saving coping choice, chosen through stress-hormone receptors in the brain's emotion circuits and stored in memory after rescue by a second receptor system. The test, they conclude, does not model depression. It models how an animal weighs a threat and adapts, which makes it a tool for studying coping itself.
europmc-pmc4807546:
Gill Harvey and Alison Kitson revisit a framework for putting research into practice in Implementation Science in 2016. Their PARIHS framework, first published in 1998, was among the first to spell out that getting proof used in clinics is a many-sided problem, with local context at its heart. It has been widely used, and also criticized, which the authors now answer with a revised version.

The integrated framework, i-PARIHS, reworks how proof itself is described, brings individuals and teams inside the picture, and splits context into finer layers. Facilitation, the work of helping change happen, becomes the engine that runs the framework. Case studies test whether the new version reads clearly and covers real projects. The paper is offered openly for debate in the field.
europmc-pmc4826446:
Tomoki Otani and four co-authors compare brain building across primates in Cell Stem Cell in 2016. Cortex size differs hugely among primates, and with it, some argue, mental power. The team grew cortical stem cells from humans and three other primates, in flat layers and in three-dimensional organoids, and traced what each founding cell produced.

Primate progenitors keep dividing for a long stretch while also turning out early neurons, unlike rodents, whose expansion phase mostly ends before neuron making begins. The length of that double-duty phase differed by species and set how many neurons one progenitor yielded. The program ran from inside the cells, unchanged by the culture setting. Cortex size, the authors conclude, is tuned at the level of each progenitor's output.
europmc-pmc4853446:
Mohamed Elshikh and co-authors built a plate method in 2016 to measure the weakest dose of a biosurfactant that stops bacteria. Biosurfactants are soap-like compounds made by microbes. Their color and poor dissolving can spoil the cloudiness reads that standard dose tests rely on. The new method uses 96-well plates and resazurin, a dye that shifts color with living cells.

Standard antibiotics, tetracycline and gentamicin, gave correct known values on test strains, which checked the method. The dye read sidesteps color and solubility traps that plague crude biosurfactant samples. Labs gain a cheap, exact way to compare these green soaps as possible germ fighters and cleaners.
europmc-pmc4853546:
Daniel Wight, Erica Wimbush, Ruth Jepson, and Lawrence Doi laid out a six-step guide for building public health programs, called 6SQuID. Programs work better when design gets as much care as testing, yet guidance on design is scarce, and many models focus on personal behavior or take years to run. Their guide targets health work but aims wider.

The steps run from grasping a problem and its causes, to picking which causes can change, and onward to a plan that can be tested. Each step is meant to be practical, logical, and based on proof. Careful build work up front, the guide argues, raises the odds that a program truly helps once it reaches the public.
europmc-pmc4864946:
Laura D'Ignazio, Daniel Bandarra, and Sonia Rocha reviewed how two master gene switches, NF-kappaB and HIF, talk to each other in immune responses. Low oxygen switches on HIF, while inflammation switches on NF-kappaB. The two share triggers, controls, and target genes, so their signals rarely act alone in sick tissue.

The review walks through the crosstalk in macrophages, neutrophils, and B and T cells, the main immune fighters. Joint control tunes how each cell type answers infection and damage. The same linked switches matter in chronic lung disease, liver cancer, and other ills. Drugs that hit only one arm may miss half the circuit, the review cautions.
europmc-pmc4874546:
Maral Mouzaki and co-authors studied bile acids and gut microbes in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in 2016. The disease, fat build-up in the liver without alcohol, comes with a skewed gut microbe mix. Bile acids and microbes shape each other, so the team measured both in 53 adults: 25 healthy controls, 12 with simple fatty liver, and 16 with the inflamed form, NASH.

People with NASH had higher stool bile acid levels and higher bile acid making than controls, plus a shifted ratio of bile acid types. Two microbe groups ran low in NASH, and one tracked closely with bile acid levels. Skewed microbes and bile acids travel together, raising liver injury risk.
europmc-pmc4879746:
Maria Peiris-Pagès and co-authors reviewed cancer stem cell metabolism in Breast Cancer Research in 2016. Cancer is now often viewed as a stem cell disease, where a self-renewing cell pool feeds growth and relapse. How those stem cells make energy is disputed: some studies call them sugar burners, others credit their mitochondria, the cell's main power plants.

Stem cells seem able to flip between fuel modes as their surroundings change, or hold a middle state. That flex lets them survive stress and treatment. Pinning down which mode a tumor's stem cells use, and when, is now a major research push. A locked fuel choice could be a drug target that starves relapse at its root.
europmc-pmc4943946:
Meital Nuriel-Ohayon, Hadar Neuman, and Omry Koren review how body microbes change across pregnancy, birth, and infancy. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. Pregnancy brings weight gain and shifts in hormones, metabolism, and immunity. The authors add the microbiome as a further factor that both shapes and reflects those shifts. They trace microbial change at the gut, vagina, mouth, and placenta from pregnancy through a baby's early life.

Until recently, the placenta and the unborn baby were thought germ free. Studies now report distinct microbial sets in the placenta and in a newborn's first stool. Some research links disturbed flora to pregnancy complications. The authors caution that the healthy baseline must be mapped first. Only then can harmful shifts be told from the normal change that growth brings. They expect future work to tie the microbial, hormone, and immune threads together.
europmc-pmc4960346:
Sergio Di Meo, Tanea T. Reed, Paola Venditti, and Victor Manuel Victor review the sources of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species in the body. Their review appeared in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2016. These reactive molecules play a double role. In excess they damage tissue, yet at set levels they act as signals that switch on stress defenses. Mitochondria were long cast as the main source, but recent data spread the credit.

The review shows interplay among sources, where firing one source can fire others. In many conditions all sources together drive damage, cell cleanup, and cell death programs. The authors find no firm proof that mitochondria are the chief source in general. They also note the same molecules can trigger protection against the very stress they cause. That duality, they argue, is why blunt antioxidant therapy so often disappoints.
europmc-pmc4960446:
M. O. Trépanier and four co-authors review postmortem brain evidence for inflammation in schizophrenia. Their systematic review appeared in Molecular Psychiatry in 2016. Schizophrenia affects about 1 percent of people over a lifetime. Brain inflammation is one candidate cause, backed by scans, blood markers, and drug trials. The team searched three databases to March 2016 for studies that measured inflammation markers in donated brains from patients.

Of 5,385 papers found, 119 measured such markers in postmortem tissue. Results clashed often. One glial marker, GFAP, was higher in six studies, lower in six, and unchanged in twenty-one. Similar splits ran through markers of microglia, astrocytes, and cytokines. The authors conclude the postmortem record does not settle whether brain inflammation is a core feature of the illness. They call for tighter methods and shared marker sets in future brain bank work.
europmc-pmc4990546:
Silvia Arboleya, Claire Watkins, Catherine Stanton, and R. Paul Ross review how Bifidobacterium populations change across human life. Their mini-review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. Bifidobacteria dominate the gut of healthy breast fed infants. In adults their levels fall but stay fairly stable, then drop again in old age and in several diseases. Which species lead also shifts with age; some species typify infancy, others adulthood, with Bifidobacterium longum common to both.

Supplements of bifidobacteria show benefits ranging from infection protection to effects beyond the gut. The bacteria make helpful compounds, including short chain fatty acids, conjugated linoleic acid, and bacteriocins, microbe killing proteins. The authors admit the open question plainly: is the late life decline a cause of frailty or a result of it? They map what is known stage by stage.
europmc-pmc4999546:
Marc A. Sze and Patrick D. Schloss revisit whether gut microbes really differ with obesity. Their reanalysis appeared in mBio in 2016. Two recent papers reanalyzed old datasets and found weak support for the popular claim that obesity reshapes the microbiome. Sze and Schloss gathered ten studies under systematic review rules and pooled their results with a random effects model. They tested diversity measures and the balance between the two dominant bacterial phyla.

Pooled data did show significant links between obesity and several diversity measures. The effects, though, were tiny: the diversity gap between obese and non-obese people was about two percent. The famous phylum ratio showed no association. A power analysis found only one study could reliably detect even a five percent diversity difference. The authors conclude a real signal may exist but sits near the noise floor of current study sizes.
europmc-pmc5032846:
Sharada P. Mohanty, David P. Hughes, and Marcel Salathé teach a deep learning network to spot crop disease in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2016. Crop disease threatens food supplies, yet expert scouts are scarce in much of the world. Smartphones are spreading fast, so a photo-based diagnosis could reach small farms directly. The team trained their network on a public set of 54,306 leaf photos taken under controlled conditions.

The trained model sorted leaves into 14 crop species and 26 diseases, or health, and scored 99.35 percent correct on held-out test images. That near-perfect mark was on clean, controlled photos, and the authors present it as proof of feasibility rather than a finished farm tool. Their wider point is that large public image sets, shared openly, let such models improve fast and could bring plant diagnosis to a global scale through ordinary phones.
europmc-pmc5057346:
Gert van Valkenhoef, Sofia Dias, A. E. Ades, and Nicky J. Welton automate a consistency check for network meta-analysis in Research Synthesis Methods in 2016. Network meta-analysis combines trials of many treatments at once, mixing direct head-to-head results with indirect ones inferred through shared comparators. If the two kinds of evidence disagree, the synthesis is suspect. Node-splitting tests each comparison separately, but building each model by hand is slow.

The authors give an unambiguous rule for choosing which comparisons to split, and prove it selects exactly the comparisons sitting in loops where inconsistency could arise, no more and no fewer. They also show that under their rule, writing each model becomes trivial, sidestepping multi-arm trial tangles. The result removes most of the manual labor, letting analysts spend time judging the findings instead of building models. The methods ship for routine use in evidence synthesis.
europmc-pmc5062546:
Samuel A. J. Trammell and nine co-authors test a vitamin in Nature Communications in 2016. Nicotinamide riboside is a precursor the body uses to build NAD+, a central helper molecule in energy metabolism, and it is sold widely as a supplement. Yet no study had measured how oral doses move NAD+ levels in people. The team gave single doses to mice and ran the first human pharmacokinetic trial of the compound.

In mice, the vitamin raised liver NAD+ better than its two rival precursors, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide. In one pilot volunteer, a single dose lifted blood NAD+ up to 2.7-fold. In the trial, doses of 100, 300, and 1,000 milligrams raised the blood NAD+ metabolite mix in step with dose. A byproduct called NAAD, not previously thought to sit on the path, rose sharply and proved the most sensitive sign that NAD+ stores had been refilled.
europmc-pmc5110546:
Tikam Chand Dakal, Anu Kumar, Rita S. Majumdar, and Vinod Yadav reviewed silver nanoparticles as germ killers in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. As more microbes resist standard drugs, tiny silver particles have drawn interest as a fresh weapon. Their strength depends on size, shape, surface charge, dose, and how they clump in fluid.

The review explains how the particles attack: they stick to microbe surfaces, slip inside, spawn reactive oxygen that damages cell parts, and scramble the microbes' internal signals. The same particles can also harm human cells, causing cell damage, genetic damage, and inflammation that vary by cell type. The authors call for particles engineered for safety, checks on whether microbes learn resistance, and closer study of harm to people.
europmc-pmc5121946:
Diogo Lobo-Silva, Guilhermina M. Carriche, A. Gil Castro, Susana Roque, and Margarida Saraiva reviewed a calming immune signal in the brain in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2016. Inflammation defends the brain, but inflammation that fails to switch off sits at the core of diseases from cancer to brain degeneration.

Their subject is interleukin-10, a molecule many immune cells release to limit damage from overreaction. Microglia, the brain's own immune cells, make it after sensing danger, yet how brain cells control its production is far less mapped than the same process in the rest of the body. The review gathers what is known about that control and what it means for diseases where the brain slowly breaks down.
europmc-pmc5174146:
Aneika C. Leney and Albert J. R. Heck asked what native mass spectrometry means, writing in the Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry, with the hosted text dated 2017. Mass spectrometry weighs molecules, and its electrospray form can now measure whole protein complexes kept folded and assembled as they are in the cell.

The perspective traces the term native MS to its coinage. It sets out what the term should and should not cover. The assemblies must reach the gas phase in their native quaternary state, their working arrangement of parts. Examples show the method answering structural and functional questions about protein, DNA, and RNA assemblies that other tools struggle with. The authors aim to fix the term's meaning as the field, small two decades ago, matures.
europmc-pmc5187946:
Estelle Charlier and a large team of co-authors, among them Charles J. Malemud and Ali Mobasheri, review how chondrocytes die in osteoarthritis. Cartilage has few cells and little power to repair itself, so each lost chondrocyte matters. The authors sort the death routes into apoptosis, chondroptosis, necrosis, and death tied to autophagy. Triggers include Fas signaling, interleukin-1β, tumor necrosis factor-α, leptin, nitric oxide donors, and mechanical stress on the joint.

Autophagy gets careful treatment because it can protect cartilage yet also fail. In healthy cartilage it clears damaged parts and helps chondrocytes survive. With age and disease, an imbalance between the factors HIF-1α and HIF-2α weakens that protection. The review weighs where blocking cell death might slow osteoarthritis. It also marks where the evidence is still thin. And it notes that saving chondrocytes will not help unless the surrounding cartilage matrix is preserved as well.
europmc-pmc5255946:
Daniel Trujillano and a large team of colleagues reported results from a thousand families tested by clinical whole exome sequencing in the European Journal of Human Genetics in 2017. Exome sequencing reads the protein-coding parts of all genes at once, a powerful route when a patient's condition defies standard diagnosis. The series covers 2,819 sequenced samples from families in 54 countries, with doctors' notes converted into standard phenotype terms.

A disease-causing or likely disease-causing variant was found in 307 families, 30.7 percent of the total. In another 253 families the best candidate remained a variant of unknown effect. Some patients carried two separate diagnoses in different genes at once. Yields ran higher in families where parents were related, and in severe or multi-symptom presentations, while single isolated signs fared worse. The authors recommend exome sequencing as a first-line test whenever no clear diagnosis leads.
europmc-pmc5319046:
Jian-Ping Zhang and co-authors improved a precise gene editing method in Genome Biology in 2017. To place new DNA at an exact spot, cells can copy from a donor template after a CRISPR cut. That repair path, called HDR, is often weak. It works worst in prized cells like human stem cells made in the lab.

Their trick was a donor that the CRISPR tool cuts free at both ends before repair. Freed this way, the donor worked two to five times better than round plasmid donors. They tested it in human kidney cells and in lab-made stem cells. Mid-length match arms on the donor gave near-perfect repair among all inserts. Adding a cell cycle drug pair doubled the yield again in stem cells. The paper gives clear design rules for donor shape and helper drugs.
europmc-pmc5330146:
Brent A. Neuschwander-Tetri surveyed fatty liver disease not caused by alcohol in BMC Medicine in 2017. The illness has grown beside rising obesity and the wider metabolic syndrome. It is hard to spot, its causes are tangled, and no drug is yet cleared to treat it. As hepatitis C fades, this disease is set to become the main chronic liver illness in adults and children.

The survey sums up fresh work on how the disease starts and grows. The core idea is overload: too much fat fuel reaches the liver and turns toxic, hurting cells. That harm drives swelling, scarring, and in time liver failure. Trials now test drugs at many points of this chain, from early fuel overload to late scar growth. Neuschwander-Tetri notes fresh chances in appetite control and energy use, which could help the whole syndrome at once.
europmc-pmc5349246:
Adriana Di Martino led a large team in sharing a second wave of autism brain scans in Scientific Data in 2017. Autism research needs large, open data sets to find firm patterns in brain wiring. The first exchange of this kind gave out more than a thousand data sets in 2012. That scale let labs test claims on shared ground rather than on small home sets.

The new wave adds scans from close to five hundred people with autism and more than five hundred controls, gathered at sixteen sites across the world. Each set joins resting brain scans with body scans and rich notes on traits and health. Joined with the first wave, the store holds more than two thousand full sets. Some sets add diffusion scans that trace wiring paths. The size can help split autism into true subtypes and probe sex gaps.
europmc-pmc5371246:
Peijie Lin, Michael Troup, and Joshua W. K. Ho built a fast grouping tool for single-cell data in Genome Biology in 2017. Reading genes cell by cell shows how cells differ in kind and state. A flaw dogs the data: many genes drop out of a cell's read, which leaves false zeros that blur the groups. Past fixes leaned on heavy models and slow math.

Their tool, CIDR, fills the gaps in a simple, principled way tucked inside the grouping step itself. With the gaps softened, the standard map method sorts cells far better. On fake and real data sets, CIDR beat the top rival tools on grouping accuracy. It runs in seconds for hundreds of cells and minutes for thousands, on plain gear. The team posts the tool for free download, with notes for users.
europmc-pmc5398546:
Rony Nehmé and nine co-authors report a study in PLoS ONE on mini-G proteins, small lab-built tools for studying cell receptors. The receptors, called GPCRs, pass signals from outside the cell to G proteins inside. They are easiest to study when locked in their active shape, but full G proteins are bulky and fragile. Mini-G proteins keep just the part that grips the receptor, so they hold it active in a form that is small and sturdy.

The team widened the family from one member to several, plus two mixed forms. Each paired with the right receptors and formed stable pairs that could be cleaned and sorted by size. Receptors held by a mini-G protein withstood heat better. Tagging the tools with a glow marker let the team watch pairing live and gauge grip strength.
europmc-pmc5456046:
Boughorbel and co-authors build a classifier made for lopsided data sets. Their research article appeared in PLoS ONE. Many biomedical data sets hold far more cases of one class than the other. Standard classifiers then favor the large class. Plain accuracy hides that failure. A lazy model can score high by always picking the majority. Resampling can help, but it wastes scarce minority cases.

The team instead optimizes a fairer score directly. The Matthews Correlation Coefficient suits uneven classes well. They derive the best possible Bayes classifier for that metric. The math uses a Fréchet derivative, and the method proves consistent. Tests on 64 data sets check the claim. The new classifier matched an imbalanced support vector machine on performance. It did so with a simpler design and less computing time.
europmc-pmc5470046:
Mateju and co-authors report a cell biology study in The EMBO Journal. It concerns stress granules, small cell compartments that hold RNA during stress. Faulty forms of these granules are linked to diseases such as ALS. The team asks what turns a normal granule into a harmful, solid one.

The authors find that misfolded proteins build up inside stress granules in human cells. One example is a faulty form of SOD1 linked to ALS. This build-up slows the granules and shifts them from liquid to solid. Helper proteins called chaperones block that shift, they report. Cells also clear bad granules by breaking them down.
europmc-pmc5509546:
Bushell and co-authors report a genome screen in Cell on the malaria parasite Plasmodium berghei. Many parasite genes still have no known job. Knowing which ones the parasite cannot live without guides drug hunting. The team built 2,578 tagged knockout mutants, covering half the genome. The mutants then raced each other inside mice.

Two-thirds of the genes proved needed for best growth at one life stage, they report. That share is the highest seen in any organism so far. Backup copies cluster in gene families facing the host. A public database shares the growth scores. The pattern helps explain drug wins and vaccine struggles.
europmc-pmc5511646:
Schirone and co-authors present a review in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity on cardiac remodeling. After injury, the heart reshapes its own structure and size. Early changes compensate for lost pumping power. Stretched over time, the same changes drive heart failure. Heart attack stands out as a prime trigger.

Cell death, muscle thickening, and scarring form the core processes. Faulty recycling, energy trouble, and weak mitochondria join in. Hormone systems such as renin-angiotensin fan the flames. The review maps each pathway in turn. Gene therapy attempts to retune key signals are also weighed.
europmc-pmc5635046:
