Sarica, Cerasa, and Quattrone wrote a systematic review on brain imaging. It appeared in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience. The topic is the Random Forest algorithm. Clinicians use such methods to classify Alzheimer's disease scans. The review followed PRISMA guidelines. The team searched four databases with a set query. Twelve articles from 2007 to 2017 passed selection.

Those studies applied Random Forest to single and combined scan types. Inputs included MRI measures, diffusion imaging, and PET images. On combined data, the method gave top accuracy for one task. That task was predicting which mild impairment cases turn into Alzheimer's. The authors note strengths like resistance to overfitting. They urge more direct comparisons with rival methods.
europmc-pmc5668946:
Dolzhenko and co-authors present a software study in Genome Research. It introduces ExpansionHunter for finding repeat expansions. Some diseases come from short DNA repeats grown very long. Examples include ALS and fragile X syndrome. Short sequencing reads cannot span those long repeats. Standard variant callers therefore miss them.

ExpansionHunter genotypes repeats from PCR-free genome data. It works even when expansions exceed read length. The team tested it on 3,001 ALS patients with known results. It flagged all 212 expanded samples correctly. Nearly all wild-type samples were also classified right. A second set held 152 samples with eight known expansions. The tool caught all but one of them.
europmc-pmc5681946:
Shi and co-authors test a new dressing for slow-healing wounds in diabetes. Their study uses tiny vesicles called exosomes from gum stem cells. The stem cells come from human gingival tissue. The team loaded the exosomes into a sponge made of chitosan and silk. They then tried the mix on skin wounds in diabetic rats.

The exosomes had a mean width of 127 nanometres. The sponge held moisture well and swelled as needed. Wounds treated with the loaded sponge healed faster than controls. Tissue checks showed more new skin and collagen. The treated wounds also grew the most tiny blood vessels and nerves.
europmc-pmc5701046:
Lauss and co-authors search for signs that predict who gains from a cell therapy for melanoma. The treatment, adoptive T cell therapy, uses a patient's own tumor-fighting T cells. It can give lasting responses, yet half or more of patients gain nothing. The team studied samples taken before treatment in a clinical trial.

Samples came from 27 patients with stage IV melanoma. All had failed other immune therapies before. The team used exome and transcriptome sequencing plus neoantigen prediction. Patients with more mutations and more predicted neoantigens did better. They also lived longer without disease growth. Strong immune activation signs, tied to antigen display, marked benefit as well.
europmc-pmc5758546:
Vigotsky and co-authors review how signal size in surface electromyography should be read. This method records muscle activity through the skin. Sport and rehabilitation studies often compare signal size across muscles, exercises, and loads. From such gaps, researchers often infer force, activation, or future growth in strength and size.

The authors argue that many of these inferences lack support. Signal size alone cannot show how much force a muscle makes or how it will adapt. They set out what the method can and cannot tell in acute and long term work. The review ends with practical advice, gaps in the field, and lines for better studies.
europmc-pmc5818346:
Rolfes and co-authors describe how the CDC now sizes up each flu season in the United States. Their account appeared in Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses. Older estimates came out every few years and leaned on deaths and hospital stays. Annual estimates began with the 2010-2011 season.

The method blends surveillance data, outbreak investigations, and survey rates of care seeking. Across six seasons, they estimate illnesses ranged from 9.2 million to 35.6 million. Hospitalizations ran from 140,000 to 710,000. The yearly figures also credit vaccination with illnesses and hospital stays averted. Officials use them to plan resources and sharpen surveillance.
europmc-pmc5860146:
Würtz and co-authors offer a primer on NMR metabolomics for large health studies. Their article appeared in the American Journal of Epidemiology. The method measures molecules in blood samples with nuclear magnetic resonance. One platform had already profiled over 400,000 samples when they wrote. Each sample yields more than 200 metabolic measures. These include lipoprotein details, fatty acids, and amino acids.

The authors explain how such data clarify risk factors for disease. They cover study design, analysis choices, and common pitfalls. They also show how pairing metabolic data with genetics can aid drug work. Methods such as Mendelian randomization get close attention. The primer helps researchers plan biobank-scale metabolic studies.
europmc-pmc5881046:
Danso and co-authors hunt for PET-degrading bacteria and enzymes worldwide. Their article appeared in Applied and Environmental Microbiology. PET plastic piles up in nature with little breakdown. Few enzymes that digest it are well known. The team built a search algorithm for candidate genes. It found 504 possible PET hydrolase genes in databases. A wider sweep covered 133 marine and land metagenomes.

That sweep found 349 further candidate enzymes. Four candidates were made and tested in the lab. All four worked as predicted, the team reports. Two new enzymes were stable under heat. Candidates clustered in three main bacterial phyla. The enzymes proved truly rare across environments. The richest sample held just 1.5 hits per megabase.
europmc-pmc5939046:
Sun and co-authors show how polyubiquitin chains make the protein p62 form liquid droplets. Their study appeared in Cell Research. Misfolded proteins are cleared by selective autophagy. The scaffold protein p62 gathers ubiquitin-tagged proteins into aggregates. Autophagosomes then engulf and degrade those aggregates. The team looked closely at how p62 bodies form.

They report that p62 droplets in living cells act like liquid. The droplets are round, fuse, and recover after photobleaching. Pure p62 alone did not separate into droplets in vitro. Adding a K63 polyubiquitin chain triggered the separation, they find. The process needs p62 polymerization and binding to ubiquitin. Disease-linked mutations in p62 can alter it.
europmc-pmc6008046:
Morrissey and co-authors build man-made cell catchers that make clean-up cells eat set targets. Their study was published in eLife. Standard catchers of this kind re-aim T cells to kill cancer. The team asked if other immune cells could be taught new tasks. Clean-up cells by nature eat scraps and germs. The new catchers join a grip part to an eat signal. A screen found two inner parts that drove eating well. The catchers worked no matter what their own outer parts had been.

Taught cells ate coated beads and whole cancer cells, they report. An added growth part made the eating stronger still. In mixed dish tests, cancer cell counts fell by over 40 percent.
europmc-pmc6247346:
Feigin and co-authors estimated the lifetime risk of stroke for nearly every country. Their study appeared in The New England Journal of Medicine. It uses Global Burden of Disease estimates for 195 countries. Risk was counted from age 25 onward. The team weighed stroke rates against the chance of dying from other causes first. Results cover both 1990 and 2016.

The authors report a world lifetime risk of about one in four. Risk was near equal in men and women. Blockage strokes made up most of that risk. Bleeding strokes added a smaller share. East Asia showed the highest risk, at close to two in five. Eastern sub-Saharan Africa showed the lowest. World risk also rose by about nine percent over the study years.
europmc-pmc6259046:
Crocker and co-authors tested whether involving patients and the public helps clinical trials recruit and keep people. Their review and analysis appeared in The BMJ. Involvement can mean patients shaping the question, the design, or the outreach. The team searched ten databases for studies that measured the effect. Twenty-six studies qualified, covering many trial settings.

On average, involvement raised the odds of joining a trial by a modest amount. The clearest gains came when people with lived experience of the condition took part. Their input raised joining odds far more than other forms. Results for keeping members were less firm, with fewer studies to draw on. Extra elements bundled with involvement may share the credit. The authors call for cleaner tests of which forms of involvement work best.
europmc-pmc6259146:
Dai and Mumper review plant phenolics, a large family of plant compounds with health effects. Their review appeared in Molecules. Phenolics are the most common secondary compounds in plants. More than 8,000 forms are known. They colour plants and defend them against sun and pests. People take them in through fruit, tea, wine, and many other foods.

Methods for pulling phenolics from plants fill the first part. Ways to purify, measure, and count them follow. Their antioxidant power is then weighed in detail. A long section covers cancer effects in cell and animal tests. Early human studies are included as well. The authors discuss how the compounds may work, both as antioxidants and in the reverse role. They also note effects on cell signalling that may matter more.
europmc-pmc6273146:
Yuan and co-authors review how traditional medicine feeds modern drug discovery. Their review appeared in Molecules. Systems such as Chinese medicine, Ayurveda, Kampo, and Unani have run for centuries. Each holds long records of plant and animal remedies. Modern science has tested only a small share of plant species. Yet natural products already gave drugs such as morphine, isolated in 1805.

Eight traditional systems are compared in the review. Their theories, uses, and current standing are laid out side by side. Natural products offer chemical variety that labs struggle to match. Long clinical use also gives clues on safety and dose. The authors argue that those clues speed drug hunting. New methods can test old remedies with fresh rigour. The review aims to join the two traditions in one drug pipeline.
europmc-pmc6306246:
Bakken and co-authors compare two ways of profiling single brain cells. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE. One method reads RNA from whole cells. The other reads RNA from cell nuclei alone. They used matched data from mouse visual cortex. The question was how well each method sorts cell types.

Whole cells yielded more detected genes per sample. Nuclei yielded fewer, about 7,000 genes. Closely related neuron types still separated well with nuclei. That held when intron reads were counted. Nuclear RNA made up 20 to over 50 percent of cell RNA. The authors back nuclei for frozen, archived brain tissue.
europmc-pmc6323946:
Frankish and co-authors describe GENCODE, the reference gene annotation for human and mouse genomes. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. For over fifteen years the consortium has refined these annotations. Expert manual annotators work beside automated pipelines. Experimental and computing groups feed both efforts. Public data and literature inform every gene call.

The annotations reach users through Ensembl and the UCSC browser. Download sites and programming interfaces serve them too. Accurate gene maps underpin genome biology and clinical genomics. Errors in annotation would ripple through countless studies. GENCODE aims for reference quality in both species. The article explains how that standard is kept. It also outlines access routes for new users.
europmc-pmc6345046:
Jiang and co-authors review how autophagy and the immune system shape each other. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. Autophagy is the cell's recycling and cleanup system. A set of ATG genes runs the process. In tumors, autophagy cuts both ways. It can feed cancer growth or hold it back.

Context decides which role it plays. Cell type, tissue, and tumor stage all matter. Autophagy also steers immune responses strongly. It shapes immune cell function and cytokine output. Immune signals, in turn, tune autophagy up or down. Boosting antigen display is one therapy idea. It could make killer T cells hit tumors harder. But autophagy can also help tumors hide. The review weighs both sides for treatment design.
europmc-pmc6397746:
Chen and co-authors report a research article in Molecular Cancer on gallbladder cancer. A long non-coding RNA called PVT1 drives several cancers. Its role in gallbladder cancer was largely unknown before this work.

PVT1 levels ran high in tumor tissue and cell lines. It soaks up miR-143, a small RNA that normally slows growth. That frees HK2, an enzyme that feeds the sugar use tumors rely on. Cell tests tied the chain to faster growth and spread. The authors name PVT1 as a driver worth targeting in this rare, deadly cancer.
europmc-pmc6435446:
Bengoechea and Sa Pessoa review how the hospital germ Klebsiella pneumoniae slips past the human immune system. It causes pneumonia, urine and blood infections, and sepsis, and it hits newborns, old people, and those with weak immune defenses first. More and more strains now resist the drugs used to treat them, at times leaving no drug that works.

The review walks through stealth tricks and active attacks on first-line immunity. A thick capsule and surface sugars blunt the alarm, and other systems help the germ hold on inside tissue. These tricks evolved side by side with a full immune response, which helps explain why the infections hit so hard. Knowing each trick may point to drugs that disarm the germ instead of only trying to kill it.
europmc-pmc6471246:
Homayun and co-authors review the obstacles to swallowing biopharmaceuticals, large biological drugs that patients would far rather take by mouth than by injection. Oral dosing wins on shelf life, ease, sustained delivery, and even immune response. Proteins, though, face stomach acid, digestive enzymes, mucus, and a gut wall built to keep them out.

Major routes of administration are compared first, then each oral barrier receives its newest countermeasures, from protective carriers to agents that loosen the tight junctions between gut cells. Permeation enhancers such as PIP 640 illustrate the junction approach, though how permeability is controlled remains incompletely understood. Technical choices about adding properties versus redesigning molecules close the analysis.
europmc-pmc6482146:
Rosenberg and co-authors show that the standard live-dead stain for bacteria lies when cells sit in biofilms. Propidium iodide should enter only membrane-damaged cells and mark them red, but 24-hour biofilms of Staphylococcus epidermidis and Escherichia coli read 76 and 96 percent red, implying near-total death.

Other measures disagreed: 68 percent of the cells stayed metabolically active, and 82 to 89 percent grew in culture after harvesting. Confocal microscopy exposed the trick, a coat of extracellular nucleic acids outside intact membranes soaking up the red stain over green, living interiors. The authors' instruction is blunt: viability counts for adherent cells must be validated another way, preferably by cultivation.
europmc-pmc6503746:
Choi and Lee map the jobs of the porins, the pore proteins in the outer membrane of E. coli, writing in Frontiers in Microbiology. That membrane shields the cell from toxic chemicals, and porins are its main gates. The authors built mutants lacking each porin in turn, then tested them against many antibiotics and for membrane strength.

Each porin played a distinct part. Losing OmpF made cells resistant to several antibiotics, including β-lactams, marking it as the main entry route. Losing OmpA weakened the membrane itself, so cells grew more open to many drugs. OmpC shared both jobs. Other porins mattered only for a few drugs, or not at all. The split helps explain why porin changes alter drug response in such varied ways.
europmc-pmc6560046:
Blencowe and co-authors estimate low birthweight worldwide, writing in The Lancet Global Health. Babies born under 2500 grams face higher risks of death, stunting and adult disease. A global target demands a 30% cut in low birthweight by 2025, yet no solid baseline existed to track it.

The team assembled 1,447 country-years of data covering 281 million births in 148 countries, adjusting surveys and smoothing trends. They estimate that about one in seven babies born in 2015 was low birthweight, over 20 million in all, down from roughly one in six in 2000. Some 91% were in poorer countries, led by southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. Progress is real but far too slow: the pace must more than double to reach the target.
europmc-pmc6627346:
Wimalawansa reviews how vitamin D deficiency affects oxidative stress, gene control, and ageing. His article appears in Biology. Vitamin D acts as a hormone far beyond bone. Its active form calms inflammation inside cells. It also supports mitochondrial respiration and energy output. Deficiency does the opposite on each front. Oxidative stress rises, and tissues age faster. The review links these mechanisms to epigenetic change. Gene transcription shifts through the vitamin D receptor.

The author connects deficiency to many age-related diseases. These include diabetes, hypertension, memory disorders, and some cancers. Adequate vitamin D, he argues, protects DNA and proteins. It also keeps mitochondria working in balance. He calls correcting deficiency cheap and widely beneficial.
europmc-pmc6874146:
Masucci and co-authors review tumour-associated neutrophils in Frontiers in Oncology. Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells, first responders to infection. Tumours recruit them through chemical signals. Once inside, they can take sides. One state, called N1, attacks the tumour. The other, N2, helps it grow, spread, and hide from immunity.

Patients with many of these cells, or a high ratio of neutrophils to lymphocytes in blood, tend to fare worse. Those counts now serve as rough prognostic markers. The review covers how the cells damage DNA and feed new vessel growth. It ends with treatment ideas, including blocking the signals that draw neutrophils in.
europmc-pmc6878946:
Priyam and co-authors present a friendlier face for a classic tool, in Molecular Biology and Evolution. BLAST compares a new DNA or protein sequence against databases of known ones. It underpins modern biology, yet running it on a custom dataset is fiddly for many researchers. Errors creep in through arcane settings.

Their program, Sequenceserver, wraps BLAST in a modern graphical interface. A lab can install it quickly, for one user or on a shared server. Simple built-in algorithms guard against common analysis mistakes. Results come as readable text and as visuals that show how matches align along the query. The design centres on the user rather than the machinery.
europmc-pmc6915746:
Cheng and co-authors review drugs that target epigenetic regulators in cancer. Their review appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Epigenetic changes alter gene activity without changing DNA. Such changes are heritable yet reversible. Their dysregulation is tied to many cancers.

The authors survey enzymes that methylate DNA. They also cover enzymes that acetylate or methylate histones. Each section explains how faulty enzyme action drives tumour growth. It then tracks inhibitors built against that enzyme. Some drugs already help in blood cancers. Trials now test them in solid tumours as well. The review weighs early results and open problems.
europmc-pmc6984846:
Hunter argues that infection, above all from the mouth, sits at the root of much medical disease. His address appeared in The Dental Register. He delivered it at McGill University in Montreal on October 3, 1910. It was first published in the Lancet in January 1911. The journal reprints an abstract for dental readers.

Hunter contrasts the old praise for fast surgeons with the new honour given to clean, aseptic ones. Physicians, he says, must likewise become antiseptic physicians. He sets out the principles of antiseptic surgery and medicine in turn. Oral sepsis, infection festering in the mouth, is named the chief channel of harm. Such infection, he argues, seeds inflammation across the body, from appendicitis to gall-bladder disease. Prevention through mouth cleanliness is his closing plea.
europmc-pmc7003246:
Zhang and co-authors review treatments that block a 'do not eat me' signal on cancer cells. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Many cancers coat themselves in a protein called CD47. It binds a partner on macrophages, the immune system's eating cells, and tells them to stand down.

Tumours with high CD47 tend to fare worse for patients. Blocking the CD47 and SIRPα pairing lets macrophages swallow tumour cells again. It also stirs the wider adaptive immune response. Studies of such blockers have multiplied in recent years. The authors describe the pair's structure and function, survey the inhibition studies, and weigh the promise and problems. Toxicity from hitting healthy cells is a known concern. Smarter drug designs, they argue, are the path forward.
europmc-pmc7046546:
Xu and co-authors review a gut bacterium's role in obesity for Frontiers in Microbiology. Akkermansia muciniphila lives in the mucus layer of the gut and adjusts basal metabolism. Its numbers consistently fall in obesity and metabolic syndrome, and giving it to animals improves metabolic health. Human studies are beginning to test the same idea.

Obesity, fatty liver, and type 2 diabetes are tightly bound to diet, and gut microbes influence both energy handling and immunity. The review gathers recent work on how this bacterium interacts with lipid metabolism, immune responses, and gut systems. It lays out the mechanisms proposed so far and weighs animal against human evidence. The authors present the microbe as a next-generation therapeutic candidate, while noting that the causal chain in humans still needs firmer proof.
europmc-pmc7052046:
Zhang and co-authors review the cross-talk between gut microbes and the lungs in Frontiers in Microbiology. Gut disturbances show up again and again in lung diseases, including allergy, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, and lung cancer. Whether a disturbed gut causes lung trouble or follows from it is still unsettled. Changes in gut species and their chemical products track with shifts in immunity and inflammation.

The review works through the evidence disease by disease. It explains how microbial metabolites reshape immune responses in distant lung tissue, and how inflammation can smoulder along the gut-lung axis. Animal studies with probiotics hint that tending the gut can ease lung injury. The authors close by weighing strategies that adjust gut microbes or their products as a fresh therapeutic angle for stubborn lung diseases.
europmc-pmc7052246:
Vettore, Westbrook, and Tennant review amino acid metabolism in cancer in the British Journal of Cancer. Fast-growing tumours need abundant amino acids. Beyond building proteins, amino acids supply energy, feed nucleoside production, and keep the cell's redox balance steady. Tumours often sit in nutrient-poor surroundings, so they form metabolic relationships with nearby stromal cells, sometimes symbiotic and sometimes parasitic.

Some cancers cannot make particular amino acids at all and must import them. The review uses such cases to show how cancer cells lean on, and feed, their microenvironment, both steadily and under therapy pressure. It also covers amino acid synthesis coupled to other reactions, sometimes running beyond the cell's growth needs. A final section opens an understudied area: amino acids that never enter proteins, and what they might do in cancer metabolism. The picture recasts the tumour as a trading community, not a lone consumer.
europmc-pmc7140346:
Baghban and co-authors review the complexity of the tumor microenvironment and what it means for therapy, in Cell Communication and Signaling. A tumor is not cancer cells alone: stromal cells and the extracellular matrix around them constantly trade signals. Those exchanges raise tumor diversity, drive evolution of cell clones, and build drug resistance.

Cancer cells also hijack nearby healthy cells, reprogramming them to support growth and invasion. Materials shed into the blood by tumors can serve as diagnostic tools for predicting and monitoring treatment results. The review weighs these ideas across advanced models, with special attention to 3D culture systems and lab-on-chip devices that mimic the environment better than flat dishes.
europmc-pmc7143846:
Li and co-authors measure how China's COVID-19 declaration changed the mood of social media users, in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. They analysed posts from 17,865 active Weibo users before and after 20 January 2020, using machine learning models that score emotions and thinking patterns from word use.

Negative emotions such as anxiety, depression, and indignation rose after the declaration, while happiness scores and life satisfaction fell. Sensitivity to social risk also increased. Users wrote more about health and family and less about leisure and friends. The authors offer the findings to policymakers managing public feeling during outbreaks, and to clinicians preparing support for affected groups.
europmc-pmc7242746:
Zhou and co-authors report early experience treating COVID-19 patients with a drug called interferon-alpha2b in Wuhan. Their study appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. No approved drug against the virus existed at the time, so doctors were testing what they had. The group held 77 adults in hospital with confirmed infection. Each patient breathed in the drug as a mist, took a second drug called arbidol, or received both at once.

Patients who got the interferon cleared the virus from their airways sooner than the others did. Two blood markers of inflammation, called IL-6 and CRP, also fell back to normal sooner in those patients. The team tracked fever, oxygen levels, and blood counts through each hospital stay. The study was small and early, with no untreated group for a fair contrast. Even so, the pattern suggested this drug family deserves proper trials.
europmc-pmc7245646:
Huang and Pranata pool studies on whether low lymphocyte counts predict severe COVID-19. Their meta-analysis appeared in the Journal of Intensive Care. Lymphocyte count was a marker of interest from the first reports of the disease. Hospitals needed cheap signs of who would need scarce breathing support. The team searched six databases for admission blood counts and outcomes.

Patients with severe disease had clearly lower lymphocyte counts than milder cases. The gap held for patients in intensive care as well. Those with poor combined outcomes, including death, also started lower. Age and other illnesses were checked for influence on the link. The authors conclude a low count on admission is a useful warning sign. It costs nothing beyond a routine blood test. Triage teams gain one more early signal.
europmc-pmc7246646:
Nguyen and co-authors review the idea of type 3 diabetes, the label some give to Alzheimer's disease in the brain. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The link between type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's is still debated. Poorly controlled blood sugar does raise Alzheimer's risk. Some researchers argue the connection is strong enough to rename the brain disease itself.

Both the making of toxic amyloid and its clearance depend on insulin signaling, they note. When brain cells resist insulin, energy handling falters and disease advances. A gene variant called APOE4, found in over half of Alzheimer's cases, disrupts how neurons process insulin. Diet-driven insulin resistance in the body can echo in the brain. The authors suggest insulin-based treatments deserve more trials. The review frames Alzheimer's partly as a metabolic disorder.
europmc-pmc7247346:
Diomede and co-authors review how bone growth and blood vessel growth work together. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. New bone cannot form well without new vessels. Vessels bring oxygen, minerals and growth factors to healing tissue. A protein called VEGF helps drive both vessel growth and bone growth.

The authors focus on mesenchymal stem cells and on scaffolds that hold them. Stem cells from mouth tissue get special attention. Cell products such as tiny vesicles and microRNAs also shape the coupling of the two processes. Good scaffolds need open pores so vessels can grow in. The review maps what a bone repair design must supply.
europmc-pmc7288346:
Milazzo and co-authors review histone deacetylases, enzymes that remove acetyl tags from histones and other proteins. Their review appeared in Genes. Removing those tags usually tightens chromatin and quiets gene expression, so these enzymes fine-tune which genes are active in every cell. Faults in that tuning appear in cancer, brain disorders, and genetic disease.

The authors trace the zinc-dependent family across species and tissues, and examine how each member's chemistry gives it specific targets. The enzymes work inside larger chromatin-binding complexes that form part of the cell's regulatory network. Special focus goes to drugs that block these enzymes as anti-cancer agents: how they act, where they are selective, and what their place in the wider protein network means for safety.
europmc-pmc7306546:
Hwang and co-authors examine loneliness and social isolation among older adults during the COVID-19 pandemic. Their article appeared in International Psychogeriatrics. Loneliness is the subjective feeling of being alone; social isolation is the objective thinness of a person's contacts. The two often travel together but are not the same, and both damage health.

Even before the pandemic, prevalence across Europe, the United States, and China ran from 10 to 40%, earning the label of a behavioral epidemic. Restrictions imposed to slow the virus made things worse. The authors connect loneliness to higher blood pressure, heart disease, and greater overall mortality, plus poorer sleep and mental health. They discuss what can be done for older people cut off by infection-control measures.
europmc-pmc7395146:
Shyer and co-authors review metabolic signaling in T cells in Cell Research. Immune cells patrol blood, lymph, and tissues, each place with its own chemical mix. When a T cell switches on to fight, it must rebuild its inner chemistry to match the job.

The review focuses on where metabolism happens inside the cell, not just how much. Partitioning reactions between compartments, and shipping molecules between them, intertwines with gene programs to set the cell's functional state. Lymphocyte studies illustrate the principle best, though it runs through all immunity. Understanding this geography of metabolism may explain immune failures and suggest fixes. Readers get a tour of the cell as a set of connected workshops.
europmc-pmc7407646:
Rodríguez-Gómez and co-authors review microglia as agents of brain inflammation in Cells. Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells, and their inflammatory mode contributes to several neurodegenerative diseases. Research on them spans a century, with understanding growing fast in the last two decades.

The review follows the switch from calm, homeostatic microglia to reactive ones, triggered by receptors such as TLR4 and TREM2 and by caspase-driven pathways. Newer lenses, epigenetics and immunometabolism, show how DNA marks, microRNAs, and fuel use reshape the response. Exosomes spreading inflammation and imaging methods for watching microglia in living brains get attention too. Readers get a many-angled portrait of the cells behind brain inflammation.
europmc-pmc7439246:
Barzilay and co-authors survey resilience and stress in the early COVID-19 outbreak. They built a brief survey on self-reliance, emotion control, relationships, and neighborhood. It ran online from April 6 to April 15, 2020.

In all, 3042 people took part. Worry focused most on family catching the virus, at 48.5%. Fear of passing it on unknowingly came next, at 36%. Anxiety rates were 22.2% and depression 16.1%. Health workers and others showed the same patterns. Higher resilience scores linked with less worry. A one-step rise in resilience cut the rate of anxiety by 65% and depression by 69%. The work sets a base for later studies of mental health paths.
europmc-pmc7561246:
Nadim and co-authors present a consensus report on COVID-19 linked acute kidney injury. The report comes from the 25th Acute Disease Quality Initiative workgroup. Kidney harm in COVID-19 ranges from mild signs to organ failure.

Injury needing kidney replacement therapy marks the severe end. Such injury links to high death rates in hospital. It also acts as an independent risk factor for death. Causes appear multiple and are not fully known. Surges in cases can strain dialysis supplies and staff. Daily checks of resources are advised by the group. Guidance covers diagnosis, prevention and management of injury. Future research needs are also set out clearly.
europmc-pmc7643046:
Davis and co-authors run a randomized trial of psilocybin-assisted therapy for major depressive disorder. Depression affects more than 300 million people worldwide. It is the top cause of disability globally.

Current drug treatments help many but not all patients. About 30% to 50% do not respond fully to them. Some 10% to 30% are classed as treatment-resistant. Psilocybin is a classic hallucinogen with mixed actions. It acts on serotonin and glutamate systems in the brain. Early work in cancer patients hinted at antidepressant effects. The trial tests psilocybin as an add-on to therapy. It examines efficacy for major depressive disorder in adults. Results speak to a new treatment path for stubborn depression.
europmc-pmc7779046:
Larkin and co-authors, with the FlyBase Consortium, report updates to FlyBase. FlyBase is the main online database for the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. It serves genetic, molecular, genomic, and reagent data.

New features include Pathway Reports and information on paralogs. Disease models based on orthology were added. Tables inside reports can now be customized. Overview ribbons sum up expression and disease data at a glance. Recent data updates add a developmental proteome. The GAL4 search tab was upgraded, and more Experimental Tool Reports were added. FlyBase moved genome browsing to JBrowse. Batch queries, downloads, and the Fast-Track Your Paper tool also improved.
europmc-pmc7790746:
Iljazovic and co-authors test whether a gut microbe can drive gut inflammation. Gut microbe patterns track with gut disease in many studies. It is often not clear if the microbes cause the harm or just grow well in a sick gut. The team put one microbe, Prevotella intestinalis, into mice.

Mice with the microbe got worse gut inflammation than mice without it. The microbe changed the gut mix and what the mix makes. A key fuel for gut cells, the short-chain fat acetate, fell. A gut signal called IL-18 fell with it. Giving IL-18 back to the mice eased the inflammation. The authors say the microbe harms the gut through this chain of changes.
europmc-pmc7816146:
Mutha and co-authors overview flavonoids and their role in treatment. Flavonoids are natural phenolic compounds in plants. People have used plant remedies since ancient times. Lab work ties plant phenolics and flavonoids to many healing actions.

The authors gather what is known about these compounds. They set out the classes of flavonoids found in diets and herbs. Their reported effects on the body are summed up. Uses in therapy, from prevention to drug support, are weighed. Gaps in the evidence are noted as well. The piece serves as a compact entry point to flavonoid science. Long-term intake of phenolic-rich foods was linked to protection against diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.
europmc-pmc7826746:
Tolomeo and Cascio review the many-sided role of STAT3 in cancer. STAT3 is a protein that switches genes on and off. In many tumors it stays stuck in the on state. Overactive growth signals and lost brakes cause that state.

STAT3 drives known cancer genes such as c-myc and VEGF. Drugs that block it are in development. The picture is not one-sided, though. STAT3 can also suppress tumors in some settings. Its two forms, STAT3α and STAT3β, act differently. Cell context decides which face shows. The authors warn that therapy must match the tumor type. Blanket blocking could do harm where STAT3 protects.
europmc-pmc7896046:
Wheatley and co-authors report a cohort study of immune responses after mild to moderate COVID-19. How long protection lasts after infection matters for reinfection risk and vaccine design. The team followed people who had recovered from mostly mild illness. They tracked antibodies, B cells, and T cells over time.

Binding and blocking antibodies faded over the first 4 months after infection. Key T cell groups fell over the same period. Memory B cells for the spike protein moved the other way. They built up steadily and became a large share of the memory pool. Modelling suggested blocking activity would hold above a key level in half of the group to 74 days. The authors conclude that vaccines may need to beat natural infection on strength and staying power.
europmc-pmc7910446:
Wang and co-authors present a review of arachidonic acid metabolism and its promise as a drug target. Arachidonic acid sits in cell membranes until an enzyme frees it. Other enzymes then turn it into a wide family of active signals. Those signals shape heart health, cancer growth, and diseases such as asthma and arthritis.

Three main enzyme routes do the conversion work. Their products include prostanoids, leukotrienes, and epoxyeicosatrienoic acids. Some products drive harm, while others protect tissue. The review sets out how each route works in health and disease. It gives special weight to heart disease and cancer. Early clinical studies that target these routes are also covered. The authors argue the pathways offer rich ground for new preventive and treatment drugs.
europmc-pmc7927246:
Li and co-authors report a mouse study of panaxydol, a compound from ginseng root, against acute lung injury. The injury drives uncontrolled lung inflammation and can be fatal. A form of cell death called ferroptosis helps the injury progress. The team tested whether panaxydol could blunt both the death pathway and the inflammation.

Mice given a bacterial toxin to injure the lungs fared better with panaxydol. Their lung damage, swelling, and inflammation all eased. Signs of ferroptosis fell as well. In human bronchial cells, the compound blocked toxin-driven ferroptosis and the inflammation it fed. It worked by raising the activity of a protective pathway, Keap1-Nrf2/HO-1. Blocking that pathway removed the benefit. The authors present panaxydol as a promising new candidate for treating acute lung injury.
europmc-pmc7946946:
Romano and co-authors report a meta-analysis of the gut microbiome in Parkinson's disease. Gut microbes are gaining attention as shapers of brain disease. Parkinson's often starts with gut symptoms, and its gut nerves change early. Many small studies had profiled the microbes of patients, but no shared picture had emerged. The team re-analysed the raw data to find one.

They pooled ten available datasets built on the same sequencing method. Clear shifts in the patient microbiome survived the pooling, though the total difference from controls was small. Three bacterial genera ran high: Lactobacillus, Akkermansia, and Bifidobacterium. Two groups that make short-chain fatty acids ran low. The pattern points to a pro-inflammatory gut state. That state may feed the gut symptoms that trouble many patients.
europmc-pmc7952346:
Feng and co-authors present a systematic review of the measurement quality of the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire. The tool asks people to rate their health on five dimensions. Its five-level version is newer than the classic three-level one and less tested. Health economists rely on its scores to value treatments. The review gathers the proof on how well the newer form performs.

The search found 889 publications, of which 99 were included. The studies came from 32 countries. Missing answers and floor effects were rarely a problem. The index score proved reliable in every paper that tested it. Single dimensions were less stable over time. Scores matched well with other health measures. The authors call the tool's properties excellent overall. Its responsiveness to change still needs harder testing, they say.
europmc-pmc7969646:
Bennett and co-authors present a scoping review of how lockdown changed eating habits during the COVID-19 outbreak. Fresh food was harder to reach, and people spent far more time at home. Some feared worse diets. Others noted a rise in home cooking. The review screened the research from the first lockdown to sort the patterns by population group.

From thousands of studies, 23 full papers met the rules. Four themes emerged: broad diet patterns, good habit changes, bad habit changes, and side topics such as activity and weight. Ten studies found more snacking. Eleven found good shifts, with more fresh produce and home cooking. Bad habits tracked with weight gain, poor mental health, and low activity. The authors warn that lasting changes could shape public health for years. The first lockdown cut both ways.
europmc-pmc8080646:
Lee and co-authors review pairing vessel-blocking therapy with checkpoint blockade in cancer. Checkpoint drugs free T cells to attack tumors. Yet only 20–30% of patients respond to them. The tumor's crooked blood vessels share much of the blame. They bar CD8 T cells from entering and sap those that slip in. VEGF, the vessel growth driver, also stalls dendritic cell training.

Immune cells feed the problem from the other side. M2-like macrophages and regulatory T cells pour out vessel growth factors. Killer T cells that would tidy the vessels cannot reach them. The review argues for striking both faults at once. Trials of the pairing have won FDA approval for kidney, liver, lung, and uterine cancers. Normalizing the vessel-immune cross-talk is the shared logic. The authors see the combo widening immunotherapy's reach.
europmc-pmc8190846:
Lei and co-authors survey single-cell sequencing in cancer research and its next steps. Bulk sequencing averages signals across many cells. Single-cell methods read each cell on its own, across genes, proteins, and more.

The review sums up new tools and what they have shown in cancer. They reveal the range of malignant and immune cells in a lesion. They also expose tumour diversity and how cells change over time. Circulating tumour cells get their own coverage. The authors weigh hurdles that still block wider clinical use. Progress and open problems both get a full hearing.
europmc-pmc8238046:
Moretta and co-authors present antimicrobial peptides as a fresh hope against resistant bacteria. Antibiotics remain vital, but long use breeds drug-resistant microbes. New molecules that bacteria resist less are badly needed.

All living things make these small defensive proteins. They form a first line of defence against fungi, viruses, and bacteria. The review sorts them by source, structure, and how they are made. Sources span microbes, plants, and animals. Their attack style makes resistance harder to build. The authors weigh their promise for medicine and pharmacy. Their range of shapes and charges shapes how they kill microbes.
europmc-pmc8329746:
Moore and co-authors present the ADAPT guidance for moving interventions into new contexts. Reusing a proven intervention can beat building a new one. Fit with the new setting, though, decides if it works.

Some interventions travel well, others fail on arrival. Careful adaptation aims for a good fit. The guidance rests on fresh evidence and expert consensus. It sets out when and how to adapt. Definitions open the document for clarity. Interest in adaptation is rising across health research. The paper gives that work a shared, careful method. Consensus informed the guidance beside the evidence review.
europmc-pmc8385046:
Uemura and co-authors review VEGFR1 signaling in the retina. The VEGF family has five ligands, and VEGF-A binds both VEGFR1 and VEGFR2. Most past work focused on VEGFR2. This review gives VEGFR1, long treated as a simple decoy, its own close look.

VEGFR1 appears in many retinal cell types, from vessel lining cells to microglia and pigment cells. Its levels shift under low oxygen and inflammation. Direct signaling through VEGFR1 can raise vessel leak and drive immune cells to release growth and inflammatory signals. The ligands also compete with each other for the receptor. The authors weigh what this means for retinal disease.
europmc-pmc8489046:
Jia and co-authors compare two common tests for mild cognitive impairment in older Chinese adults. The Mini-Mental State Examination and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment both screen for early thinking decline. Which suits population studies in China was not clear.

The cross-sectional study covered 4923 adults aged 55 years or older from many regions. Each person took both tests in Chinese versions. The two tests agreed well on who had impairment. Prevalence calls differed, with the Montreal test flagging more cases. Education-based cut-offs were used for both. The authors also weighed risk factors for impairment. Their work helps clinics pick the right screen.
europmc-pmc8613146:
Kumle, Võ, and Draschkow give a hands-on guide to power checks for mixed-effects models. These models handle fixed and random effects at once. No simple formula gives the chance that a test will find a real effect. That chance, called power, shapes sample size choices and trust in results.

The tutorial uses simulation to estimate power. It covers three cases: planning from past data, choosing how many test items to use, and planning with no past data. Examples span plain and generalized models in R. Code and open datasets come with the guide. The aim is sound study design for researchers who use these models.
europmc-pmc8638446:
Li and co-authors review tiny vesicles released by cancer-linked fibroblasts and their role in tumor growth. The tissue around a tumor holds many cell types. Fibroblasts linked to cancer are a major group there. They shape how tumors invade, spread, and dodge the immune system.

These fibroblasts send signals in small vesicles called exosomes. The vesicles carry nucleic acids, fats, and proteins to other cells. Their cargo can change how cancer cells behave. Vesicles in the blood may also serve as markers for diagnosis and outlook. The review covers how these vesicles link fibroblasts to cancer cells and to other tissue cells.
europmc-pmc8825346:
Afkhami and co-authors test a COVID-19 vaccine given through the nose rather than the arm. Current shots target only the spike protein. New variants can slip past that narrow defense. The team built adenovirus vaccines carrying three viral parts: spike, nucleocapsid, and RdRp. They compared nose and muscle delivery in mice. A chimpanzee adenovirus version led the field.

A single nasal dose built stronger, wider protection. It raised antibodies in the body and at the airway surface. It also seeded memory T cells in the lung and trained innate defenses. Vaccinated mice resisted the original virus and two variants of concern. The authors propose airway delivery as a next step for COVID-19 vaccines. It could guard the very site where infection starts.
europmc-pmc8864846:
Wan and co-authors trace how a chemical mark on RNA helps breast tumors hide from the immune system. The checkpoint protein PD-L1 lets tumors exhaust T cells. Steady PD-L1 supply is key to that escape. The team asked whether the m6A marking system controls PD-L1 output. They focused on the writer METTL3 and the reader IGF2BP3. Several molecular assays pinned down the chain of control.

The authors report that PD-L1 RNA is a direct target of METTL3. Removing METTL3 stripped the mark and destabilized PD-L1 RNA. The effect depended on IGF2BP3 reading the mark. Silencing either partner boosted anti-tumor immunity in cell and mouse tests. Tumor tissue data matched the lab story. PD-L1 rose alongside both proteins. The authors propose this axis as a drug target.
europmc-pmc9090746:
You and co-authors review how artificial intelligence helps find new cancer targets and new drugs. Cancer grows from complex webs of genes, proteins, and signals. AI tools can read those webs and rank which parts matter most. That ranking can point to drug targets that lab work alone might miss.

The review explains two broad tool types in plain terms. Network tools study links between cell parts, while machine learning tools find patterns in large data sets. Worked examples show both types in real cancer studies. The authors show how models can flag new drug candidates for tests. Readers get a clear frame for judging what AI can and cannot do in this field.
europmc-pmc9462846:
Lovell and co-authors present GENESPACE, a tool that tracks genes across many genomes at once. Groups now hold chromosome-scale reference genomes for many taxa. Using them side by side is still hard work. Questions span chromosome change, trait gene hunts, and speciation tests.

GENESPACE joins conserved gene order with orthology calls. That pairing predicts where each gene should sit in each genome. The team tested it at three scales of study. One case spanned 300 million years of vertebrate sex chromosome change. A second ranged across the grass family. A third compared 26 maize cultivars. The R package maps presence-absence and copy number shifts. It handles polyploid and outbred genomes well, the authors note. That fills a gap in gene family and synteny software.
europmc-pmc9911346:
Hekkelman and co-authors present AlphaFill, a method that adds missing ligands and cofactors to AlphaFold models. Predicted protein models lack small molecules that many proteins need. Hemoglobin models lack heme, and zinc fingers lack zinc ions. No ATP sits in predicted ATPases or kinases.

AlphaFill uses sequence and structure likeness to copy molecules from solved structures. It places those molecules into matching predicted models. Tests against known structures checked the approach. The team performed 12,029,789 transplants on 995,411 AlphaFold models. Results and quality scores sit in the alphafill.eu databank. Scientists can use the added molecules to form hypotheses and design experiments. The method makes predicted structures more useful for real biology.
frus-1861-d146:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 August 1861, the day Seward also wrote to him. The dispatch is document 146 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Same day writing on both ends of the Paris line was by now a habit of the record. Dayton's page reports the view from the Seine as Seward's sets the line from the Potomac. The file's strength is this doubled view of one tie. The doubled view is what makes this printed record so rich for readers now. A doubled view of one tie gives this record its rare, stereo depth.
frus-1861-d246:
In a letter dated 26 July 1861, William H. Seward gave James Shepherd Pike his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 246 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d46:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 21 May 1861. The letter is document 46 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The letter of 21 May became famous for its harsh tone toward Britain. Lincoln and Seward softened its sharpest lines before it went out. Even so, it warned London plainly against any step that aided the South. Few single letters in the volume carry such weight in the history of the war. Lincoln's edit of the letter is one of the great acts of his early war leadership.
frus-1862-d146:
On 17 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch from Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is printed as Document 146 in the Foreign Relations volume that the State Department laid before Congress with the President's yearly message.

That same day, Union and Confederate armies fought at Antietam in Maryland, the bloodiest single day of the Civil War. News crossed the Atlantic by ship, so London learned of battles days after Washington did. Dispatches from this week show the lag built into wartime statecraft, and the care both men took with news that could sway British policy.
frus-1862-d246:
On 26 December 1861 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, in a dispatch printed as Document 246 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was Seward's first Paris letter in this file.

Boxing Day 1861 was also the day Washington decided to free the envoys seized from the Trent, ending the crisis with Britain. Seward wrote to Paris as that settlement took shape. His letters to Dayton through the next year pressed one point. France should leave the American war alone and expect no Union blessing for adventures elsewhere. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d346:
Filed out of order as Document 346, a Dayton report dated 6 November 1862 went from Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. William L. Dayton was the American minister to France.

Dayton wrote two days after the Northern elections and in the week of the British cabinet's decision on the truce plan. His report thus sits at the crossing of the war's political and diplomatic threads. In the printed file it arrives late, among mid-November papers, a placement the reader must correct by its date. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d446:
On 17 February 1862 Norman B. Judd reported from Berlin to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 446 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

Judd's February report came as Union forces took Fort Donelson and opened the Tennessee River, victories that strengthened the Union's name in Europe. In Berlin he watched a Prussia busy with its own army reforms and its rivalry with Austria. His letters told Washington how the German world weighed the American war. For readers, the Berlin file is a useful contrast to London and Paris. At this court the Union's task was to keep goodwill warm. It did not have to head off harm.
frus-1862-d46:
News and judgment from Charles Francis Adams reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 11 April 1862. It was printed as Document 46 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d546:
Roest van Limburg received this reply from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 September 1862. The note is Document 546 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Seward's mid-September notes to resident ministers were written in the shadow of the Maryland campaign, four days before Antietam. His Dutch reply handled the standing business between the governments with the Department's usual exactness. For Van Limburg, a written American answer was the useful thing: it could be sent home to The Hague as the Union's stated position. The exchange illustrates why both sides valued this formal traffic. It fixed positions, prevented surprise, and kept a useful friendship in repair during the war's most anxious fortnight.
frus-1862-d646:
On 30 April 1862, Robert H. Pruyn wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Pruyn was the new American minister to Japan, picked to take over the legation from Townsend Harris. His dispatch appears as document 646 in the Foreign Relations volume that covers 1862.

A new envoy's early letters told Washington what he found on taking up his post. Pruyn's report belongs to the hand-over between the first American mission to Japan and the men who would run it through the Civil War years. It is a plain, working piece of the record that tied a far-off legation to the State Department.
frus-1863p1-d146:
On 7 April 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. A dispatch from Adams bears the same date in the volume. The letter is document 146 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward wrote in the same week Adams reported on the seized raider, though neither man yet had the other's sheet. The cross of dates is the sea mail at work. His letter fed the brief at a bright point: Britain had at last held a Southern ship. This one is Washington's half of the day's exchange, set beside London's in the printed file.
frus-1863p1-d246:
Reporting on 23 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 246 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d346:
Writing in Washington on 31 December 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 346 in the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Lyons knew that harsh words could push the two nations toward a fight neither wanted. His notes are firm on British rights but measured in tone. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war. Each side kept copies of the whole exchange, which is why the printed volume can show the argument from both desks.
frus-1863p1-d446:
The date 4 April 1863 heads a letter from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d46:
On 28 October 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote again to James M. Mason, the South's envoy in London. Benjamin headed the Confederate state office in Richmond. The letter is document 46 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A month had passed since Benjamin's last letter to Mason in this file, and the ground had shifted. Antietam was fought, and the freedom edict was on its way. Letters from Richmond had to keep envoys' hopes up as the facts grew hard. This one is part of that strain. Kept in the Union's printed record, it shows the South's London brief run from Richmond, sheet by sheet.
frus-1863p1-d546:
Writing on 1 June 1863, Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward addressed Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington in an official letter. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the early summer of 1863. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d646:
Dated 23 October 1863, document 646 is a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d146: Secretary Hull wrote to Ambassador Steinhardt in Ankara on November 20, 1943, the same day the president also wrote to him. The letter is Document 146 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A president's letter and a secretary's letter landing together marked a coordinated push on the Turkish question. The record gives the parties and the date and no topic. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d246:
The President's Log continues with the Cairo days, 22 to 25 November 1943, kept hour by hour. It opens with Roosevelt's flight from Tunis on 22 November, which ran late and worried the welcoming party at Cairo West airport.

Two fighter groups missed their rendezvous with the President's plane, which had swung south to the Nile and flown up the river over the Sphinx and the Pyramids. Roosevelt settled at Ambassador Kirk's villa near Gizeh, while the Sextant Conference met at the Mena House Hotel by the Pyramids. Churchill and the Chiangs, who had arrived the day before, called that afternoon, and a first meeting with staffs ran from nine until after eleven that night.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d346:
Alexander Kirk sent Harry Hopkins a second urgent, secret telegram from Cairo on 29 November 1943 about the held Cairo communiqué. It follows his alarmed message of the day before on the release arrangements.

The Chinese chargé has just called on Kirk to say he has cabled the text to Chungking, with orders to hold release until his own flash. Kirk reminded him that he, Kirk, was charged with giving the notice once word came from Tehran. The position now, Kirk points out, is that the text sits in the foreign offices of London and Chungking, while Washington, unless Hopkins has sent it direct, has no copy at all. He asks whether to cable the text to the State Department in advance, to be held there, or whether Tehran is handling it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d446:
American and British officials produced an agreed record on December 5, 1943. The meeting took place at the Second Cairo Conference. Both delegations checked agreed minutes before they stood. So the text states what London and Washington jointly said happened. The State Department included it in the published Cairo-Tehran papers.

A reader finds the two allies' common account of one day's work. The conference was crowded and near its end. The Tehran decisions still had to become firm plans. Records of this type anchor the history of the summit. Memoirs can blur or boast over time. An agreed record fixes what both sides signed at the time.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d46: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on October 17, 1943, two days before the Moscow Conference of foreign ministers opened in his capital. The message is Document 46 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hull, Eden, and Molotov would do the talking in Moscow, but the leaders kept their own channel open above them. The record names no subject for this letter. Its text is printed in the Foreign Relations volume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d546:
Marked secret in the printed volume, this message from President Roosevelt to Prime Minister Churchill is dated January 14, 1944. The two leaders corresponded constantly that month as invasion planning advanced. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

A secret marking on a leaders' message signals matter not meant for wider eyes, even inside their own governments. Roosevelt and Churchill kept several grades of candor in their letters, and the classified ones carried the alliance's real sensitivities. For readers, the document is part of the private layer of the partnership, preserved because the State Department's historians later judged it part of the conferences' story.
frus-1944-quebec-d146:
General Wilson, Supreme Allied Commander in the Mediterranean, sent the British and American chiefs a broad review of his theater on September 2, 1944. The first half covers Operation Dragoon, the landing in southern France. Wilson calls it an outstanding success, with some 50,000 prisoners taken and the ports of Toulon and Marseilles captured ahead of schedule.

The review then works through supply, railways up the Rhone, and the Seventh Army's advance toward Lyons. Wilson proposed transferring command in France to Eisenhower and forming the 6th Army Group. Turning to Italy, he counted some 26 German divisions facing his armies, though worn down to perhaps 17 in real strength. Air support for both fronts closes the survey.
frus-1944-quebec-d246:
Acting Treasury Secretary Daniel Bell briefed Morgenthau on September 14, 1944, on the French lend-lease negotiations, and his tone is alarm. A sixth draft agreement, agreed by State and the Foreign Economic Administration, would let long-life reconstruction goods go to France on long-term credits. Requisitions could be accepted until at least the end of the war with Japan, enabling reconstruction on a large scale.

Monnet, Bell reported, had a two-billion-dollar program ready for immediate requisitions. The July design had limited lend-lease to the end of European hostilities. War Department officials McCloy and Hilldring had stated flatly that French industrial production would be no help against Germany. Its help against Japan could be, in their phrase, put in your right eye.
frus-1944-quebec-d46:
A further Churchill message went to Roosevelt on September 1, 1944. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. It sits next to the day's other exchange.

Two messages from Churchill came in a single day. The Atlantic crossing lay ahead of him. The pattern suggests business finished in layers. One point was settled, and another was opened. The Quebec Conference had to divide hard work. It concerned the war's last phase between the allies. For readers, this companion message shows his preparation at full stretch. It came in the last week before the leaders met.
frus-1945-50-intel-d146:
On 8 April 1946 the Third Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. The State Department prints it as document 146 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

The text is the meeting as the secretaries kept it, topic by topic, with the results marked as they were reached. Such pages are often the only proof of when a choice was made, and by whom. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d246:
Dated 3 November 1947, this memorandum runs from the Assistant Executive Secretary (Lay) to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The Office of the Historian kept it as document 246 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d346:
A memorandum dated 4 June 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. The State Department prints it as document 346 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d46:
A paper prepared for the Secretary of State's Staff Committee is dated 15 November 1945. The staff committee was where the department's senior men settled questions for the secretary. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Papers written for a committee are drafted to be argued over, so they often state the options with unusual clarity. This one fed the State Department's top table as the intelligence contest moved toward decision. Readers can use it to see how the department framed the choice for itself, apart from what it told rivals. The distinction matters: what an agency says in its own room is the truest map of what it wants and what it fears.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d146:
President Roosevelt wrote to Premier Mikolajczyk on 17 November 1944, and Harriman carried the letter to London. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Roosevelt says he would rather have waited for the general postwar settlement, but he understands the premier's need for an answer now.

The position comes in numbered points. The United States stands without qualification for a strong, free, and independent Polish state. The Polish people must have the untrammeled right to order their own internal life. On frontiers, if the Polish, Soviet, and British governments reach mutual agreement, with Germany compensating Poland, Washington would raise no objection. One point is held back for the bearer: Harriman is to discuss the city of Lwów in person.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d246:
A strong China as the anchor of Asia is the long view in this briefing book paper of 13 January 1945. Its title promises an outline of long-range objectives and policies toward China. The paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Peace and security in the Far East, it argues, rest on China becoming the principal stabilizing factor there. American policy therefore aims at three things. In politics, a strong, stable, and united China, governed as its people wish. In economics, a well-knit and balanced Chinese economy, with a fuller flow of trade to the world. In culture, joint work in learning and science, as a ground for common understanding. The paper then opens out the first of these aims in detail.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d346:
Foreign ministers at Yalta turned to publicity and to Germany's future at noon on February 6, 1945, in Edward Page's minutes. Stettinius said a first press release on the Crimean Conference seemed wise. Press aide Stephen Early spoke to the plan, and a draft was attached. Molotov suggested adding the word "common" before "enemy."

Stettinius offered small cuts of his own, which Molotov accepted, though the release still needed Stalin's approval. The ministers then took up how to study the dismemberment of Germany. They agreed to refer that question to the European Advisory Commission in London. Page catches the wording games behind a famous phrase.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d446:
Freedom to move and to report home is Britain's demand for its officers in Bulgaria, in this proposal of February 10, 1945. London held two things essential. Its representatives must enjoy reasonable freedom of movement and communication. And decisions must not be taken in Britain's name without British consultation.

For Hungary, agreed statutes for the control commission had already met the first point. London proposed that identical statutes be adopted for Bulgaria. It also wanted prior consultation with British and American officers during the first period. The paper repeats, almost word for word, the British memorandum of February 1 — a sign the point had not moved.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d46: Harriman reported to Roosevelt on 8 January 1945, answering from Moscow in the summit's final preparatory month. His message is document 46 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. Reports sent this close to departure shaped the president's expectations directly, since there would be little time to correct a wrong reading of Soviet intentions later.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d146:
Harry Hopkins reported Stalin's Far East aims from Moscow in extracts of a telegram dated May 30, 1945. The extracts form document 146 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Hopkins, the President's adviser, was in Moscow on a special mission to smooth relations with Stalin before the summit.

Stalin is very anxious to discuss Japan at the coming conference, Hopkins writes. Some elements in Japan are putting out peace feelers, so the Allies should settle a joint line on Japan's surrender. Stalin expects Russia to share in the actual occupation of Japan, with agreed zones, and wants an understanding on areas of operation in Manchuria and China. The report warned Truman that Soviet entry into the Pacific war would come with a price in territory and influence.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d246:
A briefing book paper set out the American fallback positions on Libya, dated June 30, 1945. The paper is document 246 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Libya, Italy's North African colony, was one of the territorial questions the peace settlement would have to decide.

The United States proposes no program of its own, the paper says, but would support any of three solutions in order of preference. Best is returning all Libya to Italian rule, with general demilitarization. Next is partition: Tripolitania stays Italian, while Cyrenaica becomes an autonomous Senussi state under Egyptian or British trusteeship. Last is partition with Tripolitania under an international trusteeship run by Italy. Background data follow: a vast, poor desert land of 680,000 square miles, with some 100,000 Italian settlers counted in 1939.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d346:
German interim financing is the subject of a memorandum the Secretary of State sent President Truman on July 5, 1945. Four agencies, it reports, now agreed: State, Treasury, War, and the Foreign Economic Administration. Together they had settled proposals to put to the British, the French, and the Soviets on buying and paying for essential German imports.

Under the plan, the cost of imports would be a first charge on all German exports, whether from current production or stocks on hand. The memo also records a War Department caveat. The Army's duty to pay for supplies, it said, had not yet covered every import the government's broader aims in Germany required.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d446:
A British protest to Moscow is reported in Harriman's cable from Moscow, sent at midnight on July 7, 1945. The British ambassador, Sir Archibald Clark Kerr, had written Molotov on July 6 in sharp terms. His complaint concerned recent criticism in the Soviet press and radio of the Greek government, of British policy in Greece, and of General Scobie and the British troops there.

One article is named: a piece by Shalitov in New Times of June 15, on Greece. Clark Kerr described it as misleading and hostile. Harriman's brief report, repeated to Athens and London, shows Greece already serving as a Cold War battleground in print, weeks before Potsdam's Greek election plan was complete.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d46:
On June 1, 1945, President Truman sent Marshal Stalin a personal and top secret telegram, number 278, from Washington. It is document 46 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The message thanks Stalin for his note of May 30 about the date of the planned three-power meeting near Berlin.

Truman confirms that he has told Prime Minister Churchill that both he and Stalin agree to meet near Berlin around July 15. With this short cable, all three leaders had accepted the same date. The exchange shows how the Potsdam Conference was arranged: not by staffs or foreign offices, but in direct, brief messages between the heads of government themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d546:
Fred Vinson, who ran war mobilization and reconversion, sent a top secret wire to the Secretary of State on July 13, 1945. It is document 546 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Vinson wrote from Washington while the President was at sea.

Vinson traces the muddle over lend-lease back to March, when Stimson asked President Roosevelt for a plan. He cites a Quebec pledge to let Britain reconvert its economy in a fair way. He also cites Churchill's anxious cable of May 28 and Admiral Leahy's fears. Truman's July 5 order, he says, has left all the top aides confused. He asks Byrnes for advice before the order harms the shift of U.S. forces to the Pacific.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d646:
A top secret briefing paper on Palestine was written for the Potsdam Conference, dated June 22, 1945. It is document 646 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. It suggests the President raise Palestine in general terms with Churchill and ask what plans Britain has.

The paper stresses one deadline above all. The quota for Jewish immigration under the 1939 White Paper would run out by summer or early fall.
