Britain would then have to decide the key issue in the Palestine dispute. Any choice, the paper warns, risks serious disorder and even bloodshed. Zionist Jews were growing restless at the delays in a settlement. If Britain held to the White Paper and barred further immigration, moderate leaders might not restrain well-armed extremists in Palestine.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1046:
President Truman sent this memorandum to Stalin on July 27, 1945, with his coal directive to General Eisenhower attached. An acute coal famine threatens Europe this winter, he warns, unless German coal flows out in large amounts. America is already shipping coal across the Atlantic as an emergency step, despite shortages at home. The war against Japan caps what more it can send.

Truman has ordered his commander in Germany to raise output and exports, and London and Paris have done the same. He asks Stalin to join a common four-power policy. The Control Council should frame a coal production and export program for Germany as a whole. The attached directive sets a floor of 25 million tons for export by April 1946.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1146:
Poland's President Bierut and Prime Minister Osobka-Morawski signed this joint letter to President Truman on 20 July 1945. The two men headed the new government in Warsaw, the one the Soviet Union backed and the Western powers had just agreed to accept. Writing together, they spoke with the full weight of that government.

A joint letter from a head of state and a head of government is a formal reach for goodwill. Warsaw wanted American acceptance, trade, and a friendly hearing at Potsdam, where Poland's border was being set. The letter shows the new rulers courting Washington in public form. It sits oddly, and tellingly, beside the private doubts the Western envoys voiced elsewhere.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1246:
The President wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 24 July 1945. Truman's word reached the China post from the middle of the German talks. A presidential message steadied an envoy's hand like nothing else in the service.

Hurley's task in China was delicate: back the Nationalist government, press it toward unity with its communist rivals, and keep China in the war. Orders from the top set the line for that work. This note is the commander in chief tending the far end of his alliance. It shows the summit's leader ruling by cable across two oceans at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1346:
Clement Attlee wrote to President Truman on 31 July 1945, days after becoming prime minister of Britain. Attlee had beaten Churchill at the polls and taken his seat at the Potsdam table mid-conference. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Few letters in the volume carry a change of government inside them. Attlee's note opens the working tie between the new Labour government in London and Truman's White House. It also marks the strange shape of Potsdam, where one of the three delegations changed its leader halfway through. Readers can see the new prime minister step into the talks in his own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-146: Printed among the unnumbered items after document 710, this editorial note belongs to the second Potsdam volume. The historians who built the volume used such notes to explain the record's seams. They give provenance, flag missing pieces, and link kindred papers. A reader can lean on this note while crossing a dense field of staff writing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-46:
A brief undated memorandum by President Truman records a question he put to Stalin on July 20, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Like the note before it, the text is Truman's manuscript jotting on a memo from Admiral Leahy.

Question asked of Stalin after meeting on 20th, Truman writes. Had already asked him when he called. Agreed to it in a few days. The editors identify the question from the file around it. It concerned when the Soviet chiefs of staff would meet with the United States chiefs of staff. Stalin's answer, as Truman records it, promised the military meeting within a few days. The scrap is characteristic of the President's own paper trail at Potsdam: three short sentences carrying a real piece of conference business.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d746:
Arthur Schoenfeld, the American representative in Hungary, reported to the Acting Secretary of State on July 17, 1945. Document 746 opens the volume's Hungary thread. Hungary was a former enemy state under an armistice and an Allied control body. Schoenfeld watched its politics from Budapest as Potsdam began.

Reports from the former enemy capitals grounded the summit's choices. Leaders argued over lands most had never seen. Men like Schoenfeld supplied the facts. Readers get a ground-level view of a country under foreign watch. The document shows how the conference's fate was prepared in embassies as much as in palaces.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d846:
Secretary of State Byrnes wrote directly to Soviet Foreign Commissar Molotov on July 19, 1945. Document 846 is a minister-to-minister letter inside the Potsdam record. Byrnes and Molotov faced each other daily at the conference. A formal letter between them fixed words that talk left loose. It joined the second Potsdam volume.

Letters between rivals carry a special charge. Each phrase is chosen knowing the other side will parse it. Readers see diplomacy at its most deliberate. The document also shows Byrnes working every channel: plenary, committee, and now direct paper. At Potsdam, the written word between principals was itself a move in the game.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d946:
Edwin Pauley explained a puzzle in the reparations figures to the Secretary of State on July 29, 1945. American and British totals looked far apart, he writes, but the gap was only method. Britain used 1938 replacement value plus 15 percent. America used depreciated value plus the same markup, to guard against later fights over removed machinery.

Pauley offers to accept the British new cost basis, if it also governs at removal time. He reports the Ruhr holds about 45 percent of reparations due from the western zones. Still, he advises drawing from all three western zones, not the Ruhr alone. War targets lie outside it, and the Ruhr itself is hard to define.
frus-1977-80v11p1-d46:
A message from Charge d'Affaires Bruce Laingen in Tehran to Secretary of State Vance forms document 46 in Part 1 of Volume XI of the 1977-1980 series. Laingen, himself among the hostages, sent the text out through visiting ambassadors. He reports almost no contact with Iranian officials for ten days. He calls the public mood a dangerous frenzy. He warns that the mourning month of Moharram, just ahead, will raise the risk to the hostages.

Laingen urges Washington to avoid acts or words that could inflame the crowds. He sees two broad paths for Khomeini: expel the hostages after the December 2 referendum, or hold some while hinting at talks. A third, darker path, he fears, is more likely.
gao-gaoreports-b-295946:
The protest in files B-295946 and B-295946.2 reached GAO's ruling on April 25, 2005, with Sayres and Associates Corporation as the protester. The Department of Energy had awarded Navarro Research and Engineering a contract for administrative and technical support services. The buy was a section 8(a) set-aside. Sayres attacked the scoring of its past performance. GAO denied the protest. The agency properly set aside parts of the firm's past performance write-up that ran past the page limit. It also set aside a reference sent in late.

The agency had made fair efforts to reach that reference, which failed to reply in time. Page limits and deadlines, evenly applied, bind all offerors alike.
gao-gaoreports-b-296946:
CACI Technologies protested an Air Force choice to pass it by in GAO decision B-296946, dated October 27, 2005. The work was design and tech support for weapon systems. The firm had bid on first offers. The agency found its bid missed hard terms on design work. It thus barred the bid from award.

GAO denied the protest. The find that the bid missed hard terms was sound. A bid that misses such terms cannot win on first offers. It must be cut. The firm did not show the terms were met. First-offer award needs a bid that meets all hard terms on its face. That bar was not met here.
gao-gaoreports-b-297346:
Sytronics protested a Marine Corps task order for test cell upgrades in GAO decision B-297346, dated December 29, 2005. The winner was Nexjen Systems. The site was Cherry Point in North Carolina. The work was new gear and code for two T58 test cells. The buy was set aside for small firms. The winner was lower rated and lower priced.

GAO sustained the protest. Marks on the winner's plan and past work broke the call terms. Price talks also skewed to the winner. The firm had the higher tech score and the higher price. It was hurt by the skewed talks. A buy that scores one firm wrong and talks price with a tilt cannot stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-298946:
Allmond & Company protested a Drug Enforcement Administration move on accounting support services. The firm held the work under a schedule deal since 2001. The agency sought fresh bids for the next round. It did not send the request to the firm. GAO ruled in B-298946 on January 9, 2007.

The buy ran under federal supply schedule rules. Those rules set a clear bar for fair rivalry. An agency must seek bids from at least three fit schedule firms. The agency met that bar here. No rule forced it to invite the prior firm by name. Being shut out of one round broke no duty. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-309946:
Brinkmann Instruments, Inc. lost its protest under GAO decision B-309946, dated October 15, 2007. The Navy planned a sole-source buy of 33 autotitrators. The units test steam plant water on nuclear submarines. The buy went to Mettler-Toledo, Inc. The same unit was at work on 44 boats of the fleet.

GAO denied the protest. The Navy had fair ground to seek the same unit it had placed fleet-wide. One shared type aids both fleet standards and safety. A sole-source path can be sound when sameness is the need. The ruling weighs fleet safety more than a fresh race for the work.
gao-gaoreports-b-400346:
View One, Inc. lost an Army award for event work on the Spirit of America 2008 show and protested the choice. The file, B-400346, was closed by GAO on July 30, 2008. The contract, under request for proposals No. W91QV1-08-R-0016, went to Eggs & Bacon, Inc.

View One said the Army botched the trade-off of price against skill. GAO noted View One did not dispute the Army's view that its skill edge was very slight. It also gave no facts or law to back its broad claim. A protest must state its grounds in detail, so GAO dismissed this one as too thin.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-946:
Fund shifting by the Army engineers is examined in GAO-05-946, a report dated September 16, 2005. The Corps has more work than funds in recent years. Congress lets it move money from stalled projects to ready ones. Doubts arose over whether moves followed the rules. GAO counted the moves in fiscal years 2003 and 2004. It checked rule compliance, reasons, and results.

The Corps moved funds over 7,000 times, shifting over $2.1 billion. Nearly two-thirds of projects in two accounts saw money move in or out. In a sample of 271 projects, GAO found moves mostly followed guidance. Eight cases broke it, by passing limits or skipping notice to Congress. Worse, the guidance is written so most moves do not count toward notice limits. That dims oversight, GAO said. Better planning should replace reliance on shifting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1046:
Performance terms in federal grants are studied in GAO-06-1046, issued September 29, 2006. Grants must now chase long-term goals like contracts long have. Lessons from contracts are starting to shape grant design. GAO read the literature and spoke with experts. It asked what blocks accountability in grants. It catalogued the mechanisms in use. And it named strategies to spread them.

Headings give the arc. Trade-offs and challenges mark every bid to hold grantees to results. The mechanisms in use can improve both performance and accountability, GAO found. Sound strategies support picking, designing, and running those mechanisms. Case studies include a job training grant program and a child support program, plus two nonfederal contracts. Chances exist at the federal level to widen the practice, the report concludes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-446:
An aging jamming aircraft might be upgraded to cover a gap in a new one. In GAO-06-446 (April 26, 2006), GAO studies electronic warfare aircraft. The EA-6B has flown airborne electronic attack for all services since 1996. A 2002 study found the fleet would fall short of needs beyond 2009. In 2003 the Navy began building the EA-18G to replace it.

GAO tested whether that 2002 finding still holds. It judged whether the EA-18G buying approach rests on solid knowledge. Upgrading more EA-6Bs could cut risk in the new aircraft's development, GAO said. Readers get fleet counts, timing, and a fallback option.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-46:
A court ruling changed what disability exams must say about pain and fatigue. Report GAO-06-46, issued October 12, 2005, tracks the Department of Veterans Affairs and the DeLuca decision. In fiscal year 2004, regional offices asked medical centers to examine about 500,000 claimants. Joint and spine exams were among the most requested. In 2002, VA found 61 percent of such reports lacked needed detail.

The court held that limits from pain, fatigue, and flare-ups must be considered. Congress asked how much progress VA had made since 2002. GAO judged whether exam reports now carry the required facts. More progress is possible, it found. Readers get claim-level stakes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-546:
New cutters and aircraft for the Coast Guard come through the Deepwater program. In GAO-06-546 (April 28, 2006), GAO reviews changes to the Deepwater plan. The program replaces aging assets for at-sea roles. After the September 11 attacks, the Coast Guard added homeland security missions. It revised the plan to fit those duties. Changes in asset mix and delivery dates raised concern.

GAO compares the revised plans with the original plan on assets, timing, and cost. It judges the models used to build the asset mix. It tracks progress on prior GAO advice. Changes appear sound and management has improved, GAO said. Continued monitoring is still warranted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-646:
Drug aid for people with HIV and AIDS is covered in GAO report GAO-06-646, released on April 26, 2006. Under the Ryan White CARE Act, states and territories run AIDS Drug Assistance Programs. These programs buy and provide costly HIV drugs to people who qualify. Each program sets its own rules on who is covered and which drugs are offered, and some keep waiting lists.

GAO reviewed 52 of these programs and found wide differences in coverage. Income ceilings, enrollment caps, and drug lists varied a great deal from place to place. GAO also found gaps in federal oversight of drug buying. Better oversight, GAO said, would help the programs get the best prices for drugs and stretch limited funds further.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-846:
Misuse of military recruiters is the subject of GAO-06-846 (August 8, 2006). The all-volunteer force needs several hundred thousand new recruits each year. Since the Iraq war began in March 2003, some services have struggled to meet their goals. Pressure on recruiters can tempt some to bend the rules. GAO examined how well the Defense Department and the services track recruiter irregularities.

GAO found that the services lacked the data to see the full scale of the problem. Reports of misconduct were kept in separate systems with uneven detail. Three of the eight active and reserve components had missed recruiting goals in fiscal year 2005, which raised the pressure. GAO said better data would give leaders visibility over irregularities. Honest recruiting, GAO implied, protects both recruits and the force.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-946:
Safety gains from a pipeline watch program are weighed in GAO report GAO-06-946, dated September 8, 2006, a mate to the retest study issued the same day. The 2002 pipeline law set a risk-based plan for gas lines. Firms must find high-risk zones where a break would hurt most, test lines there, and fix flaws.

A 2002 law also told GAO to judge the plan's effect on public safety. GAO spoke with 51 operators and polled all state pipeline agencies. It found the program aids public safety. But the yardsticks firms report should be made more alike, so results can be fairly compared.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1046:
Equal access to rule-making facts at the Federal Communications Commission is urged in GAO report GAO-07-1046, dated September 6, 2007. The commission, known as FCC, rules on radio, TV, wire, satellite, and cable links. It makes policy through rule cases, with a public file for each.

Congress asked GAO to lay out that process. For picked cases, GAO checked if the agency kept to its own steps. It asked why some files and cases stay open for years. It read recent rules and spoke with agency staff and users. Steps are needed, GAO said, so all parties see the same record at the same time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-346:
Watch-list checks on overseas flights are getting stronger, but two screening systems risk growing apart. GAO reviewed the effort in GAO-07-346, a report dated May 16, 2007. This public version trims a November 2006 report for security reasons. Border officers now staff some foreign airports under a pilot program. They interview high-risk travelers and inspect their documents. A separate agency is building a domestic screening system.

The pilot lacks a full strategic plan, GAO found. Its goals and measures are not yet set. The two screening programs will overlap on many trips. A passenger may fly abroad and connect at home. If the systems diverge, airlines face two rule sets. Travelers face confusion, and costs rise. Key joint decisions remain unmade. Privacy notices also lag legal duties, GAO said. It repeated three fixes from its earlier report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-46:
Medicare hospital pay rates rest mostly on the program's own data, a point GAO-07-46, dated September 26, 2007, tests in depth. Hospitals get fixed sums per stay, set by diagnosis-related groups. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) reshapes those groups each year. Extra pay goes to stays that use new technology. A 2003 law told GAO to check whether outside data could sharpen the rates.

GAO asked how far CMS had used outside data for new-technology pay calls. It then asked whether data from other agencies could feed the wider rate work. Staff spoke with CMS and with bodies such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Department of Veterans Affairs. CMS had tapped outside data in some new-tech cases. Its own files stayed the main source. The report weighs where guest data helps and where it does not fit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-346:
Youth in residential facilities are the subject of GAO report GAO-08-346, released May 13, 2008. Federal funds helped states place more than 200,000 youth in such facilities in 2004, many for behavior or emotional problems. GAO surveyed state agencies on abuse incidents, licensing, and federal oversight.

Survey replies from 28 states reported at least one death in a facility in 2006. State data counted 1,503 staff abuse and neglect incidents in 2005, a figure GAO called understated. Some facilities, such as boarding schools, escape licensing, and standards often skip key risks like suicide. GAO urged better data reporting and stronger federal and state oversight. Two of the three agencies addressed generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-46:
GAO-08-46: a GAO report dated October 25, 2007 that covers a customs trade processing system. The Automated Commercial Environment (ACE) will replace and supplement the cargo systems of the Department of Homeland Security. Law required GAO to review the spending plan for the program.

The plan meets many, but not all, of the conditions set in the fiscal year 2007 appropriations act. It partly meets capital planning rules and fits the department's enterprise architecture only in part. Of 15 open GAO recommendations from the past 4 years, the department has carried out 8 and is working on 7. Redefining weak early requirements for several releases will likely delay the schedule. GAO recommended fuller quarterly reports to Congress. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-546:
Deploying soldiers with medical limits is examined in GAO report GAO-08-546, issued June 10, 2008. Army rules let commanders deploy such soldiers if steps are met. A soldier with an impairment gets a profile form grading severity; a grade of 3 or higher requires a medical board review before deployment.

Records and enforcement fall short, GAO found. About 3 percent of sampled soldiers graded 3 deployed without the required board review. Of 685 records checked, 213 profile forms were missing. About 7 percent of soldiers had profiles barring some duties yet carried grades below 3. Soldiers and units face risk when duties ignore these limits. GAO urged enforcement steps and better ombudsman access. The Defense Department agreed.
gaule-select-cases-conscience-1646:
John Gaule weighs a priest's doubts in Select Cases of Conscience Touching Witches, his book of 1646. Gaule was a church man in the east, in the midst of the great hunt. Folk brought him hard asks: is my sick bairn bewitched, is my dream a sign, should I shun my next door dame? He replies from the Good Book with care, and with more doubt than the hunt's chiefs liked at that hot hour.

He warns gainst rash claims and cruel tests in plain words. That nerve, in that year, took grit. The book is a rare cool voice from the hunt's own turf.
gaule-select-cases-of-conscience-1646:
John Gaule was a Puritan minister who wrote Select Cases of Conscience Touching Witches and Witchcrafts in 1646. He wrote against Matthew Hopkins, the self-styled Witchfinder General whose hunt was then filling English gaols. Gaule's manual is pastoral: it sorts hard cases for troubled consciences.

He distinguishes true witchcraft, as he believed scripture taught it, from melancholy, fraud, and the lies of frightened witnesses. His tests would have acquitted most of the people Hopkins sent to the gallows in those years. The book shows a churchman using his own tradition's tools to slow a witch-hunt.
gaule-select-cases-of-conscience-english:
John Gaule, a minister in Huntingdonshire, published his Select Cases of Conscience in 1646. Those were the years of Matthew Hopkins, the self-styled Witchfinder General, whose hunt swept eastern England. Gaule's cases examine the scruples that witch-hunting raised in a pastor's mind, and they argue against the hunt's methods.

Gaule questions the tests, the confessions, and the haste of the finders. His protest is the first English clerical voice raised from inside the persecution itself. He wrote at real personal risk, since Hopkins's party answered critics sharply. Conscience set down in print gives the book its force. It shows resistance beginning within the church that blessed the trials.
greaves-pyramidographia-1646:
Oxford scholar John Greaves traveled to Egypt and measured the pyramids with care. His Pyramidographia appeared in 1646, among the first English studies of the sites. He brought tools, patience, and a love of exact fact.

Greaves records sizes, passages, and chambers in sober detail. He tests old tales against his own tape and eye. His numbers corrected centuries of loose guessing by travelers. The prose is plain for its age. The book marks a turn: Egypt studied by measure, not just marvel. It remains vital for the history of Egyptology.
guizot-civilization-europe-hazlitt-1846:
Francois Guizot's History of Civilization in Europe appears in William Hazlitt's translation of 1846. The book prints Guizot's famous Sorbonne lectures of 1828. Guizot traces European civilization from Rome's fall to the French Revolution. Europe, he argues, grew by the clash and balance of many forces: church, kings, towns, and free thought.

No single power ruled all, and so liberty survived and grew. The lectures made Guizot famous and shaped liberal history across Europe. Hazlitt, son of the essayist, gave the work its English form. The book is the classic liberal account of Europe's rise. Its breadth still impresses students of civilization.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
Chapter eight of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands shows Flanders in a forlorn condition. Parma's soldiers, the finest veterans in Europe, cannot be paid. There was no pretence, Motley writes, of keeping them lodged or clothed. Their general implored his sovereign for money enough to buy the soldiers shoes.

Spaniards and Italians were asked to march foodless and barefoot on frozen swamps in January. The loyal provinces had harvested utter ruin as obedience's reward. Bruges and her sister cities starve behind their loyalty. Meanwhile Parma negotiates secretly with the malcontent nobles. Motley balances pity for the soldiers with contempt for the system that wastes them. This chapter is the dark ground of his history: war eating the land it claims to govern, while the free provinces prosper by contrast.
howards-end-pg2946:
E. M. Forster's novel of the Schlegel sisters and the Wilcox family is hosted here in a second edition, distinct from the other copy in this library. The text opens directly on the first chapter, without front matter. Helen Schlegel is staying at Howards End, the Wilcox family's small Hertfordshire house, and the story starts, as Forster says, with her letters to her sister.

The chapters that follow are the same novel: Margaret's deepening tie to the widowed Mr. Wilcox, the clerk Leonard Bast and his disastrous evening, and the contest over who shall finally hold the house. Readers comparing copies will find the wording of the novel itself, in a plainer dress than the companion edition. The duplication is of the edition, not of the tale.
huntingdon-witches-examinations-1646:
Huntingdon's accused witches were questioned in 1646, at the crest of the East Anglian hunt led by Matthew Hopkins. The Witches of Huntingdon prints their examinations and confessions in full. The county town saw the panic at its most intense that year.

Confession follows confession in these pages, as the hunt's methods pressed the accused to name themselves and others. Hopkins and his helpers filled gaols across the east with just such work. The pamphlet lets readers judge the words the courts took as proof. It stands as a key record of England's worst witch year.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
Volume 4 of In the Fire of the Forge, the Nuremberg romance by Georg Ebers, opens on a June morning after a storm. Ebers fills the city gates with peasants bringing vegetables, wains of grain and charcoal, herds, laden donkeys, and carts of milk and honey crossing a dyke still soft from night rain. The air has cooled, though the sun is already fierce in this stretch.

Chapter XV lingers on small acts of morning faith and trade. Maidservants open shutters and set flowers at windows, bowing as a priest passes to mass. A barefoot Capuchin friar begs at kitchen doors, and each cook who fills his sack feels her household blessed for the day. Ebers builds his medieval city from such traffic before returning to the Ortlieb sisters and their knights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-israel-46: Aaron Israel was an American rabbi born at Lancaster, Pennsylvania, on November 20, 1859. His father was a native of Hesse-Darmstadt who had served many years in the army. Israel studied at the Hebrew Union College at Cincinnati. He was rabbi at Fort Wayne, Indiana, from 1883 to 1887, and at Buffalo, New York, from 1887 on. He wrote on the Jews and Arabs and the Renaissance, and translated works on the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abensur-jacob-2: Jacob Abensur was in all likelihood a son of Daniel Abensur. Like his father, he served as Polish minister resident at Hamburg, in his case after 1695. In 1701 he set up private religious services in his own house. That step split the Portuguese congregation of the city. Its elders asked the authorities to step in and stop the break, but their plea came to nothing. The entry takes that account from the archives of the Hamburg state archive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abodah-of-the-d:
The 'Abodah of the Day of Atonement forms a key part of that day's Musaf service. It rests on the Mishnah Yoma account of the high priest's Temple rite. Leviticus xvi gives the base for the whole rite.

Readers follow the rite step by step. The high priest prepares for seven days, washes, and changes garments. He confesses over a bullock, draws lots over two goats, and enters the Holy of Holies with incense and blood. One goat bears the people's sins into the wild. The service ends with prayers for the Temple's return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-nahmias: David Nahmias' responsa supply the setting in which this Abraham Nahmias turns up. The stub itself does little more than name his one known labor and send readers onward to the opening Nahmias, Abraham article. That labor was translating the commentary on Aristotle's Metaphysics written by Thomas Aquinas. No century, city, or second work is recorded in the lines provided, which keeps his profile to a single scholarly task.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abtalion-ottavi:
Abtalion Ottaviano of Modena was an Italian Hebrew scholar born in Modena in 1529. He died in Ferrara in 1611. His family came from France and moved to Italy in an expulsion. His father Mordecai was a learned rabbi and a noted doctor in Bologna. Abtalion, the youngest of four sons, moved to Ferrara. He won fame there for Hebrew learning and wide studies.

His best known act came in 1581. Pope Gregory XIII had ordered all Jews to give up the Talmud and like books to be burnt. Jewish groups chose Abtalion as their envoy, since he knew Latin well. He spoke before the pope in a long, fine Latin address. The speech moved the court, and the order was withdrawn. The entry also reports a tale that Elijah once showed himself to him in his youth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akrabah-1046: Akrabah was a city one day's journey north of Jerusalem. It is probably the Akrabattene named by Josephus. In the years before Jerusalem fell, that district saw many bloody fights. Judeans and Samaritans clashed there again and again. Early texts spell the name in two ways, Akrabah and Akrabat. The entry warns against a mix-up: this place is not the Biblical Akrabbim, which lies on the southeastern border of Judea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-lysim: Alexander Lysimachus was an alabarch, the brother of the philosopher Philo. He was the father of Julius Alexander and of Tiberius Julius Alexander. He held office under the emperors Tiberius and Claudius. Caligula put him in prison. Claudius freed him and restored him to office, for he had served Claudius's mother Antonia as procurator. He once refused a loan to Herod Agrippa I., but granted it to Agrippa's wife Cypros. The gates of the Sanctuary were adorned by him in gold and silver.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alkalai-joseph-: Joseph ben David Alkalai lived in Turkey early in the nineteenth century. He wrote a book called Amar Yoseph. It holds notes on Maimonides. It also holds Talmud notes sorted by letter. A set of sermons rounds out the book. The book came out at Salonica in 1831. The entry is short and gives no dates for his birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alzey-1346:
Alzey is a town in Rhein-Hessen in Germany. It stands on the river Setez. Its Jewish group first shows in a book of martyrs. That book lists Alzey among towns hit in 1349. That year was a year of terror for Jews. Named members show up by 1383. The group stayed small for centuries.

Jews were driven from the Palatinate in 1391. None from Alzey show in a count of 1550. A group formed again late in the 1600s. The first synagogue rose in 1791. A rule of 1748 capped Jewish families at three. By 1901 about 320 Jews lived in the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ankava-jacob-be: Jacob ben Amram Ankava was a translator who lived in Algeria in the nineteenth century. He turned a Spanish treatise into Arabic. Its subject was the laws that Jewish women must observe. He gave the work the title Dat Yehudit, Laws for the Jewess. It was printed at Algiers in 1855. The entry is very short and rests on Zedner's catalog of Hebrew books in the British Museum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apollinaris-or-: Apollinaris, or Apollinarius Claudius, was bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia in the year 170. He wrote an Apology for the Christian Faith and addressed it to the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. He also wrote two books Against the Jews. Other works took on pagans and the Montanist and Encratite heresies. Every one of these books is now lost, the entry states. Its record rests on Eusebius, Jerome, and later church bibliographers whom it names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aryeh-loeb-1846: Aryeh Loeb was a dayyan, a religious judge, at Lublin in Poland in the seventeenth century. He wrote Likkute ha-Or, Collection of Light, in two volumes. The first volume appeared at Lublin in 1667 under the title Ha-Maor ha-Katan, The Lesser Light. It comments on the laws of Kiddush ha-Hodesh, the consecration of the new moon, in Maimonides. The second volume, Ha-Maor ha-Gadol, The Greater Light, stayed unpublished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashima-1946:
Ashima was one of the gods of the men of Hamath. After Sargon settled them in Samaria, following 722 B.C., they set up his image there, as Second Kings chapter 17 records. Jewish tradition explains the name as a short-haired goat, which led some to picture a sort of eastern Pan, a god of woods and shepherds. The entry calls that guess highly improbable.

Other matches have been tried. Some link the name to Ashmun, or Eshmun, the Phenician god. Others tie it to Tashmitu, the Babylonian goddess who was wife to Nabu, god of learning. Kittel's view wins most favor here: an Aramaic god, likely tied to the river Ashmaya near Tyre. Beyond the Bible verse, the entry admits, nothing sure is known.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-assyria-2046:
Assyria took its name from Asshur, a city west of the Tigris. From that city grew a kingdom and then an empire. The entry tells Assyria's story with Israel in view. It sets out three spans: quiet years to 1500 B.C., growth to 745, and supremacy to 607. For Israel, the key parts are the Syrian wars, the fall of the northern kingdom, and Judah's years as a vassal.

Kings of Israel and Judah met Assyria as allies, rebels, and tribute payers. Ahab fought beside Damascus against Shalmaneser II. about 854 B.C. Jehu submitted about 842. Tiglath-pileser III. later remade the empire and pressed west. In the end the Medes and Chaldeans destroyed Nineveh and split the empire. The entry closes on Assyria's mark on Judah's religion and on the Old Testament books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auspitz-jacob-2:
Jacob Auspitz was a writer on geography. He lived at Budapest, Hungary, in the first quarter of the nineteenth century. His book "Beër ha-Luḥot," Explanation of the Tablets, came out at Vienna in 1818. It holds five maps of the Bible lands, copied from a Latin source, with full notes of his own.

The maps show the spread of mankind after the Flood, the wanderings of the Hebrew tribes in the desert, and their camps. Two more maps show the Mediterranean with the planned division of Palestine, and Palestine itself from Jewish and Gentile sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baal-peor-2246:
Baal-peor was the name of a Canaanite god. Peor was a mountain in Moab, and Beth-peor was the place at its foot. The god took his name from the place where he was worshiped. Israel, just before entering Canaan, was drawn for a short time into his service. The book of Numbers tells that story with shame.

It is commonly held that this worship called for sensual license. The entry grants that the evil at Peor was flagrant. But it warns that all Ba'al worship urged the same sin, and Peor may have been no worse than many shrines. Rabbinic lore adds a grotesque detail. The worship, it says, meant baring in public what people most take care to hide. One tale tells of a foreign ruler who, on hearing of the rite, set his soldiers on the worshipers and killed them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baeza-2346: Baeza, a city in the province of Jaen, Spain, had a large Jewish community as early as Moorish rule. The entry is short and grim. That community suffered much in the war between Castile and Mohammed al-Naṣir in 1212. In 1391 many Jews of Baeza were slain, and the rest were spared only if they accepted baptism. Five years later only Maranos remained. In 1473 many of those fell to mob fury, as at Cordova, while the count de Cabra, the city's governor, saved others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baron-jonas-254: Jonas Báron, a Hungarian physician and surgeon, was born at Gyöngyös on November 23, 1845. He lectured on surgery at the University of Budapest. His father was secretary of the Jewish community in Gyöngyös. In 1870 he acted as medical assistant at various Budapest hospitals. From 1871 to 1873 he served the Jewish hospital there, and since 1874 he has been its senior surgeon. He wrote a work on surgical pathology and therapeutics (Budapest, 1871). His articles appeared in Budapest medical journals and in the "Wiener Med. Presse" and "Wiener Med. Wochenschrift."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-michael-27:
Michael Beer was a German poet born in Berlin on Aug. 19, 1800. He was a brother of the composer Meyerbeer and of the astronomer Wilhelm Beer. At eighteen he wrote his first tragedy, staged in Berlin in 1819 to a warm welcome.

His one act tragedy of 1823 won an ovation, with praise from Goethe himself. The entry reads that play as a bitter cry against the oppression of Jews in Europe. Beer traveled widely and moved in Paris salons. He died at Munich on March 22, 1833, still a young man. A second tragedy, drawn from his Italian travels, appeared in print at Leipsic in 1823 beside the first.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjacob-isaac-:
Isaac ben Jacob Benjacob, a Russian writer on books, author, and publisher, was born on Jan. 10, 1801, and died at Wilna on July 2, 1863. Raised at Wilna, he wrote poems and short pieces in pure biblical Hebrew from a young age. Time in business at Riga still left room for study and writing.

At Leipsic he published his first book and a valued edition of a classic work on the duties of the heart. Back at Wilna, he helped issue the Bible with a German rendering in seventeen volumes. His edition of a great name-list of Hebrew authors stayed the standard one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berendt-gottlie: Gottlieb Michael Berendt, a German geologist, was born in Berlin on Jan. 4, 1836. He studied mining science, and his work of 1863 gave the first geological map of the Mark Brandenburg. He later made maps of parts of the Harz range and of eastern and western Prussia. Settled at Königsberg and then at Berlin, he rose to a university chair in 1875. His name rests chiefly on study of the North German Lowland, where he was among the first to accept the glacial theory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-juliu: Julius Bernstein, a German physiologist and medical writer, was born at Berlin on Dec. 8, 1839. A son of Aaron Bernstein, he took his medical degree at Berlin in 1862. He taught at Heidelberg from 1865 and rose there to assistant professor. In 1871 he gained the chair of physiology at Halle, a post he still held in 1902. A high state title came in 1898. Counted a leader in his field, he wrote on the working of nerve and muscle, on the five senses, and a textbook of physiology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berthold-of-reg:
Berthold of Regensburg, born about 1220, was a monk and itinerant preacher who died at Regensburg on December 14, 1272. Known as "Rusticanus," he traveled widely through German lands and beyond, winning fame as the most celebrated popular preacher of the Middle Ages.

The entry focuses on his sermons' references to Jews: he opposed forced conversion and forced disputations, urged kings to guard Jewish persons and property, and praised Jewish prayer and family life. Yet it also notes his harsh words against usury and his slurs, and points to his elaborate angelology as a link between Christian and Jewish mysticism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bezer-3246: Bezer was a city of refuge in Reuben's territory. Deuteronomy and Joshua both name it so. Reuben also gave it to the Levites. The Mesha inscription calls it a Moabite city. It is probably Jeremiah's Bozrah of Moab. The entry states a plain limit. Bezer has not yet been identified. No ruins in Moab's plateau are surely its. It must also be kept distinct from Bosor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bitumen-3346: Bitumen is a substance Genesis names as mortar. It belongs to the hydrocarbon class. It forms from petroleum by evaporation and oxidation. Continued change turns it into asphalt. The Dead Sea's south end holds much asphalt. That gave the sea its name Asphaltites Lacus. Famous eastern springs lie at Hît near Babylon. Bitumen coated sun-dried bricks for durability. Boat-builders at Hît still use its springs today. The entry cites Hull on its rock source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonsenior-ibn-y: Bonsenior ibn Yahya was a chess expert about whom no life details can be obtained. His name is probably Provençal, and he lived not later than the fifteenth century. He wrote an essay on chess playing in Hebrew. It was first printed at Mantua in 1557. A French version later appeared at Paris in 1864. That edition paired his work with a chess piece by Ibn Ezra. The entry offers no birth, home, or death facts at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-broughton-hugh-:
Hugh Broughton was an English Christian divine and rabbinical scholar. Born in 1549 at Oldbury, Shropshire, he studied Hebrew at Magdalene College, Cambridge. He graduated in 1570 and won notice in London as a Puritan preacher. He died at Tottenham on Aug. 4, 1612.

His first work, A Concent of Scripture, appeared in 1588 and tried to fix Bible chronology. Traveling in Germany, Broughton debated with Jews and hoped to convert them. He disputed in a Frankfort synagogue in 1590 and with Rabbi David Farrar. He wanted to translate the New Testament into Hebrew but completed only Revelation. The entry also describes his fierce attack on the King James Version after he was passed over.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carmel-mount-40:
Mount Carmel is a ridge in Palestine running from the plain of Esdraelon to the Mediterranean Sea. It ends in a steep headland about nine miles southwest of Acre. The rock is limestone mixed with flint, and the highest point stands 1,742 feet above the sea. Oaks, pines, olives, and laurels cover its slopes.

In the Bible, Carmel fell to the tribe of Asher. Elijah there called Israel back to God and slew the priests of Baal, as I Kings xviii reports. Elisha also stayed there and met the Shunammite woman there. The account notes an altar on the mount before Baal worship entered the kingdom. Later visitors included Pythagoras and Vespasian, drawn by its sacred name. The exact site of the contest with Baal has not been fixed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catalogues-of-h:
Catalogues of Hebrew books were in frequent use among Jews in the Middle Ages. Judah ibn Tibbon, about 1200, praised his own book collection and its catalogue, and urged both on his son Samuel. Old catalogue fragments from genizot have come to light in recent years. One twelfth-century fragment lists 100 works for sale, classed as Bible, Mishnah, Talmud, Theology, Halakah, and Liturgy.

Such lists are scarce, and their scarcity leaves a gap in the history of medieval Hebrew literature. Only in the last two and a half centuries have libraries printed their catalogues. The account then lists printed catalogues of public collections by town. Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Bologna, Breslau, Cambridge, Copenhagen, and Florence all appear, with dates and manuscript counts. Private collections follow, arranged by owner name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-charger-4246: Charger renders two Hebrew words and one Greek word in the Bible versions. The first Hebrew word stands in the list of gifts from tribal chiefs at the dedication of the Tabernacle. Elsewhere that word is rendered dish. The second Hebrew word, of uncertain origin, stands in the list of vessels Cyrus returned to the Jewish exiles. The Greek word names the dish on which the head of John the Baptist was brought to Herodias, as Matthew and Mark report.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chmielnicki-bog:
Bogdan Zinovi Chmielnicki, hetman of the Zaporogian Cossacks, was born about 1595 and died at Chigirin on Aug. 16, 1675, as the entry gives it. Raised without turning to Roman Catholicism, he held fast to the Greek Orthodox faith of most Cossacks. Personal wrongs, the loss of his estate at Subotovo and harm to his family, sharpened his anger.

The entry argues that ambition to rule a freed Ukraine drove his uprising more than revenge alone. It describes how Jewish leaseholders stood between Polish landlords and peasants, drawing peasant hatred. Chmielnicki turned that anger toward Jews and Poles alike. Massacres followed, yet the entry notes he still failed to win lasting freedom for Ukraine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coen-jacob-4446: Jacob Coen was the eldest son of Abraham Coen. He served as receiver-general, or contador mayor, to Count Maurice of Nassau. Maurice ruled the United Provinces of the Netherlands as stadtholder from 1584 to 1625. Dutch Jews then held no rights of citizenship. Maurice rose above the bias of his age, the entry says. In thanks for Abraham Coen's great services, he gave the son this high office. One publication of the American Jewish Historical Society is the only source named for the brief notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-corbeil-or-4646: Corbeil, a city in the department of Seine-et-Oise, France, held Jews from an early date. They lived in a quarter called the Juderia. Records name a house given away by King Philippe Auguste in 1184. Special taxes followed in 1202, plus seal fees on deals with Christians. A treasury journal of 1298 names the tax receiver Hagin. In 1306 a Jew named Cressant owned a house on the Seine with high rent. The entry also recalls noted Talmudists, among them Judah of Corbeil and Jacob the Saint.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cremation-3846:
Cremation, the burning of the dead, was never the ruling custom among the ancient Hebrews. It was not unknown, though. The Pentateuch sets burning as a penalty for certain grave offenses. In Joshua the burning of a corpse is added to a death sentence. From such cases the entry infers that burning a body was viewed with horror. In an epidemic, it may have been used from need.

Later sections test one disputed verse in Amos about a kinsman who burns the dead. The reading is weak, the article argues. Funeral pyres of costly goods are treated next, with a ban in the Shulḥan 'Aruk for common folk. One scholar even read the Bible cases as embalming, not burning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cremieux-hector:
Hector Jonathan Crémieux was a French dramatist, born at Paris on Nov. 10, 1828. He died there in 1892, kin to Isaac Adolphe Crémieux. He studied law in Paris after the Lycée Bourbon. In Feb., 1848, he joined the revolution against the Orleanist dynasty. At twenty he held a lieutenant's post in the Garde Mobile. He kept clear of extreme politics until the coup of 1851.

His stage work began with a bold adaptation. With his brother Emile he reworked Schiller's Fiesco as a French spectacle play. Later he wrote in partnership after partnership. Melodrama, fairy pieces, and dramatized novels fill the list. Names like Ludovic Halévy and Philippe Gillet appear among his many collaborators.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dagger-4846: Dagger is defined here in one line: a short, edged, and pointed weapon for stabbing. The entry is only a few lines long. It says the word is given in the Ehud episode in Judges as the English equivalent of a Hebrew term. That term, ḥereb, is elsewhere rendered sword. The entry then points the reader to the article on Sword for the fuller treatment. No kinds, makers, or other uses are described. Readers learn the weapon's shape, its one Bible scene, and where to read more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-hoday:
Hodaya's son David, a prince of the Davidic house, lived at Mosul about 1150 to 1220. His long genealogy, preserved in an excommunication he issued, traces his line back through the exilarchs to King David, though the entry warns the list is incomplete and incorrect.

When the exilarch Daniel died childless, David and his brother Samuel both claimed the office, and the choice was still open when the traveler Pethahiah visited Mosul about 1175. David protected Samuel ben Ali of Bagdad, the leading eastern opponent of Maimonides. His excommunication of about 1191 targeted Samuel's enemies. Al-Ḥarizi, visiting in 1217, praised David as exilarch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutsch-mordeca: Enoch Judah's son Mordecai Deutsch was rabbi of Kolin, Bohemia, and of the smaller communities under it. He flourished at the beginning of the eighteenth century. He wrote one work, "Mor Deror" (Flowing Myrrh). It gives novellae, fresh comments, on six Talmudic treatises: Ketubot, Baba Ḳamma, Baba Meẓi'a, Ḥullin, Yoma, and Shebu'ot. The book was printed at Prague in 1738. The short entry cites Steinschneider, Zedner, and Walden, and gives no dates of birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dubno-5346:
Dubno is a town in the government of Volhynia, Russia. The census of 1897 counted 13,785 people there, including 5,608 Jews. Trade and industry feed most of those Jews. The entry counts 902 artisans and 147 day-laborers. Jews appear at Dubno from the early seventeenth century.

In 1650 Dubno held 47 Jewish taxable households against 141 Christian ones. The town has a Jewish hospital but only small religious schools. Much of the entry is a long roll of Dubno rabbis from 1600 on. It opens with Isaiah ha-Levi Hurwitz, author of Shene Luhot ha-Berit. Later names include martyrs of 1649 and scholars who moved between great Volhynian pulpits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eger-czech-cheb:
Eger, in Czech Cheb, is a Bohemian town on the river of the same name. In 1890 it held 17,148 people, among them 508 Jews. The oldest paper naming its Jews dates to March 12, 1314. That paper barred them from a new street near the monastery.

By about 1332 rich Jews had settled thickly in Eger. They soon formed a quarter of the town. They kept a high school, a synagogue, and a cemetery. Black Death charges reached Eger in March 1349. A monk's preaching fired the mob, and in 1350 nearly all the Jews were killed. Their books went to the Imperial Library at Prague.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-b-malai: Eleazar ben Malai was a Palestinian scholar of the fourth century. His name appears only once in the Babylonian Talmud. There he passes on a homily of Simeon ben Lakish against corrupt courts. The homily reads a verse from Isaiah part by part. Judges take bribes, scribes write false papers, and lawyers twist the law. The entry adds a doubt about his very name. Some editions read Simlai in place of Malai. That leaves it unsure if Malai was his true father's name at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-ben-benj: Elijah ben Benjamin ha-Levi was a Turkish rabbi. He lived at Constantinople in the sixteenth century. In 1526 he followed his teacher Elijah Mizrahi as rabbi there. He made the first collection of prayers for the Romanian rite. That prayer book came out at Constantinople in 1510. He added many poems of his own to it. His book of rulings holds 451 responsa in all. Only a part of those were ever printed. Other works of his stayed in handwriting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-en-sof-boundles: En Sof is a Cabala term for God before creation. It means the boundless or endless One in Hebrew. It names God prior to any showing of Himself in the world. The phrase most likely comes from Ibn Gabirol's words. Azriel ben Menahem first put it to this use. He held that God has no wish, thought, word, or act. The Zohar calls En Sof the nameless being in its pages. Before form, God was alone and like nothing else. No name, letter, or mark may stand for Him then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-esau-5846:
Esau was Jacob's elder twin brother, and his name shifts with Edom in the Bible. Genesis explains Edom, meaning red, from his birth and from the red stew he ate. The entry admits the true sense of Esau is unknown. Born red and hairy, he grew into a skillful hunter. Hungry one day, he sold his birthright to Jacob for a meal.

The long entry then follows rabbinic tales about Esau. In those tales he plots against Jacob even before birth. Isaac favors him, but Rebekah swaps Jacob in for the blessing. Esau weeps and wins a lesser blessing, then vows to kill his brother. The brothers later make peace and part, Esau settling in Seir. No death of Esau is recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eye-5946:
The eye is named more than 800 times in the Bible, and this long entry gathers what those mentions teach. The Bible describes the eye only from the outside, the entry notes. Its parts get homely names: the pupil is the little man, whose image shows in the eye. Lashes, lids, sockets, and brows are each pinned to verses.

Sight weakens with age, grief, and tears, the entry shows from many texts. Joy makes the eyes light up, and wine makes them red. A son closed his dead father's eyes. Later parts of the entry take up eye disease and care in ancient Israel. Blindness was common, though its true spread cannot be fixed from the verses. Priestly rules for a spot on the eye are also cited.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fear-of-man-604:
Fear of man, as this entry treats it, is chiefly the respect owed to parents, elders, teachers, and rulers. Scripture and Talmud both press respect for parents hard. The Talmud ranks honor for parents beside honor for God, since parents stand as God's agents on earth. In early Israel the family carried the state, and parents acted near to judges.

Death once punished the son who struck or cursed a parent, and the stubborn son who would not obey. Respect is also owed to the aged face, to teachers, whose fear ranks as fear of Heaven, and to rulers. Pray for the kingdom's peace, one saying runs, since without fear of rule men would swallow each other alive. Plain cowardly fear, by contrast, is scorned in the texts quoted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fischels-meir-6:
Meïr Fischels, an Austrian Talmudist, died at Prague on Dec. 16, 1769. His surname marks him as a son of Ephraim Fischel of Bunzlau. His family traced its line back to Rabbi Löw of Prague. The entry calls him one of the greatest Talmudists of his time. Great communities in Europe invited him, but he refused them all. He stayed in Prague as head of its great court.

Fischels ran a school at Prague for more than forty years. Students came to it from far countries. Even the chief rabbi deferred to his rulings. In the great ghetto fire of 1754 he lost the manuscripts of all his works. He never got over that loss, the entry says. His grave in the old cemetery bears a mausoleum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fortress-6246:
A fortress is a permanent fort or fortified place. The Israelites, entering the land west of the Jordan, found many walled cities they could not take. They settled in open places and fled to forests and caves when attacked. In time they took the Canaanite strongholds, among them Jerusalem. David fortified that city anew. Hezekiah and Manasseh later walled the rest of it. The Maccabeans and Herodians added a third wall.

Kings built new fortresses to guard the borders and the roads in. Solomon raised Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer, and other towns for that purpose. Rehoboam fortified fifteen cities south and west of Jerusalem. Samaria, built by Omri on a mountain top, fell to the Assyrians only after a siege of three years. The entry then describes the works themselves. Walls of great stones carried battlements and towers. Gates had heavy wooden doors and bolts of brass or iron.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frensdorff-solo:
Solomon Frensdorff was a German Hebraist born at Hamburg on February 24, 1803. He died at Hanover on March 23, 1880. At the gymnasium of his home town he was brought into Hebrew letters by Isaac Bernays. Bernays shaped his later stand toward Judaism and religion at large. Frensdorff studied philosophy and Semitic languages at Bonn. There he came to know Abraham Geiger, who praised his character and learning in many letters. In 1837 he became head master of the Jewish religious school at Hanover.

In 1848 Frensdorff was named head of the new Jewish teachers' seminary at Hanover. He kept that post until his death. His life's work was the close study and printing of Masoretic books. Those books are prized for their exactness. They include a work on Hebrew pointing and accents, printed in 1847. A second Masoretic work followed in 1864. His great Masora volume, with a Masoretic dictionary, came out in 1876.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gabbatha-or-gab:
Gabbatha is a place name tied to more than one site. One town matches the biblical Gibeah, named in the Septuagint and in Josephus. Ancient place lists place one Gabbatha near Sepphoris, one east of the Daroma, and one about twelve miles from Eleutheropolis. Near the last stood a tomb said to be that of the prophet Habakkuk.

A second sense comes from John xix. 13. There Gabbatha is the Hebrew name for the Pavement in Jerusalem. Pilate gave his final judgment on Jesus at that spot, before the governor hall. The entry notes that the Greek and Hebrew names do not match well. Gabbatha may have marked a nearby part of the upper city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gebweiler-6546:
Gebweiler, a town of Alsace in the Colmar district, first names its Jewish community in a paper of 1270. Its synagogue is first named in 1333. Jews there suffered in the attacks of 1349. None seem to have lived there for the next few centuries. In the Thirty Years War three Jewish families won leave to stay for a time, at a steep weekly fee.

By 1706 four Jewish families lived at Gebweiler, and by 1741 ten. In 1784 only seven families, 40 people in all, remained. By 1903 the count had grown to 83 families. A new synagogue rose in 1870-71. The dead rest in the burial ground at Jungholz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldenberg-samu: Samuel Löb Goldenberg was an Austrian Hebraist. He was born at Bolechow, Galicia, in 1807. He died at Tarnopol on Jan. 11, 1846. His fame rests on one journal, "Kerem Ḥemed." He founded it and edited its seven volumes between 1833 and 1843. The entry says the journal opened a new epoch in Hebrew letters. It offered readers work of a fully scientific kind. Its writers included Rapoport, Krochmal, Zunz, Luzzatto, and Geiger. Their clear, classic Hebrew broke with older habits. Their critical spirit also struck at Ḥasidism in Galicia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-greeting-forms-:
Greeting, in this entry, means the fixed ways people address each other on meeting. Among the ancient Hebrews the form turned on how close the two people were. Greetings could hold a health inquiry, a kiss, a blessing, or a deep bow. Joseph asked his brothers after their welfare in Genesis. David sent Nabal a triple wish of peace. Boaz greeted his harvesters with "The Lord be with you."

Rabbinic teaching then takes over. The Ethics of the Fathers urges greeting every man first with peace. Johanan ben Zakkai greeted even Gentiles in the street. Rules cover how pupils greet a teacher. Kissing on the forehead was favored over mouth or cheek. Prostration was the deepest form of all. The entry ends with house customs: the answer must always differ from the greeting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hammer-7146:
Hammer is covered here as a word study: the Hebrew Bible uses several terms for the tool. "Maḳḳabah" is the stone-cutter's hewing tool, the smith's iron tool, and the Bedouin's tent-pin mallet, as in Judges iv. 21. "Paṭṭish" is a larger tool, used to smooth gold plates and to break rocks; Jeremiah calls Nebuchadnezzar the paṭṭish of the whole earth.

Two harder terms close the entry. "Halmut 'amelim," at Judges v. 26, is usually rendered hammer, but the grammar fights that sense, and the text may be corrupt. "Kelappah," at Psalms lxxiv. 6, may match an Assyrian word, and it seems to name an ax or hatchet rather than a hammer. The article is a short tour of Bible wording, not of the tool's craft.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harbona-harbona: Harbona was one of the seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus in the Book of Esther. He was ordered to bring Queen Vashti before the king. Later he pointed out the gallows Haman had built, and Haman was hanged on it. The entry also reports a rabbinic view that Harbona had first sided with Haman, then left him when the plot failed. Another tradition says the prophet Elijah appeared in Harbona's shape. A Purim song ends by asking that Harbona be remembered for good.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-havre-7346: Havre was a French seaport on the Seine estuary with a small Jewish community. Of its 118,478 people, about 50 were Jews in 1903. A dozen Jewish families first joined for the high holy days in 1850. A decree created the community in 1852. Its first synagogue was dedicated by Chief Rabbi Isidor. Growth led to a new temple in 1862, also dedicated by Isidor two years later. In 1870 the town joined the rabbinical district of Rouen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hebrew-the-7446: The Hebrew was a Jewish weekly set up in San Francisco in 1863. Philo Jacoby founded it. He was a son of Isaac Jacoby, a rabbi in Pomerania. The paper was still published by its founder at the time of writing. The entry calls it the oldest Jewish paper on the Pacific coast. Rabbis and the founder's brother were among its editors over the years. In religion it took a conservative line. No circulation figures or sample contents are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heltay-franz-75: Franz Heltay, born at Szentes on March 15, 1861, was a Hungarian deputy. He studied law and political economy at Budapest. He joined the staff of two papers, then edited a review of political economy. From 1887 he also edited the Railway News, the trade paper of the Hungarian commerce ministry. He sat on the ministry's statistics committee and tariff board. He was vice-president of the Journalists' Pension Fund. His chief work revised the trade laws. In 1896 voters sent him to the Hungarian Reichstag.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hess-isaac-7646:
Isaac Hess, born in Lauchheim in 1789, worked for Jewish emancipation in Württemberg. Trained for the rabbinate at Fürth for four years, he turned to school reform. In 1817 he urged King William to create a central bureau for Jewish education. The king named a commission on Jewish religious affairs.

Hess sent a second memorial in 1821 that reached its goal. In 1823 he moved to Ellwangen, where no Jew had lived before. Town hostility forced the governor to protect him from violence. He also projected the Ellwangen Jewish orphan asylum, founded in 1831. He died on Oct. 6, 1866.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-theodor-: Theodor Hirsch, born at Altschottland, near Danzig, on Dec. 17, 1806, was a German historian. After embracing Christianity, he studied theology, history, and geography at Berlin. He taught history at Danzig for thirty-two years from 1833. The city charged him in 1850 with sorting and guarding its archives. His main work treated Danzig's trade and crafts under the German Order, printed in 1858. He also co-edited five volumes of Prussian historical writings. In 1865 he taught at Greifswald and directed its library. He died on Feb. 17, 1881.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-honey-7846:
Honey is often named in the Old Testament as a choice food, the entry says. It was eaten alone and with other foods. In pastry it took sugar's place. Canaan is praised many times as a land flowing with milk and honey.

Palestine had many wild bees, and bees were likely kept there in Bible times too. Some passages may mean fruit syrup rather than bee honey. First fruits of honey went to the sanctuary, but honey was barred from sacrifices for its fermenting trait. Honey serves as a figure for God's words, wisdom, and a friend's speech. Talmud notes cover its taste, healing use, and hive care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hurwitz-hayyim-: Hayyim Dob Hurwitz was a Russian economist and journalist born about 1864 at Gorki. His father, a religion teacher, meant him for the rabbinate. The boy chose modern studies instead. He attended local schools, then drifted about 1880 to Berlin and Vienna for languages and philosophy. In 1898 his sketches of Russian Jewish life drew notice in Hebrew journals. His two-volume Ha-Mamon of 1900 set out the modern economic system in clear Hebrew. In 1903 he became subeditor of a Yiddish daily at St. Petersburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-shem-tob-sh:
Shem-Tob ben Joseph ibn Shem-Tob was a Spanish cabalist who lived about 1390 to 1440. He headed a school in Spain and fathered Joseph and Isaac ibn Shem-Tob. He fought rationalist philosophy with zeal. His Book of Beliefs, printed at Ferrara in 1556, attacks the Aristotelian reading of Judaism.

The book praises the Cabala as the true teaching handed down by tradition. It blames philosophy and its enlightenment for Jews leaving the faith and for the age's persecutions. Harsh verdicts fall on Maimonides, Abraham ibn Ezra, and Levi ben Gershon. His survey of cabalistic history names older writers whose existence is not proven by the naming. Moses Alashkar answered him sharply in print the same year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibzan-8046: Ibzan was a judge of Israel for seven years after Jephthah. He came from Beth-lehem and had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He was buried in his home town. Since the town is not called Bethlehem of Judah, it may be the Bethlehem in Zebulun. Talmudic teachers identify Ibzan with Boaz. The puzzle that Boaz seems to have had one child is answered by a tale. All Ibzan's children died in his lifetime, the tale says, because he had not invited Manoah to their weddings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-inheritance-yer:
Inheritance among the early Hebrews followed custom: the next of kin took the dead man's estate, and the first-born son usually took headship and the family property. A childless man might name a trusted friend instead, as Abraham nearly named his slave Eliezer. A father could also favor one child, as Abraham sent his concubines' children away with presents so Isaac would inherit undisturbed.

The daughters of Zelophehad brought the case that fixed the biblical order: son, then daughter, then brothers, then father's brothers, then the nearest kinsman. The rabbis built on it, ruling that whoever comes first transmits the right to his descendants. A widow did not inherit from her husband in the early scheme; the husband, though, is his wife's heir.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-iron-8146:
Iron-working, with brass-working, is ascribed by Genesis to Tubal-cain, yet the entry argues the Israelites learned the art from others. Solomon had to bring Hiram from Tyre to make the Temple's brazen implements. Only as the Israelites settled in towns and Canaanite cities opened to them did metal crafts develop among them, and brass came before iron in utensils and armor.

Iron seems to have replaced brass late; the oldest passage presupposing its use is II Sam. xii. 31. It served for axes, sickles, swords, bolts, chains, plowshares and the sheathing of war-chariots, which the Canaanites already fielded. Figuratively, Egypt is the "iron furnace," a tyrant an iron rod, and Daniel's fourth beast has iron teeth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-iscovescu-barbu:
Barbu Judah Iscovescu was a Rumanian painter born in 1816 at Bucharest who died on Oct. 24, 1854, at Constantinople. The son of a house-painter, he learned that trade from his father. He then went to Vienna and Paris to study drawing and painting. Back in Bucharest, he and Rosenthal were among the first to spread the plastic arts in Rumania.

In Paris he had fallen in with young Wallachians who later launched the Rumanian revolution of 1848. He joined them on his return and ran missions for the revolutionary committee. When Russian troops crushed the rising, he was banished to Constantinople with the others. He died in exile there. At his wish, he was buried in the Greek Orthodox cemetery, in one grave with two fellow exiles. Two leading men of the revolution wrote his epitaph in verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-bar-natro: Jacob bar Natronai was Gaon of Sura from 911 to 924. He took the post at a low hour. His predecessor, Shalom bar Mishael, had died, and the academy had grown poor and lost most of its students. Jacob held the gaonate for thirteen years. Halevy showed, the entry adds, that he is not the same man as Amram ben Solomon, as Grätz had held. Beyond the dates of his office and that correction, the entry records nothing of his rulings or writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jedidiah-gottli: Jedidiah Gottlieb ben Abraham Israel was a Galician preacher and Masorite who lived at Lemberg in the seventeenth century. The short entry names two works by him and nothing more of his life. One book gives fifty homiletic readings on a verse in Deuteronomy and was printed at Cracow in 1641 and again at Lublin in 1645. The other is a commentary on the Masorah in four parts, set in alphabetical order and printed in 1644.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joktan-8746:
Joktan was the younger son of Eber and the ancestor of thirteen Arabic tribes named in Genesis. Several of those tribes, such as Hazarmaveth, Sheba, Ophir, and Havilah, have been matched to real peoples and places. His name seems to mean the younger or the smaller. One Midrash reads it instead as that he humbles himself, and says his humility won him those thirteen tribes.

His line settled from Mesha toward Sephar, a mountain of the east, in Arabia by the plain reading. In Arabic writing Joktan bears the name Kahtan. Arab family men there call him the first king of Yemen and father of the true southern Arabs. A tale that his son married into Ishmael's line was likely made later to bind north and south Arabs together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-jaco: Joseph ben Jacob, also called Bar Satya, was gaon of Sura about 930 to 936 and again from 942 to 948. The exilarch David ben Zakkai chose him near 930 to take the place of the deposed Saadia. When the exilarch made peace with Saadia in 936, Joseph lost the post but kept its income. After Saadia died in 942, Joseph was named gaon once more. In 948, as the academy at Sura sank into poverty and decay, he left for Bassora, where he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-low-lob-l:
Judah Low ben Bezaleel, known as der Hohe Rabbi Low, was an Austrian Talmudist and mathematician born in Posen in the second decade of the sixteenth century. He died at Prague on August 22, 1609. From 1553 to 1573 he served as Moravian Landesrabbiner at Nikolsburg, guiding both town affairs and Talmud study. He gathered the Moravian statutes on elections, taxes, and luxury to confirm them.

Low never speaks of himself in his books, so his life is little known. The Moravian towns treated him as an authority long after he left for Prague. On February 23, 1592, the emperor called him to an audience at the castle, where the talk seems to have turned on cabalistic subjects. He later became chief rabbi of Poland at Posen. His works include a book on Jewish ethics printed at Prague in 1596.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judans-the-8946: The Judaeans was a society set up in New York on January 28, 1897, on the lines of the Maccabaeans in London. Its aim was to advance the intellectual and spiritual interests of Jews. Its rules required that at least three-fourths of its members work in letters, the arts, or science, or hold a known profession. Its first president was Henry M. Leipziger, with Richard J. H. Gottheil as first vice-president. It printed a full report of its first two years in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judenhut-9046:
The Judenhut was a tall, cone-shaped hat, generally yellow, that Jews were forced to wear as a badge. It followed the decrees of the fourth Lateran Council of 1215, which ordered that every Jew wear a distinguishing mark. The Synod of Vienna in 1267 affirmed the rule, and Pope Paul IV in 1555 fixed the hat's color as yellow.

From the thirteenth century on, paintings and prints show Jews by their pointed hats. The Jewish singer Suesskind von Trimberg wrote that he walked in the Jewish manner, in a long mantle and pointed hat. A few favored Jews won leave to skip the badge. Venice, for one, let the doctor Jacob Mantino wear a black doctor's cap for two months.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalifa-moses-be:
Moses ben Malka Kalifa was a poet and writer on religious debate. He was born at Safi, in Morocco, late in the seventeenth century. Orphaned young, he had means of his own. He traveled through Morocco and studied at Fez. His teachers there were Judah ben 'Aṭṭar and Samuel Ẓarfati.

At home again, Kalifa kept up his studies under Joseph Bueno of Mescuta. His blunt speech angered the governor of Safi. He had to flee to Agadir, a fortress on the coast. Plague struck that place in 1728. In one day he lost his wife Deborah and his daughter Estrella. The entry names two works he left in manuscript. One comments on the prayer book and holds poems. The other treats religious controversy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaufmann-moses-: Moses Jekuthiel Kaufmann was a Polish Talmudist born at Krotoschin. His birth falls near the middle of the seventeenth century. He was also known as Kaufmann Kohen Krotoschin. He married into the family of Abraham Abele Gombiner. He served as rabbi at Kutno, in Poland. His notes on the Shulḥan 'Aruk fill four parts. They came out between 1693 and 1701. His notes on Yoreh De'ah saw print twice in his line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kherson-5246:
Kherson is a Russian city on the right bank of the Dnieper, near its mouth. It is the capital of the government of the same name. Prince Potemkin founded it in 1778. Jews had leave to settle in New Russia from 1769. Some were among the first people of the new city. By 1781 they had formed a community.

The entry describes the town's prayer houses, hospital, and schools. Rabbi Faitel Blumenfeld widened the Talmud Torah to worldly subjects. A state panel met at Kherson in 1881 on the Jewish question. Christian merchants there praised the Jewish farmers as honest neighbors. The panel voted for free Jewish residence across Russia. Jews led the town's timber and grain trades. In 1890 the city held 72,451 people, about 25,000 of them Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kirschbaum-elie: Eliezer Simon Kirschbaum was an Austrian physician and writer. He was born at Sieniawa, in Galicia, in 1797. He died at Cracow in 1860. After studying philosophy and medicine in Berlin, he settled as a physician in Cracow. As "Der Berliner Doctor" he soon gained an extensive practise and a fortune. To secure the estate of Siemota, he adopted Christianity and assumed the name "Sigismund." His wife remained a law-abiding Jewess throughout her life. His German works include "Der Jüdische Alexandrinismus" of 1841.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kolisch-baron-i:
Ignaz von Kolisch, a Hungarian merchant, journalist, and chess master, was born at Presburg on April 6, 1837, and died at Vienna on April 30, 1889. In business he founded a Vienna bank body in 1869 and a Paris commission house in 1873, gaining large wealth. At chess his bright, attacking play won first prize at Cambridge in 1860.

Two near misses against the strongest players frame his chess fame. In 1861 he lost to Anderssen by a single game and drew with Paulsen. In 1867 at Paris he took the lead, beating both Winawer and Steinitz. The entry adds that he founded a Vienna newspaper and wrote for it under a pen name built from his initials.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kulisher-reuben: Reuben Moiseiyevich Kulisher, a Russian physician and educator born at Dubno in 1828, died at Kiev on Aug. 9, 1896. He won a gold medal at the Jitomir gymnasium in 1848 and graduated in medicine at St. Petersburg in 1856. He was one of three Jews then named military surgeons. Army hospital posts at Lutsk and Kiev followed. From 1869 to 1876 he did science work for the government abroad. He also pushed hard for steady schooling for Russian Jews, which made him enemies among the Orthodox.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lasch-gershon-9: Gershon Lasch, a German teacher and author born in 1803, died at Halberstadt on March 3, 1883. In 1823 he became instructor at the Jewish school in Halberstadt. Later he rose to professor there. Small school books came first. His named works give two synagogue speeches dated 1841, a history of the Halberstadt Jewish school dated 1847, and a book drawing God's laws out of the Ten Commandments, dated 1857. The school history was written for the school's fifty-year jubilee, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levin-joshua-ho:
Joshua Hoschel ben Elijah Zeeb Levin, a Lithuanian Talmudist and author, was born at Wilna on July 22, 1818. He died at Paris on Nov. 15, 1883. He studied under Elijah Kalischer, then settled at Volozhin. There he lectured on Talmud and wrote several works. In 1871 he was called to the rabbinate of Praga, near Warsaw.

Late in life Levin went to Paris, meaning to travel on to the Holy Land. At Israel Salant's request he stayed and preached to the Russo-Polish community there. His Wilna books include a life of Elijah of Wilna from 1856, a full concordance to both Talmuds, notes on the Midrash Rabbah, and glosses to the Mishnah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levin-robert-ra:
Rahel Levin, a German writer, was born at Berlin on June 19, 1771, and died there on March 7, 1833. Her father, a rich jeweler, ruled his home with a hard hand. Rahel grew close to the daughters of Moses Mendelssohn and to Henriette Herz. Her home became a meeting place for leading minds.

Guests at her salon included the Humboldts, Tieck, Jean Paul Richter, and Schleiermacher. She met Goethe at Carlsbad in 1795. In 1814 she married Karl August Varnhagen von Ense, after converting to Christianity. Their Vienna home drew the Prussian envoys to the Congress. The entry notes that she wrote little for print herself. Her force lay in the circle she held together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-liboschutz-jaco: Jacob Liboschütz, a Russian physician, was born in 1741. He died at Wilna on Feb. 10, 1827. He studied at the University of Halle and went to St. Petersburg. His faith barred him from settling in that city, so he set up at Wilna and won fame there. When Professor Frank left Wilna, someone asked in whose charge he had left the public health. Frank answered, in God and the Jew, meaning Liboschütz. The entry also calls him a diplomat and a giver to charity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowengard-max-1:
Max Löwengard, a German rabbi who changed sides in his era's religious fight, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Württemberg, he was a friend of the novelist Berthold Auerbach. He was also a keen student of Schelling's philosophy. He died at Basel on May 25, 1876.
