Salinity's lone starring role simplifies the monitoring managers must sustain.
plos-pone-0351846:
Ming Liu and colleagues found a protein that helps stomach cancer cells survive a common chemotherapy drug. The drug is known as 5-FU. The protein is called PTPRE, and it runs high in gastric tumors. The team studied it in cancer cells and in mouse tumor grafts. They traced how it protects the cells from a form of iron-driven cell death.

The protein switches on a chain of signals inside the cell. That chain ends at a second protein, TRIB3. With the chain active, the iron-driven death route stays shut. The drug then loses one of its ways to kill, and resistance sets in. Blocking the chain could hand the drug its power back. The work names each link, which is what drug developers need first.
plos-pone-0351946:
Lei Hua, Yongshou Tao, and Liangru Shen studied three mineral-linked blood markers across the stages of a modern syndrome. The syndrome ties heart, kidney, and metabolic disease into one tangle. Data came from over fifteen thousand adults in a United States health survey. A genetic method added a second strand. It uses inherited variants to test whether a marker may help cause disease, not just follow it.

One marker stood out: alkaline phosphatase. It climbed step by step with the syndrome's stage, from early risk to advanced disease with kidney harm. Calcium and phosphorus followed their own patterns. The genetic strand singles the enzyme out still further. A cheap, common blood test may deserve a second look as this syndrome's gauge. Stage-aware markers help doctors read a condition that otherwise blurs into its parts.
plos-pone-0352146:
Jia Wang and Xiaoyang Dong publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for a trial of ear-based nerve stimulation to help stroke survivors move again. Stimulating the vagus nerve through the skin of both ears may beat the usual one-ear approach, judging by earlier small studies. Their planned multicentre trial will enrol one hundred and fourteen patients whose stroke left one side of the body weak.

Patients will be assigned at random to stimulation of both ears, one ear, or a control treatment, with patients and assessors kept unaware of who got what. The trial aims for the full limb picture, not just the arm. Results should show whether the bilateral method deserves a place in stroke rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0352246:
David Sjöström and seven colleagues set out a trial protocol, published in 2026, for psilocybin therapy in anorexia nervosa. Anorexia is a severe eating disorder that often begins in adolescence. It carries high death and relapse rates. Standard psychological and nutritional care helps many patients, yet outcomes stay disappointing. Psilocybin has shown early promise in other rigid, treatment-resistant conditions.

The planned trial enrols people aged sixteen to thirty-five whose anorexia has already relapsed. Half receive two psilocybin sessions with structured psychological support, plus usual care. The other half receive usual care alone. Safety and tolerability come first among the outcomes. Symptom change, mood, and brain-related measures are also tracked. As a protocol, the paper reports no results. It lays out a careful test of whether psychedelic-assisted therapy can be run safely in this fragile group.
plos-pone-0352346:
Jay Kirkham led a team of seven authors studying how North Atlantic right whales feed, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These whales are critically endangered, so knowing how they find and take food helps protect them. The team combined motion tags on free-swimming whales with camera checks and machine learning.

Kirkham's method lets researchers read feeding events straight from tag data, without watching each whale. That means feeding can be tracked at scale, in places and seasons observers rarely reach. Knowing where and how right whales feed guides shipping and fishing rules meant to keep them alive. With so few whales left, each gain in understanding carries unusual weight.
plos-pone-0352446:
Anna-Chiara Barta and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One DNA barcoding study updating Austria's inventory of woodlice, the land-dwelling crustaceans that recycle dead plant matter in soils. Austria's species list had not been reviewed in nearly fifty years. The team generated more than five hundred genetic barcodes from fresh specimens and even managed to sequence DNA from historic museum specimens.

The barcodes covered about three-quarters of the known Austrian species and added two species never before recorded in the country. Genetic splits inside several named species were deep enough to suggest hidden, unrecognized species, and in one case the team found matching subtle body differences to back the split. Older museum material worked best with a repaired short-barcode method. The dataset now anchors Austria's national barcode library for soil wildlife monitoring.
plos-pone-0352646:
Guangming Shi and four colleagues test a microbe-based method for strengthening weak loess soil. Their 2026 study uses soil from China's Ili River Valley. That loess is loose, salty, and prone to collapse and erosion. The technique coaxes bacteria to precipitate calcium carbonate, a natural cement. Three orders of applying bacteria and cementing solution were compared in the laboratory.

Applying both solutions at once worked best. Treated samples gained roughly three-fifths more compressive strength than untreated soil. Cohesion rose by over half as well. Under the microscope, the winning method built a continuous, dense cement network. It filled voids and bridged soil particles evenly. Stepwise treatments left patchy cement instead. The authors call the work preliminary, but it points to a greener way to stabilise hazard-prone loess ground.
plos-pone-0353746:
Omar Saadani and six colleagues pair faba beans with helpful root bacteria. Their goal is to clean soil poisoned by lead and cadmium. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The beans grew in soil spiked at three levels. Some plants got a three-strain bacterial mix. The mix promotes plant growth and tolerates metals. The bacteria colonise the roots. They help the plant thrive in hostile ground.

The partnership worked best in the middle soil. Shoots grew heavier there. Root nodules flourished. The shoots pulled up far more lead and cadmium than plain plants. Cadmium uptake rose several times over. Protective chemistry in the roots rose too. In heavier soil the gains faded. That marks the practical limit of this gentle cleanup method.
plos-pone-0353846:
Chunhui Luo and six colleagues treat grey cast iron with laser-driven cavitation and test whether the treated surface resists corrosion better, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The process fires laser pulses into liquid so collapsing bubbles hammer the metal surface, hardening it without contact. The team varied laser energy and focus, and tried the treatment with and without a thin aluminium shield layer laid over the iron.

The shield clearly helped, shielding the surface from laser burn and bubble erosion, and corrosion resistance improved as laser energy rose — up to a point, after which it fell away again. Focus distance mattered less. For foundries, the recipe suggests a cheap surface upgrade for iron parts that must survive wet, corrosive work.
plos-pone-0353946:
Isabel Cervantes-Camacho and five colleagues reconstruct the life history of lane snapper in the Gulf waters off southern Mexico, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The fish supports busy commercial and recreational catches off Yucatan, yet basic facts like lifespan and natural death rates were missing. From more than a thousand landed fish, the team aged several hundred by counting yearly rings in their ear stones.

Ages ran from youngsters under a year to sixteen years in females. Comparing several growth curves with Bayesian methods, the classic von Bertalanffy model fit both sexes best. Solid age and growth numbers let managers set catch rules that a fishery can sustain instead of guessing.
plos-pone-0354146:
Kerle-Malcharek and colleagues, in a 2026 study, show how animal tracking tags can save battery by thinking before they transmit. Tags that ride on wild animals collect rich movement data, and newer tags send it by WiFi, which drains power fast. Sending everything shortens the tag's working life.

Their fix puts a tiny decision tree, a simple machine learning model, on the tag itself. The tree reads sensor data and recognizes a chosen behavior, such as feeding or resting. The tag then sends only data tied to moments that matter and holds back the rest. On a current commercial tag, this filtering cut energy use for transmission by a clear margin in realistic tests. Gyroscope data, usually processed later on a computer, proved especially useful on the tag. The team shares a full pipeline, from training data to tag-ready software, so other animal researchers can copy the trick.
plos-pone-0354246:
Wei Zhang and Liangli Chen published this 2026 mathematics paper on solving two-dimensional equations that mix integrals and derivatives, a class arising in physics and engineering. Their method builds solutions from barycentric rational interpolation, a scheme prized for being steady and exact, paired with a precise counting rule.

They derived the full solution procedure, proved error bounds and that it settles, and tested the method on worked examples. Results matched the theory, confirming it was highly exact for both straight-line and nonlinear versions of these equations. Zhang and Chen aim the method at problems where older solvers lose precision.
plos-pone-0354346:
Adelle Holder, Henry DeBruin, and Jesse Sestito tackle a bottleneck in computer-aided design in this 2026 PLOS ONE methods paper. Bayesian optimisation searches for good designs by testing one candidate at a time, which wastes time when many tests could run in parallel. Existing parallel versions are usually built from scratch, ignoring a large library of proven one-at-a-time methods.

Their fix wraps any compatible sequential method in a penalty scheme that steers each batch of tests apart, so the batch covers fresh ground instead of repeating itself. Two converted methods matched established parallel tools on solution quality and beat them on real time. Designers gain a shortcut: upgrade familiar methods rather than rebuild them.
plos-pone-0355046:
Anh Dang Thuc Phan and five colleagues published this 2026 study of herbal medicine use among patients with long-term diseases in Vietnam. More than six hundred patients at two large hospitals described which herbal products they took and whether they told their doctors. The team then checked flagged herb and drug combinations against several interaction databases.

Many patients never disclosed their herbal use, and the databases often disagreed about the same combinations, leaving regional plants poorly covered. Phan calls for routine questions about herbs during care, better clinician training, and safety tools that include local botanical knowledge.
plos-pone-0355546:
Rebecca Gordon and co-authors use an adoption study to separate how parental stress reaches children through birth ties, womb environment, and daily rearing. Stress in parents can echo in children's self-control, but the pathway matters for any remedy. Their 2026 study follows families in a long-running adoption cohort where children were placed near birth.

The design links birth mothers' life stress to teenagers' effortful control through the children's daily cortisol rhythm, a stress-hormone pattern. It then asks whether adoptive mothers' or fathers' own stressful events strengthen or soften that chain. Because birth and rearing parents differ, genetic and prenatal routes can be told apart from household ones. The authors frame the work as a map for targeted family support.
plos-pone-0355646:
Yaxiang Gong, Jiafu Wen, and Wenqi Liu test in 2026 a new way to make a plant compound called puerarin dissolve better in water. Poor dissolving limits how well the compound can be taken by mouth. Their method melts the material while blasting it with sound, then checks the result with light tests and several tools that probe crystal shape and heat behaviour.

Treated puerarin dissolved more and faster, with smaller grains that tended to clump. Its crystal form changed to a water holding form, and part of it lost ordered structure altogether. The authors link the gain to those two changes and suggest the method could improve oral products.
plos-pone-0355846:
Debrup Ghosh and colleagues collected soils from twenty sites across the Indo-Gangetic Plain in India and watched how iron escapes from them over time under different moisture levels. Iron matters because crops there often go short of it even in iron-rich ground, since it locks into minerals that roots cannot use. Their 2026 incubation study paired release measurements with chemical models of iron's forms.

Wetter soil and longer incubation both changed how much iron came free. Acidic conditions and salt content held iron back, while clay-rich soil that holds more water released more. The findings help explain why iron fertilizer often disappoints in these soils and suggest moisture management as part of the fix for iron-hungry crops.
plos-pone-0355946:
Saadi M Saleh and a multinational team survey more than six thousand doctors across twelve Middle East and North African countries about chest pain. Doctors carry heavy stress and heart risk themselves, yet no large regional study had measured their own symptoms. A standard angina questionnaire sorted pain into definite and possible categories, and validated scales screened for anxiety and panic alongside work and health habits.

About one in eight doctors met the bar for definite angina-type pain, and nearly half reported possible angina-type pain, strikingly high for a working population. Panic disorder was the single strongest predictor, ahead of physical illness, lost sleep, anxiety, obesity, and female sex, and every kind of nicotine use added risk. Saleh and colleagues call physician chest pain a workforce warning, not just a personal one.
plos-pone-0356046:
The PLOS One Editors issued a retraction notice in 2026 for an article on AptaFluorescence, a fluorescent imaging protocol using aptamers, short DNA strands that bind targets, to visualize biomolecules. After publication, concerns were raised about figures two through four and the reliability of the reported fluorescence results.

Listed problems include partly overlapping figure panels, signal strengths that clash with raw image files, and missing exposure times, which makes signal comparisons hard to judge. The counts also rested on technical rather than biological repeats, with few images and cell counts varying widely. The first author admitted errors in preparing two figures and supplied a corrected one, while the editors record the concerns that led to retraction.
plos-pone-0356146:
Qin Yu and Tao Mai build a translation system aimed at the hardest words in English news. The targets are culturally loaded terms, metaphors, and institutional names. Such items lack support in training data. Such long-tail items drift in meaning or lose their cultural charge in standard machine translation. Their design first squeezes text into a sparse code. The code spotlights cultural elements. Then it rebuilds the translation step by step. A diffusion process does the rebuilding, guided by gates and a cultural knowledge base.

On long news sentences, the system beat three mainstream rivals on two standard quality scores. On unseen vocabulary, it kept accuracy and recall well above the baselines. So the authors report. Yu and Mai present the hybrid as a route to translations that carry culture, not just words.
plos-pone-0356246:
Ahmad Adawy and seven colleagues trace how a marker on white blood cells changes after liver surgery in mice, in this 2026 study. Neutrophils, the first-responder immune cells, can either injure the liver or help it regrow after part is removed. The team combined gene-activity data with direct cell measurement in mouse livers after seventy percent of the organ was removed. They focused on a surface protein called Cd14, which earlier screens had flagged in activated liver neutrophils.

Both the gene and the protein surged in liver neutrophils, peaking a day after surgery. The protein was linked to two signaling pathways known to drive liver cell division, which led the authors to identify it as a badge of a pro-regeneration neutrophil type. They propose Cd14 as a possible therapeutic target for boosting liver regrowth after surgery, while noting the finding comes from mouse work.
plos-pone-0356546:
Dominic Dankwah Agyei and colleagues surveyed 237 researchers in Ghana about diamond open access, the publishing model where neither readers nor authors pay. Their 2026 cross-sectional study asked what researchers know about the model, where they learned it, and how they judge its benefits, then looked for patterns by age, rank, institution, and qualifications.

Awareness was thin. Two thirds had never heard of diamond open access, over half had never published open access at all, and few could identify the standard open license. Most who knew the model heard of it from colleagues, not institutions. Knowledge rose with seniority and qualifications. The authors call on Ghanaian universities to teach open publishing properly and fund it, rather than leaving equity in publishing to chance.
plos-pone-0356646:
Rabina Baraili and co-authors brew silver nanoparticles using leaf and root extracts of a spiny shrub, aiming for a greener route to a useful material. Chemical recipes for such particles often leave harsh residues, while plant extracts can both form and coat them. The team confirmed particle formation by color change and light readings, then sized and mapped the particles with several instruments.

Leaf-made and root-made particles were both tiny and round, coated by plant compounds that kept them stable. Leaf particles fought oxidation best in a standard test, and both kinds blocked harmful bacteria strongly. A shrimp test showed the leaf version was also the more toxic of the two. Baraili and colleagues say the green recipe works, while dosing care will decide safe uses.
plos-pone-0356746:
Valia Pernidaki and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on fathers' mental health when a preterm birth threatens or happens. Mothers' distress in that situation is well documented; fathers are an afterthought. Just over one hundred men completed depression and anxiety scales during pregnancy and six weeks after the birth. They were sorted into a term-birth group and two risk groups: threatened preterm birth ending at term, and threatened ending early.

During pregnancy, fathers whose babies did arrive early carried clearly higher depression and anxiety than controls, while the threatened-but-term group showed weak signs of depression. Both risk groups had more men crossing the elevated-depression threshold than controls did. After birth, depression gaps closed, but anxiety stayed higher in the actual preterm group, and the threatened-but-term fathers sat in between. A threatened preterm birth alone, they conclude, marks a father for support.
plos-pone-0357046:
Qian Wen and co-authors design fast-settling equation systems for solving a broad class of balance problems in math, called mixed equilibrium problems. Such problems model fair points where competing effects cancel, from traffic to markets. Their systems are built to reach solutions fast. One reaches the answer within a finite time. The other reaches it within a time the user fixes in advance. Both hold no matter where the system starts, under stated conditions on the problem's shape.

The authors prove existence and uniqueness of the answer, show the underlying system is stable, and turn it into a step-by-step algorithm with steady convergence. Computer tests found the preset-time version fastest of the variants. An application to recovering sparse signals showed the method working outside pure theory. The paper is fully mathematical, aimed at optimization specialists.
plos-pone-0357146:
Senad Kolar and coauthors published a 2026 pilot study in PLOS ONE on whether autism evaluations by video still work when the connection is bad. Telehealth widens access to diagnosis, but a freezing screen could hide the fleeting behaviors assessors must catch. Using a fiber-optic test setup, the team created four freeze patterns by throttling the signal, then had blinded psychologists score children's videos under each degraded condition.

Scoring eroded gradually rather than collapsing. Past clear technical thresholds, freezes grew frequent. The items most at risk were the time-sensitive ones. Spontaneous joint attention, blending gaze with behavior, and echoed or unusual language were several times more likely to be marked unscorable. Yet overall scores stayed stable, no single item failed significance after correction, and raters agreed strongly under mild conditions. Video assessment is supported as a first-line option while connections stay above the identified thresholds, preferring wired links.
plos-pone-0357346:
Titilayo T Tajudeen led a team of four authors mapping retreating coastal forests, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Coastal forests are shrinking under pressure from storms, sea level rise, and land clearing. Satellites can track that retreat, but reading their images by hand is slow. The team applied convolutional neural networks to different kinds of satellite imagery.

Tajudeen's AI-generated maps give conservationists the retreat's true extent, free from guesswork. Comparing imagery types shows which source gives the most reliable map for the least cost. Coastal forests protect shorelines and store carbon, so their loss is a double blow. Timely maps let agencies target planting and protection where retreat is fastest, and prove losses that ground surveys would miss.
plos-pone-0357446:
Patrick Addo-Fordjour leads a national study of forest loss in Ghana covering the years from the mid twenty tens to the mid twenty twenties. Published in 2026, the work uses satellite images to map land cover across the whole country rather than a few reserves. That wider view matters because past estimates for Ghana varied a lot and left policy makers unsure of the scale of loss.

Ghana lost a large stretch of forest over the decade, and yearly loss sped up in the second half of the period. Farm growth caused most of the clearing, while mining caused a smaller share but grew fastest of all land uses. Addo-Fordjour and colleagues say the pattern threatens carbon storage and needs direct land-use action.
plos-pone-0358046:
Cleofé Peña-Gómez, Bernat Sunyer-Grau, and Marc Argilés studied how light color affects the brain, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Light does more than let us see; different wavelengths reach brain systems that control eye movement and attention. The team measured how exposure to different wavelengths changes activity in those cortical areas.

Peña-Gómez and her colleagues found wavelength-specific effects on the systems that aim the eyes and focus attention. That matters for lighting design in schools and offices, and for screen habits that fill evenings with blue-rich light. It also informs therapies that use light to shift alertness. The study adds brain-level evidence to a field often guided by comfort alone.
plos-pone-0358246:
Alejandro Leyva and M Khalid Khan Niazi subtyped pancreatic cancer patient by patient, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Pancreatic cancer needs finer subtypes if treatment is to be matched to each tumor. The pair integrated three data layers for each patient: RNA expression, methylation-based clues to replication timing, and the tumor's appearance under the microscope.

Leyva's multi-layer integration sorts tumors more precisely than any single data type could. Patient-specific subtyping matters because two tumors with the same name can behave very differently. Better sorting can guide trials, pairing each subtype with drugs aimed at its biology. Pancreatic cancer's poor outcomes make every gain in precision count, and integration methods like this are a plausible route.
plos-pone-0358546:
Margaret Wingerd and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about a gut parasite in pet cats. Giardia duodenalis infects domestic cats across the United States and Canada. The authors measure its prevalence and judge its zoonotic potential, the chance of it passing to people.

A parasite shared between cats and humans matters for households, especially where children or people with weak immunity live with pets. Prevalence figures tell veterinarians how often to expect this infection and test for it. Public health readers also gain from knowing how much of the human risk from Giardia plausibly comes through cats.
plos-pone-0358646:
Jingcong Li and three colleagues improve the neural networks that solve physics equations by teaching them where to concentrate, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Physics informed networks learn a solution while respecting the governing equation at sampled points, but they spread effort evenly and under learn the hard regions. Their system closes a feedback loop. The equation's own error at each point estimates how difficult that point is. That estimate stretches the physical constraint around hard points. It also shifts training weight toward them.

Tested across five network designs on three one dimensional problems, the method took the lowest error on every benchmark. It cut the runner up method's aggregate error by roughly a fifth to three fifths, depending on the problem. Higher dimensional and fluid test cases followed. The principle is portable: a solver that notices its own confusion can spend its budget where confusion lives.
plos-pone-0358746: Monfort Sanchez and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a low-cost way to check cell barriers. Labs often grow cells in a flat sheet to mimic the linings of the gut or lungs. The team tested cheap, clinic-approved glowing dyes as a way to judge whether those sheets stay sealed. A cheap, safe check could widen barrier testing in labs with small budgets.
plos-pone-0359346:
Maxime Colomb and Julien Perret published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It describes systematic modelling of building land use at large scale, enriched with historical detail. The work fuses massive and heterogeneous datasets, records from many sources that were never designed to fit together.

Land use histories tell planners how neighborhoods grew and which uses persisted or vanished. Building that record by hand for a whole city is impossible, so an automated, systematic model is the only route. Urban historians and planning offices are the readers who gain a past-aware map of building use from this fusion work.
plos-pone-0359546: Arteaga-Jordá and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a review on nurses and workplace change. The planned review will map how planned communication can strengthen nurses' sense of professional identity. That identity, in turn, is meant to drive cultural change inside health organizations. The protocol follows the JBI approach for scoping reviews. Clear plans help later readers trust the review's map.
plos-pone-0359646:
Jolinda Pollock and co-authors characterized in 2026 a strain of Escherichia coli bacteria taken from dairy bred calves that had fallen ill. The strain belongs to the O78 group and resembles types known for causing disease in poultry. The calves showed an atypical form of colisepticaemia, a blood infection by E. coli that usually follows a more familiar pattern.

The team describes the strain's traits in detail, including the fact that it resists multiple antibiotics. A poultry-like strain turning up in calves raises questions about how such bacteria move between animal species and through farm environments. Multidrug resistance in farm animals also matters beyond the farm, since resistance can travel through food chains and waste into wider circulation.
plos-pone-0359846: Sangsiwarit and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE lab study on blood disease and infection risk. They took neutrophils, a front-line white blood cell, from people with beta-thalassemia. Outside the body, they exposed those cells to Pythium insidiosum, a water mold that can cause severe illness. They then checked how the cells' working behavior changed. The results bear on why these patients may fight this infection poorly.
plos-pone-0359946:
Gideon Nwankwo and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on maternal healthcare in Nigeria. It studies what decides whether women keep using maternal care steadily, from pregnancy through delivery and beyond. The evidence comes from Nigeria's 2024 Demographic and Health Survey.

Many women start antenatal care but drop out before skilled delivery, breaking the continuum where risk peaks. National survey evidence shows which social and economic factors hold women in care or push them out. Nigerian health planners designing maternal programs are the readers who can act on those determinants.
pmc-10657446:
Naito and co-authors compare setup poses for a handheld hip navigation tool. The tool needs a 3D frame set while the patient lies in a set pose. Surgery itself ran with patients on their side. Early cases set the frame in the side pose. Later cases set the frame with patients on their backs.

The study held 129 cementless hip replacements in a row. Cup tilt error averaged 3 point 9 degrees for side setup. Back setup cut that error to 2 point 9 degrees. Front tilt error also fell, from 4 point 8 to 3 point 2 degrees. Safe zone rates matched at 94 and 95 percent.
pmc-10658946:
Hua Wang, Xiao-Li Hu, Qiu-Fang Li, Jie Zhou, and Ming-Yuan Wu report a two thousand twenty-three analysis of a mutual aid human milk bank for preterm infants. Donor milk protects fragile babies when mothers cannot supply enough. Matching supply, demand, and cost had not been documented for this model.

Four years of records covered more than thirteen hundred donors and roughly twenty-four hundred litres of qualified milk. Nearly all donors were mothers of preterm babies themselves. Recipients averaged about nine days on donor milk. Former recipients increasingly returned as donors, and gut complication rates in recipients fell across the period.
pmc-10670746:
Jian Li and seven co-authors give a quantum private comparison protocol that needs no shared key, built on GHZ-like states. Such protocols let two users check if their secrets match, with safety from quantum rules. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

Older plans first run a key sharing step, which costs time and quantum resources. The new plan codes secrets with unit steps instead. Decoy photons guard the channel against eavesdroppers. Its quantum efficiency reaches a high mark the authors cite. They claim gains over many past plans in both efficiency and resource use, with no key to share first.
pmc-10692146:
Joan Pous and co-authors published this study in 2023. It reveals a redox switch inside p38α, a stress-signaling protein. Hundreds of past structures showed this kinase in its reduced state, often with drugs or partners bound. The new work captures the oxidized state, where two sulfur-bearing residues link into an internal bridge. That bridge is conserved across vertebrates, hinting at a real job.

The bridge leaves the active site untouched. Instead, it partly unwinds a short helix and shifts the docking groove where partners attach. Flipping between the two states could tune the protein's activity with the cell's redox mood, beyond the known on-switch. The oxidized form also exposes a hidden pocket. The authors map that pocket as a fresh target for drug design against this much-studied kinase.
pmc-10693546:
Sakha Pezhhanfar, Mir Ali Farajzadeh, Mahdi Kheirkhah Ghaleh, and two colleagues debut a new absorbent material for chemical analysis in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Their study is the first to apply the metal-organic framework MIL-68, built with gallium, to a test method. The task is pulling out and concentrating parabens, common preservatives, from mouthwash and hydrating gel samples before measurement. Test settings were tuned and performance figures noted, with computer modeling used to explain the uptake process.

The workflow treats the parabens, loads them onto a few milligrams of the framework, then releases them into methanol for gas chromatography with flame detection. Enrichment factors reached two hundred to three hundred thirty, with recoveries of forty to sixty-six percent. A clear plus is that the material absorbs both treated and untreated parabens, sparing an extra step. A software check of the method's green impact accompanies the chemistry.
pmc-10699646:
Anthony Ochen and co-authors wrote a study from 2023 on family planning use among Ugandan women and what drives it. Use sat near thirty percent in 2020, the lowest in East Africa, despite government pushes. The team mined the 2016 national demographic and health survey, which interviewed over eighteen thousand women of childbearing age across all fifteen regions. They modeled which traits came with current use of any method, and of modern methods.

About twenty-nine percent used some method, and twenty-seven percent used a modern one. Use climbed with age, peaking in the early forties. Schooling mattered: women with secondary schooling used at nearly twice the odds of those without. The richest households showed a similar lift. Simply knowing methods exist also raised the odds. The authors point to schooling, household wealth, and plain awareness as the levers to pull.
pmc-10700046:
Antje Chiu-Werner and Menna Jones studied how land use reshapes mammal diets in Tasmania in a 2023 paper. Native and invasive species share landscapes changed by farming and forestry. What each animal eats shows how those pressures rewire food webs.

The team examined nine native and two invasive mammal species across six regions and several land uses. They read diets two ways: DNA in droppings and chemical isotopes in blood. Smaller species' diets varied by region, with land use refining the menu further. Isotope patterns in predators and omnivores also tracked land use. Studying many species at once reveals community-level shifts that single-species work would miss.
pmc-10701946:
A Polish surgical team led by L. Bobrzynski tests ways to define a textbook outcome after stomach cancer surgery, in a twenty twenty-three paper. A textbook outcome means every part of care went as hoped, from full tumor removal to a smooth recovery. Many definitions exist, and the team asked which one best predicts survival. They reviewed records of 1,743 patients treated at two academic centers.

A definition that joined ten measures of full removal and smooth recovery fit the data best. Patients who met it lived a median of about sixty-nine months, against twenty for those who did not. The edge held after age, health, and tumor facts were counted. The team also built a chart to predict who will reach a textbook outcome.
pmc-10704046:
Bibi Sumera Keenoo reflects on professionalism in medical education in a 2023 essay. As a medical educationalist, she trains future clinicians to be competent and ethical. Professionalism, she writes, is the bedrock of that formation.

She uses Gibbs' reflective model to work through her experiences. One incident drives the piece: a student spoke disrespectfully to a classmate, showing little empathy. The moment stirred disappointment and worry about the culture of the setting. She weighs what such episodes taught her about values in training. The essay closes with strategies to foster respect, compassion, and collaboration.
pmc-10704646:
Yatao Wu, Xiuli Luo, Pan Chen, and Fang Zhang test how two unusual call features in female frogs differently affect male vocal behaviour. Their 2023 playback study uses a torrent frog species whose females, unusually, call often and richly.

Female calls contain frequency jumps and subharmonic components, both products of nonlinear voice production. Males were played calls of each type while their answering behaviour was recorded. Calls with subharmonics drew more short and answering calls from males. Calls with frequency jumps instead triggered more staccato calls. Most males answered first with short calls regardless of type. Approaching males switched call types depending on which feature they heard, showing distinct functions for each.
pmc-10704746:
Tyler Kozisek, Luke Samuelson, Andrew Hamann, and Angela Pannier compared four ways to load two working genes into human stem cells without using viruses, in this 2023 study. Stem cells from fat and marrow are hard to modify, yet pairs of genes could let them attack diseases with two drivers at once. The team tried separate gene packages, in one or two delivery particles, plus single packages that carry both genes in one string.

Getting both genes on at once proved hard by any route, well below single-gene success. Two designs did clearly better: separate packages bundled into one particle, and one package using a self-cutting linker between the genes. The ranking held across donors and tissue sources, giving builders a tested starting point.
pmc-10707646:
Klaudia Marek and co-authors wrote a review from 2023 on the crowded shelf of scales and tools for judging hand recovery after stroke. Stroke can leave a hand paralyzed, weak, floppy, or stiff, and many measures claim to track the return of function. Yet no shared guidance tells clinicians which to pick. Teams choose by habit, and some still use home-grown scores that were never verified.

The review sorts the measures by what they test and flags the ones that add objectivity, including chart-based readouts. Proven devices anchor the field: muscle signal recorders, joint angle gauges, and grip strength meters. Newer trends add camera-based pose tracking, artificial intelligence, and custom grip sensors. Scales first proven in bone and joint surgery are crossing over to stroke care. The authors aim the map at adults in rehab and the teams who must defend their outcome claims.
pmc-10709646:
Max Winokan, Louie Slocombe, Jim Al-Khalili, and Marco Sacchi simulated how a bacterial enzyme guards DNA against a sneaky source of mutation, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Protons hopping across a base pair's bonds can flip it into a rare form that mispairs at copying. Earlier models said the flip is feasible but fleeting, and they ignored the machinery around the DNA.

Their multi-scale simulations placed the base pair inside the helicase that unwinds DNA before copying. The protein setting raised the energy cost of the flip sharply, shifting the balance back to the normal form. They argue the action is dominated by quantum tunneling, with no reshaping of the surroundings. One protein residue emerges as a quiet guardian against mutation.
pmc-10712946:
Pooja Joshi and four co-authors test whether blocking a calcium channel in heart cells can stop sudden death in failing hearts. Sudden death from fast, chaotic heart beats is a top cause of death, and current drugs help too little. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

The team used guinea pigs whose heart failure mirrors key signs in people, with long heart signal times and leaky calcium channels. Sick animals got the drug dantrolene or a placebo, early or later in illness. The authors tracked chaotic beats, sudden death, heart signals, and pump strength. Blocking the channel cut calcium leak and uneven recovery, and helped the heart work better.
pmc-10714646:
Junping Ye and a large team study identical twins who differ in mental illness in this two thousand twenty-three paper. One twin may develop schizophrenia or bipolar disorder while the other does not. Since the twins share their genes, such gaps hint at chemical marks on DNA. The mark in focus is a modified base called 5hmC, which helps control gene activity. The team asked whether this mark leans toward one copy of a gene.

They combined a method that labels the mark with full genome reads from blood. Samples came from twin pairs split by these disorders. Shifts in the mark at control regions tracked with the twins' differing traits. The study links epigenetic marks to genetic variants in a new way. It may help explain why identical genomes can yield unlike minds.
pmc-10715646:
Gebremeskel and Gebretatios probe why HIV-positive women miss cervix screening in Ethiopia. Cervix cancer is the second top cancer harm for women there. Screening use stays low in the study zone despite that toll. The team sought traits that set screened and unscreened women apart.

The study ran in public hospitals in the Tigray central zone. It held 400 unscreened cases and 400 screened controls. All women were HIV-positive and in hospital care. Forms logged health, home, and clinic facts for each woman. Traits that tracked with screening were weighed in the pool. Results may guide outreach to lift screening rates.
pmc-10716246:
Marcela Gómez and eight colleagues published a mosquito virus survey in two thousand twenty-three in the Colombian Orinoco. Mosquitoes carry viruses that threaten people, plus others that infect only insects. Rural savanna where people, livestock, and wildlife mix is under-surveyed.

Long-read sequencing profiled viruses in six mosquito genera of public health interest. Insect-only viruses dominated the mix, led by one family across all samples. A shared core set of insect viruses appeared in every species. One of them made up nearly nine tenths of the virus signal in a single Culex species. The authors frame the catalogue as a baseline for spotting disease-carrying viruses early in this region.
pmc-10716946:
Cox and co-authors set out a protocol to review all gene studies in critically ill patients. Intensive care patients vary widely in traits, course, and outcomes. Gene differences may explain part of that spread and reveal patient subgroups.

The review will search PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for matching studies. It will follow the HuGE Review Handbook for methods and reporting. Any gene study of adults admitted acutely to medical or surgical intensive care counts. Two reviewers will screen studies and judge bias risk on their own. The final piece will chart study designs and patient groups.
pmc-10718446:
Charlotte Skau Pawlowski and co-authors wrote a 2023 scoping review of how playgrounds shape children's basic movement skills, such as balance, running, throwing, and catching. Those skills run low in children in rich countries, and playgrounds may help build them. The team searched four databases and kept 14 studies that fit their rules.

The studies point to design lessons. Playgrounds should mix features that train balance, climbing, throwing, and catching, so each skill gets practice. Spreading features across a wide area gives each child room and makes children travel between features, which builds running skills. Natural play settings may help as well. The authors warn that the evidence is still thin and call for stronger studies with standard skill tests.
pmc-10726346:
Lukáš Kývala and three co-authors simulate how single missing atoms wander and merge in phosphorene, a one-atom-thick phosphorus sheet. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Defects shape what two-dimensional materials can do, and they are usually plentiful.

Direct quantum simulations are too slow to watch defects move for long. The team trained neural network models on quantum data, keeping near-quantum accuracy at a fraction of the cost. Their microsecond-long runs show single vacancies racing along the zigzag direction of the sheet, not the crosswise one. That matches the energy barriers for each hop. Vacancies that meet fuse into double vacancies, which sit more stably and barely move. Several merging paths turned up, some with short-lived middle forms.
pmc-10728046:
Yoon, Park, and Roh pooled evidence on fixing thigh bone fractures that occur around hip replacement stems in twenty twenty-three. These periprosthetic fractures are a common complication of hip arthroplasty. The Vancouver system sorts them by pattern; B1 and B2 types differ in whether the implant is loose, which affects whether plate fixation alone suffices.

The team combined ten comparative studies head-to-head and thirty-nine studies in a proportional analysis. Reoperation risk, nonunion, and deep infection did not differ significantly between the two patterns. Pooled reoperation rates were about nine percent for B1 and eight percent for B2, with nonunion at four percent in both. The authors conclude open reduction and internal fixation is a feasible treatment for both fracture types with acceptable complication rates.
pmc-10729046:
Dan-Yang Wang and co-authors lay out a trial plan testing whether a chest wall nerve block protects the aging brain after lung surgery, in a protocol from two thousand twenty-three. Confusion and memory slips often follow big surgery in older patients, and pain is a suspected driver. The block numbs the chest wall and has eased pain after chest operations.

About two hundred fifty-six older patients at one Shanghai hospital will be split by chance into block and standard care. Brain trouble within a week is the main measure, with pain and recovery scores beside it. Three-month brain checks and blood sugar tests round out the plan.
pmc-10730146:
Meade and six co-authors reviewed gut microbiome markers of response to advanced therapies in inflammatory bowel disease in twenty twenty-three. Many patients lose response to these drugs over time. Stool microbes measured before treatment might predict who will do well, guiding precision care.

Earlier reviews linked microbes to disease activity, but this one focused on prediction before response is judged. Recurring themes included plentiful bacteria that make short-chain fatty acids, which feed the gut lining. Opportunistic bacteria also mattered, as did pathways for making butyrate, a key fatty acid. Other candidate markers included bile acids, amino acids, and fats. Gut fungi and viruses were covered as newer frontiers. The authors present these themes as leads for future biomarkers.
pmc-10733946:
Srujan Basavapura Ravikumar and co-authors published this sensor study in 2023. They built an electric sensor to measure risperidone, a drug used for psychosis, in tablet samples. The sensing layer is a double perovskite, a crystal with the formula Sm2CuZrO6, made by a gel route. Such crystals pass charge fast and can speed the reactions a sensor reads.

Tests with several scan methods confirmed the crystal's build and its electric traits. The sensor read the drug across a wide low range, down to a very small floor, with keen sensitivity. It picked the drug out from other stuff, held steady, and gave like readings on repeat runs. On real tablets it found the drug with sound recovery rates. The authors offer the sensor as a cheap check for drug quality.
pmc-10735346:
Martha Abshire Saylor, Cynthia Boyd, Sydney Dy, and Valecia Hanna look at the ethics of advance care planning talks, in this two thousand twenty-three presentation. Advance care planning counts, but primary care visits with older adults who have dementia and other complex conditions leave room for it, squeezing its logistical and ethical hard parts. Dilemmas map onto the four principles of ethics (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice), and proof to guide clinicians and families is scarce.

The team drew on the SHARE trial, which recorded and wrote out planning talks among trained facilitators, ninety-two patients with severe cognitive impairment (mean age eighty-eight years), and their family caregivers. The team coded the talks for ethical points, in a qualitative way, and read the themes. The talk reports the themes, aiming to widen practice for leading talks, guided by medical ethics and a health care system frame.
pmc-10735846:
Alyssa Aguirre and six co-authors test how well ChatGPT answers real questions from dementia caregivers, in a 2023 study. Caregivers often post questions about daily care, memory loss, and confusion on social media. The team picked twenty-five such posts that stood for common needs. They fed each post to the chatbot in March 2023 and saved the replies for scoring.

Three clinicians with long experience in dementia care scored each reply on four points. They checked facts, grasp of the main need, useful steps, and follow-up advice. Most replies earned full marks, and the rest lost just one point. The authors call the quality high but note the small sample and narrow topic range. A larger test is planned in their wider project.
pmc-10736246:
Researchers studied whether well-educated adult children go with healthier older parents in a 2023 paper. Family advantage is usually traced from parent to child, but help may flow back up the generations. The study used linked panel data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe, covering 2004 to 2020.

The sample held nearly 90,000 parents aged fifty or more across 29 countries, tied to their children in over 200,000 pairs. Parents whose children had more schooling scored lower on a forty-item frailty index. The link was strongest among parents with little schooling of their own, above all mothers. The authors suggest that public spending on the young may pay health dividends to the old.
pmc-10736446:
Mushira Khan and Ajla Basic published a study in 2023 on mindful aging in South Asian American older adults, a population among the fastest growing in the United States, yet relatively understudied. The study uses a framework blending four prominent theories of later life with mindfulness practices.

The researchers interviewed thirty-two community-dwelling adults aged fifty or older. Major changes marked their later years: adjusting to life after a spouse's death, a perceived loss of role and status in the family, reduced finances, and limited mobility from emerging health problems. Despite those changes, most expressed an overall sense of peace and gratitude. They viewed aging as a natural path that brings wisdom. They maintained ties through phone applications, volunteered at their places of worship, and helped adult children with housework and child care. A lack of culturally fitting activities to join was the main barrier they named.
pmc-10736646:
Ashwin Kotwal and five co-authors link social isolation with self-neglect among older adults in a 2023 national survey study. Self-neglect, poor care of one's body and home, may signal needs that relationships would normally meet. The team used a large 2015 survey of Americans living at home, with in-person checks of personal and household condition.

Among more than thirty-six hundred older adults, isolation was scored from household contact, network ties, and community activity. For women, isolation came with clearly higher odds of both body neglect and household neglect. For men, no such link appeared. The authors ask why the risk splits by gender and suggest that stronger social ties could help prevent neglect in women.
pmc-10737146:
Renae Smith-Ray and co-authors studied pharmacist help for older adults in a 2023 paper on drug adherence. High blood pressure, high blood fats, and type 2 diabetes are common in older Americans, yet many do not take their drugs as told. Poor adherence links to more deaths, more care use, and higher costs.

The team tracked a large drug store chain's program where pharmacists stepped in to aid adherence. Patients were Medicare drug plan members aged 65 or more with fills for at least one of the three ills. Good adherence meant drugs were on hand at least 80 percent of days. A before-and-after contrast with a matched group showed the help lined up with better adherence.
pmc-10737646:
Janelle Fassi wrote this conference paper, published in 2023, about an online activity that paired younger and older adults during the COVID-19 pandemic. The study asked whether meeting across generations online could soften ageism on both sides.

Sixteen older adults and fifteen younger adults took part in the virtual activity. A smaller group filled in ageism surveys before and after. Older adults' biased views toward younger adults dropped in a clear way. Views toward older adults did not shift in the survey scores. Written answers told a warmer story, with both groups reporting more respect and fewer stereotypes. Fassi notes the activity is workable, but a larger group is needed to prove its effect.
pmc-10738146:
Margarita Maria Osuna and Jennifer Ailshire introduce a set of studies on health and aging in Latin America, from twenty twenty-three. Aging there is fast, and it comes with high poverty and low schooling for many older adults. The studies cover four large middle-income countries in the region.

One study links early-life conditions to health in old age in Brazil. Another compares thinking scores for men and women in Mexico and the United States. A third looks at healthy life span for Indigenous people in Chile. The last compares self-reported and measured health in Colombia. Together they show which groups face the poorest health in later life.
pmc-10738546:
Hae Sagong, Myoung-Gi Chon, and Pao-Feng Tsai explore frailty among older Korean American immigrants in a 2023 study. Older immigrants face language barriers, low health literacy, and care systems unlike those back home. The team asked what shapes frailty in this group.

They interviewed nine older adults in Lee County, Alabama, where Korean health services are limited. The talks covered health literacy, activity, diet, and mental health, and standard tests added background detail. Health literacy scores differed sharply between the Korean and English test versions. The analysis found seven themes, including limits on social life, health habits, and doctor visits from language and a new care system.
pmc-10738646:
Tian Qiu, Daniel Elbich, Jessie Alwerdt, and Jonathan Hakun test whether sitting harms thinking differently depending on the timescale. They combined two weeks of ecological momentary assessment with thigh-worn activity monitors in 161 adults aged nineteen to eighty-eight. Cognition was probed six times daily with ultra-brief processing speed and working memory tasks.

Moment to moment, more sedentary time meant slower processing speed for participants over sixty-five, and swapping sitting for walking or standing helped briefly. Across days, however, more sedentary days came with better processing speed and working memory in both age groups. Cross-sectionally there was no association at all. The authors argue sedentary behavior's cognitive effects flip sign with timescale, complicating blanket advice.
pmc-10740846:
Xiuwen Guo and eight colleagues published a computer vision paper in two thousand twenty-three on classifying wound images. Sorting wound types automatically feeds online diagnosis tools. Standard neural networks mix fine texture and broad shape in the same layers, losing information.

Their network splits the job: one branch hunts high-frequency detail and texture using proven backbones, while a second extracts low-frequency structure with custom dilated blocks. A fusion module merges both streams for the final call. Accuracy reached ninety-eight percent for two-class sorting, ninety-two for three classes, and about eighty-three for four. The authors say the design beats earlier state-of-the-art methods on all three tasks.
pmc-10740946:
A team including Kinga Mazurkiewicz-Zapałowicz tests whether fungi that kill insects can slow a pig parasite's eggs. The parasite, a large roundworm, spreads through eggs that grow in soil. The team kept the eggs with five fungal species for four weeks and watched their growth under a microscope. None of the fungi killed the eggs or grew on their shells.

Three species did slow egg growth for the first two weeks. One species made the widest range of enzymes that break down tissue. The paper weighs the fungi as a mild brake on the worm, not a cure.
pmc-10741846:
Sabrina Rossi and co-authors reviewed immunotherapy for small-cell lung cancer in two thousand twenty-three. The disease responds well to chemotherapy at first, and adding immunotherapy gave a small survival gain in key trials. Many questions remain, including where radiotherapy fits.

Two common markers, PD-L1 and tumor mutation burden, have not proven reliable for picking responders, the authors find. A newer split of the disease by key transcription factors may explain behavior better, but clinical use is still far off. The review weighs patient traits and possible biomarkers that could identify who benefits most. The authors call the era mixed, with more shadows than light so far.
pmc-10741946:
Ella Bruun and seven co-authors compare grip strength in young adults born early versus on time in a 2023 study. Being born preterm links to weaker muscles and more illness across life. Hand grip is a simple, trusted gauge of muscle strength for such checks.

The study enrolled thirty-eight preterm-born adults and thirty-nine matched peers. Grip ranks fell below average far more often in the preterm group. Within that group, women showed notably weaker grips than men. Vitamin D levels were measured, and the team repeated testing after a year of supplements. The work tests whether the vitamin closes any of the strength gap. Early results frame preterm birth as a lasting factor in adult fitness.
pmc-10742046:
Alexey Pigolev and co-authors published this wheat study in 2023. Emmer wheat is a nourishing old grain, but dry spells hurt it. Jasmonates are plant stress hormones. The team gave emmer two genes from a model plant that make the hormone's building blocks. Plants with either gene made more of the active hormone when their leaves were wounded.

Oddly, one gene's boost did not raise the early hormone stock in the leaf's green parts, hinting it was used up fast. Both plant lines grew alike: the first leaves ran short, the fourth ran long. Both also bore dry, salty stress from a lab drought agent better than plain plants. The authors say tuning a crop's own hormone output is a workable path to hardier grain.
pmc-10743146:
Guillermo Ripoll, Begoña Panea, and María Ángeles Latorre study, in twenty twenty-three, how consumers perceive the color of dry-cured ham, and what counts as a just noticeable difference. Color drives buying decisions for cured meats. Ham slices were measured instrumentally and photographed. Consumers scored and matched the photos, and reported their food involvement, familiarity with cured ham, and background traits. Consumers were clustered by involvement level, and the noticeable difference threshold was computed per cluster. An interpretable machine learning method linked visual scores to instrument readings.

The threshold came out at a color distance of about six units, lower for younger people. Involvement also shifted it. Machine learning beat plain regression when psychographic traits were included. Lightness and hue angle were the most important color variables.
pmc-10745446:
Courteney Hamilton and Marc Bomhof test, in a 2023 study, whether a fiber added to a drink after exercise can curb appetite and later eating. Fiber of this type is known to shift gut hormones tied to fullness. Volunteers did a forty-five minute evening workout, then drank sweetened milk with or without the fiber.

Hunger ratings fell more after the fiber drink than after plain sweetened milk. Blood tests showed rises in two fullness hormones and a drop in a hunger hormone after exercise with fiber. Next-morning breakfast intake tended to be lower, though not clearly. Gas ratings rose, so the benefit came with a mild gut side effect.
pmc-10747046:
Victor Huarcaya leads a team on a tiny dual laser sensor for space missions. Their work from twenty twenty-three deals with precise motion sensing. Future Earth watch missions could gain from such sharp tools.

Laser readout can sense shifts far below a picometer. That beats the best charge based sensing by a wide margin. Sharp sensing needs laser tone noise cut by huge factors. The team built the sensor on one compact glass block. A fiber feed and a known design form the set up. Better motion sensors could aid climate and water work.
pmc-10747146:
Conor Cristant and co-authors test whether squirting silicone, rather than pouring it, makes cleaner MRI test phantoms. Phantoms mimic body tissue so scanners can be calibrated. Poured silicone traps air bubbles that spoil the fake tissue. A twin-syringe extruder laid down samples at varied speeds and nozzle sizes.

Void share shifted with the extrusion settings, as hoped. More voids dragged the T1 relaxation time down in a clear inverse pattern. Dielectric traits and T2 times were logged beside the void counts. Extruded samples held fewer bubbles than poured ones overall. The setup points to bubble-light phantoms built on demand.
pmc-10755846:
Yu Ma and colleagues reported in 2023 the first X-ray-driven pyroelectric effect in a single ferroelectric material. Pyroelectric materials turn temperature swings from absorbed light into electric signals, which suits self-powered detectors and imagers. The effect was well known under visible light, but reaching it with X-rays had proved hard and rare. The team's material is a layered perovskite built from lead, bromine, and two organic parts, with strong built-in polarization.

Under X-rays the material answered with no outside power at all. Its sensitivity reached 225 microcoulombs per gray per square centimeter, and it could sense doses near 83 nanograys per second. That floor sits about sixty-six times below the level medical imaging requires. The authors present the result as a new mode for X-ray detection and a guide for future light-sensing devices.
pmc-10757146:
Izel Yilmaz and co-authors examine killer T cells taken from the lymph nodes that drain breast tumors, in a 2023 study. A T cell's working state decides how well a patient answers immune therapy. Immune responses start in these nearby nodes, yet most testing uses blood samples instead, which may miss the local picture.

Using many-color cell sorting on fresh node and blood samples, the team profiled the cells' surface markers. The nodes held a distinct set of killer T cells rich in two markers, PD-1 and CXCR5. Cells carrying both, often with two more markers, looked like worn-out helper-style cells. Most of them bore the marks of central memory cells. Only small shares carried two other checkpoint markers. The authors argue that nodes, not just blood, should be sampled when judging a patient's immune state.
pmc-10797346:
Visona and seven co-authors measure asbestos burden in lungs of women exposed outside work near an Italian plant, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Women in Italy show high mesothelioma rates from home and environmental exposure. Lung fiber data for women were scarce. The team examines lungs of forty-two women who died of mesothelioma near Broni.

Samples come from forensic autopsies and are read by electron microscopy with chemical analysis. Six samples show no asbestos at all. Amosite is the most common type, ahead of crocidolite and chrysotile. Home plus environmental exposure yields higher burdens than environment alone. Burden rises with exposure duration and disease latency. The authors warn that clearance skews readings, above all for chrysotile.
pmc-10800546:
Qinmengge Li and co-authors present a study whose head gives the year as 2023. The catalog lists it under 2024. The topic is the company that skin diseases keep. Insurance claims databases transformed data handling, yet nobody had mined one systematically for skin disease pairings. The team studies fourteen skin and skin-related conditions. Their data cover thirteen million skin patients plus two million sampled controls. Records span 2001 to 2018 in a de-identified US claims warehouse.

A case-control design tests which diseases travel with each skin condition. Changes in those links over time are tracked, along with demographic patterns. Dermatologists get a population-scale comorbidity map. Shared pairings hint at shared causes; unique ones warn of specific risks. Screening guidance can follow the map: which skin patients merit checks for which hidden diseases. Claims data lack lab detail, but scale exposes links no clinic cohort could.
pmc-10811046:
Zanelli and a large team review the rare pairing of two genetic marks in blood cancers in twenty twenty-three. One mark defines classic chronic myeloid leukemia. The other drives its Philadelphia negative kin. Long thought to exclude each other, they sometimes co occur.

The pair can show at once, or surface in sequence under treatment. Their mix fools clinicians into reading progress or drug failure where neither holds. Two fresh cases from the authors' practice anchor the review. Clues from clinic, lab, and marrow signs are laid out. Clone interplay and outcomes close the survey.
pmc-10811146:
Rogelio Puente-Diaz and Judith Cavazos-Arroyo study how the kind of gift people receive shapes gratitude, in work published in 2023. Gifts of experiences, such as trips or meals, differ from material gifts, such as objects. The authors ask whether experience gifts feel more supportive of a person's freedom and values, and whether that feeling raises gratitude.

In the first study, people who recalled an experience gift rated it as more autonomy supportive than a material gift, and that rating linked to stronger gratitude. A second study found that recalling a gift matched to one's true values beat recalling an ordinary gift on both counts. A third study tested whether the giver's motives change the effect. The work applies a theory of basic human needs to gift giving.
pmc-10822946:
Yexin Mao, writing alone in 2024, weighs why two lands ruled by vote hit back at COVID-19 in such unlike ways. He sets the United States next to South Korea in a case study built on a most-like plan.

Both are rich lands ruled by vote with strong health care, which makes their split paths a puzzle. Data came from state texts, state web sites, words by heads of state, and from press and school work, with each source checked next to the rest. Traits of the head, of state rules, and of shared life shaped how heads led in the crunch and how much folk stood as one. Head style and the shape of rule swayed how sense was made, how calls were made, and how work was lined up. Shared and state life shaped that oneness, and that shaped how well the crunch was dealt with.
pmc-10827846:
Huimin Yin, Qi Zhang, Yi Li, and Jun Ma published a 2024 study of severe anxiety in people hospitalized for the first time with major depression who also had abnormal blood fats. Anxiety often travels with depression and blood fat problems, and the three interact in complicated ways. The team examined more than seven hundred such patients.

About one in nine patients had severe anxiety. A past suicide attempt, being female, higher body weight, worse depression and symptom scores, and one thyroid hormone level were each linked with severe anxiety. Naming these risk factors helps hospital teams spot depressed patients who most need anxiety screening and support.
pmc-10844946:
Gouyang Bai and colleagues test whether contrast ultrasound numbers can judge rectal cancer treatment response. Their retrospective study from twenty twenty-four covers eighty-three patients. Pre-surgery chemoradiation shrinks locally advanced rectal tumours. Knowing who responded completely changes surgical planning.

All patients had contrast ultrasound and later full tumour removal. Pathology divided them into complete and incomplete responders. Only twelve achieved complete response in the series. Ultrasound parameters and a blood marker differed between groups. A cutoff value for predicting complete response was derived. Survival outcomes were analysed against the imaging groups. Non-invasive response checks could spare some patients bigger surgery.
pmc-10845046:
Chun Huang and co-authors build molecular circuits that compute powers using a new coding scheme for DNA. The paper is listed as 2024 in the catalog, but the text itself says it was published in 2023. DNA strand displacement is a known way to build tiny circuits from DNA, yet speed and scale remain hard.

Their scheme codes DNA domains under clear rules, so strands have a regular structure. A module with a set number of inputs can carry out many logic functions, which cuts design effort. They built square root and exponentiation circuits to test scale. Simulations showed faster response, simpler structure, and better scaling than a rival dual-track design. The method aims at molecular control systems that can grow more complex without becoming unworkable.
pmc-10862046:
Veena HR and co-authors tested a new way to deliver curcumin, the active part of turmeric, against gum disease germs in the lab. Their study was published in 2023. Long use of standard chemical rinses for gum disease can cause side effects, but plain curcumin dissolves poorly in water, which limits its use.

The team packed a self-mixing form of curcumin into a gel-like carrier designed to hold it at the target site. In dishes, the system stopped four kinds of gum germs at low doses, though a standard antibiotic still worked at lower doses still. Lower doses in the carrier did not clear a visible zone on test plates. Even so, the authors see promise in the slow-release design as an add-on for gum care.
pmc-11230146:
Hasan and co-authors check whether simpler lab tests can stand in for the gold standard when judging antifungal drugs against Rhizopus, the fungus behind mucormycosis. That disease surged with COVID-19, and treatment leans on knowing which drug still works. The team tested 127 isolates from two Rhizopus groups.

They compared disc diffusion and E-test strips against the reference broth method. The E-test agreed more closely overall. For the main species, agreement ran from about 92 to 99 percent across four drugs, highest for posaconazole. Disc tests tracked the reference too, just less tightly. The authors back the E-test as a practical stand-in.
pmc-11571646:
Josef Finsterer writes a letter to the editor disputing the label put on a case of Guillain-Barré syndrome after chikungunya infection. The letter appeared in twenty twenty-four. The case involved a young woman who needed breathing support for two weeks and worsened before improving on immune treatment.

Finsterer argues the nerve tests showed both fiber damage and insulation damage, which clashes with the purely fiber type named in the report. He notes that the chikungunya-linked form of the syndrome is most often the insulation type. In one outbreak study he cites, over half of patients had that type. His letter presses the authors to resolve the mismatch. It also raises further points on the patient's course and care.
pmc-11574246:
Tuğçe Kalefetoğlu Macar and Oksal Macar test a plant extract against metal poisoning in onion roots. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, uses vanadium, a metal whose industry use raises pollution risk. The test plant is the common onion, a standard lab model. Saint John's wort extract is the proposed shield, tried at two strengths.

Vanadium harmed growth, split rates, and cell health across the board. It also raised markers of oxidative stress and broke chromosomes. Extract-only groups matched the clean control group on all measures. When extract and metal were given together, the harm eased. Chemical scans list the plant compounds behind the effect.
pmc-11576846:
Zhidong Shi and co-authors present a 2024 study on two giant structures sitting at the base of Earth's mantle. These provinces, where seismic waves slow down, are the largest features inside the planet, yet their age and origin are debated. Geology hints they have stayed put for at least 200 million years.

The team simulated mantle convection with plate-like motion. Their model grew a Pacific-style ring of sinking material and two opposite basal piles resembling the real provinces. If the piles are chemical as well as hot, they creep about four times slower than the surrounding mantle. If purely hot, they move at normal speed. The sluggish chemical version fits the long stability that the geology suggests.
pmc-11579046:
Machi Suka and colleagues survey food aversions during outpatient chemotherapy. Their one-year prospective study from twenty twenty-four covers many cancer types. Chemotherapy can turn once-liked foods repellent. How often that happens, and how much it disrupts life, needed fresh numbers.

About two hundred forty patients answered food questionnaires at each visit. One in four developed a food aversion during treatment. A quarter of those patients reported daily life interference from eating problems. Aversions appeared at a median of about six weeks after starting therapy. Women and patients with digestive cancers faced higher rates. Nutrition teams can use the timing to plan early support.
pmc-11579746:
Tongbin Liu and four colleagues review bone scaffolds built from a biodegradable plastic, mussel-inspired coating, and metal particles, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Bone regeneration scaffolds must invite cells, resist bacteria, and eventually disappear. Polycaprolactone is a workable base polymer.

Polydopamine, the adhesive chemistry mussels use, coats the scaffold to improve its biological welcome. Metal nanoparticles loaded into it add antibacterial power and steer cell behavior. The review covers synthesis, protein deposition, shape variations, and matrix interactions, plus performance in cell and animal tests. Challenges for polymer-metal hybrids are cataloged frankly. The field's goal is an off-the-shelf scaffold that surgeons can trust in infected or large defects.
pmc-11584646:
Feng-Ming Zhao and others forecast lithium battery health with neural networks in 2024. Safe long battery use needs health tracking. Knowing remaining life is just as key. Voltage, current, and heat were inputs. Cycle means kept the data even. A hybrid network design was put forward.

Pattern and memory layers were joined here. Focus helped the model focus better. Life prediction error hit near zero. Scores stayed very high overall. Rival hybrid models did worse clearly. The new model also held steadier. EV batteries could benefit at once. Grid storage watching is another use.
pmc-11585546:
Gagandeep Singh and a large team of co-authors show, in a 2024 mouse study, that prior infection cuts both ways. It can protect against a later COVID variant in one genetic strain and worsen disease in another. Two female mouse lines were first exposed to a milder variant or to flu. Thirty days later both faced a severe variant.

Prior mild-variant infection shielded the engineered line but aggravated illness in the wild-type line. Prior flu protected only the wild-type line. The harmed line's lungs flooded with inflammatory signals, while the protected line's profile looked like a first infection. Antibody strength did not explain the split. Instead, a lung immune cell population had been remodeled differently in the two lines, antiviral in one and pro-inflammatory in the other. The authors say genetic background writes the reinfection script.
pmc-11585646:
Mohamed Awad and eleven colleagues traced how a bone drug can starve healing jawbone of new blood vessels, illuminating a feared side effect. Zoledronate blocks osteoclast development; some patients on such drugs develop jawbone death after dental trauma. The team's hypothesis: precursor osteoclasts normally signal blood vessels to grow into injured alveolar bone, using a chemokine pathway. Zoledronate silences that signal. Lab tests confirmed the drug lowered the signal in precursor cells.

Medium from untreated precursors pushed vessel cells to migrate and form tubes; the drug disrupted that crosstalk. Imaging of injured mouse jawbone showed reduced blood perfusion after zoledronate. The twenty twenty-four mechanism reframes jaw osteonecrosis: not just too little bone turnover, but a broken conversation between bone cells and blood vessels at the moment healing needs both.
pmc-11592846:
Md Ataur Rahman and colleagues review a stealthy defense tumors use against the immune system, in a 2024 article. The tissue around a tumor often turns acidic. That acidity dulls the killer cells sent to attack the cancer. At the same time, it recruits cells that suppress immune action, turning would-be attackers into helpers of the tumor.

The review explains how this acid shield helps explain why immune therapy fails for many patients. It then surveys ways to break the shield. Options include buffer agents that neutralize acid and drugs that block acid production or transport. Newly found genes that control acidity offer fresh targets as well. The authors argue that pairing such tactics with immune therapy could restore the attack. They call for more work on how tumors acidify their surroundings in the first place.
pmc-11603746:
Chunlin Ye and co-authors (2024) built a risk model for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma from long non-coding RNAs tied to a new form of cell death. The death mode, called disulfidptosis, differs from better-known modes. Using cancer atlas data, the team found 155 such RNAs linked to it.
