The two groups differed in survival, immune cell mix, checkpoint activity, and drug response. Patients with high scores and many tumor mutations fared worst, while low scores with few mutations fared best. Lab tests confirmed the RNAs appear at different levels in cancer cells than in normal lining cells. The authors offer the model as a guide for prognosis and personal treatment choices. They note it needs testing in real patient groups.
pmc-11603846:
Yuantang Qiu, Chun Xiao, and Jing Li study smart care in county hospitals. Their work from twenty twenty-four is set in Chongqing, China. They ask how well sick people rate the new tech based care.

The team asked many outpatients and inpatients at ten hospitals. A scale scored what folks hoped for and what they got. What they got fell short of what they hoped for. Gaps showed in skill, use, tools, and results. The team used a chart to pick where to fix first. Their aim is to guide growth of smart care.
pmc-11603946:
Yan-bo Wang and co-authors ask how low the resting heart rate should be kept in patients who have both atrial fibrillation and coronary heart disease. Their study, from two thousand twenty-four, notes that current guidance sets the rate below one hundred to one hundred ten beats per minute. Yet little work had looked at this paired group on its own.

The team went back to data from a large trial of rhythm care for atrial fibrillation. Of the patients in that trial, one thousand five hundred twenty-two had both health problems. This group had more past smoking, high blood pressure, and heart failure than those with fibrillation alone. The authors weigh the main drug and care choices for rate control in light of that added risk.
pmc-11605646:
Takuro Ehara and four co-authors report results for a drug regimen in elderly patients with brain lymphoma. Their 2024 report covers a four-drug mix called RMPV, given without whole-brain radiation. Patients were sixty-five or older and treated at one center over seven years. The plan induced remission first, then maintained it for two years.

Forty-three patients took part, most with primary brain lymphoma. Median survival reached about fifty-one months, with about nineteen and a half months before progression. Nearly three quarters reached complete response. Daily function and mental scores improved after remission. Side effects like rash, kidney strain, and nerve damage forced dose cuts in some, guiding careful use.
pmc-11608046:
Shuhui Wu and colleagues boost stem-cell vesicles with a plant compound to heal diabetic wounds, working through the gut, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The team pre-treated umbilical cord stem cells with quercetin, a plant chemical that fights inflammation, and harvested stronger vesicles.

The surprise ran through the gut: the wounds came with a disordered gut community, and the treatment set it right, raising a helpful bacterium and rebalancing fat chemistry in the blood. The authors say the gut link is not a side note but part of the cure, and a new road for wound therapy research.
pmc-11608346:
Francisco Ruiz and co-authors present a 2024 study of iron and carbon storage in mangrove soils. Mangroves store large amounts of carbon in their soils, yet farms and ponds eat into them. Iron minerals can lock carbon in place by binding it, but that lock rests on a fragile balance in wet soils.

The team studied Amazon mangroves and a site changed to pasture and shrimp ponds. Loose, poorly formed iron types held the most fragile carbon and guarded about a tenth of soil carbon. Land change broke much of that guard, as loose iron forms decayed or hardened into less useful shapes. Carbon once shielded was then open to decay. The authors warn that such change cuts the climate worth of mangroves.
pmc-11608446:
Hanran Mai and co-authors test whether a gene variant in a long noncoding RNA changes the risk of repeated miscarriage in southern Chinese women, in a study from 2024. The RNA, PRNCR1, is known from cancer work. Long noncoding RNAs have been tied to recurrent spontaneous miscarriage before, but this site's role was untested.

The study compared just over four hundred patients with about seven hundred healthy controls, typing the variant with a standard assay. Women carrying two copies of the G form had clearly lower odds of the condition than those with two A copies. Combined carrier groups also showed lower risk. The authors read the variant as protective in this population and call for work on the mechanism behind it.
pmc-11608546:
Aleksandra Kozieł and six co-authors track new HIV infections in Lower Silesia, Poland, across a decade, comparing women and men. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Men make up most cases in Poland, but the share of women has been rising.

The team reviewed records from the Wrocław HIV clinic for twenty ten, twenty sixteen, and twenty twenty. Two hundred and two patients were included, of whom twenty-seven were women. Sexual contact was the main route among women. The data covered background, transmission route, health state at diagnosis, and other infections. Many patients arrived with advanced disease, a sign of late testing. The authors press for stronger screening so infections are caught earlier, when treatment works best.
pmc-11610246:

pmc-11612046:
Jan Wallner and co-authors validate a German questionnaire that measures mindfulness during physical activity in a 2024 study. Scores related as expected to attention, self-efficacy, and sense of coherence, and active participants scored higher than inactive ones. Links to depression and anxiety were not found, which the authors say needs more study.
pmc-11612446:

Changes in seipin tied to a human fat-wasting disease break the balance. A partner protein's fat-grip site proves key for droplet birth. The study shows screening can open this hidden corner of cell fat control.
pmc-11613146:
Ping Fu and six co-authors published a 2024 study of polydatin, a plant compound, against acute myeloid leukemia. Earlier work hinted that polydatin can push cancer cells to die and can switch on autophagy, the cell’s self-cleaning system.

Tests confirmed the compound protected that protein from destruction, raising its level and switching autophagy on. In mice carrying the cancer, treatment worked and appeared safe. The authors propose polydatin as a candidate for early-stage therapy development.
pmc-11615646:
Peihua Lu and four co-authors report the safety of a low-cost cancer therapy built on sugar starvation, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Cancer cells crave far more glucose than normal cells. The protocol exploits that hunger: insulin drives blood sugar low for under an hour, and small chemo doses are given in that window, when tumors are most exposed.

Over two years, hundreds of patients with advanced cancers received thousands of sessions. No lasting harmful reaction was seen across ages and cancer types. Blood sugar settled back without wide swings in diabetic and non-diabetic patients alike. Weight, vital signs, and blood chemistry barely shifted over repeated courses. The authors judge the therapy safe, cheap, and broadly usable.
pmc-11615946:
Antony and co-authors published a 2024 study on watching acidity at the working face of a water-splitting device. Local acidity at the anode, where oxygen forms, can swing during operation and throttles efficiency. Measuring it without stopping the device is the challenge.

The team adapted scanning electrochemical microscopy, a probe that senses chemistry at a point, to read local proton levels beside an operating membrane assembly. They compared a zero-gap industrial-style setup with a looser laboratory one. The method was then extended to further questions about the device's behavior. For engineers chasing durable green hydrogen, such operando measurements show where the chemistry, not the brochure, limits performance.
pmc-11616146:
Helen Karimi and colleagues described spine care in a myeloma case in 2024. Multiple myeloma weakens bones throughout the body. Spine collapse can bend the neck badly. Chin-on-chest deformity was the presenting problem. The patient had no nerve damage. The spine also seemed mechanically stable.

Gradual realignment came before any surgery. An external brace held the correction. Surgery later added cement support inside bone. One year later symptoms had improved. Daily activities were easier as well. Hardware showed no failure on scans. Spine stability held over time. Careful staging made surgery safer.
pmc-11618346:
Ireneusz Plebankiewicz and co-authors build a solar charger sewn onto camouflage fabric for field use, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The pack pairs a solar panel with a bank of fast-charge capacitors and a converter. It was sized to charge a common power bank and to stay portable and modular.

Lab and field tests ran in poor weather, with rain and full cloud cover. The charger still hit high efficiency under broken cloud. One nine-hour day of charging delivered a solid store of energy. A full capacitor bank could feed the power bank for over twenty minutes. Output stayed stable as weather swung.
pmc-11618446:
Ebru Kahraman, Tugba Hayri-Senel, and Gulhayat Nasun-Saygili published this study in 2024. The team built a thin film that slowly releases a cancer drug. The film blends polyurethane made from plant oils with graphene oxide, a carbon sheet material, and carries the drug 5-fluorouracil.

The authors present the film as a candidate carrier for controlled drug delivery.
pmc-11619146:
Marie March and Katharine Roberts review how psychosocial care could move from general muscle and joint practice into orthopaedic surgery in a 2024 article. The authors list barriers at patient, clinician, workforce, and system levels. They discuss staffing, shared decisions, health literacy, and care for women and diverse communities. The review frames a large chance to give surgical patients more complete, fair care.
pmc-11619446:

The team advance lights by six hours every two days for male and female mice. Tags record body temperature and activity rhythms through the shifts. pmc-11620846:
Xiao and coauthors study shrub ties in pine woods on Chinese islands. Shrubs share light, water, and soil in those woods. Which shrubs help or block each next shrub shapes the grove. The woods sit in Sandu Gulf in Fujian Province.

The team mapped top shrub species and their pair ties. They also read soil and site facts for each plot. Their goal was to learn why species live side by side. Rivalry and aid both play roles in that pattern. Clear rules may help staff guard and tend those woods. Island woods face salt, wind, and thin soil stress.
pmc-11624546:
Fahamina Ahmed and four co-authors survey pharmacy students on vaccine mandates in a 2024 study. Students at Xavier University of Louisiana were asked about required COVID-19 vaccination in schools and health settings, covering ethical, legal, and practical angles. Health workers' views can shape vaccination rates and policy.

The survey went to all two hundred ninety one pharmacy students, and about half replied. Roughly half of respondents thought the vaccine should be mandatory for the public. The sixteen question survey also probed vaccine safety views, herd immunity, and student backgrounds. The authors aim to inform training and policy with future pharmacists' perspectives on mandates.
pmc-11626746:
Anam Anil Alwani and four colleagues published a community study in two thousand twenty-four on diabetes distress in Delhi, India. Diabetes distress is the emotional burden of living with the disease's daily demands. It is often missed even though guidelines urge regular screening.

Four hundred twelve adults with diabetes from one urban colony answered standard distress, self-care, and health questionnaires. About thirty-five percent had significant distress. Being female, poorer, having other illnesses, a decade or more since diagnosis, being on treatment, and lacking social support all raised the odds. The team also compared self-care, sugar control, and healthy days between distressed and non-distressed groups. The authors press for routine distress checks in city clinics.
pmc-11629146:

The molecules join pyrazole, thiazole, and thiophene units, a mix hoped to yield both germ-killing and antioxidant effects. Such multi-action agents are sought as resistance grows.

The team made seven compounds and confirmed their structures with standard lab methods. The compounds were tested against several bacteria and fungi, showing clear inhibition zones and low doses needed to stop growth. They also scored well in tests that measure mopping up of harmful radicals. Computer modeling of their electronic traits and docking into biological targets backed the lab results. The authors present them as candidate therapeutic agents.
pmc-11631546:
Tatsuma Nomura and six co-authors present a 2024 video article on closing the hole left in the stomach wall after an inner tumor is cut out by scope. The new method adds a dual action clip that can grab two edges at once. Three point fixation with this clip plus the line method seals the defect faster. The article shows the clip types step by step in figures and video. It is a practical guide for endoscopists who face the same closure problem.
pmc-11636246:
Zhang and co-authors review glow materials that may serve medicine and dentistry. Organic room-temperature phosphorescent materials glow long after light stops. The review first explains how the glow and oxygen arise. It then sums uses in imaging, tumor care, and germ control. Design can match a patient's own tissue setting in theory. Kill rates for tumors and bacteria could rise with that tuning. The authors map how the field may enter dental care.
pmc-11637346:
Bylan and co-authors published a 2024 rat study of Lebanese cannabis oil extract against kidney scarring. Kidney fibrosis drives chronic kidney disease and has no reversing treatment. Treated kidneys and hearts also showed milder tissue damage, in step with dose.

In cultured kidney podocytes, the extract rescued cells from folic acid toxicity and partly restored their movement. Chemical signals shifted in a protective direction: one growth pathway rose, a stress pathway fell. The authors call the extract protective against this fibrosis model. They note the work is preclinical and dose discipline matters.
pmc-11640346:
Jeong-Min Heo and colleagues fine-tune a recipe for seaweed chips in this two thousand twenty-four food science paper. Green laver is a seaweed with a strong sea flavor that some eaters dislike. A statistical design method searched for the best mix and process. The winning blend combined green laver, fish surimi, and flour in set shares. Flavor building blocks were also tuned for best taste. Panel scores for overall liking and crispness came out strong. The paper gives snack makers a tested path to tastier seaweed chips.
pmc-11641946:
Paula Pohl and colleagues published a 2024 study of pararamosis, a neglected tropical disease of rubber tappers in the Amazon. Over time it thickens the membrane lining the finger joints and damages cartilage, much like chronic arthritis.

Because joint inflammation drives the damage, the team studied synoviocytes, the cells of that joint lining. They examined how caterpillar toxins make these cells inflamed and how the cells interact with macrophages and cartilage cells. Understanding this inflammation could point to treatments for a disease that mainly harms poor rural workers and receives little research attention.
pmc-11642546:
Marina Kljajic leads a team that screens kidney transplant folks for Fabry disease. Their study from twenty twenty-four covers a large group of recipients. Fabry disease is a gene fault that harms many organs.

Dry blood spots were used for gene tests in the group. Women all got gene tests, as did men with low enzyme scores. The team also checked links to age, dialysis time, and kidney scores. The fault blocks a key enzyme, so waste builds in cells. Finds could catch missed cases in this at risk group.
pmc-11644346:
Fanfan Meng and colleagues published a 2024 materials study on heat-storing capsules for textiles. Phase change capsules absorb and release heat. They could keep clothing comfortable. Their weak point is slow heat flow. The team added graphene sheets to the capsule shells.

Plant cellulose fibers kept the graphene from clumping. Microscopy and spectroscopy confirmed the structure. Capsules with graphene stored heat well. Their heat conduction rose several-fold. Strength tests also showed tougher shells. Fabrics woven with the capsules regulated temperature in tests. Smart clothing for workers and soldiers could follow. The recipe uses renewable cellulose as the helper.
pmc-11645046:
Yuchang Zhu and co-authors present a 2024 paper on measuring temperature precisely with magnetic nanoparticles, without touching the sample. The particles respond to magnetic fields in a temperature-dependent way, which suits biomedical uses. The team built field setups that mix steady and alternating fields, then read the particles' response harmonics. They tuned the setup to cut measurement error and designed algorithms that convert the response into temperature.

Their joint algorithm sharpened the reading further. Under one field scheme, their optimizer ran faster and cut error by half or more against rival methods. Under a dual-frequency scheme, the temperature error fell from about a quarter of a degree to under a tenth. The authors present the method as a step toward accurate, real-time, noninvasive thermometry for medicine.
pmc-11647146:
Katrina Plamondon and Sana Shahram published a 2024 essay on why health equity work keeps missing its target, using the image of fishing with skis and digging with noodles. Equity efforts, they argue, keep intervening on the people most burdened by inequity instead of the systems that produce it. Models abound for the structural causes, the what. The missing piece is the how: daily practices that connect knowledge to action.

The authors offer five practices anyone can fold into ordinary work to act from evidence and equity at once. The essay is a provocation aimed at scholars and practitioners alike. It asks readers to notice their own attachment to mismatched tools. The point is practical, not scolding: pick up the right tool for the structural job.
pmc-11647246:
Min and co-authors show that receptors on star-shaped brain support cells, not neurons, drive a key step in visual brain wiring. Cannabinoid CB1 receptors shape how inhibitory circuits mature in the young visual cortex. They were long assumed to sit on neuron endings. The team removed the receptors from single cell types in mice. Removing them from astrocytes stalled the maturing of inhibitory transmission. It also cut the cortex's ability to shift eye dominance during the critical period.

Removing the same receptors from interneurons left both processes intact. The split pins the effect on astrocytes. The result reframes how cannabis-like signals guide early brain development.
pmc-11649346:
Shasthara Paneyala and four co-authors test bedside exams for a thigh nerve problem in a 2024 study. The condition traps a nerve and causes tingling along the outer front thigh. Three simple tests are used in clinics, but their accuracy had never been measured head to head.

The hospital study enrolled thirty patients whose diagnosis was confirmed by electrical testing. Each bedside test was scored for how often it caught true cases and cleared healthy ones. All three tests performed well, with accuracy figures in the mid-eighties to low nineties. The authors conclude the tests are simple, reliable aids. Clinics can use them to support diagnosis before ordering costlier scans.
pmc-11649746:
A team led by Eva Klvanova ran a pilot study on drug-resistance genes hiding in indoor dust. Dust was swept from homes and from workplaces: a children's hospital, a maternity hospital, and a research center. They read the genes two ways, with a fast targeted test and with full gene shotgun reading.

The targeted test found one hundred forty-three resistance genes, led by genes that defeat a common antibiotic group. Workplaces carried more than homes, and the children's hospital carried most of all. The shotgun method found far fewer genes. The authors warn that indoor dust can hold resistant germs where people spend most of their day.
pmc-11650846:
Salah and coauthors test tiny algae that may clean a drug from water. The drug is a common germ killer found in waste water. Such drug traces can harm streams, lakes, and human health. Green methods to pull the drug out are in high demand.

The team used two algae types as living filters for the drug. Best uptake came at a low drug dose in the water. Each alga had its own best acid level for uptake. Uptake pace fit a standard rate model well. The drug bound to alga cells through surface pairing. The work backs algae as a green clean-up choice.
pmc-11651146:
Fibroids are common growths in the womb, but ones growing inside the neck of the womb are rare and hard to remove. Yousef Alebrahim and co-authors report a case in this 2024 paper in which a large fibroid of this kind was taken out through the vagina instead of through the belly.

The patient was a 43-year-old woman seeking fertility treatment. Growths that hang into the vagina are often removed that way, but growths buried in the wall usually need keyhole or open surgery. The team describes how the vaginal route worked here and argues it can speed recovery in well-chosen cases.
pmc-11653646:
Michael Ashman and five colleagues describe how patients and staff shaped a review of mental health crisis services, in a commentary from twenty twenty-four. The review asked how community crisis care works, for whom, and when. A stakeholder group mixed lived and work experience. Seven members had lived it; eight worked in it.

Two researchers co-led the group, one from each side. That bridge built trust across the divide. A voluntary group backed the lived-experience members, keeping them involved. Four group meetings ran through the review. Members joined real tasks, not just talks. The authors share what worked and what strained. Their point: people who use crisis care should help judge the research on it.
pmc-11654546:
Janaina Fonseca Almeida Souza and a team of co-authors reviewed ways to raise child vaccination in Brazil. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, came as rates there were falling. They searched three large databases for past studies. They used set rules to screen what they found. In the end just six studies fit for a close read.

Half of the six dealt with a cash aid plan for poor families. The rest dealt with direct work with parents, fast checks of vaccination, and a health agent plan. The cash plan did not by itself make families meet the child health terms. Readers see which paths have proof behind them and where proof is thin.
pmc-11655146:
Ali Ghazi Atiyah, Mustafa Salah Hasan, and Maher Saber Owain report a rabbit study from two thousand twenty-four on an ointment for full-thickness skin wounds. The ointment joins Jerusalem artichoke extract, a plant material with anti-inflammatory traits, with ozone, a gas that kills germs and can spur tissue repair.

Thirty male rabbits received a round wound cut through the skin on the back. Half were left untreated, and half got the ozonated ointment twice a day for five days. Lab tests confirmed the ointment kills bacteria in a dish. Over three weeks, treated wounds shrank faster and regrew surface skin better than controls, based on both naked-eye and microscope checks. The authors support the ointment as a healing aid.
pmc-11655646:
Ayesh Madushanka, Renaldo Moura, and Elfi Kraka release QM40, a quantum data set for machine learning in drug science, in two thousand twenty-four. Learning models need huge amounts of fine data to guess molecular traits. The set covers most of the chemical space of approved drugs in the United States.

It holds near one hundred sixty-three thousand molecules of ten to forty atoms, built from the elements common in drugs. Sixteen quantum traits were computed for each at a set theory level in a standard program, matching older data sets so they can be merged. The release adds start and refined shapes, atom charges, and bond facts such as local vibration strengths. It serves as a test bed for new prediction methods.
pmc-11656246:
Natalia Cortes, Izabel Almeida Alves, and Diana Marcela Aragón review a decade of patents on emulsifiers for cosmetics. Emulsifiers hold creams and lotions together, mixing oil and water into one stable product. The team searched the Espacenet database for filings from 2013 to 2023 and examined 51 patents. They charted yearly flow, origin, and emulsifier kinds.

Filings rose over the decade, with dips in some years. A striking 86% of the patents came from China. Natural emulsifiers led the field, ahead of polymeric, synthetic, and defined-molecule kinds. The review maps how each group forms emulsions and what systems they build. It also tracks trends in their physical and chemical traits. For makers, the message is that the hunt for better emulsifiers, above all natural ones, is hot, and the patent map shows where the crowd is digging.
pmc-11657746:
Iten and co-authors check if daily coffee links to fewer heart events in atrial fibrillation. Patients with this rhythm fault often fear coffee may harm them. Data came from two large Swiss cohorts of such patients. Follow-up ran a median of 4.7 years with yearly checks. Events were grouped as stroke, heart attack, heart failure stays, and heart death.

Daily coffee drinkers had 5.09 events per 100 person-years. Non-daily drinkers had 7.49 events per 100 person-years. After adjustment, daily use linked to a 23 percent lower risk. Two to three cups a day showed the lowest risk of all. The link held for the grouped endpoint as a whole.
pmc-11660246:
Ana Brand and co-authors present a 2024 study of a coffee compound called cafestol and what digestion does to it. Cafestol sits in coffee beans and brews and has been tied to raised cholesterol and other body effects. How the gut handles it was poorly known.

The team measured cafestol in boiled coffee, then ran a lab digestion model with mouth, stomach, and gut phases. Most of the cafestol stayed open to uptake, a share above nine tenths. In the gut phase it sat mainly in its alcohol form. A new acid form of the compound arose in the mouth phase and lasted through later phases. Fine mass tools named the products. The authors claim the first such map of cafestol digestion.
pmc-11662646:
Lucy Chou-Zheng and a team of co-authors uncover how a virus disarms the CRISPR defense of bacteria. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Bacteria use CRISPR systems to shred viral genes, and viruses answer with small blocker proteins called anti-CRISPRs.

The blocker studied here is the first known one aimed at a Type III-A system. It latches onto a part of the defense machine and damps its cutting and signaling. It also travels with broken pieces of RNA, which stick to the machine during infection. Those RNA pieces bind a host enzyme that normally helps the defense. By hitting both the core machine and its helpers, the blocker gives the virus strong protection against bacterial immunity.
pmc-11666946:
Yazhou Zhao and co-authors charted a joint path to cut pollution and carbon in a 2024 study of Inner Mongolia. The Hohhot-Baotou-Ordos region is an industrial hub where smokestack output harms air and adds to climate change. Cutting both at once saves money, since many steps serve both goals.

The team weighed the cut potential of the region's industries for air pollutants and carbon dioxide. A cross-check method then sorted steps by how strongly the two cuts move together. Strong pairs form the cheapest joint path. Few past studies had mapped such paths for a whole region's industry.
pmc-11667046:
Robert Samuel and the CORMAC-2 collaborators hammer out shared meanings for anal cancer trial results, in a two thousand twenty-four consensus paper. Trials of chemoradiotherapy for anal squamous cell carcinoma report results so variably that results resist comparison.

An earlier project had agreed a nineteen-result core set across disease activity, survival, toxicity, and life impact. This phase standardized meanings for the eleven disease activity and survival results. Current meanings were harvested by systematic review, tested in a two-round Delphi survey of fifty-one experts from thirteen countries, and ratified at a consensus meeting. Uniform meanings, the authors argue, make the core set usable in real trials and improve choice data.
pmc-11667146:
Marc Wolter and co-authors report a 2024 chemistry study on chromatography columns. Liquid chromatography separates mixtures as they flow through a packed column. The packing surface decides what sticks and what passes. The team built three new silica packings with triphenyl groups. Each differs in built-in ion-exchange sites. One has none, one carries a strong anion-exchange group, and one was oxidized further into a two-way charged surface.

Click chemistry bonded the groups onto thiol-coated silica in clean steps. Element tests and separation trials characterized each packing. Mixed-mode columns can sort charged and neutral compounds in one run. That saves labs a second column and a second method. Pharma and chemical analysts get new surfaces to try on hard mixtures. The side-by-side build shows exactly what each ion site adds to retention.
pmc-11669846:
Al Mamun, Quan, Geng, Wang, Shao, and Xiao review in twenty twenty-four therapies that aim to rebuild insulation around nerve fibres after spinal cord injury. The injury severs signals between brain and body, causing lasting loss of movement, feeling, and control. Fibres rarely regrow their insulation on their own, so helping precursor cells mature into insulation makers is a key goal.

The review surveys drugs and biological factors that push those precursor cells to multiply, mature, and wrap fibres. Lab and animal studies show promise for better insulation and function. The authors weigh hurdles for clinic use, including safety, delivery routes, and mixing therapies. They back targeted insulation repair as a hopeful path, pending careful trials.
pmc-11672646:
Andrea Cappelleri and co-authors probed a surface marker in cat tumors in a 2024 study. Feline injection-site sarcomas are harsh skin cancers that grow where a cat was vaccinated or injected. A glow-guided surgery trick, aimed at a like marker, already helps vets cut these tumors out whole.

The team asked whether a shop-bought antibody for the alpha-v integrin could serve in lab checks of the cut edges. They used ten saved tissue samples from past surgeries. Clear edges are the best guard against the tumor's return. A cheap lab read of margins could lift the odds for many cats.
pmc-11673046:
Andrea Martschini and co-authors characterize, in a 2024 paper, the first enzyme from an unexplored branch of a sugar-burning enzyme family. These oxidases, which run on vitamin-derived FAD, split into two camps that share one sequence space: some burn simple sugars, others attack glycosides, sugar-tagged compounds of more value. Sorting the family tree of soil actinobacteria gives four branches, and branch two had never had a member tested.

The enzyme, from a Microbacterium strain, behaves much like its cousins in branches three and four, preferring glycosides over plain sugars. Its menu is its own, though: it efficiently oxidizes both a rooibos C-glycoside and a classic O-glycoside, a pairing no relative had shown. The authors present the profile as a new entry in the family's catalog, widening the set of feedstocks these enzymes might upgrade for industry.
pmc-11673246:
Elsa Uribe and seven co-authors compared four ways of drying blueberries, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Dried berries are a growing market, and Chile sees room to enter it. Drying, though, can strip the berries of the compounds that make them healthy.

Vacuum drying was fastest, while freeze drying best kept the deep-color pigments tied to health gains. Hot air, infrared, and freeze drying all kept two key plant compounds at the fore. All methods raised antioxidant power on one test and lowered it on another. Extracts from freeze-dried and hot-air berries slowed lung cancer cells most, and hot air best blocked a sugar-processing enzyme. The authors recommend hot-air drying as a sustainable choice.
pmc-11674046:
Omaetxebarria and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on a shuttle protein that moves cargo out of the cell nucleus. The shuttle, called CRM1, also sits in two spots inside the nucleus tied to RNA making. Past work named five key building blocks that tune its export job. The team mutate each block and watch where the shuttle gathers. They also track how well it exports real cargo from the cell. One mutant split the two inner spots apart, showing they are set independently.

Another mutant sped some cargo exports while slowing others. Two past claims fail in their tests, they report. One says a certain chemical tag is always needed for the shuttle to work. The authors call for a fresh look at how this shuttle is controlled.
pmc-11675746:
Thonaeng Molelekoa and co-authors analyze how malaria and other fevers relate to anemia in young children in Niger. Their study came out in 2024. Anemia in early childhood is a major public health problem across Africa, and its drivers shape policy.

National survey data showed nearly three quarters of children under five were anemic. Malaria was present in about one in seven children and other fevers in about one in three. Statistical modeling linked anemia to malaria, other fevers, being male, and higher birth order. Wealth, older age, city living, and media access were protective. Two regions stood out with the highest anemia shares. The authors urge combined action on infection prevention, household resources, and health education through media.
pmc-11675846:
Lanyo and a team including Lori test group antenatal care in Ghana in twenty twenty-four. Health guidance urges mothers to breastfeed only for the first six months of life. Visits during pregnancy are a chance to teach this practice. The trial compared group visits with routine one to one care.

The study enrolled one thousand seven hundred sixty-one pregnant women at fourteen health facilities. Half received eight group sessions, and half received routine care. Data were gathered before and after the program. Women in group care had much higher odds of planning to breastfeed only for six months. They also had higher odds of waiting until six months to start solid food. The authors conclude that group care helps spread the guidance.
pmc-11677046:
Signe Eekholm and co-authors published a 2024 evaluation of a tailored plan to get fundamental evidence-based nursing care done right in a hospital ward. Fundamental care, though basic, is often missed in wards, with grave consequences for patients. The plan was built from evidence and tailored to the barriers of the ward itself, in behavior and in environment.

Eight outcomes graded the plan: adoption, acceptability, appropriateness, fidelity, feasibility, reach, sustainability, and cost. Field notes, interviews, logs, and record audits fed the evaluation. The plan was adopted, liked, appropriate, and feasible. It met its marks at the individual, team, and management level. Yet fidelity and sustainability were strained by competing organizational demands and limited time. The conclusion supports tailored plans for complex barriers, with a warning about the strain.
pmc-11677646:
Sandeep Kondakala and co-authors watch two bacteria interact at the protein level, hunting for drug-free ways to curb a harmful germ. The helpful species Lactobacillus plantarum is known to fight Staphylococcus aureus, a cause of toxic shock and other infections, but the inner mechanics are murky. The team grew them together and profiled the proteins each side raised or lowered, in both the shared fluid and the cells.

The helpful species had the stronger hand: the pathogen changed far more proteins, mostly turning them down, while its own response stayed smaller. The pattern also differed by strain, since two pathogen strains from toxic shock cases did not react alike. The authors say such protein maps expose the metabolic tug of war inside mixed cultures and can guide non-antibiotic control strategies.
pmc-11678646:
Sittipath Tirasattayapitak and co-authors predicted delayed kidney graft function with machine learning in a 2024 paper. A transplanted kidney that starts slowly fares worse, so early warning matters. The team gathered clinical and biopsy data from 354 deceased-donor transplants at a Thai hospital between 2018 and 2022.

About 18 percent of recipients had delayed function. The strongest warning signs were donor weight, donor diabetes, long cold storage time, male recipient, and scarring scores in the implantation biopsy. Three learning models all beat classic regression; the gradient boosting model scored highest on discrimination, with the random forest close behind on other measures. The authors offer the models as decision support for transplant teams weighing organ offers.
pmc-11678746:
Haoyue Yang and co-authors improve, in a 2024 study, a gas sensor for oxygen-bearing vapors by dusting its surface with a second oxide. Such vapors include alcohols and ketones worth monitoring, and tin oxide sensors for them can be sharper. The team spread bismuth oxide particles evenly over tin oxide nanoparticles, building many contact faces between the two materials.

Tests showed the loaded surface holds more of the reactive oxygen ions that sensing relies on. A sensor with one percent loading answered far more strongly and quickly than plain tin oxide across several test vapors, especially at two hundred to two hundred fifty degrees. Burn and reaction studies point to adsorption and partial burning on the surface as the working steps. The authors credit the richer oxygen layer at the two-oxide boundary, and propose the design for practical vapor monitoring.
pmc-11678946:
Victoria Wahlquist and co-authors study heading exposure in youth soccer in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Heading the ball is unique to soccer, and parents worry about repeated head impacts. The team tracked female youth players over one season to see if heading predicted changes in health measures.

Players took tests of symptoms, thinking, walking, and balance before and after the season. Small gains appeared in thinking and gait, with a slight dip in balance, but none were clinically meaningful and likely reflected practice with the tests. Heading exposure in this group was low and did not predict the changes. The authors conclude that one season at this level showed no clear harm on these measures.
pmc-11679746:
Zhou and co-authors review vaccine therapies for prostate cancer. Their 2024 paper traces how these vaccines work and where trials stand. The aim is to wake the immune system to attack tumor cells. Vaccines draw interest for being targeted, safe, and able to leave lasting immune memory.

The review walks through the field's history and the main vaccine types. Recent trial results are summed up, with both gains and stalls. The tumor's immune setting and patient-to-patient gaps still block wide use. The authors close with paths the field may take next. Better patient picks and paired drugs are among the hopes.
pmc-11682746:
Sayed-Lafi and three colleagues feed pomegranate peel to common carp fighting a bacterial infection in twenty twenty-four. The peel is rich in active plant compounds eyed as feed aids. Carp ate graded peel doses for seven weeks while carrying the germ. Growth, blood traits, and immune measures were tracked.

Mid doses lifted weight gain and feed use over the plain diet. Blood cell counts rose at all peel levels. Immune and antioxidant markers improved across the board. Most blood chemistry eased downward, save one protein pair that held steady. The team calls peel feed a promising health aid for farmed carp.
pmc-11682946:
Aaron Ashbrook and four co-authors showed how boric acid kills termites by wrecking their gut microbes. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with the Eastern subterranean termite, a pest that eats wood in homes at vast cost. Boric acid is a wide used wood guard with broad kill power. Its sway on the gut web that termites need to digest wood was not known. The team fed termites treated paper at set doses.

Death rose with dose, with the top dose cut of survival sharp. Gut microbe reads showed the web thrown into disorder at those doses. Readers in pest control get the inner path of a cheap, stable poison. Gut wreck may be the true kill, not mere taste.
pmc-11686546:
Yong-Bo Yu and six co-authors test late-night snacks as nutrition care for liver cirrhosis patients in a 2024 study. People with cirrhosis are almost always malnourished, and a small snack before bed is a standard advice. The team asked whether three months of nightly snacks change body composition, a key sign of nutrition state.

Seventy patients and thirty healthy adults were measured with a body composition device. Patients started lower than healthy adults on fat mass, muscle mass, and body cell mass. After three months, the snack group gained fat mass and body cell mass against the normal-diet group, with no change in total food intake. Muscle mass, though, barely improved.
pmc-11686946:
David Lindenmayer, Ben Scheele, Elle Bowd, and Maldwyn John Evans compare bird trends across four long-term Australian studies, in a research paper from 2024. The same species can rise in one region and fall in another, complicating care decisions. The team tracked occupancy paths for eighteen species across 571 sites spanning about a thousand kilometers of latitude.

For fourteen species, the best models showed trend paths differing by study region. Oddly, the differences did not track how far a site sat from the species' comfort zone, nor local climate. The authors argue conservation needs several long studies across a species' range, since one region's trend can mislead.
pmc-11687946:
Jon Andri Lutz, Emmanouil Psathas, Benoît Rouiller, and Luis Filipe Azenha present a 2024 case report of surgery for a pinched artery at the base of the neck. An extra rib in the neck caused the pinch, a rare cause found in about five percent of such outlet cases. The artery had been forced into a bent path.

The patient was an eighteen year old woman. Surgeons used a camera through the chest to free the lower part of the first rib. They then worked from above the collarbone to free and cut the joined ribs and remove them in one piece. After removal, the artery looked normal in width and shape.
pmc-11689446:
Yeonjung Jane Lee describes how she weaves diversity, equity, decolonization, and intersectionality into teaching gerontology, the study of aging. The presentation appeared in twenty twenty-four, drawn from her work at a minority-serving institute. The pandemic and long histories of racism and ageism, she argues, force educators to reflect on their own roles.

Students will serve older adults of many cultures and life paths. Lee shares her teaching philosophy and classroom experience toward that end. The session invites students to examine how their own identities shape their service. Its aim is dialogue and practical insight for training a diverse student body well. Lee frames self-reflection as the spark of educational change.
pmc-11689746:
Ryan Brown studies, in twenty twenty-four, how hardship in childhood shapes health at midlife. He uses a thirty-year study of four hundred thirty-three Black and White women. Hardship was marked by low family means at age ten and by felt stress at age eleven. At age forty, the team checked blood sugar control and two DNA-based age clocks, drawn from saliva. Waist size at age nineteen was tested as a link in the chain.

Higher parent schooling linked to better sugar control and slower biological aging at midlife. Felt stress in childhood also linked to later outcomes. Part of that link ran through waist size in late teen years. The work covers both social and body paths.
pmc-11690046:
Wealth gaps do not close at retirement; they sharpen, argues a 2024 symposium summary by Julie Miller. By old age, a lifetime of uneven earnings and saving has compounded, and the effects spill into the next generation through gifts and inheritances.

The symposium's four talks take the problem from different sides. One covers older LGBTQ+ adults and the life events behind their finances. Another links wills, race, and uneven wealth transfer. The last two ask whether a sense of purpose softens the gaps, and how health or marriage shocks widen them. Miller frames the set as one picture of money in later life.
pmc-11690446:
Ryan Falck and co-authors use a long-running Canadian aging study to trace how the COVID-19 pandemic touched thinking skills and daily habits, in a 2024 paper. The pandemic reshuffled how people move, sit, and sleep across the whole day, and those habits feed the aging brain. The study followed more than eleven thousand cognitively healthy adults before the pandemic, with thinking tests and habit records at three points through 2021.

Comparing people whose last tests fell after the pandemic began with those tested before, the team found a split by age and sex. Men and women aged sixty-five and older in the pandemic group showed worse thinking scores and poorer daily habits than their pre-pandemic peers. Oddly, shifts in habits did not track shifts in thinking within individuals. The authors discuss what that disconnect means for protecting older adults' minds in future crises.
pmc-11691246:
Ellis Dillon and six co-authors follow family caregivers of older adults through major planned surgery, in a 2024 interview study. Thirteen caregivers spoke with the team three times: two weeks before the operation, then one and three months after. Most were spouses, and cancer was the top reason for surgery. The talks were coded for shared themes about the caregiving role and its costs.

Care swelled to fill the whole day, and many felt the marriage shift into a nurse-patient shape. Not knowing what lay ahead fed much of the distress. Caregivers asked for plain odds, clear guidance, and support at each phase, not just at discharge. The authors urge surgical teams to treat the family as part of the care unit. Better coaching, they say, would lift both caregiver and patient.
pmc-11691446:
Molly Wright and co-authors test whether inflammation links to some thinking skills more than others in older adults, in work from twenty twenty-four. Inflammation may set the stage for mild cognitive impairment and dementia. One marker, interleukin-6, was suspected to hit planning and speed hardest, but domains were rarely modeled together.

Data came from one hundred fifty-nine older adults without impairment at entry in an ongoing aging study. Blood draws two weeks apart gave an average marker level. A model grouped tests into attention, memory, and planning plus speed factors. Higher marker levels tied to worse planning and speed only. Attention and memory showed no link. The authors predict risk for one impairment type over another.
pmc-11692446:
Fayron Epps and Andy Suggs present a 2024 journal article on how marketing practice revived a dementia program for African American faith communities in Georgia. The program, later renamed ALTER, began in 2018 and missed its first-year goals for partners and participants. The lead researcher hired a branding firm to sharpen its message for church leaders, caregivers, and partner groups.

A new name, logo, and plain-language materials followed internal sessions and interviews. Over four years the program signed 83 partnerships, beating its goal by over three hundred percent. Reach grew from 7,500 people to more than 100,000, and the program spread to fourteen states.
pmc-11692646:
Brenda Schmitt, Patricia Pantoja, and Brandt Pence test a plant sugar against inflammatory aging stress in a 2024 study. Arabinose is a simple sugar found in vegetables, fruits, and grains, with reported benefits for blood sugar and gut health. Chronic low grade inflammation with aging, called inflammaging, drives many age related diseases.

In human immune cells in a dish, the sugar was added before a bacterial trigger of inflammation. At a mid dose, it lowered activity of three key inflammatory genes. It also improved mitochondrial breathing capacity under stress and protected the cells' sugar use pattern. The authors suggest the sugar eases metabolic stress in inflamed immune cells, a result needing animal follow up.
pmc-11692846:
Yanjing Liang and co-authors published a 2024 paper tracing the careers of scholars trained at a healthy aging center in Seattle. The center, at the University of Washington, has supported nursing research on aging since 1998. It has mentored more than 165 students and given over 757,000 dollars in research funding. Travel grants helped scholars share their work.

The authors surveyed eighty-seven former scholars and heard back from thirty-two. After graduating, most went into practice, and many also taught or did research. Their work includes papers in leading journals and grants from national institutes. Some led parts of the response to the COVID-19 pandemic or changed care in their clinics. Three-quarters credited the center with sharpening their research skills. The same share praised its career guidance and mentoring. The paper shows how one training center's effects ripple outward through its graduates.
pmc-11693146:
Mikael Greenwood-Hickman and six co-authors look inside a successful trial that helped older adults sit less, asking what goals participants actually set. Their study came out in 2024. Sitting dominates older adults' days, but how people change it in practice was undocumented.

Coaches recorded goals across a hundred forty participants over six months. Satisfaction ran very high, and most participants felt their health or daily functioning improve. Sessions faithfully used structured goal-setting and problem-solving. Goals leaned on outside reminders, like wristband prompts and standing desks, and on habits, like standing through a daily chore. Inner body cues were rarely used. Goals varied widely by person, which the authors say argues for tailoring rather than a single prescription.
pmc-11693346:
Nicole Derenne and co-authors check whether image-making AI still paints a biased picture of old age. Text-to-image systems often mirror social stereotypes, a pattern called digital ageism. The team fed the same set of prompts to the DALL-E 2 generator at two points a year apart. The prompts were drawn from terms used in aging care. They studied 164 images for perceived gender, race, class, and facial mood.

At both rounds, the images leaned heavily to white, middle-class men: white figures appeared five times as often as all other racial groups combined. The second round added more Asian figures, but gender and class gaps, and facial moods, barely moved. The authors conclude that bias in generated images of older adults persists despite public pushes for kinder views of aging. They note the study covers only one generator and one kind of content.
pmc-11694046:
Michelle Colder Carras and co-authors review programs that help young people use digital media in healthy ways. Their 2024 rapid review responds to concern about heavy screen use and problems such as gaming disorder. The team defines healthy use as media habits that do not cause harm.

Following rapid review guidance, the authors searched many databases and gray sources for studies and prior reviews. They focused on what helps programs work and whether results transfer to new settings. The review maps current approaches to prevent harmful use and support well-being. It also notes where evidence is thin and where stronger studies are still needed.
pmc-11696746:
Meiyan Chen and four co-authors build a sensitive test for microRNAs, tiny molecules that regulate genes and can signal disease. Their study came out in 2024. The test needs no labels and produces a fluorescent signal, meaning the sample glows in proportion to the target found.

A padlock-shaped probe first locks onto the target and closes into a circle. That circle starts a chain reaction that builds many copies of a second reaction's starting pieces. The second reaction produces long stretches that fold into structures which bind a dye and glow brightly. Because the background glow is low, small amounts stand out clearly. The whole test finished within hours in human serum samples, which suggests use in early diagnosis.
pmc-11697246:
Moses Adriko and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four data study on treating schistosomiasis in Uganda. Mass drug campaigns there long used whole districts as the planning unit. That approach put many communities in the wrong risk class and wasted medicine.

The team checked community-level records for thousands of communities in a shared database. Before checking, most communities had unknown infection status. After validation, many districts marked high risk held mostly low or non-endemic communities. Only a minority truly ranked high. The authors argue planning should shift to community units so drug requests and treatment match real local risk.
pmc-11704446:
Vivek Chinnarasan, Prasanna Bidkar, and Srinivasan Swaminathan lead a trial comparing two drugs paired with propofol in emergency brain surgery after head injury. Their study came out in two thousand twenty-four. Propofol calms the injured brain, but high doses bring side effects. A good partner drug trims the dose a patient needs.

One hundred patients who needed a clot taken out were split at random into two groups of fifty. One group got fentanyl, a classic opioid infusion. The other got dexmedetomidine, a sedative known for steadiness. Once the skull was open, the team measured brain relaxation and skull pressure. They tracked propofol use, extra pain drug needs, and a blood marker for nerve cell injury. The dexmedetomidine group used much less propofol. Such data can guide choices where habit often rules.
pmc-11709646:
Enrique Chimal Juarez and five co-authors use spatial gene mapping to compare brain tissue around amyloid deposits in blood vessels versus deposits in brain tissue itself. Their study came out in 2025. Vessel amyloid, called cerebral amyloid angiopathy, appears in most Alzheimer's cases and damages the barrier between blood and brain.

They sampled four kinds of neighborhood: support cells near vessel amyloid, near clean vessels, near tissue amyloid, and in clean tissue. Vessel amyloid regions had a gene signature clearly distinct from clean vessels. Vessel and tissue amyloid signatures overlapped partly but diverged in key pathways. A cluster of genes tracked vessel deposits specifically. The authors argue that treating the vessel disease needs targets drawn from its own signature.
pmc-11710246:
Mabel Seto and co-authors studied genes on the X chromosome that stay active in women, and their links to Alzheimer's disease, in a paper published in 2025. Women face the disease more often than men and tend to show more brain damage from it. Some X genes escape the normal silencing of one copy, which may help explain that gap.

Using brain gene data, plaque and tangle measures, and memory scores from a long-running study, the team checked more than two hundred such genes. Dozens linked to plaques, tangles, or memory decline, and most links were seen only in women. One gene stood out for links to both lower plaques and lower tangles. The results point to sex-linked biology that drug research has largely missed.
pmc-11710646:
Carmen Molina and co-authors probe a mitochondrial gene tied to Alzheimer's risk inside immune cells, in this 2025 paper. Myeloid cells, the brain's immune sentries, loom large in the disease's origins. Genetic evidence suggests lower activity of the gene, called LACTB, in these cells protects against the disease.

The team dialed the gene down in lab-grown immune cells and erased it in stem-cell-derived brain immune cells. They then profiled the cells' chemicals and fats and ran function tests. The gene shapes cell energy systems and links to a metabolite thought to be protective. Results may point to a fresh drug direction for Alzheimer's disease.
pmc-11710746:
Michael D Gallagher and co-authors report a 2025 study of gene risk for Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis. Gene scans have found hundreds of risk spots, but most sit outside genes, in DNA that acts in one cell type only. The team grew brain cells from stem cells and mapped the active DNA in each type.

Cells grown in the lab matched real human brain cells in their active DNA patterns. Microglia, the brain's immune cells, matched best, and risk spots clustered in their active zones. The team then used a CRISPR screen in lab-grown microglia to find which genes ten risk spots affect. The work points to microglia as a key site where gene risk acts.
pmc-11712646:
Daniel T Ohm and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on how two forms of one dementia eat away at the brain's layers in unlike ways. The illness changes conduct and social life first. Under the surface it can be driven by one of two bad proteins, tau or TDP-43, and the team asked whether each leaves a unlike mark.

They counted a marked class of nerve cells in thin layers of frontal brain tissue from people who had died with the illness. Links between layers ran weaker in the tau form than in the TDP-43 form. The pattern may help explain why the two forms act alike above the surface yet differ below it. Such marks could one day guide care by type.
pmc-11712846:
Danielle M Reid and Michael E Belloy published a research paper in 2025 on genes that may drive Alzheimer's disease in one sex only, working through the proteins they control. Women face higher risk of the disease, yet plain gene scans split by sex have found few firm hits. The pair added brain protein data to sharpen the search.

They merged the largest sex-split gene scan of the disease with data linking gene variants to brain protein levels. That pairing let them name genes whose protein output tracks with risk in women or in men alone. Such sex-tied genes could guide drugs built for one group rather than all. The method also shows how protein data can rescue weak gene scans.
pmc-11713346:
Chao-Yi Wu and co-authors test whether phone games can track thinking changes over time, in this 2025 paper. Their system, called MIND GamePack, holds four simple games on an iPhone. The games cover matching cards, word play, a card game, and falling blocks.

Sixty older adults took part, some with healthy thinking, some with self-noted decline, and some with mild impairment or early dementia. Each person played for at least five minutes a day over four months. The team found that learning curves in the games differed by group, which suggests that quiet home play could help trials watch thinking change between clinic visits.
pmc-11713646:
Christopher Duma and co-authors report the first patient in a new stem cell trial for Alzheimer's disease in 2025. The trial injects a patient's own fat stem cells, treated in a lab to boost growth signals, into the fluid spaces of the brain. It is the first test of this approach in humans. Safety, not cure, is the main goal at this early stage.

The first patient passed strict screening on age, disease stage, and brain scan signs. Care came in three steps: fat removal, placement of a small port under the scalp, and the cell injection. Nine patients in total will get rising doses. Reports like this one show how a bold idea moves from animal tests to careful human care.
pmc-11713846:
Kosuke Fujita and co-authors test walking speed as an early sign of change in a 2025 Japanese dementia study. Lifestyle programs that mix exercise, food, and social life may slow memory loss. Their gains take about two years to show on thinking tests, which is slow for judging a program. Walking speed drops as thinking slips, so it may give a faster signal.

The data come from a multi-center trial of older adults with mild memory problems. The program group got eighteen months of lifestyle support. The team compared change in walking speed with change in thinking scores. If the two move together, clinics could use a hallway walk test to spot benefit early and adjust care.
pmc-11726846:
Zhenzhen Li and ten co-authors review the wider effects of PCSK9 inhibitor drugs on heart and brain vessel disease, in a 2024 survey. The drugs were built to cut bad cholesterol, a main driver of heart attacks and strokes. They work by blocking a protein that would otherwise destroy the cell gates that pull cholesterol from the blood. With more gates left standing, blood levels fall sharply, beyond what statins alone achieve.

Trials show the drugs plus statins improve outcomes for heart patients and for stroke patients with narrowed brain arteries. The review also gathers proof of side benefits: less vessel inflammation, steadier plaques, and less clot formation. The authors sort the proof by organ system, heart first and brain second. They frame the drugs as multi-use tools, not just cholesterol cutters.
pmc-11727446:
Irene Mignini and co-authors review how smoking, gut microbes, and cell damage feed a common fatty liver disease, in a paper published in 2024. In this disease, extra fat builds up in the liver alongside wider metabolic trouble. Harmful oxygen by-products are known to be one of its main drivers.

Nicotine, the authors argue, makes matters worse: it raises swelling and cell damage, frees fat from belly stores, and pushes the liver to make more fat. At the same time, nicotine-driven damage reshapes the gut microbe mix, and a disturbed gut in turn helps drive the liver disease. The review maps this three-way web at the level of molecules. Its aim is to show where the chain might be broken by treatment.
pmc-11728246:
Riley Hall and co-authors review the family of severe disorders caused by faults in the TRAPP transport machinery of cells, in work from twenty twenty-four. The complex ferries cargo vesicles between cell compartments and helps start the recycling pathway. Its subunits act as switches for two Rab proteins that steer delivery.

Broken subunits cause rare but harsh brain, bone, and muscle disease, grouped as TRAPPopathies. Faults are known in many subunits, yet how they produce disease stays murky. The review gathers what is known about each variant. The authors propose fresh ideas on the damage paths and sketch the studies needed to pin the mechanisms down.
pmc-11728746:
Anh Vo and co-authors present a 2024 study on tiny carbon particles that act like several enzymes at once. The particles, called pleozymes, are made by harshly oxidizing coconut charcoal into discs a few nanometers wide. They mimic a protective enzyme, recharge a key cell molecule, and process sulfur compounds.

Earlier work showed the particles settle in mitochondria and raise both energy pathways of the cell. Here the team tracked fuel use with labeled glucose. Treated cells made more pyruvate and lactate and burned more fat, lifting total energy output. Levels of one energy carrier rose while its partner held steady. The results frame pleozymes as flexible boosters of cell metabolism, with promise in nerve disease models.
pmc-11740046:
Emily Zolfaghari, Andrew Dhanasopon, and Gavitt Woodard review how post surgery treatment is changing for early stage non small cell lung cancer, in work from twenty twenty-four. Even after full removal of small tumors, hidden spread can bring the cancer back. Which patients gain from extra therapy is the open question.

Old trials of platinum chemotherapy showed no survival gain for the smallest stages. Guidelines now reserve it for larger or high risk stage IB and IIA tumors. Targeted drugs changed the picture: three years of one agent improved survival in tumors with a key growth gene fault and won approval. Immune therapy adds more options. The authors see blood markers guiding future picks.
pmc-11774746:
Li-Ying Nong, Chen Liao, and Jian-Hong Ye report a study from two thousand twenty-four on what shapes job wellbeing for preschool teachers in China. Leadership style is one candidate: principals who share power and support staff may lift both performance and satisfaction. Evidence in early education settings was thin, so the team dug in with interviews.

They spoke with twelve teachers and twelve kindergarten leaders and built a model from the ground up using grounded theory. Empowering leadership linked positively to teacher wellbeing. The link ran through lower stress and burnout, stronger support from the organization, and a better work climate. It also fed teachers' own motivation and engagement. The authors urge principals to lead in ways that share control.
pmc-11795046:
Jan Benedict Spannenkrebs and co-authors close the loop on robot-run biology experiments in this 2024 paper. Synthetic biology needs parts whose behavior is measured over time under set conditions. Robots can gather such data fast and repeatably, but choosing the next test settings still took human work. The team built software that lets the robot platform adjust its own test parameters.

An importer feeds machine readings into a database. An optimizer then picks the next measurement points, balancing exploration with refinement. The platform tuned, on its own, the inducer dose for one bacterial system and a two-factor mix for another. A glowing protein served as the tracked product across rounds. The paper shares lessons from running full design-build-test-learn cycles without human steering.
pmc-11813346:
Mawalle Kankanamge Hasitha Madhawa Dias and co-authors study tiny sacs given off by a germ that makes fish sick, in a paper from 2025. The germ is called Edwardsiella piscicida. These sacs, known as extracellular vesicles, carry proteins and can change how the body fights infection.

The team used a fast spin method to collect the sacs and checked their size and shape. They found close to fifteen hundred distinct proteins inside, some linked to how the germ harms its host. The sacs did not poison fish cells in lab tests. In fish and cell tests, the sacs switched on genes tied to immune defense. The work points to a possible use in fish medicine.
pmc-11816946:
Melaku Birhanu Alemu and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-four on HIV testing during pregnancy care in Ethiopia. Testing and counselling in antenatal care help prevent mothers passing HIV to their babies. Many women use the service, but the share who get good-quality care, called effective coverage, was not well measured.

The team linked a national household survey with a later survey of health facilities. They scored service quality from dozens of structural and process indicators. Only about seventeen percent of women received testing during antenatal visits, and effective coverage was lower still, near eleven percent. Gaps varied sharply by region, from very low in the Somali region to over half in Addis Ababa. The authors urge quality fixes.
pmc-11825746:
Rumeng Ren and colleagues test a melon-derived tablet against fatty liver in mice. Their study from twenty twenty-five examines Hu-lu-su-pian, a modern traditional medicine tablet. The tablet is used clinically for liver ailments in China. How it fights metabolic fatty liver was not known.

Chemical profiling first identified the tablet main ingredients. A gene-driven mouse model created fatty liver for testing. Blood tests and liver tissue checks measured treatment effects. Gene activity scans then hunted the mechanism in liver tissue. A fat-storage gene called CIDEA sat at the centre of the effect. Adjusting that gene tracked with reduced liver fat. The work gives a molecular story for a long-used remedy.
pmc-11827846:
Kong and co-authors report a 2024 population study on an antibody that may guard against a cancer of the nasopharynx, the upper throat. The cancer is tied to the Epstein-Barr virus, a very common virus. Whether any antibody against the virus actually protects people was unclear before this work.

The team drew cases and matched controls from large cohorts in southern China with more than seventy-five thousand people. They measured an antibody aimed at a virus protein called gp42 and compared levels in patients and controls. Levels ran lower in patients across years before diagnosis. The team also studied the protein's receptor on throat cells and its effect on infection. The results point to a real protective role and a possible path toward prevention.
pmc-11831046:
Finding a lost person in the wilderness is a race against time, and ground teams can only cover so much land. Jan-Hendrik Ewers, David Anderson, and Douglas Thomson, in a 2024 paper, train drones to search smarter. Their algorithm uses deep reinforcement learning: the drone practices in simulation and learns flight paths that find people fastest. It starts from a map of where the missing person is likeliest to be, built from prior knowledge of the area and the person.

In experiments the learned search beat standard coverage and search planners by a wide margin in time to find. The method also lets the drone steer smoothly in any direction, rather than hopping between fixed points, which gives more natural flight paths. The authors say such gains can be the difference between life and death in real searches, and they present the approach as ready to guide real rescue drones.
pmc-12040646:
Stefan Kammermeier and co-authors compare head control on a tilting platform in two brain diseases and in healthy peers, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Seventeen patients with progressive supranuclear palsy, eleven with Parkinson's disease, and eighteen controls rode random tilts. Body part motion was tracked in 3D.

Heads in the palsy group swung several times wider than in both other groups. Their stimulus-driven head gain doubled the Parkinson's values and ran fivefold over controls. Eye state did not change the pattern. The team blames a surface-locked control plan over a space-locked one, tied to worn midbrain paths. Neck stiffness was not the driver. Readers get a sharper fall-risk story.
pmc-12181946:
Yue Zhang and co-authors upgrade a plant-based charcoal so it can pull both dyes and heavy metals out of water, in a 2024 study. Factories release wastewater laced with both kinds of pollutant, and one sorbent that catches both is prized. The team cooked wheat straw into hydrochar, then treated it with a silicon compound that adds nitrogen groups to its surface.

The treated charcoal soaked up pollutants faster and held far more than the plain version, reaching balance in about four hours. Its uptake of lead, copper, and two dyes ran from about one to nearly ten times higher than the untreated char. Surface checks confirmed the new nitrogen groups and a larger area. The authors credit those groups for the gains and offer the recipe as a simple route to better sorbents.
pmc-12257046:
Hassan and coauthors probe a kinase complex as a drug target in a fungal pathogen. The fungus causes meningitis in people with weak immunity. The kinase complex steers key cell processes in the fungus. The team used gene data to map its role in depth.

They compared gene use in normal and mutant fungal cells. Three mutant types each lacked part of the complex. Network tools mapped which proteins shift with the complex. Wide gene shifts hit growth and virulence paths. The maps flag proteins that new drugs might block. A large virtual screen can now hunt such blockers.
pmc-12396146:
Gorman, Stevenson, and Reilly use online videos to fight defeatist beliefs in a veteran. The veteran lives with serious mental illness and sought work. Defeatist beliefs can fuel low drive and job anxiety. A YouTube-based add-on targeted those beliefs directly.

The case tracks one person through vocational rehabilitation. Videos aimed to shift I cannot to I can thinking. Job anxiety fell as openness to work duties grew. Job-seeking acts also rose during the program. Ratings, interviews, and a distress scale captured change. The team discusses tech add-ons for work readiness more broadly.
pmc-12398346:
Nybacka and seven co-authors compare diet in irritable bowel syndrome patients and controls, in work published twenty twenty-five. Patients often blame food for starting or worsening gut symptoms. Many avoid trigger foods on their own, which can erode diet quality.

Habitual intake and overall diet quality were compared between patients and healthy controls. The team also explored how diet links with symptom severity. If avoidance diets leave patients short on fiber or key nutrients, dietitian guidance becomes part of care. The study separates what patients actually eat from what they fear eating.
pmc-12400346: Yuh-Shan Ho and Ali Ouchi write this 2025 comment to flag flaws in a set of bibliometric studies published in volume 29 of the World Journal of Gastroenterology. They argue those papers used poor search keywords and strategies, show evidence for the problems, and suggest better methods. They also rerun the work with stronger search strategies and present the improved results, offering the exchange as a lesson in how citation-based studies should be designed.
pmc-12663246:
Yanyan Li and nine co-authors name a gene switch that helps stomach cancer grow and spread. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Stomach cancer is a top cause of cancer death, with few good care options. The switch, PHOX1, is found at high levels in tumour tissue and tracks with worse stage and shorter life.

A chemical mark that should hold the gene down is lost in the cancer, which lets it rise. In lab cells, more of it drives growth, motion, and invasion, while less of it slows those acts. In mice, it helps tumours spread to the liver. It works by switching on a growth receptor and a signal path below it.
pmc-12664146:
Tian and a team including Wang and Rong compared three pig virus strains in twenty twenty-five from distinct family lines in young pigs. The virus harms breeding and lungs and mixes its genes with ease. One line now leads in China, yet line traits were poor-ly mapped.

Two strains gave strong fever, while the third gave a brief, mild one. Sick pigs showed high virus loads in lungs and glands after shed stopped. Gene reads split the strains: two lit up defense paths, one lit cell change paths. Line-aware guards are needed, they find.
pmc-12670846:
Colquhoun and a large team review how social marketing has been used to put research into practice in twenty twenty-five. Social marketing borrows sales tools to solve health and social problems. The field that studies how care improves in real clinics shares many goals with it. The team asked what tested uses exist and what clinics could borrow.

They screened close to five thousand papers and kept twenty-eight controlled studies. Most work dealt with food, sexual health, or exercise. Few fields outside health appeared at all. The team lists seven ideas clinics can borrow, such as design for appeal and know what the audience values. They urge more joint work across the two fields.
pmc-12691746:
Ahmed Alsaif and colleagues measure the burden of inflammatory bowel disease across Gulf Cooperation Council countries from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-one, with forecasts to twenty thirty. Their 2025 study uses Global Burden of Disease data for all six member states.

Standardised prevalence varied between countries, with Qatar and the Emirates highest and rising fastest since nineteen ninety, by roughly ninefold. Kuwait alone stayed stable or slightly declined. Women predominated in most countries, and people born in the nineteen seventies carried notably higher risk than nineteen fifties cohorts. The disease burden appeared mainly as disability rather than death. Three forecasting approaches projected continued increases, and regression linked burden differences to social and health system factors.
pmc-12693446:
Min Gi and co-authors compare the gene activity of rat lung tumors caused by carbon nanotubes, in a 2025 study. The fibers, prized in industry, can cause cancer in animals, yet the molecular routes differ by tumor type. The team profiled tumors sparked by one multi-walled type and by two double-walled types of differing length.

Clustering split the tumors cleanly: a chest-lining cancer from the multi-walled fibers stood apart from the lung adenocarcinomas. The adenocarcinomas from all fiber types shared pathways the chest cancer lacked. The chest cancer in turn raised its own distinct set. Such signatures help regulators judge which fibers act alike and which demand separate rules, a live question for worker safety.
pmc-12696046:
Abdirahman Hashi and co-authors combine two neural network styles, tuned by a wolf-pack search method, to recognize sign language gestures. Their study appeared in 2025. The system reads hand shapes with convolutional layers, follows motion over time with transformer layers, and lets the Grey Wolf method pick its settings. It was tested on two public American Sign Language data sets, covering still letters and moving signs.

Accuracy reached 99.4 percent, with matching strength on balanced scores, beating several rival tuned models. Live detection tests held up under varied conditions. Tuning by the wolf method also sped learning and improved generalization. The authors aim the work at assistive tools that translate signs for people who do not know sign language.
pmc-12700446:
Justin Schumacher and co-authors build a clinic-ready device that measures eye lens stiffness two ways at once, in this 2025 paper. Lens softening treatments for age-related focus loss cannot be judged without numbers from living eyes. No single tool gave the full mechanical picture.

The system pairs light-scattering microscopy with vibration-based elasticity imaging on a modified slit lamp. Bench tests confirmed both channels at peak performance. The team then measured a pig lens in place and, for the first time, a living human lens with both methods. The device could track how stiffening progresses with age.
pmc-12704946:
Abeer Badi Almutairi and co-authors (2025) surveyed parents in Riyadh about the human papillomavirus and its vaccine. Parents decide whether children get vaccinated, so their knowledge sets the ceiling on coverage. The team questioned 330 parents, mostly mothers, between late 2022 and mid-2023. Half said they were willing to vaccinate their children. Yet more than half had never heard enough about the virus to judge. Education predicted knowledge strongly.

Worry about side effects was common and dragged willingness down. Parents who knew more were much more willing: over two thirds of the well-informed group said yes. The authors call for campaigns built for this audience, using the channels parents actually follow. Messages must name and answer the side-effect fears, not just announce the vaccine. They frame the study as a diagnosis of why coverage lags in the capital: the gap is information, not hostility.
pmc-12706246:
Nga Huen Chan and Shamay Ng present a 2025 protocol for a trial of skin based nerve stimulation in people with long term stroke effects.
