Thinking problems and weak arm movement are common after stroke, and rehab options for both are still thin. Gentle electric pulses through the skin might wake up brain flexibility and aid recovery.

The trial has three arms and a sham control, with patients kept unaware of their group. One arm stimulates a nerve in the neck area; another targets the spinal cord through the skin. A third gets fake stimulation. The study will track thinking scores and arm function to see which active form helps, and by how much.
pmc-12709846:
Olivia Kituuka, Ian Munabi, Moses Galukande, Adelline Twimukye, and Erisa Mwaka studied informed consent for emergency surgery in Uganda in two thousand twenty-five. Staff must get consent from patients who may be unable to decide, often in crowded and rushed units. The authors asked how that process works in practice.

They spoke with sixteen staff at two large teaching hospitals and watched consent talks take place. Staff knew the rules well, but practice fell short. Greetings, risk talks, and checks of understanding were often poor, and talks took place in noisy rooms with little privacy. Staff called for procedure-specific forms and clear rules for patients with no surrogate.
pmc-12715046:
Julia Lenz and nine co-authors track 134 old sick folk with breaks of the hip ring from weak bones, for five years, to hunt what calls who will live. Hip breaks from low falls are on the rise as the share of old folk grows. Yet plans of care made for such breaks are still lack. The work took in scores for acts of day life, scores for ills held at once, home state, and break data.

Five years on, the share dead had hit 62.1 per cent. Just 37.9 per cent still lived. Those who lived had come in with scores by much more good on the Barthel Index and day life scales. They had low scores for risk in cuts and for ills held at once. The team says staff should gauge acts in the past life and ills at the door to hone calls of death risk.
pmc-12716146:
Tingyao Wang and nine co-authors review a drug called dihydroartemisinin in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The drug is known for use against malaria. The review asks if it can also slow the long path from hepatitis to liver scarring and then to liver cancer.

The authors sum up lab and animal work on how the drug acts at each stage. It calms swelling signals, slows scar forming cells in the liver, and affects fat stores and cell death paths. Two key signal paths come up again and again in the evidence. The review presents the drug as a hopeful option, while the proof stays early and mostly preclinical.
pmc-12716246:
Budi Haryanto, Febi Dwirahmadi, Triarko Nurlambang, and Al Asyary published a spatial analysis in twenty twenty-five mapping dengue fever vulnerability in two Indonesian provinces. Climate change is widening the habitat of the Aedes mosquitoes that carry dengue, and Indonesian case rates keep climbing. Knowing where risk concentrates helps aim surveillance and control.

Six areas in South Sulawesi and East Nusa Tenggara were scored on six factors, from distance to ponds and drains to building density and elevation. Experts weighted the factors in a multi-criteria spatial model. High-risk zones clustered near major water bodies and drainage, with weaker health facility access compounding danger. The maps give local programs a targeting tool for mosquito control.
pmc-12717446:
Fatima Gherbaoui and three colleagues track how weather shapes barn swallow breeding in an arid corner of Algeria over two seasons. As droughts intensify, arid-zone birds are sentinels of climate stress. The team modeled clutch size, incubation, hatching, and fledging against temperature, rainfall, and wind.

Rain was the great benefactor: more of it meant better hatching and overall reproductive success. Clutches shrank as the season advanced, incubation lengthened with rainfall, and heat cut the chance of a second nesting attempt. The authors conclude that in dry country, swallow reproduction rides on rainfall, and hotter, drier futures spell trouble for the species there.
pmc-12721746:
Matthias Begemann and colleagues reported deep genetic testing in a newborn case in 2025. Congenital hyperinsulinism makes insulin run too high. Blood sugar falls dangerously as a result. The baby was born preterm here. Two faulty gene copies were suspected. Long-read sequencing joined standard testing.

Full analysis finally pinned the diagnosis. Care choices changed on that result. Immediate management used the genetic answer. Family counselling used it as well. Recurrence risk could now be stated. Prenatal options were also discussed. The authors back comprehensive testing early. Team-based care improved the outcome.
pmc-12722146:
Heather Ravvin McKee and a large team of co-authors review the changing spectrum of epilepsy care in a paper from 2025. The review grows out of the 2025 American Epilepsy Society Annual Course, whose theme traced care from past practice to now. Its focus is how teamwork across specialties, new diagnostic tools, and surgical and non-surgical treatments are reshaping the field.

The authors gather the course's teaching points into one account. They stress gains in research and practice around the world and weigh where care is heading next. Readers get a guided tour of modern epilepsy care, from testing to treatment choices, in a single review.
pmc-12727946:
Daumann, Klöcker, and Schurade published in twenty twenty-five an study of the market for scuba diving certificates. A few large global firms sell much the same training products. The authors ask how that tight market shape affects firm conduct, prices, and results for buyers. They use a classic frame that links market structure, firm conduct, and market performance.

Using data from the trade and theory, they point to high entry barriers. Brand networks, owned training systems, and shared standards make new entry hard. They find the lead firm, PADI, holds strong market power, yet training quality stays high. Prices, though, show waste from weak competition. Even so, they see no clear need for direct state control.
pmc-12728346:
Vasiliki Manaki and colleagues report endovascular treatment of complex aortoiliac artery blockage using a bifurcated stent graft, with a literature review. Their 2025 case concerns severe disease traditionally treated by open bypass surgery.

The patient, a man in his late forties, had the most advanced lesion class in a standard consensus grading. The graft achieved complete revascularisation without complications around the procedure. One-year follow-up confirmed the vessels stayed open. Open bypass offers durable results but carries substantial operative risk, while endovascular options reduce hospital stays. Use in non-aneurysm disease remains off-label, so the authors call for long-term comparative studies to guide patient selection.
pmc-12729246:
Seiji Yahata and co-authors improved MRI room operations with lean thinking and a central tracking system in two thousand twenty-five. Lean methods come from manufacturing and aim to cut waste in a process. The team's goals were fuller appointment slots, shorter waits, and fewer referrals to outside sites.

They mapped the workflow with lean tools, held weekly short meetings, and built a system for real-time tracking of patient progress. Bookings rose by twenty-six percent and completed scans by nineteen percent, with further gains after daily refinements. Mean wait fell from forty-five days to five, and monthly outside referrals dropped from three hundred to fifty. Leadership and staff input were key, the authors say.
pmc-12729346:
Anna Lewandowska and ten co-authors gauge use of advised shots among patients with chronic disease, and how views on shots and fear of illness play in. Health guides advise a set of shots for people with long term ills, from flu to shingles shots. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team ran a cross group survey study that follows standard reporting rules. They ask which advised shots patients had taken, what shapes their stance on shots, and how strong their fear of falling sick is. They also test if fear links to stance. The aim is to show where uptake lags and what drives it, so clinics can lift coverage in this at risk group.
pmc-12729646:
Byun and six colleagues test a fermented yeast extract for hair regrowth in twenty twenty-five. Hair follicles cycle through growth and rest phases guided by dermal papilla cells. Oxidative stress and inflammation disturb that cycle and cause loss. The extract comes from yeast and collagen fermented with two Lactobacillus strains.

In stressed follicle cells, the extract raised a key antioxidant defence switch. It also calmed an inflammation pathway and an inflammasome complex. Growth signals such as IGF-1 and Wnt proteins rose several fold. In shaved animal skin, follicle counts and growth phase share increased. More follicles were in active growth than in controls. The authors propose the extract as a candidate for preventing hair loss.
pmc-12731646:
Virginia Mirra and a large team report a girl of ten whose rare vessel ill showed in odd ways due to a patchy gene flaw. Their case report appeared in twenty twenty-five. The ill, HHT, grows thin vessel tufts and bad vessel joins in organs. It is most oft passed from a parent, with two main genes at fault.

The girl came in with eye and sinus germs, plus low oxygen and a clubbed finger shape. A large lung vessel join was found, and brain sores came next. Gene tests found the flaw in just a small share of blood reads, a patch form. The team stresses gene tests when signs hint, even if the tale is odd.
pmc-12731846:
Carsten Herrmann-Pillath, a solo author, argues for a new way to think about heat, disorder, and sustainability, in a 2025 essay. The science of heat in balance, classical thermodynamics, sits inside daily engineering. Its out-of-balance branch feels remote, and its key term, entropy, stays a mystery to most people, which weakens how societies plan for sustainability.

The essay builds a framework it calls lived thermodynamics, rooted in the pragmatist thought of Charles Peirce. It swaps the classic lone system for tangles of open systems whose disorder-making is often bent by evolution and chance. Drawing on older work about power and growth in living things, it offers a sustainability test based on entropy. The aim is to bring the science of heat closer to lived choices.
pmc-12732446:
Young Lee, Soojin Kim, and Je Hyun Seo test whether psoriasis can cause age-related macular degeneration in a genetics study from 2025. The skin disease and the eye disease share immune features, but a direct causal link was untested. The team used genetic variants tied to psoriasis as natural instruments and compared their effects in large genome data sets for both conditions.

Across several statistical methods, genetic liability to psoriasis raised the odds of macular degeneration modestly. Results held after a check that removes outlying variants. The authors say inflammation deserves study as a driver of the eye disease, and that skin patients may merit eye watch.
pmc-12732946:
Chanté Johannes and co-authors present a 2025 study that built plans with university students in South Africa to get them moving more. How much students move depends on mindset, friends, the campus around them, and campus policy. Older programs often miss how these forces act as one.

A shared workshop brought students and fitness experts into one room. The group drafted plans at three levels: personal, social, and the wider setting. They agreed on dozens of recommendations in all. The team then sorted the ideas into themes for campus action. Campus planners get student-voiced plans, framed by a social ecological model, for helping students be more active in daily life.
pmc-12733046:
Gábor Krajsovszky and colleagues make new thiourea molecules built to recognize anions, as steps toward quinazolines. Thiourea and urea kin move anions by hydrogen bonds. How strong that move is rests on how acidic their NH hydrogens are. Thiourea is the more acidic of the two. Carboxylates, fluoride, and bromide strip part of its charge. Chloride does not, which hints it picks chloride out.

The team made twenty-one new thiourea compounds, by reacting amino acid ester blocks with mixed substituted phenyl isothiocyanates. Seven match molecules with no amino acids were made from aniline. How fast the reactions ran rested most on the phenyl groups. Groups that pull electrons sped the reaction up: nitro, bis(trifluoromethyl), and fluorine. Groups that give electrons slowed it down.
pmc-12733846:
Némo Bouillon and co-authors map sky blockers in wide fisheye photos, in work from 2025. Clean maps of sky versus trees and roofs feed sun forecasts and solar plant design. Pricey sky cameras and narrow local training sets have held past methods back, and their edges were coarse.

The team faked training photos from free street panoramas and taught a network with lens-aware tweaks. A boosting step then sharpened the edges. On real phone and clip-lens photos, the method scored near top marks for overlap and edge truth. It also held up on a foreign data set, which hints at broad use at low cost.
pmc-12733946:
Takeshi Teshigawara and co-authors compare two dry eye treatments before cataract surgery in a 2025 paper. Both treatments target faulty oil glands in the eyelids, which blur measurements. One is a drug drop, diquafosol; the other is pulsed light with gland expression.

The paired-eye study covered 62 patients having surgery on both eyes. Each person had one eye on drops and the other on light treatment. After surgery, the light-treated eyes landed closer to the target prescription. Success rates within tight error bands were also higher. Tear break-up time predicted accuracy best, and the authors derive useful thresholds for it.
pmc-12734746:
Yongle Xu and co-authors published this road materials study in 2025. They mixed sepiolite, a fibrous clay mineral, into asphalt to fight three flaws at once: rutting in heat, cracking in cold, and toxic fumes. Past work left the best dose and the inner workings unclear. The team tried pure and treated clay at four doses, from two to eight percent.

Plain clay blended best with the asphalt, even though treated clay had more surface area. Doses of four to six percent gave the best heat defense, and four percent cut cold cracking risk most. Low doses stretched fatigue life. The clay's pores trapped light, fume-forming parts, and its minerals blocked other fumes, cutting toxic output. Imaging showed the clay grips asphalt by touch, not by chemical change, and its fiber web firms the mix.
pmc-12735846:
Falagas and coauthors review drug resistance to a new antibiotic in lab tests. The drug treats grave belly infections and covers many germs. Teams need to know how often germs resist it in practice. The review pools lab data from studies across the world.

Four databases were searched from their start to late 2025. From 283 candidate studies, 68 gave usable data. Those studies held near 60,000 germ samples from patients. Resistance was judged by two shared lab rule sets. Rates were split by germ type and by test rule. The pool gives a base for drug choice guides.
pmc-12735946:
The authors (2025) review a hidden layer of antibiotic resistance: chemical marks that switch bacterial genes without changing the DNA letters. Such epigenetic control lets bacteria tolerate drugs briefly, then revert when the pressure lifts. That vanishing act complicates treatment and standard testing. New sequencing tools can now map the marks, called methylomes, across a genome. They reveal enzyme systems that coordinate virulence, drug pumps, and stress responses.

The review then turns to fighting back with CRISPR tools retargeted at the marks themselves. Silencing systems and mark-writing fusions can turn genes off or on in a programmable way, without mutation. Combined with gene and protein profiles, these tools expose how plasticity sustains tolerance. The authors argue that stewardship should target the reversible layer too. Drugs that fail today might work again if the marks propping up resistance can be stripped away.
pmc-12736046:
Krittima Kriengsaksri and co-authors published this study in 2025. It finds a greener way to pull a valued compound, rosmarinic acid, out of a Thai medicinal plant. Standard solvents can irritate skin and leave smells, which is a problem for skin care products.

The team tried fourteen natural deep eutectic solvents, gentle mixtures made from safe ingredients. The best blend paired propylene glycol with lactic acid. With ultrasound help, they tuned the recipe: a set water share, a set liquid-to-leaf ratio, warm temperature, and a half-hour run. The extract fought cell-damaging molecules in tests and calmed stressed skin cells in dishes. It also stayed stable for ninety days under light, air, and base stress. The authors present the method as a safer route for cosmetic ingredients.
pmc-12736546:
Ben Schram and co-authors present a 2025 field study of the body cost of a loaded march for male and female soldiers. Army loads do not shrink by sex, so the team asked what the same load costs each group. Twelve soldiers, six of each sex, marched five kilometers at a set pace with thirty kilos, three times, on flat road and rough gravel. Heart rate and oxygen use were tracked the whole way.

Loads and finish times matched across groups. Men were taller and heavier, so the same pack made a smaller share of their body weight. Models still found sex effects on mean heart rate and oxygen use. The small crew limits firm calls, yet effect sizes ran large. Kit and fitness planning gain field data here.
pmc-12737246:
Sebastián Beltran-Castillo and five colleagues published a review in two thousand twenty-five on tobacco smoke and vaping before birth. The brain's white matter forms in the womb through finely timed cell steps. Toxins crossing the placenta can derail that process, and vaping is widely misjudged as harmless in pregnancy.

The review gathers population and brain-scan findings linking prenatal exposure to altered white matter and later learning and behaviour problems. Lab work shows nicotine directly jolts the receptors of the cells that build myelin, disturbing their growth signals. Other smoke and aerosol chemicals harm support and immune cells and the tissue around them. The authors map the routes by which exposure damages the forming wiring.
pmc-12737346:
Tao He and co-authors weigh what drives the removal of dioxins from fly ash by heat treatment. Dioxins are toxic compounds left in ash from burning waste, and heat can break them down. The team pooled more than four thousand data sets from studies run between 2010 and 2025. They used pooled analysis and a path model to rank each factor's weight.

Some ash parts, such as lime and silica, helped removal, while iron-rich ash hurt it past a point. Heat between five hundred and nine hundred degrees, with mid-length runs, worked best. Ash makeup was the strongest factor of all, ahead of heat settings. Long runs past the best window cut gains. The work gives targets for cleaner, leaner ash treatment.
pmc-12740646:
Motohiko Sano and co-authors present a case report from two thousand twenty-five on mouth ulcers caused by a bone drug, and the pharmacist's role in fixing them. Bisphosphonate drugs can rarely ulcerate the mouth lining, a problem distinct from jaw bone damage. The case took place in a care home for older adults.

A ninety-one-year-old woman with dementia developed ulcers under her tongue and on the floor of her mouth that lasted two weeks. Tests ruled out cancer and confirmed a drug cause. Instead of stopping the drug, the team corrected how it was given, and the ulcers healed fully within four weeks. The authors stress teaching correct dosing technique and involving pharmacists in drug-related mouth care.
pmc-12742446:
Suany Quesada and four colleagues published a seaweed genetics study in two thousand twenty-five on a red alga of the Chilean coast. Mazzaella laminarioides holds three deeply split lineages, north, centre, and south. Where they meet and whether they still mix was unclear from earlier coarse sampling.

Twenty-nine sites between twenty-eight and forty-three degrees south were genotyped with nuclear and mitochondrial markers. The lineages proved almost fully isolated, with only a few mixed individuals even kilometres apart. One contact zone is a five-kilometre rock platform; others form a mosaic across two hundred twenty-five kilometres, centred on sandy beaches. The authors invoke earthquakes and coastal uplift in the lineages' history. They treat the three as sibling species in practice.
pmc-12743146:
Awni Alshurafa and co-authors report a 2025 case of a young man found, almost by accident, to lack a clotting factor almost entirely. The twenty-four-year-old felt perfectly well and came in only for tests before a nose operation. One clotting time came back long, yet he had no bleeding history and no family pattern of bleeding trouble.

Mixing tests corrected the abnormal result, pointing to a missing factor rather than a blocker, and assays confirmed severe factor XI deficiency. The case is a warning that this rare disorder can hide in people with no symptoms at all. Finding it before surgery lets teams plan around a bleeding risk the patient never knew he had.
pmc-12743846:
Jonas Paludo and colleagues evaluate how well a cancer drug's liquid suspension is absorbed and whether it can be delivered through feeding tubes. Their 2025 study concerns ibrutinib, used for several blood cancers and graft-versus-host disease.

Patients who struggle to swallow capsules or tablets need alternative ways to take the drug. In healthy volunteers, the suspension's absorption matched capsules at the same daily dose under fasting conditions. Dose-adjusted values were similar across formulations in patient studies too. Laboratory mock administrations through syringes and two tube types recovered nearly the full intended dose in every case. Impurities, particle size, and holding time were also checked for each delivery route.
pmc-12744946:
Zitong Xiong and Jiangtao Pu review work from two thousand twenty-five on matrine, a natural alkaloid, and its derivatives as cancer drugs. These compounds strike several core pathways that tumors use to grow. They can slow cell division, push cells into programmed death, and reshape the immune setting around a tumor.

Newer derivatives improved on the parent compound in animal models built from patient tumors, with strong tumor suppression in pancreatic and liver cancers. They also helped overcome drug resistance. Still, no registered early clinical trials exist for cancer use. Barriers include poor uptake in the body, liver toxicity, and resistance driven by tumor diversity. The authors propose smart delivery systems and precision strategies to move the field forward.
pmc-12745446:
Jungmin Lym and co-authors report a 2025 case of a dog with a rare and aggressive skin cancer treated with a dose-adjusted drug. The cancer is a T-cell lymphoma of the skin, and its Sezary form spreads cancer cells into the blood. No standard treatment guide exists for it in veterinary care.

The patient was a ten-year-old Yorkshire Terrier with skin nodules, plaques, crusts, and itch. Tissue tests confirmed the lymphoma, and a blood smear found the telltale Sezary cells. A drug called oclacitinib was started at a standard dose. Within fifteen days the dog improved markedly and the blood cells vanished. When the skin worsened a few weeks later, a much higher dose brought gains again, though a later relapse followed. The case shows a dose-linked response worth testing in more dogs.
pmc-12748946:
Jihee Choe and colleagues linked activity timing to sleep quality in 2025. Poor sleep affects health and daily life for many adults. Exercise is a known drug-free aid for sleep. But the role of timing and body clock type was unclear. The team split activity by time of day and intensity. They also split people by their daily rhythm pattern. Machine learning models then predicted that night's sleep efficiency. Explainable tools showed which activity windows mattered most.

Activity patterns predicted sleep efficiency with high accuracy in every group. Timing mattered as much as amount. Gentle activity in the evening mattered most across all groups. That window fell roughly twelve to fifteen hours after waking. The authors see a base for personal, drug-free sleep plans. Plans could match activity timing to a person's rhythm. The work also shows explainable models can untangle daily health links.
pmc-12749246:
Maowei Zhang and colleagues ran a randomized trial in twenty twenty-five testing whether village doctors could deliver talk therapy to people living with a chronic lung disease. The trial took place in communities around Xuzhou, China, in late twenty twenty-three. Village doctors were trained in cognitive behavioral therapy and then led group sessions. Patients either received the therapy plus usual care or usual care alone, and the team followed them for six months.

Patients who received therapy reported lower anxiety and lower depression scores than the control group. They also reported better quality of life and less breathlessness. A direct measure of lung function did not differ clearly between groups. The result supports training local doctors to provide mental health support alongside lung care.
pmc-12751346:
Hai-Tao Wang and five colleagues hunted for the smallest dose of a long-acting numbing drug that still blocks pain well after shoulder surgery. The drug, liposomal bupivacaine, is placed near the nerves of the neck to numb the arm. Too little fails; too much adds risk. Fifty-one patients having keyhole repair of a torn shoulder tendon took part. Each got a dose set by the last patient's result, in a biased-coin up-and-down plan.

The dose that worked for nine in ten patients came out at 10.0 milliliters, with a likely range of 9.3 to 12.5. Side effects were logged for three days after surgery. A firm number like this helps surgical teams standardize the block instead of guessing. The twenty twenty-five study turns a habit-based choice into a measured one for a common operation.
pmc-12753746:
Domenico Boccuzzi and colleagues race three cataract surgery machines against each other, in this pilot study from Naples, published in twenty twenty-five. Cataract removal by ultrasound, called phacoemulsification, depends on fluid flow inside the eye and the time the ultrasound runs. Shorter, gentler runs mean safer surgery.

One hundred forty-five patients were assigned at random to four setups built from three machines with different fluid systems. One machine, the Centurion, finished with the least ultrasound time and the lowest eye pressure, with or without its sensor handpiece. It also drew less fluid than one rival. The sensor handpiece itself added no measurable edge. The authors rank the Centurion's fluid control first among the three, while noting this was a single-center pilot whose findings merit wider testing.
pmc-12754946:
Fang Luo and co-authors tested whether electroacupuncture, needle stimulation with mild electric current, can ease the muscle metabolism problems of type 2 diabetes. They worked with rats made diabetic by a rich diet plus a drug injection. For four weeks the treatment group received daily sessions at three standard points. Other groups got a sham treatment, no treatment, or the same needling plus a drug that blocks a key energy sensor called AMPK.

Treated rats showed lower blood sugar, weight, fats, and insulin resistance, healthier muscle cells, and more cellular energy. A signaling chain through AMPK and two partner proteins switched on, and blocking AMPK erased the benefits. The authors say the pathway likely explains how the treatment helps muscle burn sugar and fat.
pmc-12766746:
Bing Xu and colleagues build a lightweight vision model that grades lychee disease severity. Their study from twenty twenty-five targets anthracnose, a fruit-rotting fungus. Hand grading is slow and subjective for packers. Field-ready models must be accurate yet small.

Their design rebuilds parts of a modern detector with cheap convolutions. A dual-path attention block sharpens lesion features. Weighted convolutions further cut computing cost. Nearly fifteen thousand fruit images trained and tested it. Two lychee varieties under varied lighting were included. Three severity grades structured the labels. Accuracy stayed very high despite the slimming. Growers gain fast, consistent, non-destructive grading.
pmc-12767246:
Gouri Panchannavar and Punnya Angadi stain mouth tissue for two switch proteins, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. They compared thirty cases of oral leukoplakia, a warning lesion, with thirty cases of mouth cancer. The proteins, E-cadherin and ZEB1, drive the shift that lets tumors spread.

Glue protein E-cadherin faded and strayed from its place as lesions turned cancerous. ZEB1 rose in the warning tissue and climbed higher still in cancer. Two ZEB1 measures sorted the groups with eighty-five percent accuracy. The authors read the pair as early flags of the spread program switching on.
pmc-12775146:
Garazi Peña Alzua and colleagues published a 2025 study creating human antibodies against the H5N1 bird flu virus now spreading worldwide. The virus has killed many wild and farmed birds and infected mammals, raising fears of a human pandemic. The researchers targeted the protein the virus uses to enter cells.

Special mice carrying human antibody genes were immunized, yielding sixteen fully human antibodies. Most recognized several variants of the virus, and nearly all neutralized it in laboratory tests. The strongest ones also protected mice when given before or after infection. Such antibodies could become treatments or emergency protection if the virus adapts to people.
pmc-12785646:
Elif Gökçen and co-authors review what fig tree extracts do to cancer cells and how, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Harsh standard drugs drive the hunt for gentler plant aids. Fig parts have a long folk medicine past and rich chemistry.

Dish studies show extracts slow growth, trigger cell death, and cut stress damage in many cancer lines. Results swing with plant part, method, dose, and time. Animal studies are few and human trials none. High doses, above all of the latex, can harm. The authors want standard extracts tested in animals and clinics. Readers get promise with plain caveats attached.
pmc-12786146:
Gabriela Breen and co-authors rebuild tiny protein capsules in the lab in a 2025 study. The capsules, called vaults, form naturally from a single main protein that joins into a shell. Making them from unfolded protein outside cells had not been done before. The team added tags to the protein so it could line up along DNA or a sugar chain, like beads on a string.

Light scattering showed particles of the expected size for vault-like shells. Microscope images, energy transfer tests, and cargo loading all backed up the result. Tagged versions mixed together formed mixed shells as well. The method could allow much larger production of these capsules, which are of interest as delivery vehicles in medicine.
pmc-12787146:
Marcin Ziolkowski and a large team compare cholesterol measures in patients on lipid lowering therapy in a 2025 study. Diagnosis of high cholesterol rests on lab values, but three common measures do not always agree on whether a patient is at goal. The team reviewed records for more than five thousand patients at a large hospital in 2024.

Most treated patients took a statin drug alone, while about a quarter used combined therapy. A mismatch between a key protein measure at goal and cholesterol still high occurred in about a quarter of untreated patients. The mismatch was less common in treated patients, and least common with combined therapy. The findings matter for judging treatment success fairly.
pmc-12789546:
Chiara Bigi and a large world team report why a kagome metal breaks spin sameness in its electron acts on its own. Kagome metals host odd electron states, and this one's bent state had no firm cause. The team joined a light based photo tool, which snaps electron bands, with high grade maths on a full play model. Tests used aimed light to split parts by orbit.

The band build showed a bend tied to one orbit set at low power bands. Maths named a d-wave Pomeranchuk shift, a group electron act, as the cause. It was driven by links in set orbits. Shifts off key band points called Van Hove points shaped the act. The 2025 finds tie orbit choice straight to the break in sameness. They give a small scale frame for bent states across the kagome clan.
pmc-12796546:
Yuichiro Yoneoka and co-authors published a case report in 2025 on a hidden tongue-base thyroid that turned a mild stroke into an airway emergency. A sixty-three-year-old man arrived with a small left-sided stroke. His protocol head scan incidentally showed a four-centimeter calcified mass at the tongue base, narrowing his throat severely.

Tests proved the mass was his only working thyroid tissue. Stroke-related weakness of the throat muscles had removed the reflexes protecting his airway. The team secured the airway with a tracheostomy under local anesthesia, then removed the mass through the jaw in one piece. He recovered well on lifelong hormone replacement. The case warns that quiet anatomy can become critical when stroke strikes.
pmc-12801446:
Qing Long and six co-authors use machine learning to find what predicts student happiness in a 2025 study. The data come from a large Chinese family panel survey, with eight hundred sixteen students used to build models and seven hundred twenty four more held back for outside validation. Forty two candidate factors spanned psychology and public health themes.

A variable selection method narrowed the field, and five tree based models competed under cross validation, with class imbalance handled by synthetic sampling. The best model was checked on internal and external sets and explained with standard importance tools. The authors argue theory guided feature choice keeps such prediction honest. Their aim is practical: point universities toward the levers that raise well being.
pmc-12804446:
Lingchen Wang, Katherine Starcevich, and Wei Yang count how Nevada's cancer deaths shifted during the pandemic's first two years. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Global excess deaths are well documented, but cause-by-cause accounts remain scarce.

Death certificates from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-one anchored the comparison. Combining cancer as main and contributing cause, deaths ran two hundred eight below expectation, a ratio of zero point nine eight. Respiratory cancers dropped notably, fourteen percent under forecast. Deaths with cancer as the underlying cause fell five hundred fifty short. Yet deaths listing cancer as a contributor rose one hundred eighty-nine above expectation. The authors read the split as cancer patients dying with, not of, their disease during COVID waves.
pmc-12805646:
Charlotte Gineste, David Reiss, and Jocelyn Laporte tested tamoxifen in myopathy mice in two thousand twenty-five. Centronuclear myopathies are rare inherited muscle disorders. No effective treatment exists for them. Tamoxifen helped mice with other genetic forms earlier. This model carries a recessive calcium-channel gene defect. Treated and untreated mice were compared over five weeks.

Muscle weakness persisted regardless of treatment. Fiber size stayed small in sick mice. Misplaced nuclei remained frequent too. Repeated contraction force actually fell with treatment. Related protein levels did not change. The drug offered no benefit in this form. It may even harm muscle function slightly.
pmc-12815746:
Five patients with disease from variants in the LAMA2 gene show how widely its effects can range, in a genotype and phenotype study published in 2025. The authors reviewed records of confirmed cases, compared features across age groups, and pulled variant data from public databases.

Every patient had delayed motor milestones, ankle contractures, and lasting motor problems. Two also had cognitive delays, three school age patients had seizures, and brain scans showed white matter changes in four. Muscle enzyme levels ran high. The paper ties variant types to the clinical picture, which helps doctors read new cases against a known pattern.
pmc-12816246:
Peng Luo and eight co-authors present a 2025 study teaching machines to spot tobacco leaf diseases from light beyond the visible. Diseased leaves cost yield and quality, and eye checks are slow. A camera that reads hundreds of wavelengths can catch chemical fingerprints of infection early, without touching the leaf.

The team imaged healthy leaves and four major diseases, from brown spot to two viruses. To keep the test honest, whole leaves, never loose pixels, were held out for checking. Several cleaning methods, wavelength picks, and classifiers were compared head to head. An explanation tool then showed which wavelengths drove each call, making the model's reasoning inspectable for agronomists.
pmc-12821846:
Ali Toffaha and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five review of fifteen years of colorectal cancer surgery in one centralized service. Keyhole surgery grew steadily as the team specialized. The study asks whether outcomes improved alongside that shift.

All planned cancer bowel resections were split into five three-year eras. Keyhole use rose from about half of cases to nearly all. Robotic surgery joined partway through the period. Cancer clearance, lymph node counts, major complications, and hospital stay were compared across eras. The long view shows what centralization and specialization did for safety and quality.
pmc-12821946:
Kerr and coauthors track immune cells used to treat advanced skin cancer. The care grows a patient own tumor-fighting cells in a lab. Those cells are then put back to attack the tumor. Some patients respond well, while others gain little.

The team read the gene codes of the infused cells in fine detail. They tracked those codes in blood through the full course of care. Their aim was to find cell traits that flag who will benefit. Past clues, such as cell counts, gave mixed results. Clear cell marks could help doctors pick patients and improve the cell product.
pmc-12822146:
Youssouf Mfopit and co-authors sequence, in a 2025 paper, the full genome of a bacterium pulled from the gut of a tsetse fly caught in Cameroon. Tsetse flies carry the parasites of sleeping sickness, and their resident microbes may sway how well they pass the parasite on. The isolate belongs to the Pseudomonas clan, a vast genus that includes both germ-fighting helpers and opportunistic pathogens.

The draft genome spans about 5.85 million bases across sixty-one pieces, with over five thousand coding sequences and no plasmid. Family tests place it as a likely new species, nearest to a known soil relative. Its genes include several for resisting antibiotics and pumping drugs out, plus clusters for making seven secondary compounds. Despite carrying some virulence-linked genes, prediction tools judge it a non-human pathogen. The authors add the genome to the record for tsetse microbiome research.
pmc-12827146:
Feng, Wang, and Zhu present a study from twenty twenty-six on neck artery plaque traits and brain white matter damage. White matter bright spots on scans mark small vessel disease in the brain. The team review one hundred eighty patients with neck artery narrowing. All get vessel scans and brain scans for comparison. Plaque thickness, length, narrowing, and calcium type are measured from the vessel scans. Bright spot severity is graded on a standard scale, with volumes split by region. Patients with severe bright spots show thicker plaques and tighter narrowing.

Plaque thickness and narrowing stay firm predictors after full adjustment. Thickness links most strongly to bright spot volume near the ventricles. Plaque length shows no clear links in their data. A rim-signed calcium type also tracks with total bright spot volume.
pmc-12827746:
Xiang Zhang and co-authors review how stomach cancer prepares distant tissue for spread to the belly lining, in a review paper published in 2025. This spread is the top cause of death in advanced stomach cancer. Fluid in the belly helps form a pre-metastatic niche, a landing pad that welcomes wandering tumor cells.

The review tracks how that niche changes over time, using organoid models watched at fine detail. It focuses on tiny vesicles shed by cells that mute immune defenses in the niche. The authors sum up organoid advances, flag open problems, and name possible treatment targets. The synthesis aims to sharpen future anti-spread therapies.
pmc-12829246:
Maha Ramadan Ali and two colleagues compare audio lessons with a self-study module for teaching menstrual health to visually impaired girls, in a trial from twenty twenty-five. Sixty menstruating students at a specialist school in Port Said were randomized. Knowledge, practices, and behaviors were scored before and after.

The self-instructional group scored higher on overall knowledge at post-test and follow-up. The audio group, however, scored higher on actual health practices. It also led on menstruation-related behaviors and restrictions. Both gaps were statistically significant. Knowledge and behavior thus responded to different formats. Positive correlations linked the outcome domains to each other. The authors suggest matching format to the outcome that matters most.
pmc-12831246:
Min Wang, Qiqi Lin, Yibin Tao, and Li Zhao published a 2025 meta-analysis comparing two tools for placing breathing tubes during surgery. A tube must pass the vocal cords safely, and a failed first attempt raises risk. The McGrath device carries a small camera, while the classic Macintosh tool relies on a direct view.

The team pooled nineteen randomized trials in adults under general anaesthesia. The camera device gave a clearly better view of the vocal cords. Yet first-attempt success and the time taken were about the same for both tools. Sore throat rates also matched. The authors conclude that a better view alone does not guarantee a faster or more successful placement.
pmc-12837046:
Fang Hu and co-authors present a 2025 study of methylmalonic acid, a metabolic leftover that builds up in colorectal cancer, and its effect on neutrophils, a front-line immune cell. Bowel cancer grows within a suppressive immune setting shaped by metabolism. How this acid steers neutrophils was poorly defined, so the team attacked the question from several sides.

They combined chemical profiling, data mining, and cell and animal tests. Cancer cell lines and two kinds of neutrophils were used to measure growth, invasion, and cell state changes. pmc-12837446:
Anil Kumar Mandal and Chitra Bahadur Budhathoki develop a school health program to stop adolescents in Nepal from starting smokeless tobacco. The team drafted teaching sessions from those findings and the literature, then pilot-tested them with sixteen students. Reliability scores exceeded 0.8 for every session objective, and over eighty percent of pilot students judged the components effective and appropriate. pmc-12839246:
Kai Yi Han and colleagues examine how brain networks talk to each other during music, in a 2025 brain-scan study. Music engages hearing, movement, and reward systems at once, yet most studies probe one network at a time. The team asked how the three connect at rest, during focused listening, and while music plays in the background of other tasks.

pmc-12840246:
Antonios Michailidis and eight co-authors review a treatment for malformed blood vessels in this 2025 paper. Such malformations are present from birth and can lower quality of life. pmc-12843346:
Agostino Rodda and co-authors try an oxygen-rich dressing in breast cancer surgery in two thousand twenty-five. Slow healing and discomfort are common woes after oncoplastic breast surgery. The dressing is a breast-shaped pad soaked in an oily matrix that leaks low levels of reactive oxygen, which aids repair.

Skin stayed well hydrated and the pad was praised for comfort and ease, with no clear gap in early complications between sides.
pmc-12844446:
Shiyuan Cheng and thirteen co-authors test an extract of the herb Smilax china against fatty liver disease in rats, in a two thousand twenty-five pharmacology paper. Metabolic-associated fatty liver disease is widespread and still lacks effective drug treatments.

Those changes activated the FXR and PPAR-alpha receptors that regulate lipid metabolism. The authors present the herb as a candidate therapy working through the gut-liver axis.
pmc-12847846:
Zicheng Qiu and co-authors present a 2025 journal article on a transformer model for forecasting traffic flow. pmc-12852546:
Jigang Yang and a large team trialed a new imaging tracer for suspected prostate cancer, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Scans guide early detection, but standard imaging can miss small early tumors. The tracer is a radioactive tag that sticks to a protein found on prostate cancer cells, lighting them up on a scan.

In the low-dose group, the scan caught every cancer the biopsy found and was right in most negative cases too. The authors present the tracer as a promising tool for first diagnosis.
pmc-12858946:
Chaochao Xie and five co-authors designed an iron catalyst with a built chiral shape. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with iron cyclopentadienone complexes. These are wide used to add or strip hydrogen in reactions. But the chiral forms lag, since a good chiral home round the iron core is hard to build. Those arms carve a chiral pocket in front of the active iron. Used on acylsilanes, the catalyst adds hydrogen with high pace and fine left right choice. Readers in green chemistry get an earth rich metal doing a job oft left to rare metals.
pmc-12864546:
Sudabeh Shokrollahi and Ahmad Amiri study how two tumor-targeting radioactive drugs cling to albumin, the blood's main carrier protein. Their study appeared in 2025. pmc-12883746:
Zhunzhun Liu and co-authors review benefit finding in adults with long-term physical diseases that are not infectious. Benefit finding means spotting good changes that grow out of hard circumstances. The lowest levels sat in the oldest groups: cancer survivors over 60, and all patients over 70. Age, sex, time since diagnosis, and study quality all helped explain the spread. pmc-12906746:
Ram Bahadur Khadka, Samrat Parajuli, and Nabin Pahari present a two thousand twenty-five viewpoint on bone and joint infection diagnosis in Nepal. Such infections, including those around implants and prosthetic joints, are hard to confirm without good laboratories. Outside major cities, facilities are scarce.

They also name the barriers to using them well. Locally adaptable strategies are proposed to sharpen diagnosis, guide treatment, and protect antibiotics in low-resource hospitals.
pmc-12920446:
Gina Cusimano, Ryan Staupe, and Nicole Sullivan sum fresh ways to read and aim long-lived plasma cells in shot design. Their review head is dated twenty twenty-five. Such cells sit in bone and gut cloth and pour germ-fit guards for decades, which makes them the core of long shield. Yet the calls that make them from plain B cells are thin known.

Shot picks known to sway long shield are summed, with how the cells form and split by kind. Fresh tech that can read cell life is laid out as the path to shots built to call such cells forth on aim.
pmc-12933046:
Nayyar, Brown, Andrade, and Lilford present a scoping review from twenty twenty-four on the economics of antimicrobial stewardship programs. Such programs curb needless antibiotic use to slow resistance. The team gather studies weighing both costs and benefits of the programs. Only eight studies from two decades qualify. pmc-12985346:
Eight doctors led by Bibissara Yerekesh present a case report on two rare mechanical failures after a heart attack went untreated. Their patient was a man of fifty-eight who slid into heart failure two months after a front-wall heart attack. Scans with several imaging methods told the story.

pmc-13038046:
Ali Garmroudi, Md Abdul Kader Tushar, Chang Liu, and Zhengwei Li review robots built partly from living tissue in a 2025 article. These biohybrid robots pair living parts, such as muscle cells, with synthetic materials, so they can adapt and respond like organisms. They discuss design choices, recent advances, and uses in health, medicine, and environmental sensing. Future progress, they argue, will need joint work across biology, materials, and engineering. The goal is smart living machines that can work inside the body or in the field.
pmc-13058646:
Eleven authors present a pooled analysis from two thousand twenty-five on how antidepressant drugs change the resting brain. pmc-13110646:

pmc-13128646:
Karolina Jakubowska-Kowal and a team of co-authors studied a hormone condition in teen girls, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. The condition affects periods, hormones, and later health. The girls in the study had been sent for checks due to excess male-type hormones or period problems.

pmc-13136746:

pmc-13138246:

pmc-13153246:

pmc-13159946:

pmc-13173246:

pmc-13179746:

pmc-13180446:

pmc-13181146:

pmc-13181246:

pmc-13187846:

pmc-13188146:

pmc-13194346:

pmc-13198146:

pmc-13198546:

pmc-13202446:

pmc-13202746:

pmc-13203646:

pmc-13208246:

pmc-13209246:

pmc-13219646:

pmc-13221446:

pmc-13222046:

pmc-13222246:

pmc-13223346:

pmc-13223846:

pmc-13225146:

pmc-13225446:

pmc-13226846:

pmc-13230846:

pmc-13234046:

pmc-13234946:

pmc-13247646:
Kim, Han, and Hwang evaluated extra counseling for suicide attempters in financial hardship, in this 2026 Journal of Korean Medical Science study. Drawn from a Korean emergency-room follow-up service, ninety-three people who had attempted suicide entered the program during or after the COVID-19 period, and forty-nine completed it. Economically vulnerable participants received six counseling sessions, including two tailored picks such as family counseling or vocational rehabilitation, while the general group received four.

Tailored support was associated with reduced suicidal ideation, particularly among vulnerable participants during the pandemic period. Hopelessness emerged as the key mechanism to address: those starting more hopeless improved differently than expected, sharpening the target. pmc-13248746:
Blaschke and a large materials team widened the pores of a metal-organic framework, reported in 2026. These crystal sponges, called MOFs, usually have tiny pores that shut out big catalyst molecules. pmc-13248846:
Pounraj Thanasekaran and co-authors review metal-organic frameworks as programmable electronic materials in a 2026 survey. These crystal lattices join metal nodes with organic links in endlessly varied ways. That freedom lets chemists dial in properties that fixed materials cannot offer.

The review covers frameworks as insulators, as semiconductors with better charge flow, and as white light emitters. pmc-13249046:
Huang and a large team used genetics to test whether chronic back pain raises dementia risk, reported in 2026. Ordinary studies cannot easily separate cause from coincidence, so the authors applied Mendelian randomization, which uses inherited gene variants as natural experiments. Data came from two population sources, and they also checked whether brain structure changes carried the effect.

Genetic liability to chronic back pain pointed toward higher Alzheimer's disease risk, roughly doubling the odds in the main estimate. The authors urge caution, since the estimate is imprecise.
pmc-13249446:
Essers and a European team measured how daily temperature moves teenagers' activity, in a 2026 study. They combined two cohorts, more than thirteen hundred Dutch adolescents and about five hundred Spanish ones, each wearing wrist accelerometers for up to nine days. Fine-grained weather modeling estimated the temperature at each home address for the same days.

Warmer days brought more light and moderate activity in both countries, on the order of five to sixteen extra minutes at the warm extreme. Vigorous exercise did not budge with temperature. pmc-13250246:
Ge, Zhao, and Zhang hunt for the molecular switches behind active generalized vitiligo, an autoimmune disease that destroys skin pigment cells. Their 2026 ImmunoTargets and Therapy paper combines protein and whole-transcriptome readings from blood samples. Three patients and three healthy volunteers supplied the discovery samples, with checks in a separate group.

pmc-13252546:
Brian W Johnston and ten co-authors review how studies define a fast, irregular heartbeat that starts in intensive care, in a paper from 2026. This rhythm fault is common in very ill patients, but studies define it in unlike ways, which blocks fair comparison. The team searched records from 1990 to 2024 and sorted definitions and outcomes in forty-four studies.

Studies differed in how long the fault must last, what heart rate counts, and how it is proven. Outcomes were mostly reported by clinicians, rarely by patients. The authors give ICU teams a shared base to align definitions with guidelines and to plan more even future studies.
pmc-13252746:
Xuye Kang, Jianying Li, and Huipan Wu survey teen sleep across China in this 2026 study. Sleep quality is sliding among Chinese adolescents, and the team set out to measure how it splits by sex and by city versus countryside.

Data covered 5,713 students aged 13 to 18, averaging about 15 years old. A standard sleep questionnaire found a third sleeping poorly. Rural teens fared worse than urban ones, at about 36 versus lower urban rates, and girls worse than boys, at about 38 percent. Fitness and mental health protected sleep, while higher body weight, sitting time, and screen time hurt it. Place and sex changed the strength of those links.
pmc-13254046:
Daniela Nürnberg and Mareike Altgassen study future memory in autistic adults in a 2026 paper. Prospective memory means remembering to do a planned action later, like buying bread when passing a bakery. Thirty autistic and 30 non-autistic adults, matched for age, gender, and non-verbal skills, did an event-based memory task and three thinking tasks.

Non-autistic adults did better on the memory task overall. In both groups, stronger executive functions, the mind's planning and control skills, tied to better memory scores, and planning task time predicted performance. The authors suggest supports such as planning training, agendas, and reminder tools.
pmc-13255346:
Amr A. Othman and a large team describe tuberous sclerosis in Egyptian patients in a 2026 case series. Tuberous sclerosis complex is a multi-organ disease caused by faults in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes, and Egyptian genetic data are scarce. The team studied 23 patients from 20 unrelated families at two centers between 2022 and 2025, using exams, imaging, and full gene sequencing.

Pale skin patches appeared in all patients, brain tubers in 96 percent, and seizures in 87 percent. Eighteen distinct gene variants were found, 16 in TSC2 and two in TSC1, and nine were new. Most variants appeared in just one family each.
pmc-13255946:
Yan Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 genetics study hunting for growth markers in male Dongfeng sika deer. The team examined variation in three candidate genes, GABRA5, SOX13, and AGL, and related it to body weight and chest circumference. They also compared gene activity between fast-growing and slow-growing animals.

Six single-letter DNA variants were found across the three genes, all moderately variable in the herd and in normal inheritance balance. Each variant linked significantly to weight or chest size, and one combined genotype pattern marked the best growers. All three genes also ran more actively in the high-growth group. The authors single out GABRA5 and AGL as the most promising candidates. The variants give breeders concrete markers for selecting faster-growing deer.
pmc-13256046:
Wang and a large team picked apart the shared genetics of sleep traits and epilepsy using genome-wide association data from European cohorts. Standard linkage and local correlation scans probed overlap between epilepsy and sleep length or insomnia. Cross-trait meta-analysis and gene-activity scans then hunted for genes shaping both sides of the link.

Mendelian randomization hinted that epilepsy risk nudges people toward shorter sleep, not the reverse, though the effect was small. The authors stress that lab tests must come before any treatment claims.
pmc-13256146:
Shiyu Hu and co-authors wrote a 2026 journal article on the world burden of COPD, a long-term lung disease that limits airflow. They used Global Burden of Disease 2021 data to count deaths and DALYs, meaning years of healthy life lost. Their focus was how much of that burden came from smoking and from secondhand smoke between 2019 and 2021, during COVID-19.

In 2021 there were about 213 million people living with COPD and 3.7 million deaths, both up from 2019. Smoking caused about 1,334,961 of those deaths, and secondhand smoke caused 266,125 more. The authors say COVID-19 did not seem to change the overall trend, but they call for continued monitoring and stronger action on tobacco use.
pmc-13257246:
Angelika Auguścik and co-authors review breast implants from an engineering standpoint in a 2026 article. Implants are among the most common long-term devices placed in the body, for reconstruction and for cosmetic surgery. Their effects reach body image and quality of life, not only anatomy.

History runs from risky early materials to silicone gel devices in the 1960s, saline options, and modern cohesive gels. Incision choices and placement planes are weighed against outcomes and complication risk. The tissue response receives close attention, from protein coating to fibrous capsule growth. Biofilm and lasting inflammation feed capsular contracture, the leading long-term problem. Rupture, infection, and a rare implant-linked lymphoma are also covered. Surgeons and materials scientists share a full picture of design trade-offs.
pmc-13257346:
Cecilie Juul Mørck Offersen leads a 2026 stroke imaging study on patients whose stroke start time is unknown. Clot-busting treatment depends on timing, and a yes-or-no scan mismatch guides many decisions. Three hundred thirty-three patients admitted over two years had automated brain scan measures compared with later recovery scores.

Lesion volume on diffusion imaging tracked improvement in stroke severity scores after treatment. A brightness measure on FLAIR scans came close to significance, while a volume ratio showed no link. Human mismatch judgments also failed to predict outcome in the cohort. The authors argue for continuous, automated measures instead of a single binary call. Stroke teams gain a nudge toward richer scan numbers, though the exploratory, single-center design calls for confirmation before protocols change.
pmc-13257446:
Alonso Rodrigo Zúñiga-Suárez and colleagues turn two wastes into bricks in a 2026 materials study from Ecuador. Gold mine tailings supplied the mineral base, and used cooking oil served as the binder. Heat-driven linking of fatty acids, called oxypolymerization, held the mix together without cement.

Builders and mining communities share the audience. Locking tailings into durable blocks could cut both waste piles and demand for conventional fired materials.
pmc-13257646:

The peptide joining step also ran with far less reagent than the published large-scale method. Temperatures stayed relatively low and times short. pmc-13258446:
Julia Bartczak and co-authors review virus-linked care paths in multiple sclerosis in a 2026 work. Epstein-Barr virus is now tied firmly to how the disease starts and lasts. Twenty-three studies on set drugs' virus effects and on test-stage virus-aimed care met the rules across four databases.

Test-stage routes hold virus-made T cell infusions, latency breaks through fat paths, and cell cleanup tuning. Vitamin D and stem cell grafts show weaker, mixed effects. pmc-13258846:
Luis Jaime Pérez-Córdoba and coauthors reinforce biodegradable packaging films with cellulose fibers from crop hulls in a 2026 study. Fibers came from yam, potato, and cassava hulls at two loading levels. The base film blends two plant derived polyesters.

Films also turned less glossy and less clear, most strongly with yam fiber. Heat stability changed only slightly across recipes. Excess fiber hurt internal uniformity in some mixes. Packaging designers learn that fiber source matters as much as fiber amount.
pmc-13259346:
Heitor Luiz Ornaghi Jr. and coauthors guess the softening heat of plastics from molecule scores in a 2026 study. That heat point guides where a plastic can serve in safe use. A set of well past one hundred plastics formed the train and test pools.

Three D shape scores gave just part splits for high and low heat groups. Flat graph scores drove the wins in the end. Links in the molecule, shape marks, and ring counts topped the best lists. Those traits fit the known physics of chain stiffness. Mix teams learn that how atoms link counts more than bulk shape for this trait.
pmc-13259446:
Kaijun Xing and coauthors pool fasting trials by age group in a 2026 meta analysis. Twenty eight randomized trials with over eighteen hundred adults tested intermittent fasting effects on body makeup and heart risk markers. Participants split into young, middle aged, and older cohorts.

Middle aged and older adults improved triglycerides, blood pressure, and insulin sensitivity most. Muscle free mass fell in both young and older groups, a caution flag. Careful reanalysis also uncovered a cholesterol rise in older groups that casual reading missed.
pmc-13261146:

pmc-13261446:

pmc-13262446:
Akram S Al-Mughalles and co-authors review tiny pores in liver blood vessel cells in a 2026 journal article. In fatty liver disease linked to metabolism, these pores are lost early, a change called capillarization.

They propose combined drug approaches and cell-specific markers to guide care that is matched to each patient.
pmc-13262546:
Jia Guo and co-authors rank exercise styles by how well they rescue sleep in sedentary adults with insomnia. pmc-13262646:
David Ledingham and colleagues grade how ready digital tremor measures are for real clinical use. Essential tremor is the commonest movement disorder, yet trials still lean on shaky rating scales. pmc-13263146:

pmc-13263246:

pmc-13263846:

pmc-13263946:

pmc-13264146:

pmc-13264246:

pmc-13264346:

pmc-13264446:

pmc-13264846:

pmc-13264946:

pmc-13265846:

pmc-13266046:

pmc-13266846:

pmc-13267546:

pmc-13267746:

pmc-13269146:

pmc-13269446:

pmc-13269646:

pmc-13269846:

pmc-13270246:

pmc-13270546:
