They sequenced ten sample isolates and compared them with global records in a family-tree analysis.

All ten sequences landed in GenBank and matched known isolates at between 98.81 and 100 percent identity. Egyptian and Turkish strains were the closest relatives. The tree placed the Iraqi isolates firmly inside the parasite's grouping alongside worldwide reference strains, confirming the species while showing little genetic diversity. The authors read the conservation as good news for tests built on this gene. They call for a broader molecular watch to follow the parasite's movement.
pmc-13314346:
Karla Alvarez and seven co-authors test dogs for a parasite's antibodies in Chile in a 2025 paper. The parasite causes nerve and muscle paralysis in dogs and is a major cause of cattle abortion worldwide, yet Chilean dog data were thin. They collected blood from well over a hundred dogs, more from countryside than town, in one southern province. A fluorescence test flagged exposure.

About a quarter of dogs tested positive. Rural dogs showed higher rates than urban ones. Age mattered: dogs three years and older were more likely positive. The authors call it the first such survey for the province and a base for control planning.
pmc-13314746:
Munkhsuvd Chimed and colleagues report a 2026 case of scarring around blood vessels that spread far beyond its usual range. Perivascular fibrosis wraps the aorta and its branches in thick soft tissue, and it can mimic big-vessel inflammation or lymph tumors on scans.

Their patient was a 55-year-old man with long-standing scarring behind the belly and a blocked lower aorta. The disease also gripped his chest aorta, a coronary artery, and the branches above the aorta, a spread seldom seen. Over 20 years of follow-up, as the report states, a narrowed coronary artery caused a full heart attack that needed a stent and bypass surgery. Tests for the usual IgG4 marker came back negative. The case shows why layered imaging matters to tell this scarring from its many doubles.
pmc-13314946:
Tarek Sallam and Ahmed M. Attiya use a physics-guided neural network to shape antenna beams, in their 2026 paper. Radar and broadcast arrays often need a cosecant-squared beam shape, which lights a zone evenly while keeping stray side lobes low.

Their method tunes only the phase of each array element, which keeps the hardware simple. A deep network trained with a loss that enforces match to the wanted pattern learns the phase set for big flat arrays. Two aims rule the training: crush side lobes and smooth ripples inside the shaped beam. The team set their method against genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization, the standard search tools named in the report. Number tests gave their approach the edge on pattern quality, by the results reported.
pmc-13315646:
Nadine Berndt, Serge Schneider, and Stefania Oliverio evaluate, in a 2026 study, what changed in Luxembourg during the first year after the country legalized cannabis in 2023. It allowed home cultivation and private use. Data streams miss part of a drug market. The team triangulated seizure laboratory results, wastewater metabolite data, toxicology from driving cases, and a survey of adults who had used cannabis recently. They compared streams before and after the reform.

Most indicators moved little. Potency in seized cannabis and resin stayed stable, wastewater loads were flat, and surveyed users reported habits, prices, and buying channels, mostly illegal ones. Only a minority grew their own or planned to. The exception stood out: cannabis-related driving cases rose significantly, with blood concentrations but patterns hinting at chronic use among some drivers. The authors conclude legalization's market footprint was modest, new initiation limited, and impaired driving the outcome demanding surveillance.
pmc-13316646:
Adilson J M de Oliveira reports a 2026 national cohort of the first 100 brachial plexus operations in Angola. It covers babies hurt at birth and adults with arm nerve injuries, treated from January 2021 to December 2025. One nerve surgeon assessed and operated on every patient.

Sixteen babies were included, most with upper trunk injuries treated by a nerve transfer, and seven reached useful strength grades at follow-up. Among 86 adults, most had complete injuries and nearly all suffered nerve pain, which eased in nine of ten after surgery. Recovery rates stayed low, blamed on long waits averaging 14 months for adults. Lessons stress full care teams, child specialists, and partnerships beyond the surgeon alone.
pmc-13317546:
Xiang Qi and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how colorectal cancer spreads to bone, a rarer landing site that brings fractures, cord pressure, and calcium crises when it comes. The cancer ranks third worldwide in frequency, and bone spread usually travels with liver or lung disease.

The review walks through the TGF-beta pathway, shape-shifting of tumor cells, the Wnt pathway, chemical beacons, and immune dealings inside the bone niche. It carefully separates proof gathered in this cancer from findings borrowed from others, and grades evidence in a table for clinical use. By naming where knowledge is solid and where it is guesswork, the authors aim to steer drug development toward targets that truly fit this disease.
pmc-13318546:
Elisabetta Cozzi and colleagues present a 2026 screening study hunting for long non-coding RNAs that help drive acute myeloid leukaemia or shape response to the drug venetoclax. Protein-coding genes in this blood cancer are well mapped, but these RNA molecules are not.

Using CRISPR interference in the MOLM-13 cell line, the team dampened 7,996 candidate RNAs and watched growth, maturation, and drug sensitivity. Altogether 58 RNAs affected growth, 4 affected maturation, and 23 changed venetoclax response in the screens reported. Four were followed up in depth, including CATG00000106133.1, tied to immune signalling, and AC009299.3, tied to drug response and poorer patient outcomes, giving new leads for prognosis and treatment.
pmc-13318646:
Günhal Şatırtav leads an international expert group whose 2026 review gives guidance on when injections for wet age-related macular degeneration can safely stop. The Vision Academy panel read the literature and agreed on recommendations plus a step-by-step algorithm.

Stopping can be considered when the eye shows no fluid, no sight loss, and no new bleeding across at least three visits at the longest treatment interval a clinic uses. People whose disease stays active, or who rely on one good eye and have relapsed before, may do better continuing. After stopping, scan and vision checks should continue at an agreed pace set with the patient, since the disease can wake again.
pmc-13318746:
Chengjian Cao and co-authors review, in 2026, natural anti-inflammatory compounds for chronic rhinosinusitis. Current treatments calm downstream inflammation but miss the immune faults driving recurrence. The review centres on a regulatory axis of three players. They are FOXP3, the complement receptor C5aR1, and the factor LIF.

Complement signalling through C5aR1 blocks new regulatory cells forming. LIF pushes the other way, raising FOXP3 and calming harmful responses. Compounds such as curcumin and rosmarinic acid act on these pathways. Bromelain and cineole already have clinical support in acute sinusitis.
pmc-13318846:
Brittney P Kokinos and co-authors examine, in 2026, early bone lesions in young pigs that model a joint disease of growing animals and children. Osteochondrosis begins as a focal failure of bone formation in growth regions. Early stages are rarely imaged before symptoms force treatment, so timing and location patterns are poorly known.

The team imaged thigh bones from pigs at several ages, using both computed tomography and magnetic resonance scans, with tissue checks in subsets. Abnormal growth plate widths appeared first, then defined growth plate lesions by twelve weeks. Lesions in the joint surface region appeared later and grew larger. A previously uncharacterised irregular lesion type was common at the oldest age. Both scan methods supported the same conclusions about developmental timing.
pmc-13319046:
Fengjiao Chen and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of ozone injections into arthritic knees, focused on how long benefits last. Sixteen randomised trials with 1,172 patients were included. Searches ran across five databases to December 3, 2025. Pain, stiffness, and function scores were tracked by follow-up time.

Benefits were clear early on. At one month, total arthritis scores improved with a standardised effect of −0.63 in the pooled result. At two months, pain, function, and pain-scale scores all improved significantly. By three months, no outcome differed significantly from control. The authors conclude the effect is time-limited rather than sustained. They offer the timeline as a guide for phased treatment planning in knee osteoarthritis care.
pmc-13319446:
Soo Jin Han and co-authors linked ultrasound features of adenomyosis to IVF outcomes in a 2026 study. In adenomyosis, tissue like the womb lining grows into the womb's muscle wall. Doctors grade its signs with a standard ultrasound checklist called MUSA. Which signs actually hurt pregnancy chances was unclear.

The team reviewed embryo transfer cycles at a Seoul center from 2022 to 2024. Three hundred patients with ultrasound signs were matched with 300 without. Of all the checklist features, only an interrupted junctional zone, the boundary layer inside the womb, independently predicted a lower chance of clinical pregnancy. That focus could sharpen counseling and treatment choices for patients with this condition.
pmc-13319946:
Lingyun Xiang and co-authors study how reward and punishment reshape learning from surprise in a 2026 brain wave study. People update beliefs when outcomes clash with what they expect, and wins and losses may not weigh those clashes in the same way. A sorting task with shifting odds was paired with scalp brain wave records and a layered math model of belief change.

People did better when learning for reward than when learning to dodge punishment. Yet punishment drove faster belief updates in the model, without turning into better scores. Brain wave marks of surprise grew stronger under punishment at key points. The split shows that fast updating alone does not mean good learning, and motive colors how the brain weighs surprise.
pmc-13320046:
Lindsey West and co-authors dig into why floating wind farms at sea stall in tangled rule systems in a 2026 study of the Celtic Sea in Britain. Floating wind could speed the shift to clean power and lift coastal areas, yet growth unfolds inside split marine rule systems that serve many aims at once. Past work named the blocks but rarely traced their deep roots.

Using ideas from the study of institutions, the team traced blocks to root traits that set who does what, who links to whom, and who holds power. Blocks fed each other as a system rather than acting as lone faults, through habits such as clinging to old paths and piling new rules on old ones. Fixes must reshape the rule system itself, with more room to learn and adapt.
pmc-13320346:
Jeong-Uk Eom and co-authors study how storage before cooking shapes harmful compounds in grilled chicken in a 2026 food safety study. Harsh heat on meat makes compounds tied to cancer risk, yet past work stared at the cooking step and skipped what storage does first. Cold and frozen holds were compared for how they prime the meat chemistry that feeds those compounds.

Two weeks in the fridge drove fat and protein decay and reshaped the pool of free building blocks and sharp carbonyl compounds in the breast meat. That primed pool then fed most of the harmful compounds when the meat was cooked. Frozen storage held decay back and cut total harmful load, bar one compound. Storage checks could flag risky meat before it hits the heat.
pmc-13320446:
Zheyu Fan and co-authors study how a withdrawn gut drug harms nerves by draining a vitamin form in a 2026 study. The drug was pulled after it was tied to a nerve illness wave in Japan in the last century. A link to lack of thiamine, a B vitamin, was long suspected but unproven. Chemical scans of cells flagged the active form of that vitamin as the chief casualty.

The drug was shown to wreck that vitamin form through stress driven chemical change, which starved cell power houses and forced a shift to sugar burning. In a mouse model of Alzheimer disease the same drain and nerve harm showed in the brain. Topping up the vitamin form or a shield compound eased the harm and even boosted plaque clearing by the drug.
pmc-13320546:
Daiji Nagayama and co-authors look back at records in a 2026 Japanese study of the weight and diabetes drug tirzepatide. The drug aids weight loss and blood sugar control, but its effect on stiff arteries was less clear. The team tracked vessel stiffness with a heart to ankle index in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Weekly treatment in 24 people, over a median of about a year, lowered the stiffness index from 8.5 to 7.8 at the median. Weight, muscle and fat measures, and blood sugar marks also fell, with the sugar mark HbA1c dropping from 6.6 to 5.6 percent at the median. Higher doses gave larger weight loss in this small group.
pmc-13321046:
Fatai Lu and colleagues test a human defence peptide against bone cancer in a 2026 study. Osteosarcoma is an aggressive bone tumour with poor outlook once it spreads or returns. The peptide LL-37, part of innate defence, can fight tumours in some settings, but its role in this cancer was undefined.

It cut colony growth, movement, and invasion, stalled the cell cycle, and triggered two forms of cell death. Gene scans showed cholesterol making was turned down, with the key enzyme SQLE sharply reduced. Mouse tumour graft work was used to check the effect in living tissue.
pmc-13321546:
Pooja Yashwant Pawar and colleagues assemble first genomes for four threatened Asian hornbills in a 2026 study. Hornbills are flagship birds of wet tropical forests, hit by hunting and habitat loss, yet whole genomes existed for only two of 32 Asian species. Long and short read sequencing were combined for the new assemblies.

Genomes for Great, Rufous-necked, Malabar Pied, and Wreathed Hornbills ran from 1.1 to 1.3 billion letters, with completeness above 95.9 percent in the report. Over 10,000 gene groups were shared, and keratin related families had expanded. Past population tracking showed falling numbers during the late Pleistocene, which sharpens the case for protection.
pmc-13321646:
Jobaida Parvin and co-authors describe spinal muscular atrophy, a gene-based muscle disease, in Bangladeshi children, in a 2026 study. The work aimed to map how the disease looks and which gene changes drive it in this group.

pmc-13321746:

Satisfaction with head nurses averaged 68.94 in specialised wards and 66.11 in general wards on the study scale, fairly high in both. Balanced leadership, mixing task and relationship focus, was most common in specialised wards, while relationship led style led in general wards. pmc-13322946:
Atthaphong Phongphithakchai and colleagues test an international kidney risk tool in Thai patients, in a 2026 validation study. Their cohort held 133 adults with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy at a tertiary centre, followed for a median of 3.4 years of care.

The tool predicts a halving of filtration rate or progression to end-stage kidney disease, and 45 patients reached that endpoint during follow-up. Both versions of the model, with and without a race term, sorted patients well and split kidney survival clearly across risk groups. Fit to observed outcomes looked broadly sound, though ranges around the estimates were wide. The authors support using the tool for risk talks in Thai practice.
pmc-13323146:

Replies came from 285 adults, mostly women with basic schooling in the reported profile. People found with either disease were referred to Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital. The authors stress that gaps in knowledge and attitudes can slow care-seeking and weaken control work.
pmc-13323446:

Transmitters may share one vesicle, sit in separate vesicle pools at one terminal, or split across different branches of the same cell. No single method proves the release route, so the field joins molecular profiling, electrical recording, fine anatomy, light-based control and live sensors.
pmc-13324446:
Wei Wang and co-authors survey genetic variants in neuroblastoma, a childhood solid tumor, in a 2026 study. The cancer varies widely between patients, and its mutation patterns in Chinese patients were little known.

pmc-13325146:
Tugba Celik Caglar and Birol Kayranli test raw date seeds as a reusable sponge for the dye Rhodamine B in a 2026 water study. Dye waste from industry harms water life, and cheap plant sorbents could cut cleanup costs.

Charge tests backed charge attraction as a main grip. Among four regeneration routes, alkali washing plus drying at 120 °C kept the surface most intact. That route still removed 88.1 percent of dye in the fourth cycle, down from 96.3 percent at first.
pmc-13325446:
Spoorthy Sandras and co-authors track metabolism inside living neuron-like cells with a fast NMR method in a 2026 study. As neurons mature, their fuel use shifts, but the change unfolds in under a minute at each step.

Maturation slowed sugar breakdown through glycolysis and raised TCA cycle activity and glutamate output. Fructose 1,6 bisphosphate marked the young state, while glutathione marked the mature one. pmc-13325646:
Djamel Bezzerga, Imran Khan, Ganie Ahmad, and Jisang Hong study a two layer magnet. Their work from twenty twenty-six uses first principle math on a new material. The base sheet is a magnet that works above room heat.

Two stacked sheets can sit in a fierce contest of states. Band form shifts with magnet order and with stack form. One stack form gives an electric tilt that can flip by sliding. The slide cost is very low, which makes switching easy. Valley traits also flip with that electric switch. Flow of charge shows a giant switch effect too.
pmc-13326946:
Roberto Bonanni and co-authors review how exercise may calm epilepsy through neurosteroids in a 2026 narrative review. Brain-made steroids tune GABA signaling, the main braking system whose failure lets seizures fire.

Those same steroids steady inhibitory transmission and may raise the seizure threshold. The authors call for trials that pin dose and mechanism down.
pmc-13327446:
Viktor Olsson and colleagues tackle a hidden source of MRI error in a 2026 methods study. They modeled fields from 0.03 to 7 tesla and gradients from 20 to 600 mT/m, splitting the error into lost signal and extra diffusion weighting. Signal loss came mostly from resampling steps that broke the built-in compensation, reaching 100 percent error in bad cases, while a design-stage waveform fix cut bias below 1 percent for most systems. Using the true waveform during analysis handled the weighting error.
pmc-13329746:
Joanne Daggy and team asked if country living shapes return trips and death among older veterans sent home from VA hospitals. It modelled return trips, death, and death after return trips with a semi-competing risk model, cutting off at 30, 90, or 365 days.

Among 99,557 patients, 28.4% lived in country areas, and only 18% of country dwellers lived within thirty minutes of a VA site against 80.3% of city dwellers. pmc-13330446:
Xiaolong Li and co-authors review how neutrophil traps help cancers resist immune therapy in a 2026 article. Traps are webs of DNA and proteins cast out by neutrophils. Inside tumours they can wall off immune cells and wear T cells down, blunting checkpoint drugs that help many patients.

Such moves could restore anti-tumour immunity, the authors propose.
pmc-13333146:
Disha C Shetty and colleagues report a 2026 case of BRASH syndrome managed with transvenous pacing and continuous renal replacement therapy. BRASH stands for bradycardia, renal failure, atrioventricular nodal blockade, shock, and hyperkalemia, a life-threatening cycle in which high potassium and nodal-blocking drugs together drive profound slow heart rate and unstable circulation. He took carvedilol, losartan, and torsemide, and was brought from a rehabilitation facility after fainting and unresponsiveness. He arrived in respiratory distress, profound shock, and bradycardia at thirty beats per minute. The case shows how pacing plus continuous renal support can break the BRASH cycle.
pmc-13336446:
Seo Yun Jang and colleagues study 2026 salt mix design for at once surface steadying in silicon-nickel-rich full cells. pmc-13336746:

Its best model, a gradient boosting machine, scored 0.919 on discrimination.

Fu notes that low albumin, open injury, diabetes, high blood pressure, and longer operations drove risk, all clinically plausible factors. He praises the pairing of discrimination with calibration and explainable outputs, but warns that the high infection rate may not travel to other hospitals. External validation must come before fixed risk cutoffs guide stronger preventive care.
pmc-13336846:
Simon W J Dietzmann and co-authors question whether some reported carbon pores are real in a 2026 analysis. Pore charts from gas uptake often show narrow micropores in activated carbons and metal-nitrogen-carbon catalysts. The authors argue many are artifacts of the math models used, not true holes.

By building carbons with known surface sites, they showed the phantom pores match gas molecules preferring certain sites. Zinc-nitrogen sites in a framework-derived carbon become nitrogen sites after zinc removal, each with its own gas pull. Comparing nitrogen, carbon dioxide, and argon uptake plus energy calculations pinned the effect down. Reading these artifacts correctly could speed work on batteries, capacitors, and catalysts.
pmc-13337046:
Zhenguang Li and colleagues built a magnetic stimulation platform in 2026 to guide stem cells in the joint toward cartilage repair. Delivered into joints, the platform aims to regrow cartilage from the body's own stem cells rather than implanted tissue. The approach could offer a less invasive option for cartilage damage and early joint disease.
pmc-13340246:

It lysed eighty-three percent of the twenty-four tested bacterial strains, a broad host range. The team measured its growth curve, stability, and killing activity. The twenty twenty-six profile suggests the phage is a clean, potent candidate for phage therapy development.
pmc-13341146:

Of 178 oysters tested, the sea toxin showed in a fifth in the first year and over a third in the last. The fresh water toxin ran near half in the first year, then fell to near none. Cases involving self-harm, suicide, violence, or homicide are set aside, so the figures cover accidents only. The survey has tracked injury patterns since 2006 to guide prevention work.

Accidents clustered outdoors, with seas and rivers together accounting for just under half of cases, and they peaked sharply in the summer months from June to August. The report pairs those patterns with breakdowns by age group and by place and timing. Han cautions that twenty-three hospitals cannot stand in for the whole country, so the numbers describe the surveyed departments rather than a national total. Even so, the summer and open-water concentration gives safety campaigns a clear target.
pmc-13393146:
Tokiaki Takemura and Kazuya Ishige identified an enzyme from a giant virus of amoebae, Acanthamoeba castellanii medusavirus, that adds the third methyl mark to the cap at the head of messenger RNA. Caps guide RNA stability and protein production, and higher cap forms were known from cell studies, but no enzyme had ever shown this third-step activity in a test tube. Sequence comparisons hinted the viral protein belonged to the cap methyltransferase family.

Kinetic tests confirmed genuine Cap3 activity with moderate grip on its substrate, a level the authors call practical for laboratory use. With the enzyme in hand they prepared messenger RNAs carrying the Cap3 structure for the first time by design. They offer the tool to researchers building modified RNAs for experiments and for therapy development, where cap design strongly shapes performance.
pmc-13394446:
Christine Lebrun-Frenay and colleagues detect silent optic nerve lesions in radiologically isolated syndrome in a 2026 multicenter study. These patients show MRI changes suggesting multiple sclerosis without symptoms, and hidden optic nerve damage could sharpen diagnosis and prognosis.

Among 179 people meeting 2023 criteria, silent optic nerve lesions appeared in about 60 percent, found most often by visual evoked potentials and optical coherence tomography, but rarely by routine MRI. The team compared 2024 McDonald criteria, with or without optic nerve assessment, against 2017 criteria. Neurologists gain a case for adding optic nerve testing to early multiple sclerosis workup.
pmc-13395446:
Sebastian Uschmann, Cord Spreckelsen, and Sven Festag build, in 2026, a guard for sharing fake eye photos safely. AI image makers can craft real-looking eyes for teaching and research, yet fakes may leak the identity of real training faces. Their two-stage system first makes eye images with a tuned Stable Diffusion model. A privacy scorer then flags fakes that sit too close to real people.

Tests used two thousand photos from 704 people. The scorer caught more than ninety-seven percent of risky fakes. Safe fakes looked less real than risky ones, which shows the trade-off plainly. The authors pitch the frame for clinics that must share images without naming patients.
pmc-13395546:
Romil R. Parikh leads a 2026 study of unmet needs among Americans who rely on long-term care services. Such services back more than nine million adults at home or in care settings. Pooled national surveys covered 61,829 adults across 27 states over several waves. People were asked plainly whether their services meet their needs and goals.

About twenty-nine percent said their needs go unmet. Gaps ran higher for people living in the community than in residential care. People with unmet needs were less often active in their community. They were also less often content with how they spend their day. The authors call for joined-up investment in a patchy system.
pmc-13395946:
Anthony D. Vaudo and co-authors spent three years in one Sierra Nevada meadow asking whether wild bees divide up pollen by its food value. Pollen supplies the protein and fat bees need, and its makeup differs a lot among plants, so bee groups might settle into distinct feeding niches.

The team tested pollen loads from four common bee subgenera for protein and lipid content and watched which flowers each group visited. Each subgenus held a clear, year-after-year nutritional lane, reached either by loyalty to certain plants or by flexible foraging. Species inside one subgenus, Pyrobombus, shared a niche, which could set them competing for the same pollen mix.
pmc-13396346:
Yu and co-authors study, in 2026, how tree grapes of the genus Cyphostemma repeatedly evolved succulence, the water-storing body plan of desert plants, as they spread from rainforest into dry lands. Combining genome assemblies with ecology and morphology, they found the genomes were reshaped from within by long terminal repeat retrotransposons. These mobile DNA sequences copy themselves into new positions, and they thrived during the genus's radiation.

These insertions expanded introns, the non-coding stretches inside genes, a pattern rarely documented in flowering plants of this group. In two species examined closely, retrotransposons accounted for 58.23 percent and 54.65 percent of total intronic repeat length respectively. Rebuilding the family tree showed 72.8 percent of succulent species shifted toward larger genome sizes over time. The authors argue the restless retrotransposons made the genomes more tolerant of change, easing the evolution of succulence under aridity.
pmc-13396446:
Yuh-Shan Ho mapped three decades of world research linking oral health and nutrition, in a 2026 bibliometric study. Teeth and diet shape each other: sore mouths change what people eat, and food choices drive decay and gum disease, yet the combined field had never been charted as a whole.

Records came from the Science Citation Index Expanded for the years 1991 to 2024, gathered with a two-tier search vocabulary. The analysis traces publication counts, citation leaders, author and country patterns, and how themes shifted over time. Such a map shows newcomers where the crowded ground lies and which questions at the mouth-diet junction remain open.
pmc-13396746:
Brandon Tan and co-authors report that ivermectin, a familiar anti-parasite drug, coincided with better wound healing and less itching in one patient. The patient has junctional epidermolysis bullosa, a blistering skin disease caused by faulty skin glue proteins. Their 2026 report sits in a field where over 21 genes and a thousand mutations have been tied to the wider condition.

Splicing faults, which garble how gene messages are cut and joined, often produce partly working proteins and mid-level disease. Because no cure exists, clinics repurpose safe, cheap drugs where they can. A single case cannot prove cause, but documented gains in healing and itch give other teams a reason to test the drug formally.
pmc-13397646:
Lusine Yaghjyan and colleagues test oral contraceptive links to stem cell markers in benign breast tissue in a 2026 study. Whether contraceptives alter stem-like cell populations in healthy breast tissue could illuminate breast cancer risk pathways.

Among 731 cancer-free women with benign breast disease in Nurses' Health Study II, contraceptive histories updated biennially since 1989 were linked to CD44, CD24, and ALDH1A1 staining in normal tissue cores. Current contraceptive use tracked with stromal CD44 expression. The paper offers a tissue-level clue to hormonal effects on breast stem biology in healthy tissue.
pmc-13398246:
Diego de Oliveira Corrêa and co-authors chain three living systems into one treatment line for pig farm wastewater. Their 2026 study joins a vertical-flow constructed wetland, a microbial fuel cell and an algae photobioreactor. Pig waste runs extremely rich in organic matter and nutrients, overwhelming single-stage treatment.

Wet, saturated running of the wetland-fuel cell stage pushed open-circuit voltage to a peak of 539 mV, proof that microbes were generating current while cleaning. With pulsed feeding, that stage removed 83 percent of suspended solids and 69 percent of chemical oxygen demand in the reported figures. Cleaner outflow then grew the alga Tetradesmus obliquus to yields of 1.1 to 1.3 grams per litre, polishing the water further.
pmc-13398546:
Oz and six colleagues test fish oil feeds in mice with a sepsis like illness in twenty twenty-six. Sepsis is a severe body wide reaction to infection that can harm many organs. Sick patients who cannot eat are fed through a vein, and the fat mix in that feed may matter. The team gave mice a germ toxin, then one of three fat mixes.

The toxin cut blood flow to the gut by more than half. Only the fish oil mix, rich in omega three fats, kept gut flow near normal. Fish oil also guarded the liver from harm. The other oils, from soy and olives, harmed the liver and spleen in some healthy mice.
pmc-13398946:
Sahil Kakar and co-authors (2025) reviewed early surgery for Pott's puffy tumor, a rare infection that swells the forehead. The condition starts as frontal sinusitis and eats into the bone, raising an abscess under the skin. Tradition says wait for the infection to cool before operating. The review asked whether the Draf III procedure, a wide endoscopic opening of the frontal sinuses, is safe during the acute phase. Five studies with nine patients qualified.

Most operations went through the nose with endoscopes. Pooled complications came to zero, though the small numbers leave the true rate uncertain. Repeat operations were rare. The authors judge early surgery safe and effective in these reports, and it may shorten the illness. They insist on caution: nine patients cannot settle the question. Larger prospective studies must confirm the result and define which patients should get the early operation.
pmc-13399246:
Michael Chaim Sklar and colleagues surveyed international medical fellows at the University of Toronto about how the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic affected them, for a 2026 report. Fellows training abroad faced the usual pandemic strain plus distance from family, travel bans, and visa worries. The survey went out in June and July 2020 to 237 fellows in internal medicine and its subspecialties.

Eighty-eight fellows, a 37 percent response rate, described wide disruption. Training objectives were disturbed for 70 percent of respondents; among them, research was suspended for 60 percent and patient exposure shrank for 56 percent, per the survey tallies. Nearly half said they would rather be in their home country. Moderate or worse anxiety was reported by 64 percent, trouble concentrating by 59 percent, and burnout by 45 percent. Half felt their own wellness was affecting the care they gave. The authors argue institutions need stronger support plans for international trainees in future crises.
pmc-13399346:
Francisco Javier Romero-Expósito and co-authors studied how the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans keeps two developmental clocks in step, reporting in 2026. As the worm grows through four larval stages, its seam cells divide on one schedule while its skin is shed and rebuilt in molts on another. The team weakened insulin signaling, a pathway that senses nutrition, using the daf-2(e1370) mutant, and timed both processes.

Reduced insulin signaling slowed everything. It delayed the seam cell divisions much more than the molts, widening the gap between the two schedules. That mismatch then produced a knock-on effect. The start of the next molt was itself postponed, which pulled the programs back into alignment at the opening of the following larval stage. The authors describe this compensatory delay as a resynchronization mechanism. The authors suggest such buffering may be a general feature of how development stays reproducible when conditions vary.
pmc-13399446:
Mika Matsuzaki, Emma Sanchez-Vaznaugh, Joel Gittelsohn, and Jessica Fanzo argue in a 2026 commentary that school nutrition policy has a digital blind spot. Children now meet food through apps, delivery platforms, social media, and influencer marketing. The authors call this online layer the digital food environment. Their own 2025 survey found one in four United States teenagers had ordered food by phone app during school hours, traffic that cafeteria rules ignore.

The authors weigh two broad responses. The other is redesign. They point to trial evidence that making nutrition information and healthier options more visible on platforms reduced the calories, fat, and sodium in online orders. They propose partnerships with delivery companies to surface healthier choices for young users, plus classroom teaching that builds deliberate decision skills. Their aim is guidance that treats the phone in a student's pocket as part of the school food environment.
pmc-13399646:
Cheryl Marise Peilin Tan and colleagues present a simplified three-front-portal method for arthroscopic Latarjet surgery. Their 2026 technical paper addresses recurrent front shoulder dislocation, treated by moving a coracoid bone block to the socket rim. The arthroscopic version is technically hard, with risks of block misplacement, screw problems, and nerve injury.

The method places portals beside the coracoid process and conjoint tendon to lower nerve and vessel injury risk, and uses specific drill guides for socket and coracoid tunnels to improve block placement. The coracoid is prepared outside the joint after cutting, for better view and control. The authors call the technique safe and reproducible for recurrent anterior dislocation, while comparative outcome data remain to be gathered.
pmc-13399746:
Di Zhang and colleagues used the MIMIC-IV intensive care database to test whether a simple insulin resistance index predicts which ischemic stroke patients bounce back into intensive care. The work is a 2026 retrospective study. Among 2,929 stroke patients in the database, 24.0 percent were readmitted to intensive care during the same hospital stay.

Modeled as a continuous score, each step up in the index carried 17 percent higher odds of readmission, with an odds ratio of 1.17 in the adjusted logistic model. Split into quarters, the pattern rose in steps: the top quarter's odds ratio reached 1.53 against the bottom quarter's, in the reported trend analysis. Adding the index to conventional severity models improved their discrimination and reclassification statistics. The authors suggest the score could help flag stroke patients who need closer monitoring after they first leave intensive care.
pmc-13399946:
Wadha Mohammed and colleagues mapped the APOE gene landscape of the Emirati population to guide safer use of new anti-amyloid Alzheimer's drugs, in a 2026 analysis. The team combined Abu Dhabi health records of 2024 Alzheimer's diagnoses and antibody prescriptions with whole-genome data from 506,734 participants in the Emirati Genome Program, calling genotypes from the two defining variants.

In 2024, 1,285 Emiratis were diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, and aducanumab had been prescribed to just eight patients across 2022 to 2024. In the genome cohort, the ε3/ε3 genotype dominated at 77.9 percent. The ε4 risk allele appeared in 14.7 percent of participants, and 0.9 percent carried two ε4 copies, the highest-risk group for ARIA. The protective ε2 allele was present in 7.5 percent of the population. The authors recommend building APOE results into the Emirati Genome Program's pharmacogenomic report so that antibody eligibility and risk counseling rest on local data rather than imported European frequencies.
pmc-13400146:
Mengmeng Jiang, Jing Qu, Moshi Song, and Guang-Hui Liu review how gene therapy could be turned against aging itself, in this 2026 article. Aging is the master risk factor behind most chronic disease. Instead of chasing each disease separately, the authors survey strategies that rewrite the genetic and epigenetic programs driving decline.

The toolkit they organize spans genome editing that permanently alters DNA, RNA modulation that adjusts gene output temporarily, and epigenetic reprogramming that resets a cell's age marks without changing its identity. Against the fourteen recognized hallmarks of aging, they map which genes push aging forward and which protect against it. They weigh each intervention class for durability against delivery difficulty, safety, cost, and ethics. Gene approaches promise longer-lasting effects than drugs or lifestyle change because they act programmably at the source. The review is candid that delivery efficiency and long-term outcomes remain unsolved.
pmc-13400646:
William Son Galanza and co-authors build, in 2026, a deep learning system that recognizes everyday activities of older adults from wearable sensors. Tracking daily routines at home can flag health changes early, letting support arrive in time. The aim was accurate recognition with as few sensors as possible.

In a small home-lab study, participants performed 14 everyday activities while wearing sensors in different combinations. Five models were compared. A two-sensor setup, at the pelvis and right hand, classified 12 activities with accuracy close to ninety percent. Five sensors covered all 14 activities at slightly lower accuracy, while a single sensor struggled. Sensor placement, the authors conclude, matters as much as sensor count.
pmc-13400746:
Saskia Kolb and a large team study, in 2026, the chromatin organizer SATB1 as a possible lever for improving engineered T cell therapy. SATB1 is essential for developing regulatory T cells, which calm immunity, and for helper T cell formation. Its effects in mature human T cells were poorly mapped.

Removing SATB1 changed gene programs in both regulatory and conventional T cells, with wider effects in the regulatory subset. Across both, cytokine production and a major signaling pathway were thrown off balance. Regulatory cells lost suppressive strength, while engineered tumor-targeting CD4 cells cleared tumors better in a humanized mouse model. Tuning SATB1, the authors propose, might simultaneously loosen brakes and press the accelerator in cell therapy.
pmc-13401146:
R S K Barnes examines, in 2026, whether the tiniest bottom-dwelling animals of the Knysna estuary in South Africa form a coherent group behaving differently from larger bottom fauna. The warm-temperate bay is the countrys top estuarine conservation site. Traditional indices treat meiofauna, animals passing through fine sieves, and macrofauna as distinct ecological units.

Five seagrass and five bare sediment sites were compared, using earlier macrofauna data from the same spots. Nematodes, copepods and ostracods made up almost all meiofauna numbers. Abundance tended to be equal or higher in seagrass and peaked in clean sands at the mouth. Each major group responded individually to estuary gradients, with no shared within-group pattern, undermining the idea of two neatly opposed faunas.
pmc-13401746:
Palak Satija examined the link between body mass index and asthma severity in children in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Nutrition shapes airway inflammation in both directions, since obesity and undernutrition can each worsen the disease course through different mechanisms.

At a tertiary paediatric centre between June 2020 and December 2021, 42 children aged 5 to 18 with doctor-diagnosed asthma were graded for severity by the Global Initiative for Asthma criteria. Their BMI was plotted on World Health Organization age and sex charts. About 60 percent had a normal BMI, while roughly 19 percent were overweight or obese and about 17 percent underweight. Rising BMI was strongly tied to greater asthma severity, and half of the overweight or obese children had moderate persistent asthma. The analysis also compared patterns between boys and girls.
pmc-13401946:
Gudly Nanda, Biswajit Mohanty, Sugyani Mohapatra, and Mamata Singh present a 2026 case of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, an ultra-rare genetic disorder where soft tissue progressively turns to bone, in a six-year-old girl. Mutations in the ACVR1 gene derail bone morphogenetic protein signalling and drive the process.

Painful inflammatory swellings flare and then ossify, joint by joint, until movement locks. Most patients are wheelchair-bound by their third decade, and chest restriction can prove fatal. Because the disease is so rare, it is often misdiagnosed, and biopsies or excisions done in error can trigger rapid worsening. The authors walk through the clinical and radiological findings that should raise the diagnosis early, using their young patient's presentation and imaging to show the characteristic pattern. They stress that early recognition is the main protection against harm caused by treatment itself.
pmc-13402046:
Khairy M Ali and co-authors asked whether the speed at which drug levels rise shapes how many Escherichia coli cells become persisters, the dormant cells that survive antibiotics. Working with the antimicrobial peptide pexiganan in small chemostats, they exposed primed and unprimed bacteria to slow and fast drug ramps. Their guess was simple: slow ramps keep cells longer at weak drug levels, which should breed more persisters.

The results matched that guess. Faster rises in drug level left fewer persisters than slower rises run in the same setup. Ali and colleagues frame the finding as proof of principle that dosing schedules, which doctors control, can change persister counts. Fewer persisters could mean fewer relapses after treatment and a slower path toward full drug resistance.
pmc-13402646:
Moran Hausman-Kedem and colleagues test whether sapropterin, sold as Kuvan for another condition, can help children with multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome, an ultra-rare ACTA2 disorder. The fault, at position R179H of the actin gene, wrecks smooth muscle, bringing severe brain vessel disease, aortic aneurysms, and weak muscle action across organs. Computer simulations and virtual drug screening flagged sapropterin as able to restore the actin building that the mutation disrupts.

In skin-derived cells from a patient, the drug improved actin organization visibly. One child then received it off-label, and follow-up showed stabilized brain vessels and clinical improvement over time. The authors call the single-patient result first-in-human support, not proof: one case cannot separate drug effect from natural course. Still, with no gene therapy yet available, a repurposed, already-approved drug offers families a lead worth testing properly.
pmc-13402846:
Mariko Tsukagoshi and colleagues test whether a national risk tool built for short-term surgical danger also forecasts long-term fate after liver cancer surgery. They reviewed 210 patients who had first-time liver removal for the disease between January 2016 and December 2022 at their center. For each person they worked out a predicted death rate from the National Clinical Database tool.

Patients flagged at 3 percent or higher relapsed sooner and died sooner than the low-risk group. They also bled more, stayed longer, and had more severe complications. In adjusted models the 3 percent flag still predicted poor survival on its own, alongside male sex and tiny vessel invasion by tumor. The authors suggest the tool, already used for consent and planning, can double as a guide to long-term outlook when weighing liver surgery.
pmc-13403346:
Hafsa Malik and colleagues compute, entirely in theory, the promise of the double perovskite Ba2MnTiO6 for solar cells, hydrogen generation, and heat harvesting. Density functional calculations checked the lead-free crystal stability through formation energy, elastic traits, and lattice vibrations, and molecular dynamics runs showed no structural decay with heat. A direct band gap of 1.236 electron volts suits visible light work, and the magnetic ground state is antiferromagnetic with strong superexchange coupling.

The headline number is a spectroscopic efficiency limit of 32.28 percent, backed by an open-circuit voltage of 0.945 volts and a fill factor of 0.877 in the modeled device. Band edges also align for hydrogen production at higher pH, and at 1200 kelvin the thermoelectric figure of merit reached 0.63 in the reported figures. The authors present the compound as a versatile energy material awaiting synthesis.
pmc-13403946:
Hirokazu Kanegane, Dan Tomomasa, and Satoshi Okada set out in 2026 how they spot and treat a rare inborn immune fault called APDS. Faults in one of two genes leave a cell switch stuck on, which over-fires immune cells. Children with the fault face repeated lung infections, swollen glands, and higher cancer risk.

Unlike many immune faults, this one has targeted drugs, among them rapamycin and blockers of the faulty switch. Early spotting thus changes a child's outlook a great deal. Clues include airway damage that starts young and weak defenses against two common herpes viruses. The guide walks clinicians through signs, lab hints, and treatment choices.
pmc-13404646:
Yanqing Li and colleagues test a traditional Chinese formula, delivered in coated nanoparticles, against artery plaque in 2026 work. The Yiqi Huoxue formula was wrapped in macrophage membrane to form particles about 100 nanometres wide. The coating aims to steer the medicine toward diseased vessel walls.

Lab checks found round, evenly spread particles with a weak negative surface charge. About 59.4 percent of the formula was packed inside, and the particles did not poison rat vessel cells at the tested dose in the reported experiments. In cell tests, treated cells resisted turning into foam cells after exposure to oxidised LDL, the fat form that drives plaque. The pathway named involves KLF4 and NF-kappaB control of muscle cell behaviour.
pmc-13404846:
Ruth Hardman and colleagues set out a 2026 protocol to evaluate community paramedics working in rural Australian clinics. The CP@clinic programme began in Canada, where paramedics screen, teach and coordinate care for people with complex needs. Rural Australia faces ageing, disadvantage and staff shortages that such a role might ease.

A realist evaluation asks how the programme works, for whom and in which settings, rather than only whether it works. The team starts from an initial programme theory built from earlier evidence. Interviews and outcome data will test which local conditions trigger helpful mechanisms. Hoped-for gains include better health, stronger primary care links and fewer emergency visits.
pmc-13404946:
Yida Wu and colleagues benchmark tools that infer cell direction from single-cell gene data, reporting in 2026. RNA velocity estimates where a cell is heading by comparing new and mature gene messages. Dozens of methods exist, and earlier comparisons were narrow or incomplete.

Their benchmark covers 19 tools and 30 methods in total. Twenty-five RNA-only methods face eight tasks, including directional consistency, timing accuracy, resistance to false signals and stability at low sequencing depth. Five methods that add other data types are judged on integration. Tests span 34 datasets, mixing 26 real and eight simulated cases. Results expose a trade-off between directional consistency and robustness to negative controls.
pmc-13405046:
Hsi-An Yang and colleagues compare treatments for swelling at the centre of the retina in retinitis pigmentosa, in a 2026 review. Retinitis pigmentosa slowly destroys vision, and fluid swelling in the macula adds further loss. Many drugs are used, from water tablets to steroid implants, with little head-to-head evidence.

Twelve studies entered a network meta-analysis, which ranks treatments by combining direct and indirect comparisons. Options included oral acetazolamide, eye drops, steroid injections and implants, and immune cell infusions. At three to four months, oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors improved vision more than anti-VEGF injections in the reported analysis. By twelve months no treatment stood out as clearly best for vision.
pmc-13405646:
Cayuan Tadeu Brandão Pinto and Luciana Regina Meireles review beef parasites that can infect people, in a 2026 food safety article. Cattle carry Sarcocystis cysts in their muscle, and some species cause gut illness or painful muscle inflammation in humans who eat undercooked beef. New species with zoonotic potential are still being described.

Routine meat inspection relies on the naked eye, which misses microscopic cysts in carcasses. The review covers parasite biology, illness in people and animals, and how common infection is in herds worldwide. Molecular tests that identify species accurately are presented as the needed upgrade. The authors frame the issue as a neglected gap in slaughterhouse practice.
pmc-13406746:
Qian Wang and a large team review glowing carbon dots made by green routes, in a 2026 comprehensive survey. Carbon dots dissolve in water, shine stably and are gentle on living tissue, suiting them to sensing and medicine. Older recipes clash with green chemistry through harsh inputs and waste.

Newer methods start from plants, fruit peel or safer synthetic ingredients, using top-down and bottom-up routes the review compares. Machine learning now tunes recipes, predicting brightness and emission colour to cut trial and error. Uses span biosensing, imaging, drug delivery and light-based therapy, with scattered roles beyond biology. Scale-up and standard quality remain open challenges, the authors conclude.
pmc-13406946:
Jin-Hong Yoo, writing in 2026, sets out an ethics framework for AI-assisted scientific writing and peer review. Large language models are reshaping how papers get written and checked, so guarding against misconduct alone no longer covers the risks involved, Yoo argues.

Credit stays human: software cannot be an author, and named authors answer for accuracy in the end. Disclosure should scale with how heavily AI was used, following a tiered scheme. Reviewers may gain speed from AI tools, provided the work happens inside closed, secure systems that protect manuscripts. Yoo also flags newer hazards, including flattering, agreeable model output and hidden prompt attacks, and closes with a revision roadmap for authors, reviewers, and editors.
pmc-13407046:
Matylda Witkowska, Juliusz Huber, and Tomasz Kotwicki report a 2026 study of patients awaiting surgery for idiopathic scoliosis. That is a sideways spinal curve with no clear cause. They compared nerve and muscle function recorded before the operation. They contrasted Lenke 1 and Lenke 3 curve patterns, and patients braced alone against those who also received physiotherapy.

Testing covered muscle activity beside the spine and in the legs, nerve conduction in the lower leg, and responses evoked by magnetic brain stimulation. Deficits showed up more in Lenke 3 curves, and the brace-only group fared worse than the physiotherapy group, though a retrospective design cannot prove cause. Knowing which muscles weaken, and on which side, could shape targeted strengthening before corrective surgery.
pmc-13407246:
Nicoleta Dubei and co-authors offer prescribers, in 2026, a practical plan for preventing gut bleeding in patients taking direct oral anticoagulants, the blood thinners now widely used for atrial fibrillation. These drugs beat older thinners on convenience, yet bleeding in the stomach or bowel remains their most common serious side effect outside the skull.

Drawing on trials, real-world studies, and guidelines from 2004 to 2025, the review ties risk to existing gut disease, other illnesses, and companion drugs such as anti-inflammatory painkillers. Among the thinners, apixaban repeatedly showed the kindest gut profile, while rivaroxaban and high-dose dabigatran bled more. Suggested defences include treating Helicobacter infection, acid-suppressing medicine for high-risk patients, dropping needless companion drugs, and matching drug choice to the individual.
pmc-13407846:
Chia-Chen Chang and team weighed online team learning against simulation-based learning for teacher training in digital health education. Their 2026 quasi-experimental work enrolls 674 primary and secondary teachers in Taiwan, with 399 in team learning and 275 in simulation learning, each in a three-hour program. Digital learning is central to teacher growth, yet which online model best builds knowledge versus confidence had been unclear.

Both groups gained clearly in teaching knowledge and teaching efficacy, but patterns split: team learning gave greater knowledge gains, while simulation gave greater efficacy gains. Mixed models confirmed distinct change patterns, with mental load tied positively to knowledge gain but negatively to efficacy. The work suggests blending teamwork for understanding with simulation for applied confidence in teacher programs.
pmc-13408146:
Okutan and co-authors check, in 2026, whether harvesting the rectus femoris tendon from the front of the thigh to rebuild a torn anterior cruciate ligament weakens that muscle a year later. They use magnetic resonance volumetry, strength dynamometry, and hop tests in 54 patients whose operations ran from December 2024 to April 2025. Mean follow-up was 15.7 months in the retrospective series.

Patients scored a mean of 84.1 on the standard knee function questionnaire and showed a side-to-side laxity difference of just 1.8 millimeters on the arthrometer in the outcome battery. Every quadriceps muscle was smaller on the operated side, but the deficits were uniform, 9.63 percent for the harvested rectus femoris versus 8.52, 7.95, and 8.08 percent for its three partners, a spread that was not statistically significant, proving no selective harm to the donor muscle. Limb symmetry exceeded 90 percent on all strength and functional measures at one year.
pmc-13408346:
Zhiqi Guo and co-authors combine fermentation with light-driven chemistry in 2026 to build an unnatural amino acid from scratch. Microbes excel at making natural products, yet their enzymes refuse many useful non-natural targets. The team split production into two modules so each half could run under conditions it prefers.

Engineered Escherichia coli first fermented a feedstock into indole-3-acetic acid, with gene copies and metabolic tweaks boosting output. A second, oxygen-free module then used light plus a redesigned enzyme to join that intermediate with serine, yielding the target compound in its mirror-image form. Because no purified enzymes or pre-made exotic substrates were needed, the design reads as a template for manufacturing other non-natural products inside living systems.
pmc-13408446:
Hui Wang, Jihong Tang, and colleagues present a 2026 deep-learning tool that infers protein levels from RNA measurements in brain tumours. Proteins do the actual work in cells, yet protein profiling is far scarcer than RNA profiling, and the two correlate only weakly. Their model, T2Pdecoder, learns a shared representation of both data types from paired examples.

Tested on glioma datasets, the model predicted measured protein levels somewhat better than RNA-only baselines and reproduced protein-level pathway patterns more faithfully. Applied to ordinary tumour RNA data, it separated patient groups with clearly different survival, and on single-cell data it reduced technical batch noise while sharpening cell-type markers. The tool offers cancer researchers a way to ask protein-level questions of the large RNA archives already available.
pmc-13410746:
Han Yan and a large team probe in 2026 whether gut microbes help cause kidney damage in diabetes, using genes as natural experiments. Watch-and-see studies had linked the two, yet cause could run either way. The method used compares people whose genes nudge microbe levels up or down across a lifetime.

Data came from genome studies of gut microbes, kidney disease, and immune cell traits. Five microbe groups and seven immune traits showed causal ties to diabetic kidney disease after strict corrections. Immune cells carried part of the effect for some microbes: one species raised risk partly by lowering a marker on regulatory T cells. The chain from gut to immune system to kidney is the paper's main message.
pmc-13410946:
Yuko Takeuchi and colleagues check in 2026 whether scan measures of rebuilt knee ligament bundles predict later graft failure in teenagers. Two-bundle repair of the cruciate ligament aims to copy natural anatomy. Failure without a new injury is the outcome patients fear most, so early warning signs hold value.

The study followed 133 patients aged 15 to 19 for at least two years after surgery. CT scans a week after operation measured the shape ratios of both graft bundles. Both ratios linked to later non-contact failure and sorted patients with fair to good accuracy. In combined models, one bundle ratio, the front-inner one, kept its link.
