Three small loops on Wnt plug into the carrier, and all three are needed for exit. Release comes when the carrier twists hard, much like a hormone receptor switching on. One Wnt type pairs up while aboard, which may tune its signal. The cycle view gives drug hunters clear steps to block or boost.
pmc-13435446:
Wei Qiu and coauthors find a brake on a fiery cell death in gum disease in 2026. Single cell data flag gum fibroblasts as the main site of this death, called necroptosis, in sore periodontal tissue. A fat hormone mimic drug, used here as AdipoAI, is tested as the brake.

The drug switches on an energy sensor that then grips the death kinase and holds it down. Treated mouse gums showed less swelling and less bone loss. Dish grown gum cells made fewer swelling signals under the drug. Downstream death marks fell in step. Local dosing at the gum may calm disease without body wide effects.
pmc-13435646:
Lalitya M Sudarsono and coauthors fit a hollow fiber rig to study a herpes drug against cytomegalovirus in 2026. The virus preys on weak patients, and best dose targets for ganciclovir were never set. Cheap dialyzer cartridges stand in for costly bespoke rigs here.

The rig grows the virus, mirrors human drug curves over time, and holds exposure steady. Virus counts by two methods track drug effect cleanly. Drug levels are read by a precise mass method. Dose hunting for this and other antivirals gains an affordable bench model. Clinics may one day dose by target, not by habit.
pmc-13436646:
Gregory Muller and coauthors track gunshot deaths by transport mode in a national trauma bank from 2007 to 2021 in 2026. The set holds 355,913 patients, with 83.7 percent arriving by ambulance. Private car arrivals form the rest, bound for top trauma centers.

Raw death rates ran far higher for ambulance patients in every period. That gap reflects worse wounds, not worse care, as adjusted math shows. The adjusted odds gap shrank over the years as field care improved. Rates still sat near nineteen percent for ambulance cases in the last period. Fair gauges must adjust for wound severity first.
pmc-13437246:
Manon Queudeville and co-authors reviewed children whose graft-versus-host disease kept raging despite steroids, and who were treated with one or two immune-calming drugs. Their 2026 report covers twelve years at one center. Of 432 transplanted children, thirty-seven developed severe stubborn disease and received a TNF blocker, the JAK blocker ruxolitinib, or both. Most, about seventy percent, got the pair at some point.

About seventy-one percent of the acute group responded by day twenty-eight, and the best rate at any point reached about eighty-nine percent. The chronic group answered at similar rates early on, though fewer held their gains or cleared disease fully. Across both forms, about seventy-three percent responded by day twenty-eight and about sixty-five percent kept a durable response. The authors present the pairing as a workable path for very sick children.
pmc-13438146:
Ivan O Nekhaev's team reassessed the Asian range of the Spanish slug in 2026, a major European pest whose presence beyond Europe was poorly resolved. Field surveys, taxonomy, and ensemble distribution models were combined, using climate plus farming, mosaic landscape, and urban cover, to test whether climate-only models had wrongly ruled out Asia. A population in the northern Tien Shan gave the first reliable Central Asian record, backed by form and gene evidence.

Climate set the broad range, but urban cover unlocked high suitability in settlement mosaics within otherwise marginal mountain and continental areas of Central Asia. Farmers and biosecurity teams get a sharper invasion map that weighs human landscapes alongside climate. Early detection in towns and farms may matter more than climate watch alone.
pmc-13438546:
Zhongxiu Wu's team traced a Miao herbal remedy in 2026 against rheumatoid arthritis using network pharmacology plus lab validation. The remedy, Lysimachia paridiformis var. stenophylla, known as ZhuiFengSan, is used for joint disease, but its targets were unclear. Compound lists were crossed with arthritis genes, yielding ninety-nine candidate targets, with five core hubs led by TNF.

Docking and dynamics showed strong binding of remedy compounds to TNF, and cell tests confirmed the remedy slowed TNF-driven joint cell migration and cut inflammatory signals including IL-6, IL-1 beta, and COX-2. Arthritis teams get a multi-target mechanism centered on TNF blockade. Human efficacy and safety still await trials.
pmc-13439846:
Léa Melataguia Mekontchou's team tracked COVID-19 effects in 2026 on logged malaria in Cameroonian children under five, using monthly tracking data from 2017 to 2022. Pandemic chaos was expected to hit malaria care, yet national and local incidence effects were not yet counted. A time series with two break points, March 2020 and January 2022, adjusted for seasons, bed nets, drug cover, visits, and rainfall.

Logged case counts fell about thirty-seven percent at pandemic onset relative to trend, then climbed about three percent per month, with local patterns varying. The drop likely reflects disrupted reporting and care access as much as true disease change. Malaria programs get a place-aware account for rebuilding tracking and services after shocks.
pmc-13440046:
Zhongcan Xiao, Leyi Zhang, Guannan Zhang, and Xiaoping Wang describe an AI agent that shepherds neutron crystal data from beamline to publishable structure, reporting in 2026. At large scattering facilities, the wait between experiment and finished structure often stretches through many hand-run steps. Their NeuDiff Agent targets the TOPAZ instrument at the Spallation Neutron Source, which studies single crystals with neutrons. The agent runs the standard reduction and refinement path under strict rules.

Only approved tools may run, and checks act as gates that block progress when results fail. Every artifact, assumption, and validation outcome is logged, giving the run a full audit trail. A proofing loop repeats until the structure file meets checkCIF criteria, the field's standard validation. The authors frame governed automation, not raw speed, as the way to cut instrument-to-publication delay.
pmc-13440246:
Catharina Johanna Alberts's team launched Cancer RADAR in 2026, a European effort to map cancer risk by migration background, where comparable data were missing. Migrant health policy needs stratified cancer figures, yet registries rarely collect them consistently. Pilot population-based registries across twenty-two countries were surveyed on sharing birth-country-stratified data for six cancers chosen for infection links or screening relevance.

Feasibility proved high. Sixty percent of registries can and will share data and another ten percent intend to retrieve it, with inequality reduction as a motive and time, resources, and legal approval as barriers. A shared protocol and anonymized analysis tool now support comparable estimates, including trends around the Ukraine war. Cancer planners get a framework for equity-focused cancer surveillance.
pmc-13440446:
Shant Torkom Yeretzian and colleagues map how economic studies count lost productivity for patients and caregivers, reporting a 2026 scoping review. Evaluations that take a societal view should include work losses, yet practice varies widely. The team screened nearly four thousand records from 2019 to 2025 and kept forty studies, plus ten guidance documents from assessment agencies. Instruments for measuring loss and methods for pricing it were catalogued side by side.

Twenty-five instruments turned up, most covering patients rather than caregivers and many covering presenteeism, working while unwell, alone. Only three instruments suited both main pricing approaches. The human capital approach is simple but can overstate losses, while the friction cost approach fits labour markets better and needs hard-to-find vacancy data. Guidance across countries split between the two. The authors urge shared standards for this neglected cost category.
pmc-13442446:
Praveen Krishna Veerasubramanian and colleagues hunt for paired drug blocks that calm T cells in a 2026 study. The TNF family holds 47 proteins that steer immune signals, yet single blocks often fail as bodies route around them. The team scored family genes for links to joint and bowel illness, gene data, drug ease, and path roles.

Ten targets rose to the top and went into a mixed cell test that mimics immune clash. Four pairs cut two T-cell signal goods, IL-2 and IFN-gamma, by a clear margin. Gene reads then showed broad drops in genes for T-cell switch-on, growth, and split. The authors argue that paired blocks can close the detours that beat single drugs. They offer the four pairs as leads for immune illness care, pending tests in living systems.
pmc-13443046:
Anjali Kumari and Mahaboobkhan Rasool review two sibling signal goods, IL-1 beta and IL-18, in osteoarthritis in a 2026 paper. Both come from the IL-1 family and drive joint decay, yet they play distinct parts. The first sparks early cartilage breakdown and cell aging, while the twin fans immune fire through the inflammasome hub.

Shared wiring runs through the MyD88 path, so the pair act as partners rather than spare copies. The review sorts joint harm into three linked phases: cytokine start, growth, and chronic grind, all tied to cell aging. Drugs that hunt the first signal have flopped in trials so far. The authors urge paired hunts and mark-guided care, since twin blocks may beat single blocks for worn joints.
pmc-13443746:
Tao Xie and colleagues report amygdala ablation that eased trauma-linked fear bias in one patient in a 2026 case paper. The man had stubborn epilepsy plus chronic PTSD, and he read vague faces as more fearful than peers did. Depth probes logged his right amygdala, then heat ablation targeted that spot.

Before the burn, his amygdala split fearful from happy faces with a late signal surge that tracked his bias. Right after the burn, his gloomy read of vague faces fell, and his PTSD scores fell with it. Seizure counts held steady through the change. Late signal size shrank in step with his fear drop. The authors flag that signal as a mark that may guide care, while one case sets the limit of the claim.
pmc-13444246:
Akash Vijayan and colleagues present a 2026 deep learning framework for automated heartbeat classification from ECG traces, tackling class imbalance, timing patterns, and beat-to-beat links that limit standard tools. Their hybrid pairs convolutional feature extraction with a hypergraph network built from nearest-neighbor beat relations, plus adaptive focal loss for rare classes.

The model scored 98.66 percent accuracy on the five-class MIT-BIH arrhythmia set and 95.46 percent on the three-class INCART set, holding steady across both benchmarks. That consistency suggests the beat-relation modeling captures patterns simpler models miss. Clinics gain a promising diagnostic aid, though prospective validation on hospital data remains.
pmc-13444646:
Limei Hu and colleagues report the case of a 72-year-old man whose gut parasite infection turned severe during steroid treatment for a blood vessel disease, published in 2026. The man had belly pain and a skin rash, and doctors first treated him for IgA vasculitis. Steroids calm that disease, yet they can let a quiet worm infection spread through the body.

When his state failed to improve, tests found the worm Strongyloides stercoralis in his sputum and stool. The two diseases can look alike, since both bring belly pain and skin spots, which helps explain the missed call. The authors stress screening for the worm before steroid treatment starts, above all where the parasite is common.
pmc-13447146:
Saad Aldosari and co-authors review 2026 records on advanced arthritis drugs at a single centre in Dammam, Saudi Arabia. People with rheumatoid arthritis often start a biologic or targeted pill after older drugs fail. How long they stay on a first drug, switch, or stop in routine Saudi care was poorly known.

One hundred seventy-five adults who were new to these drugs were followed from treatment starts between 2013 and 2023. A tumour necrosis factor blocker was the most common first choice. Estimated time on drug at five years looked broadly similar across drug classes, with no clear gap in formal tests. Loss of benefit drove most switches, while pregnancy and missed doses drove many stops, though the small cohort limits firm conclusions.
pmc-13447546:
Seher Yüksel and coauthors analyze a 2026 Turkish cohort study of immune-gene markers in chronic lymph blood cancer, a disease where local data remain scarce. The team studied 145 patients at a top center, typing IGHV gene change status and B-cell dock set patterns with gene tests and living results.

Unchanged IGHV showed in 55.2 percent, above Western rates but in line with Med cohorts, and foretold far shorter time to first treatment, 17 versus 70 months. Yet worsening-free and overall living did not worsen, thanks to rescue by modern aimed drugs. Set-pattern subsets showed region-set patterns, aiding risk sorting in left-out groups.
pmc-13448046:
Tomoe Uchida and Aya Hirata review the waist size cutoffs Japan uses to flag metabolic syndrome, in a review paper from 2026. Since 2005, Japan has required a large waist for the diagnosis, set at 85 centimeters for men and 90 for women. The same cutoffs drive a national checkup program aimed at heart risk.

The authors sorted past studies into four themes, from fat around the organs to later heart disease. Waist levels tied to organ fat and clustered risk factors tended to sit below the current cutoff for women. Studies linking waist size alone to later heart disease gave mixed results, again mostly for women. The review suggests that requiring a large waist may miss at-risk people, and that total risk burden deserves more weight.
pmc-13448646:
Lei Zhang and co-authors break high-temperature limits for polymer capacitor films by locking down charge movement in a 2026 materials study. Aromatic polymers resist heat well, yet charges leak along and between their chains under hot, high-field conditions, gutting stored energy and efficiency. Blending and crosslinking fixes are blunted by the polymers' flat, stacking-prone backbones, the authors argue.

Adding a strong Lewis acid compound at four percent by weight reorganised chain packing through coordination bonds, hydrogen bonds and steric twisting. Ordered same-type chain arrangements replaced the leaky mixed stacking pattern. Stored energy at high field reached values the authors report as beyond existing polymer composites, holding above ninety percent efficiency at both moderate and extreme test temperatures. Electric vehicles, aircraft and deep drilling converters are the target settings.
pmc-13448846:
Chang Liu and a large team ask in 2026 whether nerve damage visible in the cornea can flag patients with diabetes whose feet are at greatest risk. They studied 710 participants across diabetic foot risk categories with foot examinations, microscope scans of corneal nerves, eye surface tests, and tear fluid measurements. Nerve fiber length, density, and branching all worsened as foot risk rose.

Even the lowest-risk patients already showed impaired corneal nerves compared with controls, alongside shorter tear stability and altered tear chemistry. High-risk patients showed the strongest nerve changes. A simple model using nerve fiber length, fiber width, and a blood kidney measure identified high-risk feet with an area under the curve of 0.80. Fiber length below 5.7 millimeters per square millimeter came with over fourfold odds of high-risk status, suggesting eye scans could warn earlier.
pmc-13449146:
Adrian Ybañez and co-authors survey in 2026 what high-risk groups in Cebu, Philippines, know and do about toxoplasmosis, a parasite infection spread largely through cats. They questioned 416 people across three groups with heavy cat contact: cat owners, veterinary students, and veterinary personnel. A subset of 250 also gave blood samples for rapid antibody testing against Toxoplasma gondii.

Students showed the strongest knowledge, with 61 percent rated high, against 46 percent of personnel and 24 percent of owners, and attitudes followed the same order. Daily practice reversed the ranking, with personnel highest at 54 percent. Overall, 29.2 percent of those tested carried antibodies, rising to 43.8 percent among veterinary personnel and 39 percent among cat owners. Testing positive tracked with age, education, medical history, and how often a person handled cats.
pmc-13449346:
Xian and colleagues present a 2026 review arguing that cancer's drug resistance is bounded by development. A tumor's cell of origin, the normal cell it came from, sets limits on which states its cells can reach.

The authors sort resistance into three kinds: cells keep their lineage, cells flip back to an earlier state, or cells settle into a new stable state. Gene-wide tools can spot these flexible states, but only lab tests that try to reverse them prove a state is truly changeable. The team proposes a prime-then-kill plan: first push tumor cells into a state where they are exposed, then strike that state.
pmc-13449446:
Layng and colleagues evaluated in 2026 an electronic consult tracking tool in the emergency department of a large academic hospital. Specialist consults often stall emergency care, but measuring their turnaround is hard with ordinary notes. The team embedded a tracker in the record system to stamp each step, then checked it against manual review of over five thousand consults during a three-month validation.

Layng found the tracker logged a shorter median turnaround than any paperwork stand-in, at about 139 minutes against 179 to 273 minutes for the proxy measures. Over the next year it recorded nearly thirty-five thousand consults across 26 services. Use averaged just over half of consults each month. Overall median turnaround was 108 minutes, ranging from about an hour for intensive care to over three hours for psychiatry. The authors call the tool a feasible base for improving consult flow.
pmc-13450446:
Sheng Gao and colleagues searched for predictors of response to two treatments for central serous chorioretinopathy in 2026, a retina condition where fluid leaks under the retina and blurs vision. Options include subthreshold micropulse laser and oral spironolactone, but doctors lacked clear markers of who benefits from each. The team compared baseline traits and imaging measures.

One hundred three eyes from ninety-seven patients were split into a laser group of fifty-two eyes and a spironolactone group of fifty-one eyes. Fluid resolution and retinal thickness improved in both groups, while choroidal thickness fell only with spironolactone. Baseline fluid area predicted resolution in both groups, while other factors predicted change only with spironolactone. Clinicians gain a basis for matching patients to the treatment most likely to clear fluid.
pmc-13450946:
Tang writes this 2026 editorial, titled The Missing Axis, arguing that gestational diabetes research has a blind spot shaped like a kidney. About 14 percent of pregnancies worldwide involve gestational diabetes, and the condition is known to forecast roughly ten-fold higher type 2 diabetes risk and doubled cardiovascular risk for the mother. Kidney outcomes, Tang notes, have been comparatively ignored.

The editorial discusses a French nationwide study of 1,441,317 women who delivered in 2012 and 2013, followed for ten years, in which 7.2 percent had gestational diabetes on record. A history of the condition carried a 46 percent higher adjusted risk of later hospitalized chronic kidney disease. It also carried an 18 percent higher risk of acute kidney injury in the analysis. Risk rose with the number of affected pregnancies. Tang urges that postpartum follow-up add kidney surveillance to the usual glucose and heart watch.
pmc-13452046:
Mukhammad Amonov studies in 2026 a urine protein that may flag kidney harm from high blood pressure years before standard tests stir. The protein, nephrin, slips from the kidney's filter cells when they are hurt. His study enrolled 60 adults in Bukhara, Uzbekistan, split evenly across three pressure stages, with other kidney risks kept out.

Urine nephrin already ran high at the first stage, while the usual blood marks sat normal, and it climbed with each stage. Six months of pressure care cut the protein by about a quarter to a third, with a partial return of kidney reserve. The author offers urine nephrin as an early watch tool for clinics.
pmc-13452146:
Tobar Palacios and colleagues ask in 2026 whether adding a second treatment to steroids improves recovery from severe sudden sensorineural hearing loss. That is hearing that vanishes within days and counts as an ear emergency. In the worst grades of loss, steroids alone rarely restore hearing.

Their systematic review and meta-analysis gathered nine studies of combination therapy, including steroid injections through the eardrum paired with other treatments. Combined approaches consistently outperformed steroid treatment alone on standard hearing tests and on speech discrimination, the ability to understand words. Starting treatment early produced the best auditory outcomes. The authors caution that the studies differed widely and carried a moderate risk of bias. So the apparent advantage, while consistent, awaits confirmation in large randomized trials before it can anchor routine practice.
pmc-13452246:
Gong and co-authors map how brain networks differ between new and long-standing tinnitus in people whose hearing tests normal. Their 2026 study records resting brain waves from 45 participants: fifteen with acute tinnitus under six months, fifteen with chronic tinnitus, and fifteen healthy controls. Two analysis styles were combined: one tracking brief recurring brain states, one tracking fluctuating network connections.

Acute tinnitus tilted the brain toward its salience network, the system that flags important stimuli, while the central executive network participated less, and state transitions skewed toward salience processing. Its executive network also ran with unusual high-frequency efficiency. Chronic tinnitus looked different: transitions had normalised, overall network behaviour was more stable, and efficiency gains appeared instead at low frequencies in executive and auditory networks. The authors frame acute tinnitus as a salience-executive imbalance and chronic tinnitus as compensatory rebalancing, suggesting stage-specific biomarkers.
pmc-13452746:
Hasan Asfour and others reflected in 2026 on developing the GRAFT score for skin graft loss after skin cancer surgery. Skin grafts are common after cancer resection, yet failure remains an important complication, and integrated prediction evidence was lacking. The authors asked which preoperative factors predict failure and whether they combine into a practical bedside score.

The GRAFT score, standing for Graft Risk Assessment of Failure Tool, was developed and internally validated on a retrospective cohort of skin-graft patients after cancer resection. Predictors available before surgery were prioritized for simplicity, reproducibility, and bedside use. Anticoagulation and lower body graft location emerged among the predictors in the reported analysis. Surgeons gain a simple score to flag high-risk grafts before surgery.
pmc-13453846:
Ziang Wang and co-authors test a new way to rebuild damaged windpipes using the body itself as a growth chamber, in a research paper from 2026. Long airway gaps are hard to fix, and past lab-grown replacements lacked long-term proof. The team reviewed seven patients with end-stage airway damage or tumors near the lung.

Surgeons placed a stent between layers of treated pig skin tissue and kept it washed with antibiotic fluid through small pumps. The patients' own cells were seeded into the graft twice a week for two months. Five patients had windpipe repairs and two had bronchial repairs. Two patients died within a year from a leak, a grave warning amid hopeful signs.
pmc-13453946:
Benazir Meera and five co-authors evaluate how a horseback riding program for older adults with dementia gets delivered in real communities. The program, Riding in the Moment, pairs riders and caregivers with trained non clinical staff for social connection and gentle activity. Their 2026 project surveys the staff and volunteers who run it, before and after delivery, under a standard program reach framework.

Of the workers surveyed, 95 percent felt satisfied with their training and ready to deliver the sessions. Every item on the fidelity checklist was met, which signals tight adherence to the program design. After delivery, 74 percent were extremely satisfied and all 15 post survey respondents said they would recommend the program. Workers praised the emotional payoff and the structured training, while asking for better volunteer engagement and communication.
pmc-13454046:
Patrizia Brunner and seven co-authors profile the users of dibi, a German digital companion app for type 2 diabetes. Their 2026 analysis covers 5,744 users, of whom 2,422 consented and finished registration by December 2024, leaving 2,262 adults in the main set. Most users, 89.4 percent, had type 2 diabetes, and the largest age band was 56 to 65 years.

Men made up 57.5 percent of the group, and most users were within a year of their diagnosis. Just over half set up a medication plan, and 22.7 percent used the intake tracking tool at least once. Oral drugs alone were the most common regimen, while longer disease came with stepped up treatment. Many users confirmed intake once and never again, a pattern the authors flag. They call for adding clinical measures such as HbA1c to deepen the app's value.
pmc-13454346:
Jing Zhou and nine colleagues describe, in 2026, a material that evens out microwave heating, a task long plagued by hot and cold spots. Microwaves heat unevenly because their field is uneven, and past fixes tried to reshape that field. The new absorber instead reacts to heat itself, soaking up less energy where an object is already hot.

Tests covered flat, angled, and curved shapes, plus groups of objects heated together. Temperature spread, measured by a standard variation score, fell by more than 90 percent in the reported setups. The effect held while power ranged across a hundredfold span. Because the absorber regulates itself, no sensors or controls were needed. The authors see uses in food, materials work, and other fields where even heating matters.
pmc-13454446:
Chengxing Lu and nine colleagues report, in 2026, a binder trick that wakes up plain sulfur, selenium, and tellurium electrodes for sodium batteries. These cheap electrode materials react slowly and leak dissolved chains, so they usually need nano-structuring and lots of carbon. The team's acidic binder instead corrodes the copper foil beneath the coating on purpose.

That corrosion grows a copper chalcogenide layer that later turns into an active catalyst during cycling. In selenium cells, the layer cut a key energy barrier by about a quarter. Cells reached 96 percent of the selenium's theoretical capacity and still worked after 16,000 cycles. They also kept about 94 percent of capacity at minus 20 degrees. The authors present binder-driven surface chemistry as a general route to practical, host-free sodium batteries.
pmc-13455346:
Fierro and colleagues assessed an enhanced recovery pathway layered onto dual-opioid spinal anesthesia for caesarean birth at one Italian center. They compared 166 women treated after the pathway launched with 156 treated before it. All received spinal sufentanil plus morphine with standard painkillers, and tramadol rescue whenever pain scores reached four.

Rescue opioid need fell significantly under the pathway, with regression estimating an 84.5 percent reduction on the first postoperative day alone for women in the recovery group. Early mobilization, return of bladder and bowel function, and other recovery milestones all improved after the pathway's implementation in the retrospective comparison. More women in the pathway group also went home on the second postoperative day than in the pre-pathway cohort studied. The authors caution the design is observational, but argue pairing structured recovery with opioid-sparing spinal technique compounds the benefit.
pmc-13455446:
Ying Lin and colleagues compare side vision after three operations for strong short sight in a 2026 study. Laser reshaping and lens implants all correct moderate to high myopia well at the centre of vision, yet their effects on edge vision were less clear. The team reviewed 598 eyes of patients aged 18 to 35 treated with FS-LASIK, SMILE or a phakic lens implant. Wavefront errors were measured centrally and at 30 degrees off axis before surgery and six months after.

All three methods corrected refraction accurately with little induced astigmatism, and second-order errors fell sharply. Third-order errors rose most after FS-LASIK, then SMILE, then lens implant, while peripheral focus shifted toward farsightedness most after FS-LASIK. Lens implants thus disturbed edge optics least in this group, suggesting surgeons should weigh peripheral optics, not only central acuity, when advising young patients with high myopia.
pmc-13455546:
Farima Malekinia and co-authors report a 2026 study of harmaline, a plant alkaloid, in diabetic mice and pancreatic cells. Type two diabetes ties high blood sugar to oxidative stress and inflammation. Its antioxidant name made harmaline worth a careful test.

Cells grown under varying glucose tracked insulin release and defence strength. Mice with diabetes then got harmaline, metformin, or nothing for ten days. Harmaline boosted insulin release and antioxidant strength while cutting fat peroxidation. Pathways that steer antioxidant defence and inflammation shifted as well. Both the cell work and the mouse work pointed the same way. The results position harmaline as a plausible aid, still at the test stage.
pmc-13456646:
Martin Ezechiáš, Michal Šíma, and Jaroslav Semerád open, in a 2026 editorial, a research collection on new ways to judge the harm of emerging environmental contaminants. The flood of new chemicals, drug residues, hormone disruptors, and plastic particles has outrun classic one-chemical animal testing. Real life adds low doses over years and mixtures that interact.

Thirteen contributions make up the collection, spanning lab studies, reviews, and short reports. Several use human cell systems to trace how pollutants such as PFAS disturb immunity, replacing guesswork with mechanism. Others lean on gene-wide profiling, computer models, machine learning, and effect-based water monitoring. The editors describe a field moving from describing damage toward predicting it in human-relevant, realistic settings. They frame these new approach methods as partners to, not yet replacements for, traditional toxicology.
pmc-13456746:
Judy Martin and four colleagues report, in a 2026 case study, the first free-flap breast reconstruction performed in Mali. Rebuilding a breast with the patient's own tissue is routine in rich countries, yet Mali lacks the imaging, microscopes, and trained teams such surgery demands. The operation took place during a joint mission of Swiss and Malian plastic surgeons.

The patient was a 38-year-old woman who had lost a breast to triple-negative cancer. Surgeons moved a flap of belly tissue, vessels included, to rebuild the breast, and blood flow stayed reliable despite thin preoperative imaging. A Malian surgeon handled follow-up locally. The authors frame the case as proof of feasibility for selected patients, and as capacity building: lasting gains depend on training local teams and weaving the service into Mali's own health system.
pmc-13456946:
Martins and colleagues run a pilot study of light-based facial rejuvenation in this 2026 paper. Photodynamic therapy uses a light-sensitive cream and illumination to refresh skin, and it can also fight microbes and calm inflammation. The team treated women aged 40 to 55 whose skin showed sun-aging. They compared two cream formulas, ALA and MAL. Each was combined with amber LED light and infrared laser exposure.

The treatment proved effective across the outcomes they tracked: fine lines were reduced, wrinkles appeared smoother, and skin felt softer and firmer with less sagging after the sessions. Side effects stayed minimal throughout the pilot. Because the group was small and the design exploratory, the study is presented as a pilot, with the comparison between the two creams setting up questions for larger trials.
pmc-13457046:
ZhiTong Qu, WenQin Wang, and Jie Wang comment, in a 2026 piece, on a five-step framework linking micronutrients to immune cell behavior across health, aging, and inflammation. The framework under discussion runs from nutrient sensing through gene programming, calcium and redox signals, and inflammatory cell death, ending at an NAD-linked aging step. The commentators praise the model yet press five refinements.

Their boldest move relocates the last step. They argue the NAD, CD38, and SIRT axis is not one checkpoint among five. It is the hub where all five converge, since NAD supply steers gene marks, fuel sensing, and damage control at once. Evidence from lung disease and lupus shows the axis acting across the whole chain. They also ask the framework to admit stress hormones, wider gene mechanisms, a redox tipping circuit, and the timing of any intervention.
pmc-13457646:
Jiayi Liu, Yang Liu, Annie Yuan and Ke Ning published this 2026 review tracing treatment for spinal muscular atrophy, an inherited disease that destroys motor neurons and weakens muscles, mostly in childhood. The disease stems from loss of the SMN1 gene, with a near-twin gene, SMN2, softening or worsening severity. The authors recount the field from the first clinical descriptions in 1891 and the gene's identification in 1995 to today's approved therapies.

Three SMN-targeted treatments now exist: nusinersen, approved in 2016, the gene therapy onasemnogene abeparvovec in 2019, and the oral drug risdiplam in 2020. All improve survival and movement, especially when newborn screening allows treatment before symptoms. Yet many later-diagnosed patients respond only modestly, and lost neurons cannot be restored. The review compares the three drugs, weighs biomarkers such as neurofilament light chain, and explores non-SMN strategies and combination treatment as the next frontier.
pmc-13458046:
Yitong Jia and colleagues report a single striking case: a 30-year-old man left with a prolonged disorder of consciousness and severe limb spasticity after traumatic brain injury. Treatments rarely help both problems at once. The team implanted spinal cord stimulation leads at two levels, screened frequencies, and settled on 80 hertz for 21 days of continuous stimulation, tracking consciousness, muscle tone, brain waves, and corticospinal signals.

Over those three weeks his Coma Recovery Scale score climbed from 5 to 10, a move from deep unresponsiveness toward real responsiveness. Spasticity eased sharply on two scales, with the Ashworth grade falling from 3 to 4 down to about 1, and hip adductor tone dropping from 3 to 1. Muscle recordings quieted, EEG connectivity across frontal and temporal areas strengthened, and motor responses to magnetic stimulation arrived faster. Gains held at six months. The authors present the frequency-tuned stimulation as a candidate dual therapy needing controlled study.
pmc-13458746:
Cameron Keighron and colleagues grow human dopaminergic neurons into three-dimensional organoids and argue they model Parkinson's disease more faithfully than flat cultures. pmc-13474746:

pmc-13474846:
Shurui Hu and eight colleagues tested in 2026 whether fibre Bragg grating sensors can track heat during dental implant drilling better than standard sensors. pmc-13475846:
Ann and colleagues describe, in a 2026 letter, anesthesia care for a young child with congenital pulmonary airway malformation, a developmental lung defect with cystic lesions. pmc-13476346:
Yongzhi Zheng and co-authors test mutation value in 2026 for children with a usually favorable leukemia subtype. The study held 289 children treated across many centers from 2015 to 2023. pmc-13477046:
Chantal M Sanchez and co-authors total lifetime care burden in 2026 for New York Medicaid patients born with faulty pulmonary valves. pmc-13478046:

pmc-13479346:
Kazuki Yoshida and four co-authors traced the brain steps by which people avoid hard work, in a study published in 2026. Choices weigh gains against effort, but the order of that calculation in time was unclear. The team recorded brain waves while people did an effort choice task, and scored each person's skill at judging their own performance. Choice-linked waves appeared by about a quarter of a second after the cue.

pmc-13479446:
Marjolein Dieleman and colleagues present a 2026 population cohort study of cervical disease in young women in the northern Netherlands. Findings can help doctors judge which young women warrant testing before the screening age arrives.
pmc-13479546:
Jue Lu and colleagues report a 2026 pilot imaging study in glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain tumor, for patients receiving tumor treating fields therapy. pmc-13479646:
Tyler Nighbor and coauthors present a 2026 special communication mapping evidence gaps on e-cigarette use in the United States. The call is aimed at funders and researchers setting the next agenda.
pmc-13479746:
Bellini and colleagues in Italy studied in 2026 how wealth and schooling shape the last month of care for cancer patients. Care strength was gauged by hospital stays, emergency visits, drug use, and place of death. School level and a local hardship score stood in for social rank.

pmc-13479946:
Haili Li and coauthors published a 2026 evaluation of how fairly and efficiently health resources are spread across Anhui Province in China. Their rankings give provincial planners a basis for shifting investment northward.
pmc-13480046:
Ziyuan Chen and eight co-authors ask whether heart-and-lung fitness protects against a chronic lung disease, and how genes fit in. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The disease, COPD, slowly blocks airflow, and fitness is tied to many heart and metabolic risks.

pmc-13480246:
Dhyani Mehta and two colleagues modeled in 2026 environmental costs in BRICS economies with a cusp-logit framework. Standard emissions gauges miss the economic burden of environmental damage, especially its sudden, lopsided swings.

China and India looked innovation-steady, while Brazil, Russia, and South Africa proved more fragile, giving policymakers an early-warning lens on cost exposure.
pmc-13480746:
Cui Wang and co-authors describe a 2026 route to sponges of mixed metals that make hydrogen peroxide from air and power. pmc-13481146:
Mohamad I Nasser and co-authors report a 2026 Danish study of bone breaks in people with type 2 diabetes who also carry small-vessel damage. pmc-13482646:
Ma and colleagues listen for failing bearings in 2026 inside a cow dung briquetting machine, farm equipment that crushes manure into fuel blocks under slow, heavy, noisy loads. Early bearing faults whisper under that noise, so their method stacks three techniques, an adaptive signal decomposition, a wavelet noise filter, and a dung beetle optimizer that tunes the filter automatically. It beat either technique used alone on the same buried signals in the comparisons reported by the team. On real recordings from a machine with a spalled bearing, the 8.5 hertz fault frequency and its harmonics stood out clearly, supporting use for early warnings on farm machinery.
pmc-13482746:
Hongyang Fu and four colleagues reviewed in 2026 why lung adenocarcinoma spreads to the spine in particular. Spine spread brings pain, fractures, and cord compression with poor outlook, yet most work treats it as generic bone spread.

Exosomes may prime a spine niche before arrival, pointing to targeted prevention and care routes.
pmc-13483746:
Biaorui Su and a team of co-authors test whether blocking abnormal blood vessels, paired with early exercise therapy, beats exercise alone for a stubborn shoulder problem. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The problem follows injury, and it leaves patients with lasting pain and stiff movement.

Sixty matched patients were split into two groups. Both did twelve weeks of structured rehabilitation. One group also had the vessel-blocking procedure first, with rehab starting the next day. At every check, the combined group improved more on pain, function, movement, and quality of life. At six months its night pain score was far lower and its shoulder score far higher. The authors judge the pairing safe and effective.
pmc-13483846:
Maria Khan describes a 2026 quality improvement drive to cut false-positive blood cultures at a heart institute in Peshawar, Pakistan. Across 646 cultures, the mean contamination rate fell from 12.9 percent before the push to 6.09 percent by its end. Most cultures came from inpatient units, where the program focused its effort. The rate still sits above benchmark, and the authors note that direct observation audits would sharpen the next round.
pmc-13483946:
Wang and team built a simulation that follows hydraulic fracturing from crack growth to oil output, with special attention to where the sand ends up. Their 2026 framework couples crack growth, sand transport, and production in both directions, updating crack conductivity, meaning flow capacity, as stress and sand levels change locally.

The team then varied six pumping choices, including sand size, injection rate, and fluid thickness, to rank their influence on output. pmc-13485846:

pmc-13486046:

pmc-13486746:

pmc-13487146:

pmc-13487246:

pmc-13487346:

pmc-13487446:
Johanna Finskas and three co-authors watch daily care in a nursing home in this twenty twenty-six study. Older residents often sit most of the day, and moving too little weakens the body and mind. Care staff can help residents move, but how they do it in daily work is poorly described.

The team observed ten care workers and twelve residents in one long-term care unit over two months. They also chatted with staff during the watches. pmc-13488246:

pmc-13488846:

pmc-13491746:

pmc-13492046:

pmc-13493046:

pmc-13493846:

pmc-13494046:

pmc-13494246:

pmc-13494546:

pmc-13494646:

pmc-13494746:

pmc-13494946:

pmc-13495146:

pmc-13495246:

pmc-13495446:
