The authors offer the pairing as proof that regulatory and metabolic fixes combine.
pmc-13563846:
Yeonjoo Kwak and ten colleagues prime stem cells with chemistry and motion so the parcels they shed become stronger nerve medicine. Extracellular vesicles from mesenchymal stem cells show promise for peripheral neuropathy, but flat-dish production makes them weak and uneven. Their 2026 method bathes the cells in a growth factor, TGF-beta-3, inside a three-dimensional culture. The parcels, named MCR-EVs, were tested against ordinary vesicles in injured spinal cord slices kept alive in dishes, then in mice with a squeezed sciatic nerve, a neuropathy model.

The parcels entered slice cells, cut cell death, and restored axon markers and survival signalling better than ordinary ones. In the mice, inflammation genes quieted, microglial overactivation eased, and nerve fibres, Schwann cell markers, and muscle junctions recovered more fully. Small-RNA reads found cargo tied to regeneration and pain control. The authors propose priming as an upgrade for vesicle therapy.
pmc-13563946:
Ahmet Zengin, Cemalettin Yılmaz, and Taylan Adademir describe, in a 2026 case report, surgery for a 36-year-old man with a giant pouch on the left atrial appendage of the heart. He also had long-standing atrial fibrillation. The rare birth defect measured 66 by 46 millimeters and the patient came to care with palpitations.

Surgeons removed the pouch and performed a Cox-Maze IV procedure, an operation that creates scar lines to restore normal heart rhythm, while the patient was on a heart-lung machine. He left hospital in normal rhythm, stayed free of symptoms, and had normal heart scans at follow-up. The case shows how fixing the structure and the rhythm in one operation can work.
pmc-13564946:
Ravagli and coauthors profile royal jelly from a Sicilian black bee. Italian makers face high costs next to cheap imports. Local origin could give their jelly a market edge. Jelly from the native Sicilian bee may differ in clear ways.

The team used two spectrum tools to fingerprint the jelly. Five craft samples came from Sicilian black bees. Five mass-made and five craft samples gave contrasts. Chemical traits that set the Sicilian jelly apart were sought. Those traits could back origin claims on labels. Small sample counts mean more work is due.
pmc-13565646:
Nicola Mercanti and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, what really happens inside bag-in-box wine packages stacked on pallets under export-like heat. Exporters set chamber temperatures but rarely know the wine's own temperature. The team hid pressure and temperature sensors inside three-liter boxes for a twenty-day chamber trial at mild and hot settings.

Wine inside never reached the hot chamber's set point: top boxes settled near thirty-four degrees, bottom ones near twenty-six. Pressure rose after handling and peaked around days three to five, more at the pallet's base. Hot-stored wine lost protective sulfur compounds and gained acidity markers. Set points, the authors warn, are a poor guide to real conditions.
pmc-13565746:
Thanwarat Phophantool and co-authors offer a 2026 study joining body measures and genome-wide markers to map variety in Thai swamp buffalo. These buffalo are valuable farm genetic resources. Regional gaps were suspected but never measured both ways at once.

Nearly eight hundred animals contributed body records, and most were genotyped on a dense marker array. Shape analysis found regional gaps blurred by feeding and care. Genetic data showed a broadly shared background with clear regional structure. Inbreeding patterns differed by region, strongest in the Lower South. Combined evidence guides conservation breeding.
pmc-13566346:
Kai Feng, Yayi Xia, Jingsheng Liu, and Mingxuan Yang review how a malaria drug may steer two metal-linked forms of cell death, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. The drug is artesunate, made from artemisinin, and the two death forms depend on iron and on copper. The review pulls together lab work on cancer, brain disease, and liver scarring.

In cancer models the drug tends to push iron-linked death by upsetting iron handling and weak shields in the cell. A brake on copper-linked death has so far been seen only in models of Parkinson disease. Links between the two death paths are still mostly a working idea. Readers get a clear split between firm proof and open questions.
pmc-13566446:
José A. Mejias-Figueroa, Charlotte M. Story, and Michael B. Streiff describe, in a 2026 case report, a woman whose blood clot led to discovery of a rare genetic variant affecting protein S, a natural brake on clotting. She first had a deep vein thrombosis at thirty-five, and testing five years later showed a type III deficiency pattern plus a variant of uncertain meaning in the PROS1 gene.

The altered building block sits in a spot that forms a key bond and touches a partner protein involved in several anti-clotting jobs. That biochemical context, the authors argue, supports treating the variant as disease-causing. The case helps clinicians interpret uncertain genetic results in clotting disorders.
pmc-13566846:
Julie Baltenneck and co-authors map which genes six rot-causing bacteria cannot live without in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The bacteria rot soft plant tissue and span two genera. A gene-jumping method can find vital genes, but comparing big data sets across strains is hard.

Their pipeline, TNSEEK, automates that comparison end to end. Two hundred twenty-five genes proved vital in all six strains, mostly for basic cell upkeep. Few vital genes were shared at genus level alone, which flags distinct diets between the genera. A large set of one hundred eighty-one genes was vital in single strains only, many of unknown role. Some belong to defense systems and virus remnants in the genome.
pmc-13568246:
Wenfeng Mu, Shigang Wang, and Jiajia Huang wrote a study from 2026 on grading hands-on skill in trade training with a computer. The test case is filing, a basic task for fitter trainees. Human grading takes expert time, and photo sets with expert grades are small. A plain score from a model also tells the trainee little about what went wrong.

Their method turns the teacher's grading sheet into rules the model must obey. It reads the trainee's body pose from video and names the faults it finds. It then gives a score that can be split into the points lost for each fault. They built a set of filing videos from twenty-five trainees and tested the method by leaving one person out at a time. Its scores tracked expert grades closely, and its fault calls were right most of the time.
pmc-13568446:
Lei Shi and co-authors built a sharper way to read the beat frequency of a square helium-neon ring laser gyroscope, a sensor that measures rotation. Their method first calibrates four signal channels, correcting gain and phase, then merges them. A basic merge uses least squares, and an extended version also weighs the leftover noise in each channel.

Tests with known signals confirmed the gains from merging and the soundness of the math. Real gyroscope records were split in time order for calibration, tuning, and a final held-out check. The merged signal came out cleaner than any single channel, and two kinds of Kalman filter pinned the frequency down to within a few thousandths of a hertz. Leftover patterns tied to the carrier signal point to where the noise model still needs work.
pmc-13569446:
C. Piñero-Pérez and co-authors test, in a 2026 prospective study, whether a stool marker of gut inflammation called fecal calprotectin can predict and track gut graft-versus-host disease. The study covered 165 adults receiving donor stem cell transplants. Diagnosis normally needs invasive scope procedures. Samples were taken on set days after transplant, at disease onset, and after treatment.

The marker had no predictive value at day seven but gained accuracy by days fourteen and twenty-one, with a best cutoff on day twenty-one. Levels tracked scope severity and fell after treatment, although infections also raised them. Used alongside clinical judgment, the stool test could spare some patients invasive procedures and flag trouble earlier.
pmc-13570146:
Natascha Rosen and co-authors test, in a 2026 mouse study, whether lowering a receptor called CSF1R on immune support cells can slow chronic lymphocytic leukemia, which depends heavily on those cells. Mice bred to develop the disease carried only half the usual receptor dose, and leukemia cells from patients were also grown with altered support cells in the lab.

Receptor levels fell on blood monocytes but held steady in tissue macrophages, whose numbers barely changed. Leukemia grew slightly slower early on, yet survival matched normal mice as disease advanced, and lab cultures showed no effect on cancer cell survival or movement. Halving this signal is too weak a strategy on its own.
pmc-13570746:
Didde Boisen Andersen and colleagues defend giving rare diseases special priority in health budgets, on grounds of fairness rather than numbers. Many philosophers argue rarity itself carries no moral weight, yet health systems already pay more for rare-disease treatments. This 2026 philosophy paper develops a luck-egalitarian case: people with rare diseases suffer what the authors call bad numbers luck, an undeserved disadvantage in how research and markets serve small groups.

On that view, higher willingness to pay, adjusted priority-setting, and wider societal attention can correct an injustice, not merely indulge sentiment. Recognising bad numbers luck, they argue, clarifies the tension between fairness and efficiency that cost-effectiveness analysis leaves unresolved. The paper speaks to policymakers weighing orphan drugs against treatments for common conditions.
pmc-13570846:
Joseph L. Smith and co-authors study, in a 2026 claims analysis from a large United States insurer, cholesterol-lowering treatment in adults with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, the artery-clogging condition behind most heart attacks and strokes. Treatment patterns, cholesterol results, adherence, and costs were tracked for two years after first therapy in over four hundred thousand patients with a year of follow-up.

A striking thirty-five percent received no cholesterol treatment within a year of diagnosis, and nearly all treated patients started on a statin alone. About two thirds of statin users took their drug reliably, and reliable users mostly cost less per month than non-adherent patients. Many patients still missed cholesterol targets, marking clear room to improve routine care.
pmc-13571346:
Ken Yamazaki and colleagues describe, in a 2026 case, a 54-year-old man whose racing heart circuit ran along a surviving muscular ridge inside a largely silent right atrium. He had partial atrial standstill, a rare condition where much of the upper heart chamber produces no electrical signal, together with complete heart block.

Detailed electrical mapping found broad silent zones but one preserved ridge, formed by two known bands, serving as the narrow bridge the re-entrant circuit needed. Burning that ridge, plus a standard second line, stopped the tachycardia, and a pacemaker followed for the block. He stayed free of the rhythm problem for seven years, showing how spared anatomy can both cause and cure arrhythmia.
pmc-13571446:
Abdulla Alabed and co-authors report, in a 2026 case with a literature review, a 20-year-old woman with active ulcerative colitis who turned out to have two rare compression problems at once. Alongside her bowel flare she had lost weight and suffered nausea and vomiting, and imaging revealed both superior mesenteric artery syndrome and the nutcracker phenomenon.

In the first, the duodenum is squeezed between the aorta and a branch artery, blocking food passage. In the second, the left kidney vein is pinched in the same fork, swelling upstream. Only a handful of combined cases were known, none with ulcerative colitis. Care ranges from nutrition support to surgery, and the report maps the diagnostic trap of blaming every symptom on the known bowel disease.
pmc-13572446:
Kaixin Li, with four colleagues, details a 2026 study of sprays that slow colour change in persimmon fruit. Growers treat astringent persimmons with carbon dioxide to remove the harsh taste, yet the cure speeds ripening and peel colour shift. A spray called 1-MCP, used before harvest, blocks the ripening signal ethylene.

Three groups were compared: untreated fruit, carbon-dioxide-treated fruit, and sprayed fruit then treated with gas. The gas alone raised breath rate, ethylene output, peel colour score, and orange pigment levels, while green pigment fell. Sprayed fruit kept more green pigment and scored lower on the rest. Gene tests showed the gas switched on colour-building genes up to about twenty fold, while the spray held many of them near flat. The spray thus delays the colour shift the gas brings.
pmc-13572546:
Aswiniya Ambigapathy and Sriharipriya KC present a 2026 method for reading wireless channels in fast-moving car networks. Cars that talk to each other need clean links, but speed warps the signal through the Doppler effect. Smart surfaces that both pass and bounce signals add promise and complexity at once.

The method starts with a least squares read from neat pilot signals, then hands off to a Kalman filter, which tracks the channel as it changes. A fading model with set timing links the steps, and path loss scaling sharpens the track. In simulations, error fell by up to 25 decibels for one surface mode and near 22 for another, against base methods. The gains held across many driving conditions. The authors pitch the tracker for multi-user roads at high speed.
pmc-13573346:
Dandan Ding, with three colleagues, reviews 2026 work on artificial intelligence for MRI scans of unborn babies and the placenta. MRI gives sharp soft-tissue views when ultrasound falls short, yet fetal motion, noise, and reader differences can blur the read. Smart tools promise faster, steadier scans and reads.

A PubMed search to May 2024 kept 74 studies on fetal scans and 32 on placenta scans. In fetal work, sorting organs into maps led, with motion fixes next and disease sorting rare. Placenta work centred on judging invasion into the womb wall, then on organ mapping. Past work claimed scan time cuts up to 60 percent at like quality. The authors flag small, single-centre data sets and thin variety as the main limits to fix.
pmc-13573446:
Dewei Zou, with seven colleagues, reports on a 2026 study of insulin resistance markers and death in severe bleeding stroke. Bleeding stroke kills and disables at high rates, and insulin resistance had been tied to outcomes in the clot type of stroke, not the bleed type. The team tested several stand-in markers built from routine blood values.

Records came from a public United States intensive care database and covered 1,538 patients, with deaths in hospital near 27 percent. All markers tied to death in the joint model. One marker, SPISE, pointed the other way, with higher values linked to lower risk. Curved models showed bent links for six markers, so risk did not rise in a straight line. A sugar-fat index sorted risk best of the set. The authors rate the markers as backup flags, not main tools.
pmc-13573546:
Krimpenfort and co-authors published a 2026 study on whether doctors should judge lab results against a patient's own history instead of population ranges. A personal reference interval uses a patient's past results to set their normal band, which can be far narrower than the population's. That promises sharper detection of real change. Dutch general practitioners were asked about the idea's promise and its traps.

The researchers ran focus groups and presented case vignettes, watching how doctors reasoned with personal ranges in concrete scenarios. Benefits they saw included catching drift earlier and ignoring harmless outliers. Risks included false reassurance, extra testing, and confusion when history is short. Prerequisites emerged too: good data plumbing and clear guidance. The study maps the human factors that will decide whether a statistically attractive idea survives contact with everyday practice. Personal baselines, it suggests, will need careful design to help rather than mislead.
pmc-13574246:
James Gallagher and co-authors show that a fish's personality is largely fixed before it is born, and survives threats unchanged. Their study appeared in 2026. The team used Amazon mollies, natural clones, so genes cannot explain differences. Fish were raised with or without the threat of predators and filmed continuously for their first four weeks. Predator stress shifted the average behavior of the whole group, as expected.

Yet the spread between individuals, the individuality itself, did not shrink or grow under stress. Each fish kept its own trajectory. One surprise: which mother a fish had strongly set its swimming speed but not its hiding. The authors say non-genetic seeds planted before birth quietly fix temperament.
pmc-13575146:
Archisman Banerjee and colleagues identified a single gene, BEND4, as a marker and possible target in aggressive acute myeloid leukaemia. Current prognosis rests on chromosome and mutation markers, yet many patients lack them, and most markers cannot be drugged. Analysing gene-expression data from 1,338 patients, their 2026 study found BEND4 overexpressed in adverse-risk disease, then validated it in 350 more patients, including relapsed and refractory cases.

High BEND4 meant poorer survival and higher relapse risk, and it beat mutation- and expression-based models at prediction, with a simple lab threshold separating adverse-risk patients at 91 percent sensitivity. In cells and mice, dialling BEND4 up drove leukaemia and shortened survival, while dialling it down shrank tumours and extended life. The authors propose BEND4 as both a prognostic test and a therapeutic target.
pmc-13575246:
V Basavaraj and five colleagues test a plant seed extract against root-knot nematodes in a 2026 study. These tiny worms attack vegetable roots and can cut yields by up to 80 percent. Chemical worm killers are falling from favour over health and environmental harm, so plant-based options draw interest.

The extract came from seeds of Carissa carandas, made with methanol. In lab dishes it killed young worms and stopped eggs hatching, more strongly at higher doses and longer exposure. Microscope images showed severe damage to egg masses at the top dose. In pots of muskmelon, seed powder cut root galls by 94.26 percent at 30 days, close to a commercial product's 96.78 percent. Chemical analysis flagged fatty acids as likely active ingredients.
pmc-13575946:
Emine Kutlu and co-authors make and test three new platinum compounds in a 2026 chemistry paper. Platinum drugs are a mainstay of cancer care, and the team built theirs around pyridine, a ring-shaped partner molecule with small changes on each version. They checked the makeup of each compound with several lab methods, from light spectra to magnetic resonance.

Computer models mapped where each molecule is most reactive and how it might dock with a lung cancer protein. Two of the three compounds bound that protein more strongly. In dish tests, those two also hit lung cancer cells hardest over a day of exposure. The work also touched normal lung cells, so care is needed in reading the results. The authors say the pair merit tests in animals next.
pmc-13576946:
Ian Goodall-Halliwell and co-authors wrote a 2026 paper on a software pipeline that cleans brain scans before analysis. MRI scans must be aligned, corrected, and sorted before researchers or doctors can trust measurements from them. Many pipelines are slow or hard to run in a hospital. Their tool, MICAFlow, aims to be fast and sturdy on normal clinic hardware.

The pipeline handles both standard anatomy scans and diffusion scans that trace wiring in the brain. A key step uses deep learning outlines of brain parts to line up scans of different types. It runs in minutes without a graphics card and follows shared standards so others can repeat the work. Tests on mixed data sets checked its speed and how well the scans lined up.
pmc-13577246:
Li and coauthors test womb fluid stem cells for spine defect harm in rats. Spina bifida leaves the spine cord open to slow damage. Few care choices guard nerve cells in that state. Stem cells from womb fluid may help nerves heal.

Pups with spine lesions got stem cells or a sham shot on day one. Shots went straight into the spine cord tissue. Leg motion was scored on days 2, 7, and 14. Spine tissue was taken on day 15 for checks. Treated pups moved their back legs better than controls. Nerve harm marks also fell with stem cell care.
pmc-13577346:
Chenxiao Yue and five co-authors compare how people look at scenes when viewing freely versus searching for a goal. Their eye-tracking study came out in 2026. Where the eyes go reflects both what stands out in a scene and what the viewer intends.

Shape, location, and orientation of objects drew fixations strongly under both conditions. Meaning-related features mattered much more during goal-directed search than during free viewing. Movement patterns differed clearly between the two tasks overall. The team also trained a deep learning model that could tell which task a person was doing from their gaze pattern alone. It beat methods based on hand-crafted statistics. Such discrimination could one day help spot abnormal gaze in brain diseases.
pmc-13577746:
Jerzy Kolasinski leads a team that trials a drug to cut blood loss in breast surgery. Their trial deals with breast reduction plus implant rebuild. Blood pools and ooze can harm results after such surgery.

Women got the drug or a dummy dose before the first cut. No one knew who got which, in a triple blind plan. Blood loss in the first day was the main check. Blood marks and mishaps in a month were also logged. All women were tracked as planned in the checks. Past proof for this use was thin, they note.
pmc-13578146:
Bibiana Mello de Oliveira and a large team map how long rare illness takes to name in Brazil, in work published in 2026. They draw on a national network that logged cases from 2018 to 2025. Their study counts the gap from first signs to a firm name for the illness, and asks what makes that gap long or short.

Among near six thousand cases, the mean gap was just over six years. Teens waited longest, while those sent in during a ward stay were named faster. Gaps also split by region and by cause. On average, each person saw more than five doctors before the search ended.
pmc-13578346:
Wenjing Lu and colleagues found a calming route in Parkinson's disease: a classic brake receptor that also sends slow chemical signals. Ongoing brain swelling, driven by immune cells called microglia, worsens Parkinson's, so taming it could slow disease. Their 2026 study tested GABA-A receptors, best known for fast braking, in a toxin-induced Parkinson's model in cells and mice.

Switching on those receptors strongly curbed swelling and the nerve damage that follows. The effect ran through a slow cascade: the receptor bound phospholipase C, released calcium from cell stores, and set phosphatases loose that blocked a key swelling switch. The authors propose GABA-A signalling as a fresh drug target against brain swelling in Parkinson's and related illnesses.
pmc-13578846:
Thomas J. Williams and colleagues followed thirty Brisbane patients seeking alcohol treatment who had previously undergone weight-loss surgery. Twenty had a gastric sleeve and ten had a gastric bypass. After surgery, body mass index fell by an average of 14.5 points and metabolic conditions became less common.

Alcohol dependence scores nevertheless rose markedly, from a mean of 10.2 before surgery to 18.1 afterward, with twenty-nine patients meeting dependence criteria after surgery. Markers of liver scarring also worsened despite the metabolic gains. The authors urge careful alcohol screening before surgery and close follow-up afterward.
pmc-13580946:
Qiu, Guan, and Liu charted teen diabetes worldwide in this study from twenty twenty-six. Using the Global Burden of Disease database, they tracked adolescents aged ten to nineteen across two hundred four countries. Rates of new cases, existing cases, deaths, and healthy years lost were compared from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-three.

The burden grew substantially over those three decades. About six million adolescents lived with diabetes in twenty twenty-three. Death rates stayed flat or dipped slightly, even as illness rates climbed. Poorer regions carried the heaviest death and disability load. Boys overtook girls in new cases by the end of the period. Forecasts see illness rates rising through twenty forty.
pmc-13582346:
Li Zhang and Huadi Wang used machine learning to study career indecision among vocational college students in a 2026 paper. Students in China's higher vocational colleges often struggle to choose a career path. The team surveyed students in three provinces on nine traits, from resilience and self-belief to family career behavior and sense of the future.

Grouping methods split the students into high-, middle-, and low-resource clusters, with clearly graded levels of career difficulty. Four traits did most to separate the groups: view of the future, core self-belief, career exploration, and resilience. The analysis also traced a chain in which outlook on the future eases career difficulty through self-belief, resilience, and adaptability in sequence.
pmc-13582746:
Wei Cheng and five co-authors published a review in twenty twenty-six on the two-way conversation between nerves and pancreatic tumors. Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest cancers, and invasion along nerves appears in nearly every case of its main type. Once dismissed as a passive escape route, that nerve invasion is now seen as active crosstalk.

The authors propose a four-stage model: tumor and nerve attract each other chemically, stick and breach at their interface, remodel surrounding matrix, and rewire the nerve itself. They frame the invasion zone as a sheltered sanctuary where immunity is suppressed. Mapping those exchanges, they argue, reveals drug targets against spread, recurrence, and treatment resistance.
pmc-13582946:
Cornelia Egoldt and colleagues showed that a microtubule's shape and soundness control how it gets chemically tagged. Acetylation of tubulin at lysine 40 marks stable microtubules, added by the enzyme alpha-TAT1 and removed by HDAC6, but how the lattice itself steers those enzymes was unclear. Their 2026 study rebuilt acetylation in the test tube, using purified enzymes on microtubules with defined lattice shapes.

Alpha-TAT1 outpaced HDAC6 overall, but its efficiency dropped when microtubules were damaged. It tagged expanded lattices readily, while compacted lattices blocked it. The authors conclude that lattice shape and integrity together tune acetylation, so shifts between stretched, squeezed, intact, and damaged states rewrite the tag pattern inside cells.
pmc-13583046:
Karoline E Kokot and a large team target a gene-reading step that may make artery plaques more apt to burst. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. A burst plaque is a top cause of heart attack and stroke. Cells that line vessels can shift into a scar-like state, which is tied to weak plaques.

A complex that speeds the reading of genes is high in such shifted cells in human plaques. Blocking it in lab cells calms the shift. In heart organoids, it stops scar build-up and keeps the beat. In mice prone to plaques, it cuts plaque load and weak traits, both before and after disease sets in. Human plaque data back the link.
pmc-13583446:
Dorothea Schütterle and her nine co-authors, publishing in 2026, test whether adding cellulose particles changes how antibiotic-producing bacteria grow and what they make. Streptomyces bacteria are a top source of natural medicines, but in tanks they clump into pellets whose size affects output. Growers often add mineral particles to shrink the pellets. Whether plant-based cellulose helps was unclear.

Across 13 species, cellulose shrank pellets as hoped. But it mostly lowered the abundance of natural products, the opposite of the usual hope. Without cellulose, what a species made matched the potential written in its genome. With cellulose, that link broke. The particles stressed the cells mechanically, leaving more breakdown products. The authors warn that particle effects are species-specific, and suggest future systems that pair the bacteria with cellulose-eating partners.
pmc-13584046:
Suraj KC reports a child's swallowed bracelet in a 2026 case report. An eight-year-old boy arrived at the emergency department two hours after swallowing a linked metal bracelet by accident. Such objects often trigger urgent removal with a scope or surgery. This boy had no pain and no signs of harm, so the team chose careful waiting instead.

X-rays tracked the bracelet as it moved through his gut. By eight hours it had reached the large intestine, and by fourteen hours it sat near the rectum. The boy then passed it in his stool. The case shows that a calm watch, with repeat exams and imaging, can safely replace intervention for some complex swallowed objects.
pmc-13584846:
Kevin Yonny Avila-Robayo, Eduardo Rueda, and Jaime Plazas-Tuttle test a waste-derived charcoal for removing a toxic metal from water, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The charcoal is milled from bone char to a fine powder. It targets the most harmful form of chromium in acidic lab water.

In quick screening, the powder cleared nearly all the chromium within half an hour. Standard uptake models fit the dose data well. The leftover solid, now holding the metal, was mixed into asphalt binder at small shares without large shifts in stiffness behavior. A lab recovery test even improved with more residue. The authors are careful: leaching and metal-form checks are still needed before any reuse claim.
pmc-13585046:
Nilisha Aggarwal and co-authors compare two enzyme gels for removing decay from baby teeth without a drill. Their 2026 trial tests chemomechanical removal, where a gel softens decayed dentin so it can be lifted away while healthy tooth stays. That gentle path can ease children's fear of dental work.

Thirty young children with open decay in back baby teeth were randomly split between the two gels. Teeth were then restored with a standard filling material. The team timed each removal, graded how complete it was, and scored the children's pain and behavior. One gel is a commercial papain-based product, and the other uses bromelain, an enzyme from pineapple. Trials of this kind help dentists choose gentle options backed by evidence, not marketing.
pmc-13585846:
Yoshino and co-authors contributed a 2026 author reflections piece on Claudin 18.2, a protein target in resected pancreatic cancer. A drug aimed at this protein already works in stomach cancer, prompting interest in pancreatic tumours. Earlier reports of how many pancreatic cancers carry the protein varied wildly with method.

Reflecting on their multicentre cohort of 599 surgically removed pancreatic cancers, Yoshino reports twenty-three percent expressed the protein under trial standard scoring. Carrying the protein linked independently to better overall survival, suggesting it marks friendlier tumour biology as well as a drug target. Expression matched between primary tumours and lymph node spread in most cases. Moderate patchiness inside tumours means sampling and scoring must be standardised, the authors caution.
pmc-13586746:
Jingjing Geng and co-authors published a 2026 review on why citrus flavonoids, for all their promise, mostly fail to reach the body's tissues. These plant compounds show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in test tubes. Swallowed, though, they are transformed by gut microbes and the liver, and little survives into the blood. The review follows their metabolic fate and the tricks proposed to improve it.

The authors organize the literature along one thread: structure shapes metabolism, metabolism shapes effect. Which decorative groups a flavonoid carries decides how fast it is broken down. Strategies compared include delivery systems that shield the compounds, chemical modifications, and exploiting the gut microbiota itself. Most benefit claims still rest on cell and animal studies; human data on absorption are thinner. The review maps that gap honestly, offering researchers a structure-based guide to making citrus chemistry actually bioavailable.
pmc-13587046:
Jason Nzanzu Kikuhe and colleagues report saving a newborn whose nasal passages were blocked, in a hospital lacking equipment. Bilateral choanal atresia is a life-threatening neonatal emergency needing prompt airway work.

Their patient was a full-term girl in severe respiratory distress immediately after birth. She was diagnosed by bedside catheter testing and contrast X-rays, since CT was not on hand at first. She was steadied with an improvised oral airway fashioned from an endotracheal tube. Final surgery came after a five-day delay from money and supply barriers. Surgeons did endoscopic puncture and dilation using urethral dilators. They fashioned stents from silastic tubing. The baby went home five days after surgery, feeding orally with normal oxygen levels. Stents came out at six months. Three years of follow-up showed the passages stayed open.
pmc-13588846:
Moor and nine co-authors trace how a salt-rich diet moves two scent drugs in the body in this twenty twenty-six study. Too much salt harms heart, kidney, and bone health across the world. The best-known salt scent path was mapped, but a stress scent's part stayed dim.

Inside, charts for more than three hundred folks first hint the new link in free diets. Set salt diets then showed stress scent rise and a bone scent fall with dose. Mice dosed with a stress-scent kin also showed the bone scent fall in blood. Gene reads in bone cells tied the fall to the stress path in the cell. The team casts salt, stress scent, and bone scent as one chain.
pmc-13589146:
Xingda Yang and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-six, whether wind speed in the brooding period leaves lasting effects on Pekin ducks. Ninety healthy male ducklings, seven days old, were split into three wind treatments: still air and two speeds. Treatments ran from day eleven to day twenty-one. All ducks then shared standard conditions until day forty-two. The team recorded feed intake and weight throughout. At day forty-two, they measured body size, slaughter traits, blood variables, and gut enzyme activity.

Wind speed clearly affected weight, daily gain, feed intake, and feed efficiency at day forty-two. Ducks brooded at the highest speed were heaviest, ate most, and converted feed best. Several body measurements were also larger in that group. Breast and leg yields were not clearly affected.
pmc-13590046:
Wu and seven colleagues study a circular RNA that helps gastric cancer evade immunity in twenty twenty-six. Immune checkpoint drugs help some gastric cancer patients but fail many others. Tumor metabolism can limit how well those drugs work. The team traced how the RNA drives lactate production in tumor cells.

Lowering the RNA made T cells kill cancer cells more effectively. It also cut lactate levels inside the tumor cells. Lactate fuels a chemical mark on histones at the gene for PD-L1, a key immune brake. Through that axis, the RNA raises PD-L1 levels and shields the tumor. pmc-13591546:
